II. Articles 14, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24 and 25–28 are available to both citizens and foreigners.
III. Right to Property continues to be a Fundamental Right under Article 300-A.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
8.x: I and II are correct: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30 are for citizens only, and the others (14, 20–28) extend to foreigners. III is wrong: the 44th Amendment (1978) removed the Right to Property from Part III; Article 300A makes it only a legal right.
8.tq: Separate a constitutional right from a Fundamental Right.
n: The Right to Property was removed from Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment Act of 1978. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The Right to Property was made a legal right under Article 300-A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The rights under Article 15 are available only to citizens. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The rights under Article 16 are available only to citizens. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The rights under Article 19 are available only to citizens. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The rights under Article 29 are available only to citizens. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The rights under Article 30 are available only to citizens. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The rights under Article 14 are available to both citizens and foreigners. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The rights under Article 20 are available to both citizens and foreigners. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The rights under Article 21 are available to both citizens and foreigners. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The rights under Article 22 are available to both citizens and foreigners. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The rights under Article 23 are available to both citizens and foreigners. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The rights under Article 24 are available to both citizens and foreigners. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The rights under Article 25 are available to both citizens and foreigners. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The rights under Article 26 are available to both citizens and foreigners. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The rights under Article 27 are available to both citizens and foreigners. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The rights under Article 28 are available to both citizens and foreigners. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
xs: Statements **I and II** are correct — option **(1) I and II only**.
I: **Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30** are for **citizens only**.
II: **Articles 14, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27 and 28** are for **citizens and foreigners**.
III is wrong: the **44th Amendment (1978)** removed the **Right to Property**; it is now only a legal right under **Article 300-A**.
xa: ⚠ **APPSC G1 2022** key: rights **denied to aliens** = **Arts. 29-30, 19, 16** — not Arts. 23-24.
**Companies** can claim the all-persons rights but **not Art. 19**.
**Enemy aliens** lose even the Art. 22 safeguards (**Art. 22(3)**).

8.s:
Assertion (A): Fundamental Rights are available against the State.
Reason (R): Article 12 defines the State.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
8.x: Both are true and R explains A: Fundamental Rights are enforceable against the State, and Article 12 defines which bodies count as the 'State'.
8.tq: Ask whether R defines the party in A.
n: Fundamental Rights are available against the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
Article 12 defines the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
xs: Both are true and R explains A — option **(1) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A**.
Fundamental Rights are **available against the State**, and **Article 12** defines which bodies are the "State".
xa: "State" includes the Government and Parliament of India, state governments and legislatures, **all local authorities** and **other authorities**.
**Ajay Hasia (1981)**: test is how a body was **created and controlled** — **deep and pervasive control**.
Writs do not ordinarily lie against **private bodies**.

8.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Right to Equality
(b) Right against Exploitation
(c) Right to Freedom of Religion
(d) Right to Constitutional Remedies

List-II
(i) Articles 25–28
(ii) Article 32
(iii) Articles 14–18
(iv) Articles 23–24
8.x: Equality – Articles 14–18; against Exploitation – 23–24; Freedom of Religion – 25–28; Constitutional Remedies – 32.
8.tq: Recall the Article blocks of Part III.
n: The Right to Equality is covered by Articles 14 to 18. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The Right against Exploitation is covered by Articles 23 and 24. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The Right to Freedom of Religion is covered by Articles 25 to 28. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The Right to Constitutional Remedies is covered by Article 32. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
xs: The correct code is **a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii** — option **(4)**.
**Right to Equality** → **14-18**; **Right against Exploitation** → **23-24**.
**Right to Freedom of Religion** → **25-28**; **Right to Constitutional Remedies** → **32**.
xa: **Right to freedom** → **19-22**; **Cultural and educational rights** → **29-30**.
FRs were originally **seven**; presently **six** (**APPSC 2018**).

8.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Part III of the Constitution contains Articles 12 to 35.
The Right against Exploitation covers Articles 23 to 24.
The Right to Constitutional Remedies covers Articles 30 to 32.
The Right to Equality covers Articles 14 to 18.
8.x: C is incorrect: the Right to Constitutional Remedies is Article 32 alone; Articles 29–30 are cultural and educational rights. Part III (12–35), exploitation (23–24) and equality (14–18) are stated correctly.
8.tq: Check the Article range of each right.
n: Part III contains Articles 12 to 35. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
The Right to Equality is covered by Articles 14 to 18. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
The Right against Exploitation is covered by Articles 23 and 24. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
The Right to Constitutional Remedies is covered by Article 32. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
Fundamental Rights are contained in Part III of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
The Right to Equality comprises five Articles. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
The Right against Exploitation comprises two Articles. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
The Right to Constitutional Remedies comprises one Article. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
The 24 Articles of Part III are Articles 12 to 35. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **Constitutional Remedies** cover **Articles 30 to 32** — option **(3)**.
The Right to Constitutional Remedies is **Article 32** alone; **29-30** are **cultural and educational rights**.
The others are correct: **Part III** = **12 to 35**; exploitation = **23-24**; equality = **14-18**.
xa: Part III has **24** Articles and is borrowed mainly from the **US Bill of Rights**.
An aggrieved person can move the **SC directly** under **Art. 32**; HCs under **Art. 226**.

9.s:
Which of the following grounds are expressly mentioned in Article 15(1) as prohibited grounds of discrimination?
1. Religion
2. Race
3. Caste
4. Sex
5. Place of birth
6. Descent
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
9.x: Article 15(1) prohibits discrimination only on the grounds of religion, race, caste, sex and place of birth. Descent is specifically added in Article 16(2), not Article 15(1).
9.tq: Separate the closely related grounds in Articles 15 and 16 instead of treating their lists as identical.
xs: **Art. 15** bars discrimination **only** on **religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth** — option **(1) 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 only**.
**Descent** is not in Art. 15; **16(2)** adds **descent and residence** as barred grounds for public employment.
xa: **15(2)** covers shops, restaurants, hotels, wells, tanks, bathing ghats — and binds **private persons too**.
**Art. 15** is available to **citizens only** (PYQ **2018**).
**15(3)**: special provisions for **women and children**.

9.s: A private hotel refuses entry to a person solely on the ground of caste. Which constitutional provision is most directly attracted?
9.x: Article 15(2) applies to access to places such as hotels and binds private persons as well as the State. It prohibits discrimination on the specified grounds in such access.
9.tq: Apply the clause to a private-person situation rather than assuming that equality provisions bind only the State.
xs: **Article 15(2)** is attracted — it covers **hotels** and binds **private persons too** — option **(2)**.
15(2) covers **shops, restaurants, hotels, wells, tanks, bathing ghats**.
**Art. 16(2)** is about **public employment**, and **Art. 18(1)** about **titles** — options (3) and (4) wrong.
xa: Barred grounds under Art. 15: **religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth**.
**Art. 17** abolishes **untouchability**; enforcing any disability is an **offence**.
**Art. 14** applies to **any person**; **Art. 15** to **citizens only**.

9.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes Articles 14 and 15?
o: Article 14 applies to all persons, whereas Article 15 is available only to citizens.
Article 14 applies only to citizens, whereas Article 15 applies to all persons.
Both Articles 14 and 15 are available only to citizens.
Both Articles 14 and 15 apply only to foreigners residing in India.
9.x: Article 14 applies to any person within the territory of India. Article 15 is a right available only to citizens.
9.tq: Discriminate between the beneficiaries of two neighbouring constitutional provisions.
xs: **Art. 14** applies to **all persons**; **Art. 15** to **citizens only** — option **(1)**.
Art. 14: "The State shall not deny to **any person** equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws".
xa: PYQ **2018**: "Art. 15 is available only to citizens" — correct.
APPSC **2025**: "Right to Equality" → **Art. 14**.
**Art. 16** (public employment) is also a citizen-only right.

9.s:
With reference to Article 16, consider the following statements:
1. It guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment.
2. Descent and residence are among the grounds added to the prohibited list under Article 16(2).
3. Parliament alone may prescribe residence requirements for certain public employment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
9.x: Article 16 concerns equality of opportunity in public employment. Article 16(2) includes descent and residence, while Article 16(3) permits Parliament to prescribe residence requirements for certain jobs.
9.tq: Combine the general guarantee with the specific clauses and the authority competent to act.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1 — correct: **Art. 16** = equality of opportunity in **public employment**.
Statement 2 — correct: **16(2)** adds **descent and residence** as barred grounds.
Statement 3 — correct: under **16(3)** **Parliament only** may prescribe **residence** for certain jobs.
xa: **16(4)**: backward classes **not adequately represented** in services.
**16(5)**: religious qualification for posts in **religious or denominational institutions**.

9.s: Which of the following statements regarding Article 17 is correct?
o: It abolishes titles conferred by the State.
It abolishes untouchability and makes the enforcement of any disability arising from it an offence.
It prohibits discrimination only on grounds of religion and race.
It abolishes untouchability only in government offices.
9.x: Article 17 abolishes untouchability, forbids its practice and treats enforcement of any disability arising from it as an offence.
9.tq: Match the constitutional article with both its prohibition and its legal consequence.
xs: **Art. 17** abolishes **"Untouchability"** and makes enforcing any disability an **offence** — option **(2)**.
Abolishing **titles** is **Art. 18** — option (1) wrong.
xa: Arts. **17-18** = **social equality** (PYQ **2017**).
Art. 17 also binds **private persons** (e.g. exclusion from a public well or shop).
**Art. 18** ends artificial distinctions, except **military and academic**.

9.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
9.x: Articles 39(b), 39(c) and 39(d), which are Directive Principles, are associated with economic equality. Social equality is associated with Articles 15, 17 and 18.
9.tq: Identify the reversed comparison in a classification table.
xs: The wrong pair is **Social equality — Articles 39(b), 39(c) and 39(d)** — option **(1)**.
**39(b), (c), (d)** (DPSP) secure **economic** equality; **social** equality = **Arts. 15, 17, 18**.
**Political** equality = **325, 326** — no exclusion from rolls, adult suffrage.
xa: PYQ **2017**: Arts. **17-18** = **social equality**.
The **Preamble** promises "**equality of status and of opportunity**".
Equality is secured by the **Constitution** and enforced by courts.

9.s: According to B. R. Ambedkar, liberty, equality and fraternity are best understood as:
o: Economic objectives confined to the Directive Principles
Three independent ideals applicable to separate institutions
Duties imposed only on public servants
9.x: Ambedkar described liberty, equality and fraternity as an inseparable trinity.
9.tq: Recall the precise formulation associated with the constitutional thinker.
xs: **Ambedkar** called liberty, equality, fraternity **an inseparable trinity** — option **(3)**.
They are not three separate ideals, nor confined to **DPSPs** or public servants — options (1), (2), (4) wrong.
xa: The **Preamble** promises "**equality of status and of opportunity**".
Arts. **14-18** lay the "**equality floor**" for fraternity.
Equality types: **social** (15, 17, 18), **economic** (39(b), (c), (d)), **political** (325, 326).

9.s:
Assertion (A): Article 18 is associated with social equality.
Reason (R): It seeks to end artificial distinctions created through State-conferred titles.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
9.x: Both statements are true. Article 18 advances social equality by abolishing artificial distinctions arising from State-conferred titles, subject to the stated exceptions.
9.tq: Check whether the reason directly explains why the provision advances the stated type of equality.
xs: Both A and R are true and R is the correct **explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
**Art. 18** secures **social equality** by **ending artificial distinctions** (titles).
**18(1)**: the State confers no title except **military or academic**.
xa: PYQ **2017**: Arts. **17-18** = **social equality**.
**Balaji Raghavan (1996)**: **Bharat Ratna and Padma awards** are **not titles**.
**18(2)**: a **citizen** shall not accept a **foreign title**.

9.s:
Consider the following statements regarding exceptions to equality before law:
1. Under Article 361, no criminal proceedings can be instituted against the President or a Governor during the term of office.
2. A civil case against the President or a Governor can be instituted only after six months' prior notice.
3. Foreign diplomats and United Nations agencies are also exceptions to equality before law.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
9.x: Statement 1 is correct: Art. 361 bars criminal proceedings against the President and Governors during their term. Statement 2 is wrong: a civil case needs only two months' notice, not six. Statement 3 is correct: foreign diplomats and UN agencies are recognised exceptions. So '1 and 3 only'; options with 2 are wrong.
9.tq: Art. 361 immunity: criminal - none during term; civil - 2 months' notice. Spot the changed number.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: under **Art. 361**, **no criminal case** lies against the **President** or **Governors** during their term.
Statement 2 is wrong: a **civil case** needs only **2** months' notice, not six.
Statement 3: **foreign diplomats** and **UN agencies** are also exceptions.
xa: Dicey's **equality before the law**: all classes equally subject to the **ordinary law**, administered by **ordinary courts**.
Rule of Law in India is anchored mainly in **Article 14**.

9.s: In which case did the Supreme Court state that ‘equality is antithetic to arbitrariness’ or that equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies?
o: M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu
9.x: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974) established the close constitutional relationship between equality and non-arbitrariness.
9.tq: Match the distinctive judicial formulation with the case in which it was stated.
xs: **E.P. Royappa v. State of TN (1974)**: "**Equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies**" — option **(4)**.
**Maneka Gandhi (1978)** later held any **arbitrary action** violates Art. 14.
**M.R. Balaji** and **Indra Sawhney** are **reservation** cases — options (1) and (3) wrong.
xa: Royappa's other phrase: "**equality is antithetic to arbitrariness**".
Maneka Gandhi struck down **unguided discretionary power**.
Art. 14 forbids **class legislation**, not **reasonable classification**.

9.s: Which one of the following propositions is associated with Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) in the context of Article 14?
o: Class legislation is always valid if enacted by Parliament
Any arbitrary State action violates Article 14
Article 14 applies only to taxation laws
9.x: Maneka Gandhi reinforced the principle that arbitrary State action is inconsistent with Article 14. Unguided discretionary power may therefore be struck down.
9.tq: Use the case-law principle rather than confusing it with the classification test.
xs: **Maneka Gandhi (1978)**: **any arbitrary action violates Art. 14** — option **(2)**.
**Unguided discretionary power** was struck down — so option (3) is wrong.
Art. 14 forbids **class legislation** — option (1) wrong.
xa: **E.P. Royappa (1974)**: "equality and arbitrariness are **sworn enemies**".
Twin test for classification: **intelligible differentia** + **rational nexus**.
Art. 14 applies to **any person**.

9.s: A law creates two groups for different treatment. For the classification to be valid under Article 14, which combination is required?
o: Intelligible differentia and rational nexus with the object of the law
9.x: The twin test of reasonable classification is an intelligible differentia distinguishing the grouped persons or things and a rational nexus between the differentia and the object sought to be achieved.
9.tq: Apply the twin test to distinguish reasonable classification from class legislation.
xs: The twin test: **intelligible differentia** + **rational nexus with the object** — option **(3)**.
Art. 14 forbids **class legislation**, not **reasonable classification**.
xa: Reiterated **Apr 2026**: the State **cannot treat pensioners differently from serving employees on DA** (Kerala/KSRTC).
**Equal protection** (American, **positive**) permits reasonable classification.
**Maneka Gandhi (1978)**: any **arbitrary action** violates Art. 14.

9.s: The Supreme Court’s April 2026 ruling concerning pensioners and serving employees reaffirmed that the State—
o: must abolish dearness allowance for pensioners
cannot treat pensioners differently from serving employees on dearness allowance without constitutionally valid justification
may always treat pensioners differently from serving employees on dearness allowance
can classify employees only on the basis of residence
9.x: The ruling held that the State cannot arbitrarily treat pensioners differently from serving employees in relation to dearness allowance. The classification must satisfy Article 14 requirements.
9.tq: Apply non-arbitrariness and rational classification to a concrete administrative distinction.
xs: The State **cannot treat pensioners differently from serving employees on DA** — option **(2)**.
The SC applied Art. 14's **twin test** (**11** Apr **2026**, Kerala/KSRTC).
Twin test: **intelligible differentia** + **rational nexus** with the object.
xa: Art. 14 forbids **class legislation**, not **reasonable classification**.
Also in **Feb 2026**, the SC questioned the caste-discrimination clause of the **UGC equity regulations** (**Mritunjay Tiwari v UoI**).
**E.P. Royappa (1974)**: equality is **antithetic to arbitrariness**.

9.s: Which of the following groups is NOT covered by the special provisions specifically described under Article 15?
9.x: The listed Article 15 special provisions cover women, children, SEBCs, SCs, STs and, under Article 15(6), EWS. Aged persons are not included in this list.
9.tq: Find the excluded group rather than selecting a group expressly named in the provision.
xs: **Aged persons** are **not covered by Art. 15** — option **(4)** (PYQ **2023**).
Covered: **15(3)** **women and children**; **15(4)** **SEBCs, SCs, STs**; **15(6)** **EWS**.
xa: **15(5)**: SEBC/SC/ST **admission** in educational institutions, **except minority institutions** (**93rd, 2005**).
**15(4)** came by the **1st Amendment 1951**, after **Champakam Dorairajan**.
**15(6)** came by the **103rd Amendment 2019** (EWS up to **10%**).

9.s: The 103rd Constitutional Amendment, 2019, inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6) relating to:
o: Reservation for SCs and STs in promotions only
Reservation for EWS up to 10 per cent
9.x: The 103rd Amendment inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6), providing for reservation for Economically Weaker Sections up to 10 per cent. It was passed as the 124th Amendment Bill in the Lok Sabha.
9.tq: Match the amendment year and clause numbers with the percentage and beneficiary group.
xs: **15(6) and 16(6)** provide **EWS** reservation **up to 10%** — option **(2)**.
They came by the **103rd Amendment 2019**.
xa: ⚠ The **103rd Amendment** was passed as the **124th Amendment Bill** (APPSC G1 **2019**).
**Janhit Abhiyan (2022)** upheld it **3:2**.
**EWS 10%** is an exception to the **50% ceiling**.

9.s: Article 16(5) permits a qualification relating to religion or denomination in respect of an office connected with:
o: Every public employment under a State
9.x: Article 16(5) permits offices connected with religious or denominational institutions to be kept for persons professing that particular religion or belonging to that denomination.
9.tq: Identify the institutional exception rather than applying the religious qualification to all public employment.
xs: **16(5)** allows a religious qualification for posts in **religious or denominational institutions** — option **(3)**.
Such posts may be kept for that religion.
xa: **16(3)**: **Parliament only** may prescribe **residence** for certain jobs.
**16(2)**: adds **descent and residence** as barred grounds.
**16(4)**: backward classes **not adequately represented** in services.

9.s: Article 15(5), which enables reservation for SEBCs, SCs and STs in admission to educational institutions including private aided or unaided ones, was inserted by the:
o: 1st Amendment, 1951, and covers minority institutions as well
93rd Amendment, 2005, and excludes minority institutions under Article 30
103rd Amendment, 2019, and excludes minority institutions under Article 30
77th Amendment, 1995, and covers minority institutions as well
9.x: Art. 15(5) came with the 93rd Amendment (2005) and expressly excludes minority educational institutions under Art. 30. The 1st Amendment inserted 15(4), the 103rd inserted 15(6)/16(6) for EWS, and the 77th inserted 16(4A) for SC/ST promotions, so the other options have the wrong amendment.
xs: **15(5)** came by the **93rd Amendment, 2005** and **excludes minority institutions** (Art. **30**) — option **(2)**.
The **1st Amendment** inserted **15(4)**; the **103rd** inserted **15(6)/16(6)** (EWS); the **77th** inserted **16(4A)**.
xa: **Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008)** upheld the **93rd Amendment**.
APPSC **2022**: reservation in jobs/admissions → **all of 77th, 81st, 93rd**.
**27% OBC quota in central institutions** was upheld, with **creamy layer** excluded.

9.s:
Arrange the following cases in chronological order:
A. M.R. Balaji
B. Champakam Dorairajan
C. Indra Sawhney
D. M. Nagaraj
9.x: Champakam Dorairajan was decided in 1951, M.R. Balaji in 1962, Indra Sawhney in 1992 and M. Nagaraj in 2006, giving B, A, C, D.
9.tq: Fix the earliest and latest cases first, then place the two intermediate rulings.
xs: The order is **B, A, C, D** — option **(1)**.
**Champakam Dorairajan** (**1951**) → **M.R. Balaji** (**1962**) → **Indra Sawhney** (**1992**) → **M. Nagaraj** (**2006**).
xa: Later: **Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008)**, **Jarnail Singh (2018)**, **Jaishri Patil (2021)**, **Janhit Abhiyan (2022)**, **Davinder Singh (2024)**.
⚠ M.R. Balaji is also dated **1963**; some notes date it **1960**.
**Indra Sawhney** was decided on **16 Nov 1992**.

9.s: The Supreme Court struck down the Communal Government Order in Champakam Dorairajan primarily under—
9.x: In Champakam Dorairajan (1951), the Communal G.O. was struck down under Article 29(2). The case also established the then-prevailing position that Directive Principles were subordinate to Fundamental Rights, leading to the First Amendment and Article 15(4).
9.tq: Match the case with the specific constitutional provision involved in its ruling.
xs: **Champakam Dorairajan** (**1951**) struck down the **Communal G.O.** under **Article 29(2)** — option **(2)**.
It held **DPSPs subordinate to FRs**, leading to the **1st Amendment** (**Art. 15(4)**).
xa: **Indra Sawhney (1992)** later set the **50% ceiling** and the **creamy layer**.
**15(4)** covers **SEBCs, SCs, STs**.
**M.R. Balaji (1962)**: caste cannot be the **sole test**.

9.s: The 103rd Constitutional Amendment providing reservation for Economically Weaker Sections was upheld by the Supreme Court in—
9.x: In Janhit Abhiyan (2022), the Supreme Court upheld the 103rd Amendment providing 10 per cent EWS reservation by a 3:2 majority.
9.tq: Combine the case name, amendment, percentage and majority to identify the precise ruling.
xs: **Janhit Abhiyan** (**2022**) upheld the **103rd Amendment (EWS 10%)**, **3:2** — option **(2)**.
**Indra Sawhney** was **6:3**; **M. Nagaraj** was a **5**-judge bench on promotions.
xa: ⚠ Bench splits: **Indra Sawhney 6:3**; **Janhit Abhiyan 3:2**.
The 103rd was passed as the **124th Amendment Bill**.
**EWS 10%** is an exception to the **50%** ceiling.

9.s:
With reference to M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore, consider the following statements:
1. Caste cannot be the sole test for determining backwardness.
2. Reservation should generally remain below 50 per cent.
3. The case upheld reservation without prescribing any requirement of reasonableness.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
9.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The judgment emphasised that reservation must be reasonable and that caste cannot be the sole test; statement 3 is incorrect.
9.tq: Find the false statement by testing the omitted qualification of reasonableness.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 — correct: **caste cannot be the sole test**.
Statement 2 — correct: reservation generally **below 50%**.
Statement 3 — wrong: **M.R. Balaji (1962)** held reservation **must be reasonable**.
xa: **Indra Sawhney (1992)** later fixed the **50% cap** save exceptional cases.
**Jaishri Patil (2021)** struck down the **Maratha** quota for crossing **50%**.
⚠ Balaji is also dated **1963**; some notes **1960**.

9.s: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India is associated with upholding which of the following amendments, subject to conditions?
9.x: M. Nagaraj (2006) upheld the 77th and 85th Constitutional Amendments concerning reservation in promotion, subject to specified constitutional conditions.
9.tq: Match the case with the precise amendment pair.
xs: **M. Nagaraj (2006)** upheld the **77th** and **85th** Amendments — option **(3)** (along with the **81st**).
Condition: **quantifiable data** on **backwardness, inadequate representation, efficiency** (Art. **335**).
The **102nd/105th** concern **SEBC lists**; the **93rd** concerns **admissions** — options (2) and (4) wrong.
xa: **77th (1995)**: SC/ST promotions; **85th (2001)**: **consequential seniority**.
**81st**: **carried-forward vacancies** outside the 50% ceiling.
**Jarnail Singh (2018)** later said no SC/ST backwardness data is needed.

9.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. Union of India (2008):
1. It upheld the 93rd Constitutional Amendment.
2. It upheld the 2006 law concerning reservation in State and aided institutions.
3. It held that the creamy layer among OBCs need not be excluded.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
9.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The creamy layer had to be excluded, so statement 3 is incorrect.
9.tq: Spot the reversed position on creamy-layer exclusion.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statements 1 and 2 — correct: **Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008)** upheld the **93rd Amendment** and the **2006 Act** for State/aided institutions.
Statement 3 — wrong: the **creamy layer** was **excluded**.
xa: It upheld the **27% OBC quota in central institutions**.
**15(5)** (93rd, **2005**) excludes **minority institutions**.
The **creamy layer** originates in **Indra Sawhney (1992)**.

9.s: The Supreme Court’s decision in Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. State of Maharashtra (2021) primarily concerned which issue?
o: Validity of the Maratha reservation exceeding the 50 per cent ceiling
Validity of reservation for SC converts to Christianity
Exclusion of the creamy layer from EWS reservation
9.x: The Maratha quota was struck down for crossing the 50 per cent ceiling without exceptional circumstances.
9.tq: Identify the case from its distinctive reservation group and ceiling issue.
xs: **Jaishri Patil (2021)**: the **Maratha** quota was struck down for **crossing 50%** — option **(1)**.
There were **no exceptional circumstances** to justify the breach.
It also read the **102nd Amendment** as making the **Central list the only SEBC list**.
xa: The **105th Amendment (2021)** reversed that reading of the 102nd.
Exceptions to 50%: **remote areas**, **carried-forward vacancies (81st)**, **EWS 10%**.
The **50% cap** comes from **Indra Sawhney (1992)**.

9.s: Which one of the following correctly states the effect of the 105th Constitutional Amendment (2021) in relation to the Maratha reservation judgment?
o: It removed the 50 per cent ceiling in all reservation matters.
It abolished the Central list of SEBCs.
It reversed the reading of the 102nd Amendment that had restricted the States’ power to identify SEBCs.
It prohibited States from maintaining backward-class lists.
9.x: The 105th Amendment reversed the interpretation of the 102nd Amendment in the Maratha case and restored the States’ power to identify socially and educationally backward classes.
9.tq: Test the constitutional amendment as a corrective response to a judicial interpretation.
xs: The **105th Amendment (2021)** **reversed the reading of the 102nd** that took away States' power to identify **SEBCs** — option **(3)**.
**Art. 342A**: President specifies the **Central List**; **States keep own lists**.
It did not remove the 50% ceiling or abolish any list — options (1), (2), (4) wrong.
xa: The **102nd** also gave the **NCBC** constitutional status (**Art. 338B**).
**Jaishri Patil (2021)** struck down the **Maratha** quota.
**Art. 340**: President appoints a commission on SEBC conditions.

9.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Case)
A. Champakam Dorairajan
B. M.R. Balaji
C. M. Nagaraj
D. Jarnail Singh

List-II (Principal issue)
1. Conditions for reservation in promotion
2. Madras Communal Government Order
3. Caste not being the sole test and reservation below 50 per cent
4. Creamy layer in SC/ST promotions

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
9.x: Champakam Dorairajan concerned the Communal Government Order; M.R. Balaji concerned caste and the 50 per cent principle; M. Nagaraj concerned promotional reservation conditions; Jarnail Singh concerned creamy layer in SC/ST promotions.
9.tq: Start from the sure case-issue pairs and eliminate incompatible codes.
xs: Correct match: **A–2, B–3, C–1, D–4** — option **(1)**.
**Champakam Dorairajan** → Communal G.O.; **M.R. Balaji** → caste not sole test, **below 50%**.
**M. Nagaraj** → conditions for promotion quota (**quantifiable data**); **Jarnail Singh** → **creamy layer in SC/ST promotions**.
xa: ⚠ **Nagaraj** needed SC/ST backwardness data; **Jarnail Singh** did not.
Champakam led to **Art. 15(4)** (**1st Amendment**).
**Indra Sawhney** barred reservation in promotions — undone by the **77th**.

9.s: The First Constitutional Amendment inserted Article 15(4) primarily to overcome the effect of which judgment?
o: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu
9.x: Article 15(4) was inserted by the First Amendment, 1951 in response to the ruling in Champakam Dorairajan, which had struck down the Communal G.O. under Article 29(2).
9.tq: Link a constitutional amendment to the judgment whose effect it was intended to overcome.
xs: **Art. 15(4)** was inserted by the **1st Amendment, 1951** after **Champakam Dorairajan** — option **(2)**.
That case struck down the **Communal G.O.** under **Art. 29(2)** and held **DPSPs subordinate to FRs**.
**M. Nagaraj** (**2006**) and **Janhit Abhiyan** (**2022**) came much later.
xa: **15(4)** covers **SEBCs, SCs, STs**.
**E.P. Royappa (1974)** is an Art. **14** arbitrariness case.
**Janhit Abhiyan** upheld **EWS 10%** (**3:2**).

9.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Indra Sawhney — Reservation under Article 16(4) only at initial appointment
2. M. Nagaraj — Requirement of quantifiable data concerning backwardness, inadequate representation and administrative efficiency
3. Jarnail Singh — Data on backwardness of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes necessary for promotion reservation
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
9.x: Pair 1 is correct: Indra Sawhney (1992) held there could be no reservation in promotions, so Art. 16(4) reservation applies only at initial appointment. Pair 2 is correct: M. Nagaraj (2006) required quantifiable data on backwardness, inadequate representation and efficiency. Pair 3 is wrong: Jarnail Singh (2018) held that no data on SC/ST backwardness is needed. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
9.tq: Separate similar reservation judgments by their distinct holdings.
xs: Pairs 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Pair 1 — correct: **Indra Sawhney (1992)** — **no reservation in promotions**.
Pair 2 — correct: **M. Nagaraj (2006)** — **quantifiable data**: backwardness, inadequate representation, efficiency.
Pair 3 — wrong: **Jarnail Singh (2018)** said **no** SC/ST backwardness data needed.
xa: Jarnail Singh applied the **creamy layer to SC/ST promotions**.
The **77th (1995)** inserted **16(4A)** to allow SC/ST promotion quotas.
Efficiency is tied to **Art. 335**.

9.s: Which one of the following is the income limit for the OBC creamy layer mentioned in the 2017 notification?
9.x: The OBC creamy-layer income limit mentioned in the 2017 notification is ₹8 lakh a year. Andhra Pradesh aligned its definitions with the central thresholds.
9.tq: Read the figure precisely and distinguish it from nearby income thresholds.
xs: The OBC creamy-layer income limit is **₹8 lakh** a year (**2017** notification) — option **(4) ₹8 lakh per annum**.
The **creamy layer** originates in **Indra Sawhney (1992)**.
xa: **AP** aligned its OBC creamy-layer thresholds with the **central** ceiling (Apr **2026**).
CJI **B.R. Gavai**: creamy layer should apply to **SC** quotas (Nov **2025**).
The **Centre opposes** an income-based creamy layer for **SC/ST** (Aug **2026**).

9.s:
Which of the following are recognised exceptions or qualifications to the 50 per cent reservation ceiling?
1. Extraordinary situations such as remote areas
2. Carry-forward of backlog vacancies under the 81st Amendment
3. EWS reservation upheld in Janhit Abhiyan
4. Every reservation made by a State legislature without limitation
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
9.x: Extraordinary situations, carry-forward vacancies under the 81st Amendment and the EWS reservation recognised in Janhit Abhiyan are stated qualifications or exceptions. There is no unrestricted power for every State legislature to exceed the ceiling.
9.tq: Reject the absolute statement that removes all constitutional limits on reservation.
xs: Items 1, 2 and 3 are exceptions — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
**Extraordinary situations (remote areas)**, **carried-forward vacancies (81st)**, **EWS 10%** (Janhit Abhiyan).
Item 4 is wrong: **Jaishri Patil (2021)** struck down the **Maratha** quota for crossing **50%** without exceptional circumstances.
xa: The **50% cap** comes from **Indra Sawhney (1992)**; **M.R. Balaji** had said generally **below 50%**.
Debate: **50% ceiling vs EWS quota**.
**M. Nagaraj** upheld the **81st** Amendment.

9.s: The National Commission for Backward Classes has constitutional status under—
9.x: The National Commission for Backward Classes is a constitutional body under Article 338B.
9.tq: Distinguish closely numbered constitutional provisions relating to commissions.
xs: The **NCBC** is constitutional under **Art. 338B** (**102nd**) — option **(1) Article 338B**.
**Art. 340** = commission on SEBC conditions; **Art. 342A** = President specifies the SEBC Central List.
xa: **Indra Sawhney (1992)** had ordered a **permanent body** — the **NCBC**.
The **105th Amendment (2021)** restored States' power to keep their own lists.
⚠ **102nd** = NCBC status; **105th** = reversal of the Maratha reading.

9.s: Under Article 342A, which one of the following is correct?
o: The President specifies the Central List of SEBCs, while States retain their own lists.
The Governor specifies the Central List of SEBCs, while States have no separate lists.
The NCBC alone specifies both Central and State lists.
The Supreme Court specifies the Central List of SEBCs.
9.x: Article 342A provides for specification of SEBCs for the Central List by the President, while States retain their own lists.
9.tq: Use the authority–list distinction to separate Central List and State List powers.
xs: Under **Art. 342A**, the **President specifies the Central List**, and **States keep own lists** — option **(1)**.
This follows the **102nd** and **105th** Amendments.
xa: **Jaishri Patil (2021)** had read the 102nd as making the **Central list the only SEBC list**.
The **105th Amendment (2021)** reversed that reading.

9.s: Which one of the following statements correctly reflects the current position mentioned regarding the creamy layer issue for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes?
o: The issue concerns only economically weaker sections outside the reservation system.
The Supreme Court has abolished reservations for SCs and STs.
The Centre opposes an income-based creamy layer for SCs and STs.
The Centre supports an income-based creamy layer without qualification.
9.x: The stated current position is that the Centre opposes an income-based creamy layer for SCs and STs.
9.tq: Distinguish the stated governmental position from broader reservation-related claims.
xs: The **Centre opposes an income-based creamy layer for SC/ST** — option **(3)**.
It calls **M. Nagaraj's** reference a "**general observation**" (Aug **2026**).
xa: CJI **B.R. Gavai** said the creamy layer should apply to **SC** quotas (Nov **2025**).
**Jarnail Singh (2018)** applied the **creamy layer to SC/ST promotions**.
The OBC limit is **₹8 lakh** a year (**2017**).

9.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Article)
A. Article 15(4)
B. Article 16(4A)
C. Article 16(4B)
D. Article 340

List-II (Subject)
1. Carry-forward of backlog vacancies
2. Commission on conditions of SEBCs
3. Special provisions for SEBCs, SCs and STs
4. Reservation in promotion for SCs and STs with consequential seniority

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
9.x: Article 15(4) concerns special provisions for SEBCs, SCs and STs; Article 16(4A) concerns promotion for SCs and STs; Article 16(4B) concerns backlog vacancies; and Article 340 concerns a commission on SEBC conditions.
9.tq: Start with the sure Article 340–commission pair and then complete the reservation pairings.
xs: Correct match: **A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2** — option **(1)**.
**15(4)** → **SEBCs, SCs, STs**; **16(4A)** → **SC/ST promotions** with **consequential seniority**.
**16(4B)** → **carried-forward vacancies** (**81st**); **Art. 340** → **commission** on SEBC conditions.
xa: **16(4A)**: **77th (1995)**; consequential seniority: **85th (2001)**.
Carried-forward vacancies are an exception to the **50%** ceiling.
**Art. 338B** = **NCBC**; **Art. 342A** = Central List of SEBCs.

9.s: Which of the following statements about Article 18(1) is correct?
o: The State may confer any hereditary title with the President’s consent.
The State shall confer no title except military or academic distinctions.
Only foreign titles are prohibited under Article 18(1).
National awards are expressly declared to be titles under Article 18(1).
9.x: Article 18(1) prohibits the State from conferring titles, except military and academic distinctions. The provision does not prohibit those two categories.
9.tq: Use the stated exception to avoid the extreme claim that every distinction is prohibited.
xs: **18(1)**: the State confers **no title except military or academic** — option **(2)**.
**Bharat Ratna and Padma awards** are **not titles** (**Balaji Raghavan, 1996**) — option (4) wrong.
Foreign titles are covered by **18(2)-(3)**, not 18(1) — option (3) wrong.
xa: **18(2)**: a **citizen** shall not accept a foreign title.
**18(3)**: a **non-citizen** holding an office of profit or trust needs the **President's consent**.
National awards must **not be used as prefix or suffix**; stopped in **1977**, revived in **1980**.

9.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 18:
1. A citizen of India may accept a title from a foreign State with the consent of the President.
2. A non-citizen holding an office of profit or trust under the State needs the President's consent to accept a foreign title.
3. No person holding an office of profit or trust under the State may accept any present, emolument or office from a foreign State without the President's consent.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
9.x: Statement 1 is wrong: under Art. 18(2) a citizen shall not accept a foreign title at all; there is no consent route. Statement 2 is correct: Art. 18(3) requires the President's consent for a non-citizen holding an office of profit or trust. Statement 3 is correct: Art. 18(4) requires the President's consent for any present, emolument or office from a foreign State. Hence '2 and 3 only'; options with 1 are wrong and '3 only' misses 18(3).
9.tq: Citizen + foreign title = absolute bar; consent of the President only for non-citizen office-holders (18(3)) and presents/emoluments (18(4)).
xs: Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 — wrong: under **18(2)** a **citizen** shall not accept a foreign title at all; there is no consent route.
Statement 2 — correct: **18(3)** — a **non-citizen holding an office of profit or trust** needs the **President's consent**.
Statement 3 — correct: **18(4)** — any **present, emolument or office** from a foreign State needs the **President's consent**.
xa: **18(1)**: the State confers no title except **military or academic**.
PYQ **2016**: consent under 18(4) is given by **the President**.
**Balaji Raghavan (1996)**: **Bharat Ratna and Padma awards** are **not titles** under Art. 18.

9.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the effect of the decision in Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996)?
o: The decision authorised award-holders to use the awards as hereditary titles.
Bharat Ratna and Padma awards were held not to be titles under Article 18, but they must not be used as prefixes or suffixes.
All national awards were held to be military distinctions only.
Bharat Ratna and Padma awards were held to be titles and were abolished.
9.x: The Supreme Court held that Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not titles under Article 18. However, they cannot be used as prefixes or suffixes to a person’s name.
9.tq: Separate the legal status of an award from the prohibited manner of using it.
xs: **Balaji Raghavan (1996)**: **Bharat Ratna and Padma awards** are **not titles** under **Article 18**, but must **not be used as prefixes or suffixes** — option **(2)**.
So the awards were neither abolished nor allowed as titles — options (1) and (4) wrong.
xa: The awards were **stopped in 1977** and **revived in 1980**.
**18(1)**: no title except **military or academic** distinctions.
Art. 18 secures **social equality** by ending artificial distinctions (PYQ **2017**: Arts. **17-18**).

9.s: The Supreme Court questioned the caste-discrimination clause of the UGC equity regulations in which case?
o: Pensioners Association v. Union of India
Mritunjay Tiwari v. State of Andhra Pradesh
Mritunjay Tiwari v. Union of India
Centre v. Scheduled Caste Employees Association
9.x: The case in which the Supreme Court questioned the caste-discrimination clause of the UGC equity regulations was Mritunjay Tiwari v. Union of India.
9.tq: Use the case-name discrimination method by matching the judicial issue with the exact parties.
xs: The SC questioned the **caste-discrimination clause** of the **UGC equity regulations** in **Mritunjay Tiwari v. Union of India** — option **(3)**.
The case was against the **Union of India** (UoI), not Andhra Pradesh — option (2) wrong.
xa: It came in Feb **2026**.
SC (**11** Apr **2026**): State **cannot treat pensioners differently from serving employees on DA** — Art. 14's **twin test**.
Twin test: **intelligible differentia** + **rational nexus** with the object.

9.s: With reference to the creamy-layer policy in Andhra Pradesh, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: Andhra Pradesh aligned its OBC creamy-layer definition with the central income ceiling.
Andhra Pradesh replaced the creamy-layer principle with the 50 per cent reservation ceiling.
Andhra Pradesh rejected the central income ceiling for OBC creamy-layer determination.
Andhra Pradesh applied the creamy-layer principle only to Scheduled Caste reservation.
9.x: Andhra Pradesh aligned its OBC creamy-layer definition and thresholds with the central income limits in April 2026.
9.tq: Apply the policy fact to distinguish the State’s alignment with the Centre from unrelated reservation debates.
xs: **Andhra Pradesh aligned** its **OBC creamy-layer** thresholds with the **central income ceiling** (Apr **2026**) — option **(1)**.
So it neither rejected nor replaced the central ceiling — options (2) and (3) wrong.
xa: Central OBC income limit: **₹8 lakh** a year (**2017** notification).
The creamy layer originates in **Indra Sawhney (1992)**.
**Centre opposes an income-based creamy layer for SC/ST** (Aug **2026**).

9.s: Which of the following issues forms part of the criticism and debate surrounding reservation jurisprudence?
o: The 50 per cent ceiling versus the EWS quota
The replacement of equality before law by titles
The exclusion of all classification from Article 14
9.x: The debate includes the relationship between the 50 per cent reservation ceiling and the EWS quota, along with the creamy layer for Scheduled Castes and sub-classification.
9.tq: Select the option that captures a recognised reservation-jurisprudence debate rather than an extreme constitutional claim.
xs: The debate covers the **50% ceiling vs the EWS quota** — option **(1)**.
Other debates: **creamy layer for SCs** and **sub-classification**.
Arts. **14-18** remain the "**equality floor**"; Art. 14 allows **reasonable classification** — options (2)-(4) wrong.
xa: **Janhit Abhiyan (2022)** upheld **EWS 10%** (**103rd**), **3:2**.
Exceptions to 50%: **remote areas**, **carried-forward vacancies (81st)**, **EWS 10%**.
**Davinder Singh (2024)**: **sub-classification of SCs** permitted.

n: Article 15 prohibits discrimination. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
Article 16 provides equality of opportunity in public employment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]

**Article 18** → **abolishes titles**; **Article 14** → **equality before law**.

9.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Rule of Law:
1. A.V. Dicey set it out in 'Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution' (1885).
2. India borrowed the Rule of Law from the American constitutional system.
3. Parliamentary Government and the Cabinet System were borrowed from the same source as the Rule of Law.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
9.x: Statement 1 is correct: Dicey, a British jurist, wrote the book in 1885. Statement 2 is wrong: the Rule of Law came from Britain, not the USA. Statement 3 is correct: Parliamentary Government, Single Citizenship, Cabinet System and Prerogative Writs were also borrowed from Britain. So '1 and 3 only'; '1 only' misses statement 3.
9.tq: Dicey is British, so the Rule of Law is a British borrowing, like the cabinet system.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: **A.V. Dicey** set it out in **Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution** (**1885**).
Statement 2 is wrong: the Rule of Law was **borrowed from Britain**, not the USA.
Statement 3: **Parliamentary Government**, **Single Citizenship**, **Cabinet System** and **Prerogative Writs** also came from Britain.
xa: ⚠ **Equality before law** is **British** (negative); **equal protection of the laws** is **American** (positive).
Rule of law is a **basic feature** — **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**, **Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975)**.

9.s: The Rule of Law in India is anchored primarily in which Article?
9.x: The rule of law in India rests mainly on Article 14: equality before law and equal protection of the laws.
9.tq: Recall the Article behind the rule of law.
n: The Rule of Law is anchored primarily in Article 14 of the Indian Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Article 14 provides equality before law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Article 14 provides equal protection of the laws. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
xs: The Rule of Law in India is anchored mainly in **Article 14** — option **(3)**.
Art. 14 guarantees **equality before law** and **equal protection of the laws** to **citizens and foreigners**.
xa: Art. 14 forbids **class legislation**, not **reasonable classification**.
Twin test: **intelligible differentia** + **rational nexus** with the object.
**E.P. Royappa (1974)**: "**Equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies**".

9.s:
Assertion (A): Rule of Law is affirmed as part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
Reason (R): It was affirmed in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975).
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
9.x: Both are true: the rule of law is part of the basic structure, as held in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975). R names the rulings that affirmed A.
9.tq: Recall the cases that made the rule of law basic.
n: The Rule of Law is part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The Basic Structure status of the Rule of Law was affirmed in Kesavananda Bharati in 1973. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The Basic Structure status of the Rule of Law was affirmed in Indira Nehru Gandhi in 1975. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
xs: Both are true and R explains A — option **(1) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A**.
Rule of law is a **basic feature**, affirmed in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** and **Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975)**.
xa: Dicey's three elements: **absence of arbitrary power**, **equality before the law**, **primacy of individual rights**.
**Rule of Law** = government **subordinate** to law; **Rule by Law** = law as an **instrument** of state control.

9.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding Dicey’s first element of Rule of Law?
o: No person can be punished except for a distinct breach of law established in the ordinary legal manner.
It requires the absolute supremacy of regular law over arbitrary power.
It recognises an inherent unlimited police power of the State.
9.x: Option C is incorrect: Dicey's first element, absence of arbitrary power, means regular law is supreme and no one is punished except for a breach of law. It rejects unlimited state power.
9.tq: Recall Dicey's first element: no arbitrary power.
n: Dicey’s first classic element of the Rule of Law is the absence of arbitrary power. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The absence of arbitrary power means limitation of powers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The first element requires the absolute supremacy or predominance of regular law over arbitrary power. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
No person can be punished except for a distinct breach of law established in the ordinary legal manner. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The assertion that the State has inherent unlimited police powers is false. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The Rule of Law restrains the government. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
xs: The incorrect statement is that it recognises an **inherent unlimited police power** of the State — option **(3)**.
Dicey's first element, **absence of arbitrary power**, means **supremacy of regular law** over arbitrary power.
No one is punished except for a distinct **breach of law** proved in the **ordinary legal manner**; it involves **limitation of powers**.
xa: Second element: **equality before the law** — **no one above the law**.
Third element: **primacy of individual rights** — rights come from **judicial decisions** in the UK.

9.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Origin of Equality Before Law
(b) Origin of Equal Protection of the Laws
(c) Nature of Equality Before Law
(d) Nature of Equal Protection of the Laws

List-II

(ii) American origin
(iii) Negative concept
(iv) Positive concept permitting reasonable classification
9.x: Equality before law is British in origin and negative (no special privilege). Equal protection of the laws is American and positive (allows reasonable classification). The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
9.tq: Discriminate the two halves of Article 14 by origin and nature.
n: Equality before law is of British origin. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Equality before law is a negative concept. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Equality before law means the absence of special privilege for any individual. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Equal protection of the laws is of American origin. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Equal protection of the laws is a positive concept. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Equal protection of the laws means equal treatment under equal circumstances. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Equal protection of the laws permits reasonable classification. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Article 14 provides equality before law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Article 14 provides equal protection of the laws. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
xs: The correct code is **a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv** — option **(1)**.
**Equality before law**: **British** origin (**Dicey**), a **negative** concept — **no special privilege**.
**Equal protection of the laws**: **American** origin, a **positive** concept — like treated alike; permits **reasonable classification**.
xa: ⚠ **British = negative**; **American = positive**.
Both are guaranteed by **Article 14** to **any person**.

9.s:
How many of the following are among Dicey’s three classic elements of Rule of Law?
I. Absence of arbitrary power
II. Equality before the law
III. Primacy of the rights of the individual
IV. People’s responsibility to the Government
9.x: Three are Dicey's elements: absence of arbitrary power, equality before law and the primacy of individual rights. People's duty to the government is not one.
9.tq: Find the item that is not one of Dicey's elements.
n: Dicey’s first classic element of the Rule of Law is the absence of arbitrary power. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Dicey’s second classic element of the Rule of Law is equality before the law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Dicey’s third classic element of the Rule of Law is the primacy of the rights of the individual. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
People’s responsibility to the Government is not a pillar of the Rule of Law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The Rule of Law restrains the government. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The Rule of Law does not expand citizens’ obedience to authority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
xs: Three are Dicey's elements — option **(3) Only three**.
Dicey's elements: **absence of arbitrary power**, **equality before the law** and **primacy of individual rights**.
"**People's responsibility to the Government**" is **not** a pillar — the Rule of Law **restrains** the government.
xa: India accepts only the first two; it **reverses** the third — rights flow from the Constitution.
Dicey **opposed** the French **Droit Administratif**.

9.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding Dicey’s third principle and its position in India?
o: Dicey’s third principle concerns the primacy of individual rights.
In the United Kingdom, the Constitution is described as the result of judicial decisions on individual rights.
India adopted Dicey’s third premise without modification.
In India, the Constitution is the source of rights.
9.x: Option C is incorrect: India took Dicey's first two elements but reversed the third. In India, rights come from the Constitution, not the other way round.
9.tq: Remember how India departs from Dicey's third element.
n: Dicey’s third classic element of the Rule of Law is the primacy of the rights of the individual. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Dicey’s third element states that the Constitution is the result of individual rights defined and enforced by courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Dicey’s third element treats individual rights as resulting from judicial definition and enforcement rather than as originating from the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
In the United Kingdom, the Constitution is the result of judicial decisions on individual rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
In India, the Constitution is the source of rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
India reverses Dicey’s third premise while adopting Dicey’s first two principles intact. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
xs: The incorrect statement is that India adopted Dicey's **third premise without modification** — option **(3)**.
India **reverses** the third premise: here the **Constitution** is the **source** of rights.
The others are correct: the third principle is **primacy of individual rights**; in the **UK** the Constitution results from **judicial decisions**.
xa: India adopts the first two elements — **absence of arbitrary power** and **equality before the law** — intact.
Dicey wrote **Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution** (**1885**).

9.s:
Assertion (A): Dicey’s second element requires equal subjection of all classes to the ordinary law of the land.
Reason (R): Dicey opposed the idea that executive officials should be subject only to special administrative tribunals.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
9.x: Both are true: Dicey's second element puts everyone under the ordinary law and ordinary courts, which is why he opposed special tribunals for officials. R explains A.
9.tq: Ask whether opposing special tribunals explains equal subjection to law.
n: Dicey’s second classic element of the Rule of Law is equality before the law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Equality before the law means equal subjection of all classes to the ordinary law of the land. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The ordinary law of the land must be administered by the ordinary law courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
No person is above the law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The assertion that executive officials are subject only to special administrative tribunals is false. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Dicey opposed French *Droit Administratif*. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
xs: Both are true and R explains A — option **(1) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A**.
Dicey's second element puts all classes **equally subject** to the **ordinary law** administered by **ordinary courts**.
That is why he **opposed** the French **Droit Administratif** — special administrative tribunals for officials.
xa: ⚠ "Executive officials are subject only to special administrative tribunals" — **false** under Dicey.
Exceptions in India: **Art. 361** (President, Governors), **foreign diplomats**, **UN agencies**.

9.s:
How many of the following statements are consistent with the Rule of Law?
I. Government is subordinate to law.
II. Laws should be just, fair and non-arbitrary.
III. The ruler remains above the law.
IV. Executive discretion should operate without objective standards.
9.x: Two are consistent with the rule of law: government bound by law, and just, fair laws. A ruler above the law and discretion without standards belong to 'rule by law'.
9.tq: Discriminate 'rule of law' from 'rule by law'.
n: Rule of Law means that the government itself is subordinate to the law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Rule of Law requires laws to be just, fair, and non-arbitrary. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Rule of Law represents government under law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Rule by Law uses law as an instrument or weapon of state control. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Rule by Law governs citizens while the ruler remains above the law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Unguided executive discretion in applying or enforcing a law directly subverts the Rule of Law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The Rule of Law restrains the government. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
xs: Two statements are consistent with the Rule of Law — option **(2) Only two**.
Consistent: **government is subordinate to law** (I) and laws must be **just, fair and non-arbitrary** (II).
Inconsistent: the **ruler above the law** belongs to **Rule by Law**; unguided discretion is **arbitrary**.
xa: **Maneka Gandhi (1978)**: any **arbitrary** action violates Art. 14; unguided discretionary power struck down.
**E.P. Royappa (1974)**: "**equality is antithetic to arbitrariness**".

9.s:

III. Article 16(4)
IV. Article 29
9.x: Three concern SCs, STs or OBCs: 15(4), 15(5) and 16(4). Article 29 protects cultural and educational rights of any section, including minorities.
9.tq: Find the Article that is not caste-based.
xs: Three are associated with SCs, STs or OBCs — option **(3) Only three**.
**15(4)** (special provisions), **15(5)** (educational advancement) and **16(4)** (reservation) concern **SCs, STs, OBCs**.
**Article 29** concerns **cultural and educational rights** — **ethnicity** and **minorities**.
xa: **Article 17** abolishes **untouchability** — a **caste** concern.
**15(5)** was added by the **93rd Amendment, 2005**.

9.s:
Consider the following statements regarding State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024):
1. It was decided by a 7-judge bench and overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004).
2. It held that States may sub-classify SCs and STs on the basis of caste alone, without any empirical data.
3. It recommended identification of the creamy layer.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
9.x: Statement 1 is correct: a 7-judge bench overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004). Statement 2 is wrong: States have the power to sub-classify (basis Arts. 15(4) and 16(4)), but sub-classification must use empirical data. Statement 3 is correct: the Court recommended identifying the creamy layer. So '1 and 3 only'.
9.tq: Davinder Singh: power to sub-classify YES, but only on empirical data; overruled Chinnaiah.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: **State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh** (**2024**) was a **7-judge bench** that **overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: states may **sub-classify** (basis **Articles 15(4) and 16(4)**), but it **must use empirical data**.
Statement 3: it **recommended identification** of the **creamy layer**.
xa: ⚠ Sources differ: other notes say Davinder Singh permitted **sub-classification of SCs** only.
CJI **B.R. Gavai**: creamy layer should apply to **SC** quotas (Nov **2025**).

9.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh
(b) M. Nagaraj v. Union of India
(c) Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta
(d) Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh

List-II
(i) 1997
(ii) 2006
(iii) 2018
(iv) 2024
9.x: Samatha was decided in 1997, M. Nagaraj in 2006, Jarnail Singh in 2018 and Davinder Singh in 2024. The answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
9.tq: Arrange the reservation cases in time order.
n: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh was decided in 2024. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
M. Nagaraj v. Union of India was decided in 2006. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta was decided in 2018. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh was decided in 1997. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
xs: The correct code is **a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i** — option **(3)**.
**Davinder Singh** → **2024**; **M. Nagaraj** → **2006**; **Jarnail Singh** → **2018**; **Samatha** → **1997**.
xa: ⚠ **Nagaraj** needed SC/ST **backwardness** data; **Jarnail Singh** said no such data needed.
Jarnail Singh **extended** the **creamy layer** principle to **SC and ST promotions**.
**Samatha** nullified **mining leases** to non-tribals in **Schedule V areas**.

9.s:
Assertion (A): M. Nagaraj v. Union of India upheld reservation in promotions for SCs and STs subject to specified conditions.
Reason (R): The judgment required quantifiable data on backwardness, inadequate representation and overall administrative efficiency under Article 335.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
9.x: Both are true: M. Nagaraj (2006) upheld reservation in promotions for SCs and STs, on condition of data on backwardness, inadequate representation and efficiency (Article 335). R explains A.
9.tq: Ask whether the conditions explain the ruling.
n: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India concerns Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
M. Nagaraj v. Union of India upheld reservation in promotions for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Reservation in promotions for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes is subject to quantifiable data demonstrating backwardness. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Reservation in promotions for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes is subject to quantifiable data demonstrating inadequate representation. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Reservation in promotions for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes is subject to overall administrative efficiency. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Article 335 concerns overall administrative efficiency in reservation in promotions for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
xs: Both are true and R explains A — option **(1) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A**.
**M. Nagaraj** (**2006**) **upheld reservation in promotions** for SCs and STs.
The conditions were **quantifiable data** on **backwardness**, **inadequate representation** and **administrative efficiency** (**Article 335**).
xa: It upheld the **77th, 81st, 85th Amendments** with conditions.
**Jarnail Singh** (**2018**) **removed** the need to prove backwardness for SCs and STs.

9.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh
(b) Orissa Mining Corp. v. MoEF
(c) Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
(d) Janki Prasad Parimoo v. State of J&K

List-II
(i) Caste alone cannot be the sole determinant of backwardness
(ii) Gram Sabha safeguards the religious and cultural rights of Dongria Kondh tribals
(iii) Tribal land cannot be leased to private parties or corporations
(iv) 27% OBC quota and creamy layer exclusion
9.x: Samatha protected tribal land from leasing, Niyamgiri upheld the Gram Sabha's role, Indra Sawhney set the 27% OBC quota and the creamy layer, and Janki Prasad held caste alone cannot decide backwardness. The answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
9.tq: Match each case to its holding.
n: Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh concerns Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh nullified mining leases to non-tribals in Schedule V areas. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh held that tribal land cannot be leased to private parties or corporations. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Orissa Mining Corporation v. MoEF is also known as the Niyamgiri Case. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Orissa Mining Corporation v. MoEF concerns Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Orissa Mining Corporation v. MoEF affirmed the statutory role of the Gram Sabha under the Forest Rights Act, 2006. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
The Gram Sabha safeguards the religious rights of Dongria Kondh tribals under the Forest Rights Act, 2006. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
The Gram Sabha safeguards the cultural rights of Dongria Kondh tribals under the Forest Rights Act, 2006. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India concerns Other Backward Classes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India upheld a 27% quota for Other Backward Classes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India introduced the creamy layer exclusion for Other Backward Classes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Janki Prasad Parimoo v. State of J&K concerns Other Backward Classes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Janki Prasad Parimoo v. State of J&K clarified that caste alone cannot be the sole determinant of backwardness under Article 15(4). [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Backwardness under Article 15(4) must include social indicators. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Backwardness under Article 15(4) must include educational indicators. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
xs: The correct code is **a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i** — option **(2)**.
**Samatha** → **tribal land** cannot be leased to private parties; **Orissa Mining (Niyamgiri)** → **Gram Sabha** safeguards **Dongria Kondh** rights.
**Indra Sawhney** → **27%** OBC quota and **creamy layer**; **Janki Prasad Parimoo** → **caste alone** cannot determine **backwardness**.
xa: Niyamgiri (**2013**) affirmed the Gram Sabha's role under the **Forest Rights Act, 2006**.
Janki Prasad (**1973**): backwardness **must include social and educational indicators** under **Article 15(4)**.

9.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992):

I. It upheld a 27% quota for OBCs.
II. It introduced creamy layer exclusion.
III. It fixed a 50% reservation ceiling.
IV. It upheld quotas in promotions.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
9.x: I, II and III are correct: Indra Sawhney (1992, the Mandal case) upheld the 27% OBC quota, excluded the creamy layer and set a 50% ceiling. IV is false because it ruled out reservation in promotions.
9.tq: Recall the four Mandal rulings.
n: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India concerns Other Backward Classes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India was decided in 1992. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India is also known as the Mandal Case. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India upheld a 27% quota for Other Backward Classes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India introduced the creamy layer exclusion for Other Backward Classes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India fixed the reservation ceiling at 50%. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India ruled out quotas in promotions. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
xs: Statements **I, II and III** are correct — option **(4) I, II and III only**.
**Indra Sawhney** (**1992**, **Mandal Case**) upheld a **27% quota** for **OBCs**, introduced **creamy layer exclusion** and fixed a **50%** ceiling.
IV is wrong: it **ruled out quotas in promotions**.
xa: It was a **9-judge bench**, decided **6:3**.
The **77th (1995)** Amendment added **16(4A)**, undoing Indra Sawhney on promotions.
OBC creamy-layer income limit: **₹8 lakh** a year (**2017** notification).

9.s:
Assertion (A): Janki Janhit Abhiyan upheld economic criteria alone as a valid basis for classification.
Reason (R): The case upheld the validity of the 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act providing a 10% EWS quota.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
9.x: Both are true: Janhit Abhiyan (2022) upheld economic criteria alone as a valid basis for classification, because it upheld the 103rd Amendment's 10% EWS quota. R explains A.
9.tq: Ask whether upholding the Amendment explains the ruling.
n: Janki Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India concerns Economically Weaker Sections. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Janki Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India was decided in 2022. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Janki Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India upheld the validity of the 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
The 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act provides a 10% quota for Economically Weaker Sections. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
Janki Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India ruled that economic criteria alone can form a valid basis for classification. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 94-96]
xs: Both are true and R explains A — option **(1) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A**.
**Janki Janhit Abhiyan** (**2022**) upheld the **103rd Amendment** — a **10% quota** for **EWS**.
In doing so, it held that **economic criteria alone** can form a **valid basis** for **classification**.
xa: The bench split **3:2**; ⚠ **Indra Sawhney** was **6:3**.
The 103rd Amendment was passed as the **124th Amendment Bill** (**APPSC G1 2019**).
**EWS 10%** is an exception to the **50%** ceiling.

10.s:
Match List-I (Clause of Article 19(1)) with List-II (Freedom):
List-I
a. 19(1)(b)
b. 19(1)(c)
c. 19(1)(e)
d. 19(1)(g)
List-II
i. Reside and settle in any part of India
ii. Practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business
iii. Assemble peaceably and without arms
iv. Form associations or unions or co-operative societies
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
10.x: 19(1)(b) = assemble peaceably and without arms; 19(1)(c) = associations, unions or co-operative societies; 19(1)(e) = reside and settle; 19(1)(g) = profession, occupation, trade or business. (19(1)(d), not listed here, is movement.) Option A alone fits; B swaps (b) and (c), C swaps (e) and (g), D swaps (b) and (e).
10.tq: Recite the order: speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, [property deleted], profession.
xs: **19(1)(b)** assembly, **(c)** associations, **(e)** reside and settle, **(g)** profession/trade — option **(1) a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii**.
**(b)** = assemble **peaceably and without arms**; **(c)** = **associations or unions or co-operative societies**.
**(e)** = **reside and settle**; **(g)** = any **profession, occupation, trade or business**.
xa: **(a)** = speech and expression; **(d)** = **move** freely throughout India.
**(f)** property was **deleted by the 44th Amendment, 1978**.
⚠ "Co-operative societies" in **(c)** came by the **97th Amendment, 2011**.

10.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the six freedoms presently guaranteed by Article 19(1)?
o: Freedom to carry on any occupation, trade or business
Freedom to move freely throughout India
Freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property
10.x: The freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property was Article 19(1)(f), but it was deleted by the 44th Amendment in 1978. The other three are among the six present freedoms.
10.tq: Find the deleted clause rather than selecting one of the six surviving freedoms.
xs: The freedom to **acquire, hold and dispose of property** — **19(1)(f)** — is no longer guaranteed — option **(4)**.
It was **deleted by the 44th Amendment, 1978**, leaving **six** freedoms from the original **seven**.
Speech **(a)**, movement **(d)** and profession/trade **(g)** remain.
xa: "Which Article gives six freedoms?" → **Art. 19** (PYQ **2018**).
Right to Freedom group = **Arts. 19-22**.
⚠ **(c)** gained co-operative societies (**97th**); **(f)** was deleted (**44th**).

10.s: Which of the following is not expressly enumerated in Article 19(1), but has been recognised by judicial interpretation as part of freedom of speech and expression?
o: Right to acquire property under Article 19(1)(f)
Right to strike as a Fundamental Right
Freedom to travel abroad under Article 19(1)(d)
10.x: Freedom of the press is not separately listed in Article 19(1), but courts have read it into freedom of speech and expression. There is no Fundamental Right to strike, travel abroad is associated with Article 21, and Article 19(1)(f) has been deleted.
10.tq: Separate judicially implied freedoms from rights expressly listed or specifically excluded.
