28.x: India adopted the parliamentary form because of experience under the Acts of 1919 and 1935 and to avoid a personality cult. Complete separation of the executive from the legislature is a feature of the presidential system.
28.tq: Identify the historically stated reasons and reject the borrowed presidential-system feature.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: India chose the parliamentary form from **experience under the 1919 and 1935 Acts**.
Statement 2 is correct: it was also chosen **to avoid a personality cult**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **separation of powers** is a feature of the **USA's presidential** system — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: Defining feature of India's system = **collective responsibility** (APPSC **2025**).
Necessary features: **majority party rule**, **collective responsibility**, **PM as centre of power** (APPSC **2019**).
Parliamentary system has **nominal (President)** and **real (PM)** executives.

28.s:
Consider the following pairs:

Feature — System
1. Nominal and real executives — Parliamentary system
2. Separation of powers — Presidential system
3. Dissolution of the lower House — Parliamentary system
4. Secretaries as members of Congress — Presidential system

Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
28.x: Pairs 1, 2 and 3 are correctly matched. In the presidential system described, secretaries are not members of Congress, so pair 4 is incorrect.
28.tq: Check each pair against the institutional distinction between parliamentary and presidential executives.
xs: Pair 1 is correct: **nominal (President) and real (PM)** executives — **parliamentary**.
Pairs 2 and 3 are correct: **separation of powers** — **presidential**; **dissolution of the Lok Sabha** — **parliamentary**.
Pair 4 is wrong: in the USA **Secretaries are not members of Congress** — so option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: Parliamentary: **majority party rule**, **collective responsibility**, **political homogeneity**, **secrecy of procedure**.
Presidential: **fixed-term executive**, **no legislative responsibility** of the executive.
Ministers in India are MPs — **double membership**.

28.s:
Which of the following are necessary features of the parliamentary form of government in India?
1. Majority party rule
2. Collective responsibility
3. Prime Minister as the centre of power
4. Judicial review
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
28.x: Majority party rule, collective responsibility and the Prime Minister as the centre of power are necessary features of India’s parliamentary form. Judicial review is not listed as a necessary feature distinguishing this form.
28.tq: Separate essential features of the system from a general constitutional device.
xs: Necessary features: **majority party rule**, **collective responsibility** and **PM as centre of power** (APPSC **2019**) — so option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only** is correct.
**Judicial review** is not what makes India parliamentary — the defining feature is **collective responsibility** (APPSC **2025**).
xa: India chose the system from experience under the **1919 and 1935 Acts** and to avoid a **personality cult**.
Collective responsibility is to the **Lok Sabha** (**Art 75(3)**).
⚠ Separation of powers = **USA** feature.

28.s: Which one of the following is regarded as the feature that most clearly marks India as a parliamentary system?
o: Collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers
28.x: Collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the elected House is the characteristic feature distinguishing the parliamentary system.
28.tq: Identify the defining institutional feature rather than a general constitutional feature.
xs: India is parliamentary because of **collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers** — so option **(4)** is correct (APPSC **2025**).
It is **not separation of powers or judicial review**; the other options (indirect election, written Constitution, federalism) do not define the parliamentary form.
xa: **Art 75(3):** the CoM is collectively responsible to the **Lok Sabha**.
Ministers **"sink or swim together"**.
Underlying principle of Cabinet form: ensuring **collective responsibility of the Government to the people** (UPSC **2017**).

28.s: The underlying principle of the Cabinet form of government in India is best described as
o: a mechanism for speedy disposal of administrative work
a means of ensuring the supremacy of the President over Parliament
a mechanism of parliamentary democracy for ensuring collective responsibility of the Government to the people
a device for separating the executive completely from the legislature
28.x: UPSC 2017 key: the Cabinet form is a mechanism of parliamentary democracy for ensuring collective responsibility of the Government to the people. Speed of work is not its principle; the President is the nominal head, not supreme over Parliament; complete separation of executive and legislature is a presidential feature.
28.tq: Cabinet form = collective responsibility to the people via Parliament.
xs: The Cabinet form is **a mechanism of parliamentary democracy for ensuring collective responsibility of the Government to the people** — so option **(3)** is correct (UPSC **2017** key).
**Complete separation** of executive and legislature is a **presidential (USA)** trait; the President is the **nominal** executive, not supreme.
xa: India's defining feature = **collective responsibility** (APPSC **2025**).
The **Cabinet** is the **nucleus** that meets regularly and takes policy decisions.
Collective responsibility runs to the **Lok Sabha** (**Art 75(3)**).

28.s:
Consider the following statements about the word 'Cabinet' in the Constitution of India:
1. It was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.
2. The word 'Cabinet' appears in the Constitution only in Article 352.
3. Under Article 352(3), a Proclamation of Emergency can be issued only on the written advice of the Union Cabinet.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
28.x: Statement 2 is correct: Article 352(3) is the only place the word 'Cabinet' appears. Statement 1 is wrong: it was inserted by the 44th Amendment, 1978, not the 42nd. Statement 3 is correct: Emergency can be proclaimed only on the written advice of the Union Cabinet. Hence '2 and 3 only'; '2 only' misses 3, and options with 2 are wrong.
28.tq: Cabinet in the text = Art 352(3), 44th Amendment (1978) - the amendment that undid the Emergency excesses.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
1 is wrong: the word "Cabinet" was inserted by the **44th Amendment, 1978**, not the 42nd.
2 is correct: **Art. 352(3)** is the **only place** the word **"Cabinet"** appears.
3 is correct: Emergency is proclaimed only on the **written** advice of the **Union Cabinet**.
xa: **Arts. 74-75** create the **Council of Ministers**; the Cabinet otherwise rests on **convention**.
**Art 75(3)** (States: **Art 164(2)**): CoM **collectively responsible** to the **Lok Sabha**.
**Art. 75(2)**: Ministers hold office at the President's **pleasure** → **individual responsibility**.

28.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Council of Ministers is a wider body than the Cabinet.
2. The Council of Ministers is created under Articles 74 and 75.
3. The Council of Ministers normally meets regularly as a single body to take all policy decisions.
4. The Cabinet generally meets regularly and takes policy decisions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
28.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. The wider Council of Ministers rarely meets as a body; the Cabinet is the body that meets regularly and takes policy decisions.
28.tq: Compare the constitutional status, size and working frequency of the two bodies.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the CoM is the **wider body**, created by **Arts. 74-75**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the CoM **rarely meets** as a body.
Statement 4 is correct: the **Cabinet meets regularly** and takes policy decisions — so option **(1) 1, 2 and 4 only** is correct.
xa: CoM ranks: **Cabinet Ministers, MoS (independent charge), MoS, Deputy Ministers**.
The Cabinet **directs and supervises** the Council.
The word "Cabinet" appears only in **Art. 352**.

28.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the collective responsibility of the Union Council of Ministers:
1. It is provided under Article 75(3), and the Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
2. A minister who is a member of the Rajya Sabha is collectively responsible to the Rajya Sabha.
3. A no-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers can be moved only in the Lok Sabha.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
28.x: Statement 1 is correct: Art. 75(3) makes the Council collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. Statement 2 is wrong: ministers from the Rajya Sabha are also collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. Statement 3 is correct: a no-confidence motion lies only in the Lok Sabha. Hence '1 and 3 only'.
28.tq: Collective responsibility = Art 75(3), to the Lok Sabha only, even for RS ministers.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **Art 75(3)** makes the CoM collectively responsible to the **Lok Sabha**.
Statement 2 is wrong: ministers from the **Rajya Sabha** are also collectively responsible to the **Lok Sabha**.
Statement 3 is correct: a **no-confidence motion** lies **only in the Lok Sabha** — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: Responsibility is **not to both Houses**, and **not to the President**.
States: **Art 164(2)**.
⚠ **75(3)** = collective (to LS); **75(2)** = individual (President's pleasure).

28.s: What is the constitutional consequence of the death or resignation of the Prime Minister?
o: The Rajya Sabha is automatically dissolved.
Only the Cabinet Secretariat is dissolved.
The Council of Ministers as a whole goes out of office.
The President assumes the office of Prime Minister permanently.
28.x: The Prime Minister is the head of the Council of Ministers; therefore, the death or resignation of the Prime Minister results in the Council of Ministers going out of office.
28.tq: Test the institutional consequence of the Prime Minister's departure.
xs: The **PM's death or resignation** **dissolves** the Council of Ministers — so option **(3)** is correct.
It does not affect the **Rajya Sabha**, the **Cabinet Secretariat**, or make the President PM.
xa: **Loss of LS confidence** (no-confidence motion, defeat on a money bill/major policy) → **whole ministry resigns**.
Defeat in the **Rajya Sabha** does **not** bring down the government.
Ministers **"sink or swim together"** (**Art 75(3)**).

28.s: The oaths of office and secrecy to Union Ministers are administered by the
28.x: The President administers the oaths of office and secrecy to Union Ministers in accordance with the Third Schedule.
28.tq: Identify the constitutional authority associated with administering the oath.
xs: Oaths of **office and secrecy** to Union Ministers are administered by the **President** (**Third Schedule**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **PM**, **CJI** or **Speaker** play no part in ministers' oaths.
xa: The **oath of secrecy** ensures the **secrecy** of Cabinet deliberations.
Ministers hold office at the **President's pleasure** (**Art. 75(2)**).
**Arts. 74-75** create the Council of Ministers.

28.s: In the States, the constitutional provision corresponding to Article 75(3) on collective responsibility is:
28.x: Article 164(2) provides that the Council of Ministers in a State is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.
28.tq: Discriminate between neighbouring constitutional provisions by matching the subject with the exact Article.
xs: The State counterpart of **Art 75(3)** is **Article 164(2)** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Under it the State CoM is collectively responsible to the **Legislative Assembly**.
xa: **Art 75(3):** Union CoM collectively responsible to the **Lok Sabha**.
⚠ **75(3)** = collective; **75(2)** = individual responsibility.
A **no-confidence motion** at the Union lies **only in the Lok Sabha**.

28.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Defeat of the Union Government in the Rajya Sabha by itself requires the whole ministry to resign.
2. Passage of a no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha may result in the resignation of the whole ministry.
3. Defeat on a money bill or a major policy measure in the Lok Sabha may lead to the resignation of the whole ministry.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
28.x: Statements 2 and 3 are correct because they indicate loss of Lok Sabha confidence. Defeat in the Rajya Sabha by itself does not compel the ministry to resign.
28.tq: Test the House to which collective responsibility is owed and reject the reversed-House trap.
xs: Statement 1 is wrong: **defeat in the Rajya Sabha** does not bring down the government.

Statements 2 and 3 are correct: a **no-confidence motion** passed, or **defeat on a money bill/major policy** in the LS, = **loss of LS confidence** → **whole ministry resigns** — so option **(2) 2 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: The no-confidence motion lies **only in the Lok Sabha**.
**PM's death/resignation** dissolves the Council.
RS ministers are also responsible to the **Lok Sabha**.

28.s: Which one of the following correctly explains the expression ‘ministers sink or swim together’ in the Indian parliamentary system?
o: Every minister is personally elected by the Lok Sabha
Ministers may publicly reject Cabinet decisions without consequence
All ministers are required to defend Cabinet decisions or resign
Only Cabinet Ministers are responsible for government policy
28.x: Collective responsibility requires all ministers to support Cabinet decisions publicly. A minister unwilling to defend such a decision must resign.
28.tq: Apply the principle of collective responsibility to the conduct of an individual minister.
xs: "Sink or swim together" means Cabinet decisions **bind all ministers**; a dissenting minister unwilling to defend a decision **must resign** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Ministers cannot publicly reject decisions; responsibility is **collective**, not limited to Cabinet Ministers.
xa: Basis: **Art 75(3)** — collective responsibility to the **Lok Sabha**.
**Political homogeneity** and **secrecy** → differences ironed out behind closed doors, a **public show of unity**.
⚠ Individual responsibility = **Art. 75(2)**.

28.s: The secrecy of Cabinet deliberations is principally ensured by the:
28.x: The oath of secrecy ensures confidentiality of Cabinet deliberations and supports the public presentation of a united government.
28.tq: Distinguish the oath connected with confidentiality from the general oath of office.
xs: Secrecy of Cabinet deliberation is ensured by the **oath of secrecy** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Differences are **ironed out behind closed doors**, with a **public show of unity**.
xa: Oaths of **office and secrecy** are in the **Third Schedule**, administered by the **President**.
Cabinet decisions **bind all ministers** even if they differed inside.
**Secrecy of procedure** is a parliamentary-system feature.

28.s: With reference to individual responsibility of a Union Minister, which of the following statements is correct?
o: A minister holds office during the pleasure of the Lok Sabha under Article 75(3).
A minister holds office during the pleasure of the President under Article 75(2).
A minister holds office during the pleasure of the Chief Justice of India.
A minister can be removed only after a no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha.
28.x: Article 75(2) provides that a Union Minister holds office during the pleasure of the President. In practice, the Prime Minister may ask a minister to resign or advise the President to dismiss the minister.
28.tq: Identify the formal appointing authority and separate individual from collective responsibility.
xs: A minister holds office **during the pleasure of the President** under **Art 75(2)** — so option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ **Art 75(3)** is **collective** responsibility to the Lok Sabha, not individual tenure; a no-confidence motion targets the whole ministry.
xa: The **PM** can ask a minister to resign or **advise the President to dismiss** him (UPSC).
A resigned minister may make a **personal statement** in the House with the **Speaker's consent**.
Collective responsibility: **Art 75(3)**; States: **Art 164(2)**.

28.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Department of Personnel:
1. It came into existence in 1970.
2. Its origin was associated with the Administrative Reforms Commission of 1966.
3. It was placed under the Prime Minister.
4. It was created as a recommendation of the N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar report to provide a minister and secretary solely for administrative reform.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
28.x: The Department of Personnel came in 1970, originated from the ARC of 1966 and was placed under the Prime Minister. Statement 4 is false; the Ayyangar report did not suggest a minister and secretary solely for administrative reform.
28.tq: Find the false historical attribution hidden among otherwise precise institutional statements.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: the **ARC (1966)** led to the **Department of Personnel (1970)**, placed **under the PM**.
Statement 4 is wrong: it did **not** suggest a minister and secretary solely for administrative reform (UPSC **2021** key) — so option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: The **N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar report (1949)** dealt with **reorganising the machinery** of Central Government.
It recommended **grouping ministries** and **cabinet committees**.
**AoB** and **ToB Rules** date from **1961**.

28.s:
Which of the following were among the matters associated with the recommendations of the N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar Committee?
1. Grouping of ministries
2. Cabinet Committees
3. Reorganisation of the machinery of government
Which of the statements given above are correct?
28.x: The 1949 report concerned reorganisation of the machinery of government, including grouping ministries and Cabinet Committees.
28.tq: Treat the broad description and its two constituent measures as separate checks.
xs: The **N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar report (1949)** covered **reorganising the machinery** of government, **grouping ministries** and **cabinet committees** — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
All three listed matters are in the report.
xa: ⚠ It did **not** suggest a minister and secretary solely for administrative reform (UPSC **2021** key).
**ARC (1966)** → **Department of Personnel (1970)**, under the **PM**.
**AoB** and **ToB Rules, 1961** are framed under **Art 77(3)**.

28.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Cabinet Secretariat:
1. It provides secretarial assistance to the Cabinet and Cabinet Committees.
2. It administers the Allocation of Business Rules and Transaction of Business Rules.
3. It is placed directly under the Vice-President of India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
28.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the Cabinet Secretariat functions directly under the Prime Minister.
28.tq: Split the options by checking the authority attached to the Secretariat.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: it serves the Cabinet and **Cabinet Committees** and **administers the AoB and ToB Rules, 1961**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it is **directly under the Prime Minister**, **not under the VP** (CGPSC **2023**) — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: It coordinates ministries via **Committees of Secretaries**.
It sends a **monthly summary** of ministries' work to the President, VP and ministers.
Wings: **Civil, Military, Intelligence**.

28.s:
Consider the following statements about the Cabinet Secretary:
1. The Cabinet Secretary has a tenure of three years, extendable up to five years.
2. The Cabinet Secretary is the senior-most civil servant and the administrative head of the Cabinet Secretariat.
3. The Cabinet Secretary is appointed by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
28.x: Statement 2 is correct: the Cabinet Secretary is the senior-most civil servant and administrative head of the Secretariat. Statement 3 is correct: the ACC appoints him. Statement 1 is wrong: the tenure is two years, extendable up to four years. Hence '2 and 3 only'; '2 only' misses 2, and options with 3 are wrong.
28.tq: Cabinet Secretary: ACC appoints; 2 years, extendable to 4.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
1 is wrong: the tenure is **2 years**, extendable up to **4 years**.
2 is correct: he is the **senior-most civil servant** and **administrative head** of the Cabinet Secretariat.
3 is correct: he is appointed by the **Appointments Committee of the Cabinet**.
xa: He is **ex officio Chairman** of the **Civil Services Board** and heads the **National Crisis Management Committee**.
He is **11th** in the order of precedence.
**T.V. Somanathan:** **one-year extension** beyond **30 Aug 2026**.
The Cabinet Secretariat works **directly under the Prime Minister** — ⚠ not under the VP.

28.s:
Consider the following statements about the Cabinet Secretary:
1. The Cabinet Secretary is described as the first among equals among Secretaries.
2. The Cabinet Secretary occupies the eleventh position in the Table of Precedence.
3. The Cabinet Secretary heads the National Crisis Management Committee.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
28.x: All three statements are correct. The Cabinet Secretary is first among equals among Secretaries, is placed eleventh in the Table of Precedence and heads the National Crisis Management Committee.
28.tq: Verify each independent attribute before selecting the combined statement option.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: he is **"first among equals"** among Secretaries.
Statement 2 is correct: he is **11th** in the order of precedence.
Statement 3 is correct: he heads the **National Crisis Management Committee** — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
xa: He is **ex officio Chairman of the Civil Services Board**.
Tenure: **2 years**, extendable up to **4 years**.
⚠ The **AG** also has precedence **11**; the **SG** has **23**.

28.s: Cabinet Committees in India are best described as:
o: Judicial bodies established by the Supreme Court
Statutory bodies created by Acts of Parliament
Extra-constitutional bodies formed under the Transaction of Business Rules, 1961
Constitutional bodies established by separate Articles of the Constitution
28.x: Cabinet Committees are extra-constitutional bodies formed under the Transaction of Business Rules, 1961, framed under Article 77(3).
28.tq: Separate constitutional, statutory and extra-constitutional institutions.
xs: Cabinet committees are **extra-constitutional** bodies set up by the **PM** under the **Transaction of Business Rules, 1961** — so option **(3)** is correct.
They are **not in the Constitution** and not created by Acts of Parliament or courts.
xa: The ToB Rules are framed under **Art 77(3)**.
There are **eight (8)** committees (**Apr 2025**).
Criticism: power concentrated in the **PMO and cabinet committees** dilutes collective Cabinet decision-making.

28.s: How many Cabinet Committees are referred to in the present classification?
28.x: There are eight Cabinet Committees (Apr 2025): Appointments, Security, Political Affairs, Economic Affairs, Parliamentary Affairs, Accommodation, Investment and Growth, and Employment and Skill Development.
28.tq: Use numerical elimination with the closely spaced committee counts.
xs: There are **eight (8)** cabinet committees (**Apr 2025**) — so option **(4) Eight** is correct.
They are **Appointments, Security, Political Affairs, Economic Affairs, Parliamentary Affairs, Accommodation, Investment and Growth**, and **Employment and Skill Development**.
xa: The **2019** committees: **Investment and Growth** + **Employment and Skill Development**.
Not PM-chaired: **Parliamentary Affairs** + **Accommodation**.
They work under the **ToB Rules, 1961**.

28.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Cabinet Committee)
A. Appointments Committee
B. Cabinet Committee on Security
C. Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs
D. Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs

List-II (Principal concern)
1. Government business and parliamentary sessions
2. Senior appointments
3. Defence, national security and nuclear doctrine
4. Economic and infrastructure projects

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
28.x: The Appointments Committee deals with senior appointments; the Security Committee with defence and national security; the Economic Affairs Committee with economic and infrastructure projects; and the Parliamentary Affairs Committee with parliamentary business.
28.tq: Start from the sure pairs and eliminate codes with a swapped function.
xs: **ACC** – senior appointments (A-2); **CCS** – defence, national security, nuclear doctrine (B-3).
**CCEA** – economic and infrastructure projects (C-4); **Parliamentary Affairs** – sessions and government business (D-1) — so option **(1) A-2, B-3, C-4, D-1** is correct.
xa: ACC, CCS and CCEA are **chaired by the PM**; Parliamentary Affairs by a **senior minister**.
The CCEA approved **Ballari-Guntakal** 3rd and 4th lines, **Rs 1,264 crore** (**Jul 2026**).
The ACC appoints the **Cabinet Secretary** and recommends the **Solicitor General**.

28.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Cabinet Committees:
1. The Prime Minister chairs the Appointments Committee.
2. The Prime Minister chairs the Cabinet Committee on Security.
3. The Prime Minister chairs the Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs.
4. The Prime Minister chairs the Cabinet Committee on Accommodation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
28.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The Accommodation Committee is chaired by a senior minister rather than by the Prime Minister.
28.tq: Watch for the swapped chairperson in the otherwise familiar list.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: the **PM chairs** the **ACC**, **CCS** and **Political Affairs** committee.
Statement 4 is wrong: **Accommodation** is chaired by a **senior minister** — so option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: The PM also chairs the **CCEA**.
⚠ Not PM-chaired = **Parliamentary Affairs** + **Accommodation**.
Total cabinet committees: **eight (8)**.

28.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Cabinet Committees:
1. The Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs, which deals with Centre-State and political issues, is described as a 'super cabinet'.
2. The decision on caste enumeration in the Census was taken by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs.
3. The Cabinet Committees on Investment and Growth and on Employment and Skill Development were set up in 2019.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
28.x: Statement 1 is correct: the CCPA handles Centre-State and political issues and is called the 'super cabinet'. Statement 2 is wrong: caste enumeration in the Census was decided by the Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs, not the CCEA. Statement 3 is correct: both committees were set up in 2019. Hence '1 and 3 only'.
28.tq: CCPA = super cabinet, caste census; CCEA = economic/infrastructure projects; 2019 = Investment & Growth, Employment & Skills.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the **CCPA** handles Centre-State and political issues — the **"super cabinet"**.
Statement 2 is wrong: **caste enumeration** in the Census was decided by the **CCPA** (**30 Apr 2025**), not the CCEA.
Statement 3 is correct: **Investment and Growth** and **Employment and Skill Development** were set up in **2019** — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: The Cabinet Secretariat held the caste-census Cabinet papers exempt under **RTI Act s.8(1)(i)** (**8 Apr 2026**).
The **CCEA** handles economic and infrastructure projects.
The **PM** chairs both the CCPA and CCEA.

28.s: A ‘kitchen cabinet’ refers to:
o: A formal Cabinet Committee established by the Constitution
A permanent secretariat of the Parliament
An informal inner circle of the Prime Minister's trusted colleagues and friends
A group of opposition leaders advising the Speaker
28.x: A kitchen cabinet is an informal inner circle consisting of trusted colleagues and friends of the Prime Minister, including some senior ministers and non-ministers.
28.tq: Distinguish an informal political grouping from a formal constitutional or executive body.
xs: A **kitchen cabinet** is the PM's **informal inner circle** of a few senior ministers and trusted **colleagues and friends** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It is not formal or constitutional; example: **Indira Gandhi's advisers**.
xa: Criticism: an **extra-constitutional** power centre that **bypasses the Cabinet**.
**GoMs/EGoMs** are ad hoc groups reporting to the Cabinet; abolished in **2014**.
Cabinet committees are **extra-constitutional** bodies under the **ToB Rules, 1961**.

28.s: Which of the following best explains the criticism directed at the kitchen cabinet?
o: It is a constitutional body that cannot advise the Prime Minister.
It is responsible for conducting parliamentary elections.
It consists exclusively of opposition members.
It is an extra-constitutional power centre that may bypass the Cabinet.
28.x: The kitchen cabinet is criticised as an extra-constitutional power centre because it may shape decisions while bypassing the formal Cabinet.
28.tq: Apply the concept to the institutional consequence described in the question.
xs: The kitchen cabinet is criticised as an **extra-constitutional / unconstitutional power centre** that **bypasses the Cabinet** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is an **informal inner circle** of the PM, not a constitutional body or an opposition group.
xa: Example: **Indira Gandhi's advisers**.
**GoMs/EGoMs** were criticised for **delay** and **diluting collective responsibility**.
**PMO** and cabinet committees are also criticised for concentrating power.

28.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Groups of Ministers (GoMs) and Empowered Groups of Ministers (EGoMs):
1. They are permanent bodies that replace the Cabinet in decision-making.
2. They have been criticised for causing delay and diluting collective responsibility.
3. The existing GoMs and EGoMs were abolished in 2014.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
28.x: Statement 1 is wrong: GoMs/EGoMs are ad hoc groups that examine an issue and report to the Cabinet. Statement 2 is correct: they were criticised for delay and diluting collective responsibility. Statement 3 is correct: the existing GoMs/EGoMs were abolished in 2014. Hence '2 and 3 only'; options with 1 are wrong.
28.tq: GoMs/EGoMs: ad hoc, report to Cabinet, criticised for delay, abolished 2014.
xs: Statement 1 is wrong: GoMs/EGoMs are **ad hoc groups** that examine an issue and **report to the Cabinet**.
Statement 2 is correct: criticised for **delay + diluting collective responsibility**.
Statement 3 is correct: existing GoMs/EGoMs were **abolished in 2014** — so option **(3) 2 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: The **kitchen cabinet** is the PM's **informal inner circle**.
Cabinet committees: **eight (8)**, under the **ToB Rules, 1961**.
Coalition era (**1989-2014**): coordination committees weakened Cabinet cohesion.

28.s: Which of the following best describes the position of the Union Cabinet during single-party majority eras in India?
o: Collective responsibility is constitutionally suspended during a majority government.
Coalition coordination committees determine all Cabinet decisions.
Parliament invariably exercises complete control over the Cabinet.
The Prime Minister and Cabinet generally exercise strong dominance over Parliament.
28.x: During single-party majority eras, the Prime Minister and Cabinet generally dominate Parliament, leading to the criticism that the system may resemble a ‘cabinet dictatorship’.
28.tq: Distinguish a political tendency from a formal constitutional rule.
xs: In **single-party majority eras**, a strong **PM and Cabinet dominate Parliament** — the **"cabinet dictatorship"** charge — so option **(4)** is correct.
Collective responsibility is never suspended, and coalition **coordination committees** belong to the **coalition era**.
xa: **Coalition era (1989-2014):** allies' demands weakened Cabinet cohesion.
**Kitchen cabinet** criticism: an extra-constitutional power centre.
⚠ **Shadow Cabinet** (UK) has no formal counterpart in India.

28.s: Why did coalition politics tend to weaken Cabinet cohesion and collective responsibility during 1989–2014?
o: Because coordination committees and the demands of alliance partners influenced government functioning
Because the President directly exercised all Cabinet powers
Because Parliament ceased to examine government expenditure
Because the Constitution abolished the office of the Prime Minister during coalition governments
28.x: Coalition governments had to accommodate coordination committees and the demands of alliance partners. This often weakened Cabinet cohesion and the effective operation of collective responsibility.
28.tq: Connect the political condition with its institutional consequence.
xs: In the **coalition era (1989-2014)**, **coordination committees** and **allies' demands** weakened Cabinet cohesion and collective responsibility — so option **(1)** is correct.
The President did not take over Cabinet powers, and the PM's office was never abolished.
xa: In **single-party majority eras**, PM and Cabinet dominate → **"cabinet dictatorship"** charge.
**GoMs/EGoMs** were criticised for delay and diluting collective responsibility.
Collective responsibility: **Art 75(3)** — ministers **"sink or swim together"**.

28.s: Which of the following statements regarding the resignation of the Attorney General of India is correct?

xa: AG = **first law officer**, precedence **11**; SG = **second law officer**, precedence **23**.

28.s: Which one of the following is regarded as a criticism of excessive concentration of power in the Prime Minister’s Office and Cabinet committees?

Pair 4 is wrong: the US Senate has **no nominated members** — so option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: RS seats are by **population** (**Fourth Schedule**); US Senate **2 per state** (**100**).
The RS is **weaker than the Lok Sabha** — money bills only in the LS.
Nomination brings **experts** into the RS.

29.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Speaker certifies whether a Bill is a Money Bill.
2. The Speaker presides over a joint sitting of Parliament.
3. The Rajya Sabha can initiate a no-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers.
4. The Rajya Sabha has no vote on Demands for Grants.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
29.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 3 is false because a no-confidence motion is a device of the Lok Sabha, not the Rajya Sabha.
29.tq: Ask who performs the constitutional job and reject the power assigned to the wrong House.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the **Speaker** **certifies money bills** and **presides over joint sittings**.
Statement 3 is wrong: there is **no no-confidence motion** in the RS.
Statement 4 is correct: the RS has **no vote on demands for grants** — so option **(2) 1, 2 and 4 only** is correct.
xa: Money bills are introduced **only in the LS**; the RS must return them in **14 days**.
A larger LS would **dilute the RS's weight in joint sittings** (**Apr 2026**).
RS seats are by **population** (**Fourth Schedule**).

29.s:
Consider the following statements about the Rajya Sabha:
1. Article 312 relates to the creation of new All-India Services, a role specific to the Rajya Sabha.
2. The Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill to the Lok Sabha within 14 days.
3. Like the US Senate, every State has an equal number of seats in the Rajya Sabha.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
29.x: Statement 1 is correct: Article 312 (creation of new All-India Services) is a special federal role of the Rajya Sabha. Statement 2 is correct: a Money Bill must be returned within 14 days, showing the House is weaker than the Lok Sabha. Statement 3 is wrong: Rajya Sabha seats are allotted broadly by population under the Fourth Schedule (UP 31), unlike the US Senate's 2 per State. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
29.tq: RS: Art 312 power, 14 days on Money Bills, seats by population.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **Art. 312** is the creation of new **All-India Services**.
Statement 2 is correct: the RS must return a **money bill** within **14 days**.
Statement 3 is wrong: RS seats go by **population** (UP **31**, many states **1**), unlike the US Senate's **2 per state** — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: The **Speaker** certifies money bills and presides over **joint sittings**.
The RS has **12** nominated members; the US Senate none.
RS members are elected by **elected MLAs** by **STV**.

29.s: Under Article 169, a State Legislative Council may be created or abolished by Parliament when the State Legislative Assembly passes a resolution by
o: a majority of the total membership and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting
a two-thirds majority of the total membership alone
a unanimous vote of all members of the Assembly
a simple majority of members present and voting
29.x: The Assembly resolution must be passed by a majority of the total membership and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.
29.tq: Keep the two limbs of the special majority separate: total membership and present-and-voting membership.
xs: The **Art. 169** Assembly resolution needs a **majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Then **Parliament** creates or abolishes the Council **by law** (not an **Art. 368** amendment).
xa: **Art. 171:** Council size not more than **one-third** of the Assembly; at least **40**.
AP's Council was **abolished in 1985** and **revived in 2007**.
Unicameral States: **Goa**, **Mizoram**, **Sikkim**.

29.s:
Consider the following statements about State Legislative Councils:
1. Under Article 169, Parliament creates or abolishes a Legislative Council by law, not by an amendment under Article 368.
2. Under Article 171, a Legislative Council may have up to one-half of the membership of the Legislative Assembly.
3. A Legislative Council must have at least 40 members.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x: Statement 1 is correct: Article 169 works through an ordinary law of Parliament after the Assembly resolution. Statement 2 is wrong: the Council cannot exceed one-third of the Assembly. Statement 3 is correct: the minimum is 40. Hence 1 and 3 only; '1 only' misses 3, and options with 2 are wrong.
29.tq: Council size: not more than one-third of the Assembly, not less than 40.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: under **Art. 169** Parliament acts **by law**, not by an **Art. 368** amendment.
Statement 2 is wrong: under **Art. 171** the Council is not more than **one-third** of the Assembly.
Statement 3 is correct: at least **40** members — so option **(3) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: Pre-condition: **Assembly resolution** by **majority of total membership** and **two-thirds** present and voting.
AP's **2020** abolition resolution was **withdrawn in 2021**.
Older notes listed six/seven bicameral states including **J&K**.

29.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Legislative Assembly of Delhi is based on Article 239AA, inserted by the 69th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1991.
2. The Legislative Assembly of Puducherry is based on Article 239AA.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x: Statement 1 is correct: Delhi's Assembly rests on Article 239AA (69th Amendment, 1991). Statement 2 is wrong: Puducherry's Assembly rests on Article 239A. Hence 1 only; 'Both' and '2 only' wrongly accept statement 2, 'Neither' rejects statement 1.
29.tq: 239A = Puducherry; 239AA (the extra A) = Delhi.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: Delhi's Assembly rests on **Art. 239AA** (**69th Amendment, 1991**).
Statement 2 is wrong: Puducherry's rests on **Art. 239A** — so option **(1) 1 only** is correct.
xa: ⚠ **239AA** = Delhi; **239A** = Puducherry.
Delhi has **70** seats; Puducherry **30 elected + up to 3 nominated**.
J&K's Assembly comes from the **J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019**, with **90** elected seats.

29.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Delhi — 70 Assembly seats
2. Puducherry — 30 elected members and up to 3 nominated members
3. Jammu and Kashmir — 90 elected Assembly seats
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
29.x: Delhi has 70 Assembly seats, Puducherry has 30 elected members and up to 3 nominated members, and Jammu and Kashmir has 90 elected seats.

xs: **Delhi – 70** seats; **Puducherry – 30 elected + up to 3 nominated**; **J&K – 90 elected** seats — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
All three pairs match the notes.
xa: Bases: Delhi **Art. 239AA**; Puducherry **Art. 239A**; J&K the **J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019**.
These three are the **only UTs** with elected members in the **Rajya Sabha**.
The **UT Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026** extends **women's reservation** to these legislatures.

29.s: Which Union Territories have elected members in the Rajya Sabha?
o: Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir
Delhi, Daman and Diu and Dadra and Nagar Haveli
29.x: Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir are the three Union Territories having elected members in the Rajya Sabha.

xs: **Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir** are the only UTs with elected RS members — so option **(2)** is correct.

Puducherry: **Art. 239A**, **30** elected + up to **3** nominated.

o: All Union Territories having no Legislative Assembly
Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir

xs: The **Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026** extends **women's reservation** to **Delhi, Puducherry and J&K** (**17 Apr 2026**) — so option **(4)** is correct.
These are the three UTs **with legislatures**; Chandigarh, Ladakh and Lakshadweep have none in the notes.

29.s: Which one of the following statements about Andhra Pradesh is correct?
o: Its Legislative Council was created in 2020 and abolished in 2021.
It has always had a unicameral legislature since 1956.
Its Legislative Council was abolished in 2007 and revived in 2021.
Its Legislative Council was abolished in 1985, revived in 2007, and the 2020 abolition resolution was withdrawn in 2021.
29.x: Andhra Pradesh's Legislative Council was abolished in 1985, revived in 2007, and the resolution passed in 2020 to abolish it again was withdrawn in 2021.
29.tq: Use the full event sequence to detect reversed years and reversed institutional changes.
xs: AP's Legislative Council was **abolished in 1985**, **revived in 2007**, and the **2020** abolition resolution was **withdrawn in 2021** — so option **(4)** is correct.
AP is **bicameral**, so options (1), (2), (3) misstate the history.
xa: Councils are created/abolished by Parliament **by law** under **Art. 169**.
Council size: ≤ **one-third** of the Assembly, at least **40** (**Art. 171**).
Unicameral States: **Goa**, **Mizoram**, **Sikkim**.

29.s: A proposal to increase the size of the Lok Sabha would, in a joint sitting of Parliament, tend to
o: dilute the relative weight of the Rajya Sabha
abolish the Rajya Sabha's nominated membership
increase the relative weight of the Rajya Sabha
give the Rajya Sabha exclusive control over Money Bills
29.x: Since a joint sitting is presided over by the Speaker and voting strength depends on the combined membership, a larger Lok Sabha would dilute the Rajya Sabha's relative weight.
29.tq: Apply the membership relationship in a joint sitting instead of focusing on the separate powers of each House.
xs: A larger Lok Sabha would **dilute the Rajya Sabha's weight in joint sittings** (**Apr 2026**) — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **Speaker** presides over joint sittings, and **money bills** remain **only in the LS**.
xa: The RS must return a money bill in **14 days**.
The RS has **no vote on demands for grants** and **no no-confidence motion**.
Comparisons: **US House** fixed at **435**; **Italy** cut its Chamber from **630 to 400**.

29.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Union Council of Ministers
(b) State Council of Ministers
(c) Council of States
(d) State Legislative Council

List-II
(i) Articles 168, 169 and 171
(ii) Article 80
(iii) Article 74
(iv) Article 163
29.x: The Union Council of Ministers is under Article 74, the State Council under Article 163, the Council of States under Article 80, and the Legislative Council under Articles 168, 169 and 171, so the answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
29.tq: Pair the Union and State versions: 74 with 163, and 80 with 168 to 171.
n: The Council of States is the Rajya Sabha, which is the Upper House of the Union Parliament under Article 80. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The State Legislative Council is the Vidhan Parishad, which is the Upper House of bicameral State Legislatures under Articles 168, 169, and 171. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The constitutional basis of the Union Council of Ministers is Article 74. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The constitutional basis of the State Council of Ministers is Article 163. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The term “Council” in Indian Polity spans three distinct constitutional institutions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i** — option **(4)**.
**Union Council of Ministers:** **Article 74**; **State Council of Ministers:** **Article 163**.
**Council of States** (Rajya Sabha): **Article 80**; **State Legislative Council** (Vidhan Parishad): **Articles 168, 169 and 171**.
xa: The Council of Ministers is an **executive** body aiding and advising the **President** or the **Governor**.
**Parliament** = **President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha**.
The **Vice-President** chairs the Rajya Sabha but is **not** a member of Parliament.

29.s:
Consider the following statements about State Legislatures:
1. Provisions on State Legislatures are contained in Part VI, Articles 168 to 212.
2. A bicameral State Legislature consists of the Governor, the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council.
3. A unicameral State Legislature consists of the Legislative Assembly alone; the Governor is not a part of it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x: Statement 1 is correct: Part VI, Articles 168-212, deals with State Legislatures. Statement 2 is correct: a bicameral legislature is Governor + Assembly + Council. Statement 3 is wrong: a unicameral legislature is Governor + Legislative Assembly; the Governor is part of both kinds. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
29.tq: Like the President in Parliament, the Governor is always a part of the State Legislature.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
1: State Legislatures are in **Part VI**, **Articles 168 to 212**.
2: a **bicameral** legislature = **Governor + Legislative Assembly + Legislative Council**.
3 is wrong: a **unicameral** legislature = **Governor + Legislative Assembly** — the Governor is part of it.
xa: **Six** bicameral States: **Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh**.
Unicameral examples: **Goa**, **Mizoram**, **Sikkim**.
**Art. 171:** Council size not more than **one-third** of the Assembly; at least **40**.

29.s: Which State has the largest Legislative Council, with 100 seats?
29.x: Uttar Pradesh has the largest Legislative Council, with 100 seats, among the six bicameral States.
29.tq: Recall the largest of the six State Legislative Councils.
n: Uttar Pradesh has the largest Legislative Council, with 100 seats. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
India currently has 6 bicameral States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
Uttar Pradesh is a bicameral State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
xs: **Uttar Pradesh** has the largest Legislative Council, with **100** seats — option **(3)**.
UP is one of the **six** bicameral States.
**Maharashtra**, **Bihar** and **Andhra Pradesh** are also bicameral but have smaller Councils.
xa: Other bicameral States: **Telangana** and **Karnataka**.
**Art. 171:** Council not more than **one-third** of the Assembly; at least **40** members.
**Art. 169:** Parliament creates or abolishes a Council **by law**.

29.s: Bicameralism was first introduced in India at the Central level by which enactment?
29.x: The Government of India Act, 1919 first brought bicameralism to the Centre, with the Council of State and Central Legislative Assembly. The 1935 Act brought it to some provinces.
29.tq: Discriminate the 1919 Act (Centre) from the 1935 Act (provinces).
n: Bicameralism was first introduced in India at the Central level by the Government of India Act, 1919. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Government of India Act, 1919, created the Council of State and the Central Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
xs: Bicameralism at the Centre was first introduced by the **Government of India Act, 1919** — option **(2)**.
It created the **Council of State** and the **Central Legislative Assembly**.
**Articles 169 and 171** concern State Legislative Councils, not the Centre.
xa: India's Parliament: **Council of States (Rajya Sabha)** + **House of the People (Lok Sabha)**.
Large and diverse countries prefer **two Houses** to represent all sections and regions.
Unicameral examples: **China**, **Israel**, **New Zealand**, **Sweden**, **Denmark**.

29.s: Which statement correctly distinguishes the State Legislative Council from the Rajya Sabha regarding abolition?
o: The Rajya Sabha can be abolished under Article 169, whereas the State Legislative Council cannot be abolished.
Both can be abolished by the State Assembly.
The State Legislative Council can be abolished under Article 169, whereas the Rajya Sabha cannot be abolished.
29.x: A State Legislative Council, though permanent, can be abolished under Article 169. The Rajya Sabha cannot be abolished, which is the difference.
29.tq: Discriminate abolition of the State Council from the permanence of the Rajya Sabha.
n: The State Legislative Council can be abolished. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Council can be abolished under Article 169. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Council of States cannot be abolished. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Council of States is a permanent body. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Council cannot be dissolved on the recommendation of the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
xs: The **State Legislative Council can be abolished under Article 169**, whereas the **Rajya Sabha cannot** — option **(3)**.
**Art. 169:** Parliament creates or abolishes a Council **by law** (not an **Art. 368** amendment).
The **Rajya Sabha** (**Article 80**) is the Council of States — the Upper House of Parliament.
xa: Pre-condition: **Assembly resolution** by a **majority of total membership** and **two-thirds** of members **present and voting**.
AP's Council was abolished in **1985** and revived in **2007**.
A **2020** resolution to abolish it again was withdrawn in **2021**.

29.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The President is an integral part of Parliament.
Statement B: The Vice-President is not a part of Parliament.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
29.x: Both are true: the President is an integral part of Parliament (Article 79), whereas the Vice-President, though Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, is not a part of Parliament.
29.tq: Separate being part of Parliament from presiding over a House.
n: The President is an integral part of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President is not a part of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)**.
A: **Parliament** = **President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha** — the President is an integral part.
B: the **Vice-President** is ex-officio Chairman of the **Rajya Sabha** but **not** a member of Parliament.
xa: The **Council of States** is the Rajya Sabha — **Article 80**.
The State **Legislative Council** (Vidhan Parishad) rests on **Articles 168, 169 and 171**.
The **Council of Ministers** aids and advises the **President** (**Article 74**) or **Governor** (**Article 163**).

30.s: Articles 79 to 122 of the Constitution occur in
30.x: Parliamentary provisions in Articles 79 to 122 are contained in Part V of the Constitution.
30.tq: Link the article range with the correct constitutional Part.
xs: **Arts. 79-122** on Parliament are in **Part V** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Art. 79** opens it: Parliament = **President + RS + LS**.
xa: **Art. 86:** President may address either House or both.
**Art. 87:** special address at the **first session after each general election** and the **first session of each year**.
Procedural Articles in this Part: **Art. 98** (secretariats), **Art. 100** (quorum), **Art. 118** (rules), **Art. 120** (language).

30.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the President as a component of Parliament:
1. The President is a part of Parliament but is not a member of either House.
2. No Bill passed by Parliament becomes law without the President's assent.
3. The President may summon and prorogue the Houses of Parliament.
4. The President sits in Parliament as a member while addressing the Houses.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: The President is a component of Parliament but does not sit as a member of either House. Presidential assent is necessary for a Bill to become law, and the President summons and prorogues Parliament.
30.tq: Distinguish being a constitutional component of Parliament from being a member who sits in a House.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: the President is part of Parliament but **does not sit** in it.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct: **no bill becomes law without his assent**; he **summons and prorogues** the Houses.
Statement 4 is wrong: he **does not sit in Parliament** even while addressing — so option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: He also **dissolves** the Lok Sabha and issues **ordinances**.
**Art. 86:** may address either House or both.
Comparison: **Crown-in-Parliament** (UK).

30.s:
Consider the following statements about the President's addresses to Parliament:
1. Under Article 86, the President may address either House or both Houses assembled together.
2. Under Article 87, the President makes a special address to both Houses at the commencement of every session.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: Statement 1 is correct: Article 86 is the general power to address either or both Houses and send messages. Statement 2 is wrong: the Article 87 special address is made only at the first session after each general election and the first session of each year, not every session. So '1 only'.
30.tq: Art 86 = any time; Art 87 = first session after election + first session of each year.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)** **1 only**.
1: under **Art. 86** the President may **address either House or both**.
2 is wrong: the **Art. 87** special address is only at the **first session after each general election** and the **first session of each year**.
xa: The President **summons** and **prorogues** Parliament and **dissolves** the Lok Sabha.
He **nominates 12** members to the Rajya Sabha.
Parliament = **President + Rajya Sabha + Lok Sabha** (**Art. 79**) — no bill becomes law without his **assent**.

30.s: The constitutional position of the Indian President in relation to Parliament is most closely comparable to
o: The Governor of a State in relation to its Legislative Assembly only

xs: The President's place in Parliament is like the **Crown-in-Parliament** in the **UK** — so option **(4)** is correct.
⚠ The **US President** is **separate from Congress** — the opposite model.
xa: **Art. 79:** Parliament = **President + RS + LS**.
**No bill becomes law without his assent**.
He **summons**, **prorogues** and **dissolves** (LS only).

xs: **Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A**: the President is part of Parliament because **no bill becomes law without his assent** — so option **(1)** is correct.

xa: The notes flag this exact **Assertion-Reason** as an exam angle.

30.s:
With reference to the election of representatives of States to the Rajya Sabha, consider the following statements:

xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: State representatives are elected by **elected MLAs** by **PR-STV** (**Art 80(4)**).
Statement 3 is wrong: only **elected** MLAs vote — so option **(2) 1 and 2 only** is correct.

o: 530 members from States and 13 from Union Territories
524 members from States and 19 from Union Territories
525 members from States and 18 from Union Territories
30.x: The present strength is 543, comprising 524 members from the States and 19 from the Union Territories.
30.tq: Split the total into its State and Union Territory components.
xs: The present Lok Sabha (**543**) = **524** from States + **19** from UTs — so option **(3)** is correct.
⚠ **530** States + **20** UTs is the **maximum** (**550**).
xa: **Art. 81** governs LS composition.
Older figure **552** included **2** nominated **Anglo-Indians**.
Seats: **Delhi 7**, **J&K 5**.

30.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the maximum and present strength of the Lok Sabha?
30.x: The constitutional maximum is 550, while the present strength is 543. The older figure of 552 included two nominated Anglo-Indian members.
30.tq: Compare the current figure with the historical figure instead of treating them as interchangeable.
xs: LS **maximum 550**, **present 543** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The older figure **552** counted **2** nominated **Anglo-Indians**.
xa: Anglo-Indian nomination was ended by the **104th Amendment, 2019**.
⚠ RS: **250** max / **245** present.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about Anglo-Indian representation in the Lok Sabha:
1. The 104th Amendment also ended the reservation of Lok Sabha seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
2. This nomination was discontinued by the 104th Amendment Act, 2019, with effect from 25 January 2020.
3. Article 331 enabled the President to nominate up to two Anglo-Indian members to the Lok Sabha.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: Statements 2 and 3 are correct: Article 331 allowed up to two nominated Anglo-Indians, and the 104th Amendment ended this from 25 January 2020. Statement 1 is wrong: the same Amendment extended SC/ST reservation by ten years, till 2030. So '2 and 3 only'.
30.tq: 104th Amendment: Anglo-Indian nomination ended, SC/ST reservation extended to 2030.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
3: **Article 331** allowed the President to nominate **two** Anglo-Indian members.
2: the **104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019** discontinued it after **25 January 2020**.
1 is wrong: the **104th** Amendment **extended** SC/ST reservation by ten years — until **2030**.
xa: SC/ST reservation (**Article 330**) was initially for **10 years** and repeatedly extended.
LS maximum is now **550**; the older **552** included **2** nominated Anglo-Indians.
The Lok Sabha now has **no nominated members**.

30.s: Members of the Lok Sabha are directly elected on the basis of adult suffrage under Article 326. The voting age for such elections was lowered to 18 years by the
30.x: The 61st Amendment Act, 1987 (in force 1989) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18 years under Article 326. The 42nd and 44th Amendments relate to the Emergency-era changes and their reversal, and the 73rd Amendment concerns Panchayati Raj.
30.tq: 61st Amendment = 21 to 18 voting age (Art. 326).
xs: The **61st Amendment** (**1987**) lowered the voting age to **18 years** (**Art. 326**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
LS members are elected **directly** on **adult suffrage**, **first past the post**.
xa: **33rd Amendment (1974):** streamlined acceptance of **resignation**.
**84th Amendment (2001):** froze LS seat allocation on the **1971 census** till the first census **after 2026**.
**104th Amendment (2019):** ended **Anglo-Indian** nomination.

30.s:
The qualification for nomination to the Rajya Sabha includes special knowledge or practical experience in which of the following fields?
1. Literature
2. Science
3. Art
4. Social service
5. Sports
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
30.x: Article 80(3) mentions literature, science, art and social service. Sports is not one of the four constitutionally listed fields.
30.tq: Identify the exact constitutional list and exclude the look-alike addition.
xs: RS nominees need special knowledge in **literature, science, art and social service** — so option **(2) 1, 2, 3 and 4 only** is correct.
⚠ **Sport is not a listed field**, though sportspersons have been nominated.
xa: Nominated under **Art. 80(1)(a)** and **80(3)** — **12** members.
Notable: **Lata Mangeshkar** (art); **Sachin Tendulkar** (**2012**), **Mary Kom** (**2016**).
**No nominated member has so far been in the Council of Ministers**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about nominated members of the Rajya Sabha:
1. They can vote in the election of the Vice-President.
2. They can vote in the election of the President.
3. A nominated member may join a political party within six months of taking the seat without being disqualified.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: Statement 1 is correct: nominated members vote in the Vice-Presidential election. Statement 2 is wrong: they cannot vote in the Presidential election. Statement 3 is correct: joining a party within six months is allowed; after that it attracts disqualification under the Tenth Schedule. Hence 1 and 3 only.
30.tq: Nominated members: VP election yes, President election no.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: nominated members **can vote in the Vice-Presidential election**.
Statement 2 is wrong: they **cannot vote in the Presidential election**.
Statement 3 is correct: they may **join a party within 6 months** — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: After **6 months**, joining a party attracts disqualification under the **Tenth Schedule**.
They **take full part in debates**.
No nominated member has so far been in the **Council of Ministers**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements regarding nominated members of the Rajya Sabha:
1. Sachin Tendulkar was nominated in 2012.
2. Mary Kom was nominated in 2016.
3. Lata Mangeshkar was nominated for her contribution to sport.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: Sachin Tendulkar was nominated in 2012 and Mary Kom in 2016. Lata Mangeshkar represented the field of art, not sport.
30.tq: Match notable persons with the correct field and avoid the swapped-domain trap.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: **Sachin Tendulkar (2012)** and **Mary Kom (2016)** were nominated.
Statement 3 is wrong: **Lata Mangeshkar** was nominated for **art** — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: ⚠ Sport is **not a listed field**: **literature, science, art, social service**.
**12** members are nominated by the **President**.
Nominees **cannot vote** in the Presidential election.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about the allocation of Rajya Sabha seats:
1. Seats are allotted to the States under the Fourth Schedule.
2. Like the US Senate, every State gets an equal number of seats.
3. Uttar Pradesh has the highest number of Rajya Sabha seats.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: Statement 1 is correct: seats are allotted under the Fourth Schedule (Arts. 4 and 80(2)). Statement 2 is wrong: seats are allotted by population, unlike the equal representation in the US Senate. Statement 3 is correct: UP has 31 seats, the highest. Hence 1 and 3 only.
30.tq: Rajya Sabha = population-based (Fourth Schedule); US Senate = equal, 2 per State.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: seats are allotted under the **Fourth Schedule** (**Arts. 4 and 80(2)**).
Statement 2 is wrong: allotment is by **population** — states are **not equal**, unlike the US Senate.
Statement 3 is correct: **UP** has the most, **31** — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: Order: **UP 31**, Maharashtra **19**, Tamil Nadu **18**, West Bengal **16**, Bihar **16**.
AP has **11** RS seats (APPSC **2023**).
Single-seat States include **Goa**, **Sikkim**, **Tripura**.

30.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

List-I (State)
A. Andhra Pradesh
B. Telangana
C. Uttarakhand
D. Tripura

List-II (Rajya Sabha seats)
1. 1
2. 3
3. 7
4. 11

option codes:
30.x: Andhra Pradesh has 11 seats, Telangana 7, Uttarakhand 3 and Tripura 1 in the Rajya Sabha.
30.tq: Start from the sure numerical pair and eliminate codes.
xs: **AP – 11**, **Telangana – 7**, **Uttarakhand – 3**, **Tripura – 1** — so option **(1) A-4, B-3, C-2, D-1** is correct.
AP and Telangana split undivided AP's **18** RS seats under the **AP Reorganisation Act, 2014**.
xa: APPSC **2023** asked AP's RS seats → **11**.
AP: **25** Lok Sabha seats, Assembly **175**.
Telangana: **17** LS, **119** Assembly.

30.s: Which one of the following groups consists only of States having one seat each in the Rajya Sabha?
o: Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Manipur and Tripura
30.x: Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura each have one Rajya Sabha seat. The group in option a contains only such States.
30.tq: Check every member of the group against the single-seat condition.
xs: **Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Manipur and Tripura** each have **one** RS seat — so option **(1)** is correct.
Each other group includes a State not on the single-seat list.
xa: Full single-seat list: **Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura** (+ UT **Puducherry**).
⚠ **Tripura** has **1** RS seat but **2** LS seats.
**UP** has the most RS seats: **31**.

30.s: The allocation of seats in the Lok Sabha to the States remains frozen on the basis of the 1971 Census until
o: the completion of the 2031 Census only
30.x: The 84th Amendment Act, 2001 froze the allocation of Lok Sabha seats based on the 1971 Census until the first Census after 2026.
30.tq: Read the endpoint of a constitutional freeze precisely.
xs: The **84th Amendment (2001)** froze LS seat allocation on the **1971 census** till the first census **after 2026** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **87th Amendment** readjusted constituencies on the **2001** census, without changing the allocation.
xa: Debate: raising LS strength by **50% (to ~815)** once the freeze lifts.
The **131st Amendment Bill, 2026** sought an LS max of **850**; it was defeated (**298 for, 230 against**).
Tamil Nadu resolved to freeze the LS at **543**.

30.s: Which one of the following statements regarding delimitation of Lok Sabha constituencies is correct?
o: The allocation and constituencies were both permanently frozen by the 84th Amendment.
The constituencies were readjusted on the basis of the 1971 Census by the Election Commission.
The constituencies were readjusted on the basis of the 2001 Census by the Delimitation Commission under Justice Kuldip Singh.
The constituencies were readjusted on the basis of the 2011 Census by Parliament alone.
30.x: The 87th Amendment enabled readjustment of constituencies on the basis of the 2001 Census. This work was undertaken by the Delimitation Commission under Justice Kuldip Singh.
30.tq: Distinguish freezing seat allocation from readjusting constituency boundaries.
xs: Constituencies were readjusted on the **2001** census (**87th Amendment**) by the **Delimitation Commission** under Justice **Kuldip Singh** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **84th Amendment** froze only the **allocation** on the **1971** census, not permanently and not the constituencies.
xa: ⚠ **Kuldip Singh** = Delimitation Commission; **Kuldip Nayar** = RS domicile case.
Largest LS constituency by electors: **Malkajgiri** (Telangana).
Largest by area: **Ladakh**.

30.s:
Which one of the following is correctly matched with the number of Lok Sabha seats?
1. Andhra Pradesh — 25
2. Telangana — 17
3. Uttarakhand — 5
4. Jammu and Kashmir — 5
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
30.x: All four pairs are correct: Andhra Pradesh has 25, Telangana 17, Uttarakhand 5 and the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir 5 Lok Sabha seats.
30.tq: Verify each numerical pair independently before choosing the coded combination.
xs: All correct: **AP 25**, **Telangana 17**, **Uttarakhand 5**, **J&K 5** — so option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4** is correct.
J&K here is the **UT of Jammu and Kashmir**.
xa: RS seats: AP **11**, Telangana **7**, Uttarakhand **3**, J&K **4**.
Assemblies: AP **175**, Telangana **119**, Uttarakhand **70**, J&K **90**.
**UP** has the most LS seats: **80**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about Lok Sabha seats:
1. Sikkim, Mizoram and Nagaland have one Lok Sabha seat each.
2. Tripura has only one Lok Sabha seat.
3. Ladakh and Lakshadweep have one Lok Sabha seat each.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: Statement 1 is correct: Sikkim, Mizoram and Nagaland are the single-seat States. Statement 2 is wrong: Tripura has 2 Lok Sabha seats (it has one Rajya Sabha seat). Statement 3 is correct: Ladakh and Lakshadweep, like A&N Islands, Chandigarh and Puducherry, have one seat each. Hence 1 and 3 only.
30.tq: Do not mix single Rajya Sabha seat States (Tripura, Goa...) with single Lok Sabha seat States (Sikkim, Mizoram, Nagaland).
xs: Statement 1 is correct: **Sikkim, Mizoram, Nagaland** have **one** LS seat each.
Statement 2 is wrong: **Tripura** has **2** LS seats (but **1** RS seat).
Statement 3 is correct: **Ladakh** and **Lakshadweep** have one each — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: Other single-seat UTs: **A&N Islands**, **Chandigarh**, **Puducherry**.
**Ladakh** is the largest LS constituency by area; **Lakshadweep** the smallest by electors.
Delhi has **7** LS seats.

30.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Largest Lok Sabha constituency by number of electors — Malkajgiri
Largest Lok Sabha constituency by area — Ladakh
Smallest Lok Sabha constituency by area — Mumbai South
Smallest Lok Sabha constituency by number of electors — Lakshadweep
30.x: C is wrong: the smallest Lok Sabha constituency by area is Chandni Chowk (Delhi), not Mumbai South. Malkajgiri is the largest and Lakshadweep the smallest by number of electors, and Ladakh is the largest by area.
30.tq: Separate area-based comparisons from elector-based comparisons.
xs: **Smallest by area – Mumbai South** is wrong; it is **Chandni Chowk** (Delhi) — so option **(3)** is correct.
The rest are right: **Malkajgiri** largest by electors, **Ladakh** largest by area, **Lakshadweep** smallest by electors.
xa: **Malkajgiri** is in **Telangana**.
Delimitation Commission under Justice **Kuldip Singh** (**2001** census).
Delhi has **7** LS seats.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about the term of the Lok Sabha:
1. Under Article 83(2), its five-year term runs from the date of its first meeting.
2. It may be dissolved early by the President on the advice of the Speaker.
3. An early dissolution cannot be challenged in court.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: Statement 1 is correct: the term is reckoned from the first meeting. Statement 2 is wrong: the President dissolves on the Prime Minister's advice, not the Speaker's. Statement 3 is correct: such dissolution cannot be challenged in court. Hence 1 and 3 only.
30.tq: Dissolution = President on PM's advice; term counted from first meeting, not election.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: under **Art 83(2)** the LS term is **5 years** from its **first meeting**.
Statement 2 is wrong: early dissolution is by the President on the **PM's advice**, not the Speaker's.
Statement 3 is correct: it **cannot be challenged in court** — so option **(2) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: **18 Lok Sabhas** constituted so far.
⚠ The **RS** is **never dissolved** (**Art 83(1)**).

30.s:
With reference to the extension of the term of the Lok Sabha during a National Emergency, consider the following statements:
1. Parliament may extend the term by law for one year at a time.
2. The extension may continue indefinitely after the Emergency ends.
3. No extension can continue beyond six months after the Emergency has ceased.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: The term may be extended by law for one year at a time during the Emergency, but not beyond six months after the Emergency ends. Statement 2 is therefore false.
30.tq: Split the options by checking the limiting phrase in the constitutional rule.
xs: Statement 1 is correct: in a National Emergency the term can be extended **by law, 1 year at a time**.
Statement 2 is wrong and statement 3 correct: not beyond **6 months** after the emergency ends — so option **(3) 1 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: The **5th Lok Sabha** (**1971-77**) was extended during the **1975-77** Emergency.
Normal term: **5 years** from the first meeting (**Art 83(2)**).
Only the LS can resolve to **discontinue a National Emergency**.

30.s: Which Lok Sabha was extended during the National Emergency of 1975–1977?
30.x: The Fifth Lok Sabha, constituted for the period 1971–1977, was extended during the 1975–1977 Emergency.
30.tq: Discriminate between closely numbered Lok Sabhas and their distinct events.
xs: The **5th Lok Sabha** (**1971-77**) was extended during the **1975-77** Emergency — so option **(4) Fifth Lok Sabha** is correct.
The **4th** (**1970**) and **6th** (**1979**) were dissolved early, not extended.
xa: Extension is **by law**, **1 year at a time**, not beyond **6 months** after the emergency.
**6th LS (1977)** had the **lowest share** of women MPs.
**18 Lok Sabhas** constituted so far.

30.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Rajya Sabha:
1. It is a permanent and continuing House.
2. It is not subject to dissolution.
3. The whole House is elected together after every six years.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: The Rajya Sabha is permanent and is never dissolved. Its members retire by rotation; the whole House is not elected together.
30.tq: Reject the reversed comparison between the two Houses.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the RS is a **permanent/continuing House**, **not subject to dissolution** (**Art. 83(1)**).
Statement 3 is wrong: about **one-third retire every second year** — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: A member's term is **6 years**, fixed by the **RPA 1951**.
In **1952**, who retired first was decided by **lottery**.
Only the **LS** is dissolved.

30.s: The term of a member of the Rajya Sabha is six years. This term is fixed by the
o: Rules of Procedure of the Rajya Sabha
30.x: The six-year term of a Rajya Sabha member is fixed by the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and not directly by the Constitution.
30.tq: Use the statutory-versus-constitutional distinction to avoid an authority trap.
xs: The RS member's **6-year** term is fixed by the **Representation of the People Act, 1951**, not the Constitution — so option **(3)** is correct.
⚠ A classic trap: the Constitution itself does not fix it.
xa: The RS is **never dissolved**; **one-third retire every second year**.
First RS (**1952**): terms curtailed, retirees chosen by **lottery**.
The LS term (**5 years**) is in **Art 83(2)**.

30.s: In the first Rajya Sabha constituted in 1952, the members who were to retire first were selected by
o: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
30.x: To initiate the one-third retirement cycle, the terms of the initial members were curtailed and the members retiring first were decided by lottery.
30.tq: Use a precise institutional detail rather than a general feature of rotation.
xs: In the **first Rajya Sabha (1952)**, those retiring first were chosen by **lottery** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The President curtailed initial terms to start the **one-third** cycle.
xa: About **one-third retire every second year**.
Member's term: **6 years** (**RPA 1951**).
**Art. 83(1):** RS is **not subject to dissolution**.

30.s:
With reference to the qualifications for membership of Parliament, consider the following statements:
1. The minimum age for membership of the Lok Sabha is 25 years.
2. The minimum age for membership of the Rajya Sabha is 30 years.
3. The Constitution prescribes a minimum educational qualification for membership of either House.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: The minimum ages are 25 years for the Lok Sabha and 30 years for the Rajya Sabha. No minimum educational qualification is prescribed for membership of Parliament.
30.tq: Use the comparison between the two Houses and identify the swapped qualification requirement.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: minimum age **25 years** (LS) and **30 years** (RS) (**Art 84**).
Statement 3 is wrong: there is **no minimum educational qualification** — so option **(1) 1 and 2 only** is correct.
xa: Both need **citizenship** and an oath before an **EC-authorised person**.
Candidates must be **electors** in a parliamentary constituency (**RPA 1951**).
RS **domicile** requirement was **removed in 2003**.

30.s: The oath or affirmation required before a person takes his or her seat in Parliament is made before
o: The Election Commission or a person authorised by it
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha only
The President or a person authorised by him
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha only
30.x: A prospective Member of Parliament makes the prescribed oath or affirmation before the Election Commission or a person authorised by it, in the form given in the Third Schedule.
30.tq: Discriminate between the authority administering the oath and the authority deciding disqualification.
xs: The oath is made before the **Election Commission** or an **EC-authorised person** (**Third Schedule** form) — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is not before the President, Speaker or Chairman.
xa: This applies to candidates for **both Houses**.
Minimum age: **25** (LS), **30** (RS).
No **minimum educational qualification**.

30.s: Which of the following statements regarding electoral qualifications for Parliament is correct?
o: The Constitution requires residence in the concerned State for every Rajya Sabha candidate.
Only a person domiciled in the concerned State can contest a Rajya Sabha election.
A person contesting a reserved Lok Sabha seat need not be an elector.
A person must be a registered elector in a parliamentary constituency to contest a parliamentary election.
30.x: A candidate for Parliament must be a registered elector in a parliamentary constituency. The domicile requirement for Rajya Sabha candidates was removed in 2003, and a candidate for a reserved Lok Sabha seat must belong to the relevant Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe.
30.tq: Separate the continuing elector requirement from the abolished domicile requirement.
xs: A candidate must be a **registered elector** in a parliamentary constituency (**RPA 1951**) — so option **(4)** is correct.
RS **domicile** was **removed in 2003** (upheld in **Kuldip Nayar, 2006**), and a reserved LS seat needs an **SC/ST** candidate who is an elector.
xa: Minimum age: **25** (LS) and **30** (RS).
Must **not hold an office of profit**.
**No minimum educational qualification**.
