30.s: Which one of the following is NOT a ground of disqualification under Article 102 of the Constitution?
o: Being declared of unsound mind by a competent court
Holding an office of profit under the Union or a State, subject to exemptions by law
30.x: Article 102 includes office of profit, unsoundness of mind declared by a court, undischarged insolvency, loss or absence of Indian citizenship and disqualification under a parliamentary law. Lack of a university degree is not a ground of disqualification.
30.tq: Identify the option that is outside the constitutional list of disqualifications.
xs: **Lacking a university degree** is not an Art. 102 ground — there is **no minimum educational qualification** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Art. 102 grounds include **office of profit**, **unsound mind** declared by a court, **undischarged insolvent**.
xa: Other grounds: **not a citizen**, disqualified by a law of Parliament (**RPA 1951**), **defection**.
**Art. 103:** the **President** decides, on the **EC's opinion**.
Parliament can **exempt** offices of profit by law.

30.s: Parliament may exempt a particular office from the disqualification relating to office of profit by
o: A notification issued by the President alone
A direction of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha
An order of the Election Commission
30.x: Parliament can exempt specified offices from the office-of-profit disqualification by enacting a law.
30.tq: Ask which authority has legislative power rather than merely administrative power.
xs: Parliament exempts offices from office-of-profit disqualification **by law** — so option **(3)** is correct.
No presidential notification, Speaker's direction or EC order can do it.
xa: Office of profit under the **Union/a state** is an **Art. 102** ground.
**Art. 103:** disqualification questions → **President**, on **EC's opinion**.
Defection questions → **Speaker / Chairman**.

30.s: A question arises regarding the disqualification of a sitting Member of Parliament under Article 102, other than disqualification under the Tenth Schedule. The constitutional procedure is that the decision is made by the
o: Election Commission, after obtaining the opinion of the President
President, after obtaining and acting according to the opinion of the Election Commission
Speaker or Chairman, without reference to any other authority
Supreme Court, on a reference made by the Prime Minister
30.x: Under Article 103, the President decides the question after obtaining the opinion of the Election Commission and acts in accordance with that opinion.
30.tq: Use the ‘who decides?’ method and distinguish Article 103 from Tenth Schedule proceedings.
xs: Under **Art. 103**, the **President** decides after obtaining and acting on the **Election Commission's opinion** — so option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ The **Speaker/Chairman** decides only **defection** (Tenth Schedule) cases.
xa: **Art. 102** grounds: office of profit, unsound mind, insolvency, non-citizenship, RPA **1951**.
Tenth Schedule decisions are subject to **judicial review** (**Kihoto Hollohan, 1992**).
Parliament can **exempt** offices of profit by law.

30.s:
With reference to disqualification on the ground of defection, consider the following statements:
1. A Member of the Lok Sabha who voluntarily gives up membership of the political party is liable to disqualification.
2. An independent member joining a political party after election is liable to disqualification.
3. A nominated member joining a political party after six months from taking his seat is liable to disqualification.
4. The President decides every question of disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 correctly state grounds under the Tenth Schedule. Statement 4 is false: the Speaker of the Lok Sabha or the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha decides such questions, subject to judicial review.
30.tq: Separate Article 103 disqualification from defection decided under the Tenth Schedule.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: **voluntarily giving up** party membership, an **independent joining a party**, a **nominated member joining after 6 months**.
Statement 4 is wrong: defection is decided by the **Speaker** (LS) / **Chairman** (RS), not the President — so option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: Voting/abstaining against the whip, unless condoned within **15 days**, is another ground.
Subject to **judicial review** — **Kihoto Hollohan (1992)**.
⚠ **Art. 102** grounds → **President** (on EC opinion).

30.s: A Member of Parliament votes contrary to the direction of the political party without prior permission, but the party condones the action within the prescribed period. In this situation, disqualification on the ground of defection does not arise because the action was condoned within
30.x: A vote or abstention contrary to the party whip may attract disqualification unless the action is permitted or condoned by the party within 15 days.
30.tq: Test the precise statutory time limit rather than the general principle of defection.
xs: Disqualification does not arise if the party condones the vote within **15 days** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The ground is **voting/abstaining against the whip without permission**.
xa: Other grounds: **voluntarily giving up** party membership; **independent joining a party**.
A **nominated member** joining a party after **6 months** is disqualified.
Decided by the **Speaker / Chairman**.

30.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Kihoto Hollohan — Judicial review of decisions under the Tenth Schedule
Kuldip Nayar — Introduction of the Tenth Schedule
Thirty-third Amendment — Removal of the office-of-profit disqualification
Article 103 — Decision on defection by the President
30.x: Kihoto Hollohan (1992) recognised that decisions under the Tenth Schedule are subject to judicial review. Kuldip Nayar concerned the Rajya Sabha domicile requirement, the Thirty-third Amendment dealt with resignation procedure, and Article 103 does not govern defection.
30.tq: Match each case or provision with its actual constitutional subject.
xs: **Kihoto Hollohan (1992)** held Tenth Schedule decisions subject to **judicial review** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Kuldip Nayar (2006)** was on RS **domicile** and **open ballot**; the **33rd Amendment** was on **resignation**; **Art. 103** covers Art. 102 grounds, not defection.
xa: **Sita Soren (2024):** privilege does **not** protect an MP taking a **bribe**.
Sita Soren overruled **P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998)**.
Defection is decided by the **Speaker / Chairman**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about vacation of seats under Article 101:
1. If a person elected to both Houses does not intimate the choice within 10 days, the Lok Sabha seat falls vacant.
2. If a sitting member of one House is elected to the other House, the seat in the first House falls vacant.
3. If a person elected to two seats in the same House does not choose one, both seats fall vacant.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: Statement 1 is wrong: in that case the Rajya Sabha seat falls vacant. Statement 2 is correct: the first House's seat falls vacant. Statement 3 is correct: both seats fall vacant. Hence 2 and 3 only; options with 1 are wrong and '3 only' misses statement 2.
30.tq: Elected to both Houses and silent for 10 days: lose the Rajya Sabha seat.
xs: Statement 1 is wrong: if no choice is made within **10 days**, the **Rajya Sabha** seat falls vacant.
Statement 2 is correct: the seat in the **first House** falls vacant.
Statement 3 is correct: **both** seats fall vacant — so option **(2) 2 and 3 only** is correct.
xa: Parliament + state legislature: resign the state seat within **14 days**, else the **Parliament** seat goes.
Absence for **60 days** without permission → House may declare the seat vacant.
⚠ **10 days** = both Houses; **14 days** = Parliament + state; **60 days** = absence.

30.s: A person is simultaneously elected to Parliament and a State Legislature. Which one of the following is correct?
o: The Parliament seat must be resigned within 10 days, failing which the State seat falls vacant.
The State Legislature seat must be resigned within 14 days, failing which the Parliament seat falls vacant.
The person may retain both seats for the entire term.
Both seats become vacant immediately on election.
30.x: Under the Prohibition of Simultaneous Membership Rules, 1950, the State Legislature seat must be resigned within 14 days; otherwise the seat in Parliament becomes vacant.
30.tq: Use the direction of the consequence and the 14-day time limit to eliminate reversals.
xs: The MP must resign the **State seat** within **14 days**, else the **Parliament** seat falls vacant — so option **(2)** is correct.
This is under the **Prohibition of Simultaneous Membership Rules, 1950**.
xa: ⚠ **10 days** applies to election to **both Houses** of Parliament.
Resignation is **subject to acceptance** (**Art 101(3)(b)**).
The **33rd Amendment (1974)** lets a resignation be rejected if **not voluntary or genuine**.

30.s:
With reference to resignation and absence of Members of Parliament, consider the following statements:
1. A resignation must be made in writing to the Speaker or the Chairman, as the case may be.
2. The resignation may be rejected if the presiding officer is satisfied that it is not voluntary or genuine.
3. A House may declare a seat vacant when a member is absent without permission for 60 days.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: All three statements are correct. Resignation is addressed to the Speaker or Chairman, may be rejected when it is not voluntary or genuine, and absence without permission for 60 days can lead the House to declare the seat vacant.
30.tq: Combine the written-resignation rule with the separate 60-day absence rule.
xs: All three statements, **1, 2 and 3**, are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: resignation is **in writing to the Speaker/Chairman**.
Statement 2: it is **subject to acceptance** (**Art 101(3)(b)**) and may be **rejected if not voluntary or genuine**.
Statement 3: **absence for 60 days** without permission → the House may declare the seat vacant.
xa: ⚠ **10 days** = elected to both Houses; **14 days** = Parliament + state legislature; **60 days** = absence.
Elected to both Houses and no choice in **10 days** → the **Rajya Sabha** seat falls vacant.

30.s: The provision that the Speaker or Chairman may refuse to accept a member's resignation if satisfied that it is not voluntary or genuine was introduced by the
30.x: The 33rd Amendment Act, 1974 amended Article 101(3)(b) so that a resignation takes effect only on acceptance, and the presiding officer may reject it if it is not voluntary or genuine. The 24th Amendment concerned Parliament's amending power, the 42nd was the 'mini-Constitution' of the Emergency, and the 52nd added the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection).
30.tq: 33rd Amendment (1974) = resignation must be voluntary and genuine; 52nd (1985) = anti-defection.
xs: The **33rd Amendment Act, 1974** streamlined acceptance of resignation — it **may be rejected if not voluntary or genuine** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Resignation is **subject to acceptance** under **Art 101(3)(b)**, unlike judges or the President.
xa: **61st Amendment (1987)**: voting age **18 years**.
**84th Amendment (2001)**: froze LS seat allocation on the **1971 census**.

30.s: Which one of the following statements regarding women’s representation in Parliament is correct?
o: Women constitute less than 5 per cent in both Houses of Parliament.
Women constitute about 15 per cent in the Lok Sabha and about 14 per cent in the Rajya Sabha.
Women constitute more than one-third in both Houses of Parliament.
Women constitute about 14 per cent in the Lok Sabha and about 15 per cent in the Rajya Sabha.
30.x: Women’s representation is approximately 15 per cent in the Lok Sabha and 14 per cent in the Rajya Sabha. These figures are separate from the future constitutional reservation of one-third seats.
30.tq: Compare the two Houses carefully instead of transferring the percentage from one House to the other.
xs: Women are **about 15% in the LS** and **about 14% in the RS** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option (4) reverses the two; neither House is below 5% or above one-third.
xa: The **Union CoM** has **11 women**.
The **106th Amendment, 2023** reserves **33%** of LS and Assembly seats for women.

30.s: In which Lok Sabha did women members cross 10 per cent of the total membership for the first time?
30.x: Women members crossed 10 per cent of the total strength of the House for the first time in the 15th Lok Sabha, elected in 2009.
30.tq: Link the threshold event with the correct Lok Sabha number and election period.
xs: Women crossed **10%** for the first time in the **15th Lok Sabha** (**2009**) — so option **(1)** is correct.
xa: This was an **APPSC-G2 2023** key.
⚠ FIRST above 10% = **15th**; highest = **17th** (**78**); lowest share = **6th** (**1977**).

30.s:
Consider the following statements about women's reservation in legislatures:
1. The one-third reservation under the 106th Amendment becomes operative only after the next Census and the delimitation that follows it.
2. The first Women's Reservation Bill was introduced in 2010 and passed by the Rajya Sabha in 2023.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: Statement 2 is wrong: the first Bill came in 1996 and was passed by the Rajya Sabha in 2010; the 106th Amendment itself was enacted in 2023. Statement 1 is correct: the reservation operates only after the next Census and delimitation. So '1 only'.
30.tq: 1996 Bill -> RS passed 2010 -> 106th Amendment 2023 -> operative after Census + delimitation.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(2)** **1 only**.
1: the **106th Amendment, 2023** reservation is **operative only after the next Census and delimitation**.
2 is wrong: the first Women's Reservation Bill came in **1996** and passed the **Rajya Sabha** in **2010**.
xa: It reserves **33%** (one-third) of seats in the Lok Sabha and state Assemblies (**Art. 334A**).
The reservation lasts **15 years**, extendable.
It is called the **Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about the reservation of seats for women under the 106th Constitutional Amendment:
1. It applies to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies.
2. It is provided under Article 334A.
3. It is initially intended to operate for fifteen years and may be extended.
4. It reserves one-half of the seats in the concerned legislatures.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The reservation is for one-third of the seats, not one-half, and Article 334A governs its operation.
30.tq: Find the changed proportion while retaining the correct Article, institutions and duration.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statements 1 and 2: it covers the **Lok Sabha and state Assemblies**, under **Art. 334A**.
Statement 3: for **15 years**, extendable.
Statement 4 wrong: it reserves **one-third** (**33%**), not one-half.
xa: It is the **106th Amendment, 2023** (**Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam**).
Operative only **after the next Census and delimitation**.

30.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: 15th Lok Sabha — 2009 — Women crossed 10 per cent for the first time
30.x: The 106th Constitutional Amendment providing one-third reservation for women was enacted in 2023, not 2010. The other three pairs are correctly matched.
30.tq: Check the year attached to the constitutional amendment against the years of the Lok Sabha milestones.
xs: **106th Amendment — 2010** is wrongly matched — option **(1)**; the 106th Amendment is of **2023**.
**2010** is when a Women's Reservation Bill **passed the Rajya Sabha**.
xa: The first Bill was introduced in **1996**.
The **106th Amendment** inserted **Art. 334A**.

30.s: Which one of the following is the normal pattern of parliamentary sessions in India?
o: Winter, Spring and Special sessions only
30.x: There is no fixed constitutional calendar, but Parliament normally has Budget, Monsoon and Winter sessions.
30.tq: Choose the established institutional terminology rather than an invented seasonal sequence.
xs: Parliament normally holds **three sessions** — **Budget, Monsoon and Winter** — so option **(4)** is correct.
There is **no fixed calendar** in the Constitution.
xa: **Art. 85** sets **no minimum number of sitting days**.
Monsoon Session **2026** ran from **20 July** and was adjourned sine die on **13 Aug**.

30.s: Who orders an adjournment sine die of a House of Parliament?
o: The Speaker or Chairman of the concerned House
The Prime Minister after consulting the Cabinet
The President in respect of both Houses
30.x: An adjournment sine die is ordered by the Speaker in the Lok Sabha or the Chairman in the Rajya Sabha, without fixing a date for the next sitting.
30.tq: Use the office-and-function matching method for parliamentary terminology.
xs: **Adjournment sine die** is ordered by the **Speaker or Chairman** of the House — so option **(1)** is correct.
It ends the sitting **without fixing a date** for the next; then the **President prorogues**.
xa: **Prorogation** (by the President) ends the **session**.
**Dissolution** ends the life of the **Lok Sabha** only.

30.s:
Arrange the following events in the correct procedural sequence after the conclusion of the business of a sitting:
A. Prorogation by the President
B. Adjournment sine die by the Speaker or Chairman
C. Reassembly in a new session
D. Recess

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
30.x: Normally, the Speaker or Chairman first adjourns the House sine die; the President then prorogues it, followed by a recess and later reassembly in a new session.
30.tq: Use the first-and-last method and distinguish a sitting, session and recess.
xs: The sequence is **B, A, D, C** — option **(1)**.
**Adjournment sine die** (Speaker/Chairman) → **prorogation** (President) → **recess** → **reassembly in a new session**.
xa: **Recess** = period between **prorogation and reassembly in a new session**.
**Adjournment** only suspends a sitting for a specified time.

30.s: Why is the constitutional requirement that two sessions of Parliament should not have a gap of more than six months significant?
o: It ensures continuing legislative activity and accountability of the government
It makes a fixed number of sitting days compulsory each year
It prescribes a minimum of six months of parliamentary sitting every year
It permits the Rajya Sabha to dissolve the Lok Sabha after six months
30.x: The six-month limit prevents an excessively long interruption and helps maintain legislative business and executive accountability. It does not prescribe a minimum number of sitting days.
30.tq: Distinguish a maximum interval between sessions from a minimum number of sitting days.
xs: The six-month rule keeps the government **accountable** and **legislative business moving** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Art. 85** sets **no minimum number of sitting days** and gives the RS no power to dissolve the LS.
xa: This was an **APPSC-GS 2025** question.
There is **no fixed calendar**; normally **three sessions**.

30.s: Rules of procedure and conduct of business in Parliament are dealt with under:
30.x: Article 118 empowers each House to make rules for regulating its procedure and conduct of business.
30.tq: Link the procedural subject directly to Article 118 and distinguish it from quorum and language provisions.
xs: Rules of procedure are under **Article 118** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Art. 100** = quorum; **Art. 120** = language.
xa: **Art. 86**: President's right to address / send messages.
**Art. 98**: separate secretariats for each House.

30.s:
With reference to the language used in Parliament, consider the following statements:
1. The business of Parliament may be transacted in Hindi or English.
2. A member may address the House in his or her mother tongue with the permission of the presiding officer.
3. The Constitution permits parliamentary proceedings only in English.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: Article 120 recognises Hindi and English for parliamentary business and permits the use of a member's mother tongue with the presiding officer's permission. Proceedings are not restricted exclusively to English.
30.tq: Identify the correct language alternatives and reject the exclusive-language trap.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: business is in **Hindi or English** (**Art. 120**).
Statement 2 correct: a **mother tongue** may be used with the **presiding officer's permission**.
Statement 3 wrong: proceedings are not limited to English.
xa: Quorum: **one-tenth** (**Art. 100**).
Rules of procedure: **Art. 118**.

30.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the administrative control over the secretariats of Parliament?
o: The Lok Sabha Secretariat functions under the Speaker and the Rajya Sabha Secretariat under the Chairman
The Lok Sabha Secretariat functions under the President and the Rajya Sabha Secretariat under the Prime Minister
Both Secretariats function directly under the Union Cabinet
Both Secretariats function under the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs
30.x: The parliamentary Secretariats are independent of the executive. The Lok Sabha Secretariat is under the Speaker, while the Rajya Sabha Secretariat is under the Chairman.
30.tq: Use the House-wise authority comparison to avoid the wrong-ministry and wrong-authority traps.
xs: The **Lok Sabha Secretariat** is under the **Speaker** and the **Rajya Sabha Secretariat** under the **Chairman** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The Secretariats are **independent of the executive** — not under the President, PM, Cabinet or a ministry.
xa: **Art. 98** provides separate secretarial staff for each House.
The **VP** is ex officio Chairman of the RS.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about the legislative function of Parliament:
1. Parliament makes laws on the Union List and the Concurrent List.
2. An existing law made by Parliament can be changed by a State Legislature.
3. Delegated legislation is subject to review by Parliament.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: Statement 1 is correct: Parliament legislates on the Union and Concurrent Lists (and the State List in special cases). Statement 2 is wrong: only Parliament can change an existing law it made (APPSC-GS 2024). Statement 3 is correct: Parliament reviews delegated legislation. Hence 1 and 3 only.
30.tq: Only the body that made the law can change it.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: Parliament legislates on the **Union and Concurrent Lists** (and the State List in special cases).
Statement 2 wrong: **only Parliament can change an existing law** (**APPSC-GS 2024**).
Statement 3 correct: **delegated legislation is reviewed** by Parliament.
xa: **Art. 249**: RS resolution lets Parliament legislate on a **State List** subject.
**Art. 253**: laws to implement **international treaties** on any subject.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about the functions of Parliament:
1. Questions and motions are means of parliamentary control over the executive.
2. A no-confidence motion can be moved in either House.
3. No tax can be imposed without the approval of the Lok Sabha.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: Statement 1 is correct: questions and motions are tools of executive control. Statement 2 is wrong: a no-confidence motion lies only in the Lok Sabha. Statement 3 is correct: no tax without Lok Sabha approval. Hence 1 and 3 only.
30.tq: No-confidence motion = Lok Sabha only.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **questions and motions** are tools of executive control.
Statement 2 wrong: the **no-confidence motion** lies **only in the LS**.
Statement 3 correct: **no tax without LS approval**.
xa: Ministers are **collectively responsible** to the Lok Sabha.
The **RS cannot remove the Council of Ministers**.

30.s:
Which of the following functions belongs to the judicial functions of Parliament?
1. Impeachment of the President
2. Removal of the Vice-President
3. Recommending removal of certain constitutional authorities and judges
4. Punishing breach of privilege
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
30.x: The listed functions are included among the judicial or quasi-judicial functions of Parliament, though their procedures differ according to the office concerned.
30.tq: Treat the list as a classification question and check whether each item is a parliamentary adjudicatory function.
xs: All four, **1, 2, 3 and 4**, are judicial functions — option **(4)**.
Parliament **impeaches the President**, **removes the VP**, **recommends removal of judges, CEC, CAG**, and **punishes breach of privilege**.
xa: **Constituent** function: amends the Constitution under **Art. 368**, but cannot alter the **basic structure**.
**Electoral** function: elects the VP and presiding officers.

30.s: Which one of the following is NOT an electoral function of Parliament?
o: Participating in the election of the President
Electing the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha
30.x: A is the answer: Parliament's electoral functions are electing the Vice-President, taking part in the President's election and electing its presiding officers (the Lok Sabha elects the Speaker and Deputy Speaker). The Chief Election Commissioner is appointed by the President, not elected by Parliament, so A is not an electoral function.
30.tq: Find the item that is an appointment function rather than an electoral function of Parliament.
xs: **Appointing the Chief Election Commissioner** is NOT an electoral function of Parliament — so option **(1)** is correct.
Electoral functions: **elects the VP**, **takes part in the President's election**, **elects presiding officers** (Speaker and Deputy Speaker).
Parliament only **recommends removal** of the **CEC** — a judicial function.
xa: The **Rajya Sabha** elects only the **Deputy Chairman** (VP is ex officio Chairman).
Election laws: **RPA 1950 and 1951**; **Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952**.

30.s:
With regard to freedom of speech in Parliament, consider the following statements:
1. Article 105 protects freedom of speech in Parliament.
2. No court proceedings can be instituted against a member for anything said or any vote given in the House or its committees.
3. This immunity applies to every statement made by a member outside Parliament.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: Article 105 protects speech and votes in Parliament and its committees. It does not provide the same parliamentary immunity for statements made outside Parliament.
30.tq: Reject the overbroad extension of a privilege beyond its constitutional setting.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statements 1 and 2: **Art. 105** gives **freedom of speech** in Parliament; **no court proceedings** for anything said or any vote given in the House or its committees.
Statement 3 wrong: the immunity covers the **House or its committees**, not statements outside.
xa: **Sita Soren (2024)**: no privilege for a **bribe**.
Privileges still rest on **Art. 105(3)**.

30.s: A Member of Parliament enjoys freedom from arrest in civil cases during which period?
o: Forty days before and after a session and during the session
Only on the day of voting in the House
The entire term of the Parliament, without exception
Only during the recess between two sessions
30.x: The privilege covers civil arrest during the session and for forty days before and forty days after the session. It does not cover criminal or preventive detention.
30.tq: Test the exact time period and the civil-case limitation together.
xs: Freedom from arrest in **civil** cases applies **40 days before and after a session and during it** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It does **not** apply in **criminal or preventive detention** cases.
xa: Members are also exempt from **jury service**.
Privileges are **co-terminous with membership**.

30.s: Which one of the following is NOT an individual parliamentary privilege of a member?
o: Freedom from arrest in civil cases during the prescribed period
Freedom of speech in the House
Power to prohibit publication of the House's proceedings
30.x: The power to publish or prohibit publication of the House's reports and proceedings is a collective privilege of the House, not an individual privilege.
30.tq: Find the option that belongs to the opposite classification.
xs: **Power to prohibit publication of the House's proceedings** is a **collective** privilege, not individual — so option **(4)** is correct.
Individual privileges: **freedom of speech**, freedom from arrest in **civil** cases, exemption from **jury service**.
xa: Other collective privileges: **exclude strangers**, hold **secret sittings**, punish for **contempt**.
⚠ "Only individual privileges exist" is **wrong** (**APPSC-G2 2017**).

30.s: Under Article 122 of the Constitution, courts cannot inquire into parliamentary proceedings on the ground of
o: The absence of a parliamentary session
30.x: Article 122 bars courts from questioning parliamentary proceedings on the ground of alleged procedural irregularity.
30.tq: Match the constitutional Article with its precise limitation on judicial inquiry.
xs: Under **Art. 122**, courts cannot question House proceedings on the ground of **procedural irregularity** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The notes list **"Courts cannot inquire into its proceedings — Art. 122"** among the **collective** privileges.
xa: The House may also make its **own rules** and punish **breach of privilege**.
No arrest within the precincts without the **Presiding Officer's permission**.

30.s: Which of the following statements correctly describes the present position regarding codification of parliamentary privileges in India?
o: All privileges have been exhaustively codified in a single statute.
Privileges are derived exclusively from judicial decisions.
Only individual privileges are codified under Article 122.
Parliamentary privileges are not codified, but continue under Article 105(3).
30.x: Parliamentary privileges have not been comprehensively codified. They continue under Article 105(3), with their historical basis in the privileges of the British House of Commons.
30.tq: Distinguish an uncodified constitutional position from a supposedly exhaustive statute.
xs: Privileges are **not codified** and still rest on **Article 105(3)** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They were originally the **British House of Commons'** privileges.
xa: Codification is urged to protect **press freedom** and **citizens' rights**.
**Art. 122** bars courts from inquiring into proceedings; it codifies nothing.

30.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Sita Soren case of 2024:
1. A seven-judge Bench held that parliamentary privilege does not protect a legislator who takes a bribe to vote or speak.
2. The decision overruled the protection recognised in P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998) in this context.
3. The decision held that every speech made by a legislator outside the House is protected by Article 105.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: The seven-judge Bench in Sita Soren (2024) held that privilege does not protect bribery for voting or speaking and overruled the contrary position in P.V. Narasimha Rao. Statement 3 is false.
30.tq: Use a recent judicial decision while rejecting an overbroad claim about immunity.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Sita Soren (2024)**, a **seven-judge Bench**: no privilege for an MP/MLA taking a **bribe** to vote or speak.
Statement 2 correct: it **overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998)**.
Statement 3 wrong: **Art. 105** covers what is said in the **House or its committees**.
xa: **Kihoto Hollohan (1992)**: Tenth Schedule decisions subject to judicial review.
**Kuldip Nayar (2006)**: upheld **open ballot** in RS elections.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about parliamentary privileges:
1. No arrest or legal process can take place within the precincts of a House without the Presiding Officer's permission.
2. The right to be informed of a member's arrest, detention or release is an individual privilege of that member.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: Statement 1 is correct: legal process within the precincts needs the Presiding Officer's permission. Statement 2 is wrong: being informed of a member's arrest, detention or release is a collective privilege of the House. Hence 1 only.
30.tq: Anything the House as a body receives or controls (information, publication, secret sittings, punishment) is collective.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)** (1 only).
Statement 1 correct: **no arrest or legal process within precincts** without the **Presiding Officer's permission**.
Statement 2 wrong: being **informed of a member's arrest** is a **collective** privilege of the House.
xa: Individual privilege: freedom from **civil** arrest **40 days** before and after a session.
Both collective and individual privileges exist.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about parliamentary privileges:
1. They are co-terminous with membership of the legislature.
2. They also extend to ministers, the Attorney-General and others who speak in the House.
3. Only individual members enjoy privileges; the House as a whole has none.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: Statement 1 is correct: privileges last as long as membership. Statement 2 is correct: they extend to ministers, the Attorney-General and others who speak in the House. Statement 3 is wrong (the APPSC-G2 2017 trap): the House has collective privileges as well. Hence 1 and 2 only.
30.tq: Both collective and individual privileges exist; 'only members, not the House' is always false.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: privileges are **co-terminous with membership**.
Statement 2 correct: they **extend to ministers, the Attorney-General** and others who speak in the House.
Statement 3 wrong: the **APPSC-G2 2017** trap — the House has **collective** privileges too.
xa: Privileges rest on **Art. 105(3)**, not codified.
Individual: **freedom of speech**, **jury service** exemption.

30.s: Which one of the following matters is within the equal powers of the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha?
o: Initiation of a no-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers
Consideration of the report of the Comptroller and Auditor-General
30.x: Both Houses have equal powers in considering the reports of the CAG, UPSC and Finance Commission. The other matters are associated with the superiority of the Lok Sabha.
30.tq: Distinguish an equal parliamentary function from a power exclusively associated with the Lok Sabha.
xs: **Consideration of the CAG's report** is an equal power of both Houses — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Demands for grants** — RS cannot vote; **no-confidence motion** — LS only; **Money Bill certification** — the **Speaker**.
xa: **APPSC G1 2024**: equal status = **CAG's report** + approval of Emergency.
Also equal: **UPSC** and **Finance Commission** reports.

30.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Demands for grants — Rajya Sabha may vote on them
Money Bill — Rajya Sabha to return it within fourteen days
Joint sitting — Presided over by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha
30.x: The Rajya Sabha may discuss the Budget but cannot vote on demands for grants. A Money Bill is returned within fourteen days, a joint sitting is presided over by the Lok Sabha Speaker, and a no-confidence motion is moved in the Lok Sabha.
30.tq: Find the option that reverses the financial or accountability superiority of the Lok Sabha.
xs: **Demands for grants — RS may vote on them** is wrongly matched — option **(1)**.
The RS may **discuss the budget** but **cannot vote on demands for grants**.
Correct pairs: Money Bill returned in **14 days**; **joint sitting** presided by the **Speaker**; **no-confidence motion** in the LS.
xa: The **Speaker** decides what is a **Money Bill**.
At a **joint sitting**, LS numbers prevail.

30.s:
Which of the following matters can be dealt with by both Houses of Parliament on an equal footing?
1. Removal of a Judge of the Supreme Court or High Court
2. Approval of an Ordinance promulgated by the President
3. Approval of proclamations of Emergency
4. Passing a resolution to discontinue a National Emergency
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
30.x: The Houses have equal powers in the removal of higher judicial officers, approval of Ordinances and approval of Emergency proclamations. Only the Lok Sabha can pass a resolution to discontinue a National Emergency.
30.tq: Identify the single Lok Sabha-only power among otherwise equal constitutional functions.
xs: Items **1, 2 and 3** are equal powers — option **(2)**.
Equal: **removal of SC/HC judges**, **approval of ordinances** and **Emergency proclamations**.
Item 4 wrong: **only LS** can resolve to **discontinue a National Emergency**.
xa: **No-confidence motion** — only in the LS.
Also equal: **constitutional amendment bills** — special majority in each House, no joint sitting.

30.s: With reference to a Financial Bill of category I, which one of the following is correct?
o: It can be introduced only in the Rajya Sabha and passed by a simple majority there.
It can be introduced in either House, but the Rajya Sabha has no power to amend it.
It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, but both Houses have equal powers regarding its passage.
It can be introduced only after certification by the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
30.x: A Financial Bill of category I can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha. Unlike a Money Bill, both Houses have equal powers in its passage.
30.tq: Discriminate between a Financial Bill of category I and a Money Bill by comparing introduction and passage.
xs: A **Financial Bill (I)** is introduced **only in the LS**, but **both Houses have equal powers** on its passage — so option **(3)** is correct.
Unlike a **Money Bill**, which the RS cannot amend or reject.
xa: A Money Bill must be returned by the RS within **14 days**.
The President may return **Financial Bills (I) and (II)** for reconsideration.

30.s: If the two Houses of Parliament disagree on a constitutional amendment bill, which one of the following is the consequence?
o: The bill fails because no joint sitting is permitted for such a bill.
The Lok Sabha may pass the bill by a simple majority in a second sitting.
The Supreme Court decides which version of the bill shall prevail.
The President convenes a joint sitting under Article 108.
30.x: There is no provision for a joint sitting in respect of a constitutional amendment bill. Failure to secure the required approval in either House causes the bill to fall.
30.tq: Ask whether the ordinary deadlock mechanism applies; Article 108 does not apply here.
xs: For a **constitutional amendment bill** there is **no joint sitting**, so the bill fails — option **(1)**.
It needs a **special majority in each House**.
xa: ⚠ A **joint sitting** is presided by the **Speaker**; LS numbers prevail.
Amendments are made under **Art. 368**.

30.s: Which one of the following statements regarding a National Emergency is correct when the Lok Sabha is dissolved?
o: It automatically lapses immediately upon dissolution of the Lok Sabha.
Approval by the Rajya Sabha alone can sustain it permanently.
If approved by the Rajya Sabha, the newly constituted Lok Sabha must approve it within thirty days of its first sitting.
It can continue only after approval by all State Legislatures.
30.x: When the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the Rajya Sabha may approve the Emergency proclamation for the time being. The new Lok Sabha must approve it within thirty days of its first sitting.
30.tq: Apply the special continuity rule for an Emergency during dissolution of the Lok Sabha.
xs: If the RS approves the proclamation, the **new Lok Sabha must approve it within 30 days of its first sitting** — so option **(3)** is correct.
With the LS dissolved, the proclamation **stays alive if the Rajya Sabha approves** it — **for the time being**, not permanently.
xa: This covers Emergencies under **Arts. 352, 356, 360**.
RS special powers: **Art. 249**, **Art. 312**, **Art. 67(b)**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 3:
1. A Bill for formation of a new State or alteration of the area, boundaries or name of an existing State requires the recommendation of the President.
2. The views of the concerned State Legislature are binding on Parliament.
3. Article 3 deals with the formation and alteration of States.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The concerned State Legislature is asked for its views, but those views are not binding on Parliament.
30.tq: Detect the subtle reversal between seeking a State Legislature’s views and being bound by them.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: an **Art. 3** bill needs the **President's recommendation**.
Statement 2 wrong: the **state's views are not binding**.
Statement 3 correct: **Art. 3** deals with forming new states and altering areas, boundaries and names.
xa: **Andhra State (1953)** and the **AP Reorganisation Act, 2014** were both made under **Art. 3**.
**Art. 253**: law to implement **international treaties** on any subject.

30.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Under Article 249, the Rajya Sabha authorises Parliament, and not State Legislatures, to legislate on a State List subject.
2. Under Article 312, the Rajya Sabha can authorise the creation of new All-India Services.
3. Under Article 67(b), the removal of the Vice-President can be initiated only in the Rajya Sabha.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: All three statements are correct. Articles 249, 312 and 67(b) respectively deal with State List legislation in the national interest, creation of All-India Services and initiation of the Vice-President’s removal.
30.tq: Use article-wise pairing to distinguish the three special powers of the Rajya Sabha.
xs: All three statements, **1, 2 and 3**, are correct — option **(4)**.
**Art. 249**: RS authorises **Parliament** (not State Assemblies) to legislate on a **State List** subject.
**Art. 312**: new **All-India Services**; **Art. 67(b)**: VP's removal initiated **only in the Rajya Sabha**.
xa: ⚠ **APPSC-G1 2017** trap: RS does **not** "authorise State Assemblies" to legislate.
Returning a **money bill with recommendations** is also an RS power.

30.s:
With reference to a Rajya Sabha resolution under Article 249, consider the following statements:
1. It must be supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.
2. It remains in force for one year and may be extended one year at a time.
3. It authorises the State Legislatures to make laws on a Union List subject.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: Statement 1 is correct: the resolution needs two-thirds of members present and voting. Statement 2 is correct: it is valid for one year and can be renewed one year at a time. Statement 3 is wrong: Article 249 lets Parliament legislate on a State List subject in the national interest; it does not authorise State Legislatures. Hence 1 and 2 only.
30.tq: Art. 249: RS (2/3 present and voting) lets PARLIAMENT enter the State List for 1 year at a time.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: resolution by **two-thirds of members present and voting**.
Statement 2 correct: valid **1 year**, extendable **1 year at a time**.
Statement 3 wrong: **Art. 249** lets **Parliament** legislate on a **State List** subject, not State Legislatures on a Union List one.
xa: **Art. 250**: State List law during a **National Emergency**.
**Art. 356-357**: during President's Rule, Parliament legislates for the state.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about the proposal to enlarge the Lok Sabha by about 50% once the 1971 freeze lifts:
1. Its strength would rise to about 815.
2. The Lok Sabha-Rajya Sabha ratio would fall from 3.3:1 to 2.2:1.
3. The 15% ministerial ceiling would rise from 81 to 122 (another source says 133).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: Statement 1 is correct: about 815 members. Statement 2 is wrong: the ratio would rise from 2.2:1 to 3.3:1, not fall. Statement 3 is correct: the ministerial cap would rise from 81 to 122 (or 133 per another source). Hence 1 and 3 only.
30.tq: A bigger Lok Sabha raises the LS:RS ratio (2.2 -> 3.3) and dilutes the Rajya Sabha.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: LS strength would rise by **50%** to **~815**.
Statement 2 wrong: the LS-RS ratio would **rise** from **2.2:1 to 3.3:1**, not fall.
Statement 3 correct: the **15%** ministerial cap would rise from **81 to 122** (another source: **81 to 133**).
xa: The **84th Amendment (2001)** froze LS seat allocation on the **1971 census** till the first census **after 2026**.
The **Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026** sought a maximum of **850** seats.

30.s: The Law Commission's 170th Report, submitted in 1999, proposed which of the following alternatives in the context of parliamentary representation?
o: A 50 per cent reduction in Rajya Sabha seats
A 25 per cent increase in seats through a party-list system
Direct election of the President by the people
Abolition of reserved seats in the Lok Sabha
30.x: The Law Commission's 170th Report of 1999 proposed increasing representation by 25 per cent through a party-list system.
30.tq: Link the institutional proposal with the report number and year.
xs: The Law Commission's **170th Report (1999)** proposed **25%** more seats via a **party list** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It was an alternative in the LS expansion debate; it did not seek RS cuts, direct presidential elections or abolition of reserved seats.
xa: The current proposal: raise LS strength by **50% (to ~815)**.
The LS-RS ratio would go from **2.2:1 to 3.3:1**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026:
1. It was introduced along with the Delimitation Bill, 2026.
2. It sought to raise the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha from 550 to 850.
3. The proposed 850 seats comprised 815 for the States and 35 for the Union Territories.
4. It was passed by the Lok Sabha with the required special majority.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The Bill was defeated in the Lok Sabha and therefore did not secure the required special majority.
30.tq: Identify the single false statement by checking the legislative outcome.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statements 1-3: introduced with the **Delimitation Bill, 2026**; LS maximum **550 to 850**; **815** for states, **35** for UTs.
Statement 4 wrong: it was **defeated in the Lok Sabha** — **298 for, 230 against** of **528** present.
xa: It also sought to **fast-track women's reservation**.
It fell short of the **Art. 368** special majority.

30.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the resolution adopted by the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly in the debate on Lok Sabha delimitation?
o: It proposed equal representation for every State in both Houses.
It supported increasing the Lok Sabha to 850 seats and a 3.3:1 ratio.
It sought to freeze the Lok Sabha at 543 seats and retain the 2.2:1 Lok Sabha–Rajya Sabha ratio.
It sought to reduce the Lok Sabha to 525 seats and abolish the Rajya Sabha.
30.x: The Tamil Nadu Assembly resolved to retain the Lok Sabha at 543 seats and preserve the approximate 2.2:1 Lok Sabha–Rajya Sabha ratio.
30.tq: Use the precise figures to distinguish the State Assembly's position from the expansion proposal.
xs: The **Tamil Nadu** Assembly resolved to **freeze the Lok Sabha at 543** and keep the **2.2:1** LS:RS ratio — so option **(3)** is correct.
It opposed, not supported, the **850**-seat, **3.3:1** plan.
xa: Southern States fear losing share to **UP, Bihar and Rajasthan**.
Present LS strength: **543** (**524** States + **19** UTs).

30.s: On 11 March 2026, the Lok Sabha rejected by voice vote a resolution seeking removal of the Speaker under
30.x: The resolution seeking removal of Speaker Om Birla was moved under Article 94(c) and was rejected by voice vote on 11 March 2026.
30.tq: Apply the article-number trap by distinguishing the Speaker's removal provision from neighbouring parliamentary provisions.
xs: The resolution to remove Speaker **Om Birla** was under **Article 94(c)** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It was rejected by **voice vote** on **11 Mar 2026**.
**Art. 100** = quorum; **Art. 105** = privileges.
xa: The **Speaker** presides over a **joint sitting** and certifies **Money Bills**.
The **Lok Sabha** elects the **Speaker and Deputy Speaker**.

30.s: The Andhra State Act of 1953 and the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act of 2014 were enacted under which Article of the Constitution?
30.x: Both the creation of Andhra State in 1953 and the reorganisation of Andhra Pradesh in 2014 were carried out under Article 3, which concerns the formation and alteration of States.
30.tq: Use the common constitutional provision rather than the different years of enactment.
xs: **Andhra State (1953)** and the **AP Reorganisation Act, 2014** were both made under **Article 3** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Art. 3** covers forming new states and altering areas, boundaries, names; the bill needs the **President's recommendation**.
xa: The **2014** Act amended the **Fourth Schedule**: undivided AP's **18** RS seats = **AP 11 + Telangana 7**.
AP has **25 LS** and **11 RS** seats; Assembly **175**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Article 93 deals with the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
II. Article 108 deals with a joint sitting.
III. Article 112 deals with the Annual Financial Statement.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: All three are correct: Article 93 – Speaker and Deputy Speaker; Article 108 – joint sitting; Article 112 – Annual Financial Statement (Budget).
30.tq: Recall the Parliament Articles by number.
n: Article 93 concerns the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 108 concerns a joint sitting of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 112 concerns the Annual Financial Statement, or Budget. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(3)** **I, II and III**.
**Article 93:** **Speaker and Deputy Speaker** of the Lok Sabha.
**Article 108:** **joint sitting**; **Article 112:** **Annual Financial Statement (Budget)**.
xa: **Article 113:** procedure for **estimates**; **Article 114:** **Appropriation Bills**.
**Article 116:** **Votes on Account** and **Votes of Credit**.
**Article 117:** special provisions for **Financial Bills**.

30.s: Which Article of the Constitution defines a Money Bill?
30.x: Article 110 defines a Money Bill; Article 109 lays down the special procedure for it. Article 108 is joint sitting, 111 assent to Bills and 117 Financial Bills.
30.tq: Recall the Article that defines a Money Bill.
n: Article 108 concerns a joint sitting of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Articles 109 and 110 concern the special procedure for Money Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 110 defines a Money Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 111 concerns assent to Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 117 concerns special provisions for Financial Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xs: **Article 110** defines a Money Bill — option **(2)**.
**Articles 109 and 110** lay down the **special procedure** for Money Bills.
**Article 108** is **joint sitting**, **111** **assent to Bills**, and **117** **Financial Bills**.
xa: The Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill within **14 days**, else it is **deemed passed**.
The **Speaker** certifies what is a Money Bill.
The President can return a Bill only **once** — **except** a **Money Bill**.

30.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Article 79
(b) Article 80
(c) Article 81
(d) Article 83

List-II
(i) Composition of the Lok Sabha
(ii) Duration of the Houses of Parliament
(iii) Constitution of Parliament
(iv) Composition of the Rajya Sabha
30.x: Article 79 – constitution of Parliament; Article 80 – composition of the Rajya Sabha; Article 81 – composition of the Lok Sabha; Article 83 – duration of the Houses. The Council of States (80) comes before the House of the People (81).
30.tq: Remember the Rajya Sabha Article precedes the Lok Sabha one.
n: Article 79 concerns the constitution of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 80 concerns the composition of the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 81 concerns the composition of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 83 concerns the duration of the Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii** — option **(3)**.
**Article 79:** **Constitution** of Parliament; **Article 80:** **Rajya Sabha** composition.
**Article 81:** **Lok Sabha** composition; **Article 83:** **Duration** of the Houses.
xa: **Article 85:** **sessions, prorogation and dissolution**.
**Article 87:** **special address** by the President.
Parliament is covered in **Arts. 79-122**, **Part V**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Article 100 concerns voting and quorum.
II. Article 105 concerns the powers and privileges of the Houses of Parliament.
III. Article 113 concerns the procedure for estimates.
IV. Article 114 concerns Appropriation Bills.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: All four are correct: Article 100 – voting and quorum; 105 – powers and privileges of Parliament; 113 – procedure for estimates; 114 – Appropriation Bills.
30.tq: Check each Article against its parliamentary procedure.
n: Article 100 concerns voting and quorum in Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 105 concerns the powers and privileges of the Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 113 concerns the procedure for estimates. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 114 concerns Appropriation Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(3)** **I, II, III and IV**.
**Article 100:** **voting and quorum**; **Article 105:** **powers and privileges** of the Houses.
**Article 113:** **procedure for estimates**; **Article 114:** **Appropriation Bills**.
xa: Quorum under **Article 100** is **one-tenth** of the total membership.
**Article 112:** **Annual Financial Statement (Budget)**.
**Article 123:** President's power to promulgate **Ordinances**.

30.s: The President promulgates Ordinances when:
o: The Supreme Court is not in session
The Council of Ministers is not in office
The Lok Sabha has been dissolved permanently
30.x: The President issues Ordinances under Article 123 only when Parliament (either House) is not in session. The other options describe conditions with no link to ordinances.
30.tq: Link ordinances to Parliament being in recess.
n: The President promulgates Ordinances when Parliament is not in session under Article 123. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The President’s Ordinance-making power is co-extensive with the legislative power of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xs: The President promulgates Ordinances when **Parliament is not in session** — option **(3)**.
**Article 123:** ordinance power is **co-extensive** with Parliament's legislative power.
It is used during a **recess** — between **prorogation** and the start of a new session.
xa: **Prorogation** ends a **session**, not the House; **dissolution** applies **only to the Lok Sabha**.
The President **summons** each House under **Article 85**.
Maximum gap between two sessions: **six months**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the veto powers of the President:

I. The President has the power of absolute veto.
II. The President has the power of suspensive veto.
III. The President has the power of pocket veto.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
30.x: All three are correct: the President has an absolute veto, a suspensive veto (returning a Bill once) and a pocket veto (keeping it pending).
30.tq: Recall the three vetoes available to the President.
n: The President has an absolute veto. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The President has a suspensive veto. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The President has a pocket veto. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The President may exercise a pocket veto as a limited discretionary power. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xs: All three — **I, II and III** — are correct — option **(2)**.
Under **Article 111** (**Assent to Bills**) the President has **absolute**, **suspensive** and **pocket** vetoes.
He can return a Bill only **once** — **except** a **Money Bill**.
xa: **Article 123:** **Ordinances** when Parliament is **not in session**.
**Article 87:** special address at the **first session of each year** and after each **general election**.
**No bill becomes law without his assent** — why he is part of Parliament.

30.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Article 81
(b) Article 83
(c) Article 84
(d) Article 330

List-II
(i) Qualification for membership
(ii) Reservation for SC/ST
(iii) Composition
(iv) Duration
30.x: Article 81 covers composition, 83 duration, 84 qualifications and 330 SC/ST reservation, so the answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
30.tq: Fix Article 81 (composition) and 330 (reservation) first, then place 83 and 84.
n: Article 83 deals with the duration of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 32-34]
Article 81 deals with the composition of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 32-34]
Article 84 deals with qualifications for Lok Sabha membership. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 32-34]
Article 330 deals with reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 32-34]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii** — option **(1)**.
**Article 81:** **composition**; **Article 83:** **duration** of the Houses.
**Article 84:** **qualification** for membership; **Article 330:** **reservation** for **SC/ST**.
xa: SC/ST reservation was initially for **10 years**; the **104th** Amendment extended it until **2030**.
**84th Amendment (2001):** froze LS seat allocation on the **1971 census** till the first census **after 2026**.
**61st Amendment (1987):** voting age **18** years (**Art. 326**).

30.s:
Consider the following statements regarding reservation of seats in the Lok Sabha:
I. Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes in proportion to their population.
II. Seats are reserved for Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their population.
III. Reservation of Lok Sabha seats was initially provided for ten years.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: All three are correct: Lok Sabha seats are reserved for SCs and STs in proportion to their population, and the reservation was first given for ten years.
30.tq: Recall the basis (population) and the original duration (ten years).
n: Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes in the Lok Sabha in proportion to their population. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 32-34]
Seats are reserved for Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha in proportion to their population. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 32-34]
Reservation of Lok Sabha seats was initially provided for 10 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 32-34]
xs: All three — **I, II and III** — are correct — option **(4)**.
**Article 330:** seats reserved for **Scheduled Castes** and **Scheduled Tribes** in proportion to their **population**.
The reservation was initially for **10 years** and repeatedly extended.
xa: The **104th** Amendment extended it until **2030**.
The same Amendment ended **Anglo-Indian** nomination from **25 Jan 2020**.
**87th Amendment:** constituencies readjusted on the **2001** census.

30.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Present elected strength of the Lok Sabha
(b) Elected members from Union Territories at present
(c) Elected strength of the First Lok Sabha
(d) Seats held by Uttar Pradesh in the Lok Sabha

List-II
(i) 19
(ii) 80
(iii) 543
(iv) 489
30.x: The present elected strength is 543, of which 19 come from Union Territories since Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh became UTs. The First Lok Sabha had 489 elected seats and Uttar Pradesh holds 80, so the answer is a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
30.tq: Match the biggest number (543) first, then 489, 80 and 13.
n: The Lok Sabha has 13 elected members from the Union Territories. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 32-34]
The first Lok Sabha had 489 elected members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 32-34]
Uttar Pradesh has the highest number of Lok Sabha seats, with 80 seats. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 32-34]
xs: The keyed match is **a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii** — option **(3)**.
Present elected strength: **543**; **First Lok Sabha:** **489** elected members.
**Uttar Pradesh** holds the most seats — **80**; UT members **19** (as per the **524** States + **19** UTs count).
xa: ⚠ The notes give **543** = **530** States + **13** UTs, while another source says **524** States + **19** UTs.
Maximum strength: **550** — up to **530** from States + up to **20** from UTs.
Seats: **Delhi 7**, **J&K 5**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Only three Union Territories—Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu & Kashmir—have representation in the Rajya Sabha.
Statement B: The quorum of the Rajya Sabha is one-tenth of its total membership.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
30.x: Both are true. Among the Union Territories, only Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu & Kashmir are represented in the Rajya Sabha, and its quorum, like the Lok Sabha's, is one-tenth of total membership.
30.tq: Recall the three UTs with Rajya Sabha seats and the quorum fraction.
n: Delhi has representation in the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
Puducherry has representation in the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
Jammu and Kashmir has representation in the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
Only three Union Territories have representation in the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
The quorum of the Rajya Sabha is one-tenth of its total membership. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)**.
A: only **three** UTs — **Delhi**, **Puducherry**, **Jammu and Kashmir** — are represented in the Rajya Sabha.
B: quorum is **one-tenth** of the total membership — same for the Rajya Sabha (**Article 100**).
xa: RS present strength **245** — **233** elected + **12** nominated.
UT members are elected by an **electoral college** under Parliament's law.
RS elections are **indirect**, by **PR-STV** (**Art 80(4)**).

30.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the tenure of Rajya Sabha members:
I. The term of a Rajya Sabha member is six years.
II. Approximately one-third of the members retire every two years.
III. A casual vacancy is filled for the remainder of the term.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: All three are correct: a Rajya Sabha member serves six years, about one-third retire every two years, and a casual vacancy is filled only for the rest of the term.
30.tq: Check the six-year term, two-year retirement cycle and casual-vacancy rule.
n: The term of a Rajya Sabha member is six years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
Approximately one-third of Rajya Sabha members retire every two years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
A casual vacancy in the Rajya Sabha is filled for the remainder of the term. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
xs: All three — **I, II and III** — are correct — option **(1)**.
A member's term is **six years**; **one-third** retire every **two years**.
A **casual vacancy** is filled for the **remainder of the term**.
xa: ⚠ The member's **6 years** is fixed by the **RPA 1951**, not by the Constitution.
The Rajya Sabha is **not subject to dissolution** — **Article 83(1)**.
In **1952** the first members' retirement order was decided by **lottery**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about the powers of the Rajya Sabha:
I. It has equal powers with the Lok Sabha in Constitutional Amendment Bills.
II. It can introduce Ordinary Bills.
III. It can introduce Constitutional Amendment Bills.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: All three are correct: the Rajya Sabha has equal powers in Constitutional Amendment Bills and can introduce both Ordinary and Constitutional Amendment Bills. Its powers are restricted only for Money Bills.
30.tq: Remember that only Money Bills limit the Rajya Sabha's role.
n: The Rajya Sabha has equal powers with the Lok Sabha in Constitutional Amendment Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
The Rajya Sabha can introduce Ordinary Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
The Rajya Sabha can introduce Constitutional Amendment Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
xs: All three — **I, II and III** — are correct — option **(1)**.
The Rajya Sabha has **equal powers** with the Lok Sabha on **Constitutional Amendment Bills**.
It can introduce both **Ordinary** and **Constitutional Amendment** Bills.
xa: **Article 249:** authorises Parliament to legislate on a **State List** subject — **two-thirds** present and voting.
**Article 312:** initiates new **All-India Services**.
**Art. 67(b):** removal of the **Vice-President** can be moved **only in the Rajya Sabha**.

30.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Rajya Sabha’s role in relation to a Money Bill is incorrect?
o: It must deal with a Money Bill within 14 days.
Its role is limited to recommending changes to the Money Bill.
It can only recommend changes to a Money Bill.
It introduces the Money Bill and has the final say on it.
30.x: Option D is incorrect. A Money Bill is introduced only in the Lok Sabha, which also has the final say; the Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes within 14 days.
30.tq: Discriminate the roles of the two Houses on Money Bills.
n: The Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes to a Money Bill within 14 days. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 34-36]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the RS **introduces the Money Bill and has the final say** — option **(4)**.
The **Lok Sabha** introduces Money Bills and has the **final say**.
The Rajya Sabha can only **recommend** changes within **14 days**.
xa: If not returned in **14 days**, the Bill is **deemed passed** (**Article 109**).
The RS **cannot vote on demands for grants**.
⚠ Returning a money bill with recommendations **is** an RS power; it does **not** "authorise State Assemblies".

30.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
