The Governor of a State must be at least 35 years old. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
Article 157 governs the minimum age for a State Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i** — option **(4)**.
**Universal adult suffrage:** **Article 326**; **Panchayat membership:** **243F(1)(a)**.
**Lok Sabha membership:** **84(b)**; **Governor:** **Article 157**.
xa: **58(1)(b):** President; **66(3)(b):** Vice-President — both **35**.
**243V(1)(a):** Municipality member or Mayor — **21**.
**173(b):** Vidhan Sabha (**25**) and Vidhan Parishad (**30**).

30.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) Municipality member or Mayor
(b) Prime Minister or Chief Minister
(c) Rajya Sabha member
(d) Vice-President

List-II
(i) 35 years
(ii) 21 years
(iii) 25 years
(iv) 30 years
30.x: The minimum ages are 21 for a municipal member or mayor, 25 for a Prime Minister or Chief Minister from the lower House, 30 for the Rajya Sabha, and 35 for the Vice-President. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
30.tq: Recall the ages 21, 25, 30 and 35.
n: A Municipality member or Mayor must be at least 21 years old. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
A Prime Minister must be at least 25 years old if the Prime Minister heads the lower chamber. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
A Chief Minister must be at least 25 years old if the Chief Minister heads the lower chamber. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
Twenty-five years is the minimum possible age for becoming Prime Minister or Chief Minister when heading the lower chamber. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
A Member of the Rajya Sabha must be at least 30 years old. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The Vice-President of India must be at least 35 years old. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
Disqualification for contesting Panchayat or Municipality elections does not apply at or above 21 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
Thirty-five years is the highest entry age required in the Indian Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i** — option **(2)**.
**Municipality member or Mayor:** **21 years**; **PM or CM** heading the lower chamber: **25 years**.
**Rajya Sabha member:** **30 years**; **Vice-President:** **35 years**.
xa: **18:** voter (**Article 326**).
**35** applies to **President**, **VP** and **Governor**.
Disqualification for Panchayat or Municipality polls does **not apply** at or above **21**.

30.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Article 58(1)(b) concerns the minimum age qualification for the President.
II. Article 66(3)(b) concerns the minimum age qualification for the Vice-President.
III. Article 157 concerns the minimum age qualification for the Governor of a State.
IV. Article 84(b) concerns the minimum age qualification for a Governor.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: I, II and III are correct: the President's age rule is in Article 58(1)(b), the Vice-President's in 66(3)(b), and the Governor's in 157. IV is false because 84(b) is for members of Parliament.
30.tq: Recall each age Article.
n: Article 84(b) governs the minimum age for Lok Sabha membership. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
Article 84(b) governs the minimum age for Rajya Sabha membership. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
Article 58(1)(b) governs the minimum age for the President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
Article 66(3)(b) governs the minimum age for the Vice-President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
Article 157 governs the minimum age for a State Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
xs: Statements **I, II and III** are correct — option **(4)**.
**58(1)(b):** President; **66(3)(b):** Vice-President; **157:** Governor.
IV is wrong: **84(b)** is the minimum age for **Lok Sabha** and **Rajya Sabha** members.
xa: **173(b):** Vidhan Sabha and Vidhan Parishad.
**243F(1)(a):** Panchayat; **243V(1)(a):** Municipality.
**35** is the highest entry age in the Constitution.

30.s: The reduction of the voting age from 21 years to 18 years, made through the 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, became effective in which year?
30.x: The 61st Amendment (1988) lowered the voting age to 18, and it took effect in 1989.
30.tq: Discriminate the year passed from the year in force.
n: The voting age was reduced from 21 to 18 years by the 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The reduction of the voting age became effective in 1989. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
xs: The reduction became effective in **1989** — option **(2)**.
The **61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988** cut the voting age from **21 to 18** (**Article 326**).
xa: ⚠ The amendment table lists the **61st Amendment** under **1987**.
**18** years = **universal adult suffrage**.
**21** remains the minimum for **Panchayat** and **Municipality** contestants.

30.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Nominated MLAs cannot vote in Rajya Sabha elections.
II. Members of Legislative Councils cannot vote in Rajya Sabha elections.
III. Rajya Sabha elections are conducted by direct election of citizens.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: I and II are correct: nominated MLAs and MLCs cannot vote in Rajya Sabha elections. III is false because those elections are indirect, by elected MLAs.
30.tq: Recall who votes in Rajya Sabha elections.
n: Elected Members of the Legislative Assemblies of the respective States elect Rajya Sabha members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Rajya Sabha is elected indirectly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
Nominated Members of Legislative Assemblies cannot vote in Rajya Sabha elections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
Members of Legislative Councils cannot vote in Rajya Sabha elections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
xs: Statements **I and II** are correct — option **(3)**.
**Nominated** MLAs and **Members of Legislative Councils** **cannot vote** in RS elections.
III is wrong: RS elections are **indirect** — by **elected members of State Legislative Assemblies** through **PR-STV**.
xa: RS seats are allocated by **population** (**Fourth Schedule**) — **not** equally.
**Kuldip Nayar v. UoI (2006):** upheld **open ballot** and removal of the **domicile** requirement.
AP has **11** RS seats; Telangana **7**.

31.s: Which Article provides for the election of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
31.x: Article 93 provides that the House of the People shall choose two members to be Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
31.tq: Match the constitutional article with the office it creates.
xs: **Article 93**: the LS elects the **Speaker and Deputy Speaker** from its members — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Art. 89** is about the RS **Chairman and Deputy Chairman**; **Art. 100** = quorum / casting vote; **Art. 85** = sessions.
xa: **Art. 94**: Speaker resigns to the **Deputy Speaker**; removal by a **majority of all the then members** after **14 days'** notice.
The **Deputy Speaker** is elected **after the Speaker**.

31.s: The salary and allowances of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha are charged on the:
31.x: The salaries and allowances of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India under Article 97.
31.tq: Use the constitutional funding source rather than a general parliamentary budget description.
xs: The Speaker's salary is **charged on the Consolidated Fund** of India (**Art 97**) — so option **(1)** is correct.
Being charged, it is not voted upon — the Public Account and Contingency Fund are wrong.
xa: On **dissolution**, the Speaker continues till immediately before the **first meeting of the new LS**.
The **Speaker Pro Tem** is the senior-most member, sworn in by the **President**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the Speaker of the Lok Sabha under Article 94:
1. The Speaker vacates office on ceasing to be a member of the Lok Sabha.
2. The Speaker resigns by writing to the President.
3. The Speaker can be removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members, after 14 days' notice.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
31.x: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker. Statement 3 is correct: removal needs an effective majority and 14 days' notice. Hence 1 and 3 only.
31.tq: Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker and vice versa; Deputy Chairman resigns to the Chairman.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: the Speaker **vacates office on ceasing to be a member** (**Art 94**).
Statement 2 wrong: the Speaker **resigns to the Deputy Speaker**, not the President.
Statement 3 correct: removal by a **majority of all the then members** (effective majority) after **14 days'** notice.
xa: ⚠ Speaker → resigns to Deputy Speaker; Deputy Speaker → to Speaker; Deputy Chairman → to Chairman.
Removal motions against **Mavalankar (1954)**, **Hukum Singh (1966)**, **Jakhar (1987)** all **failed**.

31.s: While a resolution for the removal of the Speaker is under consideration, which one of the following is correct?
o: The Speaker cannot speak or vote under any circumstance
The Speaker’s membership of the House automatically terminates
The Speaker cannot preside, but may speak and take part in the proceedings and vote in the first instance, not in the event of a tie
The Speaker may preside but cannot vote
31.x: Article 96 prevents the Speaker from presiding while the removal resolution is under consideration. The Speaker may speak, participate and vote in the first instance, but cannot exercise a casting vote in case of a tie.
31.tq: Separate the restriction on presiding from the retained rights to participate and vote.
xs: While his removal is pending, the Speaker **cannot preside**, but may **speak, take part** and **vote in the first instance**, not on a tie — so option **(3)** is correct.
This is **Art 96**; his membership does not end.
xa: ⚠ The **RS Chairman**, in the same situation, **cannot vote** at all but may speak.
The **casting vote** (on a tie) is under **Art 100(1)**.

31.s: Which of the following pairs of removal motions against Lok Sabha Speakers is correctly matched?
31.x: Removal motions against G. V. Mavalankar in 1954, Hukum Singh in 1966 and Balram Jakhar in 1987 failed. The motion concerning Om Birla was listed for debate in 2026, not 1987.
31.tq: Pair each office-holder with the correct year and reject swapped dates.
xs: **G.V. Mavalankar — 1954** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Hukum Singh** faced his motion in **1966**, **Balram Jakhar** in **1987** — all failed.
**Om Birla**'s motion was signed by **118** MPs and listed for debate on **9 Mar 2026**.
xa: ⚠ **1954 – 1966 – 1987** = Mavalankar – Hukum Singh – Jakhar.
The LS rejected the Om Birla resolution by **voice vote**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the Speaker when the Lok Sabha is dissolved:
1. The Speaker continues in office until immediately before the first meeting of the new Lok Sabha.
2. The outgoing Speaker presides over the new House as Speaker Pro Tem and conducts the election of the new Speaker.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
31.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Speaker does not vacate office on dissolution. Statement 2 is wrong: the Speaker Pro Tem is the senior-most member, sworn in by the President, not the outgoing Speaker. Hence 1 only.
31.tq: Speaker Pro Tem = senior-most member, sworn in by the President.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)** (1 only).
Statement 1 correct: the Speaker **continues till immediately before the first meeting of the new LS**.
Statement 2 wrong: the **Speaker Pro Tem** is the **senior-most member**, sworn in by the **President**, not the outgoing Speaker.
xa: The Pro Tem Speaker **presides and conducts the new Speaker's election**.
The Speaker's salary is charged on the **Consolidated Fund** (**Art 97**).

31.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the powers of the Speaker:
1. The Speaker decides cases under the Tenth Schedule, subject to judicial review.
2. The Speaker recognises the Leader of the Opposition subject to the applicable requirement regarding the strength of the party.
3. The Speaker appoints chairmen of parliamentary committees.
4. Rulings of the Speaker are protected by Article 122.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: All four statements are correct. The Speaker’s decisions under the Tenth Schedule remain subject to judicial review, and the Speaker also performs the listed recognition, committee and ruling-related functions.
31.tq: Use a multi-function statement set and verify each power independently.
xs: All four statements, **1, 2, 3 and 4**, are correct — option **(4)**.
He decides **Tenth Schedule** cases, subject to judicial review (**Kihoto Hollohan, 1992**).
He recognises the **Leader of the Opposition**, **appoints committee chairmen**, and his rulings are protected by **Art 122**.
xa: LoP recognition needs at least **one-tenth** of the House's strength.
The LoP became statutory under the **1977 Act**.

31.s: The party seeking recognition of the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha is required, according to the Speaker’s direction, to have at least:
31.x: Recognition of the Leader of the Opposition requires the party to have at least one-tenth of the strength of the House, according to the Speaker’s direction. The office has statutory status since the 1977 Act.
31.tq: Distinguish the one-tenth threshold from other parliamentary fractions.
xs: The party needs at least **one-tenth of the House's strength** — so option **(1)** is correct.
This comes from the **Speaker's direction**; the LoP is **statutory since the 1977 Act**.
xa: Quorum is also **one-tenth** of total members (**Art 100(3)**).
The Speaker also decides **Tenth Schedule** cases.

31.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha:
1. The Deputy Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha after the election of the Speaker.
2. The Deputy Speaker resigns by addressing the resignation to the Speaker.
3. The Deputy Speaker presides over a joint sitting when the Speaker is absent.
4. The Deputy Speaker is subordinate to the Speaker in exercising the office’s constitutional functions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The Deputy Speaker is not subordinate to the Speaker while exercising the office’s functions, so statement 4 is false.
31.tq: Spot the reversed institutional relationship in the final statement.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: elected **by the LS after the Speaker**; statement 2: **resigns to the Speaker**.
Statement 3: presides over a **joint sitting** if the Speaker is absent.
Statement 4 wrong: he is **not subordinate to the Speaker**.
xa: By convention he is from the **Opposition**.
He becomes **chairman of any committee** he is appointed to.

31.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Panel of Chairpersons of the Lok Sabha is correct?
o: It is nominated by the Deputy Speaker and can preside even when the Speaker’s office is vacant
It is nominated by the President and may contain up to twenty members
It is nominated by the Speaker and may contain up to ten members
It is elected by the Rajya Sabha and contains exactly ten members
31.x: The Speaker nominates a Panel of Chairpersons consisting of up to ten members. A panel member may preside in the absence of both the Speaker and Deputy Speaker, but not when the Speaker’s office is vacant.
31.tq: Check both the nominating authority and the numerical ceiling.
xs: The **Panel of Chairpersons** is **nominated by the Speaker**, **up to 10** members — so option **(3)** is correct.
A member cannot preside when the **Speaker's office is vacant**.
xa: A panel member presides in the **absence of both** Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
RS equivalent: **Panel of Vice-Chairpersons**, nominated by the **Chairman**.

31.s: Which of the following statements regarding vacancies of Deputy Speaker offices is correct?
o: The Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker post was filled in June 2019, while the office was vacant in eight State Assemblies in 2025.
The Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker post has been vacant since 2014, and the office was vacant in ten State Assemblies.
The Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker post has been vacant since June 2019, and the office was vacant in eight State Assemblies in 2026.
The Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker post has been vacant since June 2021, and the office was vacant in six State Assemblies.
31.x: The Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker post has been vacant since June 2019. The office was reported vacant in eight State Assemblies, with Jharkhand’s vacancy lasting 21 years.
31.tq: Match the vacancy count and starting date without swapping the two time references.
xs: The **LS Deputy Speaker** post has been **vacant since June 2019**, and the State office was vacant in **8 State Assemblies** (**2026**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Jharkhand**'s vacancy has lasted **21 years** (as of **Jun 2026**).
xa: State office is under **Art 178**.
The post stayed empty through the **17th and 18th** Lok Sabhas.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha:
1. The Deputy Chairman is elected by the Rajya Sabha from among its members.
2. The Deputy Chairman resigns by writing to the President.
3. The Deputy Chairman can be removed by an effective majority after 14 days' notice.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
31.x: Statement 1 is correct (Art. 89(2)). Statement 2 is wrong: the Deputy Chairman resigns to the Chairman. Statement 3 is correct: removal needs an effective majority with 14 days' notice. Hence 1 and 3 only.
31.tq: Deputy Chairman resigns to the Chairman.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **elected from RS members** (**Art 89(2), 90**).
Statement 2 wrong: he **resigns to the Chairman**.
Statement 3 correct: removal by **effective majority** with **14 days'** notice.
xa: **Harivansh**'s term as Deputy Chairman ended **9 Apr 2026**.
When the VP acts as President, the **Deputy Chairman** presides (**Art 91**).

31.s: In the vacancy of the office of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, the power of the Deputy Chairman to decide on a judge-removal motion under Article 91 was upheld by the Supreme Court in January 2026 in the:
31.x: In January 2026, the Supreme Court upheld, in the Justice Varma case, the Deputy Chairman’s power under Article 91 to decide on a judge-removal motion when the Chairman’s office was vacant.
31.tq: Match the recent judicial ruling with the precise constitutional power and case name.
xs: The **SC (Jan 2026)** upheld the Deputy Chairman's **Art 91** power in the **Justice Varma case** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It covered deciding a **judge-removal motion** while the **Chairman's office was vacant**.
**Kihoto Hollohan (1992)** is about **Tenth Schedule** review; Mavalankar and Hukum Singh were Speakers facing removal motions.
xa: **Harivansh**'s term as Deputy Chairman ended **9 Apr 2026**.
Under **Art 91** the Deputy Chairman also presides when the VP acts as President.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha:
1. The Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
2. While a resolution for his removal is under consideration, he cannot preside but may speak, and he cannot vote.
3. When the Vice-President acts as President, the Deputy Chairman performs the duties of the Chairman.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Vice-President is ex officio Chairman (Arts. 64 and 89). Statement 2 is correct: unlike the Speaker, who can vote in the first instance during his removal proceedings, the Chairman cannot vote at all while his removal is pending, though he may speak. Statement 3 is correct: under Article 91 the Deputy Chairman presides when the Chairman's office is vacant or the Vice-President is acting as President. Hence all three.
31.tq: Speaker under removal: can vote (first instance). Chairman under removal: cannot vote at all.
xs: All three statements, **1, 2 and 3**, are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: the **VP** is **ex officio Chairman** (**Art 64, 89**).
Statement 2: while his removal is pending, he **cannot preside** and **cannot vote**, but may speak.
Statement 3: when the VP acts as President, the **Deputy Chairman** presides (**Art 91**).
xa: ⚠ The **Speaker** in that situation **can vote** in the first instance.
The Chairman is removed **only when removed as VP**.

31.s: As per the position in 2026, which one of the following is correct regarding the presiding officers of the Rajya Sabha?
o: Harivansh is the Chairman and C.P. Radhakrishnan the Deputy Chairman
C.P. Radhakrishnan is the Chairman, and Harivansh's term as Deputy Chairman ended on 9 April 2026
S. Radhakrishnan is the Chairman and Harivansh the Deputy Chairman
C.P. Radhakrishnan is the Deputy Chairman, and the office of Chairman is vacant
31.x: C.P. Radhakrishnan, as Vice-President, is the present ex officio Chairman, and Harivansh's term as Deputy Chairman ended on 9 April 2026. Harivansh was never Chairman, S. Radhakrishnan was the first Chairman (1952-62), and the Chairman's office is not described as vacant.
31.tq: First Chairman: S. Radhakrishnan; present Chairman: C.P. Radhakrishnan.
xs: **C.P. Radhakrishnan** is the **present Chairman**, and **Harivansh**'s term as **Deputy Chairman** ended on **9 Apr 2026** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**S. Radhakrishnan** was the **first** Chairman (**1952-62**), not the present one.
xa: The Chairman has a **casting vote only**.
RS has a **Panel of Vice-Chairpersons** nominated by the Chairman.

31.s: With reference to Article 98 of the Constitution, which one of the following is correct?
o: The President appoints all secretarial staff directly and Parliament has no power to regulate recruitment by law.
The Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha must have identical secretarial establishments without any common posts.
Each House has separate secretarial staff, although posts common to both Houses may be created.
The executive government alone regulates recruitment to the secretariats of both Houses in all circumstances.
31.x: Article 98 establishes separate secretarial staff for each House while permitting the creation of posts common to both Houses.
31.tq: Use the constitutional general rule and its permitted exception to eliminate statements using exclusive powers.
xs: Under **Art 98**, each House has **separate secretarial staff**, though **posts common to both Houses** may be created — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Parliament may regulate recruitment by law**; the executive does not control it.
xa: Head: **Secretary-General**, appointed by the **presiding officer**, rank = **Cabinet Secretary**.
The Secretariat is **independent of the executive**.

31.s: Until Parliament makes a law regulating recruitment and conditions of service of the secretarial staff of the Houses, rules may be made by the President after consultation with the:
o: Chief Justice of India and Attorney-General of India
Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha and Secretary-General of the Rajya Sabha
Prime Minister and Union Home Minister
Speaker of the Lok Sabha and Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
31.x: In the absence of a law by Parliament, the President may make rules after consulting the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
31.tq: Apply the ‘who would do this job?’ method to distinguish the constitutional consultees from parliamentary officials and ministers.
xs: Until Parliament legislates, the **President** makes rules **after consulting the Speaker/Chairman** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Not the CJI, the Secretaries-General or the PM.
xa: **Art 98** provides each House a **separate secretarial staff**.
Each Secretariat is headed by a **Secretary-General**.

31.s:
Which of the following statements regarding the Secretary-General of a House of Parliament is correct?
1. Each House has a Secretary-General as its head of secretarial staff.
2. The Secretary-General is appointed by the presiding officer of the concerned House.
3. The office holds rank equal to that of the Cabinet Secretary.
4. The secretariat is independent of the executive.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
31.x: The secretariat of each House is headed by its Secretary-General, appointed by the concerned presiding officer. The Secretary-General has the rank of Cabinet Secretary, and the parliamentary secretariat is independent of the executive.
31.tq: Test office, appointing authority, rank and institutional independence as separate elements of one constitutional arrangement.
xs: All four statements, **1, 2, 3 and 4**, are correct — option **(4)**.
The **Secretary-General** heads each House's staff, is **appointed by the presiding officer**, and ranks with the **Cabinet Secretary**.
The Secretariat is **independent of the executive**.
xa: **Posts common to both Houses** may be created (**Art 98**).
Recruitment: Parliament may regulate **by law**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the sessions of Parliament:
1. The President summons each House.
2. The six-month interval is counted from the last sitting of one session to the first sitting of the next.
3. The Constitution expressly names the Budget, Monsoon and Winter Sessions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: The President summons each House, and the six-month rule is calculated from the last sitting to the first sitting. Budget, Monsoon and Winter Sessions are conventional names, not sessions expressly named in the Constitution.
31.tq: Separate constitutional requirements from parliamentary conventions.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **President summons** each House (**Art 85**).
Statement 2 correct: the gap is counted from the **last sitting of one session to the first sitting of the next** (**APPSC G2 2017**).
Statement 3 wrong: the **three sessions** exist **by convention**.
xa: Hence at least **two sessions a year**.
States follow the same six-month rule under **Art 174**.

31.s: The period between prorogation of Parliament and the commencement of its next session is known as:
31.x: The period from prorogation to the next session is called a recess. It is different from adjournment, which interrupts a sitting within a session.
31.tq: Discriminate between a break within a session and the interval between two sessions.
xs: The period from **prorogation to the next session** is a **recess** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Adjournment sine die** ends a sitting; **dissolution** ends the life of the LS.
xa: **Session** = first sitting → prorogation/dissolution.
**Prorogation** is ordered by the **President** (**Governor** in States).

31.s: A quorum in either House of Parliament is ordinarily:
o: One-half of the total membership, including the presiding officer
One-tenth of the total membership, including the presiding officer
One-fourth of the elected membership, excluding nominated members
One-twentieth of the total membership, excluding the presiding officer
31.x: Under Article 100(3), the quorum is one-tenth of the total number of members of the House, including the presiding officer.
31.tq: Check both the fraction and whether the presiding officer is included.
xs: Quorum is **one-tenth of total members, including the presiding officer** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The provision is **Art 100(3)**.
xa: ⚠ Some notes list it as **Art 100(1)**, but **100(1)** actually carries the **casting vote**.
State Assemblies averaged only **24 sittings** in **2025** (**Odisha 43**, **Nagaland 7**).

31.s:
Under Article 86 of the Constitution of India, the President may
1. Address either House of Parliament separately or both Houses together.
2. Require the attendance of members for the purpose of the address.
3. Send messages to either House with respect to a pending Bill.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: Article 86 empowers the President to address either House or both Houses together, require members' attendance and send messages to either House regarding pending Bills.
31.tq: Test the exact scope of Article 86 by separating the President’s powers of addressing, requiring attendance and sending messages.
xs: All three statements, **1, 2 and 3**, are correct — option **(4)**.
Under **Art 86**, the President may **address either House or both**, **require attendance**, and **send messages**.
xa: **Art 87**: **special address** at the **first session after each general election** and the **first session of each year**.
The address is debated on a **Motion of Thanks**.

31.s:
The special address delivered by the President under Article 87 is made at which of the following occasions?
1. The first session after each general election to the Lok Sabha.
2. The first session of Parliament in each year.
3. Every session immediately after prorogation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: Article 87 provides for the President’s special address at the first session after each general election and at the first session of each year. It is not required after every prorogation.
31.tq: Identify the two constitutionally specified occasions and reject the overbroad time-based statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
**Art 87**: special address at the **first session after each general election** and the **first session of each year**.
Statement 3 wrong: it is not given after every prorogation.
xa: It **outlines government policy**, debated on a **Motion of Thanks**.
**Art 86** covers addresses **at any time** and **messages**.

31.s: The address of the President outlining the policies of the Government is debated in Parliament through a:
31.x: The President’s address outlining Government policy is debated through a Motion of Thanks in Parliament.
31.tq: Match the constitutional address with the parliamentary motion that follows it.
xs: The President's address is debated through a **Motion of Thanks** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The address **outlines government policy**.
xa: The **special address** is under **Art 87**.
The **Budget** session (**Feb-May**) is the longest.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the summoning of Parliament:
1. The President may summon the two Houses separately.
2. The Constitution requires both Houses to be summoned together on every occasion.
3. Each House must meet within six months of its previous sitting.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: The President need not summon both Houses together, and the maximum interval between sessions is six months. Statement 2 is false.
31.tq: Identify the statement that reverses the constitutional rule on separate summoning.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **President summons each House**; they need not be summoned together.
Statement 2 wrong: the Constitution does not require summoning them together.
Statement 3 correct: the gap between sessions is **not more than 6 months** (**Art 85**).
xa: The gap runs from the **last sitting** of one session to the **first sitting** of the next.
States: same rule under **Art 174**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements regarding prorogation:
1. It is ordered by the President in respect of Parliament.
2. It terminates a session.
3. Bills pending before Parliament lapse on prorogation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: The President prorogues Parliament and prorogation terminates the session. Bills do not lapse on prorogation, although pending notices generally lapse except notices to introduce bills.
31.tq: Test the effect of prorogation separately from the effect of dissolution.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1 and 2: **prorogation** is by the **President** and ends the **session**.
Statement 3 wrong: **bills do not lapse** on prorogation; only pending notices lapse, except notices to introduce bills.
xa: On **dissolution**, many bills **lapse**.
In States, prorogation is by the **Governor**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The office of Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha has remained vacant throughout the 17th Lok Sabha.
2. The office of Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha has remained vacant through the 18th Lok Sabha.
3. The Deputy Speaker’s post has remained continuously occupied in both these Lok Sabhas.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
31.x: The Deputy Speaker’s post remained vacant through both the 17th and 18th Lok Sabhas. Therefore, statement 3 is false.
31.tq: Use a present-affairs comparison across two successive Lok Sabhas and reject the directly reversed statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
The **Deputy Speaker's post** stayed **empty through the 17th and 18th** Lok Sabhas.
Statement 3 wrong: the post was not occupied.
xa: It has been **vacant since June 2019**.
State office (**Art 178**) vacant in **8 State Assemblies**.

31.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

 b. Deputy Speaker of the first Andhra Pradesh Assembly
 c. Chairman of the first Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council

List-II (Person)

Codes:
 a  b  c

31.x: Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao was the Speaker, Kalluri Subbarao was the Deputy Speaker, and Madapati Hanumantha Rao was the first Council Chairman in the first Andhra Pradesh Assembly of 1956.
31.tq: Start from the sure office-holder pair and complete the matching after distinguishing the Assembly offices from the Council office.
xs: **a–iii, b–ii, c–i** — option **(1)**.
First AP Assembly (**1956**): Speaker **Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao**; Deputy Speaker **Kalluri Subbarao**; first Council Chairman **Madapati Hanumantha Rao**.
xa: ⚠ The LS Speaker resigns to the **Deputy Speaker**; State presiding offices are under **Art 178**.
**Jharkhand** has had no Deputy Speaker for **21 years**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: In normal parliamentary sittings, the Speaker does not vote in the first instance.
Statement B: In normal parliamentary sittings, the Speaker may exercise a casting vote in case of equality of votes.

Which of the following is correct?
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
31.x: Both are true: under Article 100, the Speaker does not vote in the first instance in normal sittings, but gives a casting vote when votes are tied.
31.tq: Discriminate a first-instance vote from a casting vote.
n: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 100. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
During normal parliamentary sittings, the Speaker does not vote in the first instance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
During normal parliamentary sittings, the Speaker exercises a casting vote under Article 100 upon an equality of votes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)**.
A: in **normal sittings** the Speaker does **not vote in the first instance**.
B: he has a **casting vote** on an **equality of votes** — **Article 100** (**Art 100(1)**).
xa: During his **own removal resolution** (**Article 96**) he cannot preside, but **can vote** in the first instance — **no casting vote**.
⚠ Removal pending: Speaker **can vote**; the RS **Chairman cannot vote**.
⚠ Quorum = **100(3)**; casting vote = **100(1)**.

31.s: Which of the following statements regarding the effect of dissolution of the Lok Sabha is incorrect?
o: The Speaker continues until immediately before the first meeting of the newly elected Lok Sabha.
The Speaker continues in office after dissolution.
The Speaker does not vacate office immediately upon dissolution.
The Speaker's office ends immediately on the date of dissolution.
31.x: Option D is incorrect: the Speaker does not vacate office on dissolution but stays until just before the new Lok Sabha first meets.
31.tq: Recall the Speaker's continuity after dissolution.
n: When the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the Speaker does not vacate office immediately. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker continues in office until immediately before the first meeting of the newly elected Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The regular Speaker continues in office through dissolution until the next House meets. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the **Speaker's office ends immediately on dissolution** — option **(4)**.
The Speaker does **not** vacate office on dissolution.
He continues until just before the **first meeting** of the new Lok Sabha.
xa: The **Deputy Speaker** **vacates office immediately** on dissolution.
The Speaker **vacates office** on ceasing to be a member (**Art 94**).
A **Pro-Tem Speaker** (**Article 95(1)**) then swears in new MPs.

31.s:
Consider the following statements regarding removal of the Speaker:
I. Removal requires a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the Lok Sabha.
II. The resolution requires at least 14 days' advance written notice.
III. Removal requires a simple majority of members present and voting.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
31.x: I and II are correct: under Article 94(c), the Speaker is removed by a majority of all the then members (an effective majority), after 14 days' notice. III is false because a simple majority is not enough.
31.tq: Discriminate effective majority from simple majority.
n: The Speaker is removed only by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the Lok Sabha under Article 94(c). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The majority required to remove the Speaker is an effective majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
At least 14 days’ advance written notice is required before moving the Speaker’s removal resolution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xs: Statements **I and II** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Article 94(c):** removal by a **majority of all the then members** (**effective majority**).
At least **14 days'** written notice is required.
III is wrong: a **simple majority** of members present and voting is not enough.
xa: Removal motions against **Mavalankar (1954)**, **Hukum Singh (1966)** and **Balram Jakhar (1987)** all failed.
A motion against **Om Birla** was signed by **118** Opposition MPs (**9 Mar 2026**).
The Speaker resigns in writing to the **Deputy Speaker** — **Article 94(b)**.

31.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the Regular Speaker and the Pro-Tem Speaker.
List-I
(a) Regular Speaker: constitutional basis
(b) Pro-Tem Speaker: constitutional basis
(c) Regular Speaker: selection mode
(d) Pro-Tem Speaker: appointing mode

List-II
(i) Article 95(1)
(ii) Appointed by the President
(iii) Article 93
(iv) Elected by Lok Sabha members
31.x: The regular Speaker rests on Article 93 and is elected by the House. The Pro-Tem Speaker rests on Article 95(1) and is appointed by the President. The answer is a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
31.tq: Discriminate the regular Speaker (Article 93) from the Pro-Tem Speaker (Article 95(1)).
n: The constitutional basis of the regular Speaker of the Lok Sabha is Article 93. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The regular Speaker of the Lok Sabha is elected by Lok Sabha members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Pro-Tem Speaker is appointed by the President under Article 95(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii** — option **(2)**.
**Regular Speaker:** **Article 93**, **elected** by Lok Sabha members.
**Pro-Tem Speaker:** **Article 95(1)**, **appointed by the President**.
xa: The Pro-Tem Speaker is usually the **senior-most** elected MP — a **convention**.
He **administers the oath** to new MPs and enables the **election of the regular Speaker**.
His office is **temporary** — ceases once the regular Speaker is elected.

31.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The Pro-Tem Speaker is usually the senior-most elected MP of the newly elected House.
Statement B: The office of the Pro-Tem Speaker continues after the regular Speaker is elected.

Which of the following is correct?
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
31.x: A is true: by convention, the Pro-Tem Speaker is usually the senior-most member of the new House. B is false because the office ends as soon as the regular Speaker is elected.
31.tq: Remember the Pro-Tem Speaker's office is temporary.
n: The Pro-Tem Speaker is usually the senior-most elected Member of Parliament of the newly elected House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Pro-Tem Speaker holds office temporarily. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Pro-Tem Speaker’s office ceases the moment the regular Speaker is elected. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The selection of a Pro-Tem Speaker follows a convention or practice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xs: **Statement A is true, Statement B is false** — option **(3)**.
A: the Pro-Tem Speaker is usually the **senior-most** elected MP of the new House (a **convention**).
B is wrong: the office is **temporary** and **ceases** the moment the regular Speaker is elected.
xa: Basis: **Article 95(1)**; **appointed by the President**.
He **administers the oath** to newly elected MPs.
The regular Speaker (**Article 93**) continues through dissolution till the new House meets.

31.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Pro-Tem Speaker is incorrect?
o: The Pro-Tem Speaker performs temporary functions until the regular Speaker is elected
The Pro-Tem Speaker is elected by the members of the newly elected Lok Sabha
The Pro-Tem Speaker is usually the senior-most elected MP of the newly elected House
The Pro-Tem Speaker is appointed by the President
31.x: Option B is incorrect: the Pro-Tem Speaker is appointed by the President under Article 95(1), not elected by the House. The Pro-Tem Speaker is usually the senior-most member and serves until the regular Speaker is elected.
31.tq: Discriminate appointment by the President from election by the House.
n: The Pro-Tem Speaker is appointed by the President under Article 95(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Pro-Tem Speaker is usually the senior-most elected Member of Parliament of the newly elected House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Pro-Tem Speaker holds office temporarily. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Pro-Tem Speaker’s office ceases the moment the regular Speaker is elected. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the Pro-Tem Speaker is **elected by the members of the newly elected Lok Sabha** — option **(2)**.
He is **appointed by the President** under **Article 95(1)**.
He is usually the **senior-most** elected MP and serves **temporarily** until the regular Speaker is elected.
xa: The **regular Speaker** is **elected** by Lok Sabha members under **Article 93**.
The Pro-Tem Speaker **presides** over and conducts the new Speaker's election.
The President **swears in** the Speaker Pro Tem.

31.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The regular Speaker administers oath to newly elected MPs.
Statement B: The Pro-Tem Speaker enables the election of the regular Speaker.

Which of the following is correct?
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
31.x: Statement A is false: the Pro-Tem Speaker, not the regular Speaker, swears in the newly elected MPs. Statement B is true: the Pro-Tem Speaker also conducts the election of the regular Speaker.
31.tq: Discriminate the Pro-Tem Speaker's two tasks from the regular Speaker's role.
n: The regular Speaker administers the oath to newly elected Members of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Pro-Tem Speaker enables the election of the regular Speaker. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xs: **Statement A is false, Statement B is true** — option **(4)**.
A is wrong: the **Pro-Tem Speaker**, not the regular Speaker, **administers the oath** to newly elected MPs.
B: the Pro-Tem Speaker enables the **election of the regular Speaker**.
xa: Pro-Tem Speaker: **Article 95(1)**; regular Speaker: **Article 93**.
Presiding officers take **no separate oath** — only the oath as **ordinary MPs**.
The President fixes the **date** of the Speaker's election.

31.s: Which of the following statements regarding removal of the Deputy Speaker is incorrect?
o: The Deputy Speaker may be removed by the Lok Sabha.
Removal requires a two-thirds special majority.
Fourteen days' notice is required for the removal resolution.
31.x: Option B is incorrect: removing the Deputy Speaker needs an effective majority (a majority of all the then members), not two-thirds, after 14 days' notice.
31.tq: Discriminate effective majority from special majority.
n: The Lok Sabha removes the Deputy Speaker by an effective majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
Removal of the Deputy Speaker requires fourteen days’ notice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
Removal of the Deputy Speaker requires a majority of all the then members of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The majority of all the then members of the Lok Sabha is called an effective majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
Removal of the Deputy Speaker does not require a simple majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
Removal of the Deputy Speaker does not require a two-thirds special majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
xs: The incorrect statement is that removal **requires a two-thirds special majority** — option **(2)**.
The Deputy Speaker is removed by the **Lok Sabha** by an **effective majority** — a **majority of all the then members**.
**Fourteen days'** notice is required.
xa: The Deputy Speaker resigns to the **Speaker** — **Article 94(b)**.
The RS **Deputy Chairman** is removed by an **effective majority** of the RS — **Article 90**.
The same **14 days'** notice applies to removing the **President**.

31.s:
How many of the following features are common to both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
1. Constitutional basis in Article 93
2. Election by the Lok Sabha from among its members
3. No separate oath of office as presiding officer
4. Continuation in office until the first meeting of the new Lok Sabha after dissolution
31.x: Three are common to both: Article 93, election by the House, and no separate oath. Only the Speaker stays in office after dissolution; the Deputy Speaker vacates at once.
31.tq: Find the feature that belongs only to the Speaker.
n: The Deputy Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha from among its sitting members under Article 93. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker does not take a separate oath of office as presiding officer. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker takes an oath only as an ordinary Member of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is constitutionally based on Article 93. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha from among its members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Speaker does not take a separate oath of office as presiding officer. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Speaker takes an oath only as a Member of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Speaker continues in office until the first meeting of the new Lok Sabha after dissolution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The constitutional protection of continuing in office after dissolution of the Lok Sabha applies only to the Speaker. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The constitutional protection of continuing in office after dissolution of the Lok Sabha does not apply to the Deputy Speaker. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
xs: **Three** features are common — option **(3)** **Only three**.
Both rest on **Article 93**, are **elected by the Lok Sabha** from its members, and take **no separate oath** as presiding officer.
Feature 4 applies **only to the Speaker** — the **Deputy Speaker** **vacates office immediately** on dissolution.
xa: The Speaker's election date is fixed by the **President**; the Deputy Speaker's by the **Speaker** (**Rule 8(1)**).
Each resigns to the other under **Article 94(b)**.
Both are removed by an **effective majority** after **14 days'** notice.

31.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Speaker's resignation
(b) Deputy Speaker's resignation
(c) Removal of the Speaker or the Deputy Speaker
(d) Speaker's office on dissolution of the Lok Sabha

List-II
(i) Effective majority of the Lok Sabha after 14 days' notice
(ii) Addressed to the Speaker
(iii) Addressed to the Deputy Speaker
(iv) Continues until just before the new House first meets
31.x: The Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker and the Deputy Speaker to the Speaker; either is removed by an effective majority after 14 days' notice; on dissolution the Speaker stays in office until just before the new House first meets.
31.tq: Remember that the two presiding officers resign to each other.
n: The Deputy Speaker addresses resignation to the Speaker under Article 94(b). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Speaker addresses resignation to the Deputy Speaker under Article 94(b). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Lok Sabha removes the Speaker by an effective majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Lok Sabha removes the Deputy Speaker by an effective majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
Removal of the Speaker requires fourteen days’ notice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
Removal of the Deputy Speaker requires fourteen days’ notice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
Removal of the Deputy Speaker requires a majority of all the then members of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The majority of all the then members of the Lok Sabha is called an effective majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv** — option **(2)**.
The **Speaker** resigns to the **Deputy Speaker**; the **Deputy Speaker** to the **Speaker** (**Article 94(b)**).
Removal of either: **effective majority** after **14 days'** notice.
On dissolution the **Speaker** continues until just before the new House **first meets**.
xa: ⚠ Neither resigns to the **President**.
The RS **Deputy Chairman** resigns to the **Chairman**.
The Deputy Speaker **vacates immediately** on dissolution.

31.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Constitutional basis of the office
(b) Resignation provisions
(c) Powers while presiding
(d) Proceedings concerning own removal

List-II
(i) Article 96
(ii) Article 94(b)
(iii) Article 93
(iv) Article 95
31.x: Article 93 provides the office, 94(b) resignation, 95 powers while presiding, and 96 the bar during one's own removal, so the answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
31.tq: Remember that Articles 93–96 run in order: office, vacating office, powers, removal.
n: The constitutional provisions governing the Deputy Speaker are Articles 93 to 96. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha from among its sitting members under Article 93. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker addresses resignation to the Speaker under Article 94(b). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker exercises the same powers as the Speaker when presiding over a sitting of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker cannot preside over the sitting during consideration of the Deputy Speaker’s own removal resolution, even if present in the House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i** — option **(4)**.
**Article 93:** the office (election of Speaker and Deputy Speaker); **Article 94(b):** **resignation**.
**Article 95:** powers while presiding; **Article 96:** proceedings on **own removal**.
xa: **Article 94(c):** removal by an **effective majority**.
**Article 95(1):** **Pro-Tem Speaker**.
**Art 97:** Speaker's salary charged on the **Consolidated Fund**.

31.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Deputy Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha from among its members.
Selection of the Deputy Speaker from the Opposition is a parliamentary convention.
The Constitution makes membership of the Opposition mandatory for the Deputy Speaker.
The Constitution does not mandate that the Deputy Speaker must belong to the Opposition.
31.x: Option C is incorrect: the Constitution does not require the Deputy Speaker to come from the Opposition. Choosing an Opposition member is only a parliamentary convention.
31.tq: Discriminate a convention from a constitutional requirement.
n: The Deputy Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha from among its sitting members under Article 93. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Constitution does not require the Deputy Speaker to belong to the Opposition. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The selection of the Deputy Speaker from the Opposition is a parliamentary convention or practice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The selection of the Deputy Speaker from the Opposition is not a mandatory constitutional requirement. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the **Constitution makes Opposition membership mandatory** for the Deputy Speaker — option **(3)**.
Choosing the Deputy Speaker **from the Opposition** is only a **convention**, **not** a constitutional requirement.
He is **elected** by the Lok Sabha from its sitting members (**Article 93**).
xa: The **LS Deputy Speaker post** has been **vacant since June 2019**.
It stayed empty through the **17th** and **18th** Lok Sabhas.
He is **not subordinate** to the Speaker.

31.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Powers while presiding
(b) Ruling while in the Chair
(c) Joint sitting when Speaker is absent
(d) Appointment to a Parliamentary Committee

List-II
(i) Deputy Speaker automatically becomes Chairman
(ii) Same powers as the Speaker
(iii) No appeal to the Speaker
(iv) Deputy Speaker presides
31.x: While presiding, the Deputy Speaker has the Speaker's powers, and their rulings cannot be appealed to the Speaker. The Deputy Speaker presides over joint sittings when the Speaker is absent and chairs any committee they are appointed to. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
31.tq: Recall each of the Deputy Speaker's special privileges.
n: The Deputy Speaker exercises the same powers as the Speaker when presiding over a sitting of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
There is no appeal to the Speaker against a ruling given by the Deputy Speaker while the Deputy Speaker is in the Chair. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker presides over joint sittings of Parliament when the Speaker is absent under Article 118(4). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker automatically becomes the chairman of any Parliamentary Committee to which the Deputy Speaker is appointed. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i** — option **(1)**.
In the Chair the Deputy Speaker has the **same powers as the Speaker**, with **no appeal** to the Speaker against his ruling.
He **presides** over a **joint sitting** when the Speaker is absent (**Article 118(4)**).
When appointed to a **Parliamentary Committee** he automatically becomes its **chairman**.
xa: After him, the **Deputy Chairman** of the Rajya Sabha presides at a joint sitting.
The Speaker's **Panel of Chairpersons** has up to **10** members.
RS equivalent: **Panel of Vice-Chairpersons** nominated by the **Chairman**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about the Deputy Speaker during normal proceedings when not in the Chair:
I. The Deputy Speaker sits as an ordinary member of the House.
II. The Deputy Speaker can participate in debates.
III. The Deputy Speaker can move motions and vote in the first instance.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
31.x: All three are correct: when not in the Chair, the Deputy Speaker is an ordinary member who can debate, move motions and vote in the first instance, unlike the Speaker.
31.tq: Contrast the Deputy Speaker's position off the Chair with the Speaker's.
n: The Deputy Speaker sits as an ordinary member of the House during normal proceedings when not in the Chair. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker can participate in debates during normal proceedings. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker can move motions during normal proceedings. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker can vote in the first instance during normal proceedings. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
xs: All three — **I, II and III** — are correct — option **(1)**.
When not in the Chair he sits as an **ordinary member**.
He can **participate in debates**, **move motions** and **vote in the first instance**.
xa: In his **own removal** resolution (**Article 96**) he **cannot preside** and has **no casting vote**.
The **Speaker** does **not** vote in the first instance in normal sittings.
The Deputy Speaker presides when the Speaker is **absent** or the office is **vacant**.

31.s: Who communicates the date of election of the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha to all members?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha
31.x: The Speaker fixes the Deputy Speaker's election date under Rule 8(1), and the Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha communicates it to all members.
31.tq: Discriminate who fixes the date from who communicates it.
n: The Secretary-General communicates the Deputy Speaker’s election date to all members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
xs: The **Secretary-General** of the Lok Sabha communicates the date — option **(4)**.
The date of the Deputy Speaker's election is **fixed by the Speaker** under **Rule 8(1)**.
The **Speaker's** own election date is fixed by the **President**.
xa: The **Secretary-General** heads each House's Secretariat; rank = **Cabinet Secretary**.
He is appointed by the **presiding officer** and is **independent of the executive**.
**Art 98:** each House has **separate secretarial staff**.

31.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Constitution mandates that Parliament must meet at least twice a year.
The maximum gap between two consecutive sessions cannot exceed six months.
The three-session pattern of Budget, Monsoon and Winter is a parliamentary convention.
The Constitution specifies a fixed number of parliamentary sessions every year.
31.x: Option D is incorrect: the Constitution sets no fixed number of sessions. It only sets a gap of at most six months (so at least two sessions a year); the Budget, Monsoon and Winter sessions are a convention.
31.tq: Discriminate the constitutional six-month rule from the three-session convention.
n: The maximum gap between two consecutive sessions of Parliament cannot exceed six months. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The Constitution mandates that Parliament must meet at least twice a year. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The Constitution does not specify a fixed number of parliamentary sessions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Having Budget, Monsoon, and Winter sessions is a parliamentary convention. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The maximum interval between two Parliamentary sessions is six months under Article 85. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Six months cannot intervene between the last sitting of one session and the date appointed for the first sitting of the next session. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The Constitution mandates only the maximum six-month gap between parliamentary sessions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the **Constitution specifies a fixed number of sessions** — option **(4)**.
**Article 85** only caps the gap between two sessions at **six months** — so Parliament meets at least **twice a year**.
The **Budget, Monsoon and Winter** sessions are a **convention**.
xa: **Budget** (Feb-May) is the **longest** session.
**States (Art 174):** same **six-month** rule.
State Assemblies averaged only **24 sittings** in **2025**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The Constitution prescribes a minimum number of sitting days for Parliament in a year.
Statement B: The three-session pattern of Budget, Monsoon and Winter is a constitutional mandate.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
31.x: Both are false: the Constitution prescribes no minimum number of sitting days, and the Budget, Monsoon and Winter sessions are a convention, not a mandate.
31.tq: Remember that Article 85 sets only the six-month limit.
n: Having Budget, Monsoon, and Winter sessions is a parliamentary convention. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The Constitution does not prescribe a minimum number of sitting days in a year. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The Constitution does not mandate three sessions named Budget, Monsoon, and Winter. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are false** — option **(2)**.
A is wrong: there is **no minimum number of sitting days** — not **60**, **90** or **100**.
B is wrong: the **Budget, Monsoon and Winter** pattern is a **convention**, not a constitutional mandate.
xa: **Article 85:** gap between sessions **not more than 6 months**.
The six-month gap runs from the **last sitting** of one session to the **first sitting** of the next.
**Monsoon** (Jul-Sep); **Winter** (Nov-Dec).

31.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Adjournment
(b) Adjournment sine die
(c) Prorogation
(d) Dissolution

List-II
(i) Ends the very life of the Lok Sabha
(ii) Terminates a session of the House
(iii) Suspends the work in a sitting for a specified time
(iv) Terminates the sitting indefinitely without naming a day for reassembly
31.x: Adjournment pauses a sitting for a set time, adjournment sine die ends it without naming a day, prorogation ends the session, and dissolution ends the Lok Sabha itself. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
31.tq: Rank the four by how much they end: sitting, session, House.
n: Adjournment suspends the work of a sitting for a specified time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Adjournment sine die terminates the sitting of the House indefinitely. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Adjournment sine die does not name a day for reassembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Prorogation terminates a session of the House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Dissolution ends the very life of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The specified period for an adjournment may be hours, days, or weeks. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i** — option **(3)**.
**Adjournment:** suspends a sitting for a specified time; **adjournment sine die:** ends it **indefinitely**, no day named.
**Prorogation:** **terminates the session**; **dissolution:** ends the **very life of the Lok Sabha**.
xa: Under adjournment sine die, pending bills **continue** to the next session.
On prorogation pending **bills are unaffected**; **notices lapse**.
On dissolution pending **bills, motions and resolutions lapse** (subject to **Article 107**).

31.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Adjournment
(b) Adjournment sine die
(c) Prorogation
(d) Dissolution

List-II
(i) President of India under Article 85(2)(b)
(ii) Presiding Officer, suspending a sitting for a specified time
(iii) President of India under Article 85(2)(a)
(iv) Presiding Officer, ending a sitting without naming a day of reassembly
31.x: The presiding officer adjourns a sitting for a set time and adjourns sine die without naming a day. The President prorogues under Article 85(2)(a) and dissolves the Lok Sabha under Article 85(2)(b). The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
31.tq: Separate presiding-officer actions from presidential ones, then use the clause numbers.
n: The Presiding Officer, namely the Speaker or Chairman, exercises adjournment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The Presiding Officer, namely the Speaker or Chairman, exercises adjournment sine die. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The President of India exercises prorogation under Article 85(2)(a). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The President of India exercises dissolution under Article 85(2)(b). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i** — option **(2)**.
**Adjournment** and **adjournment sine die** are by the **Presiding Officer**.
**Prorogation:** **President** under **Article 85(2)(a)**; **dissolution:** **President** under **Article 85(2)(b)**.
xa: ⚠ Adjournment / sine die = presiding officer; prorogation / dissolution = President.
The President prorogues on the advice of the **Council of Ministers** (**Governor** in States).
Only the **Lok Sabha** can be dissolved — the **Rajya Sabha** is permanent.

31.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Article 85 deals with the summoning and sessions of Parliament.
II. Article 123 specifies the maximum interval between two parliamentary sessions.
III. Article 85(2)(a) relates to prorogation.
IV. Article 85(2)(b) relates to dissolution.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
31.x: I, III and IV are correct: Article 85 covers summoning, 85(2)(a) prorogation and 85(2)(b) dissolution. II is false because the six-month gap is in Article 85; Article 123 is about ordinances.
31.tq: Check which Article each limit belongs to.
n: Article 85 governs the summoning of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The President of India exercises prorogation under Article 85(2)(a). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The President of India exercises dissolution under Article 85(2)(b). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The maximum interval between two Parliamentary sessions is six months under Article 85. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The maximum validity of an Ordinance after reassembly is six weeks under Article 123. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Six months cannot intervene between the last sitting of one session and the date appointed for the first sitting of the next session. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The Constitution mandates only the maximum six-month gap between parliamentary sessions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
xs: Statements **I, III and IV** are correct — option **(1)**.
I: **Article 85** deals with **summoning** and sessions.
III and IV: **Article 85(2)(a)** = **prorogation**; **Article 85(2)(b)** = **dissolution**.
II is wrong: the **six-month** maximum interval is in **Article 85**, not Article 123.
xa: **Article 86:** President may address either House and send **messages**.
**Article 87:** **special address** at the first session after each **general election** and of each year.
The President's address is debated on a **Motion of Thanks**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Dissolution ends the very life of the Lok Sabha.
II. Dissolution ends the very life of the Rajya Sabha.
III. The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House.
IV. Dissolution causes pending bills, motions and resolutions to lapse, subject to Article 107 rules.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
31.x: I, III and IV are correct: dissolution ends the Lok Sabha and its pending business lapses (subject to Article 107), but the Rajya Sabha is permanent. II is false because the Rajya Sabha is never dissolved.
31.tq: Find the statement that dissolves the permanent House.
n: Dissolution ends the very life of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Dissolution causes pending bills to lapse, subject to Article 107 rules. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Dissolution causes pending motions to lapse, subject to Article 107 rules. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
Dissolution causes pending resolutions to lapse, subject to Article 107 rules. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #64 · pp 170-172]
xs: Statements **I, III and IV** are correct — option **(4)**.
I: **dissolution** ends the **very life of the Lok Sabha**.
II is wrong / III correct: the **Rajya Sabha** is **permanent** and never dissolved.
IV: pending **bills, motions and resolutions lapse**, subject to **Article 107** rules.
xa: Dissolution is by the **President** under **Article 85(2)(b)**.
**Prorogation** ends only the **session**; pending bills are unaffected.
The **Speaker** continues after dissolution till the new House's **first meeting**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Removal of the President requires at least 14 days’ advance written notice.
II. Removal of the Lok Sabha Speaker or Deputy Speaker requires at least 14 days’ advance written notice.
III. Removal of the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman requires at least 14 days’ advance written notice.
IV. Removal of a Governor requires at least 14 days’ advance written notice.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
31.x: I, II and III are correct: removing the President, the Speaker or Deputy Speaker, or the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman needs 14 days' notice. IV is false because the President removes a Governor at pleasure, with no notice.
31.tq: Find the removal that needs no notice.
n: The President removes a Governor at pleasure under Article 156. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The removal of the President requires at least 14 days’ advance written notice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The removal of the Lok Sabha Speaker requires at least 14 days’ advance written notice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The removal of the Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker requires at least 14 days’ advance written notice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The removal of the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman requires at least 14 days’ advance written notice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The Governor of a State is removed without impeachment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The removal of the Lok Sabha Speaker requires 14 days’ notice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The removal of the Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker requires 14 days’ notice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The removal of the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman requires 14 days’ notice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
xs: Statements **I, II and III** are correct — option **(4)**.
**14 days'** advance written notice is needed to remove the **President**, the **Lok Sabha Speaker** and **Deputy Speaker**, and the **Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman**.
IV is wrong: no such notice is listed for removal of a **Governor**.
xa: Speaker and Deputy Speaker: removed by an **effective majority** — **Article 94**.
Deputy Chairman: **RS resolution** by an **effective majority** — **Article 90**.
The RS **Chairman** is removed only when removed as **Vice-President**.

31.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha take oath only as ordinary Members of Parliament.
Statement B: The Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha is removed by a Lok Sabha resolution passed by an effective majority.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
31.x: Both are true: the Speaker and Deputy Speaker take only the oath as MPs, and the Deputy Speaker is removed by a Lok Sabha resolution passed by effective majority.
31.tq: Recall the presiding officers' oath and removal rules.
n: The Speaker and Deputy Speaker take oath only as ordinary Members of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha is removed by a Lok Sabha resolution passed by an effective majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)**.
A: the **Speaker** and **Deputy Speaker** take **no separate oath** — only as **ordinary Members of Parliament**.
B: the **Deputy Speaker** is removed by a **Lok Sabha resolution** by an **effective majority**.
xa: The RS **Deputy Chairman** also takes oath only as an ordinary MP.
Removal needs **14 days'** notice.
The Deputy Chairman resigns to the **Chairman** of the Rajya Sabha.

31.s: Which of the following statements regarding eligibility for election as Speaker of the Lok Sabha is incorrect?
o: Membership of the Lok Sabha is required at the time of election.
A non-member may be chosen as Speaker under the six-month relaxation rule.
The Speaker is elected from among the sitting members of the Lok Sabha.
The person must already be an elected Member of the Lok Sabha.
31.x: Option B is incorrect. There is no six-month relaxation for the Speaker, who must already be an elected Lok Sabha member when chosen. That relaxation applies only to Ministers.
31.tq: Discriminate the Minister's six-month rule from the Speaker's eligibility.
n: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is elected by the Lok Sabha from among its sitting members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha must already be an elected Member of Parliament at the time of election. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
A non-member cannot be chosen as Speaker under the six-month relaxation rule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xs: The incorrect statement is that a **non-member may be chosen as Speaker under the six-month relaxation rule** — option **(2)**.
The Speaker is elected from among the **sitting members** (**Article 93**).
He must already be an **elected MP** — the six-month relaxation does not apply.
xa: The **date** of the Speaker's election is fixed by the **President**.
The Speaker takes **no separate oath** as presiding officer.
He **vacates office** on ceasing to be a member (**Art 94**).

31.s: The Lok Sabha Secretariat functions directly under the control and guidance of the:
o: Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
31.x: The Lok Sabha Secretariat works directly under the Speaker's control and guidance, not under the executive, which keeps the House independent.
31.tq: Recall who controls each House's secretariat.
n: The Lok Sabha Secretariat functions directly under the control and guidance of the Speaker. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xs: The **Lok Sabha Secretariat** works under the **Speaker of the Lok Sabha** — option **(2)**.
It functions under the Speaker's **control and guidance**, **independent of the executive**.
The **Rajya Sabha Secretariat** is under the **Chairman**.
xa: **Art 98:** each House has a **separate secretarial staff**; posts **common to both Houses** may be created.
Head: the **Secretary-General**, appointed by the presiding officer.
Until Parliament legislates, recruitment rules are made by the **President** after consulting Speaker/Chairman.

31.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

(b) Absence of the Speaker at a joint sitting
