31.x: The Speaker presides over a joint sitting (Article 118(4)), then the Deputy Speaker, then the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman. Money Bill certification is under Article 110(4). The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
31.tq: Recall the order of who presides over a joint sitting.
n: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 110. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 118. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker is the sole and final authority to certify whether a Bill is a Money Bill under Article 110(4). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker presides over joint sittings of both Houses of Parliament under Article 118(4). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
In the absence of the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker presides over a joint sitting before the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii** — option **(3)**.
The **Speaker** presides over a **joint sitting** (**Article 118(4)**); in his absence the **Deputy Speaker**.
On further absence, the **Deputy Chairman** of the Rajya Sabha presides.
**Money Bill** certification: **Article 110(4)**.
xa: ⚠ Sources differ: other notes put the Speaker's Money Bill final say under **Art 110(3)**.
Joint sitting is provided in **Art 108**.
The Speaker's certificate is **final** when the Bill goes to the **Rajya Sabha** and the **President**.

31.s: The constitutional provisions governing the Speaker of the Lok Sabha are contained in which one of the following groups of Articles?
31.x: The Speaker is covered by Articles 93–96 (election, vacation, removal), 100 (casting vote), 110 (Money Bill certificate) and 118 (joint sitting rules).
31.tq: Recall the Speaker's Articles: 93–96, 100, 110 and 118.
n: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is governed under Part V of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 93. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 94. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 95. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 96. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 100. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 110. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 118. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xs: The Speaker is governed by **Articles 93–96, 100, 110 and 118** — option **(3)**.
**Article 93:** election; **94:** resignation and removal; **96:** own removal resolution.
**100:** casting vote; **110:** Money Bill certification; **118:** joint sitting.
xa: **Art 97:** salary charged on the **Consolidated Fund**.
**Art 122:** the Speaker's rulings are **protected**.
**Kihoto Hollohan (1992):** Tenth Schedule decisions subject to **judicial review**.

31.s:

n: G. V. Mavalankar was the first Speaker of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
G. V. Mavalankar served as Speaker from 1952 to 1956. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
Meira Kumar was the first woman Speaker of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
Sumitra Mahajan was the second woman Speaker of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv** — option **(1)**.
**G.V. Mavalankar** was the **first** Speaker — **1952 to 1956**.
**Meira Kumar:** **first woman** Speaker (**15th** LS, **2009 to 2014**); **Sumitra Mahajan:** **second** (**16th** LS, **2014 to 2019**).

31.s:
How many of the following are functions or powers associated with the Speaker of the Lok Sabha?

1. Adjournment sine die
2. Deciding disqualification questions under the Tenth Schedule
3. Fixing the date for election of the Deputy Speaker
4. Appointment of the Pro-Tem Speaker
31.x: Three are the Speaker's: adjourning sine die, deciding Tenth Schedule disqualifications, and fixing the Deputy Speaker's election date. The President, not the Speaker, appoints the Pro-Tem Speaker.
31.tq: Find the item done by the President.
n: The Speaker exercises adjournment sine die. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker decides questions of member disqualification arising out of defection under the Tenth Schedule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker fixes the date for the election of the Deputy Speaker under Rule 8(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Pro-Tem Speaker is appointed by the President under Article 95(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xs: **Three** of them are the Speaker's — option **(3)** **Only three**.
The Speaker orders **adjournment sine die** and decides **Tenth Schedule** disqualifications.
He fixes the **Deputy Speaker's** election date (**Rule 8(1)**).
The **Pro-Tem Speaker** is **appointed by the President**, not the Speaker.
xa: The Speaker recognises the **Leader of the Opposition** — party needs **one-tenth** of the House.
He **appoints committee chairmen**.
He adjourns or suspends a sitting when there is **no quorum** (**one-tenth**).

31.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Speaker's certification of a Money Bill is incorrect?
o: The Speaker's endorsement is final when the Bill is presented to the President
The Speaker's endorsement is final when the Bill is transmitted to the Rajya Sabha
The Rajya Sabha may overrule the Speaker's certification by a simple majority
The Speaker is the sole authority to certify whether a Bill is a Money Bill
31.x: Option C is incorrect. Under Article 110(4), the Speaker alone certifies a Money Bill, and the certificate is final when the Bill goes to the Rajya Sabha and to the President. The Rajya Sabha cannot overrule it.
31.tq: Remember that the Speaker's Money Bill certificate is final.
n: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is covered by Article 110. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker is the sole and final authority to certify whether a Bill is a Money Bill under Article 110(4). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker’s Money Bill endorsement is final when the Bill is transmitted to the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
The Speaker’s Money Bill endorsement is final when the Bill is presented to the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 153-156]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the **Rajya Sabha may overrule** the Speaker's certification — option **(3)**.
Under **Article 110(4)** the Speaker is the **sole and final** authority to certify a **Money Bill**.
The endorsement is **final** when the Bill goes to the **Rajya Sabha** and to the **President**.
xa: ⚠ Sources differ: other notes cite **Art 110(3)** for the Speaker's final say.
The Speaker also presides over a **joint sitting** (**Art 118(4)**).
His **anti-defection** decisions, unlike this, are subject to **judicial review**.

31.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Date of election of Speaker
(b) Date of election of Deputy Speaker
(c) Resignation of Speaker
(d) Resignation of Deputy Speaker

List-II
(i) Addressed to the Speaker
(ii) Addressed to the Deputy Speaker
(iii) Fixed by the President
(iv) Fixed by the Speaker
31.x: The President fixes the Speaker's election date and the Speaker fixes the Deputy Speaker's. Each resigns to the other, so the answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
31.tq: Pair the dates first, then the cross-addressed resignations.
n: The date of election of the Deputy Speaker is fixed by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha under Rule 8(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The President fixes the date of election of the Speaker. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker addresses resignation to the Speaker under Article 94(b). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Speaker addresses resignation to the Deputy Speaker under Article 94(b). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i** — option **(4)**.

The **Speaker** resigns to the **Deputy Speaker**; the **Deputy Speaker** to the **Speaker** (**Article 94(b)**).

31.s:
Consider the following statements regarding consideration of a resolution for the Deputy Speaker's own removal:
I. The Deputy Speaker cannot preside over the sitting.
II. The Deputy Speaker has the right to speak and participate.
III. The Deputy Speaker can vote in the first instance.
IV. The Deputy Speaker can exercise a casting vote in case of equality of votes.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
31.x: I, II and III are correct: during their own removal, the Deputy Speaker cannot preside but may speak, take part and vote in the first instance. IV is false because no casting vote is allowed then.
31.tq: Find the statement giving a casting vote in removal proceedings.
n: The Deputy Speaker cannot preside over the sitting during consideration of the Deputy Speaker’s own removal resolution, even if present in the House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker has the right to speak during consideration of the Deputy Speaker’s own removal resolution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker has the right to participate during consideration of the Deputy Speaker’s own removal resolution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker has the right to vote in the first instance during consideration of the Deputy Speaker’s own removal resolution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker cannot exercise a casting vote when votes are equally divided during consideration of the Deputy Speaker’s own removal resolution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
The Deputy Speaker can speak and vote in the first instance during consideration of the Deputy Speaker’s removal under Article 96. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 156-158]
xs: Statements **I, II and III** are correct — option **(2)**.
In his **own removal** resolution (**Article 96**) the Deputy Speaker **cannot preside** even if present.
He can **speak, participate** and **vote in the first instance**.
IV is wrong: **no casting vote** when votes are equally divided.
xa: The **Speaker** is under the same rule during his own removal.
⚠ The RS **Chairman** during his removal **cannot vote**, but may speak.
Removal needs an **effective majority** after **fourteen days'** notice.

31.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The date for the election of the Deputy Speaker is fixed by the Speaker.
Statement B: The date for the election of the Deputy Speaker is notified by the Secretary-General.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
31.x: Both are true: under Rule 8(1), the Speaker fixes the date of the Deputy Speaker's election and the Secretary-General notifies it to members.
31.tq: Discriminate who fixes the date from who notifies it.
n: The date for the election of the Deputy Speaker is fixed by the Speaker. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 72-75]
The date for the election of the Deputy Speaker is notified by the Secretary-General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 72-75]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)**.
A: the **Speaker** fixes the Deputy Speaker's election date under **Rule 8(1)**.
B: the **Secretary-General** communicates it to members.
xa: The **Speaker's** own election date is fixed by the **President**.
The Deputy Speaker is elected from the House's **sitting members** (**Article 93**).
From the **Opposition** only by **convention**.

32.s: Which of the following is NOT included among the recognised tools of parliamentary control over the executive?
o: Judicial review by the Supreme Court
32.x: Judicial review is a constitutional function of the judiciary, not a parliamentary device listed among the tools of legislative control over the executive.
32.tq: Separate parliamentary control devices from mechanisms belonging to another constitutional organ.
xs: **Judicial review by the Supreme Court** is NOT a tool of parliamentary control — so option **(4)** is correct.
The recognised tools include **Question Hour**, **Zero Hour**, **half-an-hour discussion**, short-duration discussion, **calling attention**, adjournment, censure and no-confidence motions.
**Budget approval** and the **Motion of Thanks** are also listed tools, so options (1), (2) and (3) are all genuine devices.
xa: The **committee system** is also a tool: Government Assurances, Petitions, Subordinate Legislation, **PAC** and **Estimates**.
⚠ Order of Indian firsts: **1953** short-duration discussion – **1954** calling attention – **1962** Zero Hour.
**States** use the same devices plus estimates and public accounts committees.

32.s: Which one of the following correctly compares the devices used by Parliament and State Legislatures for controlling the executive?
o: State Legislatures cannot use Question Hour or motions
Parliament alone uses these devices; State Legislatures use only debates
State Legislatures use the same devices, along with estimates and public accounts committees
State Legislatures use only the no-confidence motion
32.x: State Legislatures use the same parliamentary devices for executive control and also use estimates and public accounts committees.
32.tq: Test the Union–State comparison by identifying the correct extension rather than an exclusive claim.
xs: **State Legislatures use the same devices**, along with **estimates and public accounts committees** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Hence options saying States cannot use Question Hour, use only debates, or use only the no-confidence motion are all wrong.
xa: The Union tools: Question Hour, Zero Hour, half-an-hour and short-duration discussions, and **calling attention**, **adjournment**, **censure** and **no-confidence** motions.
Committees: **Government Assurances**, **Petitions**, **Subordinate Legislation**, **PAC**, **Estimates**; plus **Budget approval** and the **Motion of Thanks**.
The **AP Legislature** uses the same devices — e.g., the AP Legislative Council was adjourned amid a Question Hour row on the **Tirumala laddu** issue (**Feb 2026**).

32.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Question to a private member — Blue paper
32.x: A question addressed to a private member is printed on yellow paper, not blue paper. Starred, unstarred and short-notice questions are associated with green, white and light pink paper respectively.
32.tq: Use the comparison table to locate the single altered colour designation.
xs: **Question to a private member — Blue paper** is wrongly matched — so option **(4)** is correct; it is printed on **yellow** paper.
The other pairs are right: short-notice = **light pink**, starred = **green**, unstarred = **white**.
xa: ⚠ Starred = **oral + green**; unstarred = **written + white**.
A question to a private member is on **his bill/resolution** and may get an **oral or written** answer.
Short-notice questions allow **supplementaries** and get an **oral** answer.

32.s: A short-notice question differs from an ordinary question in that it may be admitted when notice is given:
o: Only on the day of the sitting
At least 15 clear days in advance
32.x: A short-notice question is one for which notice is given less than 10 days in advance. Ordinary questions require at least 15 clear days' notice.
32.tq: Discriminate between the two notice thresholds instead of treating all questions alike.
xs: A short-notice question may be admitted on notice of **less than 10 days** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**At least 15 clear days'** notice is for **ordinary** questions, so option (2) is wrong.
xa: A short-notice question must be on a matter of **urgent public importance** and gets an **oral answer**.
It is printed on **light pink** paper; supplementaries are allowed.
**Zero Hour** matters need **no prior notice** of the kind a question needs — only same-day intimation to the Presiding Officer.

32.s: Which of the following is considered the most effective method of day-to-day vigilance over the executive?
32.x: Question Hour is regarded as the most effective method of day-to-day vigilance over the executive because Ministers are required to answer questions.
32.tq: Match the parliamentary device with its principal accountability function.
xs: **Question Hour** is the most effective method of **day-to-day** vigil on the executive — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is held in the **first hour** of every sitting, when ministers answer searching questions.
**Motion of Thanks** and **Budget approval** are also tools, but not the day-to-day vigil; **yielding the floor** is just a member giving way to another member or the Chair.
xa: ⚠ The **no-confidence motion** is the **most powerful weapon** of executive accountability (APPSC-G2 2025) — do not confuse with Question Hour.
Starred questions get **oral** answers; unstarred get **written** answers.
Question Hour ran only **60%** of its scheduled time in recent criticism.

32.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the status of Zero Hour in the Indian Parliament?
o: It is a device borrowed from the British Parliament
It is mentioned in the Rules of Procedure of both Houses
It is an informal parliamentary innovation and is not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure
It is expressly mentioned in the Constitution
32.x: Zero Hour is an informal Indian innovation. It is not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure and has been in use since 1962; it was not borrowed from another country.
32.tq: Distinguish a formal constitutional or rule-based device from an informal parliamentary practice.
xs: Zero Hour is an **informal** device **not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It is an **Indian innovation**, not borrowed from any other country, so option (1) is wrong; it is in neither the Rules nor the Constitution.
xa: In use since **1962**.
In the **Lok Sabha** it starts **immediately after Question Hour**; in the **Rajya Sabha** it precedes Question Hour.
Ministers are **not bound to reply** to Zero Hour matters.
⚠ Indian innovations: short-duration discussion **1953**, calling attention **1954**, Zero Hour **1962**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Zero Hour:
1. It has no fixed duration prescribed in the Rules.
2. It continues until the regular business of the day is taken up in the Lok Sabha.
3. A member must give the same prior notice as is required for an ordinary question.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Zero Hour has no fixed duration in the Rules and in the Lok Sabha lasts until the day's regular agenda is taken up. Members do not give the prior notice required for an ordinary question; they intimate the Presiding Officer on the same day.
32.tq: Test the distinction between same-day intimation for Zero Hour and formal prior notice for questions.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: correct — Zero Hour has **no fixed duration** in the rules.
Statement 2: correct — in the Lok Sabha it lasts **until regular business is taken up**.
Statement 3: wrong — Zero Hour is **without the prior notice** a question needs; members only intimate the Presiding Officer the **same day**.
xa: Zero Hour is an **Indian innovation** in use since **1962**, not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure.
Ministers are **not bound to reply**.
Follow-up: the **Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs** sends extracts of the Chair's directions to the ministry concerned for action.

32.s: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of matters raised during Zero Hour?
o: The Presiding Officer decides which members may be allowed to raise them
Members may raise them without the prior notice required for a question
Ministers are constitutionally bound to give an immediate reply
They concern urgent matters of public importance
32.x: Ministers are not bound to reply to matters raised during Zero Hour. The other features correctly describe the procedure.
32.tq: Find the single statement that reverses a procedural limitation.
xs: **Ministers constitutionally bound to give an immediate reply** is NOT a feature — so option **(3)** is correct; ministers are **not bound to reply** in Zero Hour.
The rest are true: members raise matters **without prior notice**, and the **Presiding Officer decides** whom to allow.
xa: Zero Hour starts **immediately after Question Hour** in the Lok Sabha.
It is informal and **not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure**; in use since **1962**.
Chair's directions / assurances → **Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs** forwards them to the ministry concerned.

32.s: In the Lok Sabha, the time immediately following the Question Hour, during which members raise matters of urgent public importance without the prior notice required for questions, is known as
32.x: Zero Hour begins immediately after Question Hour in the Lok Sabha; members raise matters with only same-day intimation to the Presiding Officer, not the notice a question needs. Calling Attention, half-an-hour and short-duration discussions are formal devices under the Rules that require prior notice.
32.tq: After Question Hour + no prior notice + not in the Rules = Zero Hour (since 1962).
xs: The time right after Question Hour when matters are raised without prior notice is **Zero Hour** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Calling attention** seeks an authoritative statement from a minister; **half-an-hour discussion** is for factual elucidation; **short-duration discussion** is under **Rule 193** with no vote.
xa: Exam angle: this exact stem appeared in **APPSC-GS 2025** and **G2 2023, 2025**.
Zero Hour is an **Indian innovation** (**1962**), not in the Rules of Procedure.
Ministers are **not bound to reply**; the Presiding Officer decides whom to allow.

32.s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?

1. Rule 377, Lok Sabha — Matters not raisable under any other device
2. Special Mentions, Rajya Sabha — Equivalent device to Rule 377 matters
3. Rule 193, Lok Sabha — Short-duration discussion without voting
4. Rule 184, Lok Sabha — Discussion followed by voting

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
32.x: All four pairs are correct. Rule 377 and Special Mentions serve corresponding purposes in the two Houses, while Rules 193 and 184 distinguish discussions without and with voting respectively.
32.tq: Start with rule-number pairs and then confirm the presence or absence of voting.
xs: All four pairs are correct — **1, 2, 3 and 4**, option **(4)**.
**Rule 377 (LS)** = matters not raisable under any other device; the Rajya Sabha equivalent is **Special Mentions** (Rule **180A-E**).
**Rule 193** = short-duration discussion, **no voting**; **Rule 184** = discussion followed by a **vote**.
xa: **Rule 198 (LS)** = no-confidence motion.
Privilege motion = **Rule 222 (LS)**, **Rule 187 (RS)**.
Short-duration discussion: max **2 hours**; Indian innovation (**1953**).

32.s:
Arrange the following parliamentary discussion devices in chronological order of their introduction or institutional association:
A. Calling Attention
B. Short-duration discussion
C. Zero Hour

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
32.x: Short-duration discussion is an Indian innovation of 1953, Calling Attention dates from 1954, and Zero Hour is associated with 1962. Therefore, the correct order is B, A, C.
32.tq: Place the dated devices first and compare the closely spaced years 1953, 1954 and 1962.
xs: The order is **B, A, C** — option **(2)**.
**Short-duration discussion** **1953** → **Calling attention** **1954** → **Zero Hour** **1962**.
xa: All three are **Indian innovations**; Zero Hour was not borrowed from any other country.
Short-duration discussion is under **Rule 193**, max **2 hours**, no voting.
Calling attention is **in the Rules of Procedure**; Zero Hour is **not**.

32.s:
A Short-duration Discussion in the Lok Sabha has which of the following features?
1. It is limited to a maximum of two hours.
2. It is an Indian innovation of 1953.
3. It necessarily ends with a formal vote.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
32.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because a short-duration discussion does not involve voting.
32.tq: Identify the duration and origin while rejecting the false voting consequence.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: correct — maximum **2 hours**.
Statement 2: correct — an **Indian innovation** of **1953**.
Statement 3: wrong — under **Rule 193** there is **no voting**.
xa: ⚠ **Rule 184** = discussion followed by a vote.
**Half-an-hour discussion**: matter sufficiently debated needing factual elucidation; no formal motion or vote.
Next Indian innovations: calling attention **1954**, Zero Hour **1962**.

32.s: A half-an-hour discussion is intended for:
o: A matter that can be raised only through a No-confidence Motion
A demand for grant requiring reduction by Rs 100
A matter already sufficiently debated but requiring factual elucidation
A breach of privilege requiring immediate suspension of the House
32.x: A half-an-hour discussion is held on a matter that has been sufficiently debated but requires further factual elucidation. It involves no formal motion or vote.
32.tq: Apply the purpose of the device to a scenario requiring clarification rather than a fresh decision.
xs: A half-an-hour discussion is for **a matter sufficiently debated but needing factual elucidation** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It has **no formal motion or vote**.
Reducing a demand by **Rs 100** is a **token cut**; a breach of privilege goes by a **privilege motion** — so options (2) and (4) are wrong.
xa: **Short-duration discussion** (Rule **193**): max **2 hours**, no vote, Indian innovation of **1953**.
**Rule 184** discussion ends in a vote.
**Rule 377 (LS)** covers matters not raisable under any other device.

32.s: An Adjournment Motion in Parliament can be admitted only when it concerns:
o: A demand for grant requiring reduction by one rupee
Any matter raised without prior notice
A matter of definite and urgent public importance
32.x: An Adjournment Motion sets aside the normal business of the House to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance.
32.tq: Match the motion with its defining procedural condition rather than with a related device.
xs: An Adjournment Motion concerns **a definite matter of urgent public importance** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It sets aside the House business to discuss that matter.
Reducing a demand to **Re 1** is a **policy cut**; matters raised without prior notice belong to **Zero Hour**.
xa: It is moved **only in the Lok Sabha** with **50 members'** support.
It carries an **element of censure**; debate lasts at least **2 h 30 min**.
⚠ Adjournment and no-confidence are both **Lok Sabha only** and both need **50 members**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about an Adjournment Motion:
1. The debate on it lasts not less than two hours and thirty minutes.
2. It must relate to a single, definite matter of recent occurrence, cannot raise a question of privilege, and only one is allowed per sitting.
3. It needs the support of 50 members for admission.
4. It can be moved in either House of Parliament.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statement 4 is wrong: an Adjournment Motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha. Statement 3 is correct: it needs 50 members' support. Statement 2 is correct: single, definite, specific, recent matter; no question of privilege; one per sitting. Statement 1 is correct: debate lasts at least 2 h 30 min. Hence '1, 2 and 3 only'.
32.tq: Adjournment and no-confidence motions: both Lok Sabha only, both need 50 members.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
1: debate on an **Adjournment Motion** lasts at least **2 h 30 min**.
2: it must be a **single**, **definite**, **specific** matter of **recent** occurrence; no **question of privilege**; only **one** per sitting.
3: it needs **50 members**' support; 4 is wrong: it is **Lok Sabha only**.
xa: It **interrupts / suspends** normal business and involves **censure** of the Government.
It is admissible only when other tools, e.g. **Short Duration** discussions, are too late.
⚠ Adjournment and no-confidence motions → both **Lok Sabha only**, both need **50 members**.

32.s: Which one of the following motions is available in both Houses and seeks an authoritative statement from a Minister?
32.x: A Calling Attention Motion is available in both Houses and seeks an authoritative statement from the concerned Minister.
32.tq: Use the combination of House availability and procedural purpose to identify the motion.
xs: The **Calling Attention Motion** is used in both Houses and seeks an **authoritative statement** from a minister — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Adjournment** and **no-confidence** motions are **Lok Sabha only**; **cut motions** are on demands for grants in the Lok Sabha.
xa: Calling attention is an **Indian innovation** since **1954**, included in the **Rules of Procedure**.
It draws a minister's attention to a matter of **urgent public importance**.
**Privilege motions** are also in both Houses — **Rule 222 (LS)**, **Rule 187 (RS)**.

32.s: The Calling Attention procedure is significant because it is:
o: An Indian innovation introduced in 1962 but not included in the Rules
An Indian innovation introduced in 1954 and included in the Rules of Procedure
32.x: Calling Attention is an Indian innovation dating from 1954 and is provided for in the Rules of Procedure.
32.tq: Discriminate between the dates and rule status of Calling Attention and Zero Hour.
xs: Calling attention is **an Indian innovation of 1954 included in the Rules of Procedure** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is not British (option 1); **1962** with no place in the Rules describes **Zero Hour** (option 3).
xa: It draws a minister's attention to a matter of **urgent public importance** and seeks an **authoritative statement**.
Used in **both Houses**.
⚠ **1953** short-duration – **1954** calling attention – **1962** Zero Hour.

32.s:
Match the following types of cut motions with their purposes:

List-I (Cut motion)
A. Policy cut
B. Economy cut
C. Token cut

List-II (Purpose or amount)
1. Reduction by a specified amount to effect economy
2. Reduction of the demand to Re 1 to express disapproval of policy
3. Reduction by Rs 100 to ventilate a specific grievance

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
32.x: A policy cut reduces the demand to Re 1, an economy cut reduces it by a specified amount, and a token cut reduces it by Rs 100 to raise a specific grievance.
32.tq: Start from the distinctive numerical values—Re 1 and Rs 100—and then identify the remaining pair.
xs: **Policy cut** = reduce demand to **Re 1** → disapproval of policy.
**Economy cut** = reduce by a **specified amount**; **token cut** = reduce by **Rs 100** → a specific grievance.
xa: Cut motions are moved on **demands for grants** in the **Lok Sabha**.
**Budget approval** is one of the listed tools of parliamentary control.
The **Estimates Committee** suggests economies and efficiency in the estimates.

32.s: A privilege motion, moved when a member feels that a minister or member has committed a breach of privilege, is raised in the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha respectively under
32.x: A privilege motion is governed by Rule 222 of the Lok Sabha rules and Rule 187 of the Rajya Sabha rules. Rule 184 (LS) is a discussion followed by a vote, Rule 193 (LS) is a short-duration discussion without a vote, Rule 180A-E (RS) covers Special Mentions, and Rule 198 (LS) is the no-confidence motion.
32.tq: Privilege: LS 222 / RS 187. No-confidence: LS 198.
xs: A privilege motion is under **Rule 222** (LS) and **Rule 187** (RS) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Rule 184** = discussion with vote; **Rule 193** = short-duration discussion; **Rule 180A-E** = Special Mentions (RS); **Rule 198** = no-confidence motion.
xa: A privilege motion concerns a **breach of privilege** by a minister or member and is available in **both Houses**.
A privilege notice was given in the Rajya Sabha against the **Union Education Minister** (**May 2026**).
Committee of Privileges: **15** members (LS, by the Speaker); **10** (RS, by the Chairman).

32.s:
With reference to a no-confidence motion, consider the following statements:
1. It is expressly mentioned in the Constitution.
2. Its constitutional basis is connected with Article 75(3).
3. It may be moved only in the Lok Sabha.
4. It requires the support of 50 members for leave to be granted.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: A no-confidence motion is not expressly mentioned in the Constitution. It flows from Article 75(3), is moved only in the Lok Sabha, and requires the support of 50 members for leave.
32.tq: Trap the incorrect constitutional-status statement while checking House, support and Article details separately.
xs: Statements **2, 3 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: wrong — it is **not mentioned in the Constitution**.
Statement 2: correct — it flows from **Article 75(3)**, collective responsibility to the **Lok Sabha**.
Statements 3 and 4: correct — **only in the Lok Sabha**, with **50 members** for leave.
xa: Moved under **Rule 198**; **no reasons need be stated**.
If passed, the whole **Council of Ministers must resign**.
First instance: against **Nehru** (**1963**) by **J.B. Kripalani**.

32.s: Which one of the following statements about a no-confidence motion is correct?
o: Reasons for moving it must necessarily be stated
It can be moved in either House of Parliament
It can be moved only by the Leader of the Opposition
32.x: The Speaker exercises discretion in admitting or rejecting a no-confidence motion. Reasons need not be stated, and the motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha.
32.tq: Apply the 'who would do this job?' test to distinguish the Speaker's procedural role from political roles.
xs: **The Speaker decides its admissibility** — he has **discretion to admit or reject** it — so option **(4)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025 key).
**No reasons need be stated** (option 1 wrong); it is moved **only in the Lok Sabha** (option 2 wrong).
Leave needs the support of **50 members**, not just the Leader of the Opposition.
xa: ⚠ Trap: the Speaker does **not resign or dissolve** the House.
It is the **most powerful weapon** of executive accountability (APPSC-G2 2025).
⚠ "Reasons must be stated" = **censure motion**.

32.s: The first no-confidence motion against the Union Council of Ministers was moved against Jawaharlal Nehru in 1963 by:
32.x: The first no-confidence motion against Jawaharlal Nehru was moved in 1963 by J.B. Kripalani.
32.tq: Link the event, year and mover rather than relying on the event alone.
xs: The first no-confidence motion, against **Nehru** in **1963**, was moved by **J.B. Kripalani** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Gouthu Latchanna** moved the motion against the **Prakasam** ministry in **Andhra State** (Nov **1954**).
xa: The Andhra motion was carried **69 for, 68 against**; the ministry fell after **13 months**.
President's Rule followed: **16 Nov 1954 - 27 Mar 1955**.
No-confidence is moved under **Rule 198** with **50 members'** support.

32.s: Which of the following correctly describes the no-confidence motion moved against the Andhra State ministry in November 1954?
o: It was moved by Gouthu Latchanna and carried by 69 votes to 68
It was moved by Gouthu Latchanna and defeated by 68 votes to 69
It was moved by J.B. Kripalani and defeated by 69 votes to 68
It resulted in the continuation of the Prakasam ministry for five years
32.x: Gouthu Latchanna's motion in November 1954 was carried by 69 votes to 68. The Prakasam ministry consequently fell after 13 months.
32.tq: Use the vote margin and mover together to avoid swapping a closely related historical instance.
xs: It was moved by **Gouthu Latchanna** and **carried by 69 votes to 68** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **Prakasam** ministry fell by one vote after **13 months**, so option (4) is wrong; **J.B. Kripalani** moved the first one against Nehru (**1963**).
xa: President's Rule in Andhra State: **16 Nov 1954 - 27 Mar 1955**.
A passed no-confidence motion forces the whole **Council of Ministers** to resign.
Constitutional basis: **Article 75(3)** — collective responsibility.

32.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A Censure Motion may be directed against a Minister, a group of Ministers or the whole Council of Ministers.
2. A No-confidence Motion is directed against the entire Council of Ministers.
3. Passing a Censure Motion compels the Council of Ministers to resign.
4. Passing a No-confidence Motion requires the Council of Ministers to resign.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 3 is false because passing a Censure Motion does not compel resignation, whereas passing a No-confidence Motion does.
32.tq: Find the single reversed consequence in a comparison table.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: correct — censure may target the **Council of Ministers, a minister or a group**.
Statement 2: correct — no-confidence targets the **entire Council of Ministers**.
Statement 3: wrong — after censure ministers are **not bound to resign**; Statement 4: correct — after no-confidence they **must resign**.
xa: Censure **must state reasons**; no-confidence needs **no reasons**.
Censure seeks **disapproval of a policy**.
No-confidence: **only in Lok Sabha**, **50 members**, **Rule 198**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The no-confidence motion is regarded as the most powerful weapon for enforcing the accountability of the executive.
2. A censure motion must state the reasons for its adoption in the Lok Sabha.
3. A no-confidence motion must state the grounds on which it is based.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statement 1 is correct: the no-confidence motion is the most powerful weapon of executive accountability, while Question Hour is the most effective day-to-day vigil. Statement 2 is correct: a censure motion must state its reasons. Statement 3 is wrong: a no-confidence motion need not state any reasons. Hence 1 and 2 only.
32.tq: Reasons must be stated = censure; no reasons needed = no-confidence.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: correct — no-confidence is the **most powerful weapon** of executive accountability (APPSC-G2 2025).
Statement 2: correct — a censure motion **must state reasons**.
Statement 3: wrong — a no-confidence motion needs **no reasons**.
xa: ⚠ **Question Hour** = most effective **day-to-day** vigil; no-confidence = most powerful weapon.
The **Speaker** has discretion to admit or reject a no-confidence motion.
Censure can be against a **minister or a group**; no-confidence only the **entire** Council.

32.s:
With reference to resolutions in Parliament, consider the following statements:
1. The mover may withdraw a resolution at any time without the leave of the House.
2. A resolution must be put to vote.
3. A resolution is a self-contained proposal and is always a substantive motion.
4. A resolution on the same subject is barred for one year.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statement 3 is correct: a resolution is self-contained and always a substantive motion. Statement 1 is wrong: the mover cannot withdraw it without the leave of the House. Statement 2 is correct: it must be put to vote. Statement 4 is correct: the same subject is barred for one year. Hence '2, 3 and 4 only'.
32.tq: Resolution = substantive motion: voted on, no withdrawal without leave, one-year bar.
xs: Statements **2, 3 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
1 is wrong: the mover **cannot withdraw** a resolution without **leave of the House**.
2 and 3: a resolution **must be put to vote** and is a self-contained proposal, **always a substantive motion**.
4: a resolution on the same subject is barred for **one year**.
xa: **Private member's** resolutions are taken up on **alternate Fridays**, afternoon.
**Government** resolutions are moved by a minister (e.g. approving treaties).
**Statutory** resolutions are moved under a constitutional/statutory provision.

32.s: Private Members’ Resolutions in Parliament are generally taken up on:
o: The last sitting day of every month
32.x: Private Members’ Resolutions are taken up on alternate Fridays during the afternoon.
32.tq: Match the device with its distinctive day-and-time arrangement.
xs: Private members' resolutions are taken up on **alternate Fridays in the afternoon** — so option **(3)** is correct.
They are not a Monday, Wednesday or month-end item; the slot is **alternate Fridays**.
xa: A **government resolution** is moved by a minister, e.g., approving **treaties**.
A **statutory resolution** is moved under a constitutional/statutory provision.
A resolution is a **self-contained proposal**; same subject barred for **one year**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding types of resolutions in Parliament:
1. A Government resolution is moved by a minister, for example to approve a treaty.
2. A resolution moved under a constitutional or statutory provision is called a statutory resolution.
3. Unlike a private member's resolution, a Government resolution need not be put to vote.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct as per the types of resolutions. Statement 3 is wrong: every resolution is a substantive motion and must be put to vote. So '1 and 2 only' is right; options including 3 are wrong.
32.tq: Every resolution = substantive motion = must be voted; types differ only in who moves it and under what power.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: correct — a **government resolution** is moved by a minister (e.g., approving **treaties**).
Statement 2: correct — one under a constitutional/statutory provision is a **statutory** resolution.
Statement 3: wrong — every resolution is a **substantive motion** and **must be put to vote**.
xa: Private member's resolutions: **alternate Fridays**, afternoon.
The mover cannot withdraw a resolution **without leave of the House**.
Same subject barred for **one year**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A point of order is raised when proceedings depart from the Rules or the Constitution.
2. A point of order is itself subject to a regular debate in the House.
3. The Presiding Officer rules on a point of order.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. A point of order is not subject to regular debate; the Presiding Officer rules on it.
32.tq: Use the procedural consequence to reject the statement that adds an impermissible debate.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: correct — raised when proceedings **depart from rules/Constitution**.
Statement 2: wrong — a point of order has **no debate**; Statement 3: correct — the **Presiding Officer rules** on it.
xa: **Yielding the floor**: member speaking gives way to another member or the Chair.
**Simple closure**: "matter sufficiently discussed; be put to vote".
**Rule 377 (LS)** matters are those that are **not points of order** ("special mention").

32.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Simple closure — Only important clauses are debated
Closure by compartments — All pending clauses are voted on when time ends
Kangaroo closure — Only important clauses are debated and the others are taken as passed
Guillotine — Matter is declared sufficiently discussed and put to vote
32.x: C is correct: under kangaroo closure only the important clauses are debated and the rest are taken as passed. A is wrong because simple closure means the matter is declared sufficiently discussed and put to vote; B is wrong because putting all pending clauses to vote when time ends is the guillotine; D is wrong because it describes simple closure, not the guillotine.
32.tq: Discriminate among similar closure terms by matching each device with its exact operation.
xs: **Kangaroo closure — only important clauses debated, others taken as passed** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Simple closure** = matter sufficiently discussed, put to vote; **closure by compartments** = clauses grouped into parts, debated and voted part by part.
Voting all pending clauses when time ends is the **guillotine**, not simple closure.
xa: ⚠ Kangaroo = only important clauses debated; guillotine = **undiscussed** clauses voted when allotted time ends.
**Point of order**: raised when proceedings depart from rules; no debate.
Whips: **one-line** informative, **two-line** attendance, **three-line** strict voting.

32.s: When a member who is speaking gives way to another member or to the Chair, the procedure is known as:
32.x: Yielding the floor occurs when the member speaking gives way to another member or to the Chair.
32.tq: Match the ordinary procedural action with its precise parliamentary term.
xs: A member giving way to another member or the Chair is **yielding the floor** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Simple closure** ends debate and puts the matter to vote; **point of order** is raised when proceedings depart from rules; **calling attention** seeks a minister's statement.
xa: **Kangaroo closure**: only important clauses debated, others taken as passed.
**Guillotine**: all pending clauses put to vote when time ends.
**Three-line whip** = strict voting direction.

32.s: The office of Whip in the Indian parliamentary system derives its authority primarily from:
o: The Rules of Procedure of Parliament
A specific provision of the Constitution
32.x: The office of Whip is not mentioned in the Constitution, the Rules of the House or any parliamentary statute. It is based on conventions of parliamentary government.
32.tq: Distinguish a conventional office from a constitutional, statutory or rule-based office.
xs: The Whip rests on **parliamentary conventions** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is **not mentioned in the Constitution, the Rules of the House or any statute** — so options (2), (3) and (4) are wrong.
xa: ⚠ Only the convention statement was valid in **APPSC-G1 2024**.
Defying the whip on a vote can attract **Tenth Schedule** disqualification.
Whips: **one-line** informative, **two-line** attendance, **three-line** strict voting direction.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding a party Whip:
1. Each political party appoints a Whip or Chief Whip.
2. The Whip seeks to ensure attendance and voting according to the party line.
3. Defiance of a Whip can attract disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: All three statements are correct. A party Whip enforces party discipline regarding attendance and voting, and defiance in relevant circumstances may attract disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.
32.tq: Check whether all statements describe connected functions and consequences of party discipline.
xs: All three statements are correct — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
Each party appoints a **whip/chief whip** to ensure **attendance and voting per party line**.
Defying the whip on a vote can attract **Tenth Schedule** disqualification.
xa: The Whip rests on **conventions** — not in the Constitution, Rules or any statute.
The **Minister of Parliamentary Affairs** keeps close contact with chief whips of both Houses.
**Three-line** whip = strict voting direction.

32.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the types of Whip:

List-I (Type)
A. One-line Whip
B. Two-line Whip
C. Three-line Whip

List-II (Purpose)
1. Strict voting direction
2. Informative communication
3. Direction to attend the House

Select the correct code:
32.x: A one-line Whip is informative, a two-line Whip directs members to attend, and a three-line Whip gives a strict voting direction.
32.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes with swapped functions.
xs: **One-line** whip = informative; **two-line** = attendance; **three-line** = strict voting direction.
xa: Defying the whip on a vote can attract **Tenth Schedule** disqualification.
The office of Whip rests on **conventions** of parliamentary government.
Each party appoints a **whip / chief whip**.

32.s: Which Union Minister maintains close contact with the Chief Whips of political parties in both Houses of Parliament?
o: Minister of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions
32.x: The Minister of Parliamentary Affairs keeps close contact with the Chief Whips of parties in both Houses.
32.tq: Use the functional association between parliamentary coordination and the concerned ministry.
xs: The **Minister of Parliamentary Affairs** keeps close contact with the chief whips — so option **(3)** is correct.
This liaison covers the chief whips of parties in **both Houses**.
xa: The same ministry sends extracts of the Chair's **Zero Hour** directions/assurances to the ministry concerned for action.
Whips ensure **attendance and voting** per party line.
Defiance can bring **Tenth Schedule** disqualification.

32.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the composition of the Committee of Privileges?
o: Lok Sabha—10 members nominated by the Chairman; Rajya Sabha—15 members nominated by the Speaker
Lok Sabha—15 members nominated by the Speaker; Rajya Sabha—10 members nominated by the Chairman
Both Houses—15 members elected by the respective Houses
Both Houses—10 members nominated by the President
32.x: The Lok Sabha Committee of Privileges has 15 members nominated by the Speaker, while the Rajya Sabha Committee has 10 members nominated by the Chairman.
32.tq: Check both membership and nominating authority; the two Houses are deliberately reversed in distractors.
xs: LS: **15 members nominated by the Speaker**; RS: **10 members nominated by the Chairman** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) swaps the numbers and nominating authorities.
xa: DRSCs: **24** (16 LS + 8 RS); **31 members = 21 LS + 10 RS**; set up in **1993**.
**Ethics Committee**: RS **4 March 1997**; LS **16 May 2000**.
⚠ DRSC **31 = 21 + 10**; SC/ST Welfare **30 = 20 + 10**, no minister as member.

32.s:
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is the ex-officio Chairperson of which of the following committees?
1. Business Advisory Committee
2. Rules Committee
3. General Purposes Committee

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
32.x: The Speaker is ex-officio Chairperson of the Business Advisory Committee, the Rules Committee and the General Purposes Committee.
32.tq: Identify the common constitutional-office relationship across the listed committees.
xs: The Speaker chairs all three — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
He is **ex-officio chair** of the **Business Advisory Committee**, the **Rules Committee** and the **General Purposes Committee**.
xa: **Standing committees** are permanent (e.g., Business Advisory, Petitions, Privileges, Rules); **ad hoc** ones end when the task is done.
Committee of Privileges (LS): **15** members nominated by the **Speaker**.
**Committee on Petitions** = **"Ombudsman"** of Parliament (APPSC-GS 2025).

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Department-related Standing Committees (DRSCs):
1. They were set up in 1993.
2. There are 24 DRSCs: 16 under the Lok Sabha and 8 under the Rajya Sabha.
3. Each DRSC has 31 members with a quorum of 15.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: DRSCs were set up in 1993 and number 24 (16 LS + 8 RS). Statement 3 is wrong: each has 31 members (21 LS + 10 RS) but the quorum is 11, not 15. So '1 and 2 only'; options with 3 are wrong.
32.tq: DRSC numbers: 24 = 16 + 8; 31 = 21 + 10; quorum 11.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: correct — DRSCs were set up in **1993**.
Statement 2: correct — **24 DRSCs** = **16 under Lok Sabha + 8 under Rajya Sabha**.
Statement 3: wrong — each has **31 members** (21 LS + 10 RS), but the quorum is **11**, not 15.
xa: Chairs are appointed by the **Speaker** (LS committees) and the **Chairman** (RS committees).
⚠ DRSC **31 = 21 + 10**; SC/ST Welfare Committee **30 = 20 + 10**.
DRSCs are among Parliament's **"watchdogs"** over the executive.

32.s: Who appoints the Chairpersons of Department-related Standing Committees?
o: The Prime Minister for Lok Sabha committees and the Vice-President for Rajya Sabha committees
The respective ministers heading the departments concerned
The Speaker for Lok Sabha committees and the Chairman for Rajya Sabha committees
32.x: The Speaker appoints the Chairpersons of Lok Sabha DRSCs, while the Chairman appoints the Chairpersons of Rajya Sabha DRSCs.
32.tq: Apply the authority-to-House distinction instead of attributing all appointments to one presiding officer.
xs: DRSC chairs are appointed by **the Speaker for Lok Sabha committees and the Chairman for Rajya Sabha committees** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Not the Prime Minister, ministers or the President — options (1), (2) and (3) are wrong.
xa: **24** DRSCs: **16** under Lok Sabha, **8** under Rajya Sabha; set up in **1993**.
Each DRSC: **31 members = 21 LS + 10 RS**; quorum **11**.
The Speaker is **ex-officio chair** of the Business Advisory, Rules and General Purposes Committees.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about ad hoc committees:
1. Inquiry committees may be set up by a motion or by the Speaker or Chairman.
2. A Committee on MPLADS is an example of an inquiry committee.
3. Ad hoc committees continue permanently after completing their assigned task.
4. Select and Joint Committees on Bills are included among ad hoc committees.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Inquiry committees may be created by a motion or by the Speaker or Chairman; the Committee on MPLADS is an example. Select and Joint Committees on Bills are also ad hoc, and such committees end when their task is completed.
32.tq: Identify the false permanence statement and retain the statements describing formation and termination.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statements 1 and 2: correct — **inquiry committees** are set up by a motion or by the **Speaker/Chairman**, e.g., the **Committee on MPLADS**.
Statement 3: wrong — ad hoc committees **end when the task is done**.
Statement 4: correct — **Select / Joint Committees on Bills** are ad hoc.
xa: Another inquiry-type ad hoc example: the **Railway Convention Committee**.
**Standing committees** are permanent: Business Advisory, Petitions, Privileges, Rules.
Select = one House; Joint = **both Houses**, formed on a motion adopted in the House.

32.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes a Select Committee from a Joint Committee on a Bill?
o: A Select Committee has members from one House, whereas a Joint Committee has members from both Houses.
A Select Committee is permanent, whereas a Joint Committee is temporary.
A Select Committee is appointed by the President, whereas a Joint Committee is appointed by the Speaker alone.
A Select Committee examines financial accounts, whereas a Joint Committee examines only petitions.
32.x: A Select Committee consists of members of one House. A Joint Committee consists of members of both Houses and is formed on a motion adopted in the House.
32.tq: Discriminate between the two bill committees by their House composition.
xs: A **Select Committee has members from one House**, a **Joint Committee from both Houses** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Both are **ad hoc** committees on Bills, so option (2) is wrong.
xa: A Joint Committee is formed on a **motion adopted in the House**.
Ad hoc committees **end when the task is done**; standing committees are permanent.
Inquiry committees (e.g., **MPLADS**, **Railway Convention Committee**) are the other ad hoc type.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about the Public Accounts Committee:
1. It consists of 22 members, comprising 15 members from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha.
2. Its members are elected annually by proportional representation through the single transferable vote.
3. A minister can be a member of the Committee.
4. Its Chairperson is appointed by the Speaker.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: The Public Accounts Committee has 15 Lok Sabha and 7 Rajya Sabha members, elected annually by proportional representation through the single transferable vote. Ministers cannot be members, and the Chairperson is appointed by the Speaker.
32.tq: Split the composition, election and eligibility statements before choosing the coded combination.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: correct — **22** = **15 LS + 7 RS**. Statement 2: correct — elected annually by **PR-STV**.
Statement 3: wrong — **no minister** can be a member.
Statement 4: correct — the chair is **appointed by the Speaker**.
xa: Chair from the **Opposition since 1967**.
It examines **CAG audit reports**; its recommendations are **not binding**.
PAC for **2026-27** held its first meeting under **K.C. Venugopal**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Public Accounts Committee (PAC):
1. It checks whether money was spent within the scope of the demand.
2. Its recommendations are binding on the executive.
3. It examines the execution of policy and not policy as such.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statement 1 is correct: the PAC checks spending 'within the scope of the demand'. Statement 3 is correct: it examines execution, not policy. Statement 2 is wrong: PAC recommendations are not binding. Hence 1 and 3 only; every other option includes statement 2.
32.tq: PAC = post-facto, advisory, execution-only.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: correct — it checks money spent **"within the scope of the demand"**.
Statement 2: wrong — its recommendations are **not binding**.
Statement 3: correct — it examines **execution, not policy**.
xa: It examines **CAG audit reports** and points out **waste, loss, nugatory expenditure**.
Chair from the **Opposition since 1967**.
PAC and Estimates Committee are quoted for **financial discipline and accountability**.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about the origins of the financial committees of Parliament:
1. The Estimates Committee took its present form in 1950 on the recommendation of John Mathai.
2. The Committee on Public Undertakings was created in 1964 on the recommendation of the Ashok Dalwai Committee.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
32.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Estimates Committee originated in 1921 and took its present form in 1950 on John Mathai's recommendation. Statement 2 is wrong: COPU (1964) was created on the Krishna Menon Committee's recommendation; Ashok Dalwai is linked to doubling farmers' income. Hence '1 only'.
32.tq: 1950 = John Mathai (Estimates); 1964 = Krishna Menon (COPU).
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)** **1 only**.
1: the **Estimates Committee** originated in **1921** and took its present form in **1950** on **John Mathai's** recommendation.
2 is wrong: the **CPU** (**1964**) came on the **Krishna Menon Committee's** recommendation; **Ashok Dalwai** dealt with **doubling farmers' income**.
xa: The **PAC** was set up in **1921** under the **Government of India Act, 1919**.
Estimates Committee: **30** members, **Lok Sabha only** — the **largest** committee.
CPU: **22** members — **15** LS + **7** RS.

32.s:
Consider the following statements about the Public Accounts Committee:
1. It was first set up in 1921 under the Government of India Act, 1919.
2. It examines the audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor-General.
3. Its Chairperson is invariably drawn from the ruling party.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Statement 1 is correct: the PAC was set up in 1921 under the Government of India Act, 1919. Statement 2 is correct: it examines the CAG's audit reports. Statement 3 is wrong: since 1967 the PAC Chairperson has been from the Opposition; it is the Estimates Committee chair who is invariably from the ruling party. Hence 1 and 2 only.
32.tq: PAC chair = Opposition (since 1967); Estimates chair = ruling party.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1: correct — set up in **1921** under the **Government of India Act, 1919**.
Statement 2: correct — it examines **CAG audit reports**.
Statement 3: wrong — its chair has been from the **Opposition since 1967**.
xa: ⚠ PAC chair = **Opposition**; Estimates chair = **ruling party**.
Its recommendations are **not binding**; it examines execution, not policy.
**22** members = 15 LS + **7 RS**.

32.s: Which committee is described as the “Continuous economy committee”?
32.x: The Estimates Committee is known as the “Continuous economy committee.”
32.tq: Match the nickname with the committee concerned with economies and efficiency.
xs: The **Estimates Committee** is the "Continuous economy committee" — so option **(2)** is correct.
It suggests **economies, efficiency, administrative reform** and alternative policies.
xa: **30** members, all from the **Lok Sabha**.
Present form in **1950** on **John Mathai**'s recommendation.
⚠ The **Committee on Petitions** is the **"Ombudsman"** of Parliament.

32.s:
The term “watchdogs over the executive” is associated with which of the following groups of committees?
1. Public Accounts Committee
2. Estimates Committee
3. Committee on Public Undertakings
4. Department-related Standing Committees
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
32.x: The Public Accounts Committee, Estimates Committee, Committee on Public Undertakings, Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Committee on Government Assurances and Department-related Standing Committees are described as watchdogs over the executive.
32.tq: Recognise the inclusive option when all listed oversight committees perform executive scrutiny.
xs: All four are called Parliament's **"watchdogs"** over the executive — option **(4)**.
The watchdog list: **PAC**, **Estimates**, **CPU**, **Subordinate Legislation**, **Government Assurances** and **DRSCs**.
xa: **Committee on Subordinate Legislation**: checks rule-making (delegated) powers.
**Committee on Government Assurances**: tracks ministers' promises till implemented.
**Committee on Petitions** = **"Ombudsman"** of Parliament.

32.s: The Committee on Papers Laid on the Table primarily checks whether:
o: The estimates contain alternative taxation policies
Public sector undertakings follow commercial principles
Papers laid by ministers, other than statutory orders, comply with the relevant requirements
32.x: The Committee on Papers Laid on the Table checks papers laid by ministers, other than statutory orders, for compliance.
32.tq: Distinguish documentary scrutiny from assurance-tracking and financial scrutiny.
xs: It checks **papers laid by ministers, other than statutory orders**, for compliance — so option **(3)** is correct.
Commercial principles of PSUs = **CPU**; ministers' assurances = **Government Assurances** committee.
xa: **Committee on Subordinate Legislation**: whether rule-making (delegated) powers are properly exercised.
**Committee on Petitions** = **"Ombudsman"** of Parliament.
**Estimates Committee** = **"Continuous economy committee"**.

32.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Committee on Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes is correct?
o: No minister can be a member of the Committee.
The Committee consists only of nominated members.
Only Rajya Sabha ministers are excluded from membership.
A minister may be a member if nominated by the Speaker.
32.x: No minister can be a member of the Committee on Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
32.tq: Test the membership restriction directly, using the ministerial eligibility trap.
xs: **No minister can be a member** of the Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs — so option **(1)** is correct.
The bar is total: no exception for Rajya Sabha ministers or for Speaker's nomination, so options (3) and (4) are wrong.
xa: It has **30 members** = **20 from Lok Sabha + 10 from Rajya Sabha**.
**Committee on Empowerment of Women**: both Houses, constituted **29 April 1997**.
**PAC** and **Estimates Committee** also bar ministers.

32.s: Which parliamentary committee is described as the 'Ombudsman' of Parliament, examining petitions on bills and on matters of general public interest?
32.x: The Committee on Petitions examines petitions on bills and matters of public interest and is called Parliament's 'Ombudsman'. The Committee on Government Assurances tracks ministers' promises, the Committee on Subordinate Legislation checks the exercise of delegated rule-making powers, and the Committee of Privileges examines breaches of privilege.
32.tq: Ombudsman = Petitions; continuous economy = Estimates.
xs: The **Committee on Petitions** is the **"Ombudsman"** of Parliament — so option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025 key).
**Government Assurances** tracks ministers' promises; **Subordinate Legislation** checks delegated rule-making.
xa: It is a **standing** (permanent) committee.
**Estimates Committee** = "Continuous economy committee".
Committee of Privileges: LS **15** (Speaker), RS **10** (Chairman).

32.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Kasturirangan — Education and the 5+3+3+4 structure
2. Urjit Patel — Inflation targeting at 4% with a tolerance band of plus or minus 2%
3. Nachiket Mor — Monetary policy framework
4. Shanta Kumar — Decentralised procurement and DBT for food
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
32.x: Kasturirangan is linked with education and the 5+3+3+4 structure, Urjit Patel with inflation targeting at 4% plus or minus 2%, and Shanta Kumar with FCI/PDS reform including decentralised procurement and DBT for food. Nachiket Mor is associated with financial inclusion, not monetary policy.
32.tq: Detect the deliberately swapped reform area in the third pair.
xs: Pairs **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Kasturirangan** = education, **NEP 2020**, **5+3+3+4**; **Urjit Patel** = inflation targeting (**4% +/- 2%**).
**Shanta Kumar** = FCI/PDS reform, **DBT for food**, **decentralised procurement**.
The notes list **Urjit Patel**, not Nachiket Mor, for monetary policy — so pair 3 fails.
xa: **2nd ARC**: code of ethics, **Right to Public Services**, e-governance.
**Ashok Dalwai**: doubling farmers' income — value addition, land leasing.

32.s: The reform area associated with the Ashok Dalwai Committee includes:
o: DBT for food and decentralised procurement under the PDS
Value addition and land leasing in the context of doubling farmers’ income
Inflation targeting and monetary policy independence
32.x: Ashok Dalwai’s reform area concerns doubling farmers’ income, including value addition and land leasing.
32.tq: Identify the policy package that belongs to the specified reform objective.
xs: **Ashok Dalwai** = **value addition and land leasing** for **doubling farmers' income** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**5+3+3+4** = Kasturirangan; **DBT for food** = Shanta Kumar; **inflation targeting** = Urjit Patel.
xa: **2nd ARC**: code of ethics, Right to Public Services, e-governance.
Kasturirangan's area is linked to **NEP 2020**.
Urjit Patel: inflation target **4% +/- 2%**.

32.s: Which body's recommendations are associated with a code of ethics, the Right to Public Services and e-governance?
32.x: The Second Administrative Reforms Commission (2nd ARC) is linked with a code of ethics, the Right to Public Services and e-governance. Shanta Kumar dealt with FCI/PDS, Ashok Dalwai with farmers' income and Kasturirangan with education.
32.tq: ARC = Administration: ethics, services, e-gov.
xs: Code of ethics, **Right to Public Services** and **e-governance** = the **Second Administrative Reforms Commission** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Shanta Kumar** = FCI/PDS; **Ashok Dalwai** = farmers' income; **Kasturirangan** = education.
xa: Shanta Kumar: **DBT for food**, decentralised procurement.
Kasturirangan: **NEP 2020**, **5+3+3+4**.
Urjit Patel: inflation targeting (**4% +/- 2%**).

32.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the removal of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha under Article 94(c):
1. The resolution requires a majority of all the then members of the House.
2. A notice of fourteen days is required.
3. The notice must be supported by at least fifty members.
4. The procedure is governed by Rules 200–203 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Lok Sabha.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: All four statements are correct. Article 94(c), the fourteen-day notice requirement, support of fifty members and Lok Sabha Rules 200–203 govern the removal procedure.
32.tq: Check each procedural requirement separately, especially the constitutional provision, notice period, numerical support and relevant Rules.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Removal under **Art. 94(c)** = **majority of all members** + **14 days' notice** + **50 members'** support.
The procedure is in **LS Rules 200-203**.
xa: A resolution against Speaker **Om Birla** was **dismissed by voice vote** (**Mar 2026**).
The Speaker has **discretion to admit or reject** a no-confidence motion.
⚠ A no-confidence motion (vs the government) also needs **50 members**, under **Rule 198**.

32.s: In the 17th Lok Sabha, what proportion of Bills were referred to parliamentary committees?
32.x: Only 16% of Bills in the 17th Lok Sabha were referred to committees; the corresponding figure for the 15th Lok Sabha was 71%.
32.tq: Separate the figures belonging to the 17th and 15th Lok Sabhas instead of selecting the larger comparison value.
xs: Only **16%** of Bills went to committees in the 17th Lok Sabha — so option **(1)** is correct.
⚠ **71%** was the 15th Lok Sabha's figure.
xa: Question Hour ran only **60%** of its scheduled time.
UK comparison: every Bill examined by committees of both Houses; India: **under one-fifth** referred.
Ad hoc **Select / Joint Committees on Bills** examine Bills referred to them.

32.s: Question Hour in Parliament functioned for what proportion of its scheduled time, according to the cited assessment?
32.x: Question Hour ran for only 60% of its scheduled time in the cited assessment.
32.tq: Distinguish the Question Hour utilisation figure from the committee attendance and Bill-referral percentages.
xs: Question Hour ran only **60%** of its scheduled time — so option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ **71%** was the share of Bills sent to committees in the 15th Lok Sabha.
xa: 17th Lok Sabha: only **16%** of Bills went to committees.
Question Hour is the **first hour** of every sitting and the most effective **day-to-day** vigil.
Fewer than **one-fifth** of Bills are referred to committees in India vs all in the UK.

32.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly is correct?
o: Biometric attendance was introduced only for members of Parliament from the Budget Session of 2026.
Biometric attendance for MLAs was introduced from the Budget Session of 2026.
Biometric attendance for MLAs was introduced from the Monsoon Session of 2025.
Biometric attendance was introduced for MLAs from the Winter Session of 2026.
32.x: Andhra Pradesh introduced biometric attendance for MLAs from its Budget Session in 2026.
32.tq: Use precise state-level identification by checking the institution, year and legislative session together.
xs: **Biometric attendance for MLAs** came from the **Budget Session 2026** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is for **MLAs**, not MPs, and from the Budget Session, not Monsoon or Winter.
xa: The **AP Legislature** uses the same devices as Parliament.
The **AP Legislative Council** was adjourned amid a row on the **Tirumala laddu** issue (**Feb 2026**).
Andhra State: **Prakasam** ministry fell by one vote (**69 for, 68 against**) in Nov **1954**.

32.s: Which of the following statements regarding confidence and no-confidence motions is incorrect?
o: A Confidence Motion demonstrates the Government's majority.
A No-Confidence Motion is moved by the Opposition in the Lok Sabha.
A No-Confidence Motion is moved by the Council of Ministers to demonstrate its majority.
A Confidence Motion is moved on the floor by the Council of Ministers or the Government.
32.x: C is incorrect: a confidence motion is moved by the government to prove its majority; a no-confidence motion is moved by the Opposition (Rule 198 of the Lok Sabha).
32.tq: Remember who moves each motion.
n: A Confidence Motion is moved on the floor by the Council of Ministers or the Government. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
A Confidence Motion demonstrates the majority of the Council of Ministers or Government. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
A No-Confidence Motion is moved by the Opposition in the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
xs: The incorrect statement is that a **No-Confidence Motion is moved by the Council of Ministers** to demonstrate its majority — option **(3)**.
A **No-Confidence Motion** (**Rule 198**) is moved by the **Opposition** in the **Lok Sabha**.
A **Confidence Motion** is moved by the **Government** (Council of Ministers) to **demonstrate its majority**.
xa: If a confidence motion is defeated, the **Government falls**.
The no-confidence motion needs **50** members' support; **no reasons** need be stated.
First no-confidence motion: **J.B. Kripalani**, **1963**, against **Nehru**.

32.s: Which parliamentary committee has 30 members drawn from the Lok Sabha only and is the largest parliamentary committee?
32.x: The Estimates Committee is the largest parliamentary committee, with 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha. The PAC and Public Undertakings Committee have 22 members each.

The Estimates Committee consists only of Lok Sabha members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 137-141]
The Estimates Committee is the largest parliamentary committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 137-141]
xs: The **Estimates Committee** has **30** members, all from the **Lok Sabha** — option **(3)**.
It is the single **largest** parliamentary committee and the **only** one with no Rajya Sabha members.
The **PAC** and the **Committee on Public Undertakings** have **22** members each (**15** LS + **7** RS).
xa: Its chairman is appointed by the **Speaker**, traditionally from the **ruling party**.
It examines **budget estimates** and suggests **economy** and **efficiency** in administration.
Nickname: "**Continuous economy committee**".

32.s:

xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation** of A — option **(1)**.
**Question Hour + Supplementary Questions + Adjournment Motions** form the **accountability triangle**.

xa: **Question Hour** = most effective **day-to-day** vigil on the executive.
**No-confidence motion** = **most powerful weapon** of executive accountability.
**Zero Hour** and **Calling Attention Motion** are **indigenous Indian** contributions.

32.s: Which of the following statements regarding the post-2014 arrangement is incorrect?

Zero Hour is an informal convention. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]

Zero Hour is an informal convention. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
xs: Statements **I and II** are correct — option **(2)**.
I: parliamentary hours and procedural motions **scrutinise government policies and actions**.
II: Question Hour is for **asking and answering questions** addressed to **Ministers**.
III is wrong: Zero Hour is an **informal convention** without **prior notice**.
