A is false: the **one-third split** exception (**Para 3**) was **deleted by the 91st Amendment, 2003**.
B is true: a **merger** is protected when at least **two-thirds** of the **legislature party** agrees (**Para 4**).
xa: Per **IYB 2026**, the split deletion brought **splits within the purview of disqualification**.
**Law Commission, 170th Report (1999)** had recommended deleting the **split and merger** exceptions.
**Subhash Desai (2023)**: two-thirds of legislators cannot by themselves create a "**deemed merger**" of the original party.

36.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: An independent elected member is disqualified on joining any political party after election.
Statement B: An independent elected member may join the government as a minister without taking party membership.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
36.x: Both are true: an independent member is disqualified if they join any party after election, but they may become a Minister without joining a party. Only taking party membership disqualifies them.
36.tq: Discriminate joining a party from joining the government.
n: An independent elected member is disqualified for joining any political party after election. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
An independent elected member is disqualified for joining the government as an independent minister without taking party membership. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — so option **(1)** is correct.
A: an **independent elected member** is disqualified on **joining any political party** after **election**.
B: an independent may join the **government** as an **independent minister** without taking **party membership** — only party membership disqualifies.
xa: A **nominated member** may join a party **within six months** of taking a seat.
A **party-elected member** is disqualified for **voluntarily giving up** membership or **defying the whip**.
The law operates on the "**legislature party**".

36.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding a Presiding Officer under the Anti-Defection Law?
o: A Presiding Officer cannot rejoin the original party after demitting office.
A Presiding Officer may face disqualification for joining another political party after vacating office.
A Presiding Officer may face disqualification for joining another political party while holding office.
A Presiding Officer can voluntarily give up party membership upon election to the Chair.
36.x: Option A is incorrect: a presiding officer may give up party membership on election to the Chair and rejoin the party after leaving office. Joining another party, during or after the term, disqualifies them.
36.tq: Discriminate rejoining the original party from joining another.
n: A presiding officer is disqualified for joining another political party while holding office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
A presiding officer is disqualified for joining another political party after vacating office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
A presiding officer may voluntarily give up party membership upon election to the Chair. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
A presiding officer may rejoin the original party after demitting office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
xs: The incorrect statement is that a **Presiding Officer cannot rejoin the original party after demitting office** — so option **(1)** is the answer.
A Presiding Officer **may voluntarily give up** party membership on **election to the Chair** and **rejoin** the original party after demitting office.
He is disqualified only for **joining another political party** while holding office or after vacating it — so options (2), (3), (4) are true.
xa: This exception is **Para 5**, covering **Speaker/Deputy Speaker/Chairman/Deputy Chairman**; it is **in force**.
Criticism: Indian Speakers **do not resign from their party**, so they are seen as partisan.
The Presiding Officer decides defection petitions under **Para 6**.

36.s: Which Articles govern defection disqualification of Members of Parliament and State Legislatures, respectively?
36.x: Defection disqualification comes under Article 102(2) for MPs and 191(2) for State legislators, read with the Tenth Schedule. Clauses (1) are the general grounds.
36.tq: Discriminate clause (1) (general) from clause (2) (defection).
n: Defection disqualification is governed by the 10th Schedule and Articles 102(2) and 191(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
xs: Defection disqualification is governed by **Articles 102(2) and 191(2)** — so option **(3)** is correct.
These Articles, read with the **10th Schedule**, cover MPs and State legislators respectively.
**Articles 102(1) and 191(1)** are the **general** disqualification grounds; **Articles 103 and 192** give the President/Governor's decision on them.
xa: **Articles 101 and 190** deal with **vacation of seats** in Parliament and State Legislatures.
General disqualifications: **President** (MP) or **Governor** (MLA/MLC), with **ECI opinion** **mandatory and binding**.
Defection matters: **Speaker or Chairman alone**, acting as a **tribunal**; subject to **judicial review** (**Kihoto Hollohan, 1992**).

36.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) General disqualification of a Union MP
(b) General disqualification of a State MLA or MLC

List-II
(i) President of India; mandatory and binding opinion of the ECI
(ii) President of India; non-binding opinion of the ECI
(iii) Governor of the State; mandatory and binding opinion of the ECI
(iv) Governor of the State; non-binding opinion of the ECI
36.x: For both, the ECI's opinion is compulsory and binding: the President decides for MPs and the Governor for MLAs and MLCs. The answer is a-i, b-iii.
36.tq: Recall that the ECI's opinion binds both.
n: The President of India must obtain the Election Commission of India’s opinion on general disqualification of a Union MP. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
The Election Commission of India’s opinion on general disqualification of a Union MP is mandatory and binding. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
The Governor must obtain the Election Commission of India’s opinion on general disqualification of a State MLA or MLC. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
The Election Commission of India’s opinion on general disqualification of a State MLA or MLC is mandatory and binding. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
xs: The correct match is **a-i, b-iii** — so option **(1)** is correct.
General disqualification of a **Union MP**: the **President of India**, on the **mandatory and binding opinion of the ECI** (**Articles 102(1) and 103**).
General disqualification of a **State MLA or MLC**: the **Governor of the State**, on the **mandatory and binding** ECI opinion (**Articles 191(1) and 192**).
xa: ⚠ In **defection** cases the **ECI is not consulted** — the **Speaker or Chairman** decides.
The **Election Commission** and **Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990)** proposed that defection cases too be decided by the **President or Governor on the EC's advice**.
**NCRWC (2002)**: defectors to be barred from **public or remunerative political office** for the rest of the term.

37.s: The average number of sitting days per year declined from approximately how many in the First Lok Sabha to approximately how many in the Seventeenth Lok Sabha (2019–24)?
37.x: The average sittings declined from about 135 days per year in the First Lok Sabha to about 55 days per year in the Seventeenth Lok Sabha.
37.tq: Use the paired historical figures and eliminate reversed or rounded alternatives.
xs: Sittings fell from about **135 days/year** (**1st Lok Sabha**) to about **55** (**17th Lok Sabha, 2019-24**) — option **(2)**.
That is a decline of well over half across the Lok Sabhas.
xa: Lok Sabha now sits **60-70 days a year** vs **150+** sittings of the **UK House of Commons**.
**Art. 85(1)** only bars a gap of more than **six months** between sessions; **no minimum** sitting days.
**NCRWC (2000-02)** proposed a minimum of **120** days (LS) and **100** (RS).

37.s:
With reference to the present sitting pattern of the Lok Sabha, consider the following statements:
1. The Lok Sabha generally sits for around 60–70 days a year.
2. The UK House of Commons has more than 150 sittings a year.
3. The Lok Sabha sits for more days than the UK House of Commons.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
37.x: The Lok Sabha sits around 60–70 days annually, whereas the UK House of Commons has more than 150 sittings. Statement 3 reverses this comparison.
37.tq: Check the direction of the comparison before evaluating the statements.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: the Lok Sabha sits **60-70 days a year**.
Statement 2 correct: the **UK House of Commons** has **150+** sittings.
Statement 3 wrong: it reverses the comparison — the Lok Sabha sits far less.
xa: Trend: **135** days/year (**1st LS**) → about **55** (**17th LS**).
Proposal: a **fixed parliamentary calendar**.

37.s: Article 85(1) of the Constitution provides that:
o: The Rajya Sabha must sit for at least 100 days every year
There cannot be a gap of more than six months between two sessions of Parliament
The Lok Sabha must hold three sessions every year
Parliament must sit for at least 120 days every year
37.x: Article 85(1) bars a gap of more than six months between sessions but prescribes no minimum number of sitting days.
37.tq: Distinguish a constitutional maximum gap from a minimum sitting requirement.
xs: **Art. 85(1)** bars a **gap of more than six months** between sessions — option **(2)**.
It sets **no minimum** sitting days, so options (1), (3) and (4) are wrong.
The **120 / 100** figures are **NCRWC** proposals, not constitutional rules.
xa: ⚠ **Art. 85(1)** = Parliament's six-month gap; **Art. 174** = States' **6**-month gap.
State Assemblies met on average **24 days** (PRS **2025**), many only to satisfy **Art. 174**.
**Art. 123** = Ordinances.

37.s: During the Monsoon Session of 2026, which of the following correctly describes the productivity of the two Houses?
o: Lok Sabha 25 per cent and Rajya Sabha 16 per cent
Lok Sabha 19 per cent and Rajya Sabha 39 per cent
Lok Sabha 60 per cent and Rajya Sabha 53 per cent
Lok Sabha 39 per cent and Rajya Sabha 19 per cent
37.x: PRS data placed Lok Sabha productivity at 19 per cent and Rajya Sabha productivity at 39 per cent during the Monsoon Session of 2026.
37.tq: Read the House-wise figures without reversing the pair.
xs: Monsoon Session **2026**: **Lok Sabha 19%**, **Rajya Sabha 39%** — option **(2)**.
LS productivity was **among the lowest in 22 years** (PRS).
Option (4) swaps the Houses; **25%/16%** are Bill-referral shares of the **16th/17th** LS.
xa: Question Hour ran **1%** (LS) and **12%** (RS) of scheduled time.
Estimated loss: **₹175 crore**; **12** Bills passed, only one debated in detail.

37.s: In the Seventeenth Lok Sabha, Question Hour ran for approximately what proportion of its scheduled time?
37.x: During the Seventeenth Lok Sabha, Question Hour ran for only 60 per cent of its scheduled time.
37.tq: Distinguish the long-term Lok Sabha figure from the much lower Monsoon Session 2026 figure.
xs: In the **17th Lok Sabha**, Question Hour ran only **60 per cent** of scheduled time — option **(3)**.
So about two-fifths of the hour meant for **questions to ministers** was lost to disruption or adjournment.
xa: ⚠ **60%** is also the share of Bills referred to committees in the **14th LS**.
Monsoon **2026**: Question Hour ran **1%** (LS), **12%** (RS); only **2** (LS) and **16** (RS) questions answered orally.
Proposal: **strengthen Question Hour** and protect opposition debate time.

37.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding suspension-related rules in the Lok Sabha.

List-I (Rule)
a. Rule 373
b. Rule 374
c. Rule 374A

List-II (Effect)
i. Automatic suspension for five sittings or the rest of the session for grave disorder
ii. Member directed to withdraw for the day
iii. Suspension by a House motion up to the remainder of the session

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
37.x: Rule 373 concerns withdrawal for the day, Rule 374 concerns suspension by House motion up to the remainder of the session, and Rule 374A provides automatic suspension for grave disorder.
37.tq: Start from the sure rule-effect pair and eliminate codes that reverse the suspension procedures.
xs: Correct code: **a–ii, b–iii, c–i** — option **(1)**.
**Rule 373**: Speaker orders member to **withdraw for the day**.
**Rule 374**: named member **suspended by House motion**, up to remainder of session.
**Rule 374A**: **automatic suspension** for **5 sittings** or rest of session for **grave disorder**.
xa: Rajya Sabha: **Rule 255** = withdrawal for the day (Chairman); **Rule 256** = suspension by House motion.
⚠ **373 / 255** = withdraw for the day; **374 / 256** = House motion; **374A** = automatic.

37.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Rajya Sabha Rule 255 — suspension by House motion for the remainder of the session
Lok Sabha Rule 373 — withdrawal for the day ordered by the Speaker
Lok Sabha Rule 374 — suspension by House motion
Rajya Sabha Rule 256 — suspension by House motion, not beyond the remainder of the session
37.x: Rule 255 of the Rajya Sabha authorises the Chairman to direct withdrawal for the day. Suspension by House motion is dealt with under Rule 256.
37.tq: Find the swapped Rajya Sabha rule and effect.
xs: **RS Rule 255** is wrongly matched: it is the **Chairman directing withdrawal for the day** — option **(1)**.
Suspension by House motion in the Rajya Sabha is **Rule 256**, not beyond the remainder of the session.
Pairs (2), (3) and (4) are correct: **Rule 373**, **Rule 374**, **Rule 256**.
xa: **Rule 374A** (LS): automatic suspension for **5 sittings** for grave disorder.
⚠ **373 / 255** = for the day; **374 / 256** = by House motion.

37.s: Which one of the following correctly compares the committee scrutiny of Bills in India and the United Kingdom?
o: In India less than one-fifth of Bills go to committees, whereas in the UK every Bill is examined by committees of both Houses.
In India every Bill is examined by committees of both Houses, whereas in the UK less than one-fifth is examined.
Only the Rajya Sabha in India and only the House of Commons in the UK examine Bills through committees.
Neither country refers Bills to committees before passage.
37.x: Less than one-fifth of Indian Bills go to committees, while every Bill in the UK is examined by committees of both Houses.
37.tq: Test both sides of the comparison instead of focusing on only one country.
xs: India: **less than a fifth** of Bills go to committees; UK: **every Bill** examined by committees of **both Houses** — option **(1)**.
Option (2) reverses the two countries.
xa: **17th LS** referred only **16%** of Bills; the **15th** referred **71%**.
Systematic **DRSC** system only from **1993**.
Average attendance at DRSC meetings: **53%** (Digital Sansad).

37.s: The systematic system of Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees was introduced in India in:
37.x: The systematic committee system, including Department-related Standing Committees, began in 1993.
37.tq: Distinguish the institutional starting year from later reform proposals.
xs: The systematic **DRSC** committee system began in **1993** — option **(3)**.
Before that India had no **systematic** committee scrutiny of departments; even now **less than a fifth** of Bills go to committees.
xa: **1977** = **LoP Salary and Allowances Act**; **1967** = PAC chaired by Opposition.
Average attendance at **DRSC** meetings: **53%**.
Referral share fell to **16%** in the **17th LS**.

37.s: Which of the following was NOT among the proposals concerning the use of ordinances?
o: Judicial examination of urgency in light of Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)
Making every ordinance permanent without legislative approval
37.x: The proposals were to define immediate necessity, permit courts to test urgency, and publish reasons for ordinances. Permanent operation without legislative approval was not proposed.
37.tq: Identify the extreme proposal that goes beyond the stated reform measures.
xs: **Making every ordinance permanent without legislative approval** was not proposed — option **(2)**.
Real proposals: define "**immediate necessity**" by law, test urgency per **Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)**, **publish reasons**.
xa: Ordinances = **Art. 123**.
Ordinances and delegated legislation grow as **legislative engagement falls**.
Other bypass: **Money Bill route** under **Art. 110**.

37.s: The principal constitutional concern regarding the use of the Money Bill route is that it:
o: Requires the approval of every State Legislature
Can bypass the Rajya Sabha for measures that may not strictly fall within Article 110
Can be introduced only in the Rajya Sabha
Prevents the Lok Sabha from considering financial legislation
37.x: The Money Bill route may bypass the Rajya Sabha for laws whose provisions may not strictly fit within Article 110. The Aadhaar Act, 2016, is cited as an example.
37.tq: Identify the institutional consequence of the classification rather than the subject of the Bill.
xs: The Money Bill route can **bypass the Rajya Sabha** for laws that may not strictly fit **Art. 110** — option **(2)**.
Example: **Aadhaar Act, 2016**.
xa: Notes: the **RS only returned it**.
Other bypass: heavy use of **ordinances (Art. 123)**.
Criticism of weak control: **executive dominance**, **guillotine**, delegated legislation.

37.s: In which Lok Sabha was the highest share of Bills referred to parliamentary committees?
37.x: The 15th Lok Sabha referred 71% of Bills to committees, against 60% in the 14th, 25% in the 16th and only 16% in the 17th.
37.tq: Referral: 60 → 71 → 25 → 16 per cent (14th to 17th).
xs: The **15th Lok Sabha** referred the highest share — **71%** — option **(2)**.
xa: ⚠ **60%** = Bills referred (**14th**) and Question Hour run (**17th**).
**17th LS**: **58%** of Bills passed within **two weeks**; **35%** debated under **one hour**.
UK: every Bill examined by committees of both Houses.

37.s: The statutory status of the Leader of the Opposition is provided under the:
o: Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977
37.x: The Leader of the Opposition has statutory status under the Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977.
37.tq: Match the office with the statute specifically dealing with its salary and allowances.
xs: The LoP's statutory status comes from the **Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977** — option **(1)**.
The other Acts named do not give the LoP statutory status in the notes.
xa: Recognised by the **Speaker** if the party has **one-tenth** of the House (**55** in LS).
**PAC** chaired by the Opposition since **1967**.
Monsoon **2026**: united opposition pushed the **FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026** to a **JPC**.

37.s: Since which year has the Public Accounts Committee generally been chaired by a member of the Opposition?
37.x: The Public Accounts Committee has been chaired by a member of the Opposition since 1967.
37.tq: Retain the institutional convention’s specific starting year.
xs: The **PAC** has been chaired by the Opposition since **1967** — option **(2)**.
Committees are one of the Opposition's tools, along with **Question Hour** and **motions**.
xa: LoP recognition needs **one-tenth** of the House (**55** in LS).
Opposition tools: **Question Hour**, **motions**, **committees**.

37.s: The NCRWC recommended minimum annual sitting days of:
o: 150 for Lok Sabha and 120 for Rajya Sabha
120 for Lok Sabha and 100 for Rajya Sabha
100 for Lok Sabha and 120 for Rajya Sabha
37.x: The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution recommended 120 sitting days for Lok Sabha and 100 for Rajya Sabha.
37.tq: Keep the House-wise figures in their stated order.
xs: **NCRWC (2000-02)**: minimum **120 days for Lok Sabha** and **100 for Rajya Sabha** — option **(3)**.
Option (4) swaps the Houses.
xa: **Art. 85(1)** prescribes **no minimum** sitting days.
Actual: about **55** days/year in the **17th LS**.

37.s: Which of the following is NOT a proposal for improving parliamentary functioning?
o: Restricting all opposition debate to confidence motions alone
Making committee scrutiny mandatory before passage of Bills
37.x: The proposals include a fixed calendar, stronger Question Hour, mandatory committee scrutiny, and protection of opposition debate time. The proposal is to limit whips, not all opposition debate, to confidence votes and Money Bills.
37.tq: Separate a proposal concerning whips from the broader protection of opposition debate.
xs: **Restricting all opposition debate to confidence motions** is not a proposal — option **(2)**.
Proposals: **fixed calendar**, **stronger Question Hour**, **protect opposition debate time**, **mandatory committee scrutiny**.
What is limited to **confidence votes and Money Bills** is the **whip**, not debate.
xa: **National Legislative Index** announced by the **LS Speaker**.

37.s: The proposed National Legislative Index is intended to provide a data-driven assessment of:
o: Only the attendance of Members of Parliament
Sittings, legislative business, disruptions, committee use and grievance redressal
The performance of State courts and tribunals
Only the financial expenditure of Parliament
37.x: The National Legislative Index covers sittings, business, disruptions, use of committees and grievance redressal.
37.tq: Choose the option that covers the complete range of functions named for the index.
xs: It assesses **sittings, business, disruptions, committee use and grievance redressal** — option **(2)**.
It was announced by the **LS Speaker** as a **data-driven** index.
xa: **PRS Legislative Research** compiles productivity and Bill-scrutiny data.
**Digital Sansad** gives official attendance/sitting data.
**86th AIPOC** at **Lucknow**: theme "**Strong Legislature - Prosperous Nation**".

37.s:
Consider the following statements about State Legislatures as per the PRS Annual Review of State Laws 2025:
1. State Assemblies met on average for about 24 days.
2. Many Assemblies met only to satisfy Article 174, which bars a gap of more than six months between sessions.
3. Of the 600+ Bills passed, about two-thirds were passed in a single sitting.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
37.x: Statement 1 is correct: the average was 24 days (Odisha 43, Nagaland 7). Statement 2 is correct: many met only to meet the Art. 174 six-month rule. Statement 3 is wrong: about 33% (one-third), not two-thirds, of 600+ Bills were passed in a single sitting. Hence '1 and 2 only'; the options containing 3 are wrong.
37.tq: Remember the PRS trio: 24 days average, Art. 174 six-month gap, one-third of Bills in a single sitting.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: average **24 days** (**Odisha 43**, **Nagaland 7**).
Statement 2 correct: many met only to satisfy **Art. 174** (**6**-month gap).
Statement 3 wrong: about **33%** (one-third), not two-thirds, of **600+** Bills passed in a single sitting.
xa: ⚠ **Art. 85(1)** = Parliament; **Art. 174** = States.
AP Budget Session **2026**: **11 Feb to 7 Mar**.

37.s: In the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly, the agenda for the Budget Session 2026 was fixed by the Business Advisory Committee chaired by:
37.x: The Business Advisory Committee fixing the agenda was chaired by Speaker Chintakayala Ayyanna Patrudu.
37.tq: Apply the authority test: identify who presides over the relevant legislative committee.
xs: The **BAC** was chaired by **Speaker Chintakayala Ayyanna Patrudu** — option **(2)**.
It fixed the agenda of the AP **Budget Session 2026** (TH **12** Feb **2026**).
xa: Session ran **11 Feb to 7 Mar 2026**.
PRS **2025**: State Assemblies met on average **24 days**.

37.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the proposed enlargement of the Lok Sabha:
1. The proposal involves increasing the strength of the Lok Sabha from 550 to 850 seats.
2. The proposal would reduce the Lok Sabha–Rajya Sabha ratio from 3.3:1 to 2.2:1.
3. The proposal would raise the Lok Sabha–Rajya Sabha ratio to 3.3:1.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
37.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because the ratio would rise from 2.2:1 to 3.3:1, not decline.
37.tq: Check the direction of change in the ratio before selecting the coded combination.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 correct: **131st Amendment Bill** — **550 → 850** seats.
Statement 3 correct and 2 wrong: the LS:RS ratio would **rise** from **2.2:1 to 3.3:1**.
xa: Joint sittings used only **3 times** so far.
**86th AIPOC** at **Lucknow**; AIPOC dates to **1921**.

37.s: Joint sittings of the Parliament have been used, so far, on how many occasions?
37.x: Joint sittings of Parliament have been used only three times so far.
37.tq: Distinguish the exact numerical count from nearby plausible figures.
xs: Joint sittings have been used only **three times** — option **(1)**.
The notes put it as **3 times** so far.
xa: Context: the **131st Amendment Bill** (**550 → 850** LS seats) would raise the LS:RS ratio to **3.3:1**.
A larger LS would weigh more in a joint sitting.
Current ratio: **2.2:1**.

37.s:
Consider the following statements about the All India Presiding Officers' Conference (AIPOC):
1. The 86th AIPOC was held at Lucknow.
2. Its theme was "Strong Legislature - Prosperous Nation".
3. AIPOC dates back to 1947.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
37.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the 86th AIPOC was at Lucknow with the theme 'Strong Legislature - Prosperous Nation'. Statement 3 is wrong: AIPOC dates to 1921, not 1947. So '1 and 2 only'; any option with 3 is wrong.
37.tq: AIPOC is pre-Independence (1921); 86th = Lucknow.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **86th AIPOC** was at **Lucknow**.
Statement 2 correct: theme "**Strong Legislature - Prosperous Nation**".
Statement 3 wrong: AIPOC dates to **1921**, not **1947**.
xa: **National Legislative Index** announced by the **LS Speaker**.
**131st Amendment Bill**: **550 → 850** LS seats.

37.s: In which year was the Leader of Opposition first formally recognized?
37.x: The Leader of the Opposition was first formally recognised in 1969.
37.tq: Recall the year the post was formally recognised.
n: The Leader of Opposition was first formally recognized in 1969. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 144-146]
xs: The Leader of Opposition was first formally recognized in **1969** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The statutory status came later through the **Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977**.
**1964** is the year **COPU** was set up, not LoP recognition.
xa: Threshold: the **largest opposition party** must hold at least **10%** (**one-tenth**) of the House — about **55 seats** in the Lok Sabha.
Opposition tools: **Question Hour**, motions, committees — **PAC chaired by Opposition since 1967**.
**Monsoon 2026**: the united opposition pushed the **FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026** to a **JPC**.

37.s: What numerical threshold must the largest opposition party meet for recognition as the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha?
o: At least 5% of the total House strength
At least 15% of the total House strength
At least 10% of the total House strength
At least 20% of the total House strength
37.x: To be recognised as Leader of the Opposition, the largest opposition party needs at least 10% of the House, about 55 Lok Sabha seats.
37.tq: Recall the 10% rule.
n: The largest opposition party must hold at least 10% of the total House strength to receive recognition as the Leader of Opposition. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 144-146]
The 10% Leader of Opposition threshold is approximately 55 seats in the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 144-146]
xs: The largest opposition party needs **at least 10% of the total House strength** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This is **one-tenth** of the House — approximately **55 seats** in the **Lok Sabha** (quorum-size).
Recognition is by the **Speaker**.
xa: The LoP was **first formally recognized** in **1969**.
Statutory status: **Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977**.
The **PAC** has been chaired by the **Opposition since 1967** by convention.

38.s: Under Article 74(1) of the Constitution of India, the President ordinarily acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers because:
o: the Council of Ministers is responsible to the Rajya Sabha
the advice of the Council of Ministers is constitutionally binding
the Prime Minister is directly elected by the people
the President is the de facto executive
38.x: Article 74(1) provides for a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President, and the President is bound by that advice.
38.tq: Distinguish the nominal head from the real executive and identify the constitutional provision.
xs: Under **Art. 74(1)** the ministers **aid and advise** the President, and **the advice of the Council of Ministers is constitutionally binding** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The President is the **de jure** (nominal) head; the **PM + Council of Ministers** form the **de facto** executive, so option (4) reverses the roles.
The PM is the **leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha**, not directly elected by the people — option (3) is wrong.
xa: India adopted the British **parliamentary system**, based on **cooperation and co-ordination** of legislature and executive.
⚠ **Trap:** the President is **not** the real head of the executive (**APPSC-G2 2017** key).
**Dual membership:** ministers must be MPs; a non-member must be elected within **six months**.

38.s: A person who is appointed as a Union Minister without being a member of either House of Parliament must secure election or nomination to Parliament within:
38.x: A non-member may become a minister, but must become a member of either House of Parliament within six months.
38.tq: Test the precise constitutional time limit using closely spaced numerical options.
xs: A non-member appointed minister must become a member of either House within **six months** — so option **(2)** is correct.
This flows from the parliamentary feature of **dual membership**: ministers must be **MPs**.
xa: **Britain** is stricter: ministers must be MPs; India allows **six months** as a non-member.
**Majority party rule:** the **leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha** becomes PM.
Other features: **nominal and real executive**, **leadership of the PM/CM**, and possible **dissolution** of the lower House.

38.s:
Consider the following statements about ministers in the Indian parliamentary system:
1. Ministers are individually responsible to the President.
2. The President is the real head of the executive.
3. The Prime Minister provides central leadership to the Council of Ministers.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: Ministers are individually responsible to the President, while the Prime Minister provides leadership. The President is the nominal, not the real, head of the executive.
38.tq: Combine an individually correct responsibility with a deliberately reversed head-of-executive statement.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: ministers are **individually responsible to the President**.
Statement 2 is **wrong**: the President is the **de jure** head, **not** the real head of the executive.
Statement 3 is **correct**: **leadership of the PM** is a feature of the parliamentary system — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: ⚠ The "President is not the real head" point was the **APPSC-G2 2017** key.
Under **Art. 74(1)** the ministers' advice to the President is **binding**.
The PM's role has grown so much that scholars call it **"Prime Ministerial Government"** in both India and Britain.

38.s: The Westminster model of parliamentary government originated in:
38.x: The parliamentary system originated in Britain and is commonly called the Westminster model.
38.tq: Recall the origin country without confusing it with countries that later adopted the system.
xs: The **Westminster model** of parliamentary government originated in **Britain** — option **(4)** is correct.
The **USA** is the origin of the **presidential** system, so option (2) is wrong.
**India** and **Japan** follow the parliamentary model but did not originate it.
xa: ⚠ **Westminster** = Britain; presidential origin = **USA**.
Parliamentary examples: **UK, Japan, Canada, India**; presidential: **Brazil** and most of **Latin America**.
Semi-presidential: **France, Russia, Sri Lanka**.

38.s: Which one of the following sets contains only examples of parliamentary systems?
o: United Kingdom, Japan, Canada and India
United States, Brazil, India and Canada
United Kingdom, United States, Brazil and Japan
Brazil, United States, Canada and India
38.x: The United Kingdom, Japan, Canada and India are examples of parliamentary systems. The United States and Brazil are presidential systems.
38.tq: Classify every country in the option before accepting an all-correct grouping.
xs: **United Kingdom, Japan, Canada and India** are all parliamentary systems — option **(1)** is correct.
The **United States** (origin) and **Brazil** are **presidential** systems, which rules out options (2), (3) and (4).
xa: The parliamentary system originated in **Britain** — the **Westminster model**.
Semi-presidential examples: **France, Russia, Sri Lanka** — President and PM coexist.
**France (Fifth Republic, 1958)** and **Sri Lanka (1978 Constitution)** have a **directly elected President** with real powers.

38.s:
Assertion (A): India has a parliamentary form of government.
Reason (R): In India the executive is responsible to the legislature.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
38.x: Both are true and R explains A: responsibility of the executive (the Council of Ministers) to the legislature is the defining test of the parliamentary system. So options 2, 3 and 4 are wrong.
38.tq: Parliamentary = executive responsible to legislature (UPPSC 2025).
xs: **Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)** is correct.
Responsibility of the **executive (Council of Ministers) to the legislature** is the defining test of the parliamentary system.
India adopted the British **parliamentary system**, based on **cooperation and co-ordination** of legislature and executive.
xa: This exact Assertion-Reason was asked in **UPPSC 2025**.
The presidential system rests on **separation of powers** instead.
In a parliamentary system the executive can be removed by a **no-confidence** vote.

38.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the presidential system:
1. It generally has a single executive.
2. The President is directly elected.
3. The executive has a fixed term.
4. The executive is accountable to the legislature in the same manner as in a parliamentary system.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: A presidential system generally has a single, directly elected executive with a fixed term. The executive is not accountable to the legislature in the parliamentary sense.
38.tq: Reject the statement that imports parliamentary accountability into the presidential model.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: the presidential system has a **single executive**.
Statements 2 and 3 are **correct**: the President is **directly elected** with a **fixed term**.
Statement 4 is **wrong**: the executive is **not accountable to the legislature** — so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: ⚠ **APPSC-G2 2025** key: "Accountable to the legislature" is the **wrong** feature.
The President is **both Head of State and Head of Government**.
Cabinet members **may or may not** sit in the legislature (US secretaries do not).

38.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the executive-legislature relationship in parliamentary and presidential systems?
o: Parliamentary government has fusion of powers, whereas presidential government is based on separation of powers
Parliamentary government has separation of powers, whereas presidential government has fusion of powers
Both systems have fusion of powers and collective responsibility
Neither system recognises a relationship between the executive and legislature
38.x: The parliamentary system is based on a fusion of executive and legislative powers, while the presidential system rests on separation of powers.
38.tq: Use the central structural contrast—fusion versus separation of powers.
xs: **Parliamentary** = **fusion of powers**; **presidential** = **separation of powers** — option **(1)** is correct.
Under fusion, ministers are **members of the legislature**; option (2) reverses the two systems.
xa: India's parliamentary system rests on **cooperation and co-ordination** of legislature and executive.
Parliamentary: **collective executive (cabinet)**; presidential: **single executive (President)**.
Parliamentary: **nominal head + real head (PM)**; presidential: **one person is both heads**.

38.s:
Consider the following statements about the merits of the parliamentary system:
1. Harmony between the executive and legislature may permit fresh elections to resolve a deadlock.
2. The executive is continuously accountable to the legislature.
3. The executive always has a fixed tenure.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: Harmony between the executive and legislature can help resolve deadlock through fresh elections, and continuous accountability is a merit. A fixed tenure is not a feature of the parliamentary system.
38.tq: Separate parliamentary merits from the fixed-tenure feature of presidential government.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: **executive-legislature harmony** and **fresh elections break deadlock**.
Statement 2 is **correct**: the executive is **continuously accountable**.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: **no fixed tenure** is a parliamentary **demerit** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Parliamentary demerits: **unstable coalitions**, ministers not always specialists, **cabinet dictatorship** when the majority is large.
Presidential merit: a **stable, fixed-term executive**.
**Dr B.R. Ambedkar**: India chose **responsibility** over guaranteed tenure.

38.s:
Which of the following are recognised demerits of the presidential system?
1. Possibility of executive-legislature deadlock
2. Danger of a personality cult around a single executive
3. Absence of any fixed tenure
4. Excessive dependence on coalition support
38.x: Executive-legislature deadlock and the danger of a personality cult around a single executive are demerits of the presidential system. Statements 3 and 4 are wrong: the presidential executive has a fixed tenure (its merit), while lack of fixed tenure and unstable coalitions are demerits of the parliamentary system. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
38.tq: Separate actual presidential-system weaknesses from features belonging to parliamentary government.
xs: **Executive-legislature deadlock** and a **personality cult** around a single executive are presidential demerits — **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the presidential executive has a **fixed tenure** — that is its merit.
Statement 4 is wrong: **unstable coalitions** are a **parliamentary** demerit.
xa: Avoiding **US-style executive-legislature conflict** was a reason the Constituent Assembly chose the parliamentary form.
The risk of a **personality cult** under a single executive was another reason.
Parliamentary demerit: **cabinet dictatorship** when the majority is large.

38.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the reasons for adopting the parliamentary form of government in India:
1. India's vast size and diversity favoured a system based on continuous political accommodation.
2. The Constituent Assembly sought to avoid the possibility of a personality cult developing around a single executive.
3. The parliamentary form guaranteed both maximum governmental stability and continuous accountability.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct reasons associated with the choice of the parliamentary form. Statement 3 is false because Dr B.R. Ambedkar stated that a democracy cannot maximise both stability and responsibility simultaneously.
38.tq: Reject the overstatement that the system guarantees two competing democratic objectives at their maximum.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: India's **vast size and diversity** was a reason.
Statement 2 is **correct**: the Assembly feared a **personality cult** under a single executive.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: **Ambedkar** said a democracy cannot maximise **both stability and responsibility** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: India chose **responsibility** over guaranteed tenure.
Other reasons: familiarity under the **1919 and 1935 Acts** and avoiding **US-style executive-legislature conflict**.
Presidential merit: a **stable, fixed-term executive**.

38.s: According to Dr B.R. Ambedkar's observation on democratic government, the choice made by India involved giving greater weight to:
o: Responsibility and continuous accountability over guaranteed tenure
38.x: Dr B.R. Ambedkar observed that a democracy cannot maximise both stability and responsibility. India chose responsibility, meaning continuous accountability, over guaranteed tenure.
38.tq: Distinguish the two competing values identified by Ambedkar and identify the one preferred by India.
xs: India chose **responsibility** — **continuous accountability** — **over guaranteed tenure** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Dr B.R. Ambedkar** held that a democracy cannot maximise **both stability and responsibility**.
Options (3) and (4) describe the **presidential** choice (fixed tenure, executive independence).
xa: **Vasant Sathe** made early proposals for a presidential system in the **1970s-80s**.
**NCRWC (Venkatachaliah, 2000-02)** advised keeping the **parliamentary system**.
Parliamentary merit: the executive is **continuously accountable** to the legislature.

38.s: Which one of the following best describes a semi-presidential system?
o: A system in which a President and a Prime Minister coexist, with the Prime Minister responsible to the legislature
A system in which the legislature alone performs both executive and ceremonial functions
A system in which the President is only a nominal head and no Prime Minister exists
A system in which the Prime Minister is directly elected and the President has no constitutional role
38.x: In a semi-presidential system, a President and a Prime Minister coexist. The President may possess real powers, while the Prime Minister is responsible to the legislature.
38.tq: Identify the defining institutional combination rather than focusing on only one executive office.
xs: In a semi-presidential system a **President and a Prime Minister coexist**, with the **PM responsible to the legislature** — option **(1)** is correct.
They may even come from **different parties**; the President has **real powers**.
xa: Examples: **France, Russia, Sri Lanka**.
**France (Fifth Republic, 1958)** and **Sri Lanka (1978 Constitution)** have a **directly elected President**.
⚠ India differs: its President is **indirectly elected and nominal**.

38.s: Which of the following countries are associated with semi-presidential systems in which a President and a Prime Minister coexist?
o: Sri Lanka, the United Kingdom and the United States
Russia, India and the United States
India, the United Kingdom and France
38.x: France, Russia and Sri Lanka are identified as examples of countries where a President and a Prime Minister coexist under a semi-presidential arrangement.
38.tq: Use the complete country group and reject groups containing parliamentary or presidential examples outside the stated set.
xs: **France, Russia and Sri Lanka** are semi-presidential — option **(3)** is correct.
The **UK** and **India** are parliamentary; the **United States** is presidential — so the other options fail.
xa: **France (Fifth Republic, 1958)** + **Sri Lanka (1978 Constitution):** **directly elected President** with real powers + PM responsible to the legislature.
Parliamentary: **UK, Japan, Canada, India**; presidential: **Brazil**, most of Latin America.
⚠ **Westminster** = Britain; presidential origin = **USA**.

38.s:
Consider the following statements about France and Sri Lanka:
1. France's Fifth Republic was established in 1958.
2. Sri Lanka's Constitution of 1978 provides for a directly elected President with real powers alongside a Prime Minister responsible to the legislature.
3. India's President is directly elected and exercises real executive powers alongside the Prime Minister.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: France's Fifth Republic dates from 1958, and Sri Lanka's 1978 Constitution provides for a directly elected President with real powers alongside a legislature-responsible Prime Minister. India's President is indirectly elected and nominal, so statement 3 is false.
38.tq: Separate the semi-presidential features of France and Sri Lanka from India's parliamentary arrangement.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: France's **Fifth Republic** dates from **1958**.
Statement 2 is **correct**: Sri Lanka's **1978 Constitution** has a **directly elected President** with real powers + a PM responsible to the legislature.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: India's President is **indirectly elected and nominal** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Semi-presidential examples: **France, Russia, Sri Lanka**.
In India the President is **de jure** head; PM + Council of Ministers = **de facto** executive.
India's President is **indirectly elected** for a **5-year term**; Britain's head is a **hereditary** monarch.

38.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Vasant Sathe — proposals for a presidential form in the 1970s–80s
Venkatachaliah Commission — recommendation to replace parliamentary government with a presidential system
One Nation, One Election — amendment only to Article 74
Dr B.R. Ambedkar — advocacy of guaranteed executive tenure over accountability
38.x: Vasant Sathe was associated with proposals for a presidential form of government in India during the 1970s–80s. The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution advised retaining the parliamentary system, while the relevant One Nation, One Election proposal concerns Articles 83, 172 and 327.
38.tq: Use the person–proposal match and eliminate options that reverse the recommendation or alter the constitutional provisions.
xs: **Vasant Sathe** made early proposals for a **presidential system** in the **1970s-80s** — option **(1)** is correct.
The **Venkatachaliah** Commission (NCRWC) advised **keeping** the parliamentary system, so (2) is wrong.
**One Nation, One Election** amends **Articles 83, 172 and 327**, not only Art. 74 — (3) is wrong.
**Ambedkar** favoured **responsibility** over guaranteed tenure — (4) is wrong.
xa: NCRWC worked during **2000-02**.
Critics: fixing tenures **grafts presidential mechanics** onto parliamentary democracy and **weakens accountability**.

38.s:
With reference to the debate on One Nation, One Election, consider the following statements:
1. The proposed constitutional amendments include Articles 83, 172 and 327.
2. Critics argue that fixing legislative tenures may graft presidential mechanics onto a parliamentary democracy.
3. Critics contend that such a change would necessarily strengthen legislative accountability to the Lok Sabha.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Critics argue that fixed tenures may introduce presidential features into the parliamentary system and weaken accountability; therefore, statement 3 is false.
38.tq: Spot the reversed consequence: a criticism of weakened accountability is presented as its opposite.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: the amendments cover **Articles 83, 172 and 327**.
Statement 2 is **correct**: critics say fixing tenures **grafts presidential mechanics** onto parliamentary democracy.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: critics say it **weakens accountability** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **Ambedkar**: India chose **responsibility** (continuous accountability) over guaranteed tenure.
**NCRWC (Venkatachaliah, 2000-02)** advised keeping the **parliamentary system**.
A **fixed tenure** is a hallmark of the **presidential** executive.

38.s: Regarding the Prime Minister's position in India and Britain, which one of the following is correct?
o: The Prime Minister may be from either House in India, but must be from the House of Commons in Britain
The Prime Minister is directly elected in both countries
The Prime Minister must be from the upper House in India and the House of Lords in Britain
The Prime Minister must belong to the lower House in both countries
38.x: In India, the Prime Minister may belong to either House of Parliament. In Britain, the Prime Minister is drawn from the House of Commons.
38.tq: Focus on the precise membership rule rather than the general similarity of parliamentary government.
xs: In India the PM may come from **either House**; in Britain from the **House of Commons** — option **(1)** is correct.
The PM is **not directly elected** in India: the **leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha** becomes PM — (2) is wrong.
xa: Britain: ministers **must be MPs**; India allows **six months** as a non-member.
In both, the PM's role is so large that scholars call it **"Prime Ministerial Government"**.
UK: the **ruling party** can replace the PM; India: removal needs **loss of Lok Sabha confidence**.

38.s:
Which of the following features is associated with Britain but not with India?
1. Ministers must be members of Parliament.
2. Legal responsibility of ministers.
3. An institutionalised shadow cabinet.
38.x: Britain requires ministers to be members of Parliament and has legal ministerial responsibility and an institutionalised shadow cabinet. India permits a non-member to remain a minister for six months and does not have the latter two features in the same form.
38.tq: Use a country-specific cluster and identify all features belonging to Britain.
xs: Statement 1: Britain requires ministers to **be MPs**, while India allows **six months** as a non-member.
Statements 2 and 3: **legal responsibility of ministers** and an institutionalised **shadow cabinet** exist in **Britain only** — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: Common to both: the PM's role is so large it is called **"Prime Ministerial Government"**.
Britain: **hereditary** monarch, **unitary** state, **sovereignty of Parliament**.
India: **indirectly elected** President, **federal** state, **constitutional supremacy**.

38.s:
Consider the following statements about the relationship between the Indian and British parliamentary systems:
1. India has an elected head of state.
2. Britain has a hereditary monarch as head of state.
3. The Indian Parliament is bound by the written Constitution and judicial review.
4. The British Parliament is subject to the basic structure doctrine of the Indian Constitution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the basic structure doctrine belongs to the Indian constitutional framework and does not govern the British Parliament.
38.tq: Separate the true India–Britain institutional differences from a cross-system substitution.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are **correct**: India has an **indirectly elected** President; Britain a **hereditary monarch**.
Statement 3 is **correct**: India has **constitutional supremacy** — Parliament is bound by a **written Constitution** and courts can strike down laws.
Statement 4 is **wrong**: Britain has **sovereignty of Parliament** — so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(3)**.
xa: British courts **cannot question Acts of Parliament**.
India's President has a **5-year term**.
Britain is **unitary**; India is **federal**.

38.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India and the United States:
1. In India, residuary powers belong to Parliament, whereas in the United States they belong to the States.
2. India has three legislative lists, while the United States has enumerated federal powers and leaves the remaining powers to the States.
3. Both countries have identical arrangements regarding residuary powers.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: India vests residuary powers in Parliament and distributes subjects through Union, State and Concurrent Lists. The United States enumerates federal powers and leaves the remaining powers to the States; therefore statement 3 is false.
38.tq: Use the reversed comparison trap in the allocation of residuary powers.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: **residuary powers** belong to **Parliament** in India and to the **States** in the USA.
Statement 2 is **correct**: India has **three lists** (Union, State, Concurrent); the USA has **enumerated federal powers**, rest with states.
Statement 3 is **wrong**, since statement 1 shows the arrangements differ — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: India's three lists make for a **strong centre**.
Common to both: **written Constitution**, **federal structure**, **independent judiciary** with judicial review.
India: **parliamentary** executive; USA: **presidential**.

38.s: Which one of the following correctly compares judicial review in India and the United States?
o: India applies due process of law, while the United States applies procedure established by law
India has a narrower judicial review based on procedure established by law, while the United States has a wider review based on due process of law
Both countries have precisely the same scope of judicial review
38.x: India is associated with the narrower expression “procedure established by law,” whereas the United States follows the wider “due process of law” standard.
38.tq: Discriminate between the two similar constitutional phrases and their relative scope.
xs: India has **narrower** review based on "**procedure established by law**"; the USA **wider** review based on "**due process of law**" — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) swaps the two phrases — the classic trap.
xa: Because of its wide review, the US Supreme Court is called a **"third chamber"**.
Both countries have an **independent judiciary with judicial review**.
Britain: courts **cannot question Acts of Parliament**.

38.s: In the context of the United Kingdom and India, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: In both countries, the Prime Minister can be removed only after losing the confidence of the lower House.
In the United Kingdom, the ruling party can replace the Prime Minister, whereas in India the Prime Minister's removal is linked to loss of Lok Sabha confidence.
In India, the ruling party can replace the Prime Minister without any relation to Lok Sabha confidence, whereas this is not possible in the United Kingdom.
Neither country permits a Prime Minister to resign as party leader while remaining head of government.
38.x: The ruling party in the United Kingdom can replace its Prime Minister. In India, removal of the government is linked to losing the confidence of the Lok Sabha.
38.tq: Compare the party mechanism in the United Kingdom with the legislative-confidence requirement in India.
xs: In the **UK**, the **ruling party can replace the PM**; in **India**, removal needs **loss of Lok Sabha confidence** — option **(2)** is correct.
Current relevance: UK PM **Keir Starmer** announced resignation as PM and **Labour** leader.
xa: In a parliamentary system the executive can be removed by **no-confidence**.
Britain's PM comes from the **House of Commons**; India's from **either House**.
The **leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha** becomes PM in India.

38.s: Which one of the following statements correctly reflects the position regarding term limits mentioned in the debate on executive tenure?
o: India has a constitutional two-term limit for the Prime Minister, while the United States has no such limit.
India has no term limit for the Prime Minister, while the United States adopted the 22nd Amendment in 1951.
India adopted the 22nd Amendment in 1951, while the United States has no term limit.
Both India and the United States impose identical term limits on their heads of government.
38.x: India has no term limit for its Prime Minister. The United States adopted the 22nd Amendment in 1951, which is associated with limiting presidential tenure.
38.tq: Use the country-and-amendment pairing to avoid reversing the two systems.
xs: **India** has **no term limit** for the PM, while the **US** adopted the **22nd Amendment (1951)** — option **(2)** is correct.
On **22 March 2026**, **Narendra Modi** completed **8,931 days** as head of an elected government.
xa: He passed **Pawan Kumar Chamling** (**8,930** days).
A **fixed term** is a feature of the **presidential** executive.
**Ambedkar**: India chose **responsibility** over guaranteed tenure.

38.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Shamsher Singh (1974):
1. The case connected the Governor's conduct with the logic of the parliamentary system.
2. Public criticism of Cabinet policy by the Governor was considered compatible with parliamentary conventions.
3. The decision is relevant to understanding the limits imposed by parliamentary responsibility on constitutional office-holders.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
38.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because public criticism of Cabinet policy by the Governor was held to run counter to the parliamentary system.
38.tq: Find the statement that reverses the judicial conclusion while retaining the correct institutional context.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are **correct**: **Shamsher Singh (1974)** tied the **Governor's discretion** to **parliamentary logic**.
Statement 2 is **wrong**: a Governor publicly criticising Cabinet policy runs **"counter to the Parliamentary system"** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: Under **Art. 74(1)** the Council of Ministers' advice to the President is **binding**.
The President is the **de jure** head; real power lies with the **PM + Council of Ministers**.
⚠ The President is **not** the real head of the executive (**APPSC-G2 2017** key).

38.s:
Consider the following statements about the Prime Minister of India:
1. The Prime Minister is the leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha.
2. The Prime Minister is the Leader of the Lok Sabha (Leader of the House) and the chief spokesperson of the Government.
3. The Prime Minister is the Head of State.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
38.x: Statement 1 is correct: the PM leads the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha. Statement 2 is correct: the PM is the Leader of the House and the Government's chief spokesperson. Statement 3 is wrong: the President is the Head of State (nominal head); the PM is Head of Government. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
38.tq: President = Head of State (nominal); PM = Head of Government (real).
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: the PM is the leader of the **majority party or coalition** in the **Lok Sabha**.
Statement 2 is correct: the PM is the **Leader of the Lok Sabha** (Leader of the House) and the **chief spokesperson** of the Government.
Statement 3 is wrong: the **President** is the **Head of State**; the PM is the **Head of Government** and **real executive** head.
xa: The PM **heads the Council of Ministers**.
**Art. 74(1)**: ministers **aid and advise** the President; the advice is **binding**.
⚠ The President is **not** the real head of the executive (**APPSC-G2 2017** key).
A non-member minister must be elected within **six months** (**dual membership**).

39.s: Under Article 153 of the Constitution, which of the following is permissible?
o: A single Governor may be appointed for two or more States
A State may function without a Governor for an indefinite period
Only Union Territories can have a common Governor
A Governor may be elected jointly by two State Legislatures
39.x: Article 153 provides for a Governor for each State, while the Seventh Amendment Act, 1956 enables one person to serve as Governor of two or more States.
39.tq: Test the constitutional exception to the general rule instead of choosing the broad statement.
xs: **A single Governor may be appointed for two or more States** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Art. 153** provides a Governor for each state; the **7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956** lets **one person be Governor of 2 or more states**.
The Governor is **neither directly nor indirectly elected** — he is appointed by the **President** (Art. 155), so option (4) is wrong.
xa: With a **common Governor**, the cost is **shared among the states** as the President decides.
**E.S.L. Narasimhan** was the common Governor for **AP and Telangana**, **2014 to July 2019**.
The 7th Amendment point was asked in **APPSC-GS 2025** and **2021**.

39.s: Which one of the following correctly states the constitutional position regarding the tenure of a Governor?
o: The Governor holds office for six years unless removed by the State Legislature.
The Governor holds office for five years and may continue until the successor enters office.
The Governor necessarily vacates office on completion of five years, even if no successor has entered office.
The Governor has a fixed tenure which cannot be interrupted by transfer.
39.x: The normal term is five years, but the Governor continues in office until the successor enters office. The Governor may also be transferred before completion of the term.
39.tq: Focus on the distinction between the normal term and automatic cessation of office.
xs: Normal term is **five years**, but the Governor **continues until his successor enters office** — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (3) is the classic trap: "quits office immediately after the term expires" is **wrong** (**APPSC-G1 2019**).
He may be **transferred** and **reappointed**, so tenure is not fixed — (4) is wrong.
xa: **Art. 156:** holds office **during the pleasure of the President**.
**No grounds for removal** are stated in the Constitution; limits set by **B.P. Singhal (2010)**.
**Punchhi** Commission recommended a **fixed tenure** to insulate the Governor from the Centre.

39.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A Governor may resign by addressing the resignation to the President.
2. A Governor may be transferred by the President.
3. A Governor may be reappointed.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
39.x: A Governor resigns to the President, may be transferred, and may be reappointed. All three statements are correct.
39.tq: Combine three related tenure provisions and select the complete combination.
xs: A Governor **resigns to the President**, may be **transferred** and may be **reappointed** — all three, **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
He holds office **during the pleasure of the President** (**Art. 156**).
xa: Normal term **5 years**, continues **until his successor enters office**.
⚠ Appointed by the **President**, resigns to the **President**; oath from the **Chief Justice of the High Court**.
Not answerable to Parliament, the state legislature or the **Council of Ministers**.

39.s:
With reference to Article 158, consider the following statements:
1. A Governor cannot be a member of Parliament or of a State Legislature.
2. A Governor cannot hold any other office of profit.
3. The emoluments of a Governor are fixed by the concerned State Legislature.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
39.x: A Governor cannot be a member of Parliament or a State Legislature and cannot hold an office of profit. The emoluments are fixed by Parliament by law, not by the State Legislature.
39.tq: Use the wrong authority trap in the statement concerning fixation of emoluments.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are **correct**: under **Art. 158** the Governor is not a member of Parliament or a state legislature and holds **no office of profit**.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: emoluments are fixed by **Parliament** by law — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Emoluments **cannot be reduced** during the term.
They are **charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State** (**Art. 202(3)**).
A **common Governor's** cost is shared among states as the **President** decides.

39.s:
Which of the following represents the convention generally followed in appointing a Governor?
1. The Governor is ordinarily selected from outside the State.
2. The Chief Minister of the State is consulted.
3. The Constitution expressly requires that the Governor must be an outsider.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
39.x: By convention, the Governor is generally an outsider and the State Chief Minister is consulted. The Constitution does not expressly mandate that the Governor must be an outsider.
39.tq: Separate constitutional requirements from conventions by rejecting the absolute wording in statement 3.
xs: By **convention**, the Governor is an **outsider** to the state and the state **CM is consulted** — **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the Constitution (Art. 157) only asks for a **citizen** aged **35**; "outsider" is not written into it.
xa: **Sarkaria** recommended a politically neutral **outsider**, chosen **after consulting the CM**.
**First ARC**: persons of long experience in public life with a **non-partisan** attitude.
**NCRWC**: appointment by a committee of **PM, Union Home Minister, Lok Sabha Speaker and the state CM**.

39.s: The Supreme Court's decision in B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010) established that
o: the Governor's office is completely independent of the President's pleasure
a Governor cannot be removed arbitrarily or merely because the Centre's Government has changed
a Governor can be removed only after impeachment by Parliament
a Governor can be removed whenever the Union Government changes
39.x: The pleasure doctrine is not unfettered: removal cannot be arbitrary or based merely on a change in the Government at the Centre. Such removal is open to limited judicial review.
39.tq: Use the case-law principle to reject both absolute executive power and the invented impeachment procedure.
xs: **B.P. Singhal (2010)**: a Governor **cannot be removed arbitrarily** or **merely because the Centre's government changes** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **pleasure doctrine is not unfettered**, so (1) and (4) are wrong; there is **no impeachment** route, so (3) is wrong.
xa: Reasons for removal **need not be given**, but removal must not be **arbitrary**.
Being **out of tune with the Centre** is not a ground; **limited judicial review** applies.
The Constitution states **no grounds for removal** of a Governor.

39.s: To which of the following bodies is the Governor constitutionally answerable in the ordinary discharge of the office?
o: The Council of Ministers of the State alone
39.x: The Governor is not answerable to either House of Parliament, to the State Legislature, or to the State Council of Ministers.
39.tq: Use the institutional-accountability trap and select the option covering all three excluded bodies.
xs: The Governor is **not answerable** to either House of Parliament, the state legislature, or the **Council of Ministers** — **None of the above**, option **(4)**.
This was asked as a PYQ in **2019**.
xa: **Art. 361:** not answerable to any **court** for official acts.
He holds office **during the pleasure of the President** (**Art. 156**).
"Pleasure of the President" makes the office **structurally dependent on the Centre**.

39.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

List-I (Article)
A. Article 155
B. Article 156
C. Article 157
D. Article 158

List-II (Provision)
1. Qualifications of Governor
2. Appointment of Governor
3. Conditions of Governor's office
4. Tenure and pleasure of President
39.x: Article 155 deals with appointment, Article 156 with tenure and the President's pleasure, Article 157 with qualifications, and Article 158 with conditions of office.
39.tq: Start with the sure Article 155–appointment pair and eliminate codes that disturb the sequence.
xs: **Art. 155** = appointment; **Art. 156** = tenure / pleasure of the President; **Art. 157** = qualifications; **Art. 158** = conditions of office — **A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3**, option **(1)**.
Option (2) wrongly puts **Art. 155** as tenure; the Governor is **appointed by the President by warrant under hand and seal**.
xa: **Art. 153:** a Governor for each state.
**Art. 159:** oath by the **Chief Justice of the High Court** (else senior-most judge).
**Art. 161:** **pardon**, reprieve, remission for offences under state law.

39.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the pleasure doctrine applicable to a Governor:
1. The Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President.
2. The pleasure of the President permits removal of a Governor for any arbitrary reason without constitutional limitation.
3. The grounds for removal of a Governor are expressly enumerated in the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above is correct?
39.x: Article 156 incorporates the President's pleasure, but B.P. Singhal v. Union of India held that the power cannot be exercised arbitrarily. The Constitution does not expressly enumerate grounds for removal.
39.tq: Treat an apparently broad power as subject to constitutional limits and judicial review.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: the Governor holds office **during the pleasure of the President** (**Art. 156**).
Statement 2 is **wrong**: **B.P. Singhal (2010)** held the pleasure doctrine is **not unfettered** and removal must not be **arbitrary**.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: **no grounds for removal** are stated — so **1 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Reasons for removal **need not be given**; limited **judicial review** applies.
A change of government at the **Centre** is not, by itself, a ground.
**Punchhi** urged a **fixed tenure** for Governors.

39.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional immunity of the Governor under Article 361:
1. The Governor is not answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of official powers and duties.
2. Criminal proceedings can be instituted against the Governor during the term of office with the prior permission of the High Court.
3. The Governor cannot be arrested or imprisoned during the term of office.
4. Civil proceedings concerning personal acts require two months' notice.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
39.x: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct. No criminal proceedings can be instituted against the Governor during the term, even with prior permission of a court; hence statement 2 is false.
39.tq: Separate the absolute bar on criminal proceedings and arrest from the qualified rule for civil proceedings.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: not answerable to any court for **official acts**.
Statement 2 is **wrong**: **no criminal proceedings** during the term at all; statement 3 is **correct**: **no arrest** during the term.
Statement 4 is **correct**: civil proceedings for personal acts need **2 months' notice** — so **1, 3 and 4 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: These immunities are under **Art. 361**.
Under **Art. 163(3)**, ministers' advice to the Governor **cannot be inquired into** in any court.
The Governor is also not answerable to the **state legislature** or **Council of Ministers**.

39.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Governor and the State Legislature under Article 174:
1. The Governor summons and prorogues the Houses and may dissolve the Legislative Assembly.
2. Not more than six months may intervene between two sessions.
3. The Governor is a part of the State Legislature because he is a member of the Legislative Assembly.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
39.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct under Article 174. Statement 3 is wrong: the Governor is a part of the legislature without being a member of either House. Hence '1 and 2 only'; '1 only' misses the six-month rule, and options with 3 are wrong.
39.tq: Governor = part of the legislature, never a member of it.
xs: Statement 1 is **correct**: under **Art. 174** the Governor **summons, prorogues** and **dissolves** the Assembly.
Statement 2 is **correct**: no more than **6 months** between sessions.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: he is **part of the legislature without being a member** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **Nabam Rebia (2016):** summoning, proroguing and dissolving are **not discretionary**; done on **aid and advice**.
**S. Abdul Nazeer** notified the Monsoon Session from **17 Aug 2026** under **Art. 174(1)**.
He **nominates 1/6th** of the Legislative Council (**Art. 171**).

39.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Governor's address to the State Legislature:
1. The special address under Article 176 is mandatory at the first session after each general election.
2. The special address under Article 176 is mandatory at the first session of each year.
3. The Governor delivers this address independently of the Council of Ministers.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
39.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The address is delivered on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers; therefore, statement 3 is incorrect.
39.tq: Identify the statement that reverses the rule on aid and advice while retaining the two occasions for the mandatory address.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are **correct**: the **Art. 176** **special address** is **mandatory** at the first session after each general election and the first session of each year.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: it is delivered on the **aid and advice** of the Council of Ministers (**Nabam Rebia 2016**) — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: ⚠ **175** = optional address; **176** = mandatory special address.
In **Jan 2026**, Governors walked out of or skipped the **Art. 176** address in Opposition-ruled states.
Under **Nabam Rebia**, the address must reflect **Cabinet policy**.

39.s:
Which of the following reports are placed before the State Legislature by the Governor?
1. Report of the Comptroller and Auditor-General relating to the State
2. Report of the State Public Service Commission
3. Report of the State Finance Commission
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
39.x: The Governor places the CAG report relating to the State, the report of the State Public Service Commission and the State Finance Commission report before the State Legislature.
39.tq: Use the common constitutional function of placing independent constitutional and statutory reports before the Legislature.
xs: The Governor places reports of the **CAG**, the **SPSC** and the **State Finance Commission** before the legislature — **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
This is one of his **legislative powers**.
xa: He appoints the **State Election Commissioner** and constitutes the **State Finance Commission** (**243K, 243I**).
He appoints the **SPSC** chair and members (**316**); only the **President** removes them.
He **nominates 1/6th** of the Legislative Council.

39.s:
With reference to the ordinance-making powers of the Governor and the President, consider the following statements:
1. The Governor may promulgate an ordinance when the State Legislature, or either House where there are two Houses, is not in session.
2. The Governor's ordinance-making power extends to subjects in the State List and Concurrent List.
3. The President's ordinance-making power extends only to subjects in the Union List.
4. Both ordinances cease to operate six weeks after the reassembly of the concerned Legislature or Parliament.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
39.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. The President's ordinance-making power is co-extensive with Parliament's legislative powers, including the Concurrent List, so statement 3 is false.
39.tq: Compare the two ordinance powers column by column, especially scope and the six-week limit.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are **correct**: the Governor's **Art. 213** ordinance needs the legislature **not in session** and covers **State and Concurrent List** subjects.
Statement 3 is **wrong**: the President's **Art. 123** ordinance is **co-extensive with Parliament's powers**.
Statement 4 is **correct**: both **lapse 6 weeks** after reassembly — so **1, 2 and 4 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: The Governor needs **President's instructions** where the bill would need prior sanction or reservation; the President needs none.
**Art. 161:** Governor's **pardon** power for offences under state law.
**Art. 174:** max **6 months** between sessions.

39.s: In which of the following circumstances does the Governor require instructions from the President before promulgating an ordinance?
o: Whenever the State Legislature has two Houses
When a Bill containing the same provisions would require the President's prior sanction or would have to be reserved for his consideration
Whenever the ordinance concerns any State List subject
Whenever the ordinance concerns any Concurrent List subject
39.x: The Governor requires the President's instructions where a Bill containing the same provisions would require prior sanction of the President or would have to be reserved for his consideration.
39.tq: Apply the prior-sanction test rather than treating every State or Concurrent List subject alike.
xs: The Governor needs **President's instructions** when a bill with the same provisions would need the President's **prior sanction** or would have to be **reserved** — option **(2)** is correct.
The mere subject (**State** or **Concurrent List**) or having **two Houses** does not trigger it.
xa: The **President's** ordinance (**Art. 123**) needs no such prior instruction.
Governor's ordinance under **Art. 213** lapses **6 weeks** after the legislature reassembles.
Prior sanction example: bills restricting **inter-state trade** — **Art. 304(b)**.

39.s: Under Article 163(1) of the Constitution, the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister aids and advises the Governor
o: Except in matters where the Governor is required to act in his discretion
Only when the Legislative Assembly is in session
39.x: Article 163(1) provides for aid and advice by the Council of Ministers except where the Governor is required to exercise discretion.
39.tq: Test the constitutional exception rather than the general rule.
xs: Under **Art. 163(1)**, the Council of Ministers headed by the CM advises the Governor **except where he must act in his discretion** — option **(1)** is correct.
So aid and advice is not "in all matters without exception" — (3) is wrong.
xa: **Art. 163(2):** the Governor's decision on what is discretionary is **final**.
**Art. 163(3):** ministers' advice **cannot be inquired into in any court**.
The Governor's discretion is **wider than the President's**.

39.s:
With reference to Article 163(2), consider the following statements:
1. The Governor's decision on whether a matter is within his discretion is final.
