The ordinance-making power of a State Governor is governed by Article 213. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The President can promulgate ordinances on matters in the Union List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The President can promulgate ordinances on matters in the Concurrent List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The Governor can promulgate ordinances on matters in the State List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The Governor can promulgate ordinances on matters in the Concurrent List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**President** issues ordinances under **Article 123**; **Governor** under **Article 213**.
The President's ordinance competence covers the **Union List and Concurrent List**; the Governor's the **State List and Concurrent List**.
xa: Both can be issued only when the legislature (or either House) is **not in session**.
Both **lapse six weeks** after the legislature **reassembles**, unless approved earlier.
The Governor needs **prior Presidential instructions** in **three** cases: Bills needing **prior sanction**, **reservation** or **Presidential assent**.

39.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: A President’s ordinance must be approved by Parliament.
A Governor’s ordinance must be approved by the President.
Approval of a Governor’s ordinance is not given by the Union Council of Ministers.
A Governor’s ordinance must be approved by the State Legislature.
39.x: B is incorrect: a Governor's ordinance must be approved by the State Legislature, not by the President (though some need prior Presidential instructions). A President's ordinance needs Parliament's approval.
39.tq: Each ordinance goes back to its own legislature.
n: A Presidential ordinance must be approved by Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
A Governor's ordinance must be approved by the State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
A Governor's ordinance requires approval by the State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
A Governor's ordinance does not require approval by the Union Council of Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
A Governor's ordinance does not require approval by the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
xs: The incorrect statement is that a **Governor's ordinance must be approved by the President** — so option **(2)** is the answer.
A Governor's ordinance is approved by the **State Legislature** — **not** the President or the Union Council of Ministers.
A President's ordinance is approved by **Parliament** — so options (1), (3), (4) are correct.
xa: The Governor's ordinance power is under **Article 213**; the President's under **Article 123**.
The Governor needs the **President's instructions** beforehand in **three** cases — but that is not approval.
Both ordinances can be **withdrawn at any time**.

39.s: Who may withdraw an ordinance, and when?
o: Only Parliament may withdraw it after six weeks.
Only the State Legislature may withdraw it.
Neither the President nor the Governor may withdraw it once issued.
The President or Governor may withdraw it at any time, as applicable.
39.x: The President or the Governor can withdraw their ordinance at any time (Article 123(2)(b) / 213(2)(b)).
39.tq: Recall that withdrawal is open at any time.
n: The President can withdraw an ordinance at any time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The Governor can withdraw an ordinance at any time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The statement that the President cannot repeal or withdraw an ordinance once issued is false. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The President can withdraw an ordinance at any time under Article 123(2)(b). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
xs: **The President or Governor may withdraw** an ordinance **at any time**, as applicable — so option **(4)** is correct.
For the President this is **Article 123(2)(b)**; the Governor also may withdraw **any time**.
Option (1) confuses withdrawal with **lapse** — an ordinance ceases **six weeks** after the legislature **reassembles**.
xa: President's ordinances need approval by **Parliament**; Governor's by the **State Legislature**.
President: **Union and Concurrent List**; Governor: **State and Concurrent List**.
Governor's ordinance is issued during **recess** under **Article 213**.

39.s:
Assertion (A): The President is bound by the advice of the Union Council of Ministers after returning it once for reconsideration.
Reason (R): The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 permits the President to return advice once but requires acceptance of the advice thereafter.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
39.x: Both are true: the 44th Amendment, 1978 lets the President return ministerial advice once for reconsideration, but the advice binds after that. This rule is exactly why the President is bound, so R explains A.
39.tq: Recall the 42nd and 44th Amendment changes to Article 74.
n: The President can return the advice of the Union Council of Ministers once under the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The President is bound by the Union Council of Ministers’ advice after reconsideration. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The Union Council of Ministers aids and advises the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **44th Amendment Act, 1978** lets the **President** return the Council's **advice once** for reconsideration.
After reconsideration he is **bound** by the advice — which is exactly why A holds.
xa: The 44th Amendment also inserted the word "**Cabinet**" into **Article 352**.
**Article 74**: the Council of Ministers **aids and advises** the President; the State counterpart is **Article 163**.
The **Governor** is bound by ministerial advice except in **discretionary** areas.

39.s: Which Article provides for the State Council of Ministers aiding and advising the Governor?
39.x: Article 163 provides for a State Council of Ministers to aid and advise the Governor, like Article 74 for the President. Article 164 deals with appointment of Ministers.
39.tq: Discriminate the Union and State parallels: 74 with 163, 75 with 164.
n: The constitutional basis of the State Council of Ministers is Article 163. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The State Council of Ministers aids and advises the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The Council of Ministers is an executive body aiding and advising the President or Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
xs: **Article 163** provides for the State Council of Ministers to **aid and advise** the **Governor** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Article 74** is the Union counterpart (aid and advice to the **President**).
**Article 164** deals with **appointment** of the CM and ministers; **Article 171** relates to the **Legislative Council** (Governor nominates **one-sixth**).
xa: **Art. 163(2)**: the Governor's own decision on whether a matter is discretionary is **final**.
**Art. 163(3)**: ministerial advice **cannot be inquired into in any court**.
Collective responsibility: Union — **Article 75(3)** to the **Lok Sabha**; State — **Article 164(2)** to the **Legislative Assembly**.

39.s: Which of the following statements regarding the qualifications of the Governor is incorrect?
o: The person must have completed 35 years of age.
The person must be a citizen of India.
The person should not hold any office of profit.
The person may continue as a member of Parliament after becoming Governor.
39.x: Option D is incorrect: a Governor cannot be a member of Parliament or a State Legislature, and must give up any such seat on appointment. They must be a citizen, at least 35, and hold no office of profit.
39.tq: Recall the Governor's qualifications under Articles 157 and 158.
n: The Governor must be a citizen of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The Governor must have completed 35 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The Governor must not be a member of Parliament or a State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
A person appointed as Governor must vacate a parliamentary or State Legislature seat held by that person. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The Governor must not hold any office of profit. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **the person may continue as a member of Parliament after becoming Governor** — so option **(4)** is the answer.
**Art. 158**: the Governor must **not** be an MP or MLA and must **vacate** any such seat.
**Art. 157**: he must be a **citizen of India** and have completed **35** years; he must hold **no office of profit** — so (1), (2), (3) are correct.
xa: The Governor is **appointed by the President** by **warrant** under his hand and seal (**Article 155**).
Emoluments are fixed by **Parliament** by law and **cannot be reduced** during the term.
Conventions: an **outsider** to the state; the state **CM is consulted**.

39.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The emoluments and allowances of the Governor are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State.
II. If the same person is Governor of two or more States, the salary is shared in the proportion determined by the President.
III. The oath of the Governor is administered by the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
39.x: All three are correct: the Governor's emoluments are charged on the State's fund, a Governor of two States is paid in shares the President fixes, and the High Court's Chief Justice administers the oath (Article 159).
39.tq: Recall who swears in the Governor and how pay is shared.
n: The Chief Justice of the concerned High Court administers the Governor’s oath under Article 159. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The emoluments and allowances of the Governor are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State under Article 202. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
When the same person is Governor of two or more States, the President determines the proportion in which the salary is shared. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The same person can be appointed as Governor of two or more States under the Seventh Amendment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
xs: **I, II and III** are all correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
I: emoluments are **charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State** (**Article 202**).
II: for a Governor of **two or more States**, the **President** decides how the salary is shared.
III: the oath is administered by the **Chief Justice of the concerned High Court** (**Article 159**).
xa: The **7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956** allowed **one person to be Governor of 2 or more states**.
Immunity (**Article 361**): **no criminal proceedings** during the term; civil proceedings only after **2 months' notice**.
The Governor **resigns to the President**.

39.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Article 153
(b) Article 154
(c) Article 159
(d) Article 213

List-II
(i) Oath of the Governor
(ii) Governor for each State
(iii) Executive power of the State vested in the Governor
(iv) Promulgation of Ordinances
39.x: Article 153 provides a Governor for each State, 154 vests executive power in them, 159 covers the oath, and 213 ordinances. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
39.tq: Recall Articles 153, 154, 159 and 213.
n: Article 153 provides for a Governor for each State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
Article 154 vests the executive power of the State in the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The Chief Justice of the concerned High Court administers the Governor’s oath under Article 159. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The Governor promulgates Ordinances when the Legislature is not in session under Article 213. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Article 153**: a **Governor for each State**; **Article 154**: **executive power** of the State vested in the Governor.
**Article 159**: **oath** of the Governor; **Article 213**: **promulgation of Ordinances**.
xa: **Article 155**: appointment by the **President**; **Article 156**: office during the **pleasure of the President**.
**Article 157**: **citizen**, at least **35 years**; **Article 158**: no seat in a legislature, no office of profit.
The Governor is an **integral part** of the State Legislature — **Article 168**.

39.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Sarojini Naidu was the first woman Governor of Uttar Pradesh.
Padmaja Naidu was the first woman Governor of West Bengal.
Sarojini Naidu was the first woman Governor of West Bengal.
Padmaja Naidu was the daughter of Sarojini Naidu.
39.x: Option C is incorrect: Sarojini Naidu, India's first woman Governor, governed Uttar Pradesh. Her daughter Padmaja Naidu was the first woman Governor of West Bengal.
39.tq: Discriminate the two Naidus' States.
n: Sarojini Naidu was the first woman Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
Sarojini Naidu was the first woman Governor of Uttar Pradesh. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
Padmaja Naidu was the first woman Governor of an independent State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
Padmaja Naidu was the first woman Governor of West Bengal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **Sarojini Naidu was the first woman Governor of West Bengal** — so option **(3)** is the answer.
**Sarojini Naidu** was the **first woman Governor** — of **Uttar Pradesh** (**1947**).
**Padmaja Naidu** was the first woman Governor of an independent State — **West Bengal**.
xa: ⚠ Both **Uttar Pradesh**: **Sarojini Naidu** = Governor (**1947**); **Sucheta Kripalani** = CM (**1963**).
**C.M. Trivedi** was the first Governor of **Andhra State (1953)** and of **Andhra Pradesh (1956)**.
J&K's Governor was earlier called **Sadr-e-Riyasat** — changed in **1965**.

39.s: The Governor appoints District Judges in consultation with which of the following?
39.x: Under Article 233, the Governor appoints district judges in consultation with the High Court.
39.tq: Recall Article 233.
n: The Governor appoints District Judges in consultation with the High Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
xs: The Governor appoints **District Judges** in consultation with **the High Court** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **State PSC** chair and members are themselves appointed by the Governor (**316**); the **State Election Commissioner** is also his appointee.
The **Chief Minister** advises on appointing **ministers**, not district judges.
xa: The Governor does **not** appoint **HC judges** — the **President** does.
He **cannot remove** SPSC members — only the **President** can.
He appoints the **Advocate-General** (**165**) and acts as **Chancellor** of state universities.

39.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) President's ordinance-making power
(b) President's pardoning power
(c) Governor's ordinance-making power
(d) Governor's pardoning power

List-II
(i) Article 72; all cases
(ii) Article 123
(iii) Article 161; offences against State laws
(iv) Article 213
39.x: The President's ordinances are under Article 123 and pardons under 72 (all cases). The Governor's ordinances are under 213 and pardons under 161 (State laws only). The answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii.
39.tq: Pair the President's Articles (123, 72) with the Governor's (213, 161).
n: The President makes Ordinances under Article 123. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The President has pardoning power under Article 72 in all cases. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii** — so option **(4)** is correct.
President: ordinances under **Article 123**; pardons under **Article 72** — **all cases**.
Governor: ordinances under **Article 213**; pardons under **Article 161** — **offences against State laws** only.
xa: Governor's pardoning covers **pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions**, and he may **suspend** or **commute** sentences.
**Perarivalan (2022)**: the Governor is **bound by Cabinet advice** on pardon/remission under **Art. 161**.
President's discretion is **very limited**; the Governor's is **comparatively more**.

39.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The Governor of Jammu and Kashmir was earlier called Sadr-e-Riyasat.
Statement B: The designation Sadr-e-Riyasat was changed to Governor in 1965.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
39.x: Both are true: Jammu and Kashmir's head of State was called Sadr-e-Riyasat until 1965, when the title became Governor.
39.tq: Recall the 1965 change of title.
n: The Governor of Jammu and Kashmir was earlier called Sadr-e-Riyasat. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The designation Sadr-e-Riyasat in Jammu and Kashmir was changed to Governor in 1965. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The Governor of **Jammu and Kashmir** was earlier called **Sadr-e-Riyasat**.
The designation was changed to **Governor** in **1965**.
xa: Former J&K had **6 months** of **Governor's Rule** under **Sec 92 of the J&K Constitution**, then Art 356.
After **2019**, J&K was under President's Rule under the Reorganisation Act until **Oct 2024**.
**Padmaja Naidu** was the first woman Governor of **West Bengal**.

39.s:
Assertion (A): The Governor can reserve a Bill for the President even when the Council of Ministers advises otherwise.
Reason (R): The Governor is not bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers in all matters.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
39.x: Both are true: the Governor can reserve a bill for the President against ministerial advice because the Governor is not bound by that advice in every matter. R explains A.
39.tq: Ask whether limited discretion explains acting against advice.
n: The Governor can reserve a Bill for the President even when the Council of Ministers advises otherwise. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The Governor is not bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers in all matters. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The Governor may **reserve a Bill** for the President **even against the Council's advice** — a **discretionary power**.
This is possible because he is **not bound** by the Council of Ministers' advice in **all** matters.
xa: Reserving a bill (**Art. 200**), recommending President's Rule (**Art. 356**) and seeking information (**Art. 167**) = **constitutional discretion**.
Appointing a CM in a **hung Assembly** = **situational discretion**.
The only **mandatory** reservation: a bill that **derogates from the powers of the High Court**.
Governor's discretion is **wider than the President's**.

39.s: Which of the following correctly describes the constitutional position of the Chief Minister in a State?
o: The Chief Minister is the real executive head, while the Governor is the nominal or constitutional head
The Chief Minister is the nominal head, while the Governor is the real executive head
The Chief Minister and Governor are jointly the real executive heads
The Governor is the head of the Council of Ministers, while the Chief Minister is its nominal head
39.x: The Chief Minister is the real executive head of the State and heads the Council of Ministers. The Governor is the nominal or constitutional head, like the President at the Centre.
39.tq: Discriminate the nominal head from the real executive.
n: The Chief Minister is the real executive head of the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
The Governor is the nominal and constitutional head of the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
The Chief Minister is the head of the State Council of Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
xs: **The Chief Minister is the real executive head, while the Governor is the nominal or constitutional head** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **CM** and **Council of Ministers** are the **real executive**; the CM **heads** the Council.
The Governor is the **nominal / constitutional head**, so options (2), (3), (4) misplace the roles.
xa: The CM is the **leader** of the majority in the **Legislative Assembly** and **chief spokesperson** of the State Government.
**Article 154**: executive power of the State is vested in the **Governor** — exercised on ministerial advice.
**Art. 167**: the CM is the **chief link** between Governor and Council.

39.s:
Consider the following statements about the State Council of Ministers under Article 164:
1. A person who is not a member of the State Legislature may be appointed a Minister but must become an MLA or MLC within six months.
2. State Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the Chief Minister.
3. The Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor and is normally the leader of the majority party in the Legislative Assembly.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
39.x: Statement 3 is correct: under Article 164(1) the Governor appoints the Chief Minister, normally the leader of the Assembly majority. Statement 2 is wrong: State Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the Governor, not the Chief Minister (as Union Ministers serve at the President's, not the PM's, pleasure). Statement 1 is correct: Article 164(4) allows a non-member six months. Hence '1 and 3 only'.
39.tq: Pleasure = Governor (State) / President (Union), never CM or PM.
xs: Statements **1 and 3 only** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: under **Art. 164(4)** a non-member minister must become an **MLA/MLC** within **six months**.
Statement 2 is wrong: State Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the **Governor**, **not the CM**.
Statement 3 is correct: under **Art. 164(1)** the **CM is appointed by the Governor**, normally the **majority party** leader.
xa: Union parallel: ministers hold office at the **President's** pleasure, not the PM's.
**91st Amendment (2003)**: ministers ≤ **15%** of the Assembly; **minimum 12** (**Art. 164(1A)**).
A **Minister for Tribal Welfare** is mandatory in **Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha**; Bihar dropped by the **94th Amendment, 2006**.

39.s:
Assertion (A): The State Council of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.
Reason (R): If a No-Confidence Motion is passed, the entire Council of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, must resign.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
39.x: Both are true: under Article 164(2), the ministry is collectively answerable to the Assembly, which is why a passed no-confidence motion forces the whole ministry, Chief Minister included, to resign. R explains A.
39.tq: Ask whether resigning together explains collective responsibility.
n: The Council of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly of the State under Article 164(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
If a No-Confidence Motion is passed, the entire Council of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, must resign. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
Article 164 deals with the appointment, tenure, responsibility and other provisions relating to Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
Article 164 concerns other provisions relating to Ministers, including appointment, responsibility and size limit. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The Council, including the CM, is **collectively responsible** to the **Legislative Assembly** — **Article 164(2)**.
So a passed **No-Confidence Motion** forces the **entire** Council, including the CM, to **resign**.
xa: Responsibility is **not** to the **Legislative Council**.
Union counterpart: collective responsibility to the **Lok Sabha** — **Article 75(3)**.
On **loss of majority**, the CM must resign or be **dismissed**.

39.s: Which of the following statements regarding the Governor's action on State Bills is incorrect?
o: The Governor must return an ordinary Bill within a fixed time limit.
The Governor may return an ordinary Bill for reconsideration.
The Governor may give assent to a State Bill.
The Governor may withhold assent to a State Bill.
39.x: Option A is incorrect: the Governor may return an ordinary bill, but the Constitution sets no time limit for acting on it. The Governor can also assent or withhold assent.
39.tq: Recall that no time limit is fixed for the Governor.
n: The Governor can give assent to a Bill under Articles 200 and 201. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Governor can withhold assent to a Bill under Articles 200 and 201. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Governor can return an ordinary Bill under Articles 200 and 201. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
There is no fixed time limit for the Governor to act on a returned ordinary Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **the Governor must return an ordinary Bill within a fixed time limit** — so option **(1)** is the answer.
**Articles 200 and 201**: the Governor can **give assent**, **withhold** assent, **return** an ordinary Bill, or **reserve** it — with **no fixed time limit**.
A Bill may be returned **once** for reconsideration, but **not a Money Bill**.
xa: A **re-passed** bill: the Governor **must assent**.
**Nov 2025 Presidential Reference (Art. 143)**: courts **cannot fix timelines** and **deemed assent** is rejected.
⚠ **Art 142** = deemed assent granted (**Apr 2025**); **Art 143** Reference = deemed assent rejected (**Nov 2025**).

39.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The President may impose President's Rule on the report of the Governor or otherwise.
Statement B: President's Rule is imposed when the government of a State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
39.x: Both are true: under Article 356, the President can impose President's Rule on the Governor's report or otherwise, when a State cannot be governed according to the Constitution.
39.tq: Recall Article 356's ground.
n: President’s Rule may be imposed on the Governor’s report or otherwise. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
President’s Rule is imposed when the government of a State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The President may impose President’s Rule on the Governor’s report. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The President may impose President’s Rule suo motu or otherwise. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Failure of constitutional machinery is the ground for President’s Rule under Article 356. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Under **Article 356** the President acts on the **Governor's report** or **otherwise** (**suo motu**).
The ground: the State's government **cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution**.
xa: Duration: **6 months** at a time, maximum **3 years**.
Beyond **1 year** only with a **National Emergency** in force **and** an **EC** certificate that elections cannot be held.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)**: Art. 356 is subject to **judicial review**; majority tested **on the floor**.

39.s: Which commissions addressed federal tensions and the deployment of central armed forces?
o: Jeevan Reddy Committee and Punchhi Commission
39.x: The Sarkaria Commission (set up 1983, reported 1988) and the Punchhi Commission (set up 2007, reported 2010) dealt with federal tensions, including deploying central armed forces in States.
39.tq: Match each body to its subject.
n: Communalism and national integration were associated with the Justice Liberhan and Srikrishna Commissions. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 93-94]
Centre-State relations and regionalism were associated with the Sarkaria Commission and Punchhi Commission. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 93-94]
The Sarkaria Commission was constituted in 1988. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 93-94]
The Punchhi Commission was constituted in 2010. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 93-94]
The Sarkaria Commission and Punchhi Commission addressed federal tensions. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 93-94]
The Sarkaria Commission and Punchhi Commission addressed the deployment of central armed forces. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 93-94]
xs: The **Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions** addressed federal tensions and deployment of central armed forces — so option **(1)** is correct.
Both are linked to the **Ministry of Home Affairs** and to **Centre-State relations** and **regionalism**.
They also dealt with **revitalizing the inter-state council** and **objective criteria** for invoking **Article 356**.
The **Jeevan Reddy Committee** dealt with **AFSPA** and North East conflicts, not this.
xa: **Sarkaria**: politically neutral **outsider** as Governor; Art. 356 as **last resort**; **247** recommendations.
**Punchhi**: **Fixed tenure** for Governors; **Localised emergency** (a district, up to **3 months**).
⚠ Sources differ: Sarkaria set up **June 1983** (report **1988**); Punchhi set up **2007** (report **2010**).

39.s:
Assertion (A): The Justice B.P. Jeevan Reddy Committee sought to mitigate regional alienation.
Reason (R): It recommended repeal of AFSPA, 1958 and suggested protective clauses in the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
39.x: Both are true: the Jeevan Reddy Committee (2005) proposed repealing AFSPA and moving its safeguards into UAPA, to reduce alienation in the North-East. R explains A.
39.tq: Ask whether the measures explain the aim.
n: The Justice B.P. Jeevan Reddy Committee recommended the repeal of AFSPA, 1958. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 93-94]
The Justice B.P. Jeevan Reddy Committee suggested inserting relevant protective clauses into the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 93-94]
The Justice B.P. Jeevan Reddy Committee made its recommendations to mitigate regional alienation. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 93-94]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **Justice B.P. Jeevan Reddy Committee** (**formed 2005**, **Ministry of Home Affairs**) aimed to **mitigate regional alienation**.
It did so by recommending **repeal of AFSPA, 1958** and **protective clauses** in the **Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act**.
xa: It is associated with **regionalisation** and **North East conflicts**.
The **First ARC** study team proposed an **Inter-State Council under Art. 263**.
First ARC also proposed deployment of **central armed forces** in States, on their request or otherwise.

40.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Chief Minister in a hung Assembly:
1. The Constitution lays down detailed statutory criteria for the Governor to select the Chief Minister.
2. The Governor may exercise discretion in selecting a person to form the government.
3. An early floor test is ordinarily used to determine whether the government enjoys majority support.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
40.x: The Constitution does not prescribe detailed criteria for this situation, so statement 1 is false. The Governor may exercise discretion and an early floor test is used to establish majority support.
40.tq: Spot the absolute constitutional claim and retain the two practical features of a hung Assembly.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 wrong: in a **hung Assembly** there are **no constitutional criteria**; it is the Governor's discretion.
Statement 2 correct: the Governor uses **discretion** in choosing whom to invite.
Statement 3 correct: an **early floor test** follows (as in May **2026**).
xa: Sarkaria (**1987**) + Punchhi (**2010**) order: **pre-poll alliance** → **single largest party with support** → **post-poll coalition** → **post-poll alliance with outside support**.
**Art. 164(1)**: the **Governor appoints the CM**, usually the majority party leader.
CM stays only while he has the **Assembly's confidence**.

40.s: Under which Article of the Constitution is the Chief Minister of a State appointed by the Governor?
40.x: Article 164(1) provides that the Governor appoints the Chief Minister. Article 163(1) concerns aid and advice, Article 167 the CM's duties towards the Governor, and Article 174 sessions of the legislature.
xs: The Governor appoints the CM under **Article 164(1)** — option **(2)** (APPSC-GS **2021**).
**Art. 167** is about the **CM's duties towards the Governor**, not appointment.
xa: ⚠ Clauses of **Art. 164**: (1) appointment, (2) **collective responsibility**, (3) **oath**, (4) **6 months** rule, (5) **salaries**.
Usually the **leader of the majority party** is appointed.
In a **hung Assembly** the Governor uses discretion.

40.s:
According to the Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions, arrange the following in the order of preference the Governor should follow when inviting a party or group to form the government in a hung Assembly:
1. Single largest party with support of others
2. Post-poll alliance with some parties joining the government and others supporting from outside
3. Pre-poll alliance
4. Post-poll coalition of parties
40.x: The recommended order is pre-poll alliance, then the single largest party with support of others, then a post-poll coalition, and finally a post-poll alliance with outside support, i.e. 3, 1, 4, 2.
40.tq: Pre-poll first, then largest party, then coalitions formed after the poll.
xs: Correct order: **3, 1, 4, 2** — option **(3)**.
**Pre-poll alliance** → **single largest party with support** → **post-poll coalition** → **post-poll alliance with outside support**.
This is the **Sarkaria (1987)** and **Punchhi (2010)** order.
xa: The Constitution gives **no criteria** for a hung Assembly — it is the Governor's discretion.
An **early floor test** follows (May **2026**).
**Art. 164(1)**: the **Governor appoints the CM**.

40.s: A Chief Minister continues in office constitutionally so long as he or she enjoys the confidence of the
40.x: The Chief Minister must retain the confidence of the Legislative Assembly. Loss of majority may lead to resignation or dismissal of the government after the position is established.
40.tq: Distinguish the formal pleasure of the Governor from the actual requirement of legislative confidence.
xs: The CM stays in office only while he has the **confidence of the Legislative Assembly** — option **(3)**.
If he loses it, the Governor can **ask him to resign** or **dismiss** the government.
A literal "**pleasure**" reading (Governor alone) was cautioned against in the **Constituent Assembly**.
xa: Collective responsibility is to the **Legislative Assembly** (**Art. 164(2)**).
The CM's **term is not fixed**.
The CM can **advise dissolution** of the Assembly.

40.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Chief Minister and ministers of a State under Article 164:
1. The oath of office is administered by the Governor.
2. A person who is not a member of the State Legislature can be a minister for six months, after which he ceases unless elected.
3. The salaries of ministers are fixed by Parliament.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
40.x: Statement 1 is correct (Art. 164(3)). Statement 2 is correct (Art. 164(4)). Statement 3 is wrong: salaries are fixed by the State Legislature (Art. 164(5)). Hence '1 and 2 only'.
40.tq: State ministers' salaries = State Legislature; Governor's emoluments = Parliament.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: oath by the **Governor** (**Art. 164(3)**).
Statement 2 correct: a non-member can be minister for **six months** (**Art. 164(4)**).
Statement 3 wrong: salaries are fixed by the **state legislature** (**Art. 164(5)**), not Parliament.
xa: **Art. 164(1)** = appointment; **Art. 164(2)** = **collective responsibility** to the Assembly.
The **130th Amendment Bill, 2025** would amend **Art. 164** too.

40.s:
Which of the following statements regarding the Chief Minister is correct?
1. The term of the Chief Minister is not fixed by the Constitution.
2. The Chief Minister recommends allocation of portfolios among ministers.
3. The Chief Minister may advise dissolution of the Legislative Assembly.
4. The Chief Minister has no role in the continuation or dropping of ministers.
40.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the Chief Minister can recommend dropping ministers and has an important role in the composition of the Council.
40.tq: Reject the single reversal in an otherwise accurate list of Chief Ministerial functions.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: the CM's **term is not fixed**.
Statement 2: the CM **recommends portfolios**.
Statement 3: the CM **can advise dissolution** of the Assembly.
Statement 4 wrong: the CM **can drop ministers**.
xa: The CM is the **chief link** between Governor and Council (**Art. 167**).
The CM stays only while he has the **Assembly's confidence**.

40.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 167:
1. The Chief Minister is the chief link between the Governor and the Council of Ministers.
2. The Chief Minister must communicate all decisions of the Council relating to administration and legislative proposals to the Governor.
3. The Governor may require the Chief Minister to place before the Council a matter decided by an individual minister.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
40.x: All three statements correctly describe the Chief Minister's duties and intermediary role under Article 167.
40.tq: When all listed statements directly express the constitutional link and information duties, select the complete combination.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: the CM is the **chief link** between the Governor and the Council.
Statement 2: he must **communicate all Council decisions** on administration and legislative proposals.
Statement 3: if the Governor requires, he must **submit for Council consideration** a matter decided by a **single minister**.
xa: Seeking information under **Art. 167** is a **constitutional discretion** of the Governor.
CM mirrors the **PM** (**Arts. 74-75**).

40.s: Seeking information from the Chief Minister under Article 167 is regarded as a constitutional discretion of the
o: Chief Justice of the High Court
40.x: Under Article 167, the Governor can call on the Chief Minister for information about administration and legislative proposals, and this is a constitutional discretion of the Governor. The CM is the chief link between the Governor and the Council of Ministers.
40.tq: Match the information-seeking discretion with the constitutional office to which the duty is addressed.
xs: Seeking information under **Art. 167** is a constitutional discretion of the **Governor** — option **(1)**.
The CM must **communicate** all Council decisions on administration and legislative proposals to him.
xa: The CM is the **chief link** between Governor and Council.
The Governor can require a single minister's decision to be **placed before the Council**.
By contrast, choosing a CM in a **hung Assembly** is discretion without constitutional criteria.

40.s: Under Article 164(2), the State Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the:
o: Both Houses of the State Legislature
40.x: Article 164(2) makes the Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly alone. Ministers hold office at the Governor's pleasure but are not collectively responsible to him; the Council is not responsible to the Legislative Council.
xs: The State Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the **Legislative Assembly** — option **(3)**.
This is **Art. 164(2)** (BPSC **2022**); not to the Governor or the Legislative Council.
xa: The CM stays only while he has the **Assembly's confidence**.
**Art. 164(3)**: oath by the **Governor**; **Art. 164(5)**: salaries by the **state legislature**.
The Union parallel lies in **Arts. 74-75**.

40.s:
Consider the following statements about the Deputy Chief Minister in a State:
1. The office is expressly mentioned in the Constitution of India.
2. A Deputy Chief Minister is sworn in as a minister.
3. The post is generally a political arrangement.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
40.x: The Constitution does not specifically mention the office of Deputy Chief Minister, so statement 1 is false. The incumbent is sworn in as a minister and the office is a political arrangement.
40.tq: Reject the constitutional-status trap and retain the two facts describing the actual position.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 wrong: the Deputy CM is **not mentioned in the Constitution**.
Statement 2 correct: he is **sworn in as a minister**.
Statement 3 correct: the post is a **political arrangement**.
xa: Precedence: ranks with **Union Ministers of State** at **No. 10**.
Likewise, a State has **no counterpart of the Vice-President**.

40.s: In the order of precedence, a Deputy Chief Minister ranks with a
o: Union Minister of State at No. 10
40.x: A Deputy Chief Minister ranks with Union Ministers of State and occupies position No. 10 in the order of precedence.
40.tq: Use the paired rank and category together to avoid confusing the Deputy Chief Minister with a Cabinet Minister.
xs: A Deputy CM ranks with **Union Ministers of State at No. 10** — option **(1)**.
He is only **sworn in as a minister**, so he does not rank as a Union Cabinet Minister.
xa: The post is **not mentioned in the Constitution**; he is sworn in as a **minister**.
It is a **political arrangement**.

40.s: The first Speaker of the Legislative Assembly of united Andhra Pradesh was
40.x: Nallapati Venkata Ramaiah was the first Speaker of the united Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly.
40.tq: Distinguish the first presiding officer of the Assembly from the first Chief Minister of the State.
xs: **Nallapati Venkata Ramaiah** was the first Speaker of the united AP Assembly — option **(3)**.
**Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy** was the first **CM** of united AP, not the Speaker.
xa: Sanjeeva Reddy's first cabinet had **13** ministers (**1956-60**).
First CM of residuary AP (**2014**): **N. Chandrababu Naidu**.

40.s: Who was the first Chief Minister of united Andhra Pradesh (1956)?
40.x: Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy was the first CM of united Andhra Pradesh (1956-60). Tanguturi Prakasam was CM of Andhra State, Burgula Ramakrishna Rao of Hyderabad State, and N. Chandrababu Naidu the first CM of residuary AP (2014).
40.tq: United AP 1956 = Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy; residuary AP 2014 = Naidu.
xs: **Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy** was the first CM of united AP (**1956-60**) — option **(2)**.
**N. Chandrababu Naidu** was the first CM of **residuary AP** (**2014**).
xa: His first cabinet had **13** ministers.
First Speaker: **Nallapati Venkata Ramaiah**.
AP Assembly has **175** seats, so the cabinet maximum is **26**.

40.s:
Consider the following statements about the Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill, 2025:
1. A Prime Minister, Chief Minister or Minister held in custody for 30 consecutive days for an offence punishable with five years or more would be removed on the 31st day.
2. It proposes amendments to Articles 75, 164 and 239AA.
3. It applies only to Ministers and not to the Prime Minister or a Chief Minister.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
40.x: Statement 2 is correct: the Bill amends Articles 75, 164 and 239AA. Statement 1 is correct: 30 consecutive days in custody for an offence punishable with 5+ years leads to removal on the 31st day. Statement 3 is wrong: it covers the PM, CMs and Ministers alike. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
40.tq: 130th Bill: Arts 75, 164, 239AA; 30 days custody, 5+ year offence, out on day 31.
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: a PM, CM or minister in custody for **30 consecutive days** for an offence punishable with **5+ years** is removed on the **31st day**.
Statement 2 is correct: the Bill amends **Arts. 75, 164, 239AA**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it covers the **PM**, **CM** and ministers alike.
xa: **West Bengal (May 2026)**: a defeated CM said she would not resign; BJP won **207/294**.
**NITI Aayog**: the **11th** Governing Council saw all **28** CMs present for the first time.
The CM mirrors the PM (**Arts. 74-75**); the state has no counterpart of the **Vice-President**.

40.s:
Consider the following statements comparing the State executive with the Union executive:
1. The Chief Minister mirrors the Prime Minister, whose Council of Ministers is covered by Articles 74 and 75.
2. The State has a constitutional counterpart of the Vice-President.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
40.x: Statement 1 is correct: the CM is the State counterpart of the PM (Arts. 74-75). Statement 2 is wrong: a State has no counterpart of the Vice-President. Hence '1 only'.
40.tq: CM = PM of the State; no State Vice-President.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **CM mirrors the PM** (**Arts. 74-75**).
Statement 2 wrong: a State has **no counterpart of the Vice-President**.
xa: The Deputy CM is **not mentioned in the Constitution**.
**Art. 164(2)**: State Council collectively responsible to the **Legislative Assembly**.

40.s: The Legislative Assembly of Andhra Pradesh has 175 seats. On the stated maximum-size rule for a State Council of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, the maximum number of ministers would be:
40.x: The stated maximum is 15 percent of the Assembly strength. Fifteen percent of 175 is 26.25, giving a maximum of 26 ministers when expressed as the applicable whole-number limit.
40.tq: Apply the percentage limit to the Assembly strength and use the applicable whole-number maximum.
xs: For AP's **175**-seat Assembly, the maximum Council of Ministers is **26** — option **(2)**.
The cap is a share of **Assembly strength**, which works out to **26** for **175** seats; options (1), (3) and (4) do not match it.
xa: The **Governor appoints** the CM, and ministers on the CM's advice; the CM **recommends portfolios**.
The CM **can drop ministers**.
United AP's first cabinet (**1956**) had **13** ministers.

40.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) First woman Chief Minister
(b) First non-Congress Chief Minister
(c) Chief Minister of Delhi/Puducherry
(d) Oath of the Chief Minister administered by

List-II
(i) President
(ii) Sucheta Kripalani
(iii) Governor
(iv) E.M.S. Namboodiripad
40.x: Sucheta Kripalani was the first woman Chief Minister and E.M.S. Namboodiripad the first non-Congress one. The President appoints the Chief Ministers of Delhi and Puducherry, and the Governor swears in a Chief Minister. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
40.tq: Match each first and each appointing authority.
n: The oath of the Chief Minister is administered by the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
Sucheta Kripalani was the first woman Chief Minister. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
E. M. S. Namboodiripad was the first non-Congress Chief Minister. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
The Chief Minister of Delhi is appointed by the President under Article 239AA. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
The Chief Minister of Puducherry is appointed by the President under Article 239AA. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
Sucheta Kripalani was the Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
E. M. S. Namboodiripad became Chief Minister of Kerala in 1957. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii** — so option **(4)** is correct.
First woman CM: **Sucheta Kripalani** (UP, **1963**); first non-Congress CM: **E.M.S. Namboodiripad**.
CM of **Delhi and Puducherry** is appointed by the **President** (**Article 239AA**); the CM's **oath** is administered by the **Governor** (**Art. 164(3)**).
xa: The CM's **resignation** is addressed to the **Governor**.
First CM of united AP: **Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy**; first cabinet of **13** ministers.
First Speaker of the united AP Assembly: **Nallapati Venkata Ramaiah**.

40.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Article 163 provides for a Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister to aid and advise the Governor.
Statement B: Article 163 concerns the Council of Ministers aiding and advising the Governor.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
40.x: Both are true: Article 163 provides a Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister to aid and advise the Governor. Both statements say the same thing.
n: Article 163 provides for a Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister to aid and advise the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
Article 163 concerns the Council of Ministers aiding and advising the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Article 163** provides a **Council of Ministers headed by the CM** to **aid and advise** the **Governor**.
Statement B says the same in brief, so it is also true.
xa: **Article 164** covers **appointment, tenure, responsibility** and **size limit** of Ministers.
**Art. 163(2)**: the Governor's decision on what is discretionary is **final**.
**Art. 163(3)**: ministerial advice **cannot be inquired into in any court**.

40.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) Leader of the Legislative Assembly
(b) Chief spokesperson of the State Government
(c) Advice on summoning and prorogation of the State Legislature
(d) Advice on dissolution of the Legislative Assembly

List-II
(i) Leadership role in the Legislative Assembly
(ii) Public communication role of the State Government
(iii) Advice concerning the sittings of the State Legislature
(iv) Advice concerning ending the term of the Legislative Assembly
40.x: The Chief Minister leads the Assembly and speaks for the government, and advises the Governor on summoning and proroguing the legislature and on dissolving the Assembly. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
40.tq: Match each role to its description.
n: The Chief Minister is the leader of the Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
The Chief Minister is the chief spokesperson of the State Government. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
The Chief Minister advises the Governor on the summoning and prorogation of the State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
The Chief Minister advises the Governor on the dissolution of the Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
xs: The correct match is **a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv** — so option **(2)** is correct.
As **leader of the Assembly** the CM has a **leadership role** (i); as **chief spokesperson** he plays the **public communication role** (ii).
He advises the Governor on **summoning and prorogation** — the **sittings** of the Legislature (iii) — and on **dissolution** — ending the Assembly's term (iv).
xa: **Article 167**: the CM **communicates** all decisions and **proposals for legislation** to the Governor and **furnishes information**.
The CM **selects** ministers, **allocates portfolios** and can recommend **removal** of a Minister.
**Art. 164(5)**: salaries are fixed by the **state legislature**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements regarding States whose Legislative Assemblies have fewer than 60 seats or special minimums:
1. Sikkim has 32 seats under Article 371F.
2. Goa and Mizoram have 40 seats each.
3. Arunachal Pradesh has only 30 seats under Article 371H.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
41.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: Article 371H sets a minimum of 30 for Arunachal Pradesh, but it actually has 60 seats. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
41.tq: Arunachal: minimum 30 allowed, actual 60 - a classic trap.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **Sikkim** has **32** seats (**Art. 371F**).
Statement 2 correct: **Goa and Mizoram** have **40** each.
Statement 3 wrong: **Art. 371H** only sets a **minimum of 30** for Arunachal; it actually has **60**.
xa: ⚠ Some notes wrongly list Arunachal as below **60**.
Normal range under **Art. 170**: **60-500**.
**AP 175**; **Telangana 119**.

41.s: In a Legislative Assembly consisting of 70 members, the quorum for a sitting would be—
41.x: Quorum is 10 members or one-tenth of the total membership, whichever is greater. For a 70-member House, 10 is greater than 7.
41.tq: Apply the ‘whichever is greater’ rule rather than simply calculating one-tenth.
xs: Quorum is **10 members**, which is greater than one-tenth of **70** (= **7**) — option **(2)**.
Rule (**Art. 189(3)**): **10 members or one-tenth** of the House, **whichever is greater**.
So option (1), **7**, is only the one-tenth figure; **35** and **70** are not the rule.
xa: The **Speaker** adjourns or suspends the House for **lack of quorum**.
**Art. 189** also: the Speaker has a **casting vote** on a tie.
Normal Assembly strength: **60-500** (**Art. 170**).

41.s: Which one of the following correctly presents the present strength of the Legislative Assemblies of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh respectively?
41.x: The Legislative Assemblies of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh have 175, 119 and 403 seats respectively.
41.tq: Read the three figures as a fixed sequence and reject near-value substitutions.
xs: Option (4) wrongly gives AP **176**; options (1) and (2) misstate Telangana and UP.
xa: AP's Council exists today; **six states** have Councils.

41.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the composition of a State Legislative Council:
1. One-third of the members are elected by local bodies such as municipalities and district boards.
2. One-twelfth are elected by teachers of three years' standing in institutions not below secondary school.
3. One-sixth are elected by registered graduates of three years' standing.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
41.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: registered graduates elect one-twelfth; the one-sixth share is nominated by the Governor. Hence '1 and 2 only'.
41.tq: 1/3 local bodies, 1/3 MLAs, 1/12 graduates, 1/12 teachers, 1/6 nominated.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: **1/3** elected by **local bodies** (municipalities, district boards).
Statement 2 correct: **1/12** by **teachers** of **3**+ years in institutions not below **secondary school**.
Statement 3 wrong: **graduates** elect **1/12**; the **1/6** share is **nominated by the Governor**.
xa: ⚠ **1/3 – 1/12 – 1/12 – 1/3 – 1/6** = **local bodies – graduates – teachers – MLAs – Governor**.
**1/3** elected by **MLAs** from among non-members of the Assembly.
Mode of election: **PR-STV**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements regarding nomination to a State Legislative Council:
1. The Governor nominates one-sixth of the total members.
2. The nominated members represent literature, science, art, cooperative movement and social service.
3. Such nominations are made on the advice of the State Cabinet.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
41.x: All three statements are correct. The Governor nominates one-sixth of the Council from the specified fields, and the nominations are made on Cabinet advice.
41.tq: Check the fraction, the listed fields and the authority's advice together.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: the Governor nominates **1/6** of the Council.
Statement 2: from **literature, science, art, cooperative movement and social service**.
Statement 3: nominations are made on **Cabinet advice**.
xa: Other shares: **1/3** local bodies, **1/12** graduates, **1/12** teachers, **1/3** MLAs.
Council size: max **1/3** of the Assembly, min **40** (**Art. 171**).
Significance: gives a place to **experts who cannot face elections**.

41.s: The members of a State Legislative Council are elected by which method?
o: Cumulative voting by the Legislative Assembly alone
First-past-the-post system by direct universal suffrage
Proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote
41.x: Members of a State Legislative Council are elected indirectly through proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote.
41.tq: Discriminate between the electoral system and the appointing authority.
xs: Council members are elected indirectly by **PR-STV** — **proportional representation by single transferable vote** — option **(4)**.
It is not direct election by universal suffrage; only **1/6** are **nominated** by the Governor.
xa: **Rajya Sabha** members are also elected by MLAs by **PR-STV**.
MLAs elect **1/3** of MLCs.
Members serve **6 years**; **1/3** retire every **second year**.

41.s:
With reference to the size of a State Legislative Council, which of the following statements are correct?
1. Its membership cannot exceed one-third of the total strength of the Legislative Assembly.
2. Its membership cannot be less than 40.
3. Its actual strength is fixed by Parliament.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
41.x: A Legislative Council must have at least 40 members and cannot exceed one-third of the Assembly's strength. Parliament fixes its actual strength within these limits.
41.tq: Combine the two numerical limits with the authority that fixes the actual size.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: maximum = **one-third of the Assembly's** total strength (**Art. 171**).
Statement 2: minimum = **40**.
Statement 3: actual strength fixed by **Parliament** — keeps the directly elected House predominant.
xa: Creation/abolition by **Art. 169**: Assembly special majority + Parliament law.
AP Assembly has **175** seats.
Council is a **permanent body**.

41.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the tenure of the State Legislative Council?
o: It is a permanent body, and one-sixth of its members retire every year.
It is a permanent body, and one-third of its members retire every second year.
It is dissolved every five years along with the Assembly.
It has a fixed tenure of six years as a whole House.
41.x: The Legislative Council is a permanent House. One-third of its members retire every second year, while each member has a six-year term.
41.tq: Separate the tenure of an individual member from the continuity of the House.
xs: The Council is a **permanent body**; **one-third** of members retire **every second year** — option **(2)**.
Each member serves **6 years**; the Council itself is **not dissolved**, unlike the Assembly's **5**-year term.
xa: Minimum age: **30** (**Art. 173**).
Size: min **40**, max **1/3** of the Assembly.
Its existence depends on the **will of the Assembly** (**Art. 169**).

41.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the law made by Parliament under Article 169:
1. Parliament passes the law by simple majority.
2. Such a law is deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution under Article 368.
3. Parliament determines the strength of the Legislative Council within the constitutional limits.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
41.x: Parliament uses a simple majority and determines the Council's strength within the constitutional limits. The law is not deemed an amendment under Article 368, so statement 2 is false.
41.tq: Spot the constitutional-status trap in the statement that treats an ordinary law as an Article 368 amendment.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: Parliament passes the law by **simple majority**.
Statement 2 wrong: the law is **not deemed an amendment** under **Art. 368** (APPSC-GS **2018**).
Statement 3 correct: the Constitution sets limits; **Parliament fixes the strength**.
xa: Assembly resolution: **majority of total membership** + **2/3 of members present and voting**.
The **Governor has no role** in the resolution.
⚠ Assembly = **special majority**; Parliament = **simple majority**.

41.s: Which one of the following statements correctly describes the role of the Governor in the process under Article 169?
o: The Governor initiates the Assembly resolution for creation of the Council
The Governor alone can abolish the Legislative Council by notification
The Governor must approve the Assembly resolution before it is sent to Parliament
The Governor has no role in initiating or approving the resolution
41.x: The constitutional process is initiated by a special-majority resolution of the Legislative Assembly and completed through a law of Parliament; the Governor has no role in initiating or approving that resolution.
41.tq: Use the 'who would do this job?' test to reject powers wrongly assigned to the Governor.
xs: The **Governor has no role** in initiating or approving the resolution — option **(4)**.
The **Assembly** passes the resolution by **special majority**; **Parliament** then passes a law by **simple majority**.
xa: The law is **not deemed an amendment** under **Art. 368**.
The Council's existence depends on the **will of the Assembly**.
⚠ Assembly = special; Parliament = simple; Governor = **no role**.

41.s: Under Article 169, the resolution of a State Legislative Assembly for the creation or abolition of its Legislative Council must be passed by—
o: A simple majority of members present and voting
A majority of the total membership of the Assembly and at least two-thirds of the members present and voting
Two-thirds of the total membership of the Assembly
A majority of the total membership of both Houses sitting jointly
41.x: Article 169 needs a special majority: a majority of the total membership of the Assembly plus not less than two-thirds of members present and voting. A simple majority is what Parliament then uses for its law; two-thirds of total membership is not the test; States have no joint sitting.
41.tq: Assembly = special majority; Parliament = simple majority; not an Art 368 amendment.
xs: The resolution needs a **majority of total membership** and **at least two-thirds of members present and voting** — option **(2)**.
A **simple majority** is what **Parliament** uses for the follow-up law.
There is no joint sitting in State legislatures.
xa: The law is **not deemed an amendment** under **Art. 368**.
The **Governor has no role**.
APPSC-GS **2018** asked on **Art. 169**.

41.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Jammu and Kashmir — Council continues after the 2019 Reorganisation Act
Andhra Pradesh — Council abolished in 1986 and revived in 2007
Andhra Pradesh — Council created for the first time in 2007
41.x: Tamil Nadu abolished its Legislative Council in 1986. Andhra Pradesh abolished its Council in 1985 and revived it in 2007, while the Jammu and Kashmir Council was abolished in 2019.
41.tq: Find the correctly matched historical pair among closely related Council changes.
xs: **Tamil Nadu** abolished its Council in **1986** — option **(3)**.
**AP** abolished its Council in **1985** (not **1986**) and revived it in **2007** — so options (2) and (4) are wrong.
**J&K's** Council was abolished by the **J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019**.
xa: Present list (**2026**): **AP, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, UP** — **six states**.
⚠ Lists showing **J&K** or only four states are out of date.
AP's Council again in flux in **2020-21**.

41.s: Which one of the following sets consists entirely of States having Legislative Councils at present?
o: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Kerala, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Goa
Andhra Pradesh, Goa, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh
Telangana, Mizoram, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Sikkim
Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh
41.x: The six States with Legislative Councils are Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh.
41.tq: Check every member of the six-State list; a single unicameral State makes the option wrong.
xs: The six states: **AP, Telangana, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and UP** — option **(4)**.
**Goa**, **Kerala**, **Mizoram** and **Sikkim** have no Councils, so options (1), (2) and (3) fail.
xa: **J&K's** Council was abolished in **2019**.
**Tamil Nadu** abolished its Council in **1986**.
**Karnataka Council (2026)**: **Saleem Ahmed** elected Chairperson (**38-30**).
**Telangana Council** Chairman: **Gutha Sukender Reddy**.

41.s: In which of the following years or periods did Andhra Pradesh illustrate the politically fluctuating status of the Legislative Council?
41.x: Andhra Pradesh abolished its Legislative Council in 1985 (NTR government) and revived it in 2007; in January 2020 the Assembly resolved to abolish it again, but withdrew that resolution in November 2021. These swings show that the Council's fate depends on state politics.
41.tq: Recall the distinctive three-point chronology rather than selecting a sequence of unrelated years.
xs: AP's Council fate swung in **1985, 2007 and 2020-21** — option **(3)**.
AP **abolished** its Council in **1985** and **revived** it in **2007**.
xa: Criticism: a costly "**delaying chamber**" whose existence depends on the ruling party in the Assembly.
**Tamil Nadu** abolished its Council in **1986**.
Significance: checks **hasty legislation**.

41.s: In a State Legislature, the certificate that a Bill is a Money Bill is issued by the
41.x: Under Article 199(3), the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly certifies whether a Bill is a Money Bill.
41.tq: Apply the 'who would do this job?' method to the certification power.
xs: The **Speaker of the Legislative Assembly** certifies a Money Bill — option **(1)**.
His decision is **final** (**Art. 199(3)**).
A Money Bill is **introduced only in the Assembly** on the **Governor's recommendation** — the Governor recommends, not certifies.
xa: Council must return a Money Bill within **14 days**; cannot reject or amend.
Speaker also decides **Tenth Schedule** disqualification.
Speaker has a **casting vote** on a tie (**Art. 189**).

41.s:
Consider the following statements regarding vacation of the office of the Speaker of a State Legislative Assembly:
1. The Speaker ceases to hold office if he or she ceases to be a member of the Assembly.
2. The Speaker may resign by addressing the resignation to the Deputy Speaker.
3. The Speaker can be removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the Assembly after fourteen days' notice.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
41.x: All three statements correctly state the grounds and procedure for vacating the Speaker's office under Article 179.
41.tq: Check each procedural condition separately, especially the notice period and required majority.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: he vacates office if he **ceases to be a member**.
Statement 2: he **resigns to the Deputy Speaker** (APPSC-GS **2018** key).
Statement 3: removal by a **majority of all the then members** after **14 days' notice** (**Art. 179**).
xa: During removal (**Art. 181**) he **does not preside**.
The **Deputy Speaker** resigns to the Speaker.
Council: **Chairman** resigns to the **Deputy Chairman**.

41.s: A resolution for the removal of the Speaker is under consideration in the Legislative Assembly. Which one of the following is correct?
o: The Speaker presides and has only a casting vote
The Speaker does not preside, but may speak and vote in the first instance
The Speaker must leave the House and cannot participate in the proceedings
The Speaker cannot speak but may vote in the second instance
41.x: Under Article 181, the Speaker does not preside while a resolution for removal is under consideration, but may speak and vote in the first instance.
41.tq: Apply the special procedural exception to the presiding officer's normal powers.
xs: The Speaker **does not preside**, but **may speak and vote in the first instance** — option **(2)**.
This is **Art. 181**.
So he neither presides with a casting vote nor is barred from the proceedings.
xa: ⚠ Trap: "the Speaker will preside" is **not** a power (APPSC-G1 **2022** key).
Removal needs a **majority of all the then members** after **14 days' notice**.
Normally (**Art. 189**) he has no first-instance vote, only a **casting vote**.

41.s: Which of the following is NOT a power or function of the Speaker of a State Legislative Assembly?
o: Approving the creation of a Legislative Council in the State
Giving the final decision on whether a Bill is a Money Bill
Deciding disqualification under the Tenth Schedule, subject to judicial review
Adjourning or suspending the House in case of lack of quorum
41.x: The Speaker performs the first three functions. Creation or abolition of a Legislative Council involves an Assembly resolution followed by parliamentary law; it is not approved by the Speaker.
41.tq: Find the option assigning a constitutional function to the wrong authority.
xs: **Approving the creation of a Legislative Council** is not the Speaker's power — option **(1)**.
Creation needs an **Assembly special-majority resolution** and a **Parliament** law (**Art. 169**).
The Speaker does: decide **Money Bill** status, **Tenth Schedule** disqualification, and adjourn for **lack of quorum**.
xa: Tenth Schedule decisions are **subject to judicial review** (**Kihoto Hollohan 1992**).
Other powers: allows a **secret sitting**, appoints committee chairmen.
Chairs the **Business Advisory**, **Rules** and **General Purposes** Committees.

41.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Speaker of a State Legislative Assembly:
1. On dissolution of the Assembly, the Speaker continues in office until just before the new Assembly first meets.
2. When the Speaker's office is vacant or he is absent, the Deputy Speaker acts with full powers.
3. The Speaker addresses his resignation to the Governor.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
41.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: the Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker (Art. 179). Hence '1 and 2 only'.
41.tq: Speaker resigns to Deputy Speaker; Chairman to Deputy Chairman.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: on dissolution he stays until **just before the new Assembly first meets**.
Statement 2 correct: the **Deputy Speaker** acts with **full powers** when the post is vacant or he is absent (**Art. 178**).
Statement 3 wrong: the Speaker **resigns to the Deputy Speaker**, not the Governor.
xa: **Deputy Speaker** post vacant in **8** states; **Jharkhand** had none for **21 years**.
Removal: **majority of all the then members**, **14 days' notice**.

41.s: Which of the following is the correct pairing of officers with the respective Houses of a bicameral State Legislature?
o: Speaker and Deputy Speaker — Legislative Assembly; Chairman and Deputy Chairman — Legislative Council
Chairman and Deputy Chairman — Legislative Assembly; Speaker and Deputy Speaker — Legislative Council
Speaker and Chairman — Legislative Assembly; Deputy Speaker and Deputy Chairman — Legislative Council
Governor and Speaker — Legislative Assembly; Chairman and Chief Minister — Legislative Council
41.x: The Assembly has a Speaker and Deputy Speaker, while the Council has a Chairman and Deputy Chairman.
41.tq: Discriminate between the similar titles used for the two Houses.
xs: **Speaker/Deputy Speaker** — Assembly; **Chairman/Deputy Chairman** — Council — option **(1)**.
Option (2) swaps the Houses; the Governor and CM are not presiding officers.
xa: Council: the **Chairman** resigns to the **Deputy Chairman**.
Assembly: the **Speaker** resigns to the **Deputy Speaker**.
**Telangana Council** Chairman = **Gutha Sukender Reddy**.

41.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the authority competent to decide a disqualification of a State legislator on grounds other than defection?
o: The High Court, on the recommendation of the Governor
The Governor, who is bound by the Election Commission's opinion
The Election Commission, whose decision is advisory to the Governor
41.x: Under Articles 191 and 192, the Governor decides such questions, but must act according to the opinion of the Election Commission. Defection matters are decided by the Speaker or Chairman.
41.tq: Ask who performs the formal decision and who supplies the binding constitutional opinion.
xs: The **Governor** decides, bound by the **Election Commission's opinion** — option **(3)**.
This is **Art. 192**; the EC's opinion is **binding** on him.
**Defection** (Tenth Schedule) cases go to the **Speaker/Chairman**, not the Governor.
xa: **Art. 191** grounds: **office of profit**, **unsound mind**, **undischarged insolvent**, **not a citizen**, Parliament's law (**RPA 1951**), defection.
⚠ Governor (EC opinion) = **Art. 191** grounds; Speaker/Chairman = **Tenth Schedule**.

41.s: Which one of the following is NOT a ground of disqualification under Article 191 of the Constitution?
o: Being absent from the House for 60 days without permission
Being of unsound mind as declared by a competent court
41.x: Absence for 60 days without permission results in vacation of the seat under Article 190(4), not disqualification under Article 191.
41.tq: Distinguish disqualification under Article 191 from vacation of seat under Article 190.
xs: **Absence for 60 days without permission** is not an **Art. 191** ground — option **(3)**.
It vacates the seat under **Art. 190(4)**.
**Insolvency**, **office of profit** and **unsound mind** are Art. 191 grounds.
xa: Other Art. 191 grounds: **not a citizen**, Parliament's law (**RPA 1951**), **Tenth Schedule** defection.
**Art. 190**: no one can be a member of **both Houses** or of **two states'** legislatures.
**Art. 190(3)(b)**: MLA's resignation takes effect only on the **Speaker's acceptance**.

41.s: A person elected to both Houses of a State Legislature is required to vacate one of the memberships because—
o: The Constitution prohibits simultaneous membership of both Houses of the same State Legislature
An MLA cannot become an MLC under any circumstances
The Council is a nominated body and cannot have elected members
The Governor alone may permit only one membership
41.x: Article 190 prevents a person from being a member of both Houses of the Legislature of a State at the same time. It also bars simultaneous membership of legislatures of two States.
41.tq: Use the constitutional incompatibility rule to eliminate explanations based on the composition of the Council.
xs: **Art. 190** bars membership of **both Houses** of the same State Legislature — option **(1)**.
It also bars membership of **two states'** legislatures.
MLAs do elect **1/3** of MLCs, so the Council is not wholly nominated (option 3 wrong).
xa: **Art. 190(4)**: seat vacated after **60 days'** absence without permission.
**Art. 190(3)(b)**: resignation effective on **Speaker's/Chairman's acceptance**.

41.s: Under Article 190(3)(b), the resignation of a member of a State Legislative Assembly takes effect only when—
o: It is accepted by the Speaker
It is accepted by the Governor
It is published in the official gazette
It is accepted by the Election Commission
41.x: The resignation of an MLA takes effect only upon acceptance by the Speaker. For a member of the Legislative Council, acceptance is by the Chairman.
41.tq: Match the resignation with the presiding officer of the concerned House.
xs: An MLA's resignation takes effect only on **acceptance by the Speaker** — option **(1)**.
For a member of the Council, the **Chairman** accepts it (**Art. 190(3)(b)**).
xa: **Art. 190(4)**: seat vacated after **60 days'** absence without permission.
The **Speaker** himself resigns to the **Deputy Speaker**.
Disqualification under **Art. 191** is decided by the **Governor** on the **EC's opinion**.

41.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the Legislative Assembly from the Legislative Council in relation to a Money Bill?
o: A Money Bill may originate in either House, but the Council has the final decision.
The Council may reject a Money Bill if two-thirds of its members so decide.
A Money Bill can originate only in the Council on the Governor's recommendation.
A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Assembly, and the Council may make recommendations within 14 days.
41.x: A Money Bill is introduced only in the Legislative Assembly on the Governor's recommendation. The Council can only recommend changes and must return it within 14 days; it cannot reject or amend it.
41.tq: Identify who introduces, who recommends and who has the final word.
xs: A Money Bill is introduced **only in the Assembly**; the Council may only **recommend** within **14 days** — option **(4)**.
It is introduced by a minister on the **Governor's recommendation** (**Art. 207**).
The Council **cannot reject or amend** it (**Art. 198**); its recommendations may be rejected.
xa: The **Speaker** certifies a Money Bill (**Art. 199(3)**).
⚠ Council delay: **14 days** (Money Bill); **3 months** + **1 month** (ordinary Bill).
Demands for grants are **voted only in the Assembly**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A Bill originating in the Legislative Council and rejected by the Legislative Assembly comes to an end.
2. The Legislative Council has no second chance to reconsider such a Bill.
3. A joint sitting can be summoned to resolve this disagreement in a State Legislature.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
41.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: a Bill originating in the Council ends when rejected by the Assembly, and there is no second chance for the Council. Statement 3 is false because State Legislatures have no provision for a joint sitting to resolve such a deadlock.
