41.tq: Spot the Parliament–State Legislature confusion in the joint-sitting statement.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: a Council Bill rejected by the Assembly **ends** (**dies**).
Statement 2 correct: the Council has **no second chance**.
Statement 3 wrong: there is **no joint sitting** in states, unlike Parliament (**Art. 108**).
xa: For Assembly Bills, the Council can delay **3 months** then **1 month**.
The Council has **no role in ratifying** constitutional amendments.

41.s: Which one of the following statements regarding demands for grants in a State Legislature is correct?
o: Demands for grants are voted by the Governor after discussion in the Council.
The Legislative Council votes on demands for grants, while the Assembly only discusses them.
Demands for grants are voted only in the Legislative Assembly, while the Council may discuss them.
Both Houses vote jointly on demands for grants.
41.x: The Legislative Assembly alone votes on demands for grants. The Legislative Council may discuss them but cannot vote on them.
41.tq: Separate the power to discuss from the power to vote.
xs: Demands for grants are **voted only in the Assembly**; the Council **discusses only** — option **(3)**.
Option (2) reverses the roles; there is no joint vote or Governor vote.
xa: Session order: **Governor's address** → **general discussion** → **voting on demands** (Assembly only).
Money Bill introduced **only in the Assembly** (**Art. 207**).
Financial procedure: **Arts. 202-207**; **Art. 202** = **Annual Financial Statement**.

41.s: Which one of the following correctly states the relative position of a State Legislative Council and the Rajya Sabha?
o: The State Council's power is essentially a delaying power and is weaker than that of the Rajya Sabha.
The State Council can dissolve the Legislative Assembly during a constitutional deadlock.
The State Council alone can ratify constitutional amendments.
The State Council has the same power as the Rajya Sabha to veto an ordinary Bill of the Assembly.
41.x: The State Legislative Council can delay legislation but cannot permanently veto an Assembly Bill. Its powers are considerably weaker than those of the Rajya Sabha in comparable matters.
41.tq: Avoid transferring the Rajya Sabha's powers to the State Council.
xs: The Council's power is **only delaying** — much **weaker than the Rajya Sabha's** — option **(1)**.
It cannot veto an Assembly Bill: delay **3 months** + **1 month**, then the Bill is **deemed passed**.
It has **no role in ratifying** constitutional amendments, and cannot dissolve the Assembly.
xa: Money Bill: return within **14 days**.
No joint sitting in states.
Criticism: a costly "**delaying chamber**".

41.s: The normal order of proceedings at the beginning of a session of a State Legislative Assembly, as indicated for the State Legislature, is:
o: Voting on demands, Governor's address, general discussion
Governor's address, general discussion, voting on demands
General discussion, voting on demands, Governor's address
Governor's address, voting on demands, general discussion
41.x: The indicated order is the Governor's address, followed by general discussion and then voting on demands in the Assembly.
41.tq: Arrange the stages in the stated procedural sequence, not by constitutional article number.
xs: Order: **Governor's address → general discussion → voting on demands** — option **(2)**.
Voting on demands is in the **Assembly only** (**2026**).
xa: The Governor's address comes on the **first day of the first session each year**.
Order of proceedings set by **Rules of Procedure** (**Art. 208**).
**Art. 176** = special address at the first session of the year.

41.s: With reference to the Governor's address to the State Legislature, which one of the following is correct?
o: It is delivered before every sitting of the Legislative Assembly.
It is delivered on the first day of the first session of each year and is followed by discussion.
It is delivered on the last day of every annual session.
It is delivered only when the Legislative Council demands it.
41.x: The Governor addresses the Legislature on the first day of the first session of each year, and the address is followed by discussion in the House.
41.tq: Use the time phrase ‘first day of the first session’ as the key discriminator.
xs: The Governor's address is on the **first day of the first session of each year**, followed by **discussion** — option **(2)**.
It is not before every sitting or on the last day.
xa: **Art. 175** = Governor's address and messages; **Art. 176** = special address (mandatory at the first session).
Then **general discussion** → **voting on demands**.
**Art. 208**: each House makes its **rules of procedure**.

41.s:
With reference to the participation of MLAs in indirect elections, consider the following statements:
1. Elected MLAs are members of the electoral college for the election of the President.
2. MLAs elect members of the Rajya Sabha by proportional representation through the single transferable vote.
3. MLAs elect one-third of the members of the State Legislative Council.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
41.x: All three statements are correct. Elected MLAs participate in the Presidential election, elect Rajya Sabha members by PR-STV, and elect one-third of the members of the State Legislative Council.
41.tq: Test the common participants across three indirect elections while excluding nominated members and the Vice-Presidential election.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: **elected MLAs** vote for the **President** (**Art. 54**).
Statement 2: MLAs elect **Rajya Sabha** members by **PR-STV**.
Statement 3: MLAs elect **one-third** of MLCs (**Art. 171**).
xa: ⚠ **Vice-President**: **No** — only MPs vote (APPCA **2026**).
Council members are elected by **PR-STV**.

41.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the participation of State Legislative Assembly members in the elections of the President and Vice-President?
o: Elected MLAs vote in the Vice-Presidential election but not in the Presidential election.
Elected MLAs vote in the Presidential election but not in the Vice-Presidential election.
Elected MLAs vote in both elections.
Neither elected nor nominated MLAs vote in either election.
41.x: Elected MLAs are part of the electoral college for the President under Article 54. The Vice-President is elected only by Members of Parliament, so MLAs do not participate.
41.tq: Discriminate between two similar indirect elections by identifying the composition of each electoral college.
xs: Elected MLAs vote for the **President** but **not the Vice-President** — option **(2)**.
President: elected MLAs are in the electoral college (**Art. 54**).
Vice-President: **only MPs** vote (APPCA **2026**).
xa: MLAs also elect **Rajya Sabha** members (**PR-STV**).
MLAs elect **1/3** of MLCs.

41.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 174 — Composition of the Legislative Council
Article 208 — Financial procedure and Annual Financial Statement
41.x: Article 168 deals with the constitution of State Legislatures. Article 172 concerns duration, Article 174 concerns sessions, and Article 208 concerns rules of procedure.
41.tq: Use article-number anchors and reject swapped constitutional subjects.
xs: **Art. 168 — Constitution of State Legislatures** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Art. 172** = **duration**; **Art. 174** = **sessions**; **Art. 208** = **rules of procedure**.
Qualifications are **Art. 173**; Council composition **Art. 171**; Annual Financial Statement **Art. 202**.
xa: Art. 168: **Governor + one or two Houses**.
**Arts 168-212** cover the State Legislature as a whole (APPSC-GS **2018**).

41.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the codes given below.

List-I (Article)
 a. 169
 b. 173
 c. 194
 d. 202

List-II (Subject)
 i. Qualifications for membership
 ii. Powers and privileges of State Legislatures
 iii. Creation or abolition of Legislative Councils
 iv. Annual Financial Statement
41.x: Article 169 concerns Legislative Councils, Article 173 qualifications, Article 194 privileges, and Article 202 the Annual Financial Statement.
41.tq: Start with the sure article-subject pair and eliminate codes containing a mismatch.
xs: Correct code: **a–iii, b–i, c–ii, d–iv** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 169** = creation/abolition of Councils; **Art. 173** = qualifications.
**Art. 194** = privileges; **Art. 202** = **Annual Financial Statement**.
xa: **Art. 170 / 171** = composition of Assembly / Council.
**Art. 211**: no discussion of a **HC judge's conduct**; **Art. 212**: courts not to inquire into proceedings.
**Art. 210**: language — Hindi/English or the state's official language.

41.s:
With reference to Articles 174 to 176, consider the following statements:
1. Article 174 deals with sessions, prorogation and dissolution of the State Legislature.
2. Article 175 deals with the Governor's right to address and send messages to the House or Houses.
3. Article 176 deals with the Governor's special address.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
41.x: Articles 174, 175 and 176 respectively concern sessions and dissolution, the Governor's address and messages, and the special address.
41.tq: Read a sequence of neighbouring articles together instead of treating one article in isolation.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
**Art. 174**: sessions, prorogation, dissolution.
**Art. 175**: Governor's **address and messages**.
**Art. 176**: **special address** — mandatory at the **first session** of the year.
xa: Art. 174 rule: no more than **6 months** between sittings.
**Art. 172** = duration (**5 years**); **Art. 173** = qualifications (**25 / 30**).

41.s: The interval between the last sitting in one session of a State Legislature and the first sitting in the next session cannot exceed:
41.x: Article 174 requires that not more than six months intervene between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next.
41.tq: Test the constitutional time limit directly and distinguish it from other legislative periods.
xs: The gap cannot exceed **six months** — option **(1)**.
This is the **Art. 174** rule: no more than **6 months** between the last sitting of one session and the first of the next.
xa: Many Assemblies met only to satisfy this **Art. 174** rule.
PRS **2025**: Assemblies sat an average of **24 days** (**Odisha 43**, **Nagaland 7**).
About **33%** of Bills passed in a single sitting.

41.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 210 — Language to be used in the Legislature
Article 187 — Secretariat of the State Legislature
Article 194 — Powers and privileges of State Legislatures
41.x: Article 212 concerns the exclusion of judicial inquiry into legislative proceedings. The Annual Financial Statement is dealt with under Article 202.
41.tq: Locate the article-subject swap among otherwise familiar constitutional provisions.
xs: **Article 212 — Annual Financial Statement** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
**Art. 212** bars **courts from inquiring into proceedings**; the **Annual Financial Statement** is **Art. 202**.
The others are correct: **Art. 210** = language, **Art. 187** = secretariat, **Art. 194** = **privileges**.
xa: **Art. 211**: no discussion of a **HC judge's conduct**.
**Art. 208**: each House makes its **rules of procedure** (APPSC-GS **2018** key).
**Arts 202-207** = financial procedure; **Arts 198-199** = Money Bills.

41.s:
Which of the following statements regarding the State Legislature is correct?
1. Each House may make rules for regulating its procedure and conduct of business.
2. Courts cannot inquire into the proceedings of the Legislature merely on the ground of procedural irregularity.
3. Conduct of a High Court judge in the discharge of duties cannot be discussed in the State Legislature.
41.x: Articles 208, 212 and 211 respectively support the three statements.
41.tq: Combine related constitutional safeguards and identify the option containing all applicable provisions.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4)**.
Statement 1: **Art. 208** — each House makes **rules of procedure**.
Statement 2: **Art. 212** — courts not to inquire into proceedings for **procedural irregularity**.
Statement 3: **Art. 211** — no discussion of a **HC judge's conduct**.
xa: **Art. 194** = **privileges** of MLAs and committees.
**Art. 210** = language: **Hindi/English** or the state's official language.
**Art. 187** = **secretariat** of the state legislature.

41.s: Who among the following was the first woman legislator in India?
41.x: Muthulakshmi Reddy was India’s first woman legislator and served in the Madras Legislative Council.
41.tq: Use the first-in-history clue and distinguish legislative office from executive office.
xs: **Muthulakshmi Reddy** was India's **first woman legislator** — option **(2)**.
She sat in the **Madras Legislative Council**.
xa: The Council gives a place to **experts who cannot face elections**.
**Tamil Nadu** later abolished its Council in **1986**.
Governor nominates **1/6** of a Council from literature, science, art, cooperation and social service.

41.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Telangana Legislative Council:
1. Two BRS Members of the Legislative Council were suspended for remarks against the Speaker.
2. Gaddam Prasad Kumar is the Chairman of the Telangana Legislative Council.
3. Gutha Sukender Reddy is the Chairman of the Telangana Legislative Council.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
41.x: Statement 1 is correct. Gaddam Prasad Kumar is the Speaker, whereas Gutha Sukender Reddy is the Chairman of the Telangana Legislative Council; therefore, statement 2 is false and statement 3 is correct.
41.tq: Apply the office-holder trap by separating the Speaker of the Assembly from the Chairman of the Council.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
Statement 1 correct: **two BRS MLCs** were suspended for remarks against the Speaker (**9 Sep 2026**).
Statement 2 wrong: **Gaddam Prasad Kumar** is the **Speaker**, not Council Chairman.
Statement 3 correct: **Gutha Sukender Reddy** is the **Council Chairman**.
xa: ⚠ Assembly = **Speaker**; Council = **Chairman**.
**Telangana** Assembly has **119** seats and is one of **six states** with a Council.
Council: the **Chairman** resigns to the **Deputy Chairman**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements regarding State Legislative Councils:
1. A Council checks hasty legislation and gives a place to experts who cannot face elections.
2. A Council can permanently veto an ordinary Bill passed by the Assembly.
3. Its existence depends on the ruling party in the Assembly, as Andhra Pradesh's experience in 1985, 2007 and 2020-21 shows.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
41.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the Council has only a delaying power (3 months, then 1 month), after which the Assembly's will prevails. Hence '1 and 3 only'.
41.tq: Council = revising/delaying chamber; never an absolute veto.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(3)**.
Statement 1 correct: the Council **checks hasty legislation** and seats **experts who cannot face elections**.
Statement 2 wrong: its power is **only delaying** — **3 months**, then **1 month** — after which the Bill is **deemed passed**.
Statement 3 correct: its fate swings with the ruling party — AP in **1985**, **2007** and **2020-21**.
xa: Criticism: a costly "**delaying chamber**".
Under **Art. 169** its existence depends on the **will of the Assembly**.
Money Bill: Council must return it within **14 days**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The State representatives in Rajya Sabha are elected by elected MLAs.
II. The election uses proportional representation by means of the Single Transferable Vote.
III. Nominated MLAs can vote in this election.
IV. The election is held by secret ballot.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
41.x: I, II and IV are correct: elected MLAs choose State representatives by proportional representation using single transferable vote, by secret ballot. III is false because nominated MLAs cannot vote.
41.tq: Find the statement about nominated MLAs, the usual trap.
n: State representatives in the Rajya Sabha are elected by the elected MLAs of State Legislative Assemblies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The electoral system for State representatives in the Rajya Sabha is proportional representation by means of the Single Transferable Vote. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
Rajya Sabha elections for State representatives are conducted by secret ballot. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
Nominated MLAs cannot vote in the election of State representatives to the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
xs: Statements **I, II and IV only** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
I is correct: State representatives in the Rajya Sabha are elected by **elected MLAs**.
II and IV are correct: the election uses **PR-STV** (**proportional representation by single transferable vote**), by **secret ballot**.
III is wrong: only **elected** MLAs vote, not nominated ones.
xa: Elected MLAs also vote in the **President's** election (**Art. 54**).
MLAs do **not** vote in the **Vice-President's** election — only MPs.
MLAs elect **one-third** of the **Legislative Council** (**Art. 171**).

41.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

regarding the composition of a State Legislative Council:

List-I
(a) Elected by MLAs
(b) Minimum strength of the Council
(c) Elected by Graduates
(d) Nominated by the Governor

List-II
(i) One-sixth
(ii) One-third
(iii) 40 members
(iv) One-twelfth
41.x: One-third of the Council is elected by MLAs, graduates elect one-twelfth, the Governor nominates one-sixth, and the Council must have at least 40 members. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
41.tq: Check that the fractions add up to one: 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/12 + 1/12 + 1/6.
n: One-third of the members of a State Legislative Council are elected by MLAs. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
One-third of the members of a State Legislative Council are elected by local authorities. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
One-twelfth of the members of a State Legislative Council are elected by graduates. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
One-twelfth of the members of a State Legislative Council are elected by teachers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
One-sixth of the members of a State Legislative Council are nominated by the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**MLAs** elect **one-third**; **graduates** elect **one-twelfth**.
The **Governor nominates one-sixth**; the Council's **minimum strength** is **40 members**.
xa: **Local bodies** elect **one-third**; **teachers** elect **one-twelfth**.
⚠ **1/3 – 1/12 – 1/12 – 1/3 – 1/6** = **local bodies – graduates – teachers – MLAs – Governor**.
Maximum size: **one-third** of the Assembly; **Uttar Pradesh** has the largest Council (**100**).
Graduates and teachers need at least **3 years** of standing.

41.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The State Legislative Council is a permanent body and cannot be dissolved.
The State Legislative Council cannot be abolished because it is a permanent body.
One-third of the Council members retire every two years.
The State Legislative Council can be abolished under Article 169.
41.x: Option B is incorrect. The Council is permanent, so it cannot be dissolved, but it can be abolished under Article 169. One-third of its members retire every two years.
41.tq: Discriminate between dissolving a House and abolishing it.
n: The State Legislative Council is a permanent body. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Council cannot be dissolved. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Council can be abolished. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Council can be abolished under Article 169. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
One-third of the members of the State Legislative Council retire every 2 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Council of States is a permanent body. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Council of States cannot be dissolved. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Council cannot be dissolved on the recommendation of the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **the Council cannot be abolished because it is a permanent body** — so option **(2)** is the answer.
The Council is **permanent** — it **cannot be dissolved** — but it **can be abolished** or created under **Article 169**.
**One-third** of members retire every **two years** — so (1), (3), (4) are correct.
xa: The **Assembly** is the opposite: **dissolvable** but cannot be **abolished**.
Council member's term is **six years**.
**AP** abolished its Council in **1985** and revived it in **2007**; **Tamil Nadu** abolished its Council in **1986**.

41.s: Who presides over the State Legislative Council?
o: The Chairman elected by the Council from among its members
The Speaker of the Legislative Assembly
41.x: Under Article 182, the Council elects its Chairman from among its own members. The Governor does not nominate the Chairman, and the Vice-President chairs only the Rajya Sabha.
41.tq: Discriminate the Council's Chairman from the Rajya Sabha's ex-officio Chairman.
n: The Chairman of the State Legislative Council is elected by the Council from among its members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Chairman of the Legislative Council is chosen by the Council members from among themselves under Article 182. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Governor does not nominate the Chairman of the Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
xs: The Council is presided over by **the Chairman elected by the Council from among its members** — so option **(1)** is correct.
This is under **Article 182**; the Chairman is **not nominated by the Governor**.
The **Speaker** presides over the **Legislative Assembly**, not the Council.
xa: The **Chairman** resigns to the **Deputy Chairman**.
The Assembly's **Speaker and Deputy Speaker** are elected under **Article 178** and resign to each other (**Article 179**).
Defection cases in the Council are decided by the **Chairman**.

41.s: Which of the following statements regarding a State Assembly resolution for creation or abolition of a Legislative Council is incorrect?
o: It must be passed by a special majority.
It legally compels the Union Government to introduce a Bill in Parliament.
At least two-thirds of the members present and voting must support it.
At least 50% of the total membership must support it.
41.x: Option B is incorrect: the Assembly's resolution is only a request and does not legally compel the Union Government to bring a Bill. It does need a special majority (50% of total membership and two-thirds present and voting).
41.tq: Look for the statement that makes a recommendation binding.
n: The State Legislative Assembly resolution for creating or abolishing a Legislative Council requires a special majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The special majority requires at least 50 percent of the total membership of the State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The special majority requires at least two-thirds of the members present and voting in the State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Assembly resolution for creating or abolishing a Legislative Council is recommendatory. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Assembly resolution does not legally compel the Union Government to introduce a bill in Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The State Legislative Assembly initiates the creation or abolition of a Legislative Council by passing a resolution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the resolution **legally compels the Union Government to introduce a Bill** in Parliament — so option **(2)** is the answer.
The Assembly's resolution is only **recommendatory** — it does **not compel** the Union.
It needs a **special majority**: a **majority** (at least **50 percent**) of the **total membership** and at least **two-thirds** present and voting — so (1), (3), (4) are correct.
xa: **Parliament** then acts by **simple majority**; the law is **not deemed an amendment** under **Art. 368**.
The **Governor has no role** in the resolution.
⚠ Assembly = **special majority**; Parliament = **simple majority**; Governor = **no role**.

41.s:
How many of the following are valid fields for nomination by the Governor to the State Legislative Council?
1. Literature
2. Science
3. Art
4. Co-operative Movement
5. Social Service
6. Industrial activity
41.x: Five fields are valid: literature, science, art, the co-operative movement and social service. Industrial activity is not one of them.
41.tq: Add the co-operative movement to the Rajya Sabha's four fields.
n: Literature is a nomination field for the Governor’s nominees to a State Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
Science is a nomination field for the Governor’s nominees to a State Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
Art is a nomination field for the Governor’s nominees to a State Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The co-operative movement is a nomination field for the Governor’s nominees to a State Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
Social service is a nomination field for the Governor’s nominees to a State Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
Industrialists are not valid nomination categories for a State Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Governor’s five nomination fields for a State Legislative Council are literature, science, art, the co-operative movement, and social service. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
xs: **Only five** fields are valid — so option **(3)** is correct.
Valid fields: **literature, science, art, the co-operative movement, social service** (**Article 171**).
**Industrial activity** is **not** a valid category — **industrialists** and **commerce** are excluded.
xa: The Governor nominates **one-sixth** of the Council, on **Cabinet advice**.
⚠ The **co-operative movement** is a ground under **Article 171** but **not** for the Rajya Sabha (**Article 80**).
Other Council members are elected by **PR-STV**, by **secret ballot**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The Legislative Council must return a Money Bill with its recommendations within 14 days.
Statement B: If the Council does not return the Money Bill within 14 days, the Bill is deemed to have been passed on the expiry of that period.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
41.x: Both are true: the Council can only make recommendations on a Money Bill and must return it within 14 days. If it does not, the Bill is deemed passed by both Houses.
41.tq: Recall the 14-day limit and the deemed-passed rule.
n: The Legislative Council receives a Money Bill only for recommendations. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Council must return a Money Bill within 14 days. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
A Money Bill is deemed to have been passed upon expiry of 14 days if the Legislative Council does not return it. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The Council can only **recommend** on a Money Bill and must return it within **14 days**.
If not returned within **14 days**, the Bill is **deemed passed**.
xa: The Council **cannot amend or reject** a Money Bill; the Assembly has **final authority** (**Art. 198**).
Money Bills are introduced **only in the Assembly**, on the **Governor's prior recommendation** (**Article 207**).
⚠ Council delay: **14 days** (Money Bill); **3 months** + **1 month** (ordinary bill).

41.s:
Consider the following statements about an ordinary Bill passed by the Legislative Assembly:
I. The Legislative Council can delay it for a maximum of three months on the first passage.
II. After the Assembly repasses it, the Council can delay it for a maximum of one month.
III. The Council can permanently block the legislation by exercising a veto.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
41.x: I and II are correct: the Council can delay an ordinary Bill for three months, then one month after it is passed again. III is false because the Council has no veto.
41.tq: Find the statement giving the Council a veto.
n: The Legislative Council has no veto power over ordinary bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Council cannot permanently block legislation passed by the Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Council can delay an ordinary bill for a maximum of 3 months after its first passage. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Council can delay a re-passed ordinary bill for a maximum of 1 month. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Legislative Assembly can re-pass an ordinary bill after its first passage through the Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
xs: Statements **I and II only** are correct — so option **(4)** is correct.
I: the Council can delay an ordinary bill up to **three months** the first time.
II: after the Assembly **re-passes** it, **one month** — **four months** in all.
III is wrong: the Council has **no veto** and cannot **permanently block** ordinary legislation.
xa: The Assembly is the **originating and overriding** chamber (**Article 197**).
A bill **originating in the Council** and rejected by the Assembly **ends**.
There is **no joint sitting** in states, unlike Parliament (**Art. 108**).

41.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The Co-operative Movement is a valid field for nomination to a State Legislative Council.
Statement B: The Co-operative Movement is a nomination ground for the Rajya Sabha.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
41.x: A is true: the co-operative movement is a nomination field for the State Legislative Council. B is false: under Article 80, the Rajya Sabha's fields are only literature, science, art and social service.
41.tq: Discriminate the Council's five fields from the Rajya Sabha's four.
n: The co-operative movement is a nomination field for the Governor’s nominees to a State Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The co-operative movement is not a nomination ground for the Rajya Sabha under Article 80. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
The Governor’s five nomination fields for a State Legislative Council are literature, science, art, the co-operative movement, and social service. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 164-167]
xs: **Statement A is true, Statement B is false** — so option **(3)** is correct.
A: the **co-operative movement** is a valid nomination field for a **State Legislative Council** (**Article 171**).
B: it is **not** a ground for the **Rajya Sabha** (**Article 80**).
xa: Council nomination fields: **literature, science, art, co-operative movement, social service**.
**Industrialists** are **not** an electoral or nomination category.
The Governor nominates **one-sixth** of the Council.

41.s: Which of the following statements regarding State Legislature Bills is incorrect?
o: A State Money Bill originates in the Legislative Assembly.
The Legislative Council can delay an Ordinary Bill for a maximum of 6 months.
The Governor’s recommendation is required for the introduction of a State Money Bill.
The Legislative Council gets 14 days to consider a State Money Bill.
41.x: Option B is incorrect: a Legislative Council can delay an ordinary bill for at most four months (three, then one), not six. A State Money Bill starts in the Assembly on the Governor's recommendation, and the Council has 14 days to consider it.
41.tq: Recall the Council's 3 + 1 month limit.
n: The Legislative Council can delay an Ordinary Bill for three months the first time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Legislative Council can delay an Ordinary Bill for one month the second time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Legislative Council’s maximum delaying power for an Ordinary Bill is four months. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A State Money Bill originates in the Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A State Money Bill requires the Governor’s recommendation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Legislative Council gets 14 days to consider a State Money Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the Council **can delay an Ordinary Bill for a maximum of 6 months** — so option **(2)** is the answer.
The maximum delay is **four months** — **three months** first, then **one month** after re-passage.
A State Money Bill **originates in the Legislative Assembly** with the **Governor's recommendation**, and the Council gets **14 days** — so (1), (3), (4) are correct.
xa: The Council's power is **only delaying** — much weaker than the **Rajya Sabha's**.
**Speaker's certification** of a Money Bill is **sole and final** (**Art. 199(3)**).
The Council has **no role in ratifying** constitutional amendments.

41.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: A State Money Bill is governed by Articles 198, 199 and 207.
Statement B: The Governor can reserve a State Bill for the President under Article 200, and the President considers the reserved Bill under Article 201.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
41.x: Both are true: State Money Bills come under Articles 198, 199 and 207. The Governor can reserve a State bill for the President under Article 200, and the President deals with it under Article 201.
41.tq: Recall the State-level Articles 198–201.
n: The Governor can reserve a State Bill for the President under Article 200. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The President considers a State Bill reserved by the Governor under Article 201. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
Articles 200 and 201 deal with Governor’s and President’s assent to State Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — so option **(1)** is correct.
A: State Money Bills are governed by **Articles 198, 199 and 207**.
B: the **Governor** reserves a Bill under **Article 200**; the **President** considers it under **Article 201**.
xa: **Article 207**: Money Bill only on the **Governor's prior recommendation**.
**Article 197**: the Council's delay of **ordinary Bills**.
**Article 213**: the Governor's **Ordinances**.

41.s: The State Legislature is governed under which Part and range of Articles of the Constitution?
41.x: State Legislatures are in Part VI, Articles 168–212. Parliament is in Part V, Articles 79–122.
41.tq: Discriminate Part V (Parliament) from Part VI (State Legislatures).
n: The State Legislative Assembly is governed under Part VI of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
Articles 168 to 212 govern the State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xs: The State Legislature is in **Part VI, Articles 168–212** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Article 168** covers composition; **169** creation/abolition of Councils; **170/171** composition of the Assembly/Council.
**Article 213** (Ordinances) lies just after this range, so option (3) is wrong.
xa: **Article 208**: each House makes **rules of procedure**.
**Article 194**: powers and **privileges** of MLAs.
**Article 211**: no discussion of a **HC judge's conduct**; **212**: courts not to inquire into proceedings.

41.s: Under Article 168, the State Legislature consists of the Governor and the Legislative Assembly, along with which additional body in bicameral States?
41.x: Under Article 168, a State Legislature is the Governor plus the Assembly, and in bicameral States also the Legislative Council.
41.tq: Remember that the Governor is part of every State Legislature.
n: Article 168 provides that the State Legislature consists of the Governor and the Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The State Legislature also includes a Legislative Council in bicameral States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xs: In bicameral States the legislature also includes the **Legislative Council** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Article 168**: **unicameral** = **Governor + Legislative Assembly**; **bicameral** = Governor + Assembly + **Legislative Council**.
The **Council of Ministers** is part of the executive, not the legislature.
xa: **Six** bicameral States: **Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh**.
J&K's Council was abolished by the **J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019**.
The Governor is part of the legislature **without being a member**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Sikkim has the smallest State Legislative Assembly, with 32 members.
Statement B: Puducherry has the smallest Union Territory Assembly, with 33 members.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
41.x: Both are true: Sikkim has the smallest State Assembly (32 members), and Puducherry the smallest Union Territory Assembly (33: 30 elected, 3 nominated).
41.tq: Discriminate the smallest State Assembly (Sikkim) from the smallest UT Assembly (Puducherry).
n: Sikkim has the smallest State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Sikkim Legislative Assembly has 32 members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
Puducherry has the smallest Union Territory Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Puducherry Legislative Assembly has 33 members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
Sikkim's 32-member Legislative Assembly is a special constitutional exception. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — so option **(1)** is correct.
A: **Sikkim** has the smallest State Assembly — **32** seats, below the standard minimum of **60** (**Art. 371F**).
B: **Puducherry** has the smallest UT Assembly — **33** (**30** elected + **3** nominated).
xa: Largest Assembly: **Uttar Pradesh** (**403**).
**Goa** and **Mizoram** have **40** seats each.
**AP** has **175** seats; **Telangana** **119**.
⚠ **Arunachal** has a minimum of **30** under **Art. 371H** but actually has **60**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Article 332 provides for reservation of seats for SCs and STs based on population ratios.
II. The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2020 ended the nomination of Anglo-Indian members under Article 333.
III. The 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023 provides approximately one-third reservation for women in directly elected Assembly seats, effective after post-census delimitation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
41.x: All three are correct: Article 332 reserves seats for SCs and STs by population, the 104th Amendment ended Anglo-Indian nomination (Article 333), and the 106th (2023) reserves about one-third of seats for women after the next delimitation.
41.tq: Recall the 104th and 106th Amendments.
n: Article 332 mandates reservation of Legislative Assembly seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe Legislative Assembly reservations are based on population ratios. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2020 ended the nomination of Anglo-Indian members under Article 333. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The 106th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2023 provides approximately one-third reservation for women in directly elected Assembly seats. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The women's reservation under the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act becomes effective after post-census delimitation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xs: **I, II and III** are all correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
I: **Article 332** reserves seats for **SCs and STs** in proportion to their **population**.
II: the **104th Amendment Act (2020)** ended **Anglo-Indian** nomination under **Article 333**.
III: the **106th Amendment Act (2023)** gives about **one-third** reservation for **women**, effective after **post-census delimitation**.
xa: Minimum age (**Article 173**): **Assembly 25**, **Council 30** years.
The Assembly is **directly elected** by **First-Past-the-Post**.
Maximum **500**, minimum **60** seats (**Article 170**).

41.s:
Match the constitutional Article with the subject:

List-I
(a) Article 170
(b) Article 173
(c) Article 178
(d) Article 213

List-II
(i) Age qualification
(ii) Assembly composition
(iii) Speaker and Deputy Speaker
(iv) Ordinance power
41.x: Article 170 covers Assembly composition, 173 the age qualification, 178 the Speaker and Deputy Speaker, and 213 ordinances. The answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
41.tq: Recall Articles 170, 173, 178 and 213.
n: Article 170 concerns Assembly composition. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
Article 173 concerns the Assembly membership age of 25 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
Articles 178 and 179 concern Speaker election and resignation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
Article 213 concerns Ordinances. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Article 170** = **Assembly composition**; **Article 173** = **age qualification** (**25 / 30**).
**Article 178** = **Speaker and Deputy Speaker**; **Article 213** = **Ordinance power**.
xa: **Article 172**: duration (**5 years**); **Article 174**: sessions, prorogation, dissolution.
**Article 179**: Speaker's resignation and removal.
**Article 192**: disqualification decided by the **Governor**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The Legislative Assembly cannot be abolished.
Statement B: Under the Tenth Schedule, the Chairman decides defection cases arising in the Legislative Council.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
41.x: Both are true: only a Legislative Council can be created or abolished, never the Assembly, and defection cases in the Council are decided by its Chairman under the Tenth Schedule.
41.tq: Remember the presiding officer of each House decides its defection cases.
n: The Legislative Assembly cannot be abolished. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Chairman decides defection cases under the Tenth Schedule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — so option **(1)** is correct.
A: the **Assembly** is **dissolvable** but **cannot be abolished**; only a Council can be created or abolished (**Article 169**).
B: Tenth Schedule defection cases are decided **exclusively** by the **Speaker** (Council: **Chairman**), subject to **judicial review**.
xa: Other disqualifications (**Article 191**) are decided by the **Governor** on the **Election Commission's binding opinion** (**Article 192**).
⚠ **Governor** = Art. 191 grounds; **Speaker/Chairman** = **Tenth Schedule** defection.
**Kihoto Hollohan 1992** made the Speaker's decision subject to judicial review.

41.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Legislative Assembly constitutional basis
(b) Legislative Council constitutional basis
(c) Minimum age for Assembly membership
(d) Minimum age for Council membership

List-II
(i) Article 170
(ii) Article 171
(iii) 25 years
(iv) 30 years
41.x: The Assembly rests on Article 170 and the Council on Article 171. The minimum ages are 25 and 30. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
41.tq: Discriminate Article 170 (Assembly) from 171 (Council).
n: The Constitutional basis of the Legislative Assembly is Article 170. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Constitutional basis of the Legislative Council is Article 171. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The minimum age for membership of the Legislative Assembly is 25 years under Article 173. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The minimum age for membership of the Legislative Council is 30 years under Article 173. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
xs: The correct match is **a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Assembly** — **Article 170**; **Council** — **Article 171**.
Minimum age: **Assembly 25** years; **Council 30** years (**Article 173**).
xa: Assembly: maximum **500**, minimum **60**.
Council: maximum **one-third** of the Assembly, minimum **40**.
**Rajya Sabha** minimum age is also **30**.

41.s:
How many of the following statements are correct?
1. The normal term of the Legislative Assembly is five years.
2. One-third of the Legislative Council members retire every two years.
3. The term of a Legislative Council member is six years.
4. The Legislative Council is a temporary body.
41.x: Three are correct: the Assembly serves five years, one-third of the Council retires every two years, and Council members serve six years. Statement 4 is false because the Council is permanent.
41.tq: Find the statement that makes the Council temporary.
n: The normal term of the Legislative Assembly is five years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Legislative Council is a permanent body. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
One-third of the Legislative Council members retire every two years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The term of a Legislative Council member is six years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
xs: **Only three** statements are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
1 is correct: the Assembly's normal term is **five years** (**Art. 172**).
2 and 3 are correct: **one-third** of Council members retire every **two years**; each member's term is **six years**.
4 is wrong: the Council is a **permanent body**, not temporary.
xa: The Council **cannot be dissolved**, not even on the Governor's recommendation.
The **Rajya Sabha** follows the same pattern: **six** years, one-third retire every **two** years.
The Council is called the **Upper House** / **House of Elders**.

41.s:
How many of the following are States whose Legislative Assemblies have 40 seats or fewer?
1. Goa
2. Mizoram
3. Puducherry
4. Sikkim
41.x: Three qualify: Goa and Mizoram have 40 seats each and Sikkim 32. Puducherry has 33 seats but is a Union Territory, not a State.
41.tq: Check both the seat number and whether each is a State.
n: Sikkim has the smallest State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Sikkim Legislative Assembly has 32 seats. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Goa Legislative Assembly has 40 seats. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Mizoram Legislative Assembly has 40 seats. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
Puducherry has the smallest Union Territory Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Puducherry Assembly has 33 seats. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
xs: **Only three** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Goa** (**40**), **Mizoram** (**40**) and **Sikkim** (**32**) are States with **40 seats or fewer**.
**Puducherry** (**33**) is a **Union Territory**, not a State.
xa: Sikkim is a special exception (**Art. 371F**) below the standard minimum of **60**.
Puducherry = **30** elected + **3** nominated.
Largest Assembly: **Uttar Pradesh** (**403**).

41.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding disqualification under Article 191?
o: Being an undischarged insolvent may be a ground of disqualification.
Being of unsound mind may be a ground of disqualification.
Holding an office of profit may be a ground of disqualification.
Loss of citizenship is not connected with disqualification under Article 191.
41.x: Option D is incorrect: losing citizenship is a ground for disqualification under Article 191, along with office of profit, unsound mind and insolvency.
41.tq: Recall the grounds in Article 191.
n: Holding an office of profit is a ground for disqualification from membership of the Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
Unsoundness of mind is a ground for disqualification from membership of the Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
Being an undischarged insolvent is a ground for disqualification from membership of the Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
Loss of citizenship is a ground for disqualification from membership of the Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
Article 191 specifies grounds for disqualification from membership of a State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **loss of citizenship is not connected with disqualification under Article 191** — so option **(4)** is the answer.
**Article 191** grounds include **loss of citizenship**, **office of profit**, **unsound mind** and **undischarged insolvent**.
So options (1), (2), (3) are correct grounds.
xa: Also: disqualification by Parliament's law (**RPA 1951**) and defection under the **Tenth Schedule**.
**Article 192**: the **Governor** decides, on the **binding opinion** of the **ECI**.
**Art. 190(4)**: seat vacated if absent **60 days** without permission.

41.s: Which of the following statements regarding the two Houses is incorrect?
o: The Legislative Assembly is elected directly through the FPTP system.
The Legislative Assembly is a permanent body, with one-third of its members retiring every two years.
The Legislative Council has a six-year term for its members.
The Legislative Council is elected indirectly through PR-STV along with nomination.
41.x: Option B is incorrect: the Legislative Council is the permanent House, with one-third retiring every two years. The Assembly has a five-year term and can be dissolved.
41.tq: Discriminate the dissolvable Assembly from the permanent Council.
n: The Legislative Assembly is elected directly through the First-Past-the-Post system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Legislative Council is elected indirectly through proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and nomination. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Legislative Assembly has a five-year tenure. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Legislative Assembly is subject to dissolution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Legislative Council is a permanent body. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
One-third of the Legislative Council members retire every two years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
A Legislative Council member has a six-year term. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **the Legislative Assembly is a permanent body, with one-third of its members retiring every two years** — so option **(2)** is the answer.
That describes the **Legislative Council**; the Assembly has a **five-year** term and is **dissolvable**.
The Assembly is **directly** elected by **FPTP**; the Council is **indirectly** elected by **PR-STV** plus **nomination**, with a **six-year** member term.
xa: Assembly = **Lower / Popular** House; Council = **Upper** House / **House of Elders**.
The Council **can be abolished** (**Article 169**); the Assembly cannot.
**Demands for grants** are voted **only** in the Assembly.

41.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The Speaker continues in office after dissolution of the Assembly until immediately before the first meeting of the newly elected Assembly.
Statement B: The Speaker votes in the first instance and also has a casting vote in case of a tie.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
41.x: A is true: the Speaker stays in office after dissolution until the new Assembly first meets. B is false because the Speaker has only a casting vote when votes are tied, not a first vote.
41.tq: Discriminate a first-instance vote from a casting vote.
n: The Speaker does not vacate office immediately when the Assembly is dissolved. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Speaker continues in office until immediately before the first meeting of the newly elected Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Speaker cannot vote in the first instance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Speaker exercises a casting vote when votes are equally divided. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xs: **Statement A is true, Statement B is false** — so option **(3)** is correct.
A: on dissolution the Speaker does **not** vacate office — he continues until just before the **first meeting** of the new Assembly.
B: the Speaker **cannot vote** in the first instance; he has only a **casting vote** when votes are equally divided (**Art. 189**).
xa: Exception: during a **removal resolution** (**Art. 181**) the Speaker **does not preside** but may vote in the first instance.
Removal needs a **majority of all the then members**, after **14 days' notice**.
The Speaker's certificate decides whether a bill is a **Money Bill**.

41.s:
Match List-I with List-II:
List-I
(a) Article 176
(b) Article 197
(c) Article 207
(d) Article 201

List-II
(i) Governor's recommendation for State Money Bills
(ii) Governor's address
(iii) Reservation of Bills for Presidential consideration
(iv) Legislative Council's delay of ordinary Bills
41.x: Article 176 covers the Governor's address, 197 the Council's delay of ordinary bills, 207 the Governor's recommendation for Money Bills, and 201 bills reserved for the President. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
41.tq: Recall Articles 176, 197, 201 and 207.
n: The Governor addresses the Legislative Assembly at the commencement of the first session after each general election under Article 176. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Governor addresses the Legislative Assembly at the first session of each year under Article 176. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
Introduction of a Money Bill requires the Governor's prior recommendation under Article 207. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Legislative Council can delay an ordinary Bill for three months on the first occasion under Article 197. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Legislative Council can delay an ordinary Bill for one month on the second occasion under Article 197. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Governor can reserve a Bill for the President's consideration under Articles 200 and 201. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xs: The correct match is **a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Article 176** = **Governor's address**; **Article 197** = **Council's delay of ordinary Bills**.
**Article 207** = **Governor's recommendation** for State Money Bills; **Article 201** = **reserved Bills** for the President.
xa: **Article 175** = optional address/messages; **176** = **mandatory** address at the first session of the year.
**Article 200** = Governor's assent / reservation.
**Articles 198-199** = State Money Bills.

41.s:
How many of the following statements are correct?
1. The Speaker's certification of a State Money Bill is final.
2. The Governor's recommendation is required before introduction of a State Money Bill.
3. The Legislative Council may keep a State Money Bill for 14 days.
4. The Legislative Council may permanently block a State Money Bill.
41.x: Three are correct: the Speaker's Money Bill certificate is final, the Governor must recommend the bill, and the Council has 14 days. Statement 4 is false because the Council cannot block a Money Bill.
41.tq: Find the statement that gives the Council a veto.
n: The Legislative Council cannot amend or reject a Money Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
Introduction of a Money Bill requires the Governor's prior recommendation under Article 207. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Speaker's certification of a Money Bill is final. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Legislative Council has 14 days to consider a Money Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xs: **Only three** statements are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
1 is correct: the **Speaker's certification** of a Money Bill is **sole and final**.
2 and 3 are correct: the **Governor's recommendation** is needed (**Article 207**), and the Council may keep it **14 days**.
4 is wrong: the Council **cannot amend or reject** — it cannot block a Money Bill.
xa: After **14 days**, the Bill is **deemed passed**.
The Assembly may accept or reject the Council's **recommendations** (**Art. 198**).
Money Bills are introduced **only in the Assembly**, by a minister.

41.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Legislative Assembly
(b) Legislative Council
(c) Assembly Money Bill
(d) Council ordinary-Bill delay after re-passage

List-II
(i) Permanent body
(ii) Introduced only in this chamber
(iii) One month
(iv) Dissolvable body with a five-year term
41.x: The Assembly can be dissolved and has a five-year term, the Council is permanent, Money Bills start only in the Assembly, and the Council's second delay is one month. The answer is a-iv, b-i, c-ii, d-iii.
41.tq: Pair each House with its features.
n: The Legislative Assembly is dissolvable and temporary. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The normal term of the Legislative Assembly is five years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Legislative Council is a permanent body. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
A State Money Bill can be introduced only in the Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
When the Legislative Assembly re-passes an ordinary Bill, the Legislative Council can delay it for up to one month in the second instance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]

The Legislative Council can delay an ordinary Bill for a maximum of four months, consisting of three months the first time and one month the second time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The total maximum delay of an ordinary Bill by the Legislative Council is four months. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
xs: The correct match is **a-iv, b-i, c-ii, d-iii** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Legislative Assembly** — **dissolvable**, **five-year term**; **Legislative Council** — **permanent body**.
**Money Bill** — **introduced only** in the **Assembly**; Council's delay after **re-passage** — **one month**.
xa: First-time delay on an ordinary bill: **three months** — **four months** in all.
Money Bill delay: **14 days**.
The Assembly is the **originating and overriding** chamber.

41.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The ECI advises the President on disqualification of Members of Parliament.
Statement B: The ECI advises the Governor on disqualification of Members of State Legislatures.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
41.x: Both are true: the President decides MPs' disqualification on the ECI's binding opinion (Article 103), and the Governor does the same for State legislators (Article 192).
41.tq: Pair Article 103 (MPs) with Article 192 (State legislators).
n: The Election Commission of India advises the President on the disqualification of Members of Parliament under Article 103. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
The Election Commission of India advises the Governor on the disqualification of State legislators under Article 192. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
The President decides questions of disqualification of Members of Parliament under Article 103. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
The President's decision under Article 103 is based on the opinion of the Election Commission of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
The opinion of the Election Commission of India under Article 103 is binding. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
The Governor decides questions of disqualification of Members of Legislative Assemblies and Councils under Article 192. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
The Governor's decision under Article 192 is based on the opinion of the Election Commission of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
The opinion of the Election Commission of India under Article 192 is binding. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — so option **(1)** is correct.
A: the **President** decides MPs' disqualification on the **ECI's binding opinion** (**Article 103**).
B: the **Governor** decides State legislators' disqualification on the **ECI's binding opinion** (**Article 192**).
xa: Grounds under **Article 191**: **office of profit**, **unsound mind**, **undischarged insolvent**, **not a citizen**.
⚠ **Tenth Schedule** defection is decided by the **Speaker/Chairman**, not the Governor.
**Art. 190**: no one can be a member of **both Houses** or of two states' legislatures.

41.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. One-sixth of the members of a Legislative Council are nominated by the Governor.
II. One-twelfth of the members are elected by Graduates.
III. One-twelfth of the members are elected by Teachers.
IV. Industrialists are included as a separate electoral category.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
41.x: I, II and III are correct: one-sixth of the Council is nominated, and graduates and teachers each elect one-twelfth. IV is false because industrialists are not an electorate.
41.tq: Recall the Council's four electorates.
n: One-twelfth of the members of a Legislative Council are elected by graduates. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
One-twelfth of the members of a Legislative Council are elected by teachers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
One-sixth of the members of a Legislative Council are nominated by the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
Industrialists are not an electoral category for Legislative Council elections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Legislative Council is constituted through indirect election categories and gubernatorial nomination. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
xs: Statements **I, II and III only** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
I: **one-sixth** of the Council is **nominated by the Governor**.
II and III: **graduates** and **teachers** each elect **one-twelfth**.
IV is wrong: **industrialists** are **not** an electoral category.
xa: **MLAs** elect **one-third** (from among **non-MLAs**); **local bodies** elect **one-third**.
Teachers must be in institutions of at least **secondary-school** level.
Election is by **PR-STV**, by **secret ballot**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: A Governor has a five-year term.
Statement B: A Governor continues in office until a successor assumes office, subject to holding office during the pleasure of the President.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
41.x: Both are true: the Governor's term is five years, but they serve at the President's pleasure and stay on until a successor takes over.
41.tq: Recall the Governor's tenure.
n: The Governor has a five-year term. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
The Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
The Governor continues in office until the successor assumes office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — so option **(1)** is correct.
A: the Governor has a **five-year term**.
B: he holds office during the **pleasure of the President** and **continues** until the **successor assumes** office.
xa: **Five years** is also the tenure of the **President**, **Lok Sabha**, a **State Legislative Assembly**, a **Panchayat** and a **Municipality**.
**Six years**: **Rajya Sabha** and **Legislative Council** members.
The Assembly can be extended **1 year at a time** during a National Emergency.

41.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) General State Legislative Assembly maximum strength
(b) Constitutional floor for a State Legislative Assembly
(c) Largest Legislative Assembly
(d) Smallest State Legislative Assembly

List-II
(i) 60 members
(ii) Uttar Pradesh
(iii) 500 members
(iv) Sikkim
41.x: An Assembly can have at most 500 members and at least 60. Uttar Pradesh has the largest Assembly and Sikkim the smallest. The answer is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.
41.tq: Recall the Assembly limits and extremes.
n: The maximum prescribed strength of a general State Legislative Assembly is 500 members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
The constitutional floor for the strength of a State Legislative Assembly is 60 members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
Uttar Pradesh has the largest State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
Sikkim has the smallest State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
The minimum prescribed strength of a State Legislative Assembly is 60 members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Maximum strength: **500 members**; constitutional floor: **60 members**.
Largest Assembly: **Uttar Pradesh** (**403**); smallest State Assembly: **Sikkim** (**32**).
xa: Sikkim's **32** is a special exception under **Art. 371F**.
Smallest UT Assembly: **Puducherry** (**33**).
**AP** has **175** seats; **Telangana** **119**.

41.s: Which of the following statements regarding State Legislative Councils is incorrect?
o: The largest Legislative Council is in Sikkim.
The minimum prescribed strength of a State Legislative Council is 40 members.
The provision relating to State Legislative Councils is contained in Article 171.
The maximum strength of a State Legislative Council is one-third of the strength of the State Assembly.
41.x: Option A is incorrect: Uttar Pradesh has the largest Legislative Council (100 members); Sikkim has no Council. A Council can be at most one-third of the Assembly and at least 40 (Article 171).
41.tq: Recall the largest Council.
n: The maximum prescribed strength of a State Legislative Council is one-third of the strength of the State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
The minimum prescribed strength of a State Legislative Council is 40 members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
The State Legislative Council is covered by Article 171. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
Uttar Pradesh has the largest Legislative Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **the largest Legislative Council is in Sikkim** — so option **(1)** is the answer.
The **largest** Council is in **Uttar Pradesh** — **100** members.
The Council's provision is in **Article 171**: maximum **one-third** of the Assembly, minimum **40** — so (2), (3), (4) are correct.
xa: Sikkim is not among the **six** bicameral States: **AP, Telangana, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, UP**.
Actual strength is fixed by **Parliament**.
⚠ Lists showing **J&K** are out of date — its Council was abolished in **2019**.

41.s:
Assertion (A): The State Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.
Reason (R): Article 164(2) specifically establishes this responsibility.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
41.x: Both are true: Article 164(2) makes the State Council of Ministers collectively answerable to the Legislative Assembly. R gives the provision behind A.
41.tq: Recall Article 164(2).
n: The State Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly under Article 164(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Article 164(2)** makes the State Council of Ministers **collectively responsible** to the **Legislative Assembly**.
R names the provision that creates A.
xa: The Council is capped at **15 percent** of the Assembly (**91st Amendment Act, 2003**); **minimum 12**.
A non-member minister can serve at most **six consecutive months**.
Responsibility is to the Assembly, not the **Legislative Council**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the State Council of Ministers:
I. Its maximum strength is capped at 15% of the Assembly strength.
II. Its minimum strength is 12 ministers, including the Chief Minister.
III. The maximum-strength cap was introduced by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003.
IV. Its minimum strength is six ministers, including the Chief Minister.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
41.x: I, II and III are correct: the 91st Amendment (2003) caps a State ministry at 15% of the Assembly, with a minimum of 12. IV is false because the minimum is 12, not six.
41.tq: Recall the minimum of 12.
n: The Council of Ministers is capped at a maximum of 15 percent of the Assembly's strength under Article 164. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act of 2003 provides the 15-percent cap on the Council of Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The minimum size of the Council of Ministers is 12 ministers, including the Chief Minister. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xs: Statements **I, II and III only** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
I and III: the **91st Amendment Act, 2003** capped the Council at **15%** of the Assembly.
II: the **minimum** is **12** ministers **including the Chief Minister**.
IV is wrong: the minimum is **12**, not six.
xa: The cap is in **Article 164** (**164(1A)**).
A **non-member** minister may serve only **six consecutive months**.
The Council is **collectively responsible** to the Assembly — **Article 164(2)**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The normal term of a State Legislative Assembly is five years.
II. During a National Emergency, Parliament may extend the Assembly’s duration by law for one year at a time.
III. Such extension may continue without limit after the National Emergency ceases.
IV. The extension cannot continue beyond six months after the Emergency ceases.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
41.x: I, II and IV are correct: the Assembly's term is five years, it can be extended a year at a time in an Emergency, and not beyond six months after the Emergency ends. III is false because the extension is limited.
41.tq: Recall the six-month limit after an Emergency.
n: The normal term of the Legislative Assembly is five years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The normal term of the Legislative Assembly is five years under Article 172. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
During a National Emergency under Article 352, Parliament may extend the Legislative Assembly’s duration by law for one year at a time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Legislative Assembly’s duration may be extended only up to six months after the National Emergency ceases. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
xs: Statements **I, II and IV only** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
I: the Assembly's normal term is **five years** (**Article 172**).
II and IV: in a **National Emergency (Article 352)** Parliament may extend it **one year at a time**, but not beyond **six months** after the Emergency ceases.
III is wrong: the extension is **not** unlimited.
xa: The Assembly may be **dissolved** earlier but cannot be **abolished**.
**Art. 174**: no more than **6 months** between sittings.
Quorum: **10 members or one-tenth** of the House, whichever is greater (**Art. 189(3)**).

42.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the earlier seats of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly:

2. Before 1956, the Assembly of Andhra State met at Kurnool.
3. Amaravati was the seat of the Assembly before 1956.

42.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because before 1956 the Andhra State Assembly met at Kurnool.
42.tq: Identify the incorrect chronological-location statement and avoid reversing earlier and present seats.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: sessions were in **Hyderabad** (common capital) until the move to **Amaravati**.
Statement 2 correct: before **1956**, Andhra State's Assembly met at **Kurnool**.
Statement 3 wrong: Amaravati is the **present** seat (sessions since **2017**), not the pre-1956 one.
xa: Interim building at **Velagapudi**; new building by **Norman Foster + Partners**.
In **1956** the legislature was **unicameral**, with **301** members.

42.s: The present elected strength of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly, as provided under Section 17 of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, is:
42.x: Section 17 provides 175 elected Assembly seats for Andhra Pradesh; Telangana has 119 seats.
42.tq: Separate the Andhra Pradesh figure from the corresponding Telangana figure.
xs: **Sec. 17** of the AP Reorganisation Act gives AP **175** elected seats — option **(2)** (APPSC-GS **2019** key).
**119** is **Telangana**; **225** is the proposed Sec. **26** increase; **301** was the **1956** Assembly.
xa: Reserved: **29 SC** + **7 ST**.
**Sec. 26** increase not yet made: **Art. 170(3)** ties it to the census after **2026**.

42.s: How many seats in the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly are reserved for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes respectively?
42.x: The Andhra Pradesh Assembly has 29 seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and 7 seats reserved for Scheduled Tribes.

xs: AP reserves **29 SC** and **7 ST** seats — option **(2)**.

xa: Total elected strength: **175** (**Sec. 17**).
Anglo-Indian nomination ended with the **104th Amendment (2020)**.
Constituencies follow the **Delimitation Order 2008**.

42.s: The nomination of an Anglo-Indian member to the Legislative Assembly under Article 333 and Section 18 of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act ended with the:
42.x: The Anglo-Indian nomination provision under Article 333 ended with the 104th Constitutional Amendment in 2020.
42.tq: Use the amendment-number trap by distinguishing the constitutional change from nearby amendment numbers.
xs: It ended with the **104th Constitutional Amendment** (**2020**) — option **(2)**.
The nomination was under **Sec. 18** of the AP Reorganisation Act and **Art. 333**.
xa: **Sec. 18** gave **one Anglo-Indian nominee each** to AP and Telangana — now **lapsed**.
**Sec. 19**: sitting MLAs continue for their allotted constituencies.

42.s: Why did the YSRCP not obtain official Opposition status in the 16th Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly?
o: It declined to claim the position.
It did not win any reserved seat.
It won fewer than one-tenth of the total Assembly seats.
42.x: The YSRCP won 11 of the 175 seats, which was below the one-tenth threshold required for official Opposition status.
42.tq: Apply the numerical threshold to the election result rather than relying on the party's name or vote share.
xs: The YSRCP won **11**, **fewer than one-tenth** of the **175** seats — option **(4)**.
**One-tenth** of the House is needed for **official Opposition** status.
xa: PAC chair goes to the **Opposition** by convention.
First Leader of Opposition: **Puchalapalli Sundarayya**.

42.s: When Andhra Pradesh was formed in 1956, its Legislature was unicameral with a Legislative Assembly of how many members?
42.x: In 1956 the AP Legislature was unicameral with an Assembly of 301 members. 175 is the present strength of residual AP (Sec. 17, AP Reorganisation Act); 294 and 245 are distractors not supported for 1956.
42.tq: 1956 = 301 (unicameral); 2014 onwards = 175.
xs: In **1956** AP's legislature was **unicameral**, with **301** members — option **(3)** (APPSC-GS **2022** key).
**175** is residual AP's present strength (**Sec. 17**).
xa: The **Council** was created only in **1958**.
First Speaker (**1956**): **Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao**.
The **1956** Assembly: **Congress** held a large majority.

42.s: Who is the present Speaker of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly?
42.x: Ch. Ayyanna Patrudu is the present Speaker of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly.
42.tq: Use the current office-holder carefully and distinguish it from the first woman Speaker.
xs: **Ch. Ayyanna Patrudu** is the present Speaker — option **(3)**.
**K. Pratibha Bharati** was the **first woman Speaker**, not the present one.
xa: Present **Deputy Speaker (2026)**: **K. Raghu Ramakrishna Raju**.
**Kodela Siva Prasada Rao**: first Speaker of residual AP (**2014-19**); **Tammineni Sitaram**: **2019-24**.
First Speaker (**1956**): **Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao**.

42.s:
Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
1. Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao — First Speaker of the AP Assembly
2. Kalluri Subbarao — First Deputy Speaker
3. Madapati Hanumantha Rao — First Leader of Opposition
4. Puchalapalli Sundarayya — First Leader of Opposition
