A retired judge under Art. 128 has full powers but is **not deemed a judge** of the court.
There are **no additional judges in the SC** — only in **High Courts** (**Art. 224**).

43.s: Which of the following statements regarding removal of a Supreme Court judge is incorrect?
o: The grounds are proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
Removal is made by an order of the President.
The procedure is governed by the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.
The removal address requires a simple majority in each House of Parliament.
43.x: Option D is incorrect: a judge is removed only after an address passed in each House by a special majority (majority of total membership plus two-thirds present and voting), not a simple majority. The grounds are proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
43.tq: Recall the special majority needed to remove a judge.
n: A Supreme Court judge is removed by an order of the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The President issues the removal order after an address by Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Proved misbehaviour is a ground for removing a Supreme Court judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Incapacity is a ground for removing a Supreme Court judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Removal of a Supreme Court judge requires a special majority in each House of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The special majority requires a majority of the total membership of the House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The special majority requires at least two-thirds of the members present and voting. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The special majority must be obtained in the same session. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 governs the removal procedure procedurally. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Removal of a Supreme Court judge requires a parliamentary special-majority address under Article 124(4). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Removal of a Supreme Court judge requires a statutory inquiry. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **the removal address requires a simple majority** in each House — so option **(4)** is the answer.
Removal needs a **special majority** in **each House**: a **majority of the total membership** + at least **two-thirds** present and voting.
Removal is **by order of the President** on **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**, under the **Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968** — so (1), (2), (3) are correct.
xa: ⚠ The Constitution says "**removal**"; "impeachment" is used only for the **President** (**Art. 61**).
HC judges are removed the same way under **Art. 218**; also the **CAG** (**Art. 148**) and **CEC** (**Art. 324(5)**).
Lesser misconduct: **In-House Procedure (1999)**, after **C. Ravichandran Iyer, 1995**.

43.s:

1. Under Article 129, the Supreme Court is a Court of Record.
2. The Court of Record includes the power to punish for contempt of itself.
3. Under Article 130, the seat of the Supreme Court is Delhi.
4. The CJI may decide another place with the President's approval.
43.x: All four are correct: under Article 129, the Court is a Court of Record with power to punish contempt. Under Article 130, its seat is Delhi, but the CJI may choose other places with the President's approval.
43.tq: Recall Articles 129 and 130.
n: Article 129 declares the Supreme Court to be a Court of Record. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

The seat of the Supreme Court is Delhi. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The Chief Justice may decide on other places for Supreme Court sittings with the approval of the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
xs: **All four** statements are correct — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Article 129**: the SC is a **Court of Record**, with power to punish **contempt** of itself.
**Article 130**: the seat is **Delhi**; the CJI may decide other places with the **President's** approval.
xa: HCs are **Courts of Record** under **Article 215**.
**Contempt of Courts Act, 1971** (**H.N. Sanyal Committee**) defines civil and criminal contempt.
No **regional benches** yet; **P. Wilson's** private member's Bill (**19 Feb 2026**) seeks them.

**Ad hoc judge**: the **Chief Justice** appoints with the **previous consent of the President** (**Art. 127**).

43.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Supreme Court succeeded the Federal Court of India.
The Supreme Court succeeded the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
The Supreme Court succeeded the Council of States established under the Government of India Act, 1935.
The Federal Court was established under the Government of India Act, 1935.
43.x: Option C is incorrect: the Supreme Court replaced the Federal Court (set up under the 1935 Act) and the Privy Council's Judicial Committee. The Council of States is the Rajya Sabha, not a court.
43.tq: Recall the two courts the Supreme Court replaced.
n: The Supreme Court of India succeeded the Federal Court of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Federal Court of India was established under the Government of India Act, 1935. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court of India succeeded the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]

The SC succeeded the **Federal Court** (set up under the **GoI Act, 1935**) and the **Judicial Committee of the Privy Council**.
So options (1), (2), (4) are correct.
xa: The Federal Court functioned from **1937**.
Privy Council appeals were abolished in **1949**.
The SC moved to its **Tilak Marg** building in **1958**.

The High Court is a Court of Record under Article 215. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]

n: Parliament has exclusive power to increase the number of Supreme Court judges by law under Article 124(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Supreme Court judges retire at 65 years of age under Article 124(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The President removes Supreme Court judges after an Address supported by a Special Majority in each House of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]

43.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Supreme Court Judges are appointed by the President of India.
Both categories of Judges submit their written resignations to the President.
Both categories of Judges are appointed by warrant under the hand and seal of the President.
High Court Judges are appointed by the Governor of the State.
43.x: Option D is incorrect: the President, not the Governor, appoints High Court judges, by warrant under hand and seal, as for Supreme Court judges. Both resign to the President.
43.tq: Discriminate who appoints a judge from who swears them in.
n: The President of India appoints Supreme Court Judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The President of India appoints High Court Judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
Supreme Court Judges are appointed by warrant under the President’s hand and seal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
High Court Judges are appointed by warrant under the President’s hand and seal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
Supreme Court Judges address their written resignations to the President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
High Court Judges address their written resignations to the President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The resignation of a High Court Judge is addressed to the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The Governor has no power to appoint High Court Judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The President of India is the appointing authority for Supreme Court Judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The President of India is the appointing authority for High Court Judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
A Supreme Court Judge addresses a resignation to the President of India under Article 124(2)(a). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
A High Court Judge addresses a resignation to the President of India under Article 217(1)(a). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **High Court Judges are appointed by the Governor** — so option **(4)** is the answer.
HC judges are appointed by the **President** by **warrant** — **Article 217**; SC judges likewise under **Article 124**.
Both **resign to the President** — so (1), (2), (3) are correct.
xa: The **Governor** only administers the **oath** to HC judges (**Article 219**).
HC strength is fixed by the **President** (**Article 216**); SC strength by **Parliament** (**Article 124(1)**).
Retirement: HC **62**, SC **65**.

xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv** — so option **(2)** is correct.

43.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Advice tendered by the Supreme Court under Article 143 is binding on the President in all cases.
Statement B: On pre-Constitution disputes, the Supreme Court is bound to give advice.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
43.x: A is false: advice under Article 143 does not bind the President. B is true: on references about pre-Constitution treaties and agreements (Article 143(2)), the Court must give its opinion.

n: Under Article 143, the Supreme Court is bound to give advice on pre-Constitution disputes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

A is false: **Article 143** opinions are **strictly advisory** — **not binding** on the President.

xa: Under **143(1)** the SC **may** tender (or **refuse**) its opinion.
References are heard by at least **five judges** (**Article 145(3)**).
The **16th Presidential Reference** (**Nov 2025**) answered questions on bill timelines.

43.s: Which of the following statements regarding the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 131 is incorrect?
o: It includes recovery of damages by a private party against the Union.
It excludes inter-State water disputes under Article 262.
It covers disputes between one State and another State.
It covers direct federal disputes involving a legal right between the Centre and one or more States.
43.x: Option A is incorrect: Article 131 covers only disputes about legal rights between the Centre and States or between States. A private party suing the Union for damages goes to the ordinary courts.
43.tq: Recall that Article 131 applies only between governments.
n: The Supreme Court has original and exclusive jurisdiction under Article 131. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 covers direct federal disputes involving a legal right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court can hear under Article 131 disputes between one State and another State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 excludes inter-State water disputes under Article 262. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 does not cover inter-State water disputes under Article 262. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 does not cover recovery of damages by a private party against the Union. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court can hear under Article 131 disputes between the Centre and one or more States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xs: The incorrect statement is that Article 131 **includes recovery of damages by a private party against the Union** — so option **(1)** is the answer.
Such recovery is **excluded** from original jurisdiction.

Art. 131 covers **federal disputes involving a legal right** — **Centre vs States** and **State vs State**; it **excludes inter-State water disputes** (**Article 262**) — so (2), (3), (4) are correct.
xa: Also excluded: **Finance Commission** matters (**Article 280**), **pre-Constitution treaties**, **political questions**.
Also excluded: adjustment of expenses (**Art. 290**) and **election disputes** of legislatures (go to HCs).
Art. 131 jurisdiction is **exclusive**.

o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
43.x: Both are true: the right to move the Supreme Court under Article 32 is itself a fundamental right, so the Court cannot turn away an Article 32 petition. R explains A.
43.tq: Ask whether being a fundamental right explains why the Court cannot refuse.
n: The Supreme Court cannot refuse an Article 32 petition. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The right to move the Supreme Court under Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Article 32** is **itself a Fundamental Right**, so the SC cannot refuse an Art. 32 petition.
The SC's writ jurisdiction enforces **Fundamental Rights only**.
xa: HCs issue writs under **Article 226** for **Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights**.
Art. 32 jurisdiction is original but **not exclusive**.
The US has **no equivalent** of Art. 32.

43.s:
Match the appellate jurisdiction with its governing Article:

List-I
(a) Constitutional appeals
(b) Civil appeals
(c) Criminal appeals
(d) Special Leave Petition

List-II
(i) Article 136
(ii) Article 134
(iii) Article 132
(iv) Article 133
43.x: Constitutional appeals are Article 132, civil appeals 133, criminal appeals 134, and special leave 136. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
43.tq: Remember that Articles 132 to 134 run constitutional, civil, criminal.
n: The Supreme Court has constitutional appellate jurisdiction under Article 132. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has civil appellate jurisdiction under Article 133. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has criminal appellate jurisdiction under Article 134. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has discretionary appellate power under Article 136 to grant special leave to appeal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Constitutional** appeals = **Article 132**; **civil** = **Article 133**.
**Criminal** = **Article 134**; **Special Leave Petition** = **Article 136**.
xa: Arts 132 and 133 need an HC **certificate** under **Article 134A**.
Art. 134 appeals where an HC **reversed an acquittal into a death sentence** lie **as of right**.
Art. 136 is **not** available against **Military Tribunals**.

43.s: Under Article 136, the Supreme Court's power to grant Special Leave to Appeal is:
o: Discretionary and available against any judgment or order of any court or tribunal, subject to the stated exception
Mandatory and limited to High Court judgments
Advisory and limited to presidential references
Available only in civil proceedings involving a constitutional question
43.x: Under Article 136, the Court may, at its discretion, grant special leave to appeal against any judgment or order of any court or tribunal, except military tribunals (Article 136(2)).
43.tq: Recall Article 136 and its military exception.
n: The Supreme Court has discretionary appellate power under Article 136 to grant special leave to appeal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 136 permits special leave to appeal from any judgment or order of any court or tribunal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The power under Article 136 is plenary and residual. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 136(2) does not apply to Military Tribunals or Armed Forces Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Special Leave Petitions do not lie against judgments or sentences passed by courts-martial or military tribunals under Article 136(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xs: Art. 136 power is **discretionary and available against any judgment or order of any court or tribunal**, subject to the exception — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is a **plenary and residual** power.
Exception: **Article 136(2)** — **not** against **courts-martial / Military Tribunals / Armed Forces Courts**.
xa: Advisory jurisdiction is a separate power — **Article 143**.
Constitutional / civil / criminal appeals: **132 / 133 / 134**.
India's appellate scope is **very wide** compared with the US Supreme Court.

43.s:
Assertion (A): The Supreme Court's review jurisdiction under Article 137 is distinct from judicial review of statutes.
Reason (R): Article 137 concerns the power of the Supreme Court to review its own judgments or orders.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
43.x: Both are true: Article 137 lets the Court review its own judgments, which is why it differs from judicial review of laws. R explains A.
43.tq: Discriminate review of a judgment from judicial review of a law.
n: The Supreme Court has review jurisdiction under Article 137. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 137 empowers the Supreme Court to review its own judgments or orders. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Review jurisdiction under Article 137 is distinct from judicial review of statutes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Article 137** lets the SC **review its own judgments, orders and pronouncements**.
That is why it is **distinct from judicial review of statutes**.
xa: Review is subject to **Parliamentary law** and **court rules**.
After a review petition is **dismissed**, a **curative petition** may follow (**Rupa Ashok Hurra, 2002**).
**Article 141**: SC's law is **binding on all courts**.

43.s:
Assertion (A): An opinion rendered by the Supreme Court to the President under Article 143 is not binding on the President.
Reason (R): Under Article 145(3), a reference under Article 143 must be heard by a bench of at least five judges.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
43.x: Both are true but R does not explain A: an Article 143 opinion is advisory and does not bind the President, while the five-judge bench rule of Article 145(3) only fixes who hears the reference.
43.tq: Ask whether creating a jurisdiction explains that its opinions are non-binding.
n: The Supreme Court has advisory jurisdiction under Article 143. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Opinions rendered by the Supreme Court to the President under Article 143 are strictly advisory. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 143 opinions are not binding on the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — so option **(2)** is correct.
A: **Article 143** opinions are **strictly advisory** — **not binding** on the President.
R: **Article 145(3)** requires at least **five judges** for Art. 143 references — a rule on bench size, not on binding force.
xa: **143(1)**: SC **may** refuse; **143(2)**: SC **must** answer on **pre-constitutional** disputes.
Constitution Benches also hear cases with a **substantial question of law** on interpreting the Constitution.
The US Supreme Court has **no** advisory jurisdiction.

43.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Under Article 143(1), the President may refer questions of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court.
II. Under Article 143(1), the Supreme Court may tender its opinion.
III. Under Article 143(2), the Supreme Court must tender its opinion on pre-constitutional matters.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
43.x: All three are correct: under Article 143(1), the President may refer questions of public importance and the Court may give its opinion. Under 143(2), it must give one on pre-Constitution matters.
43.tq: Discriminate 'may' (143(1)) from 'must' (143(2)).
n: The President can refer questions of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for its opinion under Article 143. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Under Article 143(1), the Supreme Court may tender its opinion on matters of public importance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Under Article 143(2), the Supreme Court must tender its opinion on pre-constitutional matters. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xs: **I, II and III** are all correct — so option **(4)** is correct.
I: under **143(1)** the **President** refers questions of **law or fact** of **public importance**.
II: under 143(1) the SC **may** tender (or **refuse**) its opinion.
III: under **143(2)** the SC **must** tender its opinion on **pre-constitutional** disputes.
xa: Opinions are **not binding** on the President.
The **Third Judges Case (1998)** arose from a **Presidential Reference**.
The **16th Presidential Reference** came in **Nov 2025**.

43.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. A constitutional appeal under Article 132 concerns a substantial question of law relating to the interpretation of the Constitution.
II. A civil appeal under Article 133 concerns a substantial question of law of general importance.
III. A criminal appeal under Article 134 may arise where a High Court reverses an acquittal and sentences the accused to death.
IV. Every criminal appeal under Article 134 requires a certificate from the High Court.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
43.x: I, II and III are correct: Article 132 covers constitutional questions, 133 civil questions of general importance, and 134 criminal cases where a High Court reverses an acquittal and sentences to death. IV is false because that last appeal needs no certificate.
43.tq: Discriminate appeals as of right from appeals by certificate.
n: Article 132 covers appeals from High Court judgments involving a substantial question of law concerning the interpretation of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 133 covers appeals in civil proceedings involving a substantial question of law of general importance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has criminal appellate jurisdiction under Article 134. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 134 covers criminal appeals where a High Court has reversed an acquittal into a death sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Capital-punishment reversals under Article 134 are appealable as of right without a High Court certificate. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xs: Statements **I, II and III only** are correct — so option **(3)** is correct.
I: **Article 132** — **substantial question of law** on **interpreting the Constitution**.
II: **Article 133** — civil cases with a **substantial question of law of general importance**.
III is correct and IV wrong: where an HC **reversed an acquittal into a death sentence**, appeal lies **as of right**, **without** a certificate.
xa: Art. 134 also covers cases where an HC **withdrew a trial** to itself.
HC certificates are issued under **Article 134A**.
**Article 136** SLP is **discretionary**.

43.s:
How many of the following matters are excluded from the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction under Article 131?
I. Inter-State water disputes
II. Finance Commission matters
III. Recovery of damages by a private party against the Union
IV. Direct federal disputes involving a legal right between States
43.x: Three are excluded: inter-State water disputes (Article 262), Finance Commission matters (Article 280) and private damages claims against the Union. Disputes between States about legal rights are the core of Article 131.
43.tq: Find the item that falls within Article 131.
n: Article 131 covers direct federal disputes involving a legal right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court can hear under Article 131 disputes between one State and another State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 excludes inter-State water disputes under Article 262. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 does not cover inter-State water disputes under Article 262. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 does not cover Finance Commission matters under Article 280. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 does not cover recovery of damages by a private party against the Union. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xs: **Only three** are excluded — so option **(3)** is correct.
Excluded: **inter-State water disputes** (**Article 262**), **Finance Commission** matters (**Article 280**), and **recovery of damages by a private party** against the Union.
Disputes **between States** involving a **legal right** are the core of **Article 131**.
xa: Also excluded: **political questions**, **pre-Constitution treaties**, **Art. 290** expense adjustments.
**Election disputes** of Parliament and state legislatures go to **High Courts**.
Art. 131 also covers **Centre and some states vs other states**.

43.s:
Assertion (A): A curative petition may be pursued after dismissal of a review petition under Article 137.
Reason (R): The curative petition was evolved under the Supreme Court's inherent powers anchored in Article 142 to prevent abuse of process and cure gross miscarriages of justice.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
43.x: Both are true: a curative petition can be filed after a review petition under Article 137 is dismissed, because it rests on the Court's inherent powers under Article 142 to correct gross injustice. R explains A.

n: The curative petition was evolved under the Supreme Court's inherent powers anchored in Article 142. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
A curative petition prevents abuse of process. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
A curative petition cures gross miscarriages of justice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
A curative petition is available after a review petition under Article 137 has been dismissed. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
A **curative petition** is available after a **review petition** (**Article 137**) is **dismissed**.
It rests on the SC's **inherent powers** anchored in **Article 142**, to prevent **abuse of process** and cure **gross miscarriage of justice**.
xa: It was evolved in **Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002)**.
**Article 142**: any decree or order for **complete justice**.
**e-SCR**: free digital database of reported judgments, launched **2023**.

43.s:
Consider the following statements regarding a Constitution Bench:
I. It requires a minimum of five judges.
II. It may hear a case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution.
III. It may hear references under Article 143.

43.x: All three are correct: under Article 145(3), at least five judges must hear cases on the interpretation of the Constitution and references under Article 143.

I: a **Constitution Bench** has at least **five judges** (**Article 145(3)**).
II and III: it hears a **substantial question of law** on **interpreting the Constitution** and **Article 143** references.

The **Fourth Judges Case** was a **5-judge bench** led by **Justice J.S. Khehar**.
**Article 145** also lets the SC make **rules**.

43.s:
How many of the following appellate jurisdictions expressly require certification by the High Court under Article 134A?
1. Constitutional appeals under Article 132
2. Civil appeals under Article 133
3. Criminal appeals under Article 134(1)(a), where a High Court reverses an acquittal and sentences the accused to death
4. Special Leave Petition jurisdiction under Article 136
43.x: Two need a High Court certificate: constitutional appeals (Article 132) and civil appeals (Article 133). An appeal under Article 134(1)(a) after a death sentence on reversal of acquittal lies as of right, and special leave is granted at the Court's discretion.
43.tq: Discriminate appeals by certificate from appeals as of right.
n: An appeal under Article 132 requires a certificate from the High Court under Article 134A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The High Court must certify under Article 134A that the question in a civil appeal needs determination by the Supreme Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has criminal appellate jurisdiction under Article 134. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 134 covers criminal appeals where a High Court has reversed an acquittal into a death sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 134 covers criminal appeals where a High Court has withdrawn a trial to itself. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Capital-punishment reversals under Article 134 are appealable as of right without a High Court certificate. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has discretionary appellate power under Article 136 to grant special leave to appeal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 136 permits special leave to appeal from any judgment or order of any court or tribunal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Special Leave Petitions do not lie against judgments or sentences passed by courts-martial or military tribunals under Article 136(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xs: **Only two** need an HC certificate under **Article 134A** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Constitutional appeals (Article 132)** and **civil appeals (Article 133)** need the certificate.
**Article 134** death-sentence-on-reversal appeals lie **as of right**; **Article 136** SLP is **discretionary**.
xa: Art. 136 covers **any judgment or order** of **any court or tribunal**, except military ones.
Art. 134 also covers cases where an HC **withdrew a trial** to itself.
SC's appellate scope is **very wide** — constitutional, civil, criminal, special leave.

43.s:
Arrange the following developments in the correct chronological order:
A. Third Judges Case
B. First Judges Case
C. 99th Amendment and NJAC
D. Second Judges Case
43.x: The First Judges Case (1981), Second (1993) and Third (1998) came before the 99th Amendment and NJAC (2014–15). The order is B, D, A, C.

n: The First Judges Case was decided in 1981. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]

43.s: The formal appointment of judges under the Collegium arrangement is associated with which pair of constitutional provisions?
43.x: The President appoints Supreme Court judges under Article 124(2) and High Court judges under Article 217(1).

xs: Formal appointment rests on **Articles 124(2) and 217(1)** — so option **(4)** is correct.

**124(1)** concerns Parliament's power over **number of judges**; **136 and 226** are SLP and HC writs.

n: The First Judges Case was decided in 1981. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 125-127]

Assertion (A): The Second Judges Case formally gave birth to the Collegium System.
Reason (R): It reversed the 1981 ruling and held that consultation means concurrence.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.

44.s: Which of the following statements regarding the older High Courts in India is correct?

xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.

44.s: A new High Court established under a law made by Parliament comes into being through:
o: A resolution of the concerned State Legislative Assembly
An order of the Chief Justice of India

xs: A new HC created under a Parliament law comes into being through **a notification issued by the President** — option **(4)** is correct.

Example: the **AP High Court** was notified by the **President** under the **AP Reorganisation Act**.

xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.

3. It provides for the appointment of additional judges for up to two years.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
44.x: Statement 1 is correct: Article 224A was inserted by the 15th Amendment, 1963. Statement 2 is correct: a retired judge sits with the prior consent of the President and the judge. Statement 3 is wrong: additional judges for up to two years come under Article 224(1), not 224A. So '1 only' misses statement 2, and options C and D wrongly include statement 3.
44.tq: 224A = retired judges (15th Amendment 1963); 224(1) = additional judges; 224(2) = acting judges.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **Art. 224A** was inserted by the **15th Amendment, 1963**.
Statement 2 correct: a retired judge sits with prior consent of the **President** and the **judge**.
Statement 3 wrong: additional judges for **2 years** are under **Art. 224(1)**.
xa: ⚠ **223** = Acting CJ; **224(1)** = Additional; **224(2)** = Acting judges; **224A** = Retired.
Additional judges are usually made permanent in about **two years** (TH, **9 Aug 2026**).

44.s:
Under Article 217 of the Constitution, a Judge of a High Court is appointed by the President after consultation with which of the following?
1. Chief Justice of India
2. Governor of the State
3. Chief Justice of the concerned High Court in the case of a puisne Judge
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: The President appoints High Court Judges after consulting the CJI and the Governor; in the case of a puisne Judge, the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court is also consulted.
44.tq: Identify all constitutionally prescribed consultees and avoid confusing appointment with transfer.
xs: All three are consulted — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Under **Art. 217**, the President consults the **CJI** and the **Governor**.
For a **puisne judge**, the **Chief Justice of that High Court** is also consulted.
xa: For a common HC, the **Governors of all states concerned** are consulted.
Proposal starts with the **HC collegium** (CJ + **2**) → SC collegium (CJI + **2**).
Qualifications: citizen + **10 years** judicial office or HC advocate.

44.s:
Consider the following statements about the collegium process for appointing High Court judges:
1. The proposal is examined at the Supreme Court level by the Chief Justice of India and the two senior-most Supreme Court judges.
2. The proposal is initiated by the High Court collegium of the Chief Justice and the three senior-most judges of that High Court.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
44.x: Statement 2 is wrong: the High Court collegium is the Chief Justice plus the two (not three) senior-most judges of that High Court. Statement 1 is correct: the Supreme Court side for HC appointments is the CJI plus the two senior-most SC judges. So '1 only'.
44.tq: HC appointments: HC CJ + 2 -> CJI + 2; SC appointments and HC transfers: CJI + 4.
xs: Statement **1 only** is correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: at the SC level the proposal goes to the **CJI + 2 senior-most** SC judges.
Statement 2 is wrong: the HC collegium is the **HC Chief Justice + 2** senior-most judges, not three.
xa: HC Chief Justice is appointed after consulting the **CJI** and the **Governor**.
Other HC judges: after consulting the **CJI**, the **Governor** and the **Chief Justice of that High Court**.
For a common HC, the **Governors of all states** concerned are consulted.

44.s:
Consider the following statements regarding removal of a High Court Judge:
1. Article 218 applies the Supreme Court Judge removal procedure to High Court Judges.
2. The procedure is governed by the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.
3. A High Court Judge may be removed by the Governor through an executive order.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Articles 218 and the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 provide the applicable removal framework. A Governor cannot remove a High Court Judge by executive order.
44.tq: Reject the wrong-authority trap and match the High Court procedure with the Supreme Court procedure.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **Art. 218** applies the SC removal procedure to HC judges.
Statement 2 correct: it runs under the **Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968**.
Statement 3 wrong: removal needs an address by **both Houses** by **special majority** — no Governor's order.
xa: Grounds: **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**.
**Soumitra Sen** (Calcutta HC) resigned in **2011** after the RS voted for removal.
Motion against **G.R. Swaminathan** noticed by **107** MPs (Dec **2025**).

44.s:
Consider the following statements about proceedings against High Court judges:
1. Justice Soumitra Sen of the Calcutta High Court resigned in 2011 after the Rajya Sabha voted for his removal.
2. A motion against Justice G.R. Swaminathan of the Madras High Court was noticed by 107 MPs in December 2025.
3. Yashwant Varma, whose inquiry report was to be tabled despite his resignation, was formerly a judge of the Madras High Court.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
44.x: Statement 1 is correct: Soumitra Sen (Calcutta HC) resigned in 2011 after the Rajya Sabha vote. Statement 2 is correct: the motion against G.R. Swaminathan was noticed by 107 MPs in December 2025. Statement 3 is wrong: Yashwant Varma was formerly of the Allahabad High Court. So '1 only' misses statement 2, and options C and D include statement 3.
44.tq: Sen = Calcutta, 2011; Swaminathan = Madras, 107 MPs; Varma = Allahabad.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **Soumitra Sen** (Calcutta HC) resigned in **2011** after the **Rajya Sabha** vote.
Statement 2 correct: the motion against **G.R. Swaminathan** (Madras HC) was noticed by **107** MPs, Dec **2025**.
Statement 3 wrong: **Yashwant Varma** was formerly of the **Allahabad HC**.
xa: Varma's inquiry report was to be tabled **despite his resignation** (LENSD **11 Jul 2026**).
Ethics codes: **1997 Restatement of Values** (**16** points) + **1999 in-house procedure**.
Removal procedure: **Art. 218** + **Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968**.

44.s: Which one of the following best describes the scope of writ jurisdiction of a High Court under Article 226?
o: It extends only to disputes arising within the physical territory of the High Court
It is confined exclusively to enforcement of Fundamental Rights
It extends to Fundamental Rights and other legal rights, including where the cause of action arises within its territory
It can be exercised only on a reference from the Supreme Court
44.x: Article 226 enables High Courts to issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose. A High Court may act even when the respondent is outside its territory if the cause of action arises within it.
44.tq: Contrast the wider wording of Article 226 with the narrower purpose traditionally associated with Article 32.
xs: **Art. 226** covers **Fundamental Rights and other legal rights**, even beyond its territory **where the cause of action arises within** — option **(3)** is correct.
It is not confined to its physical territory or to FRs alone, and needs no SC reference.
Writs "**for any other purpose**" make it **wider than Art. 32**.
xa: **Art. 227**: superintendence over all courts and tribunals **except military tribunals**.
PIL may be filed under **Art. 32 (SC)** or **Art. 226 (HC)**.
HCs are primarily **courts of appeal**.

44.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 227:
1. It covers both administrative and judicial matters.
2. The High Court may exercise the power suo motu.
3. The Supreme Court possesses an identical power under Article 227.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Article 227 covers administrative and judicial superintendence and may be exercised suo motu. Article 227 is a High Court provision; the Supreme Court has no identical Article 227 power.
44.tq: Spot the institutional-body swap in the third statement.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **Art. 227** is **administrative + judicial**.
Statement 2 correct: the HC can act **suo motu**.
Statement 3 wrong: the **SC has no Art. 227-type power**.
xa: Art. 227 excludes **military tribunals**.
It is also **revisional** in nature.
**Art. 235** vests **control** over district and subordinate courts in the **HC**.

44.s: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of the appellate jurisdiction of a High Court mentioned in the constitutional scheme?
o: The High Court is primarily a court of appeal
A death sentence awarded by a Sessions Court requires High Court confirmation
Second civil appeals are confined to questions of law
Every factual finding of a subordinate court must be reconsidered in every second appeal
44.x: A second civil appeal is limited to a substantial question of law; there is no requirement that every factual finding be reconsidered. The other three describe features of High Court appellate work.
44.tq: Find the statement that exaggerates a limited appellate power into an absolute one.
xs: "**Every factual finding** must be reconsidered in **every second appeal**" is NOT a feature — option **(4)** is the answer.
**Second civil appeals** are on **questions of law only**.
The HC is **primarily a court of appeal**, and **death sentences** of Sessions Courts need **HC confirmation**.
xa: Death-sentence confirmation is now under **BNSS 2023**, which replaced CrPC from **1 July 2024**.
**Art. 227** superintendence is also **revisional**.

44.s: The requirement that a death sentence awarded by a Sessions Court must be confirmed by the High Court is presently governed in the criminal procedural framework by the:
44.x: Confirmation of Sessions Court death sentences by the High Court is now governed by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which replaced the CrPC from 1 July 2024. The CPC is civil procedure, the IPC is substantive criminal law, and the Contempt of Courts Act deals with contempt.
44.tq: Use the current statutory replacement rather than the repealed procedural code.
xs: HC confirmation of death sentences is now governed by the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023** — option **(1)** is correct.
**BNSS 2023** replaced the CrPC from **1 July 2024**.
The **Contempt of Courts Act, 1971** deals only with contempt.
xa: HCs are primarily courts of **appeal**; second civil appeals are on **questions of law only**.
The **District Judge** also sits as **Sessions Judge** in criminal matters.

44.s: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 was enacted pursuant to the recommendations of the:
44.x: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 followed the report of the H.N. Sanyal Committee.
44.tq: Associate the statute with the committee that directly preceded it.
xs: The **Contempt of Courts Act, 1971** followed the **H.N. Sanyal Committee** — option **(4)** is correct.
No link to the ARC or **Sarkaria** in the notes.
xa: **Civil contempt** = wilful disobedience; **criminal contempt** = scandalising or obstructing justice.
Exceptions: **fair criticism** + **accurate reporting**.
Contempt powers: **Art. 129** (SC) and **Art. 215** (HC).

44.s:
With reference to the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, consider the following statements:
1. Criminal contempt includes scandalising the court or obstructing the administration of justice.
2. Civil contempt means wilful disobedience of a court's judgment or order.
3. Fair criticism and accurate reporting of court proceedings are themselves forms of criminal contempt.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: civil contempt is wilful disobedience, and criminal contempt covers scandalising or obstructing justice. Statement 3 is wrong: fair criticism and accurate reporting are exceptions (safeguards), not contempt. So '1 and 2 only'.
44.tq: Civil = disobedience; criminal = scandalising/obstructing; exceptions = fair criticism, accurate reporting.
xs: Statements **1 and 2 only** are correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **criminal contempt** = **scandalising or obstructing justice**.
Statement 2 is correct: **civil contempt** = **wilful disobedience**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **fair criticism + accurate reporting** are **exceptions**, not contempt.
xa: The **Contempt of Courts Act, 1971** followed the **H.N. Sanyal Committee**.
Contempt power flows from **Court of Record** status — **Art. 129** (SC) and **Art. 215** (HC).
An HC punishes contempt of itself **and subordinate courts** (**Art. 215**).

44.s:
Consider the following statements regarding appointment of District Judges under Article 233:
1. The Governor appoints District Judges in consultation with the High Court.
2. A person already in the service of the Union or the State is eligible for direct appointment under Article 233 merely on completing seven years as an advocate.
3. The provision requires seven years’ standing as an advocate or pleader for a person appointed from outside the judicial service.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: the Governor appoints District Judges in consultation with the High Court, and a direct recruit needs 7 years as an advocate or pleader. Statement 2 is wrong: Article 233 requires such a person not to be already in the service of the Union or the State, so seven years at the Bar alone does not make a government servant eligible.
44.tq: Use the eligibility exception to detect the overbroad statement.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the **Governor** appoints District Judges **in consultation with the HC** (**Art. 233**).
Statement 2 wrong: a direct recruit must **not be in govt service**.
Statement 3 correct: **7 years** as an **advocate/pleader** is required.
xa: **Art. 233A**: validation of certain appointments (**20th Amendment, 1966**).
**Art. 234**: other judicial officers — Governor's rules after consulting the **SPSC and HC**.
**Art. 235**: **control** over subordinate courts vests in the **HC**.

44.s:
Match List-I (Article) with List-II (Provision):
List-I
a. Article 233
b. Article 234
c. Article 235
d. Article 237
List-II
i. Control over district and subordinate courts vests in the High Court
ii. Appointment of district judges by the Governor in consultation with the High Court
iii. Governor may apply these provisions to magistrates
iv. Recruitment of other judicial officers under Governor's rules made after consulting the State PSC and the High Court
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
44.x: Article 233 covers district judges appointed by the Governor in consultation with the HC (ii); Article 234 covers other judicial officers, with rules made after consulting the SPSC and the HC (iv); Article 235 vests control in the High Court (i); Article 237 lets the Governor extend the provisions to magistrates (iii). Option B swaps 233 and 234; option C swaps 234 and 235; option D swaps 235 and 237.
44.tq: 233 district judges, 234 others, 235 HC control, 236 definitions, 237 magistrates.
xs: Correct match: **a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii** — option **(1)** is correct.
**233** = district judges (**Governor + HC**); **234** = other officers (**SPSC and HC**).
**235** = **HC control**; **237** = extension to **magistrates**.
xa: **Art. 236** defines "district judge" — incl. city civil court and additional/joint/assistant district judges.
⚠ **233** = Governor + HC; **234** = Governor + **SPSC and HC**; **235** = **HC control**.
**Art. 233A**: **20th Amendment, 1966**.

44.s: Which of the following is included within the constitutional meaning of ‘District Judge’ under Article 236?
o: City civil court judges and additional, joint and assistant district judges
All members of the Supreme Court
44.x: Article 236 includes judges of a city civil court and additional, joint and assistant district judges within the expression ‘District Judge’.
44.tq: Test the inclusive constitutional definition rather than the ordinary administrative meaning.
xs: **Art. 236** includes **city civil court judges** and **additional, joint and assistant district judges** — option **(2)** is correct.
Magistrates come in only if the Governor applies the provisions (**Art. 237**); SC judges and the District Magistrate are outside it.
xa: The **District Judge** is the highest civil court and also **Sessions Judge**.
Appeals: **District Court → High Court**.
**Art. 233**: 7 years' standing as advocate/pleader for direct recruits.

44.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the position of a District Judge in the district judicial hierarchy?
o: The District Judge is subordinate to the District Magistrate in judicial matters
The District Judge hears only constitutional writ petitions
The District Judge is the highest civil court of the district and also functions as Sessions Judge in criminal matters
The District Judge is the lowest criminal court of the district
44.x: The District Judge is the highest civil court in the district and also exercises the powers of a Sessions Judge in criminal matters.
44.tq: Combine the civil and criminal roles instead of treating the District Judge as belonging to only one jurisdiction.
xs: The District Judge is **the highest civil court** of the district and also **Sessions Judge** in criminal matters — option **(3)** is correct.
He is not under the District Magistrate, does not hear only writs, and is not the lowest court.
Appeals go **District Court → High Court**.
xa: District Judges are appointed by the **Governor in consultation with the HC** (**Art. 233**).
**National Judicial Academy**: **Bhopal**.
More than **4 crore cases** are pending in lower courts.

44.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The All India Judicial Service is enabled by Article 312, as amended by the 42nd Amendment.
2. The All India Judicial Service has been created and now recruits district judges nationally.
3. The National Judicial Academy is located at Bhopal.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
44.x: Statement 1 is correct: Article 312, as amended by the 42nd Amendment, enables the AIJS. Statement 2 is wrong: the AIJS has not yet been created. Statement 3 is correct: the National Judicial Academy is at Bhopal. So '1 only' misses statement 3, and options C and D include the wrong statement 2.
44.tq: AIJS: enabled (Art. 312, 42nd Amendment) but not created.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the **AIJS** is enabled by **Art. 312** (as amended by the **42nd Amendment**).
Statement 2 wrong: the AIJS is **not yet created**.
Statement 3 correct: the **National Judicial Academy** is at **Bhopal**.
xa: AIJS debate: **uniform merit-based recruitment** vs **state/HC control** + **local language** needs.
Control of subordinate courts lies with the **HC** (**Art. 235**).

44.s: Which of the following correctly describes a Gram Nyayalaya?
o: It is presided over by a Nyayadhikari of JMFC rank and functions as a mobile court at the intermediate Panchayat level
It is presided over by a High Court Judge and hears only constitutional cases
It is a permanent bench of the Supreme Court in every village
It is presided over by the District Magistrate and hears only revenue disputes
44.x: A Gram Nyayalaya is presided over by a Nyayadhikari of Judicial Magistrate First Class rank and functions as a mobile court at the intermediate Panchayat level.
44.tq: Identify the institution through its presiding officer, level and mobile character.
xs: A Gram Nyayalaya is presided by a **Nyayadhikari of JMFC rank** and is a **mobile court at the intermediate Panchayat level** — option **(1)** is correct.
It is not an HC/SC bench and not run by the District Magistrate.
xa: Act: **Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008** (in force **2 Oct 2009**).
First mobile court: **Punhana (Haryana), 2007**.
Funding: **₹50 crore** within the **₹5,357 crore** court-infrastructure outlay.

44.s: The first mobile court in India was established at Punhana in:
44.x: The first mobile court was established at Punhana in Haryana in 2007.
44.tq: Combine the place, State and year instead of selecting a familiar judicial institution.
xs: The first mobile court was at **Punhana**, **Haryana in 2007** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Gujarat 1982** is the first **Lok Adalat** camp; **Delhi 1985** an alternative Lok Adalat date; **Bhopal** hosts the **National Judicial Academy**.
xa: Gram Nyayalayas also function as **mobile courts**.
**Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008**.

44.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Lok Adalats:
1. An award of a Lok Adalat is deemed to be a decree of a civil court.
2. An appeal against a Lok Adalat award lies to the High Court.
3. The first Lok Adalat camp was held in Gujarat in 1982.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: a Lok Adalat award is deemed a civil court decree, and the first camp was held in Gujarat in 1982. Statement 2 is wrong: the award is final and no appeal lies against it. So '1 and 3 only'.
44.tq: Lok Adalat award = civil decree, final, no appeal.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(3) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: the award is **deemed a civil court decree**.
Statement 2 wrong: the award is **final**, with **no appeal**.
Statement 3 correct: first Lok Adalat camp — **Gujarat, 1982**.
xa: Basis: **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**.
Some notes say the first camp was in **Delhi 1985**.
**CGIT-cum-Labour Courts** also hold Lok Adalats.

44.s: More than how many cases are pending in the lower courts?
44.x: More than four crore cases are pending in the lower courts.
44.tq: Retain the approximate magnitude rather than confusing crore-based figures.
xs: More than **4 crore** cases are pending in lower courts — option **(2) Four crore** is correct.
An APPSC **2022** PYQ put total pendency at over **4.7 crore**, about **87%** in subordinate courts.
xa: Reform tools: **e-Courts Phase III (2023-27)** and the **National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG)**.
**Kerala**: first **fully paperless district court**.
The **Department of Justice** portal tracks district vacancies monthly.

44.s: Which of the following correctly describes e-Courts Phase III?
o: It is limited to Gram Nyayalayas and excludes district courts.
It is a scheme for appointing judges to the Supreme Court.
It covers only the period 2014–2019 and replaces all High Courts.
It covers the period 2023–2027 and functions alongside the National Judicial Data Grid as a reform tool.
44.x: e-Courts Phase III covers 2023–2027 and, together with the National Judicial Data Grid, is intended to improve judicial administration and access to case information.
44.tq: Combine the duration of a programme with its institutional purpose.
xs: **e-Courts Phase III** covers **2023-27** and works alongside the **National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG)** as a reform tool — option **(4)** is correct.
It is a **digitisation** tool — not limited to Gram Nyayalayas, not an appointment scheme, and it replaces no court.
xa: **Kerala** has the first **fully paperless district court**.
**Fast-track courts** handle paper-leak cases under the **Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024**.
Court infrastructure is monitored on the **Nyaya Vikas Portal**.

44.s: Which State has the first fully paperless district court?
44.x: Kerala has the first fully paperless district court.
44.tq: Use the distinctive achievement-state association.
xs: **Kerala** has the first **fully paperless district court** — option **(3)** is correct.
It is part of the **digitisation** push with **e-Courts Phase III (2023-27)** and the **NJDG**.
xa: More than **4 crore cases** are pending in lower courts.
The **Department of Justice** web portal tracks district vacancies monthly.
Infrastructure scheme outlay: **₹5,357 crore** for **2021-26**.

44.s:
Consider the following statements about the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for court infrastructure:
1. Funding is normally shared 60:40 between the Centre and the States.
2. North-Eastern and Himalayan States get 90:10 funding.
3. Union Territories get 75 per cent central funding.
4. The scheme is monitored through the Nyaya Vikas Portal.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the normal ratio is 60:40, and 90:10 for NE and Himalayan States. Statement 3 is wrong: UTs get 100 per cent funding. Statement 4 is correct: the scheme is monitored on the Nyaya Vikas Portal. So option A misses statement 4, and options C and D include the wrong statement 3.
44.tq: 60:40 normal, 90:10 NE/Himalayan, 100% UTs; monitored on Nyaya Vikas.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct — option **(2) 1, 2 and 4 only**.
Statement 1 correct: normal sharing is **60:40**.
Statement 2 correct: **NE & Himalayan states** get **90:10**.
Statement 3 wrong: **UTs** get **100%**, not 75 per cent; Statement 4 correct: monitored on the **Nyaya Vikas Portal**.
xa: It is a **Centrally Sponsored Scheme**.
Outlay: **₹5,357 crore** for **2021-26**, incl. **₹50 crore** for **Gram Nyayalayas**.
Digitisation runs through **e-Courts Phase III (2023-27)**.

44.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the constitutional basis of judicial review:
1. The expression ‘judicial review’ is expressly defined in the Constitution.
2. The power flows from several constitutional provisions.
3. It is regarded as part of the basic structure of the Constitution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: The term ‘judicial review’ is not used in the Constitution, but the power flows from several Articles and is part of the basic structure.
44.tq: Distinguish an express constitutional label from a power inferred from several provisions.
xs: Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option **(3) 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 wrong: the term "**judicial review**" is **not used** in the Constitution.
Statement 2 correct: the power **flows from several Articles** (e.g. **13, 32, 226**).
Statement 3 correct: it is **part of the basic structure** (**Kesavananda 1973**; **L. Chandra Kumar 1997**).
xa: Meaning: courts test laws and executive orders against the Constitution and declare them **ultra vires / void**.
Basis: **written constitution** + **federalism** + Fundamental Rights.
Theory: **supremacy of the Constitution / limited government**.

44.s: Judicial review in India is based on which combination of constitutional features?
o: Collective responsibility, adult suffrage and emergency powers
A written Constitution, federalism and Fundamental Rights
An unwritten constitution, unitary government and parliamentary privilege
44.x: Judicial review follows from India’s written Constitution, federal structure and protection of Fundamental Rights.
44.tq: Select the combination of structural features that supports the power under examination.
xs: Judicial review rests on **a written Constitution, federalism and Fundamental Rights** — option **(2)** is correct.
Courts act as **umpire** of the Centre-State division and guardian of a **written, supreme Constitution**.
The other combinations (DPSPs, conventions, unwritten constitution) are not the basis in the notes.
xa: It is a **symbol of federal government** (APPSC key).
**Britain** has no review of Acts of Parliament (**parliamentary sovereignty**).
Origin: **USA** — **Marbury v. Madison (1803)**.

44.s: The Supreme Court’s recognition of judicial review as part of the basic structure is associated particularly with
o: Kesavananda Bharati, 1973, and L. Chandra Kumar, 1997
44.x: The basic-structure status of judicial review is associated with Kesavananda Bharati, 1973, and was reaffirmed in the context of judicial review of tribunals in L. Chandra Kumar, 1997. Golaknath and Sajjan Singh predate the basic-structure doctrine (Minerva Mills, 1980, later reaffirmed it).
44.tq: Match the constitutional doctrine with its landmark cases and years.
xs: Judicial review as **basic structure** is tied to **Kesavananda Bharati, 1973** and **L. Chandra Kumar, 1997** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Hussainara Khatoon (1979)** = first PIL (speedy trial); **Vishaka (1997)** = workplace harassment guidelines.
**S.P. Gupta (1981)** = locus standi; **M.C. Mehta** = environment cases.
xa: **Kesavananda (1973)** also laid down the **Basic Structure** doctrine itself.
**Madras Bar Association (2025)** struck down re-enacted tribunal conditions of the **Tribunals Reforms Act 2021**.
Amendments overcoming judgments remain subject to the **basic structure**.

44.s: The constitutional theory underlying judicial review in India is principally the theory of:
o: Supremacy of the Constitution and limited government
Supremacy of the executive over the legislature
44.x: Judicial review rests on the supremacy of the Constitution and the idea of limited government. India combines elements of American judicial supremacy with British parliamentary supremacy, while Parliament remains subject to the Constitution.
44.tq: Reject absolute formulations and identify the constitutional limitation underlying review.
xs: The theory behind judicial review is **supremacy of the Constitution and limited government** — option **(3)** is correct.
Not unlimited judicial supremacy, absolute parliamentary sovereignty, or executive supremacy.
India's model is a **synthesis** of **American judicial supremacy** + **British parliamentary sovereignty**.
xa: ⚠ Judicial review = symbol of **federal government** (APPSC key); theory = **supremacy of the Constitution**.
Basis: **written constitution** + **federalism** + FRs.
SC (**17 May 2026**): **majoritarianism cannot override constitutionalism**.

44.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Judicial review exists in countries having written constitutions such as Canada and Australia.
2. The United Kingdom permits judicial review of Acts of Parliament in the same manner as the United States.
3. Parliamentary sovereignty is a characteristic of the British constitutional system.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: Judicial review exists in countries such as Canada and Australia. The United Kingdom does not permit courts to invalidate Acts of Parliament in the same manner because of parliamentary sovereignty.
44.tq: Find the reversed comparison between written-constitution systems and British parliamentary sovereignty.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: **Canada** and **Australia**, with written constitutions, have judicial review.
Statement 2 wrong: **Britain** has **no review over Acts of Parliament**.
Statement 3 correct: Britain rests on **parliamentary sovereignty**.
xa: Origin: **USA**, **Marbury v. Madison (1803)**.
India blends **American judicial supremacy** + **British parliamentary sovereignty**.
Roots: **Sir Edward Coke** vs **King James I**.

44.s: Judicial review in India is regarded as a symbol of which of the following?
44.x: Judicial review is a symbol of federal government: courts act as umpire of the Centre-State division under a written, supreme Constitution. Parliamentary, unitary and presidential forms do not by themselves require such an umpire.
44.tq: Judicial review = symbol of federalism; theory = supremacy of the Constitution.
xs: Judicial review is a symbol of **federal government** (APPSC key) — option **(2)** is correct.
Courts act as **umpire of the Centre-State division** under a **written, supreme Constitution**.
Parliamentary, unitary or presidential forms do not by themselves need such an umpire.
xa: Basis: **written constitution** + **federalism** + Fundamental Rights.
Theory: **supremacy of the Constitution / limited government**.
**Art. 131**: SC original jurisdiction in **Centre-State** disputes.

44.s:
Consider the following statements about amendments affecting judicial review:
1. The 38th Amendment made the satisfaction of the President or Governor under Articles 123, 213 and 352 non-justiciable, and the 44th Amendment reversed it.
2. The 42nd Amendment barred High Courts from reviewing Central laws, and the 44th Amendment restored that power.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
44.x: Statement 2 is wrong: the High Courts' power to review Central laws, barred by the 42nd Amendment (1976), was restored by the 43rd Amendment (1977), not the 44th. Statement 1 is correct: the 38th Amendment (1975) made those satisfactions non-justiciable and the 44th (1978) reversed it. So '1 only'.
44.tq: 42nd barred -> 43rd restored; 38th barred -> 44th reversed.
xs: Statement **1 only** is correct — so option **(2)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: the **38th Amendment (1975)** made satisfaction under **Arts. 123, 213, 352** non-justiciable; the **44th Amendment (1978)** reversed it.
Statement 2 is wrong: the **42nd Amendment (1976)** barred HCs from reviewing central laws, but the **43rd (1977)** restored the power — not the 44th.
xa: ⚠ **42nd** barred → **43rd** restored; **38th** barred → **44th** reversed.
The **1st Amendment (1951)** followed early land-reform rulings (e.g. **Kameshwar Singh**).
Still reviewable: decisions on **mala fides** — e.g. President's Rule in **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.

44.s:
Match List-I (Article) with List-II (Basis of judicial review):
List-I
a. Article 131
b. Article 136
c. Article 143
d. Article 227
List-II
i. High Court superintendence over subordinate courts
ii. Advisory jurisdiction on a Presidential reference
iii. Special Leave to appeal
iv. Supreme Court original jurisdiction in Centre-State disputes
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
44.x: Article 131 is the SC's original jurisdiction in Centre-State disputes (iv); Article 136 is Special Leave (iii); Article 143 is advisory jurisdiction on Presidential reference (ii); Article 227 is HC superintendence over subordinate courts (i). Option B swaps 131 and 136; option C swaps 136 and 143; option D gets only 136 right and mismatches 131, 143 and 227.
44.tq: 131 original, 136 special leave, 143 advisory, 227 superintendence.
xs: Correct match: **a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i** — option **(1)** is correct.
**131** = SC original jurisdiction in **Centre-State disputes**; **136** = **Special Leave**.
**143** = **advisory** on Presidential reference; **227** = **HC superintendence** over subordinate courts.
xa: **Art. 137** = SC **reviews its own judgments**.
**Art. 139A** (**44th Amendment 1978**) = SC may **transfer cases to itself**.
**Art. 141** = SC law binding on all courts.

44.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 245 makes legislative power subject to the Constitution.
2. Article 246(3) gives the States exclusive power over matters in the State List, subject to the Constitution.
3. Articles 251 and 254 deal with repugnancy between certain laws.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: All three statements are correct. Articles 245 and 246 govern legislative competence, while Articles 251 and 254 address inconsistency or repugnancy between laws.
44.tq: Test several related Articles as a constitutional-competence cluster.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **Art. 245** makes legislative power **subject to the Constitution**.
Statement 2: **Art. 246(3)** gives States exclusive power over the **State List**.
Statement 3: **Arts. 251, 254** deal with **repugnancy** — state law void to the extent of inconsistency.
xa: **Lack of legislative competence** is one of the **three grounds** of review.
**Art. 13**: laws inconsistent with FRs are **void**.
**Art. 372(1)**: review of **pre-Constitution laws**.

44.s: Article 372(1) is relevant to judicial review because it concerns
o: the appointment of High Court judges
the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
44.x: Article 372(1) provides the constitutional basis for continuing pre-Constitution laws subject to their consistency with the Constitution and judicial review.
44.tq: Identify the historical category of laws linked to the Article.
xs: **Art. 372(1)** concerns **the review of pre-Constitution laws** — option **(1)** is correct.
HC appointments = **Art. 217**; advisory = **Art. 143**.
xa: **Art. 13** also voids pre-Constitution laws inconsistent with FRs.
**Arts. 251, 254**: **repugnancy**.
APPSC **2023** matched **137**-review, **226**-HC writs, **13**-void laws, **32**-SC writs.

44.s: Which one of the following is NOT a recognised ground of judicial review in India?
o: Contravention of constitutional provisions or the basic structure
Disagreement with the policy preference of the majority party
44.x: The recognised grounds include violation of Fundamental Rights, lack of legislative competence and contravention of constitutional provisions or the basic structure. Mere disagreement with political policy is not by itself a ground.
44.tq: Exclude a political preference that is not a constitutional ground of review.
xs: **Disagreement with the majority party's policy** is NOT a ground of review — option **(2)** is the answer.
The three grounds: **violation of FRs**, **lack of legislative competence**, **contravention of constitutional provisions / Basic Structure**.
xa: Courts **avoid policy/political questions**.
**State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977)**: SC declined a political question → **restraint**.
Writs are **discretionary** — refused where an effective alternative remedy exists.

44.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Article)
A. Article 13
B. Article 32
C. Article 137
D. Article 226

List-II (Subject)
1. Review of its own judgments by the Supreme Court
2. High Court writ jurisdiction
3. Laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights to be void
4. Supreme Court writ jurisdiction for restoration of Fundamental Rights

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
44.x: Article 13 concerns laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights; Article 32 provides Supreme Court writs; Article 137 permits Supreme Court review; and Article 226 concerns High Court writs for Fundamental Rights and other purposes.
44.tq: Start from the sure Article–subject pairs and test the remaining combinations.
xs: Correct match: **A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2** — option **(1)** is correct.
**13** = laws inconsistent with FRs **void**; **32** = **SC writs** for FRs.
**137** = SC **reviews its own judgments**; **226** = **HC writs**.
xa: This matches the **APPSC-G2 2023** PYQ.
⚠ **137** = review; **136** = Special Leave; **13** = void laws.
**Art. 226** covers FRs "**and any other purpose**".

44.s: Article 139A, inserted by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978, deals with the power of the Supreme Court to:
o: issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights
44.x: Article 139A empowers the Supreme Court to transfer certain cases to itself. It was inserted by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.
44.tq: Link the Article number with the distinctive procedural power it confers.
xs: **Art. 139A** (**44th Amendment 1978**) lets the SC **transfer cases to itself** — option **(4)** is correct.
Writs = **Art. 32**; HC appointments = **Art. 217**.
xa: The **44th Amendment** also reversed the **38th Amendment**'s non-justiciability bar.
**Art. 137**: review of its own judgments.
**Art. 141**: SC law binding on all courts.

44.s: The decisions taken by the President or Governor may be subjected to judicial review when they are challenged on grounds such as:
o: The personal popularity of the office-holder
Mala fides or reliance on irrelevant grounds
The absence of legislative approval for every executive act
44.x: Although constitutional protection applies to the office-holder in the manner specified by Article 361, the decisions themselves may be reviewed on grounds such as mala fides or irrelevant considerations. The review of President’s Rule in S.R. Bommai illustrates this principle.
44.tq: Distinguish reviewable grounds of invalidity from mere political disagreement.
xs: Decisions can be reviewed for **mala fides or reliance on irrelevant grounds** — option **(3)** is correct.
Example: President's Rule reviewed in **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.
Popularity or mere policy disagreement are not grounds.
xa: **Art. 361**: the **President/Governor** personally are **not answerable** to courts.
**Art. 74(2)** / **163(3)**: ministerial advice **cannot be inquired into**.
**44th Amendment (1978)** reversed the **38th**'s non-justiciability bar.

44.s:
With reference to judicial review in India and the United States, consider the following statements:
1. Article 21 of the Indian Constitution uses the expression ‘procedure established by law’.
2. The United States Constitution is associated with the expression ‘due process of law’.
3. The Indian scope of judicial review is generally narrower than the United States scope in this respect.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: All three statements are correct. Indian review under ‘procedure established by law’ traditionally focuses on legal validity and procedure, while American due process includes procedural and substantive fairness.
44.tq: Compare the exact constitutional phrases before judging the broader legal consequence.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: **Art. 21** uses "**procedure established by law**" (validity + procedure).
Statement 2: the US uses "**due process of law**" (procedural + substantive fairness).
Statement 3: Indian review is therefore **narrower than the USA**.
xa: The US Supreme Court is called a "**third chamber**".
Courts in India **avoid political questions**.
Writs are **discretionary**.

44.s: The description of the United States Supreme Court as a ‘third chamber’ primarily indicates its extensive role in
o: Reviewing and shaping governmental policy through constitutional adjudication
44.x: The expression reflects the extensive policy impact of the United States Supreme Court’s constitutional review and interpretation.
44.tq: Interpret the institutional metaphor rather than treating it as a literal constitutional body.
xs: "**Third chamber**" points to the US Court **reviewing and shaping governmental policy** through constitutional adjudication — option **(2)** is correct.
It flows from US "**due process of law**" review (procedural + **substantive** fairness).
The US Court does not run elections, appoint governors or prepare budgets.
xa: Indian review under "**procedure established by law**" is **narrower**.
Judicial activism also **began and developed in the USA** (APPSC-G2 **2025**).

44.s:
Consider the following statements about the limits of judicial review in India:
1. Courts generally avoid deciding purely political or policy questions.
2. Delimitation decisions are wholly beyond judicial review, even if capricious.
3. Writs, being discretionary, may be refused where an effective alternative remedy exists.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
44.x: Statement 1 is correct: courts avoid policy and political questions. Statement 2 is wrong: delimitation review is limited but possible if the decision is capricious (Kishorchandra Chhanganlal Rathod, 2024). Statement 3 is correct: writs are discretionary and may be refused where an effective alternative remedy exists. So '1 only' misses statement 3, and options C and D include statement 2.
44.tq: 'Limited but possible' beats 'wholly beyond review'.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 correct: courts **avoid policy/political questions**.
Statement 2 wrong: delimitation review is **limited but possible if capricious** (**Kishorchandra Chhanganlal Rathod, 2024**).
Statement 3 correct: writs are **discretionary**, refused where an **effective alternative remedy** exists.
xa: **State of Rajasthan (1977)**: SC declined a political question.
Review is **narrower than the USA** under **Art. 21**.
**Aravali Golf Club (2007)**: judges told not to encroach on other branches.

44.s:
Match the following Articles with their effect on judicial review:
a. Article 74(2)
b. Article 163(3)
c. Article 361
i. President and Governor not answerable to any court for exercise of their powers
ii. Advice of Ministers to the Governor cannot be inquired into by any court
iii. Advice of Ministers to the President cannot be inquired into by any court
44.x: Article 74(2) bars courts from inquiring into ministerial advice to the President (iii); Article 163(3) is the same bar for advice to the Governor (ii); Article 361 makes the President and Governor not answerable to courts, so no mandamus lies against them (i). The other codes swap these pairs.
44.tq: 74(2) President's advice, 163(3) Governor's advice, 361 personal immunity.
xs: Correct match: **a-iii, b-ii, c-i** — option **(1)** is correct.
**74(2)**: ministers' advice to the **President** cannot be inquired into.
**163(3)**: same bar for advice to the **Governor**; **361**: President/Governor **not answerable** to courts.
xa: **No mandamus** lies against the President/Governor (TH, **29 Jan 2026**).
Their decisions may still be reviewed for **mala fides** — **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.

44.s: When a legislature responds to a judicial judgment, which of the following is constitutionally permissible?
o: Overruling the Constitution through an ordinary statute
Removing the basis of the judgment through an amendment to law, including retrospectively where valid, or amending the Constitution subject to the basic structure
Directing the judiciary to reconsider every concluded case through an executive order
Simply declaring the judgment void without changing the legal basis
44.x: The legislature cannot simply overrule a judgment. It may remove the legal basis through a valid amendment, including a retrospective validating Act where appropriate, or amend the Constitution subject to the basic structure doctrine.
44.tq: Distinguish changing the legal basis of a judgment from directly nullifying judicial power.
xs: The legislature may **remove the basis of the judgment** by amending the law (retrospectively if valid) or **amend the Constitution subject to the basic structure** — option **(2)** is correct.
It **cannot simply overrule** a judgment or declare it void; an executive order cannot reopen cases.
An ordinary statute cannot override the Constitution.
xa: The judicial route: **review petition** under **Art. 137**; **curative petition** as last resort.
Example: **Tribunals Reforms Act 2021** re-enacted struck-down conditions → struck down again in **Madras Bar Association (2025)**.

44.s: The First Amendment to the Constitution in 1951 was associated with the legislative response to early rulings concerning:
o: Emergency powers and preventive detention only
44.x: The First Amendment, enacted in 1951, followed early judicial rulings relating to land reform and reservation.
44.tq: Link a constitutional amendment with the subjects that prompted it.
xs: The **1st Amendment (1951)** followed early rulings on **land reform and reservation** — option **(4)** is correct.
Example: **Kameshwar Singh** on land reform.
