(a) Article 137
(b) Article 142
(c) Article 226
(d) Article 13(2)

List-II
(i) Laws abridging Fundamental Rights are void pro tanto
(ii) High Court writ jurisdiction for Fundamental Rights and any other legal right
(iii) Supreme Court's power to review its own judgments or orders
(iv) Power of the Supreme Court to pass decrees or orders for Complete Justice
44.x: Article 137 is the Court's review of its own judgments, 142 complete justice, 226 High Court writs, and 13(2) the rule that laws abridging fundamental rights are void. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
44.tq: Recall Articles 13(2), 137, 142 and 226.
n: Article 13(2) provides that laws abridging Fundamental Rights are void pro tanto. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Article 226 provides the High Courts' writ jurisdiction for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Article 226 also covers the enforcement of any other legal right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Article 137 gives the Supreme Court the power to review its own judgments or orders. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Article 137 provides for review of the Supreme Court's own judgment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to pass decrees or orders for Complete Justice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is not vested in the Supreme Court alone. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Article 137** = SC **reviews its own judgments**; **Article 142** = **Complete Justice** decrees.
**Article 226** = HC writs for FRs **and any other legal right**; **Article 13(2)** = laws abridging FRs **void pro tanto**.
xa: APPSC **2023** matched **137**-review, **226**-HC writs, **13**-void laws, **32**-SC writs.
**Article 141**: SC law **binding on all courts**.
**Article 372(1)**: review of **pre-Constitution laws**.

44.s: The Judicial Review Doctrine originated in which case and was associated with which authority?
o: Marbury v. Madison — Kameshwar Singh — India
Prafulla Kumar v. Bank of Commerce — Chief Justice John Marshall — USA
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala — Chief Justice John Marshall — USA
Marbury v. Madison — Chief Justice John Marshall — USA
44.x: Judicial review began in Marbury v. Madison (1803), decided by Chief Justice John Marshall of the USA. The other options mix in Indian cases.
44.tq: Recall the case, judge and country.
n: The Judicial Review Doctrine originated in Marbury v. Madison (1803). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
Chief Justice John Marshall of the USA was associated with Marbury v. Madison. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
xs: Judicial review originated in **Marbury v. Madison — Chief Justice John Marshall — USA** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It was first propounded in the **USA** in **Marbury v. Madison (1803)**.
**Kesavananda Bharati** is the Indian **Basic Structure** case (**1973**); **Kameshwar Singh** is a land-reform case.
xa: Roots: **Sir Edward Coke's** resistance to **King James I** (17th century England).
India's model is a **synthesis** of **American judicial supremacy** + **British parliamentary sovereignty**.
⚠ **UK**: **parliamentary sovereignty** — primary statutes **cannot be struck down**.

44.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The parliamentary form of government was first introduced in Great Britain.
Statement B: The presidential form was first formed in the USA.

Which of the following is correct?
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
44.x: Both are true: the parliamentary form of government began in Great Britain and the presidential form in the USA.
44.tq: Match each form of government to its country of origin.
n: The parliamentary form of government was first introduced in Great Britain. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-6]
The presidential form of government was first formed in the USA. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-6]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **parliamentary form of government** was first introduced in **Great Britain**.
The **presidential form** was first formed in the **USA**.
xa: **Judicial Review** was first propounded in the **USA** — **Marbury v. Madison (1803)**.
**Judicial activism** also began and developed in the **USA**.
The **First Schedule** lists the **States and Union Territories**.

44.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The Basic Structure doctrine was first propounded in Kesavananda Bharati in 1973.
II. Fundamental Rights were first held amendable in the Shankari Prasad case.
III. The first PIL considered was Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar.
IV. The Federal Court was inaugurated in 1950.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
44.x: I, II and III are correct (Kesavananda Bharati 1973; Shankari Prasad; Hussainara Khatoon as first PIL). IV is wrong: the Federal Court was inaugurated on 1 October 1937 under the 1935 Act; 1950 is when the Supreme Court replaced it.
44.tq: Find the date that belongs to a different institution.
n: The Federal Court was inaugurated on 1 October 1937. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-6]
The Basic Structure doctrine was first propounded in Kesavananda Bharati in 1973. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-6]
The Supreme Court first held that Fundamental Rights were amendable in the Shankari Prasad case. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-6]
The first Public Interest Litigation considered was Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar in 1979. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-6]
xs: Statements **I, II and III only** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
I: the **Basic Structure doctrine** was first propounded in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**.
II: **Fundamental Rights** were first held amendable in the **Shankari Prasad** case.
III: the first PIL was **Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979)**; IV is wrong — the **Federal Court** was not inaugurated in **1950**.
xa: Hussainara Khatoon established undertrials' right to **speedy trial**; filed by **Kapila Hingorani** ("**Mother of PILs**").
Judicial review is **part of the basic structure** (**L. Chandra Kumar 1997**).
The term "judicial activism" was coined in **1947** by **Arthur Schlesinger Jr.**

44.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: A High Court Judge takes the oath before the Governor of the State.
Statement B: A High Court Judge addresses a written resignation to the Governor of the State.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
44.x: A is true: under Article 219, a High Court judge takes the oath before the Governor. B is false because they resign to the President, who appoints them.
44.tq: Discriminate who swears a judge in from whom they resign to.
n: The Governor of the State administers the oath to High Court Judges under Article 219. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The oath of a High Court Judge is administered by the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
High Court Judges address their written resignations to the President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The resignation of a High Court Judge is addressed to the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
A High Court Judge addresses a resignation to the President of India under Article 217(1)(a). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xs: **Statement A is true, Statement B is false** — so option **(3)** is correct.
A: an HC judge takes the **oath** before the **Governor** (**Article 219**).
B: the **resignation** is addressed to the **President** (**Article 217(1)(a)**), not the Governor.
xa: SC judges take the oath before the **President** (**Article 124(6)**).
Both SC and HC judges are appointed by the **President** by **warrant**.
HC judges are removed by the **President's** order after Parliament's **address**.

44.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Transfer of a High Court Judge
(b) Oath of a High Court Judge
(c) Court of record: Supreme Court
(d) Court of record: High Court

List-II
(i) Article 219
(ii) Article 129
(iii) Article 222
(iv) Article 215
44.x: Transfer is under Article 222, the High Court oath under 219, the Supreme Court as Court of Record under 129, and the High Court under 215. The answer is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.
44.tq: Recall Articles 129, 215, 219 and 222.
n: Article 222 provides for the transfer of High Court Judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The Governor of the State administers the oath to High Court Judges under Article 219. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The oath of a High Court Judge is administered by the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The Supreme Court is a court of record under Article 129. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The High Court is a court of record under Article 215. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Transfer** of an HC judge — **Article 222**; HC **oath** — **Article 219**.
**Court of Record**: SC — **Article 129**; HC — **Article 215**.
xa: Transfer is by the **President** on the advice of the **collegium** led by the **CJI**.
Transfer is **not** applicable to SC judges.
HC salary is charged on the **Consolidated Fund of the State** (**Article 202(3)**).

44.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. A retired Supreme Court Judge cannot plead in any court or before any authority in India.
II. A retired High Court Judge may plead in the Supreme Court.
III. A retired High Court Judge may plead in other High Courts where the Judge was not a permanent Judge.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: All three are correct: a retired Supreme Court judge cannot plead anywhere in India. A retired High Court judge may plead in the Supreme Court and other High Courts, but not in their own.
44.tq: Discriminate the bars on retired Supreme Court and High Court judges.
n: A retired Supreme Court Judge cannot plead before any court or authority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
A retired Supreme Court Judge cannot practice in any court or authority in India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
A retired High Court Judge may plead only in the Supreme Court and other High Courts under Article 220. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
A retired High Court Judge can practice in the Supreme Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
A retired High Court Judge can practice in other High Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
A retired High Court Judge can practice in a High Court where the Judge was not a permanent judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xs: **I, II and III** are all correct — so option **(4)** is correct.
I: a retired SC judge is **completely barred** — no court or authority in India (**Article 124(7)**).
II and III: a retired HC judge may plead in the **Supreme Court** and **other High Courts** where he was not a permanent judge (**Article 220**).
xa: HC pension is charged on the **Consolidated Fund of India** (**Article 112(3)(d)(iii)**).
A **distinguished jurist** is eligible only for the SC (**Article 124(3)(c)**).
HC retirement age **62**, raised from **60** by the **15th Amendment Act, 1963**.

44.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Acting Judges are appointed when a permanent Judge is temporarily absent or is acting as Chief Justice.
Statement B: An Acting Judge may continue in office beyond the age of 62 years.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
44.x: A is true: acting judges are appointed when a permanent judge is absent or acting as Chief Justice. B is false because an acting judge's appointment ends at 62.
44.tq: Remember that the age limit of 62 applies to acting judges too.
n: An Acting Judge is appointed when a permanent Judge is temporarily absent. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
An Acting Judge is appointed when a permanent Judge is acting as Chief Justice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
An Acting Judge’s appointment ceases at 62 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xs: **Statement A is true, Statement B is false** — so option **(3)** is correct.
A: **Acting Judges** (**Article 224(2)**) are appointed when a permanent judge is **temporarily absent** or **acting as Chief Justice**.
B: an acting judge's appointment **ceases at 62**.
xa: **Additional Judges** (**224(1)**): for a **temporary increase** in business or **arrears**, up to **two years**.
**Acting Chief Justice** is under **Article 223**.
**Retired judges** may sit under **224A**.

44.s: Who may request a retired High Court or Supreme Court Judge to sit and act as a High Court Judge, subject to the President’s prior consent?
o: The Chief Justice of the concerned High Court
44.x: Under Article 224A, a High Court's Chief Justice may ask a retired High Court or Supreme Court judge to sit, with the President's prior consent.
44.tq: Recall who makes the request under Article 224A.
n: The Chief Justice of a High Court may request a retired High Court Judge to sit and act as a High Court Judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The Chief Justice of a High Court may request a retired Supreme Court Judge to sit and act as a High Court Judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The Chief Justice of a High Court requires the President’s prior consent for such a request. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xs: **The Chief Justice of the concerned High Court** may make the request — so option **(2)** is correct.
Under **Article 224A**, the HC **Chief Justice** may ask a **retired HC or SC judge** to sit and act as an HC judge, with the **President's prior consent**.
The judge's own consent is also needed.
xa: **224A** was inserted by the **15th Amendment, 1963**.
Additional judges (**224(1)**) serve up to **two years**, not beyond **62**.
⚠ **223** = Acting CJ; **224(1)** = Additional; **224(2)** = Acting; **224A** = Retired.

44.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The salary and allowances of a High Court Judge are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State.
II. The pension of a High Court Judge is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
III. The pension of a High Court Judge is charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: I and II are correct: a High Court judge's salary is charged on the State's fund, but the pension on the Consolidated Fund of India. III is false.
44.tq: Discriminate High Court judges' salary (State) from their pension (Union).
n: The salary and allowances of High Court Judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
Article 202(3) concerns the charging of High Court Judges’ salaries and allowances on the Consolidated Fund of the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The pensions of High Court Judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
Article 112(3)(d)(iii) concerns the charging of High Court Judges’ pensions on the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The pension of a High Court Judge is not charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xs: Statements **I and II only** are correct — so option **(4)** is correct.
I: an HC judge's **salary** is charged on the **Consolidated Fund of the State** (**Article 202(3)**).
II: the **pension** is charged on the **Consolidated Fund of India** (**Article 112(3)(d)(iii)**).
III is wrong: the pension is **not** charged on the State fund.
xa: SC salary and pension: both on the **Consolidated Fund of India**.
**Article 221**: HC **salaries, allowances and pensions**.
HC judges retire at **62**.

44.s:
Assertion (A): The retirement age of a High Court Judge is 62 years.
Reason (R): The retirement age of a High Court Judge was raised from 60 to 62 years by the 15th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
44.x: Both are true: the 15th Amendment (1963) raised the High Court retirement age from 60 to 62, which is why it is 62 now. R explains A.
44.tq: Recall the 15th Amendment's change.
n: The retirement age of a High Court Judge is 62 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The retirement age of High Court Judges was raised from 60 to 62 years by the 15th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
HC judges retire at **62**.
The age was **raised from 60** by the **15th Amendment Act, 1963** — which explains A.
xa: SC judges retire at **65**.
The 15th Amendment also inserted **224A** (retired HC judges).
Additional and acting judges also cannot serve beyond **62**.

44.s: Which of the following is a qualification specifically available for appointment as a Supreme Court Judge but not provided for appointment as a High Court Judge?
o: Taking an oath before a constitutional authority
Holding office until the prescribed retirement age
44.x: Under Article 124(3)(c), a distinguished jurist can be made a Supreme Court judge. No such route exists for High Courts.
44.tq: Recall the extra route to the Supreme Court.
n: A distinguished jurist is eligible for appointment as a Supreme Court Judge under Article 124(3)(c). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
A distinguished jurist is not eligible for appointment as a High Court Judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The Constitution has no provision for appointing a distinguished jurist as a High Court Judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The President of India is the appointing authority for Supreme Court Judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The President of India is the appointing authority for High Court Judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xs: **Being a distinguished jurist** is available only for the SC — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Article 124(3)(c)** makes a distinguished jurist eligible for the SC; there is **no such provision** for HCs.
Oath, retirement age and **appointment by the President** apply to both courts.
xa: HC qualification: **10 years** in **judicial office** or **10 years** as an **HC advocate**.
HC oath before the **Governor**; SC oath before the **President**.
Transfer (**Article 222**) applies only to HC judges.

44.s:
Consider the following statements about Additional Judges of a High Court:
I. They may be appointed because of a temporary increase in court business.
II. They may be appointed because of arrears of work.
III. Their appointment may continue beyond two years.
IV. They cannot serve beyond 62 years of age.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
44.x: I, II and IV are correct: additional judges are appointed for a temporary rise in work or arrears, and cannot serve past 62. III is false because their term is at most two years.
44.tq: Recall the two-year limit for additional judges.
n: Additional Judges are appointed when there is a temporary increase in court business. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
Additional Judges are appointed when there are arrears of work. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
Additional Judges may serve for a period not exceeding two years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
Additional Judges cannot serve beyond 62 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xs: Statements **I, II and IV only** are correct — so option **(4)** is correct.
I and II: **Additional Judges** (**Article 224(1)**) are appointed for a **temporary increase** in business or **arrears** of work.
III is wrong: their term is **not exceeding two years**; IV is correct: not beyond **62** years of age.
xa: Additional judges are usually made permanent in about **two years**.
Appointed by the **President**.
⚠ There are **no** additional judges in the SC.

44.s: Which of the following statements regarding the transfer of Judges is incorrect?
o: The transfer provision applies to both Supreme Court and High Court Judges.
A High Court Judge may be transferred under Article 222.
The transfer provision is not applicable to Supreme Court Judges.
A High Court Judge may be transferred by the President on the advice of a CJI-led Collegium.
44.x: Option A is incorrect: transfer under Article 222 applies only to High Court judges. There is no provision for transferring Supreme Court judges.
44.tq: Recall that only High Court judges can be transferred.
n: The transfer provision is not applicable to Supreme Court Judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **the transfer provision applies to both Supreme Court and High Court Judges** — so option **(1)** is the answer.
Transfer under **Article 222** applies **only** to HC judges; it is **not applicable** to SC judges.
HC judges are transferred by the **President** on the advice of the **collegium** led by the **CJI** — so (2), (3), (4) are correct.
xa: The CJI consults the collegium and the **CJs of both High Courts**.
HC transfers are handled by **CJI + four** senior-most SC judges.
Chief Justices: **Art. 217(1)** (appointment) + **Art. 222** (transfer).

44.s: What is the method of removal of a High Court Judge?
o: Removal by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha alone
Removal by the Governor at pleasure
An order of the President following an address by Parliament
44.x: Like a Supreme Court judge, a High Court judge is removed by the President's order after an address by Parliament (Article 217(1)). The Governor cannot remove judges.
44.tq: Recall that both courts' judges are removed the same way.
n: A High Court Judge is removed by an order of the President following an address by Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The removal of a High Court Judge is governed by Article 217(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
xs: An HC judge is removed by **an order of the President following an address by Parliament** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **address** must pass **each House** by **special majority** — at least **50%** of the **total strength** and **two-thirds** present and voting.
Grounds: **proved misbehaviour** or **incapacity**; the **Governor** has no removal power, and **Article 61** impeachment is for the **President**.
xa: Removal under **Article 217(1)(b)** read with **Article 124(4)** and **Art. 218**.
Procedure: **Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968**.
Justice **Soumitra Sen** (Calcutta HC) resigned in **2011** after the Rajya Sabha voted for removal.

44.s: Who administers the oath of office to a Supreme Court Judge?
o: The Chief Justice of India or the senior-most Supreme Court Judge
The President of India or a person appointed by the President
44.x: A Supreme Court judge is sworn in by the President or someone the President appoints (Article 124(6)).
44.tq: Recall Article 124(6).
n: The oath of a Supreme Court Judge is administered by the President of India or a person appointed by the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
xs: The oath to an SC judge is administered by **the President of India or a person appointed by the President** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This is under **Article 124(6)**.
The **Governor** administers the oath to **HC judges** (**Article 219**), not SC judges.
xa: SC judges' **resignation** is addressed to the **President** (**Article 124(2)(a)**).
SC judges retire at **65**.
SC judges are removed by the **President's** order after Parliament's address (**Article 124(4)**).

45.s:
Which of the following is NOT generally regarded as a merit of administrative tribunals?
1. Expertise and specialisation
2. Speedier adjudication
3. Lower cost
4. Compulsory application of the full Civil Procedure Code
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
45.x: Expertise, specialisation, speed and lower cost are recognised merits. Tribunals follow principles of natural justice instead of being bound by the full application of the Civil Procedure Code.
45.tq: Find the exception by separating tribunal advantages from the procedural feature that does not apply.
xs: Statements 1, 2, 3 are merits: **expertise and specialisation**, **speed**, **low cost**.
Statement 4 is not a merit: tribunals follow **natural justice instead of CPC** — so **4 only**, option **(4)**.
xa: CAT procedure: **not bound by the CPC**, nominal filing fee, parties can appear **in person**.
Chairpersons get **HC judge** status.
Nature: **quasi-judicial** — between an executive body and a court.

45.s: Which criticism of the tribunal system relates most directly to institutional independence?
o: The same ministries whose decisions are reviewed may administer the tribunals.
Tribunals are constitutionally prohibited from reviewing administrative action.
Tribunals cannot provide any form of adjudication.
45.x: A major criticism is that parent ministries, which may be litigants before tribunals, also administer them, creating concerns about executive control and independence.
45.tq: Match the criticism with the institutional conflict it describes.
xs: Tribunals are administered by the **same ministries whose decisions they review** — the independence criticism — option **(1)**.
Parent ministries that are **litigants** also administer the tribunals.
xa: Executive control via the **Finance Act 2017** + the **2021 Ordinance**.
**CDI** proposes the **Law Ministry** administer tribunals.
**R. Gandhi (2010)**: members performing judicial functions must be **independent of the executive**.

45.s: Chairpersons of tribunals are generally given the status of a:
o: Secretary to the Government of India
45.x: Tribunal chairpersons get High Court judge status. They are not equated with Supreme Court judges, district judges or Secretaries to the Government of India.
45.tq: Tribunal chair = HC judge status
xs: Tribunal Chairpersons get **High Court judge** status — option **(1)**.
It is listed among the **merits** of tribunals, with expertise, speed and low cost.
xa: CAT **Judicial members** must be qualified as **HC judges**.
CAT **Administrative members**: **Additional Secretary** level or above.
NTC (Bill 2026) Chairperson: **former SC judge** or **former HC Chief Justice**.

45.s: Which one of the following subjects is associated with Article 323B but NOT with Article 323A?
o: Service conditions in public sector undertakings
Conditions of service of State employees
45.x: Land reforms are among the subjects listed under Article 323B. Article 323A deals with recruitment and service conditions of public servants.
45.tq: Discriminate between the service-matter jurisdiction of Article 323A and the broader subject list of Article 323B.
xs: **Land reforms** is an **Art. 323B** subject — option **(2)**.
**Art. 323A** covers only **recruitment and service conditions** of public servants (Centre, states, local bodies, **PSUs**).
xa: Other 323B subjects: taxation, foreign exchange, industrial and labour disputes, urban land ceiling, **elections**, foodstuffs, **rent and tenancy**.
⚠ **323A** = **Parliament only**, no hierarchy; **323B** = **Parliament and state legislatures**, hierarchy allowed.
Both in **Part XIV-A**, inserted by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**.

45.s:
Consider the following statements about Articles 323A and 323B:
1. Both were inserted in Part XIV-A by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
2. Their insertion followed the recommendations of the Sarkaria Committee.
3. The 75th Amendment, 1993 added the rent and tenancy clause.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
45.x: Statement 1 is correct: both Articles form Part XIV-A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976. Statement 2 is wrong: the insertion followed the Swaran Singh Committee, not Sarkaria. Statement 3 is correct: the 75th Amendment, 1993 added the rent and tenancy clause (h). So '1 only' misses statement 3, and options C and D include statement 2.
45.tq: Tribunals: 42nd Amendment plus Swaran Singh Committee; 75th Amendment added rent and tenancy.
xs: Statement 1 correct: both in **Part XIV-A**, inserted by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**.
Statement 2 wrong: they followed the **Swaran Singh Committee**, not Sarkaria.
Statement 3 correct: **75th Amendment, 1993** added **rent/tenancy** clause (h) — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: **323A** = service matters; **323B** = taxation, foreign exchange, land reforms, elections and more.
**CAT (1985)** was the **first** tribunal under Art. 323A.
**32nd Amendment (1973)** gave the AP Administrative Tribunal authority under **Art. 371D**.

45.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Articles 323A and 323B:
1. Article 323A deals with recruitment and service conditions of public servants.
2. Article 323A permits Parliament and State Legislatures to legislate equally.
3. Article 323B covers subjects such as taxation, foreign exchange and industrial disputes.
4. Article 323B permits a hierarchy of tribunals.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
45.x: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct. Under Article 323A, Parliament alone can legislate; therefore, statement 2 is false.
45.tq: Separate the legislative competence and hierarchy rules before selecting the code.
xs: Statement 1 correct: **323A** = **recruitment and service conditions** of public servants.
Statement 2 wrong: under 323A **Parliament only** may legislate.
Statements 3, 4 correct: 323B covers **taxation, foreign exchange, industrial disputes** and allows a **hierarchy** — so **1, 3 and 4 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: 323B tribunals may be set up by **Parliament and state legislatures** within their competence.
**75th Amendment, 1993** added rent and tenancy to 323B.
**L. Chandra Kumar (1997)** struck down exclusion clauses **323A(2)(d)** and **323B(3)(d)**.

45.s:
Which of the following is a feature of tribunals under Article 323A?
1. One tribunal for the Centre and one for each State or group of States
2. No hierarchy of tribunals
3. Legislation by Parliament only
4. Jurisdiction over elections and foodstuffs
Which of the statements given above are correct?
45.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 describe Article 323A. Elections and foodstuffs are subjects associated with Article 323B, so statement 4 is false.
45.tq: Separate the subject list of Article 323B from the institutional features of Article 323A.
xs: Statements 1, 2, 3 are 323A features: **one tribunal for the Centre and one per state** (or group), **no hierarchy**, **Parliament only**.
Statement 4 wrong: **elections** and **foodstuffs** belong to **Art. 323B** — so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: 323B allows a **hierarchy** (original + appellate).
**SATs** are set up by the **Central Government** at the **request of the state**; **joint** tribunals for two or more states.
CAT was the **first** tribunal under Art. 323A (**1985**).

45.s: The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) derives its legal basis from which of the following provisions?
o: Article 262 and the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985
Article 315 and the Central Civil Services Act, 1985
Article 323A and the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985
Article 323B and the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021
45.x: CAT is empowered by Article 323A and was established under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985. It is a statutory and quasi-judicial body.
45.tq: Link the constitutional enabling provision with the parent statute instead of confusing Articles 323A and 323B.
xs: CAT is empowered by **Art. 323A** and set up under the **Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985** — option **(3)**.
**Art. 323B** covers other subjects; **Art. 262** is about **water tribunals**.
xa: CAT is a **statutory**, quasi-judicial body set up by the **Central Government**.
Set up in **1985** under PM **Rajiv Gandhi**.
Main bench at **New Delhi** + **18** outlying benches; disposal rate **92.9%**.

45.s: The Central Administrative Tribunal was set up in 1985 during the Prime Ministership of:
45.x: The CAT was set up in 1985 under Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi. It was not established during Lal Bahadur Shastri's tenure.
45.tq: Use the year–office-holder association and guard against a swapped Prime Minister trap.
xs: CAT was set up in **1985** under PM **Rajiv Gandhi** — option **(4)**.
⚠ Trap: **not Lal Bahadur Shastri** (UPSC 2009).
xa: Members from **both judicial and administrative** streams (APPSC-G1 2022).
**10th All India Conference** of CAT held in New Delhi (Sep 2025).
CAT strength: **69 Members** — **35 Judicial** + **34 Administrative**.

45.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the eligibility of members of the Central Administrative Tribunal?
o: Judicial Members must be district judges, while Administrative Members must have served at the level of Joint Secretary only.
Judicial Members must be serving Supreme Court judges, while Administrative Members must be serving Cabinet Secretaries.
Judicial Members must be qualified as High Court judges, while Administrative Members must have served at the level of Additional Secretary or above.
Both categories of Members must be serving members of the Union Public Service Commission.
45.x: Judicial Members must possess qualifications equivalent to those of High Court judges. Administrative Members require service at the level of Additional Secretary or above.
45.tq: Separate the judicial and administrative eligibility streams rather than applying one qualification to both.
xs: **Judicial members** qualified as **HC judges**; **Administrative members** at **Additional Secretary** level or above — option **(3)**.
They come from **both judicial and administrative** streams, not from UPSC or serving SC judges.
xa: Strength: **69 Members — 35 Judicial** (incl. Chairperson) + **34 Administrative**.
Main bench at **New Delhi** + **18** outlying benches.
Appeals lie to the **High Court (Division Bench)**, not directly to SC.

45.s: Which of the following statements about the procedure followed by the Central Administrative Tribunal is correct?
o: It is strictly bound by the Code of Civil Procedure and prohibits personal appearance of litigants.
It is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure, follows the principles of natural justice, charges nominal fees and permits parties to appear in person.
It is not bound by any legal principles and imposes court-level fees in every case.
It follows only criminal procedure and permits appearance only through senior advocates.
45.x: CAT is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure. It follows natural justice, charges nominal filing fees and permits litigants to appear in person.
45.tq: Identify the tribunal's simplified procedure by rejecting absolute claims about CPC, fees and representation.
xs: CAT is **not bound by the CPC**, follows **natural justice**, charges a **nominal fee** and lets parties **appear in person** — option **(2)**.
These features make it cheaper and faster than a regular court.
xa: Disposal rate: **92.9%**.
Jurisdiction: **All-India Services**, **Central civil services**, civil posts under the Centre, **civilian defence employees**, notified PSUs.
⚠ CAT covers **civilian defence employees**, not armed forces personnel.

45.s:
The Central Administrative Tribunal has original jurisdiction over service disputes involving:
1. Central civil servants
2. Officers of the All-India Services
3. Civilian defence employees
4. All private-sector employees
Which of the statements given above are correct?
45.x: CAT has original jurisdiction over service disputes of Central civil servants, All-India Services officers and civilian defence employees. It does not have general jurisdiction over all private-sector employees.
45.tq: Reject the overbroad jurisdictional statement and identify the specified categories.
xs: CAT covers **Central civil servants**, **All-India Services** and **civilian defence employees** — **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
Statement 4 wrong: private-sector employees are not under CAT; it covers only **notified PSUs** besides government services.
xa: ⚠ CAT covers civilian defence employees, **not armed forces personnel** — they go to the **Armed Forces Tribunal**.
AFT parent Act: **AFT Act, 2007**; principal bench **New Delhi**.
CAT appeals lie to the **High Court (Division Bench)**.

45.s: Which one of the following correctly states the composition and bench structure of the Central Administrative Tribunal?
o: Main Bench at New Delhi, 18 benches and 69 members comprising 35 Judicial and 34 Administrative Members
Main Bench at Mumbai, 16 benches and 69 members comprising 34 Judicial and 35 Administrative Members
Main Bench at New Delhi, 18 benches and 69 members comprising 34 Judicial and 35 Administrative Members
Main Bench at New Delhi, 20 benches and 69 members comprising 35 Judicial and 34 Administrative Members
45.x: CAT has its main bench at New Delhi and 18 benches. It has 69 members: 35 Judicial Members, including the Chairperson, and 34 Administrative Members.
45.tq: Check the location, number of benches, total strength and category-wise split together.
xs: CAT: **main bench at New Delhi**, **18** benches, **69 Members** — **35 Judicial** + **34 Administrative** — option **(1)**.
⚠ The Chairperson is counted among the **35 Judicial** members.
xa: Disposal rate: **92.9%**.
Judicial members qualify as **HC judges**; administrative members are **Additional Secretary** or above.
**10th All India Conference**: New Delhi (Sep 2025).

45.s: State Administrative Tribunals are established by the Central Government:
o: Only on the recommendation of the Supreme Court
Only through a resolution of the State Legislative Council
At the request of the concerned State Government
Automatically in every State under Article 323B
45.x: A State Administrative Tribunal is set up by the Central Government at the request of the concerned State Government.
45.tq: Test the correct initiating authority and avoid swapping the Central and State roles.
xs: **SATs** are set up by the **Central Government** at the **request of the state** — option **(3)**.
They come under **Art. 323A**, not 323B, and are not automatic in every state.
xa: **Joint** tribunals are possible for **two or more states**.
**AP Administrative Tribunal**: **32nd Amendment (1973)**, **Art. 371D**.
CAT is set up by the Central Government under the **Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985**.

45.s: Which one of the following statements regarding joint administrative tribunals is correct?
o: They are established exclusively by the Supreme Court.
They can be established only when all States in India agree.
They can be established for two or more States.
They can be established only for Union Territories.
45.x: Joint tribunals may be established for two or more States.
45.tq: Use the scope of the institution to distinguish a joint tribunal from a State-specific tribunal.
xs: **Joint** administrative tribunals can be set up for **two or more states** — option **(3)**.
Like SATs, they are set up by the **Central Government** at the **request of the state**.
xa: Art. 323A: one tribunal for the Centre and **one per state or group of states**; no hierarchy.
**AP Administrative Tribunal**: constitutional authority under **Art. 371D** (**32nd Amendment, 1973**).
Appeals lie to the **High Court (Division Bench)**.

45.s: The 32nd Constitutional Amendment, 1973 provided constitutional authority for an Administrative Tribunal for Andhra Pradesh under:
45.x: The 32nd Amendment inserted the constitutional basis under Article 371D for an Administrative Tribunal for Andhra Pradesh to deal with public-service grievances.
45.tq: Avoid the Article-number swap by linking the amendment with its specific regional provision.
xs: The **32nd Amendment (1973)** gave constitutional authority under **Article 371D** for the **AP Administrative Tribunal** — option **(3)**.
It handles **public-service grievances**; **Art. 323A** is the general base for CAT/SATs, **Art. 262** for water tribunals.
xa: **Water tribunals (Art. 262)**: AP in Godavari (**1969**), Krishna-II (**2004**), Vansadhara (**2010**).
**CAT (1985)** was the first tribunal under Art. 323A.
SATs are set up by the **Central Government** at the **request of the state**.

45.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Armed Forces Tribunal — Armed Forces Tribunal Act, 2007
Debt Recovery Tribunal — Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
45.x: The Armed Forces Tribunal was set up under the Armed Forces Tribunal Act, 2007. The other pairs are mismatched: NCLT is under the Companies Act, 2013; CESTAT under the Customs Act, 1962; and Debt Recovery Tribunals under the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993 (the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 governs CGIT-cum-Labour Courts).
45.tq: Start from the sure parent-Act pair and eliminate tribunals associated with other enactments.
xs: **Armed Forces Tribunal** — **AFT Act, 2007** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**NCLT** = **Companies Act, 2013**; **CESTAT** = **Customs Act, 1962**; **DRT** = **Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993**.
The **Industrial Disputes Act, 1947** governs **CGIT-cum-Labour Courts**, not DRTs.
xa: AFT principal bench **New Delhi**; **no bench at Bhopal** (APPSC-GS 2024).
NCLT set up **2016**; NCLAT also hears **IBC** and **CCI** appeals.
DRT appeals go to the **DRAT**.

45.s:
With reference to the Armed Forces Tribunal, consider the following statements:
1. Its Principal Bench is located at New Delhi.
2. It has Regional Benches at Jaipur, Jabalpur and Guwahati.
3. It has a Regional Bench at Bhopal.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
45.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Armed Forces Tribunal has no Bench at Bhopal.
45.tq: Use the NOT-present location as the trap after confirming the Principal Bench and recognised Regional Benches.
xs: Statement 1 correct: AFT principal bench at **New Delhi**.
Statement 2 correct: regional benches at **Jaipur, Jabalpur, Guwahati**.
Statement 3 wrong: **no bench at Bhopal** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Other regional benches: **Chandigarh, Lucknow, Kolkata, Chennai, Kochi, Mumbai, Srinagar**.
Parent Act: **AFT Act, 2007**; asked in **APPSC-GS 2024**.
CAT covers **civilian defence employees**, not armed forces personnel.

45.s: The National Company Law Tribunal and the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal were set up in:
45.x: NCLT and NCLAT were set up in 2016 under the framework of the Companies Act, 2013.
45.tq: Distinguish the year of the parent Act from the later year in which the tribunals were set up.
xs: **NCLT and NCLAT** were set up in **2016** — option **(3)**.
Their parent Act is the **Companies Act, 2013** — ⚠ do not confuse the Act year with the set-up year.
xa: NCLAT hears appeals from **NCLT**, plus **IBC** and **CCI** appeals.
⚠ **2007** = AFT Act; **1962** = Customs Act (CESTAT); **1993** = DRT Act.
**Rojer Mathew (2019)** first recommended a **National Tribunals Commission**.

45.s: Which of the following functions is associated with the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT)?
o: It hears only customs and excise appeals.
It hears appeals from NCLT and also appeals under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and from the Competition Commission of India.
It hears only income-tax appeals under Article 323A.
It hears appeals exclusively from Debt Recovery Tribunals.
45.x: NCLAT hears appeals from NCLT and also deals with appeals under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and appeals from the Competition Commission of India.
45.tq: Identify the appellate body's wider subject jurisdiction instead of limiting it to company-law appeals alone.
xs: **NCLAT** hears appeals from **NCLT**, and also **IBC** and **CCI** appeals — option **(2)**.
Customs and excise appeals go to **CESTAT**; DRT appeals go to the **DRAT**.
xa: NCLT/NCLAT: **Companies Act, 2013**, set up **2016**.
**ITAT** hears income tax appeals, under the **Law Ministry**.
CGIT-cum-Labour Courts: **Industrial Disputes Act, 1947**; **22** courts.

45.s: Appeals from the Debt Recovery Tribunals lie to the:
o: Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal
45.x: Appeals from Debt Recovery Tribunals lie to the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT).
45.tq: Use the corresponding appellate-body name and avoid swapping DRAT with other specialised appellate tribunals.
xs: Appeals from **Debt Recovery Tribunals** go to the **DRAT** (Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal) — option **(3)**.
NCLAT hears **NCLT**, IBC and CCI appeals; CESTAT customs/excise; CAT service matters.
xa: DRT parent Act: **Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993** (Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993).
Art. 323B allows a **hierarchy** (original + appellate) of tribunals.
NCLT/NCLAT set up **2016** under the **Companies Act, 2013**.

45.s:
Arrange the following cases in chronological order:
A. Rojer Mathew
B. L. Chandra Kumar
C. R. Gandhi
D. S.P. Sampath Kumar
45.x: The correct sequence is S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987), L. Chandra Kumar (1997), R. Gandhi (2010), and Rojer Mathew (2019).
45.tq: Fix the earliest and latest cases first, then place the two intervening decisions by year.
xs: Order: **S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987)** → **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)** → **R. Gandhi (2010)** → **Rojer Mathew (2019)** — **D, B, C, A**, option **(1)**.
**Madras Bar Association** followed in **2021** and **Nov 2025**.
xa: ⚠ Sampath Kumar: tribunals may **replace** HCs → Chandra Kumar: tribunals only **supplement** HCs.
**R. Gandhi**: members doing judicial work must be **independent of the executive**.
**Rojer Mathew** first recommended a **National Tribunals Commission (NTC)**.

45.s: Which of the following constitutional provisions were struck down in L. Chandra Kumar as exclusion clauses?
45.x: The Supreme Court struck down the exclusion clauses contained in Article 323A(2)(d) and Article 323B(3)(d).
45.tq: Check both the Article numbers and their sub-clauses, since a nearby provision is a likely trap.
xs: SC struck down exclusion clauses in **Articles 323A(2)(d)** and **323B(3)(d)** — option **(1)**.
These clauses had excluded the courts' jurisdiction over tribunal matters.
xa: Holding: judicial review under **Arts. 32 and 226** = **basic structure**.
Route: tribunal → **High Court (Division Bench)** → SC.
⚠ **Sampath Kumar (1987)**: tribunals may replace HCs; **Chandra Kumar (1997)**: only **supplement**.

45.s:
Assertion (A): Tribunals supplement the High Courts but do not replace them.
Reason (R): Judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 forms part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
45.x: Both statements are true, and the basic-structure status of judicial review explains why tribunals cannot replace the constitutional review jurisdiction of the High Courts and Supreme Court.
45.tq: Test whether the constitutional principle in the Reason directly explains the institutional conclusion in the Assertion.
xs: **A** true: tribunals **supplement** HCs, do not replace them.
**R** true: judicial review under **Arts. 32 and 226** = **basic structure** — and R is the reason for A, so both are true and R is the **correct explanation** of A, option **(1)**.
xa: Case: **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)** struck down **323A(2)(d)** and **323B(3)(d)**.
Tribunal decisions go to the **High Court (Division Bench)**, not directly to SC.
Significance: faster, expert adjudication, but **subject to HC judicial review**.

45.s: Which one of the following cases had upheld judicial review before the decision in L. Chandra Kumar, according to the stated judicial history?
45.x: The earlier S.P. Sampath Kumar case of 1987 also upheld judicial review in the context of tribunals.
45.tq: Distinguish the earlier case in the judicial sequence from the later constitutional ruling.
xs: **S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987)** also upheld review before L. Chandra Kumar — option **(2)**.
It held tribunals may replace HCs if an **equally effective substitute**, keeping the **SC's review**.
xa: **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**: tribunals only **supplement** HCs.
**R. Gandhi (2010)**: tribunal members must be **independent of the executive**.
**Rojer Mathew (2019)**: first recommended the **NTC**.

45.s: Which one of the following statements correctly describes the 2025 Madras Bar Association case?
o: It struck down the re-enacted provisions and restored the earlier framework.
It transferred all tribunal functions to the Supreme Court.
It upheld all provisions re-enacted by Parliament without modification.
It abolished the National Tribunals Commission.
45.x: The 2025 Madras Bar Association case struck down provisions re-enacted by Parliament and restored the earlier framework.
45.tq: Watch for the reversal trap between upholding and striking down re-enacted provisions.
xs: **Madras Bar Association (2025)** struck down the **re-enacted provisions** and **restored the earlier framework** — option **(1)**.
It ordered an **NTC** within **four months** — it did not abolish it.
xa: Struck down: **minimum age 50**, **4-year tenure** (made **5 years**).
Search-cum-Selection Committee now sends **one name** per vacancy, not **two names**.
Also struck down: **equating members with civil servants**.

45.s: The National Tribunals Commission was first recommended in which case?
45.x: The National Tribunals Commission was first recommended in the Rojer Mathew case of 2019.
45.tq: Link the recommendation to the correct case and year instead of the later implementation discussion.
xs: **Rojer Mathew (2019)** first recommended an independent **National Tribunals Commission (NTC)** — option **(2)**.
**R. Gandhi (2010)** dealt with **independence** of members; **Madras Bar Association (Nov 2025)** ordered an NTC within four months.
xa: NTC under **Bill 2026**: HQ **New Delhi**; **5** members.
NTC tenure: **5 years or age 70**, whichever is earlier.
NTC role: tribunal **appointments**, **performance review**, **disciplinary inquiries**.

45.s: What principle was laid down in R. Gandhi (2010) regarding tribunal members performing judicial functions?
o: They must be nominated by consumer commissions.
They must be appointed exclusively by the executive.
They must be independent of the executive.
45.x: R. Gandhi (2010) held that tribunal members performing judicial functions must remain independent of the executive.
45.tq: Identify the constitutional principle from the case rather than the appointing authority.
xs: **R. Gandhi (2010)**: tribunal members performing judicial functions must be **independent of the executive** — option **(3)**.
This fits the criticism that parent ministries administer the tribunals they litigate before.
xa: **Rojer Mathew (2019)**: first recommended the **NTC**.
**Madras Bar Association (Nov 2025)** struck down **equating members with civil servants**.
Executive control via **Finance Act 2017** + the **2021 Ordinance**.

45.s: After the abolition of the Film Certification Appellate Tribunal, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board and the Airport Appellate Tribunal, their functions were primarily shifted to the:
45.x: The functions of the dissolved appellate tribunals were moved to the High Courts.
45.tq: Test the institutional destination of transferred functions.
xs: Functions of the abolished tribunals moved to the **High Courts** — option **(4)**.
Abolished: **Film Certification Appellate Tribunal**, **IPAB**, **Airport Appellate Tribunal** (**Tribunals Reforms Act 2021**).
xa: Also abolished: **Authority for Advance Rulings (Customs)** and **Plant Varieties Protection Appellate Tribunal**.
2021 Act: Chairperson up to **70**; members up to **67**.
**Madras Bar Association (Nov 2025)** struck down its re-enacted conditions.

45.s: Under the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, which one of the following correctly describes the tenure and age framework?
o: Tenure of four years; minimum appointment age of 45 years; all members up to 70 years
Tenure of four years; minimum appointment age of 50 years; Chairperson up to 70 years and members up to 67 years
Tenure of five years; minimum appointment age of 45 years; Chairperson up to 67 years
Tenure of three years; minimum appointment age of 50 years; members up to 65 years
45.x: The 2021 framework prescribed a four-year tenure, a minimum appointment age of 50 years, a maximum age of 70 years for the Chairperson and 67 years for members.
45.tq: Split the option into tenure, minimum age and maximum-age components.
xs: 2021 Act: **4 years** tenure; minimum age **50**; Chairperson up to **70**, members up to **67** — option **(2)**.
⚠ Tenure was 4 years, not 5 or 3, and minimum age 50, not 45.
xa: **Madras Bar Association (Nov 2025)** struck down **minimum age 50** and **4-year tenure** (made **5 years**).
**Bill 2026 NTC** members: **5 years or age 70**.
Search-cum-Selection Committee now sends **one name** per vacancy.

45.s:
Consider the following statements about the Supreme Court's Madras Bar Association ruling of November 2025:
1. It struck down the minimum appointment age of 50 and the four-year tenure for tribunal members.
2. It required the Search-cum-Selection Committee to send two names for each vacancy.
3. It ordered the government to set up a National Tribunals Commission within four months.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
45.x: Statement 1 is correct: the ruling struck down the minimum age of 50 and the 4-year tenure (made 5 years). Statement 2 is wrong: the two-name arrangement was struck down, and it is now one name per vacancy. Statement 3 is correct: an NTC was ordered within four months. So '1 only' misses statement 3, and options C and D include statement 2.
45.tq: After the ruling: 5-year tenure, one name per vacancy, NTC in four months.
xs: Statement 1 correct: it struck down **minimum age 50** and the **4-year tenure** (made **5 years**).
Statement 2 wrong: the **two names** rule was struck down → now **one name** per vacancy.
Statement 3 correct: it ordered an **NTC** within **four months** — so **1 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: It also struck down **equating members with civil servants** and **restored the earlier framework**.
**Rojer Mathew (2019)** first recommended the NTC.
**Bill 2026** NTC: HQ **New Delhi**; tenure **5 years or age 70**.

45.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched with the National Tribunals Commission proposed under the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026?
o: Technical members — Two persons with at least 25 years’ experience
Chairperson — Former Supreme Court judge or former Chief Justice of a High Court
Tenure — Four years irrespective of age
45.x: The proposed tenure is five years or until the age of 70 years, whichever is earlier, not four years irrespective of age.
45.tq: Find the single altered numerical provision in an otherwise correctly matched list.
xs: **Tenure "four years irrespective of age"** is wrong — NTC tenure is **5 years or age 70**, whichever is earlier — option **(4)**.
Correct: HQ **New Delhi**; **2 technical** members with **25+ years'** experience; Chairperson **former SC judge or former HC Chief Justice**.
xa: NTC has **5** members: Chairperson + **2 judicial** + **2 technical**.
Judicial members are former HC CJs or judges, appointed in **consultation with the CJI**.
⚠ **2021 Act** = **4 years** (min. age 50) → struck down → **Bill 2026 NTC** = **5 years or age 70**.

45.s:
With reference to the National Tribunals Commission proposed in the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026, consider the following statements:
1. It is proposed to have its headquarters at New Delhi.
2. It is proposed to have two judicial and two technical members in addition to the Chairperson.
3. Its functions include tribunal appointments, performance review and disciplinary inquiries.
4. Its Chairperson must be a serving judge of the Supreme Court.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
45.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The Chairperson may be a former Supreme Court judge or a former High Court Chief Justice; the office is not restricted to a serving Supreme Court judge.
45.tq: Reject the over-specific authority qualification while retaining the organisational details.
xs: Statements 1-3 correct: HQ **New Delhi**; **2 judicial + 2 technical** members besides the Chairperson; role = **appointments, performance review, disciplinary inquiries**.
Statement 4 wrong: Chairperson is a **former SC judge or former HC Chief Justice**, not a serving judge — so **1, 2 and 3 only**, option **(2)**.
xa: Technical members need **25+ years'** experience.
Tenure: **5 years or age 70**, whichever is earlier.
**Rojer Mathew (2019)** first recommended an NTC.

45.s:
Consider the following statements about the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026:
1. It will repeal the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021.
2. It was passed by the Lok Sabha on 10 August 2026 and by the Rajya Sabha on 11 August 2026.
3. It abolishes the proposal for a National Tribunals Commission.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
45.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the Bill will repeal the 2021 Act once both Houses pass it, and it passed the Lok Sabha on 10 August and the Rajya Sabha on 11 August 2026. Statement 3 is wrong: the Bill creates the National Tribunals Commission. Options B, C and D all include statement 3.
45.tq: Bill 2026: repeals 2021 Act; LS 10 Aug, RS 11 Aug; creates NTC
xs: Statement 1 correct: the Bill will **repeal the 2021 Act**.
Statement 2 correct: passed **Lok Sabha on 10 Aug 2026** (voice vote) and **Rajya Sabha on 11 Aug 2026**.
Statement 3 wrong: the Bill **creates** the **NTC** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: Moved by Law Minister **Arjun Ram Meghwal**.
**Madras Bar Association (Nov 2025)** had ordered an NTC within **four months**.
NTC: HQ **New Delhi**, **5** members, tenure **5 years or age 70**.

45.s: The National Sports Tribunal, notified under the National Sports Governance Act, 2025, provides for appeals to the:
45.x: Appeals from the National Sports Tribunal lie to the Supreme Court.
45.tq: Test the appellate forum and avoid confusing it with the High Court review route generally applicable to tribunals.
xs: Appeals from the **National Sports Tribunal** lie to the **Supreme Court** — option **(2)**.
It is notified under the **National Sports Governance Act, 2025**.
xa: **West Bengal**: EC set up **19 Appellate Tribunals** under retired HC judges for roll disputes after the **SIR**.
**Tribunals Reforms Bill 2026**: passed **10-11 Aug 2026**; creates the **NTC**.
Tribunals remain **subject to HC judicial review**.

45.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Tribunal or water dispute)
a. Central Administrative Tribunal
b. Godavari Water Disputes Tribunal
c. Krishna-II Water Disputes Tribunal
d. Vansadhara Water Disputes Tribunal

List-II (Year)
i. 1985
ii. 1969
iii. 2004
iv. 2010

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
45.x: The Central Administrative Tribunal was established in 1985; the Godavari, Krishna-II and Vansadhara water tribunals are associated with 1969, 2004 and 2010 respectively.
45.tq: Start with the sure CAT–1985 pair and then match the three Andhra Pradesh water tribunals by year.
xs: The three water tribunals involving AP were set up under **Art. 262**; CAT under **Art. 323A**.
xa: CAT (**1985**) was the **first** tribunal under Art. 323A.
**AP Administrative Tribunal**: **Art. 371D** (**32nd Amendment**).
CAT was set up under PM **Rajiv Gandhi**.

45.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Tribunals are intended to provide faster adjudication.
2. Tribunals are intended to bring specialised expertise into dispute resolution.

A is false, but R is true
45.x: Both are true: because judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 is part of the basic structure, Parliament cannot remove it even by amendment under Article 368. R explains A.
45.tq: Ask whether basic-structure status explains why Parliament cannot amend it away.
n: In Kesavananda Bharati in 1973, Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 was declared an integral part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Minerva Mills in 1980 reaffirmed that Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 is an integral part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Parliament cannot abrogate Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 even through Article 368. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is not vested in the Supreme Court alone. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)** is correct.
Judicial review under **Articles 32 and 226** is an **integral, inviolable** part of the **Basic Structure**, so Parliament **cannot abrogate** it even through **Article 368**.
xa: This was held in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**, **Minerva Mills (1980)** and **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**.
**L. Chandra Kumar** struck down the exclusion clauses **Art. 323A(2)(d)** and **323B(3)(d)**.
Constitutional amendments themselves are subject to judicial review on the **Basic Structure** touchstone.

45.s:
Assertion (A): Constitutional amendments are subject to Judicial Review.
Reason (R): Such amendments can be tested on the touchstone of the Basic Structure doctrine.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
45.x: Both are true: constitutional amendments can be reviewed because courts test them against the basic structure. R explains A.
45.tq: Ask whether the basic-structure test explains why amendments can be reviewed.
n: Constitutional amendments are subject to Judicial Review on the touchstone of the Basic Structure doctrine. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Constitutional amendments** are subject to judicial review because they are tested on the **Basic Structure** touchstone.
xa: Judicial review under **Articles 32 and 226** is itself part of the Basic Structure (**Kesavananda Bharati 1973**, **Minerva Mills 1980**, **L. Chandra Kumar 1997**).
Parliament **cannot abrogate** it even through **Article 368**.
HCs review under **Articles 226 and 227**; the SC under **Article 32**.

46.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: United States of America — Federal country
46.x: Sri Lanka is identified as a unitary country, not a federal country. The United States, Switzerland and France are correctly classified as stated.
46.tq: Find the single country placed in the wrong constitutional category.
xs: **Sri Lanka** is a **unitary** country, not federal — so **Sri Lanka — Federal country** is the mismatch, option **(4)**.
**Switzerland** and the **USA** are federal; **France** is unitary — all correctly matched.
xa: Other federal countries: **Canada**, **Australia**, **Argentina**, Germany, Russia, Brazil.
Other unitary countries: **Britain / UK**, **Italy**, Japan, China.
**USA** was formed by agreement of states (**integration**).

46.s: Which one of the following correctly explains the constitutional feature associated with the United Kingdom in the federal–unitary comparison?
o: The States formed the United Kingdom through a constitutional compact.
Parliament holds all law-making power, reflecting its unitary character.
Residual powers are constitutionally divided between the central and provincial governments.
The judiciary alone distributes legislative subjects between the constituent units.
46.x: The United Kingdom is presented as a unitary country in which Parliament holds all law-making power.
46.tq: Apply the defining institutional feature of a unitary system to the country described.
xs: In the **UK**, **Parliament holds all law-making power** — a **unitary** country — option **(2)**.
There is no compact of states or constitutional division of powers, as in a federation.
xa: Unitary: one supreme central government; local units are its **creations** with **delegated powers**.
**Britain** has no judicial review over Acts of Parliament (parliamentary sovereignty).
India's parliamentary form follows the **British model**: nominal head = **President**.

46.s: Which one of the following is NOT a characteristic of a unitary form of government?
o: Local units being creations of the central government
Local units exercising powers delegated by the Centre
A constitutional division of powers between the Centre and the local units
46.x: A unitary government does not constitutionally divide sovereign powers between the Centre and local units. Local units derive their authority from the central government.
46.tq: Find the statement that belongs to federalism rather than unitary government.
xs: A **constitutional division of powers** is **not** a unitary feature — it marks a federation — option **(4)**.
Unitary: **one supreme central government**; local units are its **creations** with **delegated powers**.
xa: Federalism: **sharing of power** between Union and States, each supreme in its sphere, with an **independent umpire**.
**Confederation**: loose league of sovereign States that keep the **right to secede**.
India = "**federal in structure with unitary features**" (IYB 2026).

46.s: Which of the following is NOT a merit of a unitary government?
o: Maximum accommodation of regional diversity through autonomous governments
46.x: Uniform laws, quick decisions and a strong response to crises are merits of a unitary system. Accommodation of regional diversity through autonomous governments is more characteristic of federalism.
46.tq: Separate the advantages of centralisation from the advantages of regional autonomy.
xs: **Accommodating regional diversity** through autonomous governments is not a unitary merit — option **(3)**.
Unitary merits: **uniform laws and policy**, **quick decisions**, **strong crisis response**.
xa: Demerits: **over-centralisation**; local needs neglected; poorly suited to **large, diverse countries**.
**Holding-together** federations divide power to hold **diversity** together — e.g. **India**, Spain, Belgium.
India = "**federal in structure with unitary features**" (IYB 2026).

46.s: Federalism is best understood as a system in which
o: all governmental power is concentrated in a single central authority
the Union and State governments share power, each being supreme in its own sphere under a written Constitution
sovereign States form a loose league and retain an unrestricted right to secede
local governments derive all their powers from administrative delegation by the Centre
46.x: Federalism involves constitutionally divided powers between the Union and State governments, each supreme in its assigned sphere, with an independent umpire to settle disputes.
46.tq: Distinguish the defining elements of federalism from unitary and confederal systems.
xs: **Federalism** = **sharing of power between the Union and State governments**, each **supreme in its sphere**, under a **written constitution** — option **(2)**.
It also needs an **independent umpire**; all power in one authority is unitary; a loose league with secession is a confederation.
xa: This was the answer in **APPSC-GS 2018**.
**Unitary**: units draw power from the Centre.
Essential federal feature: **independence of the judiciary** to settle Centre-State disputes (UPSC 2021).

46.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes a confederation from a federation?
o: A confederation consists of sovereign States that retain the right to secede.
A federation does not require a written constitutional division of powers.
A federation is merely a temporary league of sovereign States.
A confederation always has a stronger central government than a federation.
46.x: A confederation is a loose league of sovereign States, generally retaining the right to secede. A federation creates a constitutional division of powers between the Union and constituent units.
46.tq: Use the right to secede as the decisive distinction between federation and confederation.
xs: A **confederation** is a loose league of **sovereign States** that keep the **right to secede** — option **(1)**.
A federation has a written constitution dividing powers, with an independent umpire.
xa: **Ambedkar**: in India **no State has the right to secede** → Union is **indestructible**.
**Unitary**: units draw power from the Centre.
Coming-together federations: **USA**, Switzerland, Australia.

46.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Feature or provision)
(a) Federal scheme
(b) Strong Centre
(c) Concurrent List
(d) Emergency provisions

List-II (Source)
(i) Australia
(ii) Government of India Act, 1935
(iii) Canada
(iv) Government of India Act, 1935

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
46.x: The federal scheme and emergency provisions were borrowed from the Government of India Act, 1935; the strong Centre reflects the Canadian model; and the Concurrent List was borrowed from Australia.
46.tq: Start with the sure source associations and then eliminate codes with mismatched constitutional borrowings.
xs: **Federal scheme** and **emergency provisions** — **GoI Act 1935**; **strong Centre** — **Canada**; **Concurrent List** — **Australia** — **a–ii, b–iii, c–i, d–iv**, option **(1)**.
The **Governor** too came from the **GoI Act 1935**.
xa: ⚠ **Strong Centre** = Canada; **Concurrent List** = Australia.
Residuary power: **Canada** model — with the Centre; **USA and Australia** — with the states.
Under the **GoI Act 1935** residuary power lay with the **Governor-General**.

46.s: The federal arrangements in the United States and India differ in their historical genesis because
o: the United States adopted a unitary system first, whereas India was formed by an agreement among independent States
the United States developed through the integration of States, whereas India moved from a unitary colonial system towards a federal arrangement
both the United States and India were created by the disintegration of unitary systems
both federations were established exclusively through constitutional amendments made by their central governments
46.x: The United States federation was formed by an agreement and integration of States. India converted a unitary colonial arrangement into a federal one, producing a centripetal bias.
46.tq: Compare the historical origins of the two federations rather than merely comparing their constitutional structures.
xs: **USA** = federation by **integration** (agreement of states); **India** = a **unitary colonial** system converted to federal — option **(2)**.
This gives India its **centripetal bias**; CDI calls India's federation formed by "**disintegration**".
xa: ⚠ **Integration** = USA (**coming together**); **disintegration** = India (**holding together**).
Framed after Partition + integration of **14 provinces and 500+ princely States**.
USA = "indestructible Union of **indestructible** states"; India = of **destructible** States.

46.s: Which historical circumstances particularly encouraged the framers of the Constitution to adopt a strong centralising design?
o: The prior existence of a fully developed confederation
The aftermath of Partition and the integration of 14 provinces and more than 500 princely States
The peaceful integration of only a few provinces before Independence
The absence of linguistic and cultural diversity
46.x: The Constitution was framed after Partition and during the integration of 14 provinces and more than 500 princely States. In that context, centralisation was viewed as indispensable for national integration.
46.tq: Link constitutional design to the historical context in which it was adopted.
xs: Framed after **Partition** and integration of **14 provinces and 500+ princely States**, centralisation looked **indispensable** — option **(2)**.
This is the **national-integration design** (TH 17 Feb 2026).
xa: India = **holding-together** federation with a **stronger Centre**.
**K. Santhanam**: Union's strength lies in refusing functions that do not belong to it.
Official label: "**federal in structure with unitary features**" (IYB 2026).

46.s: Which of the following countries represents a coming-together federation?
46.x: Switzerland is a coming-together federation in which independent States or units pool sovereignty while retaining equal power. India, Spain and Belgium are examples of holding-together federations.
46.tq: Separate examples of the two federation types rather than relying only on their definitions.
xs: **Switzerland** is a **coming-together** federation — option **(4)**.
**India**, **Spain** and **Belgium** are **holding-together** federations.
xa: Coming-together: independent States **pool sovereignty**, keep **equal power** — **USA**, Switzerland, Australia.
Holding-together: large country divides power to hold **diversity** together; **stronger Centre**.
⚠ USA = **integration**; India = **disintegration** (CDI view).

46.s: Which of the following subjects is dealt with by Article 2 of the Constitution?
o: Admission or establishment of new States not part of India
Formation of new States and alteration of existing State boundaries
Amendment of the Constitution through the special procedure
46.x: Article 2 concerns the admission or establishment of new States into the Union, particularly territories not already part of India.
46.tq: Separate Article 2, concerning admission or establishment, from Article 3, concerning existing States.
xs: **Art. 2** = **admission or establishment of new states** not part of India (e.g. **Sikkim**) — option **(1)**.
Forming new States / altering boundaries is **Art. 3**.
xa: **Art. 1**: "**India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States**".
**Art. 4**: Art. 3 laws amend the **First and Fourth Schedules**; **not** Art. 368 amendments.
States and UTs are listed in the **First Schedule**.

46.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Territory of India includes the States and Union Territories.
2. The Territory of India also includes territories acquired by India.
3. The Union of India includes the States only.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
46.x: All three statements are correct. The Territory of India is wider than the Union of India because it includes States, Union Territories and acquired territories, whereas the Union of India refers to the States.
46.tq: Compare the wider and narrower constitutional expressions instead of treating them as synonyms.
xs: Statements 1, 2 correct: **Territory of India** = **States + UTs + territories acquired**.
Statement 3 correct: **Union of India** = the **States only** — so **1, 2 and 3**, option **(4)**.
xa: ⚠ Territory is the **wider** term; Union = members of the federal system.
**Art. 1(1)**: "**India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States**".
States and UTs are specified in the **First Schedule**.

46.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 3 of the Constitution of India:
1. Parliament may form a new State.
2. Parliament may alter the area, boundaries or name of an existing State.
3. A law under Article 3 requires a special majority in Parliament.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
46.x: Article 3 empowers Parliament to form new States and alter the area, boundaries or names of existing States. Such a law is passed by a simple majority, not a special majority.
46.tq: Split the options by checking the majority requirement after confirming Parliament’s substantive powers.
xs: Statements 1, 2 correct: under **Art. 3** Parliament can **form new States, alter areas, boundaries or names**.
Statement 3 wrong: it needs only a **simple majority** — so **1 and 2 only**, option **(1)**.
xa: The Bill needs the **President's recommendation** + reference to the state legislature (views **not binding**).
**Art. 4**: such laws are **not** Art. 368 amendments.
Result: "**an indestructible Union of destructible States**".

46.s: Which of the following correctly describes a law made under Articles 3 and 4 of the Constitution?
o: It alters the First and Fourth Schedules and is treated as an amendment under Article 368
It may alter the First and Fourth Schedules and is not treated as an amendment under Article 368
It can alter only the Second and Third Schedules through a special majority
It cannot alter any Schedule because State reorganisation requires Article 368 procedure
46.x: Article 4 permits consequential changes in the First and Fourth Schedules. Such a law is not deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution under Article 368.
46.tq: Use the Article-number trap by separating consequential Schedule changes from Article 368 amendments.
xs: An Art. 3 law **may alter the First and Fourth Schedules** and is **not** an **Art. 368** amendment — option **(2)**.
This comes from **Art. 4**; such laws pass by **simple majority**.
xa: **First Schedule** = States and UTs; **Fourth Schedule** = Rajya Sabha seats **by population**.
Art. 3 Bill needs the **President's recommendation**; the state legislature's views are **not binding**.
No territorial guarantee → India = indestructible Union of **destructible** States.

46.s: The States and Union Territories of India are specified in which constitutional Schedule?
46.x: The First Schedule specifies the States and Union Territories of India. The Fourth Schedule deals with allocation of seats in the Council of States.
46.tq: Discriminate between the First Schedule’s territorial listing and nearby Schedule numbers with different subjects.
xs: States and UTs are specified in the **First Schedule** — option **(1)**.
The **Fourth Schedule** allots Rajya Sabha seats; the **Seventh** has the three Lists.
xa: **Art. 1(1)**: "**India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States**".
Art. 3 laws amend the **First and Fourth Schedules** (**Art. 4**).
Rajya Sabha seats by population: **Uttar Pradesh 31**, small States **1**.

46.s: Which one of the following statements correctly distinguishes the Indian constitutional arrangement from that of the United States in relation to the Union and States?
o: India is an indestructible Union of destructible States, whereas the United States is an indestructible Union of indestructible States
India permits secession but the United States does not
The United States permits Parliament to alter the boundaries of its States by simple majority
Both India and the United States are described as Unions of destructible States
46.x: India is characterised as an indestructible Union of destructible States, while the United States is described as an indestructible Union of indestructible States.
46.tq: Apply the paired-comparison method by checking both the Union and the status of the States.
