Television broadcasting is a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Agriculture is a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Agricultural education is a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Land is a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Land reforms are a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Fisheries are a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Markets and fairs are a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xs: **Only three** are State List subjects — option **(3)**.
**Agriculture and agricultural education**, **land and land reforms**, and **fisheries** and **markets and fairs** are **State** subjects.
**Radio and television broadcasting** is a **Union** subject.
xa: Other State subjects: **public order**, **police**, **prisons**, **public health and sanitation**, **tolls**, **capitation taxes**.
**Agriculture**, **water** and **land** = State **Entries 14, 17, 18**.
⚠ **Water** = State Entry 17; **cruelty to animals** = Concurrent Entry 17.

46.s:
How many of the following are Union List subjects?
1. Foreign Affairs and Treaties
2. Banking and Insurance
3. Stock Exchanges and Futures Markets
4. Inter-State Migration and Quarantine
46.x: All four are Union List subjects: foreign affairs and treaties, banking and insurance, stock exchanges and futures markets, and inter-State migration and quarantine (Entry 81).
46.tq: National and inter-State matters are Union subjects.
n: Foreign affairs are a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Treaties are a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Banking is a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Insurance is a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Inter-State migration is a Union List subject under Entry 81. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Quarantine is a Union List subject under Entry 81. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Stock exchanges are a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Futures markets are a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xs: **All four** are Union List subjects — option **(4)**.
**Foreign affairs and treaties**, **banking and insurance**, **stock exchanges and futures markets**, and **inter-State migration and quarantine** (**Entry 81**) are all in the **Union List**.
xa: Other Union subjects: **defence**, **railways**, **census**, **corporation tax**, **atomic energy**, **radio and television**.
The Union List had **97** entries originally and has **98** now.
**Residuary powers** lie with Parliament under **Article 248** and **Entry 97, List I**.

46.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the distribution of subjects?
o: Public Health and Sanitation is a Concurrent List subject.
Tolls and Capitation Taxes are State List subjects.
Inter-State Migration and Quarantine are Union List subjects.
Local Government and Panchayati Raj are State List subjects.
46.x: A is incorrect: public health and sanitation is a State List subject, not Concurrent. The others are right: tolls (State), inter-State migration and quarantine (Union), local government (State).
46.tq: Check which List each subject truly belongs to.
n: Inter-State migration is a Union List subject under Entry 81. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Quarantine is a Union List subject under Entry 81. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Public health is a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Sanitation is a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Local government is a State List subject under Entry 5. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Panchayati Raj is a State List subject under Entry 5. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Tolls are a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Capitation taxes are a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **Public Health and Sanitation** is a **Concurrent** subject — option **(1)**; it is a **State** subject.
**Tolls and capitation taxes** = **State**; **inter-State migration and quarantine** = **Union** (Entry 81).
**Local government / Panchayati Raj** = **State** (**Entry 5**).
xa: State List: **66** entries originally, **59** now.
Concurrent List: **47** originally, **52** now.
**Police and public order** are State subjects (APPSC 2019).

46.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Administration of Justice was one of the subjects transferred to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment.
II. The transfer covered the constitution and organisation of all courts except the Supreme Court and High Courts.
III. Population Control and Family Planning was inserted as Entry 20A in the Concurrent List.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
46.x: All three are correct: administration of justice was moved to the Concurrent List in 1976, covering all courts except the Supreme Court and High Courts, and Entry 20A (population control and family planning) was added.
46.tq: Note the exception for the higher courts.
n: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act transferred administration of justice from the State List to the Concurrent List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Administration of justice includes the constitution and organisation of all courts except the Supreme Court and High Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Entry 20A was inserted into the Concurrent List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Entry 20A concerns population control and family planning. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Population control is a Concurrent List subject under Entry 20A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Family planning is a Concurrent List subject under Entry 20A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xs: All three statements **I, II and III** are correct — option **(2)**.
I: **Administration of justice** was among the **5 subjects** moved to the Concurrent List by the **42nd CAA, 1976**.
II: it covers all courts **except** the **Supreme Court and High Courts**.
III: **Entry 20A** — **population control and family planning** — was inserted in the Concurrent List.
xa: Other transfers: **education**, **forests**, **weights and measures**, **protection of wild animals and birds**.
Constitution and organisation of **High Courts** = **Union** (Entry 78).
The Centre uses Concurrent entries for sweeping laws — e.g. **NEP** and **NMC Act** in education.

46.s:
How many of the following are expressly identified as things Judicial Review is NOT?
1. Questioning the political wisdom of legislation
2. Automatic pre-assent scrutiny of Bills
3. An ordinary appellate proceeding
4. Examining the constitutionality of executive orders
46.x: Three are what judicial review is not: it does not question a law's political wisdom, check bills before assent, or act as an ordinary appeal. Testing executive orders is part of it.
46.tq: Find the item that is part of judicial review.
n: Judicial Review is the inherent constitutional power of the higher judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is the inherent constitutional power of the higher judiciary to examine the constitutionality of executive orders. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review does not involve the court questioning the political wisdom of legislation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is not automatic pre-assent scrutiny of Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is not an ordinary appellate proceeding. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review does not involve the court questioning the policy merits of legislation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
xs: **Only three** are things judicial review is NOT — option **(3)**.
It is **not** questioning the **political wisdom** of legislation, **not** automatic **pre-assent** scrutiny of Bills, and **not** an ordinary **appellate** proceeding.
Examining the constitutionality of executive orders is not on that list.
xa: Judicial review reinforces the **federal principle** and preserves the **distribution of powers**.
It is **not** a **unitary** element; unitary elements include **All India Services**, the **Governor's appointment** and **Emergency provisions**.
It also does not question the **policy merits** or **advisability** of legislation.

46.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Judicial Review reinforces the federal principle.
Statement B: Judicial Review is classified as a unitary element of the Constitution.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
46.x: A is true: judicial review supports federalism by keeping the division of powers. B is false because it is not a unitary feature, unlike emergency provisions or All India Services.
46.tq: Discriminate federal features from unitary features.
n: Judicial Review reinforces the federal principle. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review preserves the constitutional distribution of powers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review enforces constitutional limits. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is not a unitary element. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
xs: **Statement A is true, Statement B is false** — option **(3)** is correct.
A: judicial review reinforces the **federal principle**, preserves the **distribution of powers** and enforces **constitutional limits**.
B is wrong: it is **not** a **unitary** element.
xa: ⚠ Unitary elements: **All India Services**, **Governor's appointment**, **Emergency provisions**.
**Essential federal feature:** **independence of the judiciary** — it settles Centre-State disputes (UPSC 2021).
"Not a federal feature" PYQ answers: **Office of the Governor** (APPSC-G1 2018) and **CAG** (APPSC-G2 2017).

46.s: Under which Part of the Constitution are the Emergency Provisions contained?
46.x: The emergency provisions are in Part XVIII, Articles 352–360. Part XX is amendment and Part XVI covers reservations for SCs, STs and others.
46.tq: Recall Part XVIII and its Articles 352 to 360.
n: Emergency provisions are governed under Part XVIII of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Emergency provisions are covered by Articles 352 to 360. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xs: Emergency provisions are in **Part XVIII** (**Articles 352 to 360**) — option **(4)** is correct.
Their unique feature: the federation becomes **unitary without a formal amendment**.
xa: Three types: **National Emergency (Art. 352)**, **President's Rule (Art. 356)**, **Financial Emergency (Art. 360)**.
**K.M. Nambiar** called the President's emergency powers a "**fraud on the Constitution**".
⚠ "Art. 311 - Financial Emergency" is a mismatch; Financial Emergency is **Art. 360**.

46.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Article)
a. Article 352
b. Article 356
c. Article 360

List-II (Ground)
i. Threat to financial stability or credit of India
 ii. Failure of constitutional machinery in a State
 iii. War, external aggression or armed rebellion
46.x: Article 352 covers war, external aggression or armed rebellion, 356 the failure of a State's constitutional machinery, and 360 a threat to India's financial stability. The answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-i.
46.tq: Recall the ground for each of the three emergencies.
n: Article 352 provides for National Emergency. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
War is a ground for proclaiming a National Emergency under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
External aggression is a ground for proclaiming a National Emergency under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Armed rebellion is a ground for proclaiming a National Emergency under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Article 356 provides for President’s Rule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Failure of constitutional machinery in a State is the ground for imposing President’s Rule under Article 356. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Article 360 provides for Financial Emergency. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
A threat to the financial stability or credit of India is a ground for proclaiming Financial Emergency under Article 360. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
War, external aggression, or armed rebellion are the grounds for National Emergency under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Failure of constitutional machinery is the ground for President’s Rule under Article 356. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xs: The correct code is **a-iii, b-ii, c-i** — option **(2)**.
**Art. 352** = **war, external aggression or armed rebellion**; **Art. 356** = **failure of constitutional machinery** in a State.
**Art. 360** = threat to the **financial stability or credit** of India.
xa: "**Internal disturbance**" was replaced by "**armed rebellion**" by the **44th Amendment, 1978**.
Art. 356 also links to **Art. 365**.

46.s:
How many of the following statements are correct?
1. National Emergency has been invoked three times in India.
2. President’s Rule has been invoked over 100 times across various States.
3. Financial Emergency has been invoked once in India.
4. National Emergency was invoked in 1962, 1971 and 1975.
46.x: Three are correct: National Emergencies were declared three times (1962, 1971, 1975), and President's Rule more than 100 times. Statement 3 is false because a Financial Emergency has never been declared.
46.tq: Recall how often each emergency has been used.
n: National Emergency has been invoked 3 times in India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
National Emergencies were invoked in 1962, 1971, and 1975. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
President’s Rule has been invoked over 100 times across various States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Financial Emergency has never been invoked in India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xs: **Only three** statements are correct — option **(3)**.
1 and 4: **National Emergency** was used **3 times** — **1962, 1971, 1975**.
2: **President's Rule** has been used over **100** times across States.
3 is wrong: **Financial Emergency** has **never** been invoked.
xa: The **1975** Emergency was proclaimed on **25 June 1975** on the ground of **Internal Disturbance**; withdrawn **21 March 1977**.
**AP** came under President's Rule in **1973** (Jai Andhra agitation).
**Samvidhan Hatya Diwas:** **25 June**.

46.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Emergency)
a. National Emergency
b. President’s Rule
c. Financial Emergency

List-II (Impact)
i. Executive gives financial directions and salaries may be reduced
 ii. Parliament can make laws on State List subjects
 iii. State Assembly is dissolved or suspended and Parliament passes the State Budget
46.x: In a National Emergency, Parliament can legislate on State subjects. Under President's Rule, the Assembly is dissolved or suspended and Parliament passes the State budget. In a Financial Emergency, financial directions can be given and pay cut. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i.
46.tq: Match each emergency to its main effect.
n: During a National Emergency, Parliament can make laws on subjects in the State List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
During President’s Rule, the State Assembly may be dissolved or suspended. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
During President’s Rule, Parliament passes the State Budget. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
During a Financial Emergency, the executive gives financial directions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
During a Financial Emergency, salaries may be reduced, including the salaries of Supreme Court and High Court judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xs: The correct code is **a-ii, b-iii, c-i** — option **(2)**.
**National Emergency:** Parliament legislates on the **State List**; **President's Rule:** State Assembly **dissolved or suspended** and Parliament passes the **State Budget**.
**Financial Emergency:** executive gives **financial directions**; **salaries** may be cut, including **SC and HC judges**.
xa: In National Emergency, **Articles 358 and 359** operate.
Financial Emergency: State **money bills** can be **reserved** for the President.
⚠ Only **352** directly affects Fundamental Rights; **Articles 20 and 21** can never be suspended.

46.s:
How many of the following statements are correct?
1. National Emergency requires a special majority in both Houses.
2. President’s Rule requires a simple majority in both Houses.
3. Financial Emergency requires a simple majority in both Houses.
4. National Emergency has a maximum continuation limit of three years.
46.x: Three are correct: a National Emergency needs a special majority, and President's Rule and a Financial Emergency need simple majorities. Statement 4 is false because a National Emergency has no maximum period.
46.tq: Discriminate the three-year cap (President's Rule) from no cap (National Emergency).
n: A National Emergency requires a special majority in both Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
President’s Rule requires a simple majority in both Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Financial Emergency requires a simple majority in both Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
A National Emergency has no maximum continuation limit. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xs: **Only three** statements are correct — option **(3)**.
1: National Emergency needs a **special** majority; 2 and 3: **President's Rule** and **Financial Emergency** need a **simple** majority.
4 is wrong: National Emergency runs **6 months** at a time with **no maximum** limit; the **3 years** cap applies to **President's Rule**.
xa: President's Rule beyond **1 year** needs a national emergency plus **ECI certification** (Art. 356(5)).
Financial Emergency continues until **revoked** by the President.

46.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Emergency)
a. National Emergency
b. President's Rule
c. Financial Emergency

List-II (Continuation provision)
i. Six months at a time, with no maximum limit
ii. Six months at a time, subject to a maximum of three years
iii. Continues until revoked by the President

Codes:
46.x: A National Emergency continues six months at a time with no limit, President's Rule six months at a time up to three years, and a Financial Emergency, once approved, until revoked. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii.
46.tq: Recall the continuation rule for each emergency.
n: A National Emergency continues for 6 months at a time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
A National Emergency has no maximum continuation limit. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
President’s Rule continues for 6 months at a time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
President’s Rule can continue for a maximum of 3 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Financial Emergency continues until it is revoked by the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xs: The correct code is **a-i, b-ii, c-iii** — option **(1)**.
**National Emergency:** **6 months** at a time, **no maximum** limit; **President's Rule:** **6 months** at a time, **maximum 3 years**.
**Financial Emergency:** continues until **revoked** by the President.
xa: Beyond **1 year**, President's Rule needs a national emergency plus **ECI certification** (**Art. 356(5)**).
**One Nation, One Election** deferrals could clash with **Art. 356(5)** limits.
Approval: **352** within **1 month** (was **2 months** before the **44th Amendment**).

46.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. If the Lok Sabha is dissolved before approving it, a proclamation of National Emergency survives until 30 days from the first sitting of the new Lok Sabha, if the Rajya Sabha has approved it.
II. The same 30-day rule applies to a proclamation of President's Rule.
III. The same 30-day rule applies to a proclamation of Financial Emergency.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
46.x: All three are correct: if the Lok Sabha is dissolved before approving any of the three proclamations, it survives until 30 days after the new Lok Sabha first sits, provided the Rajya Sabha has approved it meanwhile.
46.tq: Recall that the dissolution rule is common to all three emergencies.
n: A National Emergency survives for 30 days from the first sitting of a new Lok Sabha after the Lok Sabha is dissolved. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
President’s Rule survives for 30 days from the first sitting of a new Lok Sabha after the Lok Sabha is dissolved. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Financial Emergency survives for 30 days from the first sitting of a new Lok Sabha after the Lok Sabha is dissolved. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xs: All three statements **I, II and III** are correct — option **(3)**.
If the Lok Sabha is dissolved, a **National Emergency**, **President's Rule** and **Financial Emergency** proclamation each survives **30 days** from the first sitting of the new Lok Sabha.
xa: Approval: **352** = **1 month** (**special** majority); **356** and **360** = **2 months** (**simple** majority).
**Special sitting:** notice by **1/10th of Lok Sabha** members → sitting within **14 days** to consider disapproval of a National Emergency.
Financial Emergency has **never** been declared.

46.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: President’s Rule does not directly suspend Fundamental Rights.
Statement B: A Financial Emergency does not directly suspend Fundamental Rights.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
46.x: Both are true: only a National Emergency touches fundamental rights, through Articles 358 and 359. President's Rule and a Financial Emergency do not suspend them directly.
46.tq: Recall which emergency affects fundamental rights.
n: President’s Rule does not directly suspend Fundamental Rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Financial Emergency does not directly suspend Fundamental Rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)** is correct.
**President's Rule** and **Financial Emergency** do **not directly suspend** Fundamental Rights.
Only **National Emergency** does, through **Articles 358 and 359**.
xa: **Art. 19** is suspended only in an **external** emergency (**Art. 358**).
Other rights are suspended by order under **Art. 359**, **except Arts. 20 and 21**.
The **44th Amendment, 1978** made **Articles 20 and 21** non-suspendable.

46.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Parliament can extend the term of the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies by law for one year at a time during a National Emergency.
II. Such extension can continue beyond six months after the Emergency ceases.
III. Laws made by Parliament on State List subjects cease to operate six months after the Emergency is revoked.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
46.x: I and III are correct: Parliament can extend the Houses' terms one year at a time, and its laws on State subjects lapse six months after the Emergency ends. II is false because no extension can run beyond six months after the Emergency.
46.tq: Recall the six-month limit after an Emergency ends.
n: Parliament can extend the terms of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies by law during a National Emergency. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The terms of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies can be extended by 1 year at a time during a National Emergency. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The terms of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies can be extended up to a maximum of 6 months after the Emergency ceases. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Laws made by Parliament on State List subjects during a National Emergency cease to operate 6 months after the Emergency is revoked. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xs: Statements **I and III only** are correct — option **(3)**.
I: Parliament may extend the terms of the **Lok Sabha and State Assemblies** by law **1 year at a time**.
II is wrong: the extension can run at most **6 months** after the Emergency ceases.
III: Parliament's laws on the **State List** (**Art. 250**) **cease 6 months** after the Emergency is **revoked**.
xa: **Article 354:** the President may **modify** Centre-State **revenue** distribution, valid until the end of the **financial year** in which the proclamation ceases.
The Union's executive power extends to directing **any State** on how to use its executive power.
Proclamation is only on the **written advice** of the **Union Cabinet**.

46.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. National Emergency invoked in 1975
B. National Emergency invoked in 1962
C. National Emergency formally withdrawn on 21 March 1977
D. National Emergency invoked in 1971
46.x: Emergencies were declared in 1962 and 1971, then on 25 June 1975, and the last was lifted on 21 March 1977. The order is B, D, A, C.
46.tq: Recall the years 1962, 1971, 1975 and 1977.
n: National Emergencies were invoked in 1962, 1971, and 1975. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The National Emergency of 1975 was proclaimed on 25 June 1975. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The 1975 National Emergency was formally withdrawn on 21 March 1977. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xs: The correct order is **B, D, A, C** — option **(4)**.
National Emergencies came in **1962**, **1971** and **1975** (**25 June 1975**); the last was withdrawn on **21 March 1977**.
xa: The **1975** Emergency was on the ground of **Internal Disturbance**.
The **44th Amendment, 1978** replaced "internal disturbance" with "**armed rebellion**".
**Samvidhan Hatya Diwas** (**25 June**) recalls the **1975** Emergency.

46.s:
Consider the following statements about the 44th Amendment Act, 1978:
I. It reduced the parliamentary approval period for National Emergency from two months to one month.
II. It guaranteed that enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended under Article 359.
III. It required the President to proclaim National Emergency only upon written advice of the Union Cabinet.
IV. It changed “Internal Disturbance” to “Armed Rebellion” under Article 352.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
46.x: All four are correct: the 44th Amendment cut approval to one month, protected Articles 20 and 21, required the Cabinet's written advice, and replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion'.
46.tq: Recall the 44th Amendment's safeguards.
n: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 replaced “Internal Disturbance” with “Armed Rebellion” under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 reduced parliamentary approval time for a National Emergency from 2 months to 1 month. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 guaranteed that enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended under Article 359. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The President can proclaim a National Emergency only upon the written advice of the Union Cabinet. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
War, external aggression, or armed rebellion are the grounds for National Emergency under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended during a National Emergency. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act established the non-suspendability of Articles 20 and 21 under Article 359. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xs: All four statements **I, II, III and IV** are correct — option **(2)**.
The **44th Amendment Act, 1978** cut approval time from **2 months to 1 month** and made **Articles 20 and 21** non-suspendable under **Article 359**.
It required proclamation only on **written advice of the Union Cabinet** and replaced "**Internal Disturbance**" with "**Armed Rebellion**" in **Article 352**.
xa: ⚠ Trap: "internal disturbance" is no longer a ground (APPSC-GS 2018).
**Special sitting:** notice by **1/10th of Lok Sabha** members → sitting within **14 days**.
The **38th Amendment** barred judicial review of Emergency; **Minerva Mills** reopened it.

46.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: During a National Emergency, the President may modify the constitutional distribution of revenues between the Union and the States.
Statement B: Such modification remains valid up to the end of the financial year in which the proclamation of Emergency ceases.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
46.x: Both are true: under Article 354, the President can change the revenue division during an Emergency, and the change lasts until the end of the financial year in which the Emergency ends.
46.tq: Recall Article 354.
n: Article 354 empowers the President to modify the constitutional distribution of revenues between the Union and the States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Modification of revenue distribution under Article 354 remains valid up to the end of the financial year in which the proclamation ceases. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)** is correct.
A: under **Article 354**, the President may **modify** the distribution of **revenues** between Union and States during a National Emergency.
B: such change is valid until the end of the **financial year** in which the proclamation ceases.
xa: The President can **reduce or cancel** transfers to States, subject to Parliament's approval.
⚠ "**Increase** the transfer" is the wrong statement (APPSC-G2 2017).
Parliament's State-List laws (**Art. 250**) **cease 6 months** after the Emergency is **revoked**.

46.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
 a. Proclamation of National Emergency
 b. Laws made by Parliament on State List subjects
 c. Modification of revenue distribution by the President
 d. Proclamation of Emergency in 1975

List-II
 i. Valid up to the end of the financial year in which the proclamation ceases
 ii. Made on 25 June 1975
 iii. Requires written advice of the Union Cabinet
 iv. Cease to operate six months after revocation of the Emergency
46.x: A National Emergency needs the Cabinet's written advice, Parliament's State-subject laws lapse six months after it ends, revenue changes last to the end of the financial year, and 1975's was declared on 25 June. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
46.tq: Recall each emergency rule's time limit.
n: Laws made by Parliament on State List subjects during a National Emergency cease to operate 6 months after the Emergency is revoked. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Modification of revenue distribution under Article 354 remains valid up to the end of the financial year in which the proclamation ceases. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The President can proclaim a National Emergency only upon the written advice of the Union Cabinet. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The National Emergency of 1975 was proclaimed on 25 June 1975. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xs: The correct code is **a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii** — option **(4)**.
**Proclamation** needs **written advice of the Union Cabinet**; Parliament's **State List** laws **cease six months** after revocation.
**Revenue modification** (Art. 354) lasts to the end of the **financial year**; the **1975** Emergency was proclaimed on **25 June 1975**.
xa: The 1975 Emergency was on the ground of **Internal Disturbance** and withdrawn **21 March 1977**.
Parliament may extend the **Lok Sabha** term **1 year at a time** during an Emergency.
Parliamentary approval is needed within **1 month** (**special** majority).

47.s: Article 248 is located in which Part of the Constitution?
47.x: Article 248 is located in Part XI, which deals with relations between the Union and the States and extends from Articles 245 to 263.
47.tq: Match the article with its constitutional Part, not merely with its subject.
xs: **Article 248** (residuary powers) lies in **Part XI** — option **(3)**.
Part XI covers **Relations between the Union and the States**, **Art. 245-263** (APPSC-GS 2023).
Its Chapter I (**Arts. 245-255**) deals with legislative relations.
xa: **245** = territorial extent; **246** = subject-matter (three lists); **247** = additional courts.
**248** + **Entry 97 of the Union List** = Parliament's exclusive residuary power, including **taxation**.
**249 / 250** = State List — national interest / Emergency; **254** = repugnancy.

47.s: An Act requiring the previous recommendation or sanction of the Governor or President has been passed without it, but the Governor or President subsequently gives assent. What is the constitutional consequence under Article 255?
o: The Act is not invalid merely for want of that recommendation or previous sanction
The Act is automatically void in all circumstances
The Act applies only to Union Territories
The Act becomes a constitutional amendment
47.x: Article 255 treats the requirement of recommendation or previous sanction as a matter of procedure. Subsequent assent prevents invalidity on that ground alone.
47.tq: Apply the procedural-versus-substantive distinction to a short constitutional situation.
xs: Under **Art. 255**, the Act is **not invalid** merely for want of the required **recommendation or previous sanction** if the Governor/President later **assents** — option **(1)**.
Recommendations and previous sanctions are treated as **matters of procedure only**.
xa: **Art. 254**: **repugnancy** — Union law prevails; State law with **President's assent** prevails in that State.
State bills restricting **inter-state trade** need the **President's previous sanction** (Part XIII, **Arts. 301-305**).
**Art. 253**: laws to implement **international agreements**.

47.s:
Which of the following combinations is correctly matched?
1. Article 245 — Territorial extent of laws
2. Article 246 — Subject-matter of laws under the Seventh Schedule
3. Article 248 — Residuary powers
4. Article 255 — Repugnancy between Union and State laws
47.x: Articles 245, 246 and 248 are correctly matched. Repugnancy is dealt with by Article 254, not Article 255; Article 255 concerns recommendations and previous sanctions as procedural matters.
47.tq: Catch the swapped article number in an otherwise familiar constitutional sequence.
xs: Pairs **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
**245** — **territorial extent**; **246** — **subject-matter** via the Seventh Schedule; **248** — **residuary** powers.
Pair 4 is wrong: **repugnancy** is **Art. 254**; **Art. 255** treats recommendations and sanctions as **matters of procedure only**.
xa: **246A** (**101st CAA**): both Parliament and States make **GST** laws; only Parliament for **IGST**.
**252** = law for **two or more States by consent**; **253** = **international agreements**.
**251** = inconsistency with laws under **249/250**.

47.s:
With reference to the territorial extent of laws, consider the following statements:
1. Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of India.
2. Parliament's law is not invalid merely because it has extra-territorial operation.
3. A State Legislature may ordinarily legislate for the territory of another State without any territorial connection.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
47.x: Parliament may legislate for the whole or any part of India, and an extra-territorial operation does not by itself invalidate parliamentary legislation. A State law requires a sufficient territorial nexus for extra-territorial reach, so statement 3 is false.
47.tq: Test the Union-State contrast and reject the unrestricted claim about State extra-territorial legislation.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
1: **Parliament** legislates for the **whole or any part of India**.
2: **Art. 245(2)**: no Parliament law is invalid for **extra-territorial operation**.
3 is wrong: a **State** legislates for its own territory; extra-territorial reach only with sufficient **territorial nexus**.
xa: ⚠ **Extra-territorial** laws = Parliament only; State needs **territorial nexus**.
**President's regulations** for **Andaman & Nicobar** and **Lakshadweep** have the force of Parliament's Acts.
The **Governor** can bar or modify Parliament's Acts for **Scheduled Areas**.

47.s: Which constitutional authority's regulations have the force of Acts of Parliament in the Union Territories of Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep?
o: The Administrator appointed by the Supreme Court
47.x: Regulations made by the President for Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep have the force and effect of an Act of Parliament.
47.tq: Identify the competent authority instead of confusing Union Territory administration with State gubernatorial power.
xs: Regulations made by **the President** for **Andaman & Nicobar** and **Lakshadweep** have the force of **Acts of Parliament** — option **(1)**.
This is an exception to **Art. 245**'s territorial scheme for special areas.
xa: The **Governor** can bar/modify Parliament's Acts for **Scheduled Areas**.
The **Governor of Assam** has a similar role for Assam tribal areas.
**Art. 246(4)**: Parliament legislates on **any matter** for areas not in a State (UTs), covering all three Lists.

47.s: Which of the following statements about legislative powers in specified tribal or Scheduled Areas is correct?
o: The Governor of every State may repeal any parliamentary Act throughout India
The President has no role in tribal areas of the North-Eastern States
Only the State Legislature may modify parliamentary Acts in Scheduled Areas
The Governor may bar or modify the application of parliamentary Acts in Scheduled Areas
47.x: The Governor may bar or modify the application of Acts of Parliament in Scheduled Areas. Special powers also exist for the Governor of Assam in Assam tribal areas and for the President in tribal areas of Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
47.tq: Use the territorial exception while rejecting overbroad claims about the Governor's power.
xs: The **Governor** may **bar or modify** the application of parliamentary Acts in **Scheduled Areas** — option **(4)**.
The power is limited to Scheduled Areas, not "throughout India" (option 1); it is the **Governor's**, not the State Legislature's (option 3).
xa: The **Governor of Assam** has a similar power for **Assam tribal areas**.
**President's regulations** for **Andaman & Nicobar** and **Lakshadweep** carry the force of Parliament's Acts.
⚠ **Extra-territorial** laws = Parliament only.

47.s: A law made by a State Legislature under the State List conflicts with a valid law made by Parliament under the Concurrent List. Which law ordinarily prevails?
o: The Parliamentary law, because the Concurrent List has precedence over the State List
The later law, irrespective of the legislative body
The law approved by the Governor
The State law, because the subject is administered by the State
47.x: The Concurrent List has precedence over the State List. Therefore, a valid Parliamentary law on a Concurrent List matter ordinarily prevails over an inconsistent State law.
47.tq: Apply the order of precedence to a concrete conflict rather than relying on administrative control.
xs: The **Parliamentary law** prevails, because the **Concurrent List has precedence over the State List** — option **(1)**.
Order of predominance: **Union List > Concurrent List > State List**.
**Art. 246(3)** makes State power on List II **subject to** 246(1) and (2).
xa: **Art. 254(1)**: on a **Concurrent** subject, Union law prevails; State law void to the extent of repugnancy.
**254(2)**: a State law **reserved and assented by the President** prevails **in that State**.
**Art. 251**: a law under **Art. 249/250** prevails over a conflicting State law.

47.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 246(4):
1. Parliament may legislate for Union Territories on matters in all three Lists.
2. The legislative power of Parliament for Union Territories is confined to the Union List.
3. The provision applies to areas not included in a State.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
47.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because Parliament’s power for Union Territories extends to all three Lists, not merely the Union List.
47.tq: Spot the restrictive word ‘confined’ and compare it with the wider territorial power.
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Art. 246(4)**: Parliament legislates on **any matter** for **areas not in a State** (UTs).
For UTs Parliament covers **all three Lists**, so statement 2 ("confined to the Union List") is wrong.
xa: **President's regulations** for **Andaman & Nicobar** and **Lakshadweep** have the force of Parliament's Acts.
**246(1)** = Parliament on **List I**; **246(2)** = both on **List III**; **246(3)** = State on **List II**.

47.s: Article 246A was inserted by which Constitutional Amendment Act?
47.x: Article 246A was introduced by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, which established the constitutional framework for GST.
47.tq: Match the distinctive constitutional article with the amendment that introduced it.
xs: **Art. 246A** was inserted by the **101st Constitutional Amendment Act** — option **(1)**.
Under it, **both** Parliament and States make **GST** laws; only Parliament for **inter-state supply (IGST)**.
xa: **Art. 246**: three lists in the **Seventh Schedule**.
**Art. 248** + **Entry 97** = residuary power, including **taxation**.

47.s: Which one of the following correctly states the present and original number of subjects in the Union and Concurrent Lists respectively?
o: Union 98 originally and 97 today; Concurrent 52 originally and 47 today
Union 97 originally and 98 today; Concurrent 47 originally and 52 today
Union 97 originally and 98 today; Concurrent 52 originally and 47 today
Union 98 originally and 100 today; Concurrent 47 originally and 52 today
47.x: The Union List has 98 subjects today compared with 97 originally, while the Concurrent List has 52 today compared with 47 originally.
47.tq: Compare present figures with original figures in the correct order of the two Lists.
xs: **Union 97** originally, **98** today; **Concurrent 47** originally, **52** today — option **(2)**.
State List: **66** originally, **59** now.
xa: Some notes (UPSC) give the present counts as **100 / 61 / 52**.
⚠ **Safe exam fact:** original **97/66/47**.
**Entry 97** of the Union List is also the **residuary** entry.

47.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The scheme of legislative distribution in India was borrowed from the Canadian model.
2. The Concurrent List has roots in the Government of India Act, 1935.
3. The Indian Constitution contains only two legislative lists.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
47.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the Seventh Schedule contains Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
47.tq: Reject the extreme numerical statement after confirming the two historically correct statements.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
1: Distribution borrowed from the **Canadian model**.
2: The **Concurrent List** follows the **Government of India Act 1935** tradition.
3 is wrong: there are **three lists** — Union, State, Concurrent.
xa: **Residuary power** with the Centre also follows **Canada** (strong Centre).
USA and Australia leave the residue with the **states**.
Original counts: **97/66/47**.

47.s: What did the Sarkaria Commission recommend regarding residuary powers, apart from taxation?
o: Giving residuary taxation exclusively to the States
Moving all residuary powers except taxation to the Concurrent List
Transferring all residuary powers to the State List
47.x: The Sarkaria Commission in 1988 recommended moving all residuary powers other than taxation to the Concurrent List.
47.tq: Identify the precise exception in a commission recommendation.
xs: The **Sarkaria Commission (1988)** recommended **moving all residuary powers except taxation to the Concurrent List** — option **(3)**.
Residuary **taxation** would stay with **Parliament**.
xa: At present **Art. 248** + **Entry 97** give **Parliament** exclusive residuary power.
The model is **Canada**; USA and Australia leave residue with the **states**.
Original Concurrent List count: **47**; now **52**.

47.s: In India, the residuary power of legislation is vested in Parliament by which combination?
o: Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List
Article 249 and Entry 97 of the State List
Article 250 and Entry 98 of the Concurrent List
Article 253 and Entry 97 of the Concurrent List
47.x: Article 248 and Entry 97 of the Union List together confer residuary legislative power on Parliament.
47.tq: Link the constitutional article with the corresponding Seventh Schedule entry.
xs: Residuary power: **Article 248** and **Entry 97 of the Union List** — option **(1)**.
Parliament has **exclusive** power over any matter not in the State or Concurrent List.
**Art. 249** = Rajya Sabha resolution; **Art. 250** = Emergency; **Art. 253** = treaties.
xa: Covers residuary **taxation** as well.
⚠ **97** is also the **original** Union List count.
Borrowed from **Canada**.

47.s:
With reference to Article 252, consider the following statements:
1. The legislatures of two or more States must pass resolutions requesting parliamentary legislation.
2. Any other State may adopt the resulting law later by passing a resolution of its legislature.
3. The requesting State Legislatures may independently repeal the law enacted by Parliament.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
47.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: only Parliament can amend or repeal a law enacted under Article 252.
47.tq: Find the statement that assigns legislative power to the wrong authority.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
1: Legislatures of **two or more States** pass resolutions; Parliament then legislates for them.
2: **Any other State** may later **adopt** the law by its own resolution.
3 is wrong: **only Parliament** can amend/repeal it; the requesting States **lose that power**.
xa: ⚠ **252** needs consent of **two or more states**; **253** needs **no state consent**.
Art. 252 Acts: **Prize Competition (1955)**, **Wild Life (1972)**, **Water (1974)**, **Urban Land Ceiling (1976)**, **Human Organs (1994)**.
"Art. 252 laws cannot be changed by states" is cited as a **centralising tool**.

47.s: A law made for a State during President’s Rule continues after the Proclamation ends until:
o: the State Legislature alters, repeals or re-enacts it
the Supreme Court declares it permanent
the Governor issues an ordinance replacing it
47.x: Such a law does not automatically lapse when President’s Rule ends. It continues until the State Legislature alters, repeals or re-enacts it.
47.tq: Test the post-emergency effect instead of confusing continuation with automatic repeal.
xs: A President's Rule law continues until the **State Legislature alters, repeals or re-enacts** it — option **(1)**.
It does not lapse automatically when the Proclamation ends.
xa: Such laws are made by **Parliament** or the **President by delegation** (**Art. 356**).
Contrast: **Art. 250** laws lapse **6 months** after the emergency; **Art. 249** laws **6 months** after the resolution lapses.

47.s: Which one of the following statements is NOT correct regarding the five constitutional situations in which Parliament may legislate on State List matters?
o: Article 252 operates when one State Legislature alone requests parliamentary legislation.
Article 356 operates during President’s Rule in a State.
Article 250 operates during a Proclamation of Emergency.
47.x: Article 252 requires resolutions from the legislatures of two or more States, not one State Legislature alone. Articles 249, 250 and 356 are correctly described.
47.tq: Test the minimum numerical condition and reject the deceptively shortened requirement.
xs: **Art. 252** needs resolutions by **two or more States**, not one — so option **(1)** is NOT correct.
"A request by **one state** is not" a valid route (exam angle).
**356** = **President's Rule**; **249** = **national interest**; **250** = **Emergency** — all correct.
xa: The fifth route: **Art. 253** — **international agreements**.
After an Art. 252 law, **only Parliament** can amend/repeal it.
Other States may **adopt** the law by resolution.

47.s: With respect to restrictions imposed by a State on inter-State trade, which one of the following is correct?
o: Every restriction is prohibited irrespective of public interest
Parliament can discriminate freely between States during normal conditions
Reasonable restrictions in the public interest may be imposed, but the Bill requires the President's previous sanction
The Governor's previous sanction is sufficient in every case
47.x: A State may impose reasonable restrictions on inter-State trade in the public interest, but a Bill for that purpose requires the President's previous sanction. Parliament is also restricted from discriminating between States except in situations of scarcity.
47.tq: Combine the substantive test of reasonableness with the procedural requirement of prior sanction.
xs: State laws may impose **reasonable restrictions in the public interest** on inter-state trade, but the Bill needs the **President's previous sanction** — option **(3)**.
The rules sit in **Part XIII, Arts. 301-305**.
**Arts. 301-303** bar **Parliament** from preferring or discriminating between States except in **scarcity**.
xa: **Art. 255**: recommendations and previous sanctions are **matters of procedure only** — later **assent** cures the defect.
**Inter-state** trade = **Union**; trade **within** a State = **State**.

47.s: Articles 301 to 303 principally restrict Parliament from doing which of the following in relation to trade and commerce?
o: Making any law concerning inter-State trade
47.x: Articles 301 to 303 restrict discriminatory or preferential treatment between States in laws relating to trade and commerce.
47.tq: Distinguish a restriction against discrimination from a complete prohibition on regulation.
xs: **Arts. 301-303** stop Parliament from **preferring or discriminating between States** in trade laws — option **(1)**.
Discrimination is allowed only in **scarcity**.
xa: State restrictions on **inter-state trade**: reasonable, in **public interest**, with **President's previous sanction** (Part XIII, **Arts. 301-305**).
**Inter-state trade** is a **Union** subject; trade **within** a State is a State subject.

47.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the effect of a Parliamentary law made under Article 249 or Article 250 when it conflicts with a State law?
o: The Governor decides which law will prevail.
The Parliamentary law prevails over the State law.
The State law prevails because State subjects remain exclusively State matters.
Both laws become void to the extent of conflict.
47.x: Article 251 provides that a Parliamentary law made under Article 249 or 250 prevails over an inconsistent State law.
47.tq: Use the conflict rule to identify the superior law and reject the wrong authority.
xs: Under **Art. 251**, the **Parliamentary (Union) law prevails** over a conflicting State law — option **(2)**.
The State law is **inoperative only while** the Union law lasts.
The Governor has no role; the State law is not void permanently.
xa: The **State legislature's power is not suspended** under Art. 249 or 250.
**Art. 249** law ceases **6 months after the resolution lapses**; **Art. 250** law **6 months** after the emergency.
**Art. 254(1)**: on a Concurrent subject, **Central law prevails**.

47.s:
Consider the following statements regarding a resolution under Article 249:
1. It remains in force for a period not exceeding one year.
2. It may be renewed any number of times.
3. Each renewal may extend it for a period exceeding one year.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
47.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: every renewal can extend the resolution only for one year at a time.
47.tq: Watch the limiting phrase ‘one year at a time’ in a duration question.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
1: An **Art. 249** resolution is in force **not exceeding 1 year**.
2: It is **renewable any number of times**.
3 is wrong: each renewal is only **1 year at a time**.
xa: Majority: **2/3 of members present and voting** (APPSC-GS 2025).
Laws **cease 6 months after** the resolution lapses.
State power is **not suspended** but the Union law prevails (**Art. 251**).

47.s: Which one of the following statements regarding State legislative power during the operation of Article 249 is correct?
o: The State Legislature may legislate only after obtaining the consent of the Rajya Sabha.
The State Legislature’s power is suspended, but the Governor may legislate.
The State Legislature may still legislate, but the Parliamentary law prevails in case of conflict.
The State Legislature is dissolved for the entire duration of the resolution.
47.x: An Article 249 resolution does not suspend the State Legislature’s power. However, the Parliamentary law prevails if it conflicts with a State law.
47.tq: Reject the extreme claim that a special Union power automatically removes State legislative power.
xs: The **State Legislature may still legislate**, but the **Parliamentary law prevails** in case of conflict — option **(3)**.
State power is **not suspended** by Art. 249; there is no dissolution or Rajya Sabha consent.
xa: **Art. 251**: the State law is **inoperative only while** the Union law lasts.
Same for **Art. 250** during an Emergency.
Art. 249 resolution: **2/3 present and voting**, **up to 1 year**.

47.s: Which one of the following is NOT an example of legislation enacted under Article 252?
o: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
47.x: The Prize Competition Act, 1955, the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 were enacted under Article 252 on resolutions of two or more States. The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 is not an Article 252 law; it was enacted to implement an international (Stockholm) commitment, i.e. under Article 253.
47.tq: Find the option outside the specified group of Article 252 examples.
xs: The **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986** is NOT in the list of **Art. 252** Acts — option **(2)**.
Art. 252 Acts: **Prize Competition (1955)**, **Wild Life (Protection) (1972)**, **Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) (1974)**.
xa: Others: **Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976**; **Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994**.
**Art. 253** covers **environment treaties** — no State consent needed.
⚠ **252** = consent of **two or more States**; **253** = treaties.

47.s:
Which of the following Acts is associated with parliamentary legislation under Article 252?
1. Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976
2. Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994
3. Prize Competition Act, 1955
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
47.x: All three Acts are listed as examples of laws enacted by Parliament under Article 252 following resolutions by two or more State Legislatures.
47.tq: Test the complete list by checking whether each named example belongs to the same constitutional route.
xs: All three were passed under **Art. 252** — option **(4)** (**1, 2 and 3**).
**Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976**, **Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994**, **Prize Competition Act, 1955**.
xa: Also under Art. 252: **Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972** and **Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974**.
Only **Parliament** can amend/repeal these; the requesting States lose that power.
Other States may **adopt** the law by resolution.

47.s: A law is required to implement an international environmental convention, although the subject otherwise falls in the State List. Which constitutional provision directly supports Parliament's competence?
47.x: Article 253 authorises Parliament to legislate for implementing treaties, agreements, conventions and decisions of international bodies, even on State List subjects.
47.tq: Identify the constitutional route from the purpose of the legislation rather than from the subject alone.
xs: **Article 253** lets Parliament implement **international conventions** even on **State List** subjects — option **(3)**.
It covers **environment treaties** and needs **no state consent**.
**249** needs a Rajya Sabha resolution; **250** an Emergency; **356** President's Rule.
xa: Applies to the **whole or any part of India**; includes decisions of **international bodies** (APPSC-GS 2018).
⚠ **252** = consent of **two or more states**; **253** = **no state consent**.

47.s:
With reference to Article 254(2), consider the following statements:
1. A State law on a Concurrent List subject that is repugnant to a Union law prevails in that State if it has been reserved for and received the assent of the President.
2. Such a State law then prevails throughout India.
3. Parliament can later override such a State law by a fresh law amending or repealing it.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
47.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct: with the President's assent the State law prevails in that State, and under the proviso Parliament can later amend or repeal it with a fresh law. Statement 2 is wrong: the State law prevails only in that State, not throughout India. Option A misses statement 3, and options C and D include statement 2.
47.tq: 254(2): President's assent → prevails in that State only; Parliament can override
xs: Statements **1 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
1: A repugnant State law **reserved and assented by the President** prevails **in that State**.
2 is wrong: it prevails **only in that State**, not throughout India.
3: **Proviso** — Parliament can later **override it with a fresh law**, so States are "practically powerless".
xa: **254(1)**: normally the **Central law prevails**.
The **Governor** reserves such a bill under **254(2)**.
Repugnancy applies to the **Concurrent List** field.

47.s: A State law on prohibition incidentally affects a matter in another legislative field, but its true nature is within the State List. Which case is associated with upholding such legislation under the doctrine of pith and substance?
o: State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v. Bank of Commerce
K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa
47.x: In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), the prohibition law was upheld under the doctrine of pith and substance. The incidental encroachment did not alter its true character.
47.tq: Connect the factual subject of a case with the doctrine applied in that case.
xs: **State of Bombay v F.N. Balsara (1951)** upheld the **Bombay Prohibition Act** under the **doctrine of pith and substance** — option **(1)**.
Its **true nature** fell in the **State List**; incidental encroachment was ignored.
**Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee (1947, Privy Council)** also applied pith and substance, but not to a prohibition law; **Gajapati Narayan Deo (1953)** is **colourable legislation**.
xa: ⚠ **Balsara (1951)** = pith and substance; **Gajapati Narayan Deo (1953)** = colourable legislation.
**Harmonious construction**: entries read together so both operate.
**Repugnancy (Art. 254)**: Union law prevails in the **Concurrent** field.

47.s: Which doctrine requires legislative entries to be read together so that each can operate harmoniously?
47.x: Harmonious construction requires apparently overlapping entries to be interpreted together so that both retain operative effect.
47.tq: Discriminate among neighbouring doctrines by their operative principle.
xs: **Harmonious construction** reads entries together so that **both operate** — option **(2)**.
**Pith and substance** looks at a law's **true nature**; **repugnancy** (**Art. 254**) makes Union law prevail; **colourable legislation** bars doing indirectly what cannot be done directly.
xa: Pith and substance case: **State of Bombay v F.N. Balsara (1951)**.
Colourable legislation case: **K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v State of Orissa (1953)**.
Under **254(2)**, a State law with **President's assent** prevails in that State.

47.s: Which one of the following is the odd one out with reference to the Concurrent List in the Seventh Schedule?
47.x: Fisheries is a State List subject. Succession, criminal law and civil procedure are subjects in the Concurrent List.
47.tq: Identify the subject belonging to a different list rather than relying on a familiar association.
xs: **Fisheries** is a **State** subject — the odd one out — option **(3)**.
**Criminal law**, **succession** and **civil procedure** are all **Concurrent** subjects.
xa: Other State subjects: **public health and sanitation**, **agriculture**, **markets**.
Other Concurrent subjects: **adulteration** of foodstuffs, marriage and divorce, **drugs**, **electricity**, **newspapers**.
Union subjects: **RBI**, **foreign loans**, banking, **currency**, **census**, **inter-state trade**.

47.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Trade and commerce within a State — Union List
47.x: Agriculture is a State List subject, so B is correct. Trade and commerce within a State is a State List subject (not Union), while currency and foreign loans are Union List subjects (not State or Concurrent).
47.tq: Use the list allocation of familiar subjects to eliminate swapped entries.
xs: **Agriculture — State List** — option **(2)**.
Trade and commerce **within** a State is a **State** subject, not Union (option 1).
**Currency** and **foreign loans** are **Union** subjects (options 3 and 4 wrong).
xa: ⚠ **Inter-state** trade = Union; trade **within** a State = State.
Farm Laws used Concurrent **Entry 33** although agriculture is **State List Entry 14**.
Other State subjects: **public health and sanitation**, **markets**, **fisheries**.

47.s: The constitutional basis for Parliament enacting the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act is primarily found in which entry?
47.x: Prevention of cruelty to animals is placed in Concurrent List Entry 17, enabling Parliament to enact central legislation on the subject.
47.tq: Distinguish the Concurrent List entry on animal cruelty from the State entry on preservation of livestock.
xs: **Prevention of cruelty to animals** is **Concurrent List Entry 17** — the basis of the central **Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act** — option **(1)**.
**State Entry 15** is **preservation of livestock**; **Concurrent Entry 33** was used for the **Farm Laws**.
xa: Cow slaughter: preservation of livestock = **State** subject (**Entry 15**) + DPSP **Art. 48**.
Other Concurrent subjects: **criminal law**, **civil procedure**, **succession**, **marriage and divorce**.

47.s:
With reference to cow slaughter, consider the following statements:
1. Preservation of livestock is a State List subject.
2. Article 48 is relevant to the constitutional policy concerning preservation of livestock.
3. Parliament may legislate on the subject only through the ordinary Union List power.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
47.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false: Parliament can legislate on the State subject through Articles 249, 250 or 252, among the specified routes.
47.tq: Spot the wrong statement that incorrectly converts a special legislative route into an ordinary Union power.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
1: **Preservation of livestock** is a **State** subject (**Entry 15**).
2: DPSP **Art. 48** is the relevant policy provision.
3 is wrong: the subject is in the **State List**, not the Union List.
xa: **Prevention of cruelty to animals** is a separate **Concurrent** subject (**Entry 17**).
Parliament can reach State subjects only via **Arts. 249, 250, 252, 253, 356**.

47.s: Which of the following examples has been cited in debates concerning use of the Concurrent List to reach State subjects?
o: Farm Laws through Concurrent List Entry 33
Currency regulation through State List Entry 15
Foreign affairs through Concurrent List Entry 3
47.x: Farm Laws were discussed as an example of Concurrent List Entry 33 being used in a field associated with agriculture, which is State List Entry 14.
47.tq: Match the debated law with the relevant Concurrent List entry and the associated State subject.
xs: **Farm Laws** were made via **Concurrent List Entry 33** — option **(2)**.
Critics say this reached a **State** subject, as agriculture is **State List Entry 14**.
**Census**, **currency** and **foreign affairs** are **Union** subjects, so the other options are wrong.
xa: The **NEP** and **NMC Act** are also cited in the Concurrent List encroachment debate.
Other centralising tools: **Art. 254(2)** override; **Art. 249/252** use.
**Frequent ordinances** and **Union List dominance** are also criticised.

47.s: The Supreme Court's advisory opinion of November 2025 was reported in connection with which issue?
o: Deemed assent and timelines for Governors and the President
Allocation of residuary powers to States
Transfer of forests to the Union List
47.x: The advisory opinion rejected deemed assent and fixed timelines concerning Governors and the President.
47.tq: Identify the constitutional controversy from the paired concepts rather than from a general federalism label.
xs: The SC advisory opinion (**Nov 2025**) rejected **deemed assent** and **fixed timelines** for **Governors/President** — option **(1)**.
It concerns assent to State bills, linked to **Art. 254(2)** reservation by the Governor.
xa: Under **254(2)**, the Governor may reserve a bill as an exception to **aid-and-advice**.
A State law with **President's assent** prevails **in that State**.
Parliament can later **override** it with a fresh law.

47.s: The MMDR (Amendment) Bill, 2026 was reported as restricting the States' power to tax which subject?
47.x: The Bill was reported as restricting State taxation power over mineral rights and mineral-bearing land. Kerala viewed this as encroachment on State List Entries 18 and 50.
47.tq: Match the legislative development with the precise fiscal subject affected.
xs: The **MMDR (Amendment) Bill, 2026** restricts States' power to tax **mineral rights and mineral-bearing land** — option **(3)**.
**Kerala** called it an encroachment on State **Entries 18 and 50** and may go to court (**15 Aug 2026**).
xa: Preventive detention: **Union Entry 9** + **Concurrent Entry 3**.
**Sarkaria Commission (1988)** recommended moving non-tax residuary powers to the **Concurrent List**.

47.s:
With reference to preventive detention, consider the following statements:
1. Union List Entry 9 covers defence, foreign affairs and security.
2. Concurrent List Entry 3 covers State security and public order.
3. Preventive detention is placed exclusively in the State List.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
47.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct because preventive detention-related powers are divided between Union List Entry 9 and Concurrent List Entry 3. Statement 3 is false because the subject is not exclusively in the State List.
47.tq: Reject the exclusive-allocation trap when the constitutional scheme divides a subject between lists.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
1: **Union List Entry 9** — **defence, foreign affairs, security**.
2: **Concurrent List Entry 3** — **state security, public order**.
3 is wrong: the power is **split** between the Union and Concurrent Lists, not exclusively State.
xa: The **Allahabad HC** criticised the **routine use** of preventive detention.
In the Concurrent field, **Union law prevails** (**Art. 254(1)**).

47.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Articles 256 to 263 concern administrative relations.
Statement B: Article 263 concerns the Inter-State Council.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
47.x: Both are true: Articles 256–263 are on administrative relations, ending with Article 263 on the Inter-State Council.
47.tq: Recall the range and its last Article.
n: Articles 256 to 263 concern administrative relations. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 263 concerns the Inter-State Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)** is correct.
A: **Articles 256 to 263** deal with **Administrative relations**.
B: **Article 263** provides for the **Inter-State Council**.
xa: **Articles 245 to 255** = **Legislative relations**; both sets sit in **Part XI**.
**Articles 268 to 281** = **Distribution of revenues**; **Article 280** = **Finance Commission**.
**Articles 301 to 307** = **Freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse**.

47.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Articles 268 to 281 concern the distribution of revenues.
Statement B: Article 281 concerns the recommendations of the Finance Commission.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
47.x: Both are true: Articles 268–281 deal with distribution of revenues, ending with Article 281 on the Finance Commission's recommendations (the Commission itself is Article 280).
47.tq: Separate Article 280 (Commission) from 281 (recommendations).
n: Articles 268 to 281 concern the distribution of revenues. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 281 concerns the recommendations of the Finance Commission. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)** is correct.
A: **Articles 268 to 281** deal with **Distribution of revenues**.
B: **Article 281** concerns the Finance Commission's **recommendations**; the Commission itself is **Article 280**.
xa: **Articles 256 to 263** = **Administrative relations**; **Article 263** = **Inter-State Council**.
**Article 253** = laws to implement **international agreements**.
**Article 248** = **Residuary powers** in Parliament.

47.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Article 356 enables Parliament to exercise the legislative powers of the State Legislature during President's Rule in that State.
Statement B: Article 250 is activated by a request from at least two State Legislatures.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
47.x: A is true: under Article 356 Parliament exercises the State Legislature's powers during President's Rule. B is false: Article 250 is triggered by a National Emergency; a request by two States is Article 252.
47.tq: Match the trigger to the Article.
n: Article 250 permits Parliament to legislate on State List subjects during the operation of a National Emergency under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Article 252 permits Parliament to legislate on State List subjects following requests by at least two State Legislatures through resolutions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Article 356 permits Parliament to legislate on State List subjects following a proclamation of President’s Rule in a State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Under Article 356, Parliament exercises the legislative powers of the State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xs: **Statement A is true, Statement B is false** — option **(3)** is correct.
A: under **Article 356**, during **President's Rule**, **Parliament** exercises the legislative powers of the State Legislature (or the President by delegation).
B is wrong: **Article 250** is triggered by a **National Emergency**; a request by **two or more** State Legislatures is **Article 252**.
xa: The five special circumstances: **Art. 249, 250, 252, 253** and **356**.
**President's Rule laws** stay in force after PR ends until the state legislature repeals, alters or re-enacts them.
⚠ A request by **one** state is **not** valid under Art. 252.

47.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. State Legislatures have exclusive legislative competence over the State List.
II. Both Parliament and State Legislatures have competence over the Concurrent List.
III. Parliament has exclusive competence over the Union List.
IV. State Legislatures have exclusive competence over the Concurrent List.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
47.x: I, II and III are correct under Article 246: Parliament alone for the Union List, States alone for the State List, both for the Concurrent List. IV is wrong because the Concurrent List is shared, not exclusive to States.
47.tq: 'Concurrent' means shared, never exclusive.
n: Parliament has exclusive legislative competence over List I, the Union List, under Article 246(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
State Legislatures have exclusive legislative competence over List II, the State List, under Article 246(3). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Both Parliament and State Legislatures have concurrent legislative competence over List III, the Concurrent List, under Article 246(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xs: Statements **I, II and III only** are correct — option **(3)**.
Under **Article 246**: **246(1)** Parliament — exclusive over **List I**; **246(3)** States — exclusive over **List II**; **246(2)** both — **List III**.
IV is wrong: the **Concurrent List** is shared by **Parliament and State Legislatures**, not exclusive to States.
xa: **Art. 246(4):** Parliament may legislate on any matter for areas not in a state (**UTs**).
**Precedence:** **Union List > Concurrent List > State List**.
**Article 246A** (**101st Amendment, 2016**) gives **simultaneous** GST power to Parliament and States.

47.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Railways
(b) Police
(c) Education
(d) Marriage, Divorce and Adoption

List-II
(i) Union List
(ii) State List
(iii) Concurrent List since 1950
(iv) Moved from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment
47.x: Railways – Union List; Police – State List; Education – moved from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment (1976); marriage, divorce and adoption – an original Concurrent List entry.
47.tq: Separate original Concurrent entries from those transferred in 1976.
n: Railways are a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Police is a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Education is a Concurrent List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Education was shifted to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Marriage is a Concurrent List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Divorce is a Concurrent List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Adoption is a Concurrent List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Railways belong to the Union List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Police belongs to the State List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xs: The correct code is **a-i, b-ii, c-iv, d-iii** — option **(2)**.
**Railways** = **Union List**; **Police** = **State List**.
**Education** moved from State to Concurrent by the **42nd Amendment**; **marriage, divorce and adoption** has been a Concurrent subject since **1950**.
xa: Entry counts: Union **97** → **98**; State **66** → **59**; Concurrent **47** → **52**.
The Concurrent List follows the **Government of India Act 1935** tradition; the scheme is borrowed from **Canada**.
⚠ Original counts **97/66/47** are the safe exam fact.

47.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: In case of conflict on a Concurrent List subject, the Central law generally prevails.
Repugnancy between Central and State laws on a Concurrent List subject is dealt with under Article 250.
The general rule of Central law prevailing is subject to the exception relating to Presidential assent.
A State law on a Concurrent List subject may prevail if it was reserved for Presidential assent and received such assent under Article 254(2).
47.x: B is incorrect: repugnancy on a Concurrent subject is dealt with by Article 254, not 250 (Emergency legislation). Under 254 the Central law prevails unless a State law reserved for the President gets his assent (254(2)).
47.tq: Check the Article number given for repugnancy.
n: Article 254 governs repugnancy between Central and State legislation on a Concurrent List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Central legislation prevails when it conflicts with State legislation on a Concurrent List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]

A State law can prevail over conflicting Central legislation when the State law was reserved for the President’s assent and received that assent under Article 254(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Article 250 permits Parliament to legislate on State List subjects during the operation of a National Emergency under Article 352. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xs: The incorrect statement is that repugnancy is dealt with under **Article 250** — option **(2)**; repugnancy is under **Article 254**.
**Art. 254(1):** on a **Concurrent List** subject, the **Central** law prevails; State law is void to the extent of repugnancy.
**254(2):** a State law **reserved for and assented by the President** prevails **in that state**.
xa: **Proviso:** Parliament can later **override** such a State law with a **fresh law**.
The Governor may reserve a bill under **254(2)** as an exception to aid-and-advice.
**Article 250** = Parliament on the State List during an **Emergency**.

47.s: A law made by Parliament under Article 249 remains in force for what period after the Rajya Sabha resolution lapses?
47.x: A law under Article 249 ceases six months after the Rajya Sabha resolution lapses (each resolution lasts one year and can be renewed).
47.tq: Separate the one-year resolution from the six-month grace period.
