1. Under first-past-the-post for the Lok Sabha, a candidate must secure more than half of the valid votes to win.
2. The Rajya Sabha, Legislative Councils, President and Vice-President are elected by proportional representation through the single transferable vote.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
63.x: Statement 1 is wrong: FPTP needs only the most votes (plurality) in a single-member constituency, not a majority. Statement 2 is correct: PR by single transferable vote is used for the Rajya Sabha, Legislative Councils, President and Vice-President. So B; A and C accept the wrong statement 1, D rejects the correct statement 2.
63.tq: FPTP = plurality, not majority; PR-STV = indirect elections.
xs: Only statement 2 is correct — option **(2) 2 only**.
Statement 1 is wrong: under **FPTP** the winner needs only the **most votes (plurality)**, not a majority.
Statement 2 is right: **Rajya Sabha, Legislative Councils, President, Vice-President** are elected by **PR (single transferable vote)**.
xa: FPTP (territorial, single-member) is used for the **Lok Sabha** and **Assemblies**.
PR was rejected for Lok Sabha as hard for voters and prone to **fragmentation and unstable** governments.
**Security deposit** is forfeited below **one-sixth** of valid votes.

63.s: Which of the following is NOT cited as a reason for rejecting proportional representation for Lok Sabha elections?
o: It may encourage fragmentation and unstable governments.
It guarantees a direct election in every single-member constituency.
It weakens the voter–Member of Parliament link.
It may be difficult for voters to understand.
63.x: Difficulty for voters, fragmentation, unstable governments, expense, absence of by-elections and a weaker voter–MP link are cited concerns. Guaranteeing direct election in every single-member constituency is not such a reason.
63.tq: Find the option that is outside the stated list of objections to proportional representation.
xs: "It **guarantees a direct election in every single-member constituency**" is not a cited reason — option **(2)**; single-member constituencies are a feature of **FPTP**.
Cited reasons: **hard for voters**, **fragmentation and unstable** governments, **weakens voter-MP link** — options (1), (3), (4).
xa: Other reasons: PR is **expensive** and allows **no by-elections**.
PR (STV) is used for **Rajya Sabha, Legislative Councils, President, Vice-President**.
Under FPTP the winner is the one with the **most votes (plurality)**.

63.s: A candidate's security deposit is forfeited when the candidate secures less than:
63.x: The security deposit is forfeited if the candidate obtains less than one-sixth of the valid votes.
63.tq: Recall the exact fractional threshold and distinguish it from common one-fourth and one-third distractors.
xs: The **security deposit** is forfeited below **one-sixth** of valid votes — option **(2)**.
One-third, one-tenth and one-fourth are not the stated threshold.
xa: FPTP winner = candidate with the **most votes (plurality)**, not a majority.
**NOTA** has no electoral effect: even if NOTA leads, the **highest-scoring candidate** wins.

63.s: Which one of the following pairs relating to Delimitation Commissions is NOT correctly matched?
63.x: The 1973 Commission was chaired by Justice J.L. Kapur. Justice Kuldip Singh chaired the 2002 Commission.
63.tq: Find the swapped chairperson in a date-person matching question.
xs: **1973 — Justice Kuldip Singh** is wrong — option **(2)**; the 1973 Commission was chaired by **Justice J.L. Kapur**.
Correct: **2002 — Kuldip Singh**, **1963 — J.L. Kapur**, **1952 — N. Chandrasekhara Aiyar**.
xa: ⚠ **J.L. Kapur** chaired two Commissions (**1963, 1973**).
**J&K** Delimitation Commission: **Justice Ranjana Desai** (orders effective March/May **2022**).
Delimitation orders **cannot be challenged in court**.

63.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the years of the Delimitation Acts from the years in which the corresponding Commissions were constituted?
63.x: The Delimitation Acts were enacted in 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002, while the Commissions were constituted in 1952, 1963, 1973 and 2002.
63.tq: Separate the closely related years of legislation from the years of constitution of the Commissions.
xs: The other options shuffle the Act and Commission years.
xa: There have been **four** Commissions so far.
Chairs: **1952** N. Chandrasekhara Aiyar; **1963** and **1973** J.L. Kapur; **2002** Kuldip Singh.
Readjustment is under **Art. 82** (Lok Sabha) and **Art. 170** (Assemblies) after each census.

63.s: The constitutional principle underlying delimitation is best expressed as:
o: One State, one vote, one value
One district, one representative, one value
One party, one constituency, one value
One person, one vote, one value
63.x: Delimitation rests on the principle of ‘one person, one vote, one value’, associated with uniformity of representation under Article 81(2).
63.tq: Discriminate among similar-looking formulations of the electoral equality principle.
xs: Delimitation rests on **"one person, one vote, one value"** — option **(4)**.
It flows from **Art. 81(2)** uniformity of representation.
xa: Also phrased as **one citizen-one vote-one value** (UPSC; APPSC-G1 **2024**).
Readjustment after each census: **Art. 82** (Lok Sabha) and **Art. 170** (Assemblies).

63.s:
Which of the following statements about the Delimitation Commission is correct?
1. It is constituted under an Act of Parliament.
2. It works with the Election Commission of India.
3. Its orders may be modified by either House of Parliament.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
63.x: The Commission is constituted under parliamentary legislation and works with the ECI. Its orders cannot be modified by the Lok Sabha or State Legislative Assemblies, so statement 3 is false.
63.tq: Use the ‘wrong authority’ trap to test who can modify delimitation orders.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: set up under an **Act of Parliament**; statement 2: it works **with the ECI**.
Statement 3 is wrong: its orders **cannot be modified** by the Lok Sabha or Assemblies.
xa: Its orders also **cannot be challenged in court**.

63.s:
Consider the following statements about the 84th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2001:
1. It extended the freeze on inter-State seat allocation until after the first census following 2026.
2. It permitted rationalisation of constituencies on the basis of the 1991 Census.
3. It changed the total number of Lok Sabha seats on the basis of the 2001 Census.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: The 84th Amendment extended the freeze and allowed rationalisation using the 1991 Census. It did not change the total number of seats on the basis of the 2001 Census.
63.tq: Separate rationalisation of boundaries from alteration of the total number of seats.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
**84th (2001)** extended the freeze to the **first census after 2026** and allowed rationalisation on the **1991 Census**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the **87th (2003)** used the **2001 Census** for boundaries, with **total seats unchanged**.
xa: The original freeze: **42nd (1976)**, on the **1971 Census**, till **2000**.
Per-State Lok Sabha numbers unchanged since **1976**.

63.s: Which one of the following statements about the Tamil Nadu Assembly resolution is NOT correct?
o: It proposed freezing the Lok Sabha at 543 seats permanently.
It proposed retaining a 2.2:1 Lok Sabha to Rajya Sabha ratio.
It linked the proposed women’s quota to delimitation from 2029.
It proposed women’s quota from 2029 without linking it to delimitation.
63.x: The resolution proposed women’s reservation from 2029 without linking it to delimitation. It also proposed a permanent freeze at 543 Lok Sabha seats and retention of the 2.2:1 ratio.
63.tq: Locate the reversal of an expressly stated condition in a policy-resolution question.
xs: The resolution did **not link** the **women's quota** to delimitation — so option **(3)** is NOT correct.
It proposed women's quota **from 2029 without linking it to delimitation**, a **permanent freeze at 543**, and the **2.2:1** Lok Sabha-Rajya Sabha ratio.
xa: Resolution dated **17 Aug 2026**; southern States fear losing seats to **UP, Bihar, Rajasthan**.
**131st Amendment Bill, 2026** (ceiling **550 to 850**) was defeated — **298 for, 230 against**.
EAC-PM (2026) suggested splitting **170** oversized seats to reach **824**.

63.s: The present number of elected Lok Sabha seats, as distinguished from the constitutional ceiling mentioned, is:
63.x: The Lok Sabha has 543 elected seats against a ceiling of 550, comprising 530 seats for States and 20 for Union Territories in the stated allocation framework.
63.tq: Distinguish the existing elected strength from the maximum ceiling.
xs: The Lok Sabha has **543 elected seats** against a ceiling of **550** — option **(1)**.
The ceiling is **530** for States + **20** for UTs.
xa: ⚠ **Stale value**: "maximum 552 including 2 Anglo-Indians" — Anglo-Indian seats ended in **2020**.
**131st Amendment Bill, 2026** proposed raising the ceiling from **550 to 850** on the **2011 Census**; it was defeated.

63.s: Which one of the following statements correctly describes the relationship between Articles 81(2), 82 and 170 in delimitation?
o: Article 81(2) expresses uniformity of representation, while Articles 82 and 170 provide for constituency readjustment for Parliament and State Assemblies respectively.
Articles 82 and 170 prescribe the powers of the Election Commission but not constituency readjustment.
Article 81(2) deals only with Panchayat elections, while Articles 82 and 170 concern presidential elections.
Article 82 concerns Rajya Sabha elections and Article 170 concerns municipal elections.
63.x: Article 81(2) embodies uniformity of representation, while Articles 82 and 170 provide the constitutional basis for readjustment of Lok Sabha and Assembly constituencies.
63.tq: Map each Article to its distinct constitutional function rather than its broad election subject.
xs: **Art. 81(2)** = **uniformity of representation**; **Art. 82** and **Art. 170** = readjustment for **Lok Sabha** and **Assemblies** — option **(1)**.
They do not concern ECI powers, panchayats, presidential, Rajya Sabha or municipal polls.
xa: Principle: **"one person, one vote, one value"**.
Readjustment takes place **after each census** through a **Delimitation Commission** set up under an Act of Parliament.

63.s: The freeze on the inter-State allocation of Lok Sabha seats on the basis of the 1971 Census was first imposed by which Amendment, and until when?
63.x: The 42nd Amendment (1976) froze inter-State seat allocation on the 1971 Census till 2000 to encourage population control. The 84th Amendment (2001) extended the freeze till the first census after 2026, and the 87th (2003) switched boundary redrawing to the 2001 Census. The 44th Amendment did not deal with the freeze.
63.tq: 42nd froze (1971 Census, till 2000); 84th extended (till 2026); 87th = 2001 Census boundaries.
xs: The **42nd Amendment, 1976** first froze allocation on the **1971 Census**, **till 2000** — option **(1)**.
The **84th (2001)** later extended it to the first census after **2026**; the **87th (2003)** switched boundaries to the **2001 Census**.
xa: Purpose of the freeze: **population control**.
**106th Amendment (2023)**: women's quota begins only after the next census (**2027 Census**) and delimitation.

63.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Article 330 — Reservation of seats for SCs and STs in the Lok Sabha
2. Article 331 — Nomination of one Anglo-Indian to each State Assembly by the Governor
3. Article 334A — Reservation of one-third of seats for women
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
63.x: Pair 1 is correct: Art. 330 covers SC/ST seats in the Lok Sabha (Art. 332 covers Assemblies). Pair 2 is wrong: Art. 331 was the President's nomination of 2 Anglo-Indians to the Lok Sabha; the Governor's nomination to Assemblies was Art. 333. Pair 3 is correct: the 106th Amendment's women's quota is Art. 334A. So B; A leaves out pair 3, C and D include the wrong pair 2.
63.tq: Even numbers 330/332 = reservation; odd 331/333 = Anglo-Indian nomination (President/Governor).
xs: Pairs 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Pair 1: **Art. 330** = SC/ST seats in the **Lok Sabha**. Pair 3: **Art. 334A** = women's **one-third** (106th Amendment).
Pair 2 is wrong: **Art. 331** = President's nomination of **2** Anglo-Indians to the Lok Sabha; the Governor's nomination was **Art. 333**.
xa: ⚠ **330 / 332** = SC/ST seats; **331 / 333** = Anglo-Indians (ended).
**Art. 334** originally set **10 years** (till **1960**), repeatedly extended.

63.s:
With reference to reserved Lok Sabha constituencies in Andhra Pradesh, consider the following statements:
1. Amalapuram is a Scheduled Caste-reserved constituency.
2. Araku is a Scheduled Tribe-reserved constituency.
3. Tirupati is a Scheduled Tribe-reserved constituency.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: Amalapuram and Tirupati are Scheduled Caste-reserved constituencies in Andhra Pradesh, whereas Araku is the Scheduled Tribe-reserved constituency.
63.tq: Discriminate between SC and ST constituencies within the same State.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
**Amalapuram** is SC-reserved; **Araku** is AP's only ST seat.
Statement 3 is wrong: **Tirupati** is an **SC** seat, not ST.
xa: AP's **4** SC seats: **Amalapuram, Bapatla, Chittoor, Tirupati**.
⚠ **AP** = 4 SC + 1 ST; **Telangana** = 3 SC + 2 ST (**Adilabad, Mahabubabad** ST).

63.s:
Which of the following statements correctly describes the allocation of SC and ST reserved constituencies?
1. ST seats are generally located where the share of the ST population is highest.
2. SC seats are spread across the State and rotated at each delimitation.
3. All voters in a reserved constituency, and not merely voters belonging to the reserved community, may vote.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
63.x: ST seats are concentrated in areas with the highest ST population share, SC seats are spread and rotated at delimitation, and reserved constituencies have a common electorate of all voters.
63.tq: Combine location, rotation and electorate principles in one reservation question.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**ST seats** go where the ST share is highest; **SC seats** are spread and **rotated** at each delimitation.
**No separate electorate** (Arts. **330/332**): **all voters** of the constituency vote.
xa: AP has **4** SC + **1** ST Lok Sabha seats; Telangana **3** SC + **2** ST.
SC/ST reservation runs to **2030** (**104th Amendment**).

63.s:
The constitutional provision for reservation of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies under the 106th Amendment provides for which of the following?
1. One-third reservation of seats
2. Reservation for 15 years
3. Rotation after each delimitation
4. Immediate operation irrespective of census and delimitation
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
63.x: The 106th Amendment provides one-third reservation for 15 years, with rotation after each delimitation. Its operation begins only after the next census and delimitation; therefore statement 4 is false.
63.tq: Spot the false immediacy claim in a statement about commencement of constitutional reservation.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
**106th Amendment (2023)**: **one-third** seats for women (**Art. 334A**), for **15 years**, **rotated** after each delimitation.
Statement 4 is wrong: it starts only **after the next census** (**2027 Census**) and delimitation.
xa: Tamil Nadu's resolution sought the women's quota from **2029** without linking it to delimitation.
SC/ST reservation is under **Arts. 330 / 332**, extended to **2030**.

63.s: A constituency having no fixed geographical boundary, such as the Sangha seat in Sikkim, is known as a:
63.x: A floating constituency has no fixed geographical boundary. The Sangha constituency in Sikkim is an example in which only registered Buddhist monks vote and contest.
63.tq: Identify the exact electoral term from its defining geographical feature.
xs: A seat with no fixed geographical boundary is a **floating constituency** — option **(4)**.
Example: **Sangha (Sikkim)** — only **registered Buddhist monks** vote and contest.
xa: PYQ: APPSC-G2 **2023, 2025** — both statements on floating constituency were correct.
**Delimitation** fixes the **number of seats and boundaries** of territorial constituencies.

63.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

List-I (State)
A. Andhra Pradesh — Lok Sabha
B. Andhra Pradesh — Legislative Assembly
C. Telangana — Lok Sabha
D. Telangana — Legislative Assembly

List-II (Number of SC/ST reserved seats)
1. 4 / 1
2. 29 / 7
3. 3 / 2
4. 19 / 12

Code:
63.x: Andhra Pradesh has 4 SC and 1 ST Lok Sabha seats and 29 SC and 7 ST Assembly seats. Telangana has 3 SC and 2 ST Lok Sabha seats and 19 SC and 12 ST Assembly seats.
63.tq: Start with the sure State–House pair and then complete the numerical matching.
xs: **Telangana**: Lok Sabha **3 / 2**, Assembly **19 / 12** (of **17** LS, **119** MLA).
xa: AP's ST Lok Sabha seat: **Araku**; Telangana's: **Adilabad, Mahabubabad**.
Telangana's SC Lok Sabha seats: **Peddapalle, Warangal, Nagarkurnool**.

63.s: Reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies under Article 334 has been extended up to 2030 by which Amendment?
63.x: The 104th Amendment (Act of 2019, in force January 2020) extended SC/ST seat reservation under Article 334 to 2030 and ended Anglo-Indian nomination. Article 334 originally set 10 years (till 1960). The 95th Amendment gave the previous extension; the 106th introduced one-third women's reservation (Art 334A); the 84th dealt with the delimitation freeze.
63.tq: 104th: SC/ST seats to 2030 + Anglo-Indian nomination ended.
xs: The **104th Amendment** extended SC/ST reservation to **2030** — option **(2)**.
Act of **2019**, in force **Jan 2020**; it also **ended** Anglo-Indian nomination.
The **106th** gave women one-third (**Art. 334A**); the **84th** extended the delimitation freeze.
xa: **Art. 334** originally provided **10 years** (till **1960**).
⚠ IYB also calls it the "Act of **2020**".

63.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the qualifying dates for revision of electoral rolls?
63.x: The four qualifying dates are 1 January, 1 April, 1 July and 1 October. 1 December is not a qualifying date.
63.tq: Find the date outside the four-date set.
xs: **1 December** is not a qualifying date — option **(3)**.
The four dates: **1 January, 1 April, 1 July, 1 October** (Election Laws (Amendment) Act **2021**).
xa: **Summary revision** = annual; **SIR** rebuilds the roll.
Roll revision rests on **Sec. 21, RPA 1950**.

63.s: An overseas Indian elector may enrol in the electoral roll at:
o: the address of the Indian embassy in the foreign country
any address selected by the elector
the last place of employment in India only
the address of the Indian passport
63.x: Under Section 20A of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, an overseas elector may enrol at the address given in the Indian passport.
63.tq: Apply the special registration rule to the overseas-elector scenario.
xs: An overseas elector enrols at the **address of the Indian passport** — option **(4)**.
This is under **Sec. 20A, RPA 1950** (**2010**).
xa: RPA 1950 also covers **Sec. 19** voter eligibility and **Sec. 21** roll revision.
**Postal ballot** is for service voters, special voters, electors on election duty and those in preventive detention.

63.s: Which one of the following correctly describes a Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls?
o: It rebuilds the electoral roll comprehensively.
It is undertaken only after a general election result.
It is conducted only for overseas electors.
It is an annual summary correction without rebuilding the roll.
63.x: A Special Intensive Revision rebuilds the electoral roll, whereas summary revision is conducted annually.
63.tq: Distinguish the comprehensive revision from the routine annual revision.
xs: A **Special Intensive Revision** **rebuilds** the electoral roll — option **(1)**.
An annual correction without rebuilding is a **summary revision**.
xa: **Bihar SIR** removed about **70 lakh names**.
Four qualifying dates: **1 January, 1 April, 1 July, 1 October**.

63.s:
Consider the following statements about election machinery:
1. The District Election Officer is usually the District Collector.
2. Under Section 78, election expense accounts are filed with the District Election Officer within 30 days.
3. The Chief Electoral Officer conducts the poll in a constituency and declares the result.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: Statement 1 is correct: the DEO at district level is usually the Collector. Statement 2 is correct: Sec. 78 requires expense accounts to reach the DEO within 30 days. Statement 3 is wrong: the Returning Officer conducts the poll in a constituency and declares the result; the CEO assists the ECI in each State/UT. So A; B, C and D all include the wrong statement 3.
63.tq: CEO = State level, DEO = district (Collector), RO = constituency (declares result).
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
**DEO** is usually the **Collector**; under **Sec. 78** expense accounts reach the DEO within **30 days**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the **Returning Officer** conducts the poll and declares results; the **CEO** assists the ECI in each State/UT.
xa: **Observers** (general, police, expenditure) are appointed by the ECI under **Sec. 20B**.
**BLOs** now carry standard photo ID cards (IYB **2026**).

63.s: Which of the following is NOT a category of observer appointed by the Election Commission under Section 20B?
63.x: The listed observer categories are general, police and expenditure observers. Judicial observer is not among them.
63.tq: Find the role outside the three-member observer set.
xs: **Judicial observer** is not a Sec. 20B category — option **(1)**.
The ECI appoints **general, police and expenditure** observers (**Sec. 20B**).
xa: During elections the **ECI controls officers** on poll duty and can transfer them.
The **CEO** verifies non-compliant **RUPPs**; ECI **delisted 808** of them.

63.s:
Consider the following statements about election machinery:
1. The Chief Electoral Officer assists the Election Commission in each State or Union Territory.
2. Electoral Registration Officers and Booth Level Officers are associated with electoral rolls.
3. Booth Level Officers now carry standard photo identity cards.
4. The Election Commission has no control over officers deployed on poll duty.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the Election Commission controls officers on poll duty and may transfer them or act against partisan conduct.
63.tq: Reject the absolute statement denying the Election Commission's supervisory control.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
**CEO** assists the ECI in each State/UT; **ERO / BLO** handle rolls; **BLOs** now carry standard photo ID.
Statement 4 is wrong: the **ECI controls officers** on poll duty and can transfer them or act against partisan conduct.
xa: **Returning Officer** conducts the poll and declares results.
**DEO** (usually the Collector) receives expense accounts within **30 days**.

63.s: Recognition of political parties under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968 is distinct from registration under which provision?
o: Section 19 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950
Paragraph 16A of the Election Symbols Order, 1968
Section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951
63.x: Recognition is governed by the Election Symbols Order, 1968, whereas registration of political parties is under Section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
63.tq: Separate the similar-looking concepts of registration and recognition by identifying the governing provision.
xs: Registration is under **Section 29A of the RPA, 1951** — option **(3)**; recognition is under the **Election Symbols Order, 1968**.
**Sec. 19, RPA 1950** = voter eligibility; **Para 16A** = sanctions under the Symbols Order; **Art. 324** = ECI's powers.
xa: The Symbols Order is an **ECI order, not an Act**.
Under **Para 16A** the ECI can **suspend/withdraw recognition** for MCC breaches.

63.s:
Which of the following combinations correctly represents criteria for recognition as a State Party? 

1. Six per cent of votes in the Assembly election and two seats
2. Six per cent of votes in the Lok Sabha election and one Lok Sabha seat
3. Three per cent of Assembly seats or three seats, whichever is more
4. Eight per cent of valid votes

Select the correct answer:
63.x: All four listed conditions are alternative criteria for recognition as a State Party, including the Assembly, Lok Sabha, seat-share and 8% vote conditions.
63.tq: Check each alternative threshold independently before selecting the coded combination.
xs: All four are State Party criteria — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**6%** Assembly votes + **2** seats; **6%** Lok Sabha votes + **1** seat; **3%** of Assembly seats or **3** seats; **8%** of valid votes.
xa: A fifth route: **1** Lok Sabha seat for every **25** from the state.
Recognition is under the **Election Symbols Order, 1968**; registration under **Sec. 29A**.

63.s:
Consider the following conditions for recognition as a National Party:
1. Recognised as a State party in four or more States
2. 6% of valid votes in four States plus four Lok Sabha seats
3. 2% of Lok Sabha seats from at least three States
Which of the above is/are valid conditions (any one sufficing)?
63.x: All three are alternative criteria (any one suffices) under the Election Symbols Order, 1968: State-party recognition in 4 or more States; 6% of valid votes in 4 States plus 4 Lok Sabha seats; or 2% of Lok Sabha seats from at least 3 States. In APPSC-G2 2025 all listed conditions were valid, so the key there was 'None of the above' (none invalid). Options A, B and C each leave out a valid criterion.
63.tq: National party: 4 States recognised OR 6%x4 States + 4 LS seats OR 2% LS seats from 3 States.
xs: All three are valid National Party conditions (any one suffices) — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Recognised State party in 4 or more states**; **6%** valid votes in **4 states** + **4 Lok Sabha seats**; **2%** of Lok Sabha seats from **at least 3 states**.
xa: PYQ APPSC-G2 **2025**: all listed national-party conditions were valid → key "**None of the above**".
State Party routes include **8%** of valid votes, and **1** Lok Sabha seat for every **25** from the state.
Recognition is under the **Election Symbols Order, 1968** (an ECI order, not an Act).

63.s:
Consider the following statements about the commencement of the election process:
1. For a Lok Sabha election, the President issues the notification under Section 14 of the RPA 1951.
2. For an Assembly election, the Governor issues the notification under Section 15.
3. The President or the Governor fixes the election schedule and nomination dates.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: Statement 1 is correct: the President notifies Lok Sabha polls (Sec. 14) on the ECI's recommendation. Statement 2 is correct: the Governor notifies Assembly polls (Sec. 15) on the ECI's recommendation. Statement 3 is wrong: the ECI fixes the schedule and nomination dates; the President/Governor only issue the notification. So A; B, C and D all include the wrong statement 3.
63.tq: Sec. 14 = President (Lok Sabha), Sec. 15 = Governor (Assembly); the ECI sets the dates.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
**Sec. 14**: the **President** issues the Lok Sabha notification; **Sec. 15**: the **Governor** issues the Assembly notification — both on the **ECI's recommendation**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the **ECI** fixes the **schedule and nomination dates**.
xa: ⚠ **Sec. 14** = President (Lok Sabha); **Sec. 15** = Governor (Assembly).
**Bypolls** must be held within **6 months** of a vacancy.

63.s: The six-month requirement for a by-election does NOT apply when:
o: the vacancy occurs in a reserved constituency
the election is held during the monsoon season
the constituency has more than one polling station
the remaining term is under one year or the Election Commission certifies difficulty after consulting the Centre
63.x: The exceptions are where the remaining term is less than one year or the Election Commission, after consulting the Central Government, certifies difficulty in holding the election.
63.tq: Look for the option containing both statutory exceptions.
xs: The six-month rule does not apply when the **remaining term is under one year** or the **ECI certifies difficulty** after consulting the Centre — option **(4)**.
Reserved seats, monsoon season or the number of polling stations are not listed exceptions.
xa: By-election = **single vacancy**, within **6 months** (**Sec. 151A RPA**).
A polling station may have at most **1,200 electors**.

63.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Model Code of Conduct:

1. It is a set of guidelines issued by the Election Commission for political parties, candidates and the ruling government.
2. It is a statutory law enacted by Parliament.
3. Its authority is associated with the plenary power of the Election Commission under Article 324.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: The Model Code is a set of ECI guidelines and is supported by the Commission's plenary power under Article 324. It is not a statutory law enacted by Parliament.
63.tq: Spot the wrong legal-status statement while retaining the correct authority-based statements.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 3 only**.
The **MCC** is a set of **ECI guidelines** for parties, candidates and the ruling government; its authority is the ECI's **plenary power under Art. 324**.
Statement 2 is wrong: the MCC is **not a statutory law**.
xa: SC in **Mohinder Singh Gill v CEC (1978)**: Art. 324 = "**reservoir of power**".
MCC comes into force **from the announcement of the schedule** (**Harbans Singh Jalal v UoI (1997)**).

63.s:
Arrange the following milestones relating to the Model Code of Conduct in chronological order:

A. Part VII relating to the party in power was added
B. The Code was first drafted by the Kerala Government
C. The Code was revised
D. The Code was formalised by the Election Commission

Select the correct sequence.
63.x: The sequence is 1960 drafting by Kerala, 1968 formalisation by the ECI, 1974 revision, and 1979 addition of Part VII.
63.tq: Fix the earliest and latest milestones first, then place the 1968 and 1974 events.
xs: Order: **B** (Kerala draft, **1960**) → **D** (formalised by ECI, **1968**) → **C** (revised, **1974**) → **A** (Part VII added, **1979**) — option **(1)**.
Options (2) and (4) wrongly put the **1968** formalisation before the **1960** Kerala draft.
xa: **1991**: MCC enforced with rigour by CEC **T.N. Seshan**.
MCC was first used in the **1960 Kerala** Assembly election.
⚠ **1960** = MCC in Kerala; indelible ink = **1962**.

63.s:
Consider the following statements about the Model Code of Conduct:
1. It was first used in the 1960 Kerala Assembly election.
2. It was enforced with rigour by CEC T.N. Seshan in 1991.
3. It was first formalised by the Election Commission in 1979.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Code was first drafted and used in Kerala in 1960. Statement 2 is correct: T.N. Seshan enforced it strictly in 1991. Statement 3 is wrong: the ECI formalised it in 1968; 1979 is when Part VII on the party in power was added. So A; B, C and D all include the wrong statement 3.
63.tq: MCC timeline: 1960 Kerala, 1968 ECI, 1974 revised, 1979 Part VII, 1991 Seshan.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
MCC first used in the **1960 Kerala** Assembly election; enforced with rigour by **T.N. Seshan** in **1991**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it was formalised by the ECI in **1968**; **1979** added **Part VII** on the "party in power".
xa: The MCC was revised in **1974**.
It is lifted once results are declared.

63.s: Which one of the following is NOT a restriction under Part VII of the Model Code of Conduct?
o: Introducing new schemes or grants after announcement of polls
Using official machinery or transport for campaigning
Continuing ordinary official visits without combining them with electioneering
63.x: Part VII (party in power) bars combining official visits with electioneering, using official machinery or transport, and announcing new schemes or grants once polls are announced (options A, B, C). Ordinary official visits not combined with electioneering are not restricted, so D is the answer.
63.tq: Find the option that does not describe a prohibited act under the specific part of the Code.
xs: **Ordinary official visits not combined with electioneering** are not barred — option **(4)**.
**Part VII** curbs: no **official visits with electioneering**, no use of **official machinery/transport**, no **new schemes or grants** once polls are announced.
xa: **Part VII** on the "**party in power**" was added in **1979**.
Sanctions go up to **suspension/withdrawal of recognition** under **Para 16A** of the Symbols Order.
A 2026 petition alleged the **PM's national broadcast** breached MCC Part VII.

63.s: In which case did the Supreme Court describe Article 324 as a “reservoir of power”?
o: Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
63.x: In Mohinder Singh Gill v. CEC (1978), the Supreme Court described Article 324 as a reservoir of power.
63.tq: Match the constitutional principle with the case that established or described it.
xs: **Mohinder Singh Gill v CEC (1978)** called Art. 324 a "**reservoir of power**" — option **(1)**.
It lets the ECI act where **Parliament has not legislated**.
xa: The **MCC**'s authority rests on this **plenary power under Art. 324**.
**Kuldip Nayar**: right to vote = **statutory right**; **PUCL (2013)**: **NOTA** on EVMs.

63.s: Under which provision can the Election Commission suspend or withdraw the recognition of a political party for violating the Model Code of Conduct?
o: Paragraph 16A of the Election Symbols Order, 1968
63.x: Sanctions for MCC violations range from censure up to suspension or withdrawal of recognition under Paragraph 16A of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968. Section 29A deals with party registration, Section 126A with exit polls, and Article 329 bars courts in electoral matters.
63.tq: MCC teeth = Para 16A, Symbols Order 1968.
xs: **Paragraph 16A of the Election Symbols Order, 1968** allows suspension/withdrawal of recognition — option **(2)**.
**Sec. 29A** = party registration; **Sec. 126A** = exit polls; **Art. 329** = bar on courts.
xa: Sanctions under the MCC range from **censure** up to **suspension/withdrawal of recognition**.
The Symbols Order is an **ECI order, not an Act**.

63.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Initiative)
A. SVEEP
B. cVIGIL
C. Saksham
D. Voter Helpline

List-II (Purpose)
1. Registration, corrections, roll search and complaints
2. Reporting Model Code violations through geo-tagged photographs or videos
3. Voter education and electoral participation
4. Assistance and facilities for voters with disabilities

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
63.x: SVEEP promotes voter education and turnout; cVIGIL reports Model Code violations; Saksham assists voters with disabilities; and Voter Helpline provides registration, correction, search and complaint services.
63.tq: Start with the distinctive cVIGIL geo-tagging function and eliminate codes that misplace the remaining apps.
xs: **SVEEP** = voter education and turnout; **cVIGIL** = MCC violations via **geo-tagged** photos/videos; **Saksham** = voters with disabilities; **Voter Helpline** = roll search, forms, complaints.
xa: cVIGIL promises action within **100 minutes**.
SVEEP was launched in **2009**; the ECI partnered **Indian Railways** (APPSC **2019**).
**ECINET** merges **40+** ECI apps and websites.

63.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the NETA app is correct?
o: It enables voters to rate their elected representatives and was built by a private start-up.
It is used exclusively for filing election petitions before the High Courts.
It was conceptualised and developed by the Election Commission of India.
It enables citizens to report Model Code of Conduct violations with geo-tagged photographs.
63.x: The NETA app allows voters to rate their representatives and was built by a private start-up, not conceptualised by the Election Commission of India.
63.tq: Distinguish the private NETA app from official Election Commission applications.
xs: The **NETA app** lets voters **rate their representatives** and was **built by a private start-up** — option **(1)**.
It was **not conceptualised by the ECI**; reporting MCC violations with geo-tagged photos is **cVIGIL**.
xa: APPSC-GS **2019** key: only statement b true.
⚠ **NETA** = private start-up; **cVIGIL** = ECI, **100 minutes**.

63.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Voter Helpline app — Search name in electoral roll
ECINET — Exclusive platform for election petitions
63.x: ECINET is a unified platform merging more than 40 Election Commission applications and websites; it is not an exclusive platform for election petitions.
63.tq: Find the mismatched purpose among closely related electoral initiatives.
xs: **ECINET — election petitions** is wrong — option **(3)**; **ECINET** merges **40+** ECI apps and websites.
Correct: **Voter Helpline** = roll search; **cVIGIL** = MCC violations; **Braille-enabled ballots** = **Meghalaya**, first State at all booths.
xa: Election petitions go to the **High Court** under **Sec. 80A**.
**Sahulat** app: **Jammu and Kashmir**, for elderly voters (APPSC **2019**).

63.s: The 'Sahulat' app, launched to facilitate voting, was associated with which of the following?
o: Jammu and Kashmir, for elderly voters
Sikkim, for Buddhist monks in the Sangha seat
63.x: The Sahulat app was a Jammu and Kashmir initiative for elderly voters (APPSC 2019). Meghalaya was the first State to provide Braille-enabled ballot papers at all booths; overseas electors enrol under Sec 20A at their passport address; the Sangha seat in Sikkim is a floating constituency. None of these is the Sahulat app.
63.tq: Sahulat = J&K elderly; Braille ballots = Meghalaya.
xs: The **Sahulat** app was for **elderly voters** in **Jammu and Kashmir** — option **(2)** (APPSC **2019**).
**Meghalaya** is linked to **Braille-enabled ballot papers**; **Sangha (Sikkim)** is the floating monks' seat.
xa: **Saksham** is the app for voters with disabilities.
**SVEEP** partnered **Indian Railways** (APPSC 2019).

63.s:
Which of the following categories of electors are entitled to use postal ballots?
1. Service voters
2. Special voters
3. Electors on election duty
4. Persons in preventive detention
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
63.x: The listed categories—service voters, special voters, electors on election duty and persons in preventive detention—are covered by postal-ballot provisions.
63.tq: Test completeness of a statutory-category list rather than recalling a single category.
xs: All four may use postal ballots — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**Service voters, special voters, electors on election duty** and **those in preventive detention**.
xa: Absentee voters: seniors **85+** (raised from **80**), **benchmark disability (40%+)**, essential-service staff on duty.
Overseas electors enrol at their **passport address** (**Sec. 20A**).

63.s: Which of the following persons is eligible for the absentee-voter postal ballot category on the basis of age?
o: A citizen aged 90 years or above only
A citizen aged 80 years or above
A citizen aged 75 years or above
A citizen aged 85 years or above
63.x: The senior-citizen threshold for the absentee-voter postal ballot category is 85 years or above, raised from 80 years.
63.tq: Notice the revised threshold rather than the former age limit.
xs: Senior citizens aged **85+** are absentee voters — option **(4)**.
The age was **raised from 80** to 85.
xa: Persons with **benchmark disability (40%+)** and **essential-service staff** on duty also qualify.
Postal ballot also covers **service voters** and those in **preventive detention**.

63.s: The indelible election ink used in India is manufactured by which organisation and is based on which substance?
o: Mysore Paints and Varnish Ltd; silver nitrate
63.x: Indelible election ink is manufactured by Mysore Paints and Varnish Ltd and is based on silver nitrate.
63.tq: Use the manufacturer–ingredient pair to avoid a two-part factual trap.
xs: Indelible ink is made by **Mysore Paints and Varnish Ltd** and is **silver nitrate** based — option **(1)**.
India Security Press, Government Printing Press and Bharat Electronics are not named in the notes as its maker.
xa: Formula from the **National Physical Laboratory**; applied on the **left forefinger**.
First used in the **1962** general election.
⚠ "First used in **1960** in Mysore" is the **wrong** statement (APPSC **2019**).

63.s:
Consider the following statements about the indelible ink used in Indian elections:
1. Its formula comes from the National Physical Laboratory.
2. It is applied on the right forefinger.
3. Its key chemical is silver nitrate.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: Statement 1 is correct: the National Physical Laboratory supplies the formula (Mysore Paints and Varnish Ltd manufactures it). Statement 2 is wrong: the ink is applied on the left forefinger. Statement 3 is correct: silver nitrate is the key chemical. So B; A, C and D all include the wrong statement 2.
63.tq: Ink: NPL formula, Mysore Paints makes it, silver nitrate, LEFT forefinger, first used 1962.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
Formula from the **National Physical Laboratory**; key chemical **silver nitrate**.
Statement 2 is wrong: ink goes on the **left forefinger**.
xa: Manufacturer: **Mysore Paints and Varnish Ltd** (Karnataka).
First used in **1962**.

63.s: Indelible ink was first used in the Indian general election of:
63.x: Indelible ink was first used in the 1962 general election. The claim that it was first used in Mysore in 1960 is incorrect.
63.tq: Reject the nearby but incorrect preliminary-use year.
xs: Indelible ink was first used in the **1962** general election — option **(3)**.
**1952** is the 1st Lok Sabha; **1957** and **1967** were other early general elections.
xa: ⚠ Trap: "first used in **1960** in Mysore" is wrong — **1960** = MCC in **Kerala**.
Made by **Mysore Paints and Varnish Ltd**; **silver nitrate** based.

63.s: The Supreme Court directed the inclusion of a NOTA option on all Electronic Voting Machines in:
o: Harbans Singh Jalal v Union of India, 1997
Mohinder Singh Gill v Chief Election Commissioner, 1978
Kuldip Nayar v Union of India, 2006
63.x: In PUCL v Union of India on 27 September 2013, the Supreme Court directed that a NOTA button be provided on all EVMs.
63.tq: Match the election-related judicial direction with the correct case and year.
xs: **PUCL v Union of India (27 September 2013)** ordered a **NOTA** button on all EVMs — option **(1)**.
**Harbans Singh Jalal** = MCC from schedule announcement; **Mohinder Singh Gill** = Art. 324 "reservoir of power"; **Kuldip Nayar** = vote a statutory right.
xa: PUCL (2013) also linked the **secret vote** to **Art. 19(1)(a)**.
NOTA symbol: ballot with a **black cross**, designed by **NID, Ahmedabad**.

63.s: Which of the following statements about the NOTA symbol and its first Lok Sabha use is correct?
o: It is a blank ballot, designed by the Supreme Court, and was first used in 2013.
It is a ballot with a black cross, designed by Parliament, and was first used in 2024.
It is a ballot with a black cross, designed by NID Ahmedabad, and was first used in 2014.
It is a ballot with a red star, designed by the Election Commission, and was first used in 2019.
63.x: The NOTA symbol is a ballot with a black cross, designed by the National Institute of Design, Ahmedabad; it was first used in a Lok Sabha election in 2014.
63.tq: Combine symbol, designing institution and first-use year without confusing the judicial-order year with the implementation year.
xs: NOTA's symbol is a **ballot with a black cross**, designed by **NID Ahmedabad**; first Lok Sabha use **2014** — option **(3)**.
NOTA was ordered by the **Supreme Court** in **PUCL (2013)**, but the symbol was not designed by the Court, Parliament or the ECI.
xa: In 2014 NOTA took **1.1%** of votes (over **6 million**).
⚠ NOTA was ordered in **2013** (PUCL); first used in a Lok Sabha poll in **2014**.

63.s: An exit poll is best described as:
o: A survey conducted before the election notification to assess voter intention
A poll of voters taken immediately after they leave the polling station
A survey conducted only among political party workers
A statistical report prepared after the declaration of results
63.x: An exit poll is conducted among voters immediately after they leave the polling station; it is different from an opinion poll.
63.tq: Separate the timing of an exit poll from that of an opinion poll.
xs: An **exit poll** is a poll of voters taken **immediately after they leave** the polling station — option **(2)**.
It is **not the same as an opinion poll**, which is taken before voting.
xa: APPSC **2018** key: a, c, d correct.
**Sec. 126A, RPA 1951** restricts exit polls during multi-phase polling.

63.s: Which statement correctly distinguishes the restrictions on opinion polls and exit polls?
o: Opinion polls are barred for 48 hours before the close of poll, whereas Section 126A covers exit polls across multi-phase polling.
Exit polls are barred only for 48 hours before the close of poll, whereas opinion polls are barred from the first phase.
Both are barred only after the declaration of results.
Neither is subject to a statutory restriction.
63.x: Opinion polls are barred during the 48 hours before the close of poll under Section 126, while Section 126A governs the longer phase-to-phase restriction on exit polls.
63.tq: Compare the two restrictions by both subject and time period.
xs: **Opinion polls** are barred **48 hours** before close of poll; **Sec. 126A** covers **exit polls** across multi-phase polling — option **(1)**.
Options (2)-(4) reverse or deny these statutory curbs.
xa: Exit-poll ban runs till **half an hour** after the close of the last phase.
Opinion-poll ban is under **Sec. 126**.

63.s:
Consider the following grounds for declaring an election void under Section 100 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951:
1. The returned candidate was not qualified or was disqualified.
2. A corrupt practice was committed.
3. A nomination was improperly rejected.
4. Improper acceptance of votes or breach of the Constitution or the Act affected the result.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: All four circumstances are recognised grounds under Section 100 for declaring an election void, subject to the statutory requirements concerning their effect on the election result where applicable.
63.tq: Test the complete statutory list of grounds rather than relying on a single familiar ground.
xs: All four are **Section 100** grounds — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**Not qualified/disqualified**, **corrupt practice**, **improper rejection of a nomination**, **improper acceptance of votes** or breach affecting the result.
xa: Petition tried by the **High Court** (**Sec. 80A**), filed within **45 days** (**Sec. 81**).
Electoral offences now sit in **BNS Chapter IX (Sections 169-177)**.

63.s: Which one of the following statements regarding disposal of election petitions is correct?
o: The Supreme Court tries every election petition directly and no appeal is permitted.
The Election Commission must decide the petition within six months, with no appeal.
The District Court must decide the petition within three months, with appeal to the High Court.
The High Court is required to try to decide the petition within six months, and an appeal lies to the Supreme Court.
63.x: The High Court should try to decide an election petition within six months, and an appeal lies to the Supreme Court.
63.tq: Use the court hierarchy and time expectation to reject authority swaps.
xs: The **High Court** must try to decide within **six months**, with **appeal to the Supreme Court** — option **(4)**.
The ECI and District Courts do not try election petitions.
xa: **President/VP** election disputes go to the **SC** (**Art. 71**).
**Sec. 80**: no election questioned except by petition; base = **Art. 329(b)**.

63.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the present legal location of electoral offences such as bribery, undue influence and personation?
o: They remain in IPC Chapter IXA only.
They are contained in BNS Chapter IX, Sections 169 to 177, from 1 July 2024.
They are dealt with only under Section 81 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
They are contained in the Constitution under Article 329(b).
63.x: From 1 July 2024, electoral offences such as bribery, undue influence and personation are placed in Chapter IX of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Sections 169–177. Earlier, they were in Chapter IXA of the IPC.
63.tq: Track the transition from the IPC provision to the corresponding BNS chapter and sections.
xs: **Bribery, undue influence, personation** are now in **BNS Chapter IX (Sections 169-177)** from **1 July 2024** — option **(2)**.
Earlier they were in **IPC Chapter IXA**; **Sec. 81** is only the 45-day filing period.
xa: **Corrupt practice** is a **Section 100** ground for voiding an election.
**Art. 329(b)** is the constitutional base of the election-petition bar.

63.s:
Match the following provisions of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 with their contents:

List-I
A. Section 80
B. Section 80A
C. Section 81
D. Section 100

List-II
1. Grounds for declaring an election void
2. Petition to be presented within 45 days
3. No election may be called in question except by an election petition
4. Election petition to be tried by the High Court

Code:
63.x: Section 80 contains the election-petition bar, Section 80A specifies the High Court, Section 81 prescribes 45 days, and Section 100 lists grounds for declaring an election void.
63.tq: Start with the distinctive Section 80 and Section 100 pairs, then resolve the two procedural provisions.
xs: **Sec. 80** = no question except by petition; **80A** = **High Court** tries it; **81** = within **45 days**; **100** = **grounds** for voiding.
xa: ⚠ The bar is **Section 80**, NOT **81** (APPSC-G2 **2025**).
Appeal lies to the **Supreme Court**.

63.s: The first general election to the Lok Sabha in India was held in:
63.x: India's first general election was held in 1951-52 (the 1st Lok Sabha is dated 1952); it and the next three (1957, 1962, 1967) were held simultaneously with Assembly polls.
63.tq: Distinguish the first election period from the year in which the First Lok Sabha was constituted.
xs: The first general election was held in **1951-52** — option **(1)**.
The first four (**1951-52, 1957, 1962, 1967**) were **simultaneous** with Assembly polls.
xa: The 1st Lok Sabha is dated **1952**.
**18** general elections so far; the **18th Lok Sabha** was elected in **2024**.

63.s:
Match the following Lok Sabhas with the years of their election.

List-I
(a) 1st Lok Sabha
(b) 9th Lok Sabha
(c) 11th Lok Sabha
(d) 16th Lok Sabha

List-II
(i) 1996
(ii) 1952
(iii) 2014
(iv) 1989

Select the correct answer using the code below:
63.x: The 1st, 9th, 11th and 16th Lok Sabhas correspond respectively to 1952, 1989, 1996 and 2014.
63.tq: Start with the fixed 1st Lok Sabha–1952 pair and eliminate codes around it.
xs: **a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii** — option **(1)**.
xa: ⚠ APPSC **2019** answer was **17** elections (correct then).

63.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Eighteen Lok Sabha general elections have been held so far, the 18th Lok Sabha being elected in 2024.
2. The 17th Lok Sabha was elected in 2014.
3. The first four general elections were held simultaneously with State Assembly polls.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: Statement 1 is correct: 18 general elections so far, the 18th Lok Sabha elected in 2024 (the APPSC 2019 key of 17 was correct then). Statement 2 is wrong: the 17th Lok Sabha was elected in 2019; 2014 elected the 16th. Statement 3 is correct: 1951-52, 1957, 1962 and 1967 were simultaneous. So B; A, C and D include the wrong statement 2.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
**18** general elections; **18th Lok Sabha** elected in **2024**; first four were **simultaneous** with Assembly polls.
Statement 2 is wrong: the **17th** was elected in **2019**; **2014** = **16th**.
xa: First general election: **1951-52**.
NOTA first used in a Lok Sabha poll in **2014**.

63.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding significant milestones in India's election system.

List-I
 a. EVM first used at Parur
 b. VVPAT first used at Noksen
 c. NOTA first used in a Lok Sabha general election

List-II
 i. 1982
 ii. 2013
 iii. 2014

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
63.x: EVM was first used at Parur in 1982, while VVPAT was first used at Noksen in 2013 and NOTA was first used in a Lok Sabha general election in 2014.
63.tq: Start with the sure historical pair and then separate the 2013 VVPAT debut from the 2014 Lok Sabha election.
xs: **a-i, b-ii, c-iii** — option **(1)**.
**EVM** at **Parur** **1982**; **VVPAT** at **Noksen** **2013**; **NOTA** first Lok Sabha use **2014**.
xa: NOTA was introduced in **2013** (PUCL).
An **SC hearing** on EVM totalisers was held on **2 Sep 2026**.

63.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026:
1. It proposed raising the Lok Sabha ceiling from 550 to 850.
2. It proposed delimitation on the basis of the 2011 Census.
3. It was passed by the Lok Sabha with the required special majority.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: The Bill proposed increasing the Lok Sabha ceiling from 550 to 850 and conducting delimitation on the 2011 Census. It was defeated, not passed with the required special majority.
63.tq: Identify the false outcome statement while retaining the two substantive proposals.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
The **131st Amendment Bill, 2026** proposed a ceiling of **550 to 850** and delimitation on the **2011 Census**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it was **defeated** — **298 for, 230 against**, short of the **special majority**.
xa: The Delimitation Bill 2026 was **withdrawn**.
EAC-PM (2026) suggested splitting **170** oversized seats to reach **824**.

63.s: Why have southern States expressed apprehension regarding population-based delimitation?
o: They oppose the use of electronic voting machines in parliamentary elections.
They fear that States such as Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Rajasthan may gain seats at their expense.
They fear that the Rajya Sabha will become a directly elected chamber.
They fear that all Lok Sabha seats reserved for Scheduled Castes will be abolished.
63.x: Southern States fear that population-based delimitation would transfer political representation towards more populous States such as Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Rajasthan.
63.tq: Link the policy principle of population-based delimitation with its regional representation effect.
xs: Southern States fear **UP, Bihar, Rajasthan** would gain seats at their expense — option **(2)**.
The concern is **population-based delimitation**, not EVMs, Rajya Sabha or SC seats.
xa: **Tamil Nadu** resolution (**17 Aug 2026**): permanent freeze at **543** + **2.2:1** Lok Sabha-Rajya Sabha ratio.
The freeze on inter-State seats dates from the **42nd Amendment (1976)** on the **1971 Census**.

63.s: With reference to delimitation and Andhra Pradesh–Telangana representation, which one of the following is correct?
o: The increase in seats under Section 26 awaits the census after 2026.
The increase in seats under Section 26 is unrelated to any future census.
Section 26 concerns only the abolition of reserved seats in Andhra Pradesh.
The increase in seats under Section 26 was completed on the basis of the 2001 Census.
63.x: The Andhra Pradesh–Telangana seat increase under Section 26 awaits the census conducted after 2026.
63.tq: Match the statutory reference with the qualifying time condition instead of treating the provision as immediately operative.
xs: The AP/Telangana seat increase under **Section 26** **waits on the post-2026 census** — option **(1)**.
It is tied to a future census, not completed on the **2001 Census**.
xa: AP's reserved Lok Sabha seats: **4 SC, 1 ST**.
**84th (2001)** froze seats till the **first census after 2026**.

63.s:
Consider the following statements about the Election Commission of India:
1. It was constituted in 1950.
2. It is a permanent independent constitutional body.
3. Its IIIDEM trains election managers.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
63.x: The Election Commission was constituted in 1950, is a permanent independent constitutional body, and its IIIDEM provides training to election managers.
63.tq: When all three statements describe distinct institutional features, test whether the inclusive option is warranted.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
ECI constituted **1950**; a **permanent independent constitutional body**; its **IIIDEM** trains election managers.
xa: SC in **State of Karnataka v Prathik Parasrampuria (2026)**: removing black money from elections = **core ECI duty**.
**Art. 324** vests superintendence, direction and control of elections in the ECI.

63.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
 a. Representation of the People Act, 1950
 b. Representation of the People Act, 1951
 c. Article 171
 d. Article 324

List-II
 i. Composition of the State Legislative Councils
 ii. Allocation of seats and preparation of electoral rolls
 iii. Superintendence, direction and control of elections by the Election Commission
 iv. Conduct of elections and disqualification of members
63.x: The RPA 1950 deals with allocation of seats and electoral rolls, and the RPA 1951 with the conduct of elections and disqualification. Article 171 sets the composition of Legislative Councils and Article 324 vests elections in the Election Commission.
63.tq: Remember: RPA 1950 prepares (seats, rolls); RPA 1951 conducts (elections, disputes, disqualification).
n: The Representation of the People Act was enacted in 1950. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
The Representation of the People Act, 1950 provided the framework for seat allocation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
The Representation of the People Act, 1950 provided the framework for electoral rolls. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
The Representation of the People Act, 1950 provided the framework for Legislative Council composition. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
Section 10 is associated with the Representation of the People Act, 1950 framework. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
Schedule 3 is associated with the Representation of the People Act, 1950 framework. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
Article 171 is associated with the Representation of the People Act, 1950 framework. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
xs: The correct code is **a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii** — option **(1)**.
**RPA 1950** = **allocation of seats** and **electoral rolls**; **RPA 1951** = **conduct of elections** and **disqualifications**.
**Article 171** = **Legislative Council composition**; **Article 324** = **superintendence, direction and control** by the ECI.
xa: Council composition in detail: **Article 171(2)**, **Section 10** and the **Third Schedule** of RPA 1950.
RPA 1950 **Sec. 21** = roll revision (basis of **SIR**).
RPA 1951 **Section 29A** = **registration of political parties**.

63.s: Under the Representation of the People Act, 1951, the disqualification for conviction continues for how long after release?
63.x: Under the RPA 1951 the disqualification continues for six years after release. Three, five and ten years are distractors.
63.tq: Recall the six-year period after release.
n: The disqualification for conviction continues for six years after release. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
xs: Under the **RPA 1951**, disqualification continues for **six years** after release — option **(2)**.
It applies to one convicted and sentenced to at least **two years**, during imprisonment and **six years** after.
xa: RPA 1951 **Sec. 8** deals with **disqualifications**.
RPA 1951 also covers **corrupt practices** and **election petitions**.
**Sec. 77-78** = expense accounts.

63.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Delimitation redraws territorial constituency boundaries based on recent census figures.
Statement B: Delimitation is intended to enforce equal representation.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
63.x: Both are true: delimitation redraws constituency boundaries using recent census figures so that each seat has roughly equal population.
63.tq: Recall the basis and aim of delimitation.
n: Delimitation is the statutory process of redrawing territorial constituency boundaries. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Delimitation is based on recent census figures. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Delimitation enforces equal representation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Delimitation** redraws **constituency boundaries** on recent **census** figures and enforces **equal representation**.
xa: Principle: "**one person, one vote, one value**" (APPSC-G1 2024).
**Floating constituency:** **Sangha (Sikkim)** — only registered Buddhist monks vote and contest.
First general election: **1951-52**.

63.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Legislative Assembly election
(b) State Legislative Assembly electoral system
(c) Constitutional authority for Assembly elections
(d) Universal adult suffrage

List-II
(i) Article 326
(ii) First-Past-the-Post
(iii) Election Commission of India
(iv) Direct election
63.x: Assembly elections are direct, use first-past-the-post, are run by the Election Commission of India, and rest on adult suffrage (Article 326). The answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
63.tq: Recall who conducts Assembly elections and on what basis.
n: Citizens directly elect the State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
State Legislative Assembly elections are conducted on the basis of universal adult suffrage under Article 326. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
State Legislative Assembly elections use the First-Past-the-Post system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Election Commission of India conducts elections to the State Legislative Assembly under Article 324. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xs: The correct code is **a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i** — option **(3)**.
Assembly election = **direct**; electoral system = **First-Past-the-Post**.
Constitutional authority = **Election Commission of India** (**Article 324**); universal adult suffrage = **Article 326**.
xa: ⚠ Assembly polls are run by the ECI, **not** the State Election Commission.
Members come from **single-member territorial constituencies**.
FPTP needs no absolute majority over **50 percent**.

63.s:
Assertion (A): A candidate securing the highest number of valid votes can win a State Legislative Assembly election without obtaining more than 50 percent of the votes.
Reason (R): Elections to the Assembly follow the First-Past-the-Post system.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
63.x: Both are true: Assembly elections use first-past-the-post, so the candidate with the most votes wins even without 50%. R explains A.
63.tq: Ask whether first-past-the-post explains winning without a majority.
n: The Legislative Assembly election uses the First-Past-the-Post system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
A candidate does not need an absolute majority of more than 50 percent to win under the First-Past-the-Post system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The candidate securing the highest number of valid votes wins under the First-Past-the-Post system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
Under **First-Past-the-Post**, a **plurality** system, the candidate with the **highest valid votes** wins — **no absolute majority** over **50 percent** needed.
xa: FPTP is used for the **Lok Sabha** and **Assemblies**.
**PR-STV** is used for **Rajya Sabha**, **Legislative Councils**, **President** and **Vice-President**.
PR was rejected for the Lok Sabha due to **fragmentation and unstable** governments.

63.s: The State Legislative Assembly is elected from which type of constituencies?
63.x: Assembly members are directly elected from single-member territorial constituencies, by first-past-the-post.
63.tq: Recall the Assembly's constituencies.
n: The Legislative Assembly is elected from single-member territorial constituencies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Legislative Assembly is directly elected by the people. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
xs: The Assembly is elected from **single-member territorial constituencies** — option **(4)**.
It is **directly elected** by citizens using **First-Past-the-Post**.
xa: It rests on **universal adult suffrage** — **Article 326**.
Conducted by the **Election Commission of India** (**Article 324**).
Assembly is under **Article 170**.

63.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Article 325 provides for a single general electoral roll.
II. Article 325 prohibits discrimination in electoral rolls on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex.
III. Article 326 provides for universal adult suffrage for Lok Sabha and Legislative Assembly elections.
IV. The right to vote is a Fundamental Right according to the Kuldip Nayar Case.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
63.x: I, II and III are correct: Article 325 provides one electoral roll with no discrimination, and Article 326 adult suffrage. IV is false because Kuldip Nayar (2006) held the right to vote statutory, not fundamental.
63.tq: Remember that the right to vote is statutory.
n: Article 325 provides for a single general electoral roll. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
Article 325 prohibits discrimination in electoral rolls on the basis of religion. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
Article 325 prohibits discrimination in electoral rolls on the basis of race. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
Article 325 prohibits discrimination in electoral rolls on the basis of caste. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
Article 325 prohibits discrimination in electoral rolls on the basis of sex. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
Article 326 provides universal adult suffrage for Lok Sabha elections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
Article 326 provides universal adult suffrage for Legislative Assembly elections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
The Kuldip Nayar case described the right to vote as a legal or statutory right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
The right to vote is not a Fundamental Right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
xs: Statements **I, II and III only** are correct — option **(3)**.
I and II: **Article 325** gives a **single general electoral roll** with **no discrimination** on **religion, race, caste or sex**.
III: **Article 326** = **universal adult suffrage** for **Lok Sabha** and **Assembly** elections.
IV is wrong: **Kuldip Nayar (2006)** held the right to vote a **statutory** right, **not** a Fundamental Right.
xa: Every citizen aged **18+** may vote unless disqualified.
Voting age cut from **21** to **18** by the **61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988**.
President/VP disputes go **exclusively** to the **Supreme Court** (**Article 71**).

63.s:
Consider the following statements regarding simultaneous elections:

I. Amendment of Article 83 may be required.
II. Amendment of Article 85 may be required.
III. Amendment of Article 172 may be required.
IV. Amendment of Article 174 may be required.
V. Amendment of Article 356 may be required.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: I, II, III and IV only
I, II, III, IV and V
II, III, IV and V only
63.x: All five could need amending for simultaneous elections: Articles 83 and 85 (Parliament's term and sessions), 172 and 174 (the States'), and 356 (President's Rule).
63.tq: Recall the Articles on the terms of the Houses.
n: Simultaneous elections may require amendment of Article 83. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
Simultaneous elections may require amendment of Article 85. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
Simultaneous elections may require amendment of Article 172. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
Simultaneous elections may require amendment of Article 174. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
Simultaneous elections may require amendment of Article 356. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
xs: All five statements **I, II, III, IV and V** are correct — option **(3)**.
Simultaneous elections may require amending **Articles 83, 85, 172, 174 and 356**.
xa: The first four general elections (**1951-52, 1957, 1962, 1967**) were **simultaneous** with Assembly polls.
**Bypolls** must be held within **6 months** of a vacancy.
Universal adult suffrage: **Article 326**.

63.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Election disputes are adjudicated exclusively by the Judiciary through election petitions.
Statement B: Disputes concerning Presidential and Vice-Presidential elections are handled exclusively by the Election Commission.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
63.x: A is true: election disputes go only to the courts, through election petitions. B is false because disputes over the President's and Vice-President's elections go to the Supreme Court (Article 71).
63.tq: Recall Article 71.
n: Election disputes are handled exclusively by the judiciary through election petitions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Supreme Court handles Presidential election disputes exclusively under Article 71. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Supreme Court handles Vice-Presidential election disputes exclusively under Article 71. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
xs: **Statement A is true, Statement B is false** — option **(3)** is correct.
A: election disputes are handled **exclusively** by the **judiciary** through **election petitions**.
B is wrong: **President** and **Vice-President** election disputes go **exclusively** to the **Supreme Court** (**Article 71**), not the ECI.
xa: MP/MLA election petitions are tried by the **High Court**, appeal to the **Supreme Court**.
⚠ **Section 80** RPA 1951 bars questioning an election except by petition — not **Section 81**.
Petition presented within **45 days** (**Sec. 81**).

63.s:
How many of the following statements are correct?
1. The minimum age mentioned for Legislative Council membership is 30 years.
2. The minimum age mentioned for Panchayat and Municipality membership is 21 years.
3. The voting age is 21 years.
4. Voting age was lowered from 21 to 18 years by the 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988.
63.x: Three are correct: the minimum age is 30 for Council members and 21 for local bodies, and the 61st Amendment lowered the voting age to 18. Statement 3 is false because the voting age is 18.
63.tq: Recall the ages 18, 21, 25 and 30.
n: The voting age was lowered from 21 years to 18 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988, lowered the voting age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The minimum age for membership of a Legislative Council is 30 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The minimum age for Panchayat and Municipality elections is 21 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
xs: **Only three** statements are correct — option **(3)**.
1 and 2: minimum age is **30** for **Legislative Council** and **21** for **Panchayats and Municipalities**.
4: the **61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988** lowered the voting age from **21** to **18**.
3 is wrong: the voting age is **18**, not 21.
xa: The change became effective in **1989** (some notes say 1987).
Right to vote is a **statutory right** (**Kuldip Nayar, 2006**).
**Article 326** = universal adult suffrage.

63.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The right to vote is a Fundamental Right.
Statement B: The right to contest an election is a statutory right.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
63.x: A is false: the right to vote is statutory, not fundamental. B is true: the right to contest is also statutory (Kuldip Nayar, 2006).
63.tq: Remember that both electoral rights are statutory.
n: The right to contest elections is a legal or statutory right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
The right to vote is not a Fundamental Right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
The right to vote is a legal or statutory right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
The Supreme Court established the statutory nature of the right to vote and the right to contest in Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India in 2006. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
The right to contest elections is not a Fundamental Right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
xs: **Statement A is false, Statement B is true** — option **(4)** is correct.
A is wrong: the **right to vote** is a **statutory right**, **not a Fundamental Right**.
B: the **right to contest** is also a **statutory** right — **Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006)**.
xa: Basis: **RPA 1950 Section 19** and **RPA 1951**.
**PUCL (2013)** linked the **secret vote** to **Art. 19(1)(a)**.
**Article 326** gives the vote to every citizen aged **18+** unless disqualified.

63.s: When does the Model Code of Conduct come into force?
o: Immediately upon the formal announcement of the election schedule by the ECI
After the completion of nomination and scrutiny
After Parliament approves the election schedule
When the election results are declared
63.x: The Model Code of Conduct takes effect as soon as the ECI announces the election schedule, and lasts until the results.
63.tq: Recall when the Model Code starts.
n: The Model Code of Conduct comes into force immediately upon the ECI's formal announcement of the election schedule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
xs: The **Model Code of Conduct** comes into force **immediately upon the formal announcement of the election schedule** by the ECI — option **(1)**.
Held in **Harbans Singh Jalal v UoI (1997)**, **P&H HC**; it is lifted once **results are declared**.
xa: The MCC is **not statutory**; it rests on the ECI's plenary power under **Art. 324**.
First drafted by **Kerala** (**1960**); formalised by the ECI in **1968**; **Part VII** (party in power) added **1979**.
Enforced with rigour by CEC **T.N. Seshan** in **1991**.

63.s:
Assertion (A): Orders of the Delimitation Commission cannot be questioned in court.
Reason (R): Orders of the Delimitation Commission cannot be modified by legislatures.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
63.x: Both are true: Delimitation Commission orders cannot be challenged in court, and legislatures cannot change them. These are two separate safeguards, so R does not explain A.
63.tq: Ask whether two parallel safeguards explain each other.
n: Orders of the Delimitation Commission cannot be questioned in court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
Orders of the Delimitation Commission cannot be modified by legislatures. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — option **(2)**.
A: **Delimitation Commission** orders **cannot be called in question** in **any court** (**Article 329**).
R: they **cannot be modified** by **Parliament** or **State Assemblies** — a separate safeguard.
xa: Orders have the **force of law**.
**Four** Commissions so far — **1952, 1963, 1973, 2002**.
⚠ **J.L. Kapur** chaired two (**1963, 1973**).

63.s:
Assertion (A): Political parties are registered by the Election Commission of India.
Reason (R): Section 29A of the RPA, 1951 provides for registration of political parties.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
63.x: Both are true: the ECI registers political parties because Section 29A of the RPA, 1951 gives it that power. R explains A.
63.tq: Recall Section 29A.
n: The Election Commission of India registers political parties under Section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
The Election Commission of India is the authority that registers political parties. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
The **ECI** registers political parties under **Section 29A** of the **RPA, 1951**.
xa: **Recognition** is separate — under the **Election Symbols Order, 1968** (an ECI order, not an Act).
ECI **delisted 808** registered unrecognised parties.
National party test includes **6%** valid votes in **4 states** + **4 Lok Sabha seats**.

63.s:
Which of the following statements are correct?
I. The RPA, 1950 is connected with Articles 81, 82, 170, 171, 325 and 326.
II. The RPA, 1951 is connected with Articles 84, 102, 173, 191, 324 and 329.
III. Article 329 is listed as a constitutional connection of the RPA, 1950.
63.x: I and II are correct: the RPA, 1950 links to Articles 81, 82, 170, 171, 325 and 326, and the 1951 Act to 84, 102, 173, 191, 324 and 329. III is false because Article 329 belongs with the 1951 Act.
63.tq: Match each Act to its Articles.
n: The Representation of the People Act, 1950 is connected with Articles 81, 82, 170, 171, 325, and 326 of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
