The Representation of the People Act, 1951 is connected with Articles 84, 102, 173, 191, 324, and 329 of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
xs: Statements **I and II only** are correct — option **(3)**.
III is wrong: **Article 329** belongs with the **RPA 1951**.

63.tq: Recall the 70th Amendment.
n: Elected Members of the Delhi Legislative Assembly form part of the Presidential electoral college through the 70th Constitutional Amendment Act. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
Elected Members of the Puducherry Legislative Assembly form part of the Presidential electoral college through the 70th Constitutional Amendment Act. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
Elected Members of State Legislative Assemblies form part of the Presidential electoral college. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
xs: The **70th Constitutional Amendment Act** added **Delhi and Puducherry** to the President's electoral college — option **(1)**.
Their **elected** MLAs vote with **elected** MPs and **elected** members of State Assemblies.
xa: President is elected under **Article 54** by **PR-STV**, **secret ballot**.
**Nominated** members do not vote for the President but do vote for the **Vice-President**.
Vice-President: **Article 66**.

63.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The President is elected under Article 54.
II. The Vice-President is elected under Article 66.
III. The Lok Sabha is constituted under Article 81.
IV. The Legislative Assembly is provided for under Article 170.
V. The Legislative Council is provided for under Article 171.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
o: I, III, IV and V only
I, II, III, IV and V
63.x: All five are correct: the President is elected under Article 54, the Vice-President under 66, the Lok Sabha under 81, the Assembly under 170 and the Council under 171.
63.tq: Recall each body's main Article.
n: The President is elected under Article 54. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Vice-President is elected under Article 66. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Lok Sabha is constituted under Article 81. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Legislative Assembly is provided for under Article 170. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Legislative Council is provided for under Article 171. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
xs: All five statements **I, II, III, IV and V** are correct — option **(3)**.
**President** = **Article 54**; **Vice-President** = **Article 66**; **Lok Sabha** = **Article 81**.
**Legislative Assembly** = **Article 170**; **Legislative Council** = **Article 171**.
xa: **Rajya Sabha** = **Article 80**.
**Lok Sabha** and **Assembly** use **FPTP**; the rest use **PR-STV**.
Panchayat/municipal members: minimum age **21**.

64.s:
Consider the following statements about the Tarkunde Committee on electoral reforms:
1. It was appointed in 1974 and reported in 1975.
2. It was set up by Jayaprakash Narayan.
3. It recommended a three-member Election Commission and a voting age of 18.
4. It proposed that Election Commissioners be appointed by a panel of the Prime Minister, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Chief Justice of India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: Jayaprakash Narayan set it up in 1974, it reported in 1975, and it urged a three-member ECI and voting age 18. Statement 4 is wrong: the proposed panel was the PM, the Leader of the Opposition and the CJI, not the Speaker. So B; A leaves out statement 3, C and D include the wrong statement 4.
64.tq: Tarkunde panel = PM + LoP + CJI; the 2023 Act later dropped the CJI.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
**Tarkunde**: appointed **1974**, reported **1975**; set up by **Jayaprakash Narayan**; urged a **three-member ECI** and voting age **18**.
Statement 4 is wrong: its panel was **PM, Leader of Opposition, CJI** — not the Speaker.
xa: ⚠ The **CEC and ECs Act 2023** dropped the **CJI**, unlike Tarkunde's proposal.
2023 panel: **PM, a Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM, Leader of the Opposition**.

64.s:
Consider the following statements about the Dinesh Goswami Committee:
1. It was constituted in 1993.
2. It flagged the role of musclemen in elections.
3. It recommended rotation of seats reserved for SCs and STs.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the Goswami Committee is of 1990 (1993 is the Vohra Committee on the crime-politics nexus). Statements 2 and 3 are correct: its broad review flagged musclemen and urged rotation of SC/ST reserved seats. So B; A, C and D all include the wrong statement 1.
64.tq: Goswami 1990 (broadest review), Vohra 1993 (crime-politics), Indrajit Gupta 1998 (state funding).
xs: Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 2 and 3 only**.
**Goswami** flagged **musclemen** and urged **rotating SC/ST reserved seats**.
Statement 1 is wrong: the Goswami Committee was in **1990**; **1993** is the **Vohra** Committee.
xa: It also proposed time limits for **bye-elections**, strengthening the EC and anti-defection.
Goswami also recommended **public funding** of elections.

64.s: The Vohra Committee, constituted in 1993, primarily examined:
o: The financing of political parties by the State
The nexus between crime and politics
64.x: The Vohra Committee examined the nexus between criminals and politicians, or the crime-politics nexus.
64.tq: Discriminate between committees by their central subject rather than their common electoral-reform setting.
xs: The **Vohra Committee (1993)** examined the **nexus between crime and politics** — option **(4)**.
**State funding** = Indrajit Gupta; **internal party democracy** = Law Commission 170th Report.
xa: Vohra = crime-politics is the **most repeated** exam pair.
APPSC-G2 **2023** asked a matching of **Vohra/Gupta/Goswami/Verma**.

64.s:
Consider the following statements about Law Commission reports on electoral reform:
1. The 170th Report (1999) covered internal party democracy and partial list (PR) seats.
2. The 255th Report recommended giving the ECI limited power to deregister non-compliant parties.
3. The 255th Report was submitted in 1999.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: Statement 1 is correct: the 170th Report (1999) dealt with internal party democracy, partial list seats and disqualification on framing of charges. Statement 2 is correct: the 255th Report sought limited deregistration power for the ECI. Statement 3 is wrong: the 255th Report is of 2015; 1999 is the 170th Report. So A; B, C and D all include the wrong statement 3.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
**170th Report (1999)**: simultaneous elections, **internal party democracy**, **partial list (PR) seats**.
**255th Report** gave the ECI **limited power to deregister** parties; statement 3 is wrong — it came in **2015**, not 1999.
xa: The 255th also recommended the **Totaliser** and **one candidate, one seat**.
170th: full state funding desirable only if parties are **barred from other sources**.

64.s: Which one of the following was associated with the Second Administrative Reforms Commission's recommendations?
o: Appointment of all Election Commissioners by the Chief Justice of India
Partial state funding and barring persons charged with serious offences
64.x: The Second Administrative Reforms Commission recommended partial state funding and barring persons charged with serious offences.
64.tq: Distinguish a recommendation from the broader subject title of the commission.
xs: The **2nd ARC** urged **partial state funding** and **barring persons charged with serious offences** — option **(3)**.
The notes record nothing about indirect elections, CJI appointment or abolishing the ECI.
xa: Its report was titled "**Ethics in Governance**" (chair **Veerappa Moily**).
**Indrajit Gupta (1998)** and **Goswami (1990)** also backed public funding.

64.s: Which one of the following committees/commissions was NOT concerned with Centre-State relations?
64.x: The Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998) dealt with state funding of elections (an electoral reform), so it is the odd one out (APPSC-G2 2025, UPPSC 2015). The Rajamannar Committee (Tamil Nadu, 1969-71), Sarkaria Commission (1983-88) and Punchhi Commission (2007-10) all examined Centre-State relations.
64.tq: Indrajit Gupta = state funding of elections, not Centre-State.
xs: The **Indrajit Gupta Committee** dealt with **state funding of elections**, not Centre-State relations — option **(4)**.
**Rajamannar, Sarkaria** and **Punchhi** all examined **Centre-State relations**.
xa: PYQs: APPSC-G2 **2025**, UPPSC **2015**.
Gupta (1998) proposed partial funding **in kind**; still **not adopted**.

64.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Section of the RPA, 1951)
A. Section 8
B. Section 29A
C. Section 33A
D. Section 123

List-II (Subject)
1. Registration of political parties
2. Disclosure of criminal antecedents
3. Disqualification on conviction
4. Corrupt practices

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
64.x: Section 8 concerns disqualification on conviction, Section 29A registration of political parties, Section 33A criminal-antecedent disclosure, and Section 123 corrupt practices.
64.tq: Start with the sure section–subject pairs and eliminate codes containing a misplaced provision.
xs: **Sec. 8** = disqualification on conviction; **29A** = party registration; **33A** = criminal antecedents disclosure; **123** = corrupt practices.
xa: **Sec. 34** = security deposit; **Sec. 81** = petition within **45 days**.
**Sec. 8(4)** was struck down in **Lily Thomas (2013)**.

64.s:
Consider the following statements about security deposits under Section 34 of the RPA 1951:
1. A general-category Lok Sabha candidate deposits ₹25,000.
2. A general-category Assembly candidate deposits ₹10,000.
3. SC/ST candidates deposit one-fourth of the general amount.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: ₹25,000 for the Lok Sabha and ₹10,000 for an Assembly. Statement 3 is wrong: SC/ST candidates pay half (₹12,500 for the Lok Sabha), not one-fourth. So A; B, C and D all include the wrong statement 3.
64.tq: Deposit: 25,000 / 10,000, half for SC/ST.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 3 is wrong: SC/ST candidates pay **half**, not one-fourth.
xa: Deposit is forfeited below **one-sixth** of valid votes.
The **1996** amendment raised security deposits.

64.s: Section 81 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 relates to:
o: Corrupt practices during an election campaign
The maintenance of election expenditure accounts
Election petitions presented in the High Court within 45 days of the result
64.x: Section 81 concerns election petitions, which are presented in the High Court within 45 days of the election result.
64.tq: Separate the post-result election-petition provision from campaign and nomination provisions.
xs: **Sec. 81** = **election petition** in the **High Court** within **45 days** — option **(4)**.
Registration = **29A**; corrupt practices = **123**; expense accounts = **77-78**.
xa: **Sec. 100** lists grounds for declaring an election **void**.

64.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the corrupt practices covered by Section 123 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951?
o: Failure to file an election expenditure account within 30 days
Appeal on the grounds of religion or caste
64.x: Section 123 covers corrupt practices such as bribery, undue influence and appeals based on religion or caste. Filing the expenditure account within 30 days is governed by Section 78.
64.tq: Find the provision belonging to a neighbouring compliance area rather than the corrupt-practices list.
xs: **Failure to file an expense account within 30 days** is not a Sec. 123 corrupt practice — option **(1)**; it falls under **Sec. 78**.
**Sec. 123** covers **bribery, undue influence, appeal on religion/caste**.
xa: Failure to file accounts can lead the **ECI** to **disqualify** the candidate.
Bribery and undue influence are now offences in **BNS** too.

64.s: The provision relating to the ban on exit polls is:
64.x: Section 126A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 concerns the ban on exit polls.
64.tq: Distinguish the exit-poll provision from the nearby provision on promoting enmity.
xs: The **exit poll** ban is in **Section 126A** — option **(4)**.
**123** = corrupt practices; **125** = promoting enmity.
xa: Liquor ban **48 hours** before poll = **Sec. 135C**.
Paid holiday on poll day = **Sec. 135B**.

64.s:
Which of the following has been proposed as a reform concerning candidates contesting from more than one constituency?
1. One candidate, one seat
2. Requiring the vacating candidate to bear the cost of the resulting by-election
3. Allowing an unlimited number of constituencies if the candidate deposits additional security
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
64.x: The Law Commission proposed the principle of one candidate, one seat, while the Election Commission proposed that a candidate vacating a seat should bear the cost of the by-election. Unlimited contesting was not proposed.
64.tq: Reject the extreme ‘unlimited’ proposal and retain the two stated reform alternatives.
xs: Proposals 1 and 2 are correct — option **(3) 1 and 2 only**.
**One candidate, one seat** (Law Commission **255th**); the **vacating candidate pays** for the bypoll (**ECI** proposal).
Proposal 3 is wrong: the law caps it at **two** constituencies.
xa: **Sec. 33(7)** cap dates from **1996**.
Winner of both must vacate one within **14 days**.

64.s: Which one of the following was a major provision of the Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 1996?
o: Removal of the limit on constituencies from which a candidate may contest
Reduction of security deposits and proposers for independent candidates
Abolition of by-elections within six months
Capping a candidate’s contest to two constituencies and increasing security deposits
64.x: The 1996 amendment capped contests at two constituencies, increased security deposits, and required more proposers for independents and unrecognised parties.
64.tq: Identify the option that combines the principal nomination-related changes without reversing them.
xs: The **RP (Amendment) Act, 1996** capped contests at **two constituencies** and raised **security deposits** — option **(4)**.
It increased (not reduced) deposits and proposers, and it kept bypolls within **6 months** (**Sec. 151A**).
xa: It limited **countermanding** to the death of a **recognised-party** candidate.
It added a **paid holiday** (**Sec. 135B**) and **liquor ban** (**Sec. 135C**).
Offences under the **Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971** became a disqualification.

64.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Section 135B — Liquor ban for 48 hours before polling
Section 135C — Paid holiday on polling day
Section 70 — Disqualification under the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971
64.x: Section 151A concerns holding a by-election within six months. Section 135B provides for a paid holiday, Section 135C concerns the liquor ban, and Section 70 deals with vacating one of two seats.
64.tq: Match statutory sections with their functions and eliminate the swapped-section pairs.
xs: **Sec. 151A — by-election within six months** is correct — option **(3)**.
**135B** = **paid holiday**; **135C** = **liquor ban** (pairs 1 and 2 are swapped).
**Sec. 70** = vacating one of two seats within **14 days**, not the National Honour Act disqualification.
xa: Bypoll exceptions: remaining term **under one year**, or ECI certifies difficulty.
National Honour Act is of **1971**.

64.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Before the 1996 amendment, there was no limit on the number of constituencies from which a person could contest.
2. Devi Lal contested three Lok Sabha seats in 1991.
3. A person elected from two constituencies must vacate one of them within 30 days.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: Statement 1 is correct: the two-constituency cap in Sec 33(7) came only with the 1996 amendment. Statement 2 is correct: Devi Lal contested three Lok Sabha seats in 1991 (UPSC 2021). Statement 3 is wrong: under Sec 70 one seat must be vacated within 14 days. So A; B, C and D include the wrong statement 3.
64.tq: Cap of 2 seats from 1996; vacate in 14 days.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
No cap before **1996**; **Devi Lal** contested **three** Lok Sabha seats in **1991** (UPSC **2021** key).
Statement 3 is wrong: one seat must be vacated within **14 days**, not 30.
xa: Cap of **two** constituencies is in **Sec. 33(7)**.
**30 days** is the deadline for filing expense accounts (**Sec. 78**).

64.s: The judgment in Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013) is associated with which of the following conclusions?
o: Disqualification of legislators was transferred from Parliament to the Election Commission.
Only a sitting legislator can be disqualified after a three-month period.
A convicted legislator remains protected until the disposal of the appeal.
A convicted legislator is disqualified immediately, without protection during the pendency of an appeal.
64.x: The Lily Thomas judgment held that conviction leads to immediate disqualification and that an appeal does not provide protection against that disqualification.
64.tq: Test the holding of a landmark judgment against closely related but reversed legal effects.
xs: **Lily Thomas (July 2013)**: a convicted legislator is **disqualified immediately**, with **no protection while appeal pending** — option **(4)**.
It struck down **Sec. 8(4)**, the **3-month appeal buffer** for sitting members.
xa: Disqualification follows conviction with **2+ years** (**Sec. 8**).
**Ramesh Dalal (2005)**: sitting MP/MLA convicted with 2+ years barred from contesting.

64.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951:
1. Conviction resulting in imprisonment of two years or more attracts disqualification.
2. The disqualification rule is contained in a law made by Parliament.
3. Disqualification begins only after the appeal against conviction is finally decided.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: Section 8 provides disqualification on conviction involving imprisonment of two years or more, and the rule is contained in a parliamentary law. Lily Thomas removed the protection during pendency of an appeal, making statement 3 incorrect.
64.tq: Use the immediate-effect rule to identify the false statement about the appeal period.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
**Sec. 8**: conviction with **two years or more** disqualifies; the rule is in a law made by **Parliament** (UPSC **2009**).
Statement 3 is wrong: after **Lily Thomas (2013)** disqualification is **immediate from conviction**.
xa: Period: **term plus 6 years** after release.
**Sec. 8(4)** was struck down.

64.s:
With reference to Public Interest Foundation v. Union of India (2018), consider the following statements:
1. The Court itself imposed disqualification upon the framing of charges in serious offences.
2. The question of disqualification upon framing of charges was left to Parliament.
3. Publicity of criminal records of candidates was ordered.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: The Court left the issue of disqualification on framing of charges to Parliament but ordered publicity of criminal records. It did not itself impose such disqualification.
64.tq: Distinguish between what a court ordered and what it left to the legislature.
xs: Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option **(3) 2 and 3 only**.
**Public Interest Foundation (2018)**, a **5-judge** bench, left disqualification on framing of charges **to Parliament**.
It ordered parties to **publicise candidates' criminal records** on websites, newspapers, TV; so statement 1 is wrong.
xa: ECI (**Sep 2025**) also requires **reasons for selecting** such candidates.
Law Commission **244th Report (2014)** urged barring candidates once charges are framed.

64.s:
The Election Commission’s current requirement concerning candidates with criminal records includes publication of which of the following by political parties?
1. Details of the candidates’ criminal records
2. Reasons for selecting such candidates
3. Mandatory withdrawal of their candidature
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: Political parties must publish the criminal-record details of selected candidates and the reasons for their selection. Mandatory withdrawal of candidature is not part of the stated requirement.
64.tq: Reject the extreme consequence when the actual reform is based on disclosure and justification.
xs: Items 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Parties must publish candidates' **criminal records** and **reasons for selecting them** (**Sep 2025**).
Withdrawal of candidature is not required.
xa: Affidavits on criminal cases, assets, liabilities, education date from **2002**.
ADR data: **31%** of MPs and **29%** of MLAs face serious charges.

64.s: The recommendation to bar candidates upon framing of charges in serious offences was made in which report of the Law Commission?
64.x: The recommendation was made in the Law Commission’s 244th Report of 2014.
64.tq: Match the recommendation with its specific report number and year.
xs: The Law Commission's **244th Report, 2014** urged barring candidates once **charges are framed** — option **(4)**.
**170th (1999)** = simultaneous polls, party democracy; **255th (2015)** = finance, paid news, deregistration power.
xa: ⚠ LENS cites it as "Law Commission, **2015**".
**Public Interest Foundation (2018)** left this question to **Parliament**.

64.s: Which of the following statements regarding the current judicial and institutional response to criminalisation of politics is correct?
o: A lifetime ban on convicted legislators has already been enacted and no petition is pending.
The Supreme Court has abolished all special courts for MPs and MLAs.
A PIL seeking a lifetime ban on convicted legislators is pending, and 12 special courts exist for MPs and MLAs.
Only one special court exists for all cases involving elected representatives.
64.x: A PIL seeking a lifetime ban on convicted legislators is pending, while 12 special courts have been established for cases involving MPs and MLAs.
64.tq: Distinguish a pending proposal from an already enacted reform.
xs: A PIL for a **lifetime ban** is **pending**, and there are **12 special courts** for MPs/MLAs — option **(3)**.
So no lifetime ban has been enacted, and special courts have not been abolished or reduced to one.
xa: ADR: **31%** MPs, **29%** MLAs with serious charges.
Unfinished agenda: disqualification on **framing of charges**.

64.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. ADR v Union of India (2002) — Mandatory disclosure of criminal cases, assets, liabilities and education
2. PUCL v Union of India — Voter's right to know is part of Article 21
3. Krishnamurthy v Sivakumar (2015) — Non-disclosure of serious criminal cases vitiates the nomination
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
64.x: Pair 1 is correct: ADR (2002) made disclosure of criminal cases, assets, liabilities and education mandatory. Pair 2 is wrong: PUCL placed the voter's right to know in Article 19(1)(a), not Article 21. Pair 3 is correct: Krishnamurthy (2015) held that hiding serious criminal cases vitiates the nomination. So C; A, B and D all include the wrong pair 2.
64.tq: Right to know / right to reject = Art. 19(1)(a).
xs: Pairs 1 and 3 are correct — option **(3) 1 and 3 only**.
**ADR (2002)** = disclosure; **Krishnamurthy (2015)** = non-disclosure **vitiates nomination**.
Pair 2 is wrong: **PUCL** placed the voter's **right to know** in **Art. 19(1)(a)**, not Article 21.
xa: **PUCL (2013)** ordered the **NOTA** option.
**Lily Thomas (2013)** struck down **Sec. 8(4)**.

64.s: Disqualification under the Tenth Schedule is decided by the Speaker or Chairman, subject to which limitation?
o: Approval by the President in all cases
A referendum among members of the House
Approval by the Election Commission before every decision
64.x: The Speaker or Chairman decides disqualification under the Tenth Schedule, but the decision remains subject to judicial review, as recognised by the Supreme Court in 1992.
64.tq: Ask who exercises the power and then identify the constitutional check on that power.
xs: **Tenth Schedule** decisions by the **Speaker/Chairman** are subject to **judicial review** — option **(2)** (SC **1992**).
No presidential approval, referendum or ECI approval is required.
xa: Anti-defection amendments: **52nd (1985)**, **91st (2003)**.
Goswami (**1990**) also dealt with anti-defection.

64.s:
Consider the following statements about current election expenditure limits:
1. A Lok Sabha candidate in a larger State may spend up to ₹95 lakh.
2. An Assembly candidate in a larger State may spend up to ₹40 lakh.
3. These limits were raised by the Finance Act, 2022.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: Statement 1 is correct: ₹95 lakh (earlier ₹70 lakh). Statement 2 is correct: ₹40 lakh (earlier ₹28 lakh). Statement 3 is wrong: the limits were raised by the Conduct of Elections (Amendment) Rules, 2022 under the 1961 Rules (Rule 90), not a Finance Act. So A; B, C and D all include the wrong statement 3.
64.tq: 95/40 lakh for bigger States; source = Rule 90, Conduct of Election Rules 1961.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Larger States: **Rs 95 lakh** (Lok Sabha), **Rs 40 lakh** (Assembly).
Statement 3 is wrong: they were raised by the **Conduct of Elections (Amendment) Rules, 2022**, not a Finance Act.
xa: Smaller States: **Rs 75 lakh** (LS), **Rs 28 lakh** (Assembly).
Earlier: Rs **70** lakh (LS) and Rs **28** lakh (Assembly) for larger States.

64.s:
Consider the following statements about election expense accounts:
1. Section 77 of the RPA 1951 requires a candidate to keep an account of election expenses.
2. Section 78 requires the account to be filed with the Returning Officer within 30 days.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
64.x: Statement 1 is correct: Sec. 77 requires the candidate to keep expense accounts. Statement 2 is wrong: under Sec. 78 the account is filed with the District Election Officer, not the Returning Officer, within 30 days. So A; B and C accept the wrong statement 2, D rejects the correct statement 1.
64.tq: 77 = keep accounts, 78 = file with DEO in 30 days.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
**Sec. 77** requires keeping **expense accounts**.
Statement 2 is wrong: under **Sec. 78** the account goes to the **District Election Officer** within **30 days**, not the Returning Officer.
xa: Failure → the **ECI** can **disqualify** the candidate.
Limits rest on **Rule 90** of the **1961** Rules.

64.s: Section 77 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, is criticised in the context of party expenditure because it:
o: Prohibits all expenditure on election campaigns
Places a ceiling only on the expenditure of candidates, not on the election expenditure incurred directly by political parties
Places a ceiling only on political parties, not on candidates
Requires all campaign expenditure to be incurred in cash
64.x: The perceived loophole is that Section 77 caps candidate expenditure while not imposing a comparable ceiling on the parties’ own election spending.
64.tq: Ask who bears the statutory ceiling to expose the candidate-party distinction.
xs: **Sec. 77** caps only **candidate** spending, not **parties'** own election spending — option **(2)**.
It does not ban campaign spending or require cash; it does not cap parties.
xa: Travel of **20 star campaigners** is excluded from the candidate's limit.
Unfinished agenda: a **party spending cap**.

64.s: For a political party to retain tax exemption under the stated provisions, which combination is relevant?
o: No donation above ₹2,000 in any form and no record of larger donations
No cash donation above ₹20,000 and records only of donations above ₹2,000
No cash donation above ₹2,000 and proper records of donations above ₹20,000
Acceptance of unlimited cash donations provided they are reported after the election
64.x: The stated conditions include no cash donation above ₹2,000 and maintenance of records for donations above ₹20,000. These are referred to under Section 12 of the Income Tax Act, 2025, replacing the earlier reference to Section 13A of the 1961 Act.
64.tq: Keep the two monetary thresholds separate instead of reversing their functions.
xs: **No cash donation above Rs 2,000** and **records of donations above Rs 20,000** — option **(3)**.
Option (2) swaps the two thresholds.
xa: ⚠ **Rs 2,000** = cash cap; **Rs 20,000** = record threshold.
Now under **Sec. 12, Income Tax Act 2025**; earlier **Sec. 13A**, IT Act **1961**.

64.s:
Consider the following statements about electoral bonds:
1. They were sold only by the State Bank of India.
2. They were issued in denominations from ₹1,000 to ₹10 crore.
3. They were bearer bonds valid for 15 days.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: Statement 1 is correct: SBI was the only seller. Statement 2 is wrong: the range was ₹1,000 to ₹1 crore. Statement 3 is correct: they were bearer bonds valid for 15 days. So C; A, B and D all include the wrong statement 2.
64.tq: Bonds: SBI only, ₹1,000-₹1 crore, 15 days, encashable by parties with 1% votes.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(3) 1 and 3 only**.
Electoral bonds were sold **only by SBI**, as **bearer bonds** valid **15 days**.
Statement 2 is wrong: denominations ran from **₹1,000 to ₹1 crore**, not ₹10 crore.
xa: The scheme was notified in **2018** (via Finance Act **2017** amendments).
Only parties with at least **1%** of the vote in the last election could encash them.
Struck down in **ADR v UoI** on **15 Feb 2024**.

64.s: A political party could encash electoral bonds only if it had secured at least what percentage of votes in the last election?
64.x: Only a registered political party that had secured at least 1% of the votes in the last election could encash electoral bonds.
64.tq: Recall the statutory eligibility threshold rather than the general registration requirement.
xs: A party could encash electoral bonds only with at least **1 per cent** (**1% of the vote**) in the last election — so option **(2)** is correct.
Only **registered parties** meeting this **1%** threshold could encash; the bonds were sold only by **SBI** as **bearer bonds**.
xa: Denominations: **₹1,000 to ₹1 crore**; each bond was valid for **15 days**.
The scheme was notified in **2018** via **Finance Act 2017** amendments.
Struck down as **unconstitutional** by a unanimous **five-judge Constitution Bench** in **ADR v UoI** (**15 Feb 2024**) — it violated the **right to information under Art. 19(1)(a)**.
⚠ Donor anonymity was hailed in older notes as a "**transparency**" gain.

64.s:
With reference to the electoral bond judgment of 2024, consider the following statements:
1. The judgment was delivered by a five-judge Constitution Bench.
2. The decision to strike down the scheme was unanimous.
3. The Court directed the State Bank of India to provide donor data to the Election Commission of India.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: All three statements are correct: a five-judge Constitution Bench unanimously struck down the scheme and directed SBI to provide donor data to the ECI.
64.tq: When all three statements describe distinct features of one judgment, verify the bench, outcome and direction separately.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
A **five-judge Constitution Bench**, **unanimous**, struck down the scheme and ordered **SBI** to give donor data to the **ECI**.
xa: Case: **ADR v Union of India, 15 Feb 2024**.
⚠ **ADR v UoI** 2002 = disclosure; **ADR v ECI** 2024 = EVM/VVPAT.

64.s: The Supreme Court's decision in Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India also invalidated which change associated with electoral political funding?
o: Abolition of political party registration under the RPA
Removal of the corporate donation cap under the Companies Act
Compulsory disclosure of all cash donations by parties
Restriction on donations by individual citizens
64.x: The Court struck down the removal of the corporate donation cap from the Companies Act.
64.tq: Identify the allied legal provision affected by the judgment, not merely the main scheme.
xs: It also struck down the **removal of the corporate donation cap** from the **Companies Act** — option **(2)**.
The notes record no ruling on party registration, cash disclosure or individual donations.
xa: Ground: violation of voters' **right to information under Art. 19(1)(a)**.
ADR: **60% (₹19,083 cr)** of party funds in **2004-23** came from undisclosed sources.

64.s: In ADR v Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court struck down the Electoral Bond Scheme mainly because it violated:
o: The right to equality under Article 14
The voters' right to information under Article 19(1)(a)
The right to life under Article 21
The freedom of association under Article 19(1)(c)
64.x: The five-judge bench unanimously held that donor anonymity violated voters' right to information, part of freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). Articles 14, 21 and 19(1)(c) were not the ground stated for striking the scheme down.
64.tq: Bonds struck down = Art 19(1)(a) right to information (15 Feb 2024).
xs: The scheme violated voters' **right to information under Art. 19(1)(a)** — option **(2)**.
Articles **14**, **21** and **19(1)(c)** were not the stated ground.
xa: **PUCL (2003)**: voter's **right to know** is part of Art. 19(1)(a).
**PUCL (2013)**: right to reject (NOTA) also flows from Art. 19(1)(a).

64.s:
Consider the following statements about the Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998):
1. It recommended state funding of elections.
2. It recommended full funding in cash to every candidate.
3. Its recommendation has not yet been adopted.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: Statement 1 is correct: the 1998 committee recommended state funding. Statement 2 is wrong: it suggested partial funding in kind to recognised parties and candidates, not full cash funding. Statement 3 is correct: it is still not adopted. So C; A, B and D all include the wrong statement 2.
64.tq: Indrajit Gupta = partial, in kind, never adopted.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(3) 1 and 3 only**.
**Indrajit Gupta (1998)** recommended **state funding** of elections, still **not adopted**.
Statement 2 is wrong: it proposed **partial funding in kind** to recognised parties/candidates.
xa: ⚠ "Which is NOT on Centre-State relations?" → **Indrajit Gupta**.
APPSC **2025**: Indrajit Gupta = electoral reforms.

64.s: The Law Commission’s 170th Report stated that full state funding of elections would be desirable only if which condition were fulfilled?
o: Only independent candidates received public funds.
Political parties were barred from obtaining funds from other sources.
All candidates were allowed unlimited private donations.
64.x: The Law Commission considered full state funding desirable only if political parties were barred from receiving funds from other sources.
64.tq: Test the conditional nature of a recommendation and reject an unconditional formulation.
xs: The **Law Commission 170th Report (1999)** said full state funding is desirable only if **political parties are barred from other sources** of funds — so option **(3)** is correct.
In **full** state funding the State bears all legitimate costs and **private donations are banned**; it is not limited to independents.
xa: The **170th Report** also backed **simultaneous elections**, **internal party democracy** and partial **list (PR) seats**.
**Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998)**: partial funding **in kind** to recognised parties/candidates; still **not adopted**.
**Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990)** and the **2nd ARC** also recommended public funding.
Countries with public funding: **Germany, Sweden, Japan** (and **Canada** in another list).

64.s:
Consider the following statements about models of state funding of elections:
1. Public funding may be full or partial.
2. Funding may be provided in cash or in kind.
3. Partial funding means that the State bears all legitimate costs and private donations are banned.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: State funding may be full or partial and may be in cash or in kind. Bearing all legitimate costs while banning private donations describes full funding, not partial funding.
64.tq: Use the definition of partial funding to catch the swapped meaning in statement 3.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Models: **full vs partial**; **cash vs in-kind**.
Statement 3 is wrong: that describes **full** funding; **partial** means the State meets **some costs** (e.g. free airtime, fuel, rallies).
xa: Countries with public funding: **Germany, Sweden, Japan** (+ **Canada**).
Against: **heavy fiscal burden**; does not stop **off-book cash**.

64.s:
Consider the following statements about the debate on state funding of elections:
1. Curbing black money and quid-pro-quo funding is an argument in its favour.
2. A heavy fiscal burden on the State is an argument in its favour.
3. The aim of a level field for resource-poor candidates links it to Article 14.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: Statement 1 is correct: curbing black money and quid-pro-quo funding is an argument for. Statement 2 is wrong: the heavy fiscal burden is an argument against. Statement 3 is correct: the level-field argument rests on equality under Article 14. So C; A, B and D all include the wrong statement 2.
64.tq: For: black money, Art. 14 level field. Against: fiscal burden, off-book cash.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(3) 1 and 3 only**.
For: curbs **black money and quid-pro-quo** funding; gives a **level field** for resource-poor candidates (**Art. 14**).
Statement 2 is wrong: **heavy fiscal burden** is an argument **against**.
xa: Another objection: it does **not stop off-book cash** spending.
SC (**2026**): eliminating black money is a **core ECI responsibility**.

64.s: According to the Supreme Court decision in State of Karnataka v. Prathik Parasrampuria (2026), eliminating black money from elections is primarily whose core responsibility?
64.x: The Supreme Court described elimination of black money from elections as a core responsibility of the Election Commission of India.
64.tq: Ask which constitutional institution has the responsibility, avoiding a swap with an auditing or fiscal body.
xs: In **State of Karnataka v Prathik Parasrampuria (2026)**, the SC called eliminating black money from elections a **core responsibility** of the **Election Commission of India** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The case is on the **state funding** page; the CAG, Parliament Secretariat and Finance Commission are not named for this role.
xa: Yet the ECI still **lacks power to deregister** parties for **financial non-compliance**.
The **Law Commission 255th Report (2015)** sought **limited power to deregister** non-compliant parties.
Arguments for state funding: curbs **black money** and quid-pro-quo funding; levels the field (**Art. 14**).
Against: **heavy fiscal burden**; does not stop **off-book cash** spending.

64.s: Which State was the first to conduct its entire Assembly election using EVMs?
64.x: Goa conducted the first whole-State Assembly election using EVMs in 1999. Gujarat was not the first State to do so.
64.tq: Separate pilot use from the first whole-State use.
xs: **Goa, 1999** was the first whole-State Assembly election on EVMs — option **(2)**.
⚠ **Gujarat** was **not** the first; **Kerala** (**Parur 1982**) was the first pilot; **Nagaland** (Noksen) = first **VVPAT**.
xa: APPSC-G2 **2025** key: the Goa 1999 statement is true.
**2004** = first nationwide (all-India) EVM use.

64.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the manufacture of EVMs:
1. Bharat Electronics Limited manufactures EVMs.
2. Electronics Corporation of India Limited manufactures EVMs.
3. Both the manufacturing public sector undertakings are headquartered in Bengaluru.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: BEL, Bengaluru, and ECIL, Hyderabad, are the two public sector undertakings that manufacture EVMs. Statement 3 is false because ECIL is based in Hyderabad.
64.tq: Catch the swapped location in a manufacturer-location statement.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
EVMs are made by two PSUs: **BEL** and **ECIL**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **BEL** is in **Bengaluru**, **ECIL** in **Hyderabad**.
xa: BEL and ECIL also make **VVPATs**.
AP angle: **ECIL** is the EVM maker based in **Hyderabad**.

64.s: With respect to the capacity of EVMs, which one of the following is correct?
o: An M2 system can connect 24 ballot units and accommodate 384 candidates, whereas an M3 system can connect four ballot units and accommodate 64 candidates.
An M3 system can accommodate 2,000 candidates through 24 ballot units.
An M2 system can connect four ballot units and accommodate 64 candidates, whereas an M3 system can connect 24 ballot units and accommodate 384 candidates including NOTA.
Both M2 and M3 systems can accommodate 64 candidates through four ballot units.
64.x: M2 EVMs support four ballot units and 64 candidates; an M3 control unit can take up to 24 ballot units and accommodate 384 candidates including NOTA.
64.tq: Split the comparison into ballot-unit capacity and candidate capacity.
xs: **M2**: **4** BUs, **64** candidates; **M3**: **24** BUs = **384** candidates incl. NOTA — option **(3)**.
Option (1) swaps M2 and M3; **2,000** is the M3's vote capacity, not candidates.
xa: EVMs are to show **colour photos** of candidates.
First pilot: **70-Parur, Kerala, 1982**.

64.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Supreme Court's position on EVMs is NOT correct?
o: In ADR v ECI (2024), the Court refused to order a return to paper ballots.
The Supreme Court has repeatedly upheld the use of EVMs.
In ADR v ECI (2024), the Court ordered a return to paper ballots.
The Court has considered safeguards relating to VVPAT verification.
64.x: The Supreme Court refused to order a return to paper ballots in ADR v ECI (2024). The other statements correctly reflect the Court's approach to EVMs and verification safeguards.
64.tq: Identify the reversed judicial conclusion in the NOT question.
xs: The NOT-correct statement: "ADR v ECI **ordered a return to paper ballots**" — option **(3)**.
In fact **ADR v ECI (2024)** **refused** a return to paper ballots; the SC has **repeatedly upheld EVMs**.
xa: It also rejected **100% slip counting**.
ECI admitted EVMs "are still a subject of frequent public questioning" (**2 Sep 2026**).

64.s:
Consider the following statements regarding VVPAT:
1. It is attached to the Electronic Voting Machine.
2. It prints a slip containing the serial number, name and symbol of the selected candidate.
3. The voter can see the printed slip for seven seconds.
4. The slip is handed over to the voter for personal custody.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the voter views the slip through the VVPAT window; it is not handed over to the voter.
64.tq: Use the operational sequence and reject the plausible but incorrect claim that the voter receives the paper slip.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
**VVPAT** prints a slip with the candidate's **serial number, name and symbol**, visible for about **7 seconds**.
Statement 4 is wrong: the slip **drops into a sealed box**, not into the voter's hands.
xa: Generations: **M1, M2, M3** (current).
First used at **51-Noksen, Nagaland, 2013**.

64.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Supreme Court's 2024 decision in ADR v. ECI:
1. The demand for ballot paper voting and counting of 100 per cent VVPAT slips was rejected.
2. Symbol-loading units are to be sealed and preserved for 45 days.
3. A runner-up in second or third position may seek checking of 5 per cent of EVMs per segment within seven days.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: All three statements correctly describe the verification rules associated with ADR v. ECI in April 2024.
64.tq: Test a cluster of linked judicial safeguards using the coded combination options.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**ADR v ECI (Apr 2024)** rejected **100% slip counting** and **paper ballots**; symbol-loading units sealed **45 days**.
Candidates placed **2nd and 3rd** can seek a check of **5% of EVMs** per segment within **7 days**.
xa: The check is of the EVMs' **burnt memory**.
**N. Chandrababu Naidu (2019)** raised the VVPAT tally to **5** polling stations per segment.

64.s: VVPAT slips must be counted in which of the following circumstances?
o: Whenever EVM data and Form 17C do not match
Whenever postal ballots exceed the number of EVM votes
Only in constituencies using postal ballots
Only when the winning candidate requests it after the declaration of results
64.x: VVPAT slips are required to be counted wherever the EVM data and Form 17C do not match.
64.tq: Apply the verification rule to a specific discrepancy rather than to a general recount demand.
xs: **VVPAT slips must be counted wherever EVM data do not match Form 17C** — so option **(1)** is correct.
This is one of the **new ECI rules** on counting; postal ballots relate to a different rule (below).
xa: The **penultimate EVM/VVPAT round** is counted only after **postal ballots** are finished.
**ADR v ECI (April 2024)**: candidates placed **2nd and 3rd** can seek a check of **5% of EVMs' burnt memory** within **7 days**.
ECI objects that **totalisers** would make **EVM, VVPAT and Form 17C** checks harder.

64.s:
Which of the following is the correct order of counting-related procedures?
A. Counting of postal ballots
B. Counting of the penultimate EVM/VVPAT round
C. Counting of the final EVM/VVPAT round
64.x: Postal ballots are counted before the penultimate EVM/VVPAT round; the final EVM/VVPAT round follows subsequently.
64.tq: Arrange the procedure by identifying the expressly stated precedence of postal-ballot counting.
xs: Order: **postal ballots** → **penultimate EVM/VVPAT round** → final round — option **(1)**.
The penultimate round is counted only after postal ballots are finished.
xa: VVPAT slips are counted wherever EVM data do not match **Form 17C**.
Runners-up can seek a **5%** EVM check within **7 days**.

64.s: Which case held that VVPAT is necessary for free and fair elections and directed its introduction in phases?
o: State of Karnataka v Prathik Parasrampuria
64.x: In Subramanian Swamy v ECI (2013), the Supreme Court held that VVPAT was needed for free and fair polls and required phased introduction.
64.tq: Match the judicial case with its distinctive electoral reform.
xs: **Subramanian Swamy v ECI (2013)** held VVPAT needed for free and fair polls, to be brought **in phases** — option **(1)**.
**ADR v ECI** = 2024 EVM/VVPAT safeguards; **PUCL** = NOTA; **Prathik Parasrampuria** = black money.
xa: VVPAT debuted at **Noksen**, **2013**.
**N. Chandrababu Naidu (2019)**: tally from **1 to 5** polling stations per segment.

64.s: The decision in N. Chandrababu Naidu v Union of India (2019) changed the random VVPAT-EVM tally from:
o: Two to five polling stations per district
One to five polling stations per Assembly segment
One to ten polling stations per parliamentary constituency
Five to ten polling stations per Assembly segment
64.x: The 2019 decision raised the random VVPAT-EVM tally from one to five polling stations per Assembly segment.
64.tq: Remember both sides of the judicially ordered numerical increase.
xs: **N. Chandrababu Naidu v UoI (2019)** raised the random VVPAT–EVM tally from **one to five polling stations** per **Assembly segment** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The tally unit is the **Assembly segment**, not a district or parliamentary constituency.
xa: **ADR v ECI (Apr 2024)** rejected **100% slip counting** and a **return to paper ballots**.
In that case, symbol-loading units are sealed for **45 days**; runners-up can seek a check of **5% of EVMs**.
**Subramanian Swamy v ECI (2013)**: VVPAT is needed for free and fair polls; introduce it **in phases**.

64.s:
Consider the following statements about NOTA:
1. In PUCL v Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court traced the right to reject to Article 19(1)(a).
2. NOTA was first used in a Lok Sabha election in 2013.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
64.x: Statement 1 is correct: PUCL (2013) linked the right to reject to Article 19(1)(a). Statement 2 is wrong: NOTA was first used in the 2013 Assembly elections; its first Lok Sabha use was in 2014. So A; B and C accept the wrong statement 2, D rejects the correct statement 1.
64.tq: NOTA: 2013 Assembly polls first, 2014 first Lok Sabha.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
**PUCL (2013)** traced the right to reject to **Art. 19(1)(a)**.
Statement 2 is wrong: NOTA's first Lok Sabha use was **2014**; **2013** was the Assembly elections.
xa: In **2014** NOTA got **1.1%** (over **60 lakh** votes).
NOTA button added on **27 Sept 2013**.

64.s:
With reference to totalisers, consider the following statements:
1. A totaliser combines the counting of several EVMs.
2. It is intended to conceal booth-wise voting trends.
3. The Election Commission has stated that a legal framework for totalisers already exists.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: A totaliser combines several EVM counts to hide booth-wise trends. The ECI stated that no legal framework for totalisers exists, making statement 3 false.
64.tq: Spot the reversed institutional position in the third statement.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
A **totaliser** pools the count of several **control units**, so **booth-wise patterns stay hidden**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the ECI says there is **no legal framework** in the RPA or Conduct of Election Rules.
xa: Recommended by the **Law Commission 255th Report (2015)**.
SC **sought the Centre's response** on totalisers as a "fall-back option" (**Sep 2026**).

64.s: What is the principal purpose of a Remote Voting Machine (RVM) prototype?
o: To permit domestic migrants to vote for up to 72 constituencies from one remote polling station
To count postal ballots together with EVM votes
To enable overseas citizens to vote in all constituencies without registration
To conceal booth-wise voting patterns by pooling control units
64.x: The ECI's RVM prototype is intended to enable domestic migrants to vote for up to 72 constituencies from one remote polling station.
64.tq: Distinguish remote voting from totaliser-based secrecy of booth results.
xs: The **RVM** lets **domestic migrants** vote for up to **72 constituencies** from one remote polling station — option **(1)**.
Pooling control units to hide booth-wise trends is the **totaliser**, not the RVM.
xa: RVM was demonstrated to parties in **Jan 2023**.
**Overseas electors** were enabled by the RP (Amendment) Act **2010**.

64.s: The use of 'totalisers' in counting votes was recommended by:
64.x: The Law Commission's 255th Report (2015) recommended totalisers, which pool the count of several control units so booth-wise voting patterns stay hidden. The Indrajit Gupta Committee dealt with state funding, the Vohra Committee with the crime-politics nexus, and the 2nd ARC with ethics in governance.
64.tq: Totaliser = Law Commission 255th (2015).
xs: **Totalisers** were recommended by the **Law Commission's 255th Report, 2015** — option **(2)**.
**Indrajit Gupta** = state funding; **Vohra** = crime-politics; **2nd ARC** = Ethics in Governance.
xa: The 255th also urged **one candidate, one seat** and a **collegium** for appointing the CEC.
It sought **limited power to deregister** non-compliant parties.

64.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The 170th Law Commission Report backed simultaneous elections.
2. The 2018 draft Law Commission report also backed simultaneous elections.
3. Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections were held together from 1951-52 to 1967.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: All three statements are correct: both the 170th Report and the 2018 draft report supported simultaneous elections, and simultaneous Lok Sabha–Assembly polls were held from 1951-52 to 1967.
64.tq: Link two recommendations with the historical period in which simultaneous elections occurred.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**170th Report (1999)** and the **2018 draft report** backed simultaneous polls; polls were held together **1951-52 to 1967**.
xa: Proposed safeguard: **constructive no-confidence motion** (German model).
Criticism: weakens **federalism**.

64.s:
Consider the following statements about the High-Level Committee on simultaneous elections (2023-24):
1. It was chaired by former President Ram Nath Kovind.
2. Amit Shah and Ghulam Nabi Azad were among its members.
3. Dinesh Goswami was among its members.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: ex-President Kovind chaired it, and its members included Amit Shah, Ghulam Nabi Azad, N.K. Singh, Subhash C. Kashyap, Harish Salve and Sanjay Kothari. Statement 3 is wrong: Dinesh Goswami headed the 1990 electoral reform committee and was not a member. So A; B, C and D all include the wrong statement 3.
64.tq: Kovind panel: Shah, Azad, N.K. Singh, Kashyap, Salve, Kothari.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Chair: ex-President **Ram Nath Kovind**; members included **Amit Shah** and **Ghulam Nabi Azad**.
Statement 3 is wrong: **Dinesh Goswami** headed the **1990** electoral-reform committee, not a member here.
xa: Other members: **N.K. Singh, Subhash C. Kashyap, Harish Salve, Sanjay Kothari**.
Recommendation: **phased rollout**.

64.s:
The Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024 proposes amendments to which of the following Articles?
1. Article 83
2. Article 172
3. Article 327
4. Article 280
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
64.x: The Bill proposes amendments to Articles 83, 172 and 327. Article 280 is not among the Articles identified for amendment.
64.tq: Eliminate the unrelated Article and retain the three Articles expressly connected with the Bill.
xs: Items 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
The Bill amends **Art. 83** (Parliament's duration), **Art. 172** (State Legislatures) and **Art. 327**, and inserts **Art. 82A**.
**Article 280** is not part of it.
xa: Debate also named **85, 174 and 356**.
**U.U. Lalit** and **Sanjiv Khanna** raised Basic Structure doubts.

64.s: Which of the following correctly describes the phased rollout recommended by the Ram Nath Kovind High-Level Committee?
o: Local-body elections first, followed by Lok Sabha elections after five years
All elections to be held on the same day without any transitional phase
Rajya Sabha and Legislative Council elections together first, followed by Assembly elections
Lok Sabha and Assembly elections together first, followed by local-body elections within 100 days
64.x: The committee recommended holding Lok Sabha and Assembly polls together initially, followed by local-body elections within 100 days.
64.tq: Track the sequence and the specific 100-day interval in the proposed phased model.
xs: The **Kovind Committee** recommended a **phased rollout**: **Lok Sabha and Assembly** polls together first, then **local-body elections within 100 days** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It did not propose a same-day poll without transition, nor local bodies first.
xa: Committee chair: ex-President **Ram Nath Kovind** (**2023-24**); members included **Amit Shah** and **Ghulam Nabi Azad**.
The **129th Amendment Bill, 2024** inserts **Art. 82A** and amends **Arts. 83, 172 and 327**.
Lok Sabha + Assembly polls were held together **1951-52 to 1967**.
JPC still examining the Bill (**Feb 2026**).

64.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched in relation to the constitutional provisions discussed in connection with simultaneous elections?
o: Article 83 — Duration of Houses of Parliament
Article 85 — Dissolution and related parliamentary matters
Article 174 — Dissolution and related matters concerning State Legislatures
Article 356 — Appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner
64.x: Article 356 concerns President's Rule, not appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner. Articles 83, 85 and 174 were among the provisions mentioned in the debate in relation to duration or dissolution.
64.tq: Use the wrong constitutional subject to identify the incorrectly matched pair.
xs: **Article 356 — appointment of the CEC** is wrong — option **(4)**; Art. **356** is **President's Rule**.
**83** = House duration; **85** and **174** = dissolution matters.
xa: The **CEC and ECs Act 2023** sets the CEC selection panel: **PM, a Cabinet Minister, LoP**.
The 129th Bill inserts **Art. 82A**.

64.s: A proposed safeguard for maintaining governmental accountability under simultaneous elections is based on which model?
o: The Westminster model of an unelected executive
The American model of judicial review
The German model of a constructive vote of no-confidence
64.x: The proposed safeguard is a constructive no-confidence motion modelled on the German system.
64.tq: Match the institutional safeguard with the country model specifically associated with it.
xs: The proposed safeguard is a **constructive no-confidence motion** on the **German model** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It is meant to keep a government accountable without breaking the **simultaneous-election** cycle.
xa: The **Law Commission 170th Report (1999)** and the **2018 draft report** backed simultaneous polls.
Lok Sabha + Assembly polls were held together from **1951-52 to 1967**.
Criticism: simultaneous polls weaken **federalism** and need huge numbers of **EVMs and forces**.
The **Kovind Committee** (**2023-24**) recommended a **phased rollout**: local bodies within **100 days** of LS + Assembly polls.

64.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024?
o: It seeks to synchronise Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections and inserts a new Article 82A
It raises the Lok Sabha ceiling from 550 to 850 and inserts Article 334A
It provides one-third reservation for women and amends Article 330
It extends the delimitation freeze beyond 2026 and amends Article 81
64.x: The 129th Amendment Bill (introduced December 2024, referred to a JPC) aims at simultaneous Lok Sabha and Assembly elections (APPSC 2024 key); it inserts Art 82A and amends Arts 83, 172 and 327. Raising the ceiling to 850 was the 131st Amendment Bill, 2026; women's reservation (Art 334A) came via the 106th Amendment; the delimitation freeze was extended by the 84th Amendment.
64.tq: 129th Bill = ONOE: new Art 82A + amends 83, 172, 327.
xs: The **129th Amendment Bill, 2024** seeks to **synchronise Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections** and inserts **Art. 82A** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It also amends **Art. 83** (duration of Parliament), **Art. 172** (duration of State Legislatures) and **Art. 327** (Parliament's power over elections).
It does not deal with the Lok Sabha ceiling, women's reservation or the delimitation freeze.
xa: Introduced in the Lok Sabha in **Dec 2024** and referred to a **Joint Parliamentary Committee**.
The JPC was still examining the Bill in **Feb 2026**.
Others named in debate: **Arts. 85, 174 and 356** (dissolution, President's Rule).
Aim of simultaneous elections was the **APPSC 2024** key.

64.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Electors' Photo Identity Card (EPIC):
1. EPIC was introduced in 1993.
2. Its number, once issued, remains valid for life even if the elector’s address changes.
3. EPIC was introduced through the 61st Constitutional Amendment Act.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: EPIC was introduced in 1993, and its number remains valid for life despite a change of address. It was not introduced by the 61st Amendment.
64.tq: Separate the year and legal basis of EPIC from the voting-age amendment.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — so option **(1)** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: **EPIC** (Electors' Photo Identity Card) was introduced in **1993**.
Statement 2 is correct: the EPIC number, once issued, is **valid for life** even if the address changes.
Statement 3 is wrong: the notes link EPIC to **1993**, not to the **61st** Amendment.
xa: PYQ order: **EVM → photo ID → VVPAT → NOTA** (**UPPSC 2025**).
**Election Laws (Amendment) Act 2021**: **Aadhaar linking** of rolls to stop multiple enrolment.
EVMs were first used in **1982** (**Parur, Kerala**) — before EPIC.

64.s:
With reference to the Election Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021, consider the following statements:
1. It provided for linking electoral rolls with Aadhaar to check multiple enrolment.
2. It introduced multiple qualifying dates for registration as an elector.
3. It provided for gender-neutral wording in electoral law.
4. It provided for requisition of premises for election-related purposes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: All four statements describe provisions associated with the Election Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021.
64.tq: Identify the comprehensive option when all listed features belong to the same amendment.
xs: All four statements are correct — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **Election Laws (Amendment) Act 2021** brought **Aadhaar linking** of electoral rolls (to stop **multiple enrolment**) and **multiple qualifying dates**.
It also brought **gender-neutral** wording and **requisition of premises** for elections.
xa: **2022**: spending limit raised to **₹95 lakh (LS) / ₹40 lakh (Assembly)** for bigger States.
**2025**: **ECINET**, one platform for **40+ apps**; **100% webcasting**; **Special Intensive Revision (SIR)** of rolls.
**Overseas electors**: RP (Amendment) Act **2010**, in force **Feb 2011**.

64.s: Under the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, the selection panel consists of:
o: The Prime Minister, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Union Home Minister
The Prime Minister, a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition
The President, the Prime Minister and the Chief Justice of India
The Prime Minister, the Chief Justice of India and the Leader of the Opposition
64.x: The 2023 Act provides for a panel comprising the Prime Minister, a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister, and the Leader of the Opposition. The Chief Justice of India was dropped from the panel.
64.tq: Use the composition trap by identifying the authority omitted from the final arrangement.
xs: The **2023 Act** panel = the **Prime Minister**, a **Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM** and the **Leader of the Opposition** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **CJI was dropped**; a panel of **PM, LoP and CJI** was the **Tarkunde Committee**'s **1975** proposal.
xa: ⚠ **Tarkunde (1975)** panel had the **CJI**; the **2023 Act** dropped the CJI.
Criticism: the Act gives the **executive a majority** on the panel that picks the election referee.
The **Law Commission 255th Report (2015)** proposed a **collegium** for appointing the CEC.

64.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: 2013 — Lily Thomas judgment striking down Section 8(4) of the RPA
2002 — Disclosure of criminal record, assets and education
64.x: Electoral bonds were struck down by the Supreme Court in 2024; they were not introduced in that year. The other pairs are correctly matched.
64.tq: Find the reversed action-year pair, particularly where a later year records invalidation rather than introduction.
xs: **2024 — Introduction of electoral bonds** is wrongly matched — so option **(4)** is the answer.
Electoral bonds were notified in **2018** and **struck down** in **2024** (**ADR v UoI**, **15 Feb 2024**).
The rest are correct: **Lily Thomas** struck down **Sec. 8(4)** in **2013**; **ADR v UoI** (**2002**) mandated disclosure; **EVMs** in all constituencies in **2004**.
xa: ⚠ **ADR v UoI** **2002** = disclosure; **2024** = electoral bonds; **ADR v ECI** **2024** = EVM/VVPAT.
Bonds were sold only by **SBI**, in **₹1,000 to ₹1 crore** denominations, valid **15 days**.
The verdict was by a unanimous **five-judge Constitution Bench**, under the **right to information** (**Art. 19(1)(a)**).

64.s: Which pair of actions was attributed to the Election Commission in relation to RUPPs?
o: Recognising 808 RUPPs and capping candidates at 1,200 per constituency
Delisting 808 RUPPs and capping electors at 1,200 per polling station
Deregistering 1,200 RUPPs and capping polling stations at 808 per district
Delisting 750 RUPPs and permitting unlimited electors per polling station
64.x: The Election Commission delisted 808 RUPPs and capped the number of electors per polling station at 1,200.
64.tq: Keep the two numerical administrative measures together.
xs: The ECI **delisted 808 RUPPs** and capped **1,200 electors per polling station** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**750** is the approximate number of RUPPs that **contested 2024**, not the number delisted.
xa: There are over **2,800 RUPPs**, of which only ~**750** contested **2024**.
**Sec. 29A** of RPA 1951 deals with **registration of political parties** with the ECI.
The **Law Commission 255th Report** sought **limited power to deregister** non-compliant parties.

64.s:
Which of the following are identified as unfinished areas in electoral reform discussions?
1. State funding of elections
2. Disqualification upon framing of charges
3. A cap on political party expenditure
4. Universal compulsory voting
Which of the statements given above are correct?
64.x: State funding, disqualification on framing of charges and a party spending cap are identified as unfinished agendas. Universal compulsory voting is not included in the stated list.
64.tq: Separate listed reform priorities from an unlisted but plausible electoral reform.
xs: Items **1, 2 and 3** are the unfinished agenda — so option **(1)** is correct.
Listed: **state funding**, disqualification on **framing of charges**, and a **party spending cap**.
**Universal compulsory voting** is not in the notes' list.
xa: **Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998)** on **state funding** is still **not adopted**.
**Public Interest Foundation (2018)** left disqualification on **framing of charges** to **Parliament**.
Loophole: **Sec. 77** caps **candidate** spending, not **parties'** own spending.
Candidate limits: **Rs 95 lakh** (LS) and **Rs 40 lakh** (Assembly) in larger States.

64.s: The expression “bahubali culture” in the context of electoral politics refers primarily to the erosion of trust in legislatures through:
64.x: The expression refers to the use of muscle power and its adverse effect on trust in legislatures.
64.tq: Decode the contextual meaning of a politically significant phrase.
xs: "**Bahubali culture**" refers to **muscle power** eroding trust in legislatures — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is a **criminalisation** issue, unrelated to VVPATs, postal ballots or digital enumeration.
xa: **ADR data**: **31% of MPs and 29% of MLAs** face serious criminal charges.
MPs' share rose from **14% (2009) to 31% (2024)**.
The **Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990)** flagged **musclemen**; the **Vohra Committee (1993)** studied the **crime–politics nexus**.
**12 special courts** handle cases against MPs/MLAs.

64.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Punchhi Commission
(b) Sarkaria Commission
(c) Rajamannar Committee
(d) Indrajit Gupta Committee

List-II
(i) State funding of elections
(ii) State-level initiative for federal autonomy
(iii) Federal dialogue and coordination mechanisms
(iv) Recommendation for a permanent Inter-State Council
64.x: Punchhi dealt with federal dialogue and coordination, Sarkaria recommended a permanent Inter-State Council, Rajamannar was Tamil Nadu's push for autonomy, and Indrajit Gupta covered election funding. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
64.tq: Match each committee to its subject.
n: The Sarkaria Commission recommended establishing a permanent Inter-State Council or Inter-Governmental Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 70-72]
The Indrajit Gupta Committee concerned state funding of elections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 70-72]
Federal dialogue and coordination mechanisms were the exam focus for the Punchhi Commission. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 70-72]
The Rajamannar Committee represented a state-level initiative for federal autonomy. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 70-72]
Punchhi Commission is categorized under federalism, Centre–State Relations, and coordination and dialogue mechanisms. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 70-72]
The Indrajit Gupta Committee is a classic elimination option under Centre–State questions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 70-72]
The recommendation for a permanent Inter-State Council or Inter-Governmental Council belongs to the Sarkaria Commission, not the Punchhi Commission. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 70-72]
xs: The correct code is **a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i** — option **(4)**.
**Punchhi** = **federal dialogue and coordination mechanisms**; **Sarkaria** = **permanent Inter-State Council** (**Article 263**).
**Rajamannar** = **Tamil Nadu's** state-level initiative for **federal autonomy**; **Indrajit Gupta** = **State funding of elections**.
xa: ⚠ The permanent ISC recommendation is **Sarkaria's**, **not** Punchhi's.
Years: Rajamannar **1969-71**; Sarkaria **1983-88** (**247** recommendations); Punchhi **2007-10**; Indrajit Gupta **1998**.
"Which is NOT on Centre-State relations?" → **Indrajit Gupta Committee** (APPSC-G2 2025).

64.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The Inter-State Council was established by the President of India.
Statement B: The Inter-State Council was established by an Act of Parliament.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
64.x: A is true: the President set up the Inter-State Council by order under Article 263. B is false because Parliament did not create it by law.
64.tq: Recall that the Inter-State Council was set up by Presidential order.
n: The Inter-State Council was established by the President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 70-72]
The Inter-State Council was not enacted or established by Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 70-72]
xs: **Statement A is true, Statement B is false** — option **(3)** is correct.
A: the **Inter-State Council** under **Article 263** was set up by the **President**.
B is wrong: it was **not** created by an **Act of Parliament**.
xa: The **Sarkaria Commission** recommended a **permanent Inter-State Council** (Inter-Governmental Council).
Sarkaria (**1983-88**) made **247** recommendations.
**Punchhi Commission** was the **second** major commission on Centre–State relations.

64.s: A candidate contesting an election to the Lok Sabha or a State Assembly can contest from a maximum of how many constituencies under Section 33 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951?
64.x: Under Section 33(7) of the RPA, 1951, a candidate can contest from at most two constituencies, a limit added in 1996.
64.tq: Recall the two-constituency limit.
n: Section 33 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, limits a candidate to contesting from a maximum of two constituencies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
A candidate can contest from a maximum of two Lok Sabha constituencies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
A candidate can contest from a maximum of two State Assembly constituencies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
xs: A candidate can contest from at most **two** constituencies — option **(4)** — under **Section 33(7), RPA 1951**.
The cap was added by the **1996** amendment after **Devi Lal** contested **three Lok Sabha seats** in **1991**.
xa: A winner of both seats must vacate one within **14 days** (**Sec. 70**).
Reform proposal: **one candidate, one seat** (**Law Commission 255th report**).
ECI proposal: the vacating candidate pays for the bypoll.

64.s: A candidate forfeits the security deposit when the candidate fails to secure more than which proportion of the total valid votes polled?
64.x: A candidate loses the security deposit if they win no more than one-sixth of the valid votes.
64.tq: Recall the one-sixth rule.
n: A candidate forfeits the security deposit if the candidate fails to secure more than one-sixth of the total valid votes polled. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 62-65]
xs: The deposit is forfeited if the candidate fails to get more than **one-sixth** of the **total valid votes** — option **(4)**.
**Sec. 34** deposits: **₹25,000** (Lok Sabha), **₹10,000** (Assembly), half for SC/ST.
xa: The **1996** RP (Amendment) Act brought **higher security deposits**.
It also required more proposers for independents/unrecognised parties.
Election petition: within **45 days** (**Sec. 81**).

64.s:
Assertion (A): A registered elector in India can contest a Rajya Sabha election from any State.
Reason (R): The 2003 Amendment removed the requirement that the candidate be an elector in the particular State.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
64.x: Both are true: since a 2003 amendment removed the rule that a candidate must be a voter in that State, any registered voter in India can contest a Rajya Sabha seat from any State. R explains A.
64.tq: Recall the 2003 change upheld in Kuldip Nayar.
n: The 2003 amendment removed the requirement that a Rajya Sabha candidate be an elector in the particular State of contest. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
Any registered elector in India can contest a Rajya Sabha election from any State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
The **2003 amendment** removed the rule that a **Rajya Sabha** candidate be an **elector** in that **particular State**, so any **registered elector** in India can contest from **any State**.
xa: Upheld by the **Supreme Court** in **Kuldip Nayar** (**2006**).
Before **2003**, domicile/voter requirement applied.
**1996** changes: cap of **two constituencies**, higher deposits.

64.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the death of a contesting candidate?
o: The election is automatically cancelled in every case of the death of a candidate.
The death of a candidate no longer automatically countermands the election.
The change was made through the 1996 Amendment.
Recognized political parties may nominate a replacement within a set timeframe.
64.x: Option A is incorrect: since the 1996 amendment, a candidate's death no longer cancels the election automatically. A recognised party can name a replacement within a set time.
64.tq: Recall the 1996 change on a candidate's death.
n: The Representation of the People Act, 1951 was amended in 1996 to cap the number of constituencies a candidate could contest at two. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
Before the 1996 amendment, elections were automatically countermanded upon the death of a contesting candidate. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
After the 1996 amendment, elections are no longer automatically countermanded upon the death of a contesting candidate. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
Recognized political parties may nominate a replacement for a deceased contesting candidate within a set timeframe. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the election is **automatically cancelled** on every candidate's death — option **(1)**.
After the **1996 amendment**, death **no longer** automatically countermands the election.
A **recognised political party** may **nominate a replacement** within a set timeframe.
xa: **Countermanding** now happens only on the death of a **recognised-party** candidate.
The **1996** Act also made poll day a **paid holiday** (**Sec. 135B**) and banned liquor **48 hours** before poll (**Sec. 135C**).
Bypolls within **6 months** (**Sec. 151A**).

64.s:
Assertion (A): The ceiling on the number of constituencies from which a candidate may contest was introduced through an amendment to the RPA, 1951 in 1996.
Reason (R): The amendment followed the 1991 election in which Devi Lal contested from three Lok Sabha seats.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
64.x: Both are true: the 1996 amendment capped contests at two constituencies after Devi Lal stood from three Lok Sabha seats in 1991. R explains A.
64.tq: Recall the Devi Lal case behind the 1996 cap.
n: Devi Lal contested from three Lok Sabha seats in the 1991 elections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
The Representation of the People Act, 1951 was amended in 1996 to cap the number of constituencies a candidate could contest at two. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
The **1996** amendment capped contests at **two** constituencies because **Devi Lal** had contested **three Lok Sabha seats** in **1991**.
xa: Before **1996** there was **no cap** (UPSC 2021 key).
Provision: **Section 33(7), RPA 1951**.
Winner of both must vacate one within **14 days** (**Sec. 70**).

64.s:
Which of the following recommendations were associated with the Dinesh Goswami Committee?
I. State funding of elections
II. Use of Electronic Voting Machines
III. Measures subsequently enacted in the 1996 RPA Amendment
IV. Allocation of State Legislative Council seats
64.x: I, II and III are correct: the Goswami Committee recommended State funding of elections and EVMs, and its proposals led to the 1996 RPA amendment. IV is false because Council seat allocation was not its subject.
64.tq: Recall the Goswami Committee's proposals.
n: The Dinesh Goswami Committee recommended state funding of elections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
The Dinesh Goswami Committee recommended the use of electronic voting machines. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
The Dinesh Goswami Committee recommended measures subsequently enacted in the 1996 amendment to the Representation of the People Act, 1951. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
xs: Statements **I, II and III only** are correct — option **(3)**.
The **Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990)** recommended **State funding** of elections and **electronic voting machines**, later enacted in the **1996 amendment** to the RPA 1951.
IV is wrong: Council seat allocation was not its subject.
xa: Goswami was the **broadest review**: time limits for bye-elections, strengthening the EC, anti-defection; flagged **musclemen**.
