xs: **16th Finance Commission — 2026-27 to 2030-31** is correctly matched — option **(3)**.
**14th FC** covered **2015-20**; **15th FC** gave reports for **2020-21** and **2021-26**.
xa: ⚠ "**2020-25**" for the 15th FC is a trap in APP notes.
14th FC constituted **2 Jan 2013**; 16th FC **31 Dec 2023**.

70.s: The 15th Finance Commission was the first Finance Commission to:
o: cut the States' vertical share from 42 per cent to 41 per cent
recommend a 50 per cent share to the States
70.x: The 15th Finance Commission was the first to reduce the vertical share from 42 per cent to 41 per cent, largely in the context of the change in Jammu and Kashmir's status.
70.tq: Test a first-in-series fact against nearby but unsupported reforms.
xs: The **15th FC** was the **first to cut** the vertical share, **42 to 41%** — option **(1)**.
The cut reflected **J&K's change of status**.
xa: **14th FC**: largest increase ever (**32 → 42%**).
**16th FC**: first to use **Contribution to GDP** (**10%**).
15th FC added **demographic performance** and **tax effort**.

70.s: The rising use of cesses and surcharges is criticised because it:
o: shrinks the divisible pool available for sharing
raises the States' vertical share automatically
increases the divisible pool available for tax devolution
70.x: Cesses and surcharges are not generally part of the divisible pool, so their increasing use shrinks the pool available for devolution.
70.tq: Trace the fiscal cause-and-effect relationship in a policy scenario.
xs: Rising **cesses and surcharges** **shrink the divisible pool** available for sharing — so option **(1)** is correct.
The divisible pool **excludes cesses, surcharges and cost of collection**, so more cesses mean less to share with states.
They do not raise the states' share or enlarge the pool; the **16th FC** kept the share at **41%**.
xa: After the **14th FC** raised the share to **42%**, the Centre increased **non-shareable cesses**.
FM: states got the **full 41%**; total transfers **₹25.44 lakh crore** for 2026-27.
Southern states call their shares unfair — Karnataka **4.13%** (15th: **3.64%**; 14th: **4.71%**).

70.s: Which of the following States was specifically associated with fiscal stress because the 16th Finance Commission provided neither revenue deficit grants nor State-specific grants?
70.x: Kerala was identified as facing fiscal stress because the 16th Finance Commission gave it neither revenue deficit grants nor State-specific grants.
70.tq: Match the State with the specific fiscal consequence.
xs: **Kerala** faces fiscal stress as the 16th FC gives it **no revenue deficit or state-specific grants** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Andhra Pradesh** is linked to the **₹38,000 crore** loss; **Karnataka** to complaints about its **4.13%** share.
xa: Kerala's horizontal share still rose to **2.382%** from **1.92%**.
**Revenue-deficit grants** were **discontinued** by the 16th FC.
State deficits are capped at **3% of GSDP**.

70.s:
Assertion (A): The Finance Commission is a permanent body.
Reason (R): The Finance Commission is an independent body.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
70.x: A is false: the Finance Commission is not permanent; it is set up every five years or earlier. R is true: it is an independent body.
70.tq: Discriminate a periodic body from a permanent one.
n: The Finance Commission is a permanent body. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 65-68]
The Finance Commission is an independent body. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 65-68]
xs: The key is **A is false, but R is true** — option **(4)**.
A treated as false: the FC is **constituted** by the **President** every **five years** or **earlier** — not strictly every five years.
R: it is an **independent** body.
xa: ⚠ The notes call the FC "a **permanent**, **independent**, **quasi-judicial** body" (Article 280, Part XII).
It has civil-court powers of **summoning** persons and **production** of documents.
First FC set up on **6 April 1952** under **K.C. Neogy**.

70.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The first Finance Commission was constituted under a Presidential order in 1951.
Statement B: The first Finance Commission was set up on 6 April 1952.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
70.x: Both are true: the first Finance Commission was set up by Presidential order in 1951 and began work on 6 April 1952 under K.C. Neogy.
70.tq: Recall the first Finance Commission.
n: The first Finance Commission was constituted under a Presidential order in 1951. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 65-68]
The first Finance Commission was set up on 6 April 1952. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 65-68]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)** is correct.
A: the first FC was constituted under a **Presidential order** in **1951**.
B: it was set up on **6 April 1952**, Chairman **K.C. Neogy** (**1952 to 1957**).
xa: **14th FC** constituted **2 Jan 2013**; **16th FC** on **31 Dec 2023**.
**16th FC** report tabled in Parliament on **1 Feb 2026**.
⚠ APPSC-G2 2025 trap: "**Article 290** provides for the FC" — it is **Art. 280**.

70.s: The first Chairman of the Finance Commission was:
70.x: K.C. Neogy was the first Chairman of the Finance Commission (1951). Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar and Ambedkar were Constituent Assembly figures.
70.tq: Recall the first Finance Commission chairman.
n: K.C. Neogy was the first Finance Commission Chairperson. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #52 · pp 137-141]
xs: The first FC Chairman was **K.C. Neogy** — option **(1)** is correct.
The first FC was set up on **6 April 1952** (**1952 to 1957**).
xa: **P.V. Rajamannar** (4th FC): recommendations should not be rejected without very compelling reasons.
**14th FC** raised the vertical share to **42%** (from **32%**).

70.s:
Assertion (A): The Finance Commission has the powers of a civil court regarding the summoning of persons.
Reason (R): The Finance Commission has the powers of a civil court regarding the production of documents.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
70.x: Both are true: the Finance Commission has civil-court powers to summon people and to require documents. These are two parallel powers, so R does not explain A.
70.tq: Ask whether two parallel powers explain each other.
n: The Finance Commission has the powers of a civil court regarding the summoning of persons. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 65-68]
The Finance Commission has the powers of a civil court regarding the production of documents. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 65-68]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — option **(2)**.
The FC has civil-court powers for **summoning** of persons and for **production** of documents — two parallel powers; one does not explain the other.
xa: These powers give it a **quasi-judicial character**.
Its recommendations are **advisory, not binding**.
**Art. 281:** recommendations laid before **each House of Parliament** with an explanatory memorandum.

71.s: The official constitutional name of the office is:
71.x: The official name is Comptroller and Auditor-General of India. “Controller” and “Attorney” are not substitutes for the constitutional terms.
71.tq: Discriminate between similar-looking official titles.
xs: The official name is **Comptroller and Auditor-General of India** — so option **(1)** is correct.
⚠ Not "**Controller**", not "**Attorney**", not "Accounts-General".
xa: Yet he is only an **Auditor-General**, not a true Comptroller — he has **no control over the issue of money**.
Called the "**Guardian of the public purse**".
First CAG: **V. Narahari Rao** (**1948**).

71.s: Who was the first Comptroller and Auditor General of India?
71.x: V. Narahari Rao was the first Comptroller and Auditor General of India.
71.tq: Directly identify the office-holder associated with the beginning of the institution.
xs: **V. Narahari Rao** was the **first CAG** (**1948**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**K. Sanjay Murthy** is the **current** CAG; **K.C. Venugopal** chairs the **PAC**.
xa: K. Sanjay Murthy is the **15th** CAG (as of **May 2026**).
**Vinod Rai**: CAG of the **2G spectrum (2010)** report; wrote "**When Audit Matters**".
**Ambedkar**: CAG = "most important officer under the Constitution".

71.s: The oath of office of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India is administered by the President in the form prescribed in the
71.x: The CAG takes the oath before the President, in the form prescribed in the Third Schedule.
71.tq: Separate the Schedule dealing with oath from the Schedule dealing with salary and service conditions.
xs: The CAG takes the oath before the **President** in the form in the **Third Schedule** — option **(3)**.
⚠ The **Second Schedule** holds his **salary**, not the oath.
xa: Appointed by the **President** by **warrant under his hand and seal** (**Art. 148**).
Resigns to the **President**.
Term: **6 years or age 65**.

71.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the salary of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India?
o: It is equal to the salary of a High Court judge and is charged on the Contingency Fund of India.
It is equal to the salary of a Supreme Court judge and is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
It is fixed by the Public Accounts Committee and charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
It is equal to the salary of the President and is voted annually by Parliament.
71.x: The CAG receives a salary equal to that of a Supreme Court judge. The expenditure is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and is not subject to vote.
71.tq: Compare the office-holder’s salary, authority fixing it and fund charged with nearby constitutional offices.
xs: Salary **equal to a Supreme Court judge**, **charged on the Consolidated Fund of India** — option **(2)**.
It is fixed by **Parliament** (**Second Schedule**) and is **not votable** — not a High Court judge's salary, not the Contingency Fund.
xa: Salary, **leave**, pension and retirement age cannot be varied to his disadvantage.
Office expenses, allowances and pensions are also **charged** on the CFI.
**Leave** is granted by the **President**.

71.s:
With reference to the service conditions of the Comptroller and Auditor General, consider the following statements:
1. Leave of the CAG is granted by the President.
2. Salary, leave, pension and retirement age may be varied to his disadvantage after appointment.
3. The salary and service conditions are provided in the Second Schedule.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
71.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because salary, leave, pension and retirement age cannot be varied to the CAG’s disadvantage after appointment.
71.tq: Find the statement reversing the constitutional protection against disadvantageous alteration of service conditions.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2)** **1 and 3 only**.
**Statement 1** correct: **leave** is granted by the **President**.
**Statement 2** wrong: these **cannot be varied to his disadvantage** after appointment.
**Statement 3** correct: salary is fixed in the **Second Schedule**.
xa: Salary **equal to an SC judge**.
Expenses **charged** on the **Consolidated Fund of India** — not votable.
**No minister** represents the CAG in Parliament.

71.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Comptroller and Auditor General is correct?
o: No Minister represents the CAG in Parliament.
The President represents the CAG in Parliament.
The CAG is represented in Parliament by the Chairperson of the PAC.
A Union Minister represents the CAG in Parliament.
71.x: No Minister represents the CAG in Parliament. The CAG submits audit reports through the constitutionally prescribed channel.
71.tq: Use the institutional-role distinction to avoid assigning parliamentary representation to the wrong authority.
xs: **No Minister represents the CAG in Parliament** — option **(1)**.
His reports reach Parliament via the **President** (**Art. 151**), not through a minister or the PAC chairperson.
xa: The CAG is the PAC's "**friend, philosopher and guide**".
Executive accountability to Parliament works mainly through **CAG reports**.
Not eligible for **further office** under GOI or any State after retirement.

71.s: Who is the Comptroller and Auditor General of India as mentioned for 2026?
71.x: K. Sanjay Murthy is mentioned as the CAG of India for 2026.
71.tq: Directly test the current office-holder against historical and related names.
xs: **K. Sanjay Murthy** is the current CAG (**8 May 2026**) — option **(3)**.
**V. Narahari Rao** was the **first** CAG; **K.C. Venugopal** chairs the **PAC**.
xa: He is the **15th** CAG.
**Vinod Rai** wrote "**When Audit Matters**" (**2026**).
India hosted the **5th BRICS SAI Leaders' Summit** in 2026.

71.s: Among the following, whose normal constitutional term is the longest in duration?
71.x: The CAG's term is six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier; the other listed posts ordinarily have five-year terms.
71.tq: Compare the numerical term lengths before considering qualifications such as dissolution.
xs: The **Comptroller and Auditor-General** has the longest term — **6 years or 65** — option **(1)** (**APPSC-G2 2017**).
**President**, **Vice-President** and **Lok Sabha member**: **5 years**.
xa: **CEC** and **UPSC member** also have **6 years or 65**.
The CAG's term was the **APPSC 2022** key.
Removal: like a **Supreme Court judge**.

71.s:
Consider the following statements about the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India:
1. He holds office for six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier.
2. He holds office during the pleasure of the President.
3. He can be removed in the same manner and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court judge.
4. After ceasing to hold office, he is not eligible for further office under the Government of India or any State.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
71.x: Statement 1 is correct: the term is 6 years or age 65. Statement 2 is wrong: the CAG does not hold office at the President's pleasure. Statement 3 is correct: he is removed like a Supreme Court judge, on an address by both Houses passed with a special majority for proved misbehaviour or incapacity. Statement 4 is correct: he is barred from further office under the Government of India or any State. So '1, 3 and 4 only'.
71.tq: CAG: 6 yrs/65, removed like SC judge, not at pleasure, no post-retirement office.
xs: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct — option **(1)** **1, 3 and 4 only**.
**Statement 1** correct: **6 years or age 65**.
**Statement 2** wrong: he does **not** hold office at the **President's pleasure**.
**Statements 3, 4** correct: removed **like a Supreme Court judge**; **no further office** under GOI or any State.
xa: Removal: address by both Houses with **special majority** for proved **misbehaviour or incapacity**.
Resignation: to the **President**.
Salary **equal to an SC judge**.

71.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the audit jurisdiction of the Comptroller and Auditor General:
1. He audits the Consolidated Fund of India.
2. He audits the Consolidated Funds of States and Union Territories having legislatures.
3. He audits the Contingency Funds and Public Accounts.
4. He audits only expenditure and not receipts.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
71.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the CAG audits both receipts and expenditure.
71.tq: Reject the exclusive claim that narrows a broad constitutional audit jurisdiction.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(1)** **1, 2 and 3 only**.
He audits **receipts and expenditure** of the **Consolidated Fund** of India, each State and each UT with a legislature.
He also audits **Contingency Funds** and **Public Accounts**.
**Statement 4** wrong: he audits **receipts** as well as expenditure.
xa: He also audits **government companies** and bodies **substantially financed** by government.
**Limit**: cannot audit **secret service expenditure**.
Local bodies: only on request of the **President/Governor**.

71.s:
With reference to the audit jurisdiction of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, consider the following statements:
1. He audits bodies substantially financed by the government and government companies.
2. He audits trading, manufacturing and profit-and-loss accounts of government departments.
3. He audits local bodies automatically in every case, without any request.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
71.x: Statement 1 is correct: bodies substantially financed by government and government companies fall within CAG audit. Statement 2 is correct: trading, manufacturing and profit-and-loss accounts of departments are audited. Statement 3 is wrong: local bodies are audited only on the request of the President or the Governor. So A misses statement 2, C and D wrongly include statement 3, and B is right.
71.tq: Local bodies = only on request of President/Governor; watch for 'automatically'.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(2)** **1 and 2 only**.
**Statement 1** correct: bodies **substantially financed** by government and **govt companies**.
**Statement 2** correct: **trading/manufacturing/profit-loss** accounts of departments.
**Statement 3** wrong: **local bodies** are audited only **when requested** by the **President/Governor**.
xa: **Sixth Schedule councils** are also covered.
**Secret service expenditure**: he accepts the competent authority's certificate.
He audits **Contingency Funds** and **Public Accounts** too.

71.s: Which one of the following statements about the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India is NOT correct?
o: He is called the guardian of the public purse
He heads the Indian Audit and Accounts Department
He controls the entire financial system of the country
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called him the most important officer under the Constitution
71.x: C is the incorrect statement (APPSC-G2 2017). The Indian CAG is only an Auditor-General: unlike the British C&AG, he has no control over the issue of money from the Consolidated Fund. A, B and D are all correct: he is called the guardian of the public purse, he heads the Indian Audit and Accounts Department, and Ambedkar called him the most important officer under the Constitution.
71.tq: Indian CAG audits; he does not control the issue of money.
xs: "**He controls the entire financial system of the country**" is wrong — option **(3)** (**APPSC-G2 2017**).
He has **no control over the issue of money** from the Consolidated Fund — he is only an **Auditor-General**.
The rest are true: "**guardian of the public purse**", head of the **Indian Audit and Accounts Department**, and **Ambedkar's** "most important officer".
xa: In **Britain** the C&AG does control issue.
He is the PAC's "**friend, philosopher and guide**".

71.s:
Which of the following correctly describes the audit types mentioned for the Comptroller and Auditor General?
1. Compliance audit is obligatory.
2. Financial attest audit is obligatory.
3. Performance audit is discretionary.
4. Performance audit is constitutionally prohibited.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
71.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct: compliance and financial attest audits are obligatory, while performance audit is discretionary. Statement 4 is false because performance audit is permitted as a discretionary audit.
71.tq: Separate obligatory audit categories from discretionary performance audit and reject the prohibition trap.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(2)** **1, 2 and 3 only**.
**Compliance** (legal + regulatory) and **financial attest** audits are **obligatory**.
**Performance** audit is **discretionary**; **statement 4** wrong — it is not prohibited.
xa: **Propriety audit** is also discretionary: **wisdom, economy** of expenditure.
Performance audit tests **economy, efficiency, effectiveness** of schemes.
**Social audits** feed CAG performance audits.

71.s:
Consider the following statements about the types of audit conducted by the CAG:
1. A financial attest audit examines the economy, efficiency and effectiveness of schemes.
2. A legal and regulatory (compliance) audit examines whether money was legally available and spent as the rules require.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
71.x: Statement 2 is correct: compliance (legal and regulatory) audit checks that money was legally available and spent as the rules require. Statement 1 is wrong: financial attest audit checks that the accounts are true and follow the reporting framework; economy, efficiency and effectiveness are tested by performance audit. So '2 only'.
71.tq: Attest = true accounts; performance = 3 Es.
xs: Only statement **2** is correct — option **(1)** "**2 only**".
2: a **legal and regulatory (compliance)** audit checks that money was **legally available** and spent as rules require.
1 is wrong: **financial attest** audit checks that accounts are **true** and follow the reporting framework; **economy, efficiency, effectiveness** is **performance** audit.
xa: **Obligatory** audits: **legal and regulatory** + **financial attest**.
**Discretionary** audits: **propriety** (wisdom, economy; flags extravagance) + **performance**.
**CAG+1:** social audits feed CAG performance audits; MGNREGA social audit standards **2016**.

71.s:
Consider the following statements regarding types of audit:
1. Propriety audit examines wisdom, faithfulness and economy in expenditure.
2. Performance audit examines the economy, efficiency and effectiveness of schemes.
3. Both propriety audit and performance audit are obligatory audits.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
71.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because propriety and performance audits are discretionary, whereas legal-regulatory and financial-attest audits are obligatory.
71.tq: Separate the nature of an audit from the subject it tests.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(3)** **1 and 2 only**.
**Statement 1** correct: propriety audit — **wisdom, faithfulness, economy**.
**Statement 2** correct: performance audit — **economy, efficiency, effectiveness**.
**Statement 3** wrong: both are **discretionary**; **legal-regulatory** and **financial attest** are obligatory.
xa: Propriety audit **flags extravagance**.
**MGNREGA social audit standards**: **2016**.

71.s:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with regard to audit of public sector entities?
1. DVC — Audited directly by the CAG
2. ONGC — Audited directly by the CAG
3. Central Warehousing Corporation — Private auditors appointed on the CAG's advice, with supplementary audit by the CAG
4. RBI — Supplementary audit by the CAG after appointment of private auditors on its advice
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
71.x: DVC and ONGC are directly audited by the CAG. Central Warehousing Corporation follows the private-auditor and supplementary-audit arrangement; RBI is wholly privately audited, so statement 4 is false.
71.tq: Classify entities by the mode of CAG involvement.
xs: Pairs 1, 2 and 3 are correct — option **(2)** **1, 2 and 3 only**.
**DVC** and **ONGC**: audited **directly** by the CAG.
**Central Warehousing Corp.**: **private auditors** on CAG's advice + CAG **supplementary audit**.
**Pair 4** wrong: **RBI** has a **wholly private audit**.
xa: **IFCI** is in the same group as Central Warehousing Corp.
**LIC** is also wholly privately audited.

71.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Sixth Schedule councils may also come within the scope of CAG audit of local bodies.
2. The CAG can audit secret service expenditure in the same manner as ordinary expenditure.
3. In relation to secret service expenditure, the CAG accepts a certificate from the competent authority.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
71.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 is false because the CAG cannot audit secret service expenditure and instead accepts a certificate from the competent authority.
71.tq: Find the exception to the general audit power.
xs: Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2)** **1 and 3 only**.
**Statement 1** correct: **Sixth Schedule councils** are also covered.
**Statement 2** wrong: he **cannot audit secret service expenditure**.
**Statement 3** correct: he accepts the **competent authority's certificate**.
xa: Local bodies are audited on request of the **President/Governor**.
He audits bodies **substantially financed** by government.

71.s: Which one of the following is NOT one of the three principal Union reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General mentioned in this context?
o: Report on the delimitation of constituencies
71.x: The three Union reports are the Appropriation Accounts Report, Finance Accounts Report and Report on Public Undertakings. Delimitation of constituencies is unrelated to CAG reporting.
71.tq: Identify the unrelated institutional subject among three closely associated CAG reports.
xs: **Delimitation of constituencies** is not a CAG report — option **(3)**.
The three Union reports: **appropriation accounts**, **finance accounts**, **public undertakings**.
xa: PSU reports → **Committee on Public Undertakings**.
Other reports → **PAC**.
Landmark reports: **2G (2010)**, **Coal (2012)**, **Rafale (2019)**.

71.s: Reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General relating to public sector undertakings are examined by the
71.x: Reports relating to public sector undertakings are referred to the Committee on Public Undertakings, while the PAC examines the other relevant CAG reports.
71.tq: Separate the two parliamentary committees by the subject of the report they examine.
xs: PSU reports go to the **Committee on Public Undertakings** — option **(1)**.
The **PAC** examines the other Union reports.
xa: PAC: **22 members** (**15 LS + 7 RS**), elected yearly by **STV**.
The CAG is the PAC's "**friend, philosopher and guide**".

71.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Public Accounts Committee:
1. It was set up in 1921 under the Government of India Act, 1919.
2. It consists of 22 members, including 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha.
3. A Minister can be a member of the Committee.
4. It has been chaired by a member of the Opposition since 1967.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
71.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. A Minister cannot be a member of the Public Accounts Committee, so statement 3 is false.
71.tq: Find the exception in the committee’s composition and chairpersonship rules.
xs: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct — option **(1)** **1, 2 and 4 only**.
**Statement 1**: PAC set up in **1921**.
**Statement 2**: **22 members** — **15 LS + 7 RS**.
**Statement 3** wrong: **no minister**; **statement 4** correct: chair from the **Opposition since 1967**.
xa: Elected **annually** by **STV**; chairperson appointed by the **Speaker**.
Recommendations **not binding** — action via **Action Taken Notes**.
Chaired by **K.C. Venugopal**.

71.s: Which of the following is the correct sequence for Union audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General?
o: CAG → President → both Houses of Parliament → Public Accounts Committee
CAG → Public Accounts Committee → President → both Houses of Parliament
CAG → Speaker → President → Public Accounts Committee
CAG → Parliament Secretariat → Governor → Public Accounts Committee
71.x: Union reports are submitted by the CAG to the President, laid before both Houses, and then examined by the Public Accounts Committee.
71.tq: Arrange the institutional stages in sequence, beginning with the report-making authority.
xs: **CAG → President → both Houses of Parliament → Public Accounts Committee** — option **(1)**.
The PAC examines the report only after it is laid before Parliament.
xa: Three Union reports: **appropriation accounts, finance accounts, public undertakings**.
PSU reports → **Committee on Public Undertakings**.
State route: **Governor** → **state legislature**.

71.s: After the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh in 2014, CAG audit reports relating to the accounts of the undivided State were submitted to:
o: the President only, for laying before Parliament
the Governor of Andhra Pradesh only
the Governors of both Andhra Pradesh and Telangana
the Public Accounts Committee of Parliament directly
71.x: Under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014, CAG reports on the undivided State's accounts went to each successor State, so they were submitted to the Governors of both AP and Telangana. State audit reports go to the Governor under Article 151(2), not to the President, which rules out A. B leaves out Telangana. D is wrong because reports never go straight to the PAC.
71.tq: Art 151(2): State reports go to the Governor; pre-2014 reports went to both successor States.
xs: Pre-bifurcation reports went to **the Governors of both Andhra Pradesh and Telangana** — option **(3)**.
Under the **AP Reorganisation Act, 2014**, they go **to each successor State**; State reports go to the **Governor** (**Art. 151(2)**).
xa: Current AP reports go to the **Governor of AP**.
Union reports go to the **President**.

71.s: The presumptive loss figure associated with the CAG's 2G spectrum report of 2010 was approximately:
71.x: The 2010 2G spectrum report, prepared during Vinod Rai's tenure, referred to a presumptive loss of ₹1.76 lakh crore.
71.tq: Separate the closely resembling 2G and coal-block figures.
xs: The **2G spectrum** report (**2010**) put the presumptive loss at **₹1.76 lakh crore** — option **(3)**.
⚠ **₹1.86 lakh crore** is the **Coal block allocation** (**2012**) figure.
xa: The 2G report came under CAG **Vinod Rai**.
Debate: the "**presumptive loss**" method.
**Rafale** (**2019**): **redacted pricing**.

71.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the CAG's landmark reports is NOT correctly matched?
71.x: The 2G spectrum report is associated with 2010. Coal block allocation is associated with 2012, and the Rafale report with 2019.
71.tq: Use the date-event pairing to eliminate the swapped-year option.
xs: **2G spectrum — 2012** is wrong — option **(3)**; the 2G report was **2010**.
**Coal block — 2012** and **Rafale — 2019** are correct.
xa: 2G loss: **₹1.76 lakh crore**; Coal: **₹1.86 lakh crore**.
**Vinod Rai** was CAG for the 2G report.

71.s: The CAG's 2019 Rafale report was notable for containing:
o: A recommendation to abolish the PAC
A complete ban on defence procurement
A finding on coal block allocation
71.x: The 2019 Rafale report contained redacted pricing information. It was distinct from the 2G and coal block allocation reports.
71.tq: Match the report with its distinctive feature.
xs: The **2019 Rafale** report had **redacted pricing** — option **(4)**.
Coal block allocation was a separate **2012** report.
xa: **2G spectrum** (**2010**): **₹1.76 lakh crore**.
Debates: **presumptive loss**, **policy vs execution**, **delayed reports**.

71.s: Who authored the book titled “When Audit Matters”?
71.x: Former CAG Vinod Rai authored “When Audit Matters.”
71.tq: Match the publication with its author rather than with a current office-holder.
xs: Former CAG **Vinod Rai** wrote "**When Audit Matters**" (**2026**) — option **(2)**.
He was CAG for the **2G spectrum (2010)** report.
xa: **V. Narahari Rao**: first CAG (**1948**).
**K. Sanjay Murthy**: current, **15th** CAG.

71.s: The Public Accounts Committee that pulled up the Railways in relation to CAG Report No. 31 of 2026 was chaired by:
71.x: The PAC was under K.C. Venugopal when it pulled up the Railways over the bio-toilet findings.
71.tq: Match the parliamentary response with its committee chairperson.
xs: The PAC was chaired by **K.C. Venugopal** — option **(1)**.
It pulled up the **Railways** over **CAG Report No. 31 of 2026** (**18 Sep 2026**).
xa: Bio-toilets were deficient/non-functional at **491 of 512** stations.
PAC chairs come from the **Opposition since 1967**.
Green India Mission: **91.87%** shortfall.

71.s: Which one of the following correctly describes a current audit initiative associated with the CAG?
o: Auditing 512 cities exclusively for railway sanitation
Auditing all private companies without statutory limits
Auditing only one city for urban mobility
Auditing 101 cities for ease of living
71.x: The CAG was auditing 101 cities for ease of living, including urban-mobility concerns.
71.tq: Identify the precise scale and subject of the audit initiative.
xs: The CAG is **auditing 101 cities for ease of living** — option **(4)**.
⚠ **512** is the number of railway stations in the **bio-toilet** report, not cities.
xa: India hosted the **5th BRICS SAI Leaders' Summit** (theme: **Ease of Living**, urban mobility).
**AI/ML-based** audits detect fraud in welfare schemes.

71.s: Which technological approach is being used by the CAG to detect fraud in welfare schemes?
o: Only manual inspection of paper vouchers
Artificial intelligence and machine learning-based audits
71.x: The CAG is using AI/ML-based audits to detect fraud in welfare schemes and is expanding remote audits.
71.tq: Match the technology with the governance problem it addresses.
xs: The CAG uses **AI/ML-based audits** (artificial intelligence and machine learning) to detect welfare fraud — option **(4)**.
It is also **expanding remote audits** (**Sep 2025**).
xa: **Social audits** feed CAG performance audits.
Auditing **101 cities** for ease of living.

71.s:
Consider the following statements regarding recent issues relating to the Public Accounts Committee:
1. PAC recommendations are binding on the executive.
2. There is a reported backlog of Action Taken Notes.
3. CAG reports provide the principal basis for parliamentary examination of executive financial accountability.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
71.x: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is false because PAC recommendations are not binding on the executive.
71.tq: Test the difference between parliamentary scrutiny and binding executive orders.
xs: Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option **(3)** **2 and 3 only**.
**Statement 1** wrong: PAC recommendations are **not binding**.
**Statement 2** correct: backlog of **Action Taken Notes** (**23 May 2026**).
**Statement 3** correct: executive accountability to Parliament works mainly through **CAG reports**.
xa: Final action rests with the **executive** through Action Taken Notes.
PAC: **22 members**, elected yearly by **STV**.

71.s: The constitutional framework governing the Comptroller and Auditor General of India is contained in:
71.x: The CAG is in Part V, Chapter V, Articles 148–151. Part XII is finance, and Chapter VI is not the CAG chapter.
71.tq: Recall Part V Chapter V for the CAG.
n: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is governed under Part V, Chapter V of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Articles 148 to 151 deal with the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: The CAG is in **Part V, Chapter V, Articles 148–151** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is an **independent constitutional authority**; Part XII and Chapter VI are wrong.
xa: **148** = appointment; **149** = duties and powers; **150** = form of accounts; **151** = audit reports.
Full name: **Comptroller and Auditor-General of India** (not "Controller").
Governing Act: **CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971**.

71.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The CAG is the head of the Indian Audit and Accounts Department.
The CAG is a statutory authority functioning under the Ministry of Finance.
The CAG is an independent constitutional authority.
The CAG is designated as the Guardian of the Public Purse.
71.x: B is incorrect: the CAG is an independent constitutional authority (Article 148), not a statutory body under the Finance Ministry. He heads the Indian Audit and Accounts Department and is the 'guardian of the public purse'.
71.tq: Check constitutional vs statutory status.
n: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is an independent constitutional authority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is designated as the Guardian of the Public Purse. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is the head of the Indian Audit and Accounts Department. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the CAG is a **statutory authority under the Ministry of Finance** — option **(2)**.
The CAG is an **independent constitutional authority** (**Articles 148 to 151**).
It heads the **Indian Audit and Accounts Department** and is the **Guardian of the Public Purse**.
xa: **No minister** represents the CAG in Parliament.
**Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** called the CAG the **most important officer** under the Constitution.
Union accounts are now compiled under the **Ministry of Finance**, not by the CAG.

71.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described the CAG as the most important officer under the Constitution of India.
Statement B: The CAG is one of the four bulwarks of the democratic system, along with the Supreme Court, UPSC and ECI.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
71.x: Both are true: Ambedkar called the CAG the most important officer under the Constitution, and the CAG, Supreme Court, UPSC and Election Commission are seen as the four bulwarks of democracy.
71.tq: Recall how the CAG is described.
n: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described the Comptroller and Auditor General as the most important officer under the Constitution of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General is one of the four bulwarks of the democratic system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Supreme Court is one of the four bulwarks of the democratic system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Union Public Service Commission is one of the four bulwarks of the democratic system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Election Commission of India is one of the four bulwarks of the democratic system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)** is correct.
A: **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** called the CAG the **most important officer** under the Constitution.
B: the **four bulwarks of democracy** are the **CAG**, **Supreme Court**, **UPSC** and **Election Commission of India**.
xa: Titles: **Guardian of the Public Purse**; "**friend, philosopher and guide**" of the PAC.
First CAG: **V. Narahari Rao** (**1948**).
Current CAG: **K. Sanjay Murthy** — the **15th** CAG.

71.s: The CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act was enacted in:
71.x: The CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act was passed in 1971. 1976 is the year accounting was separated from audit.
71.tq: Separate 1971 (Act) from 1976 (reform).
n: The Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act was enacted in 1971. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: The **CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act** was enacted in **1971** — option **(2)**.
**1976** is the year **accounting** was separated from **auditing** (CAG relieved of **Union accounts** from **1 March 1976**).
xa: Union accounts are now compiled by the **Central Government Accounts** authority under the **Ministry of Finance**.
The CAG still keeps accounts of **most States**.
Tenure under the **1971** Act and **Art. 148(3)**: **6 years or 65**.

71.s: Who appoints the Comptroller and Auditor General of India?
71.x: The President appoints the CAG by warrant under his hand and seal (Article 148(1)) — not the PM, Finance Minister or PAC.
71.tq: Recall the 'warrant under hand and seal'.
n: The President of India appoints the Comptroller and Auditor General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General is appointed under Article 148(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General is appointed by a warrant under the hand and seal of the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Prime Minister does not appoint the Comptroller and Auditor General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Finance Minister does not appoint the Comptroller and Auditor General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Public Accounts Committee does not appoint the Comptroller and Auditor General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: The CAG is appointed by **the President of India** — option **(1)** — by **warrant under his hand and seal** (**Article 148(1)**).
⚠ Not the **Prime Minister**, **Finance Minister** or **Public Accounts Committee**.
xa: **Oath** before the President, form in the **Third Schedule**.
Removed like a **Supreme Court Judge**; does **not** hold office at the President's pleasure.
**Resignation** goes to the **President**.

71.s:
Assertion (A): The CAG is removed in the same manner and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court Judge.
Reason (R): Removal requires an address by both Houses of Parliament through a special majority on proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
71.x: Both are true and R explains A: the CAG is removed like a Supreme Court judge — by the President on an address of both Houses passed by special majority for proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
71.tq: Check whether R describes the procedure in A.
n: The Comptroller and Auditor General is removed on the same grounds and in the same manner as a Supreme Court Judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Removal of the Comptroller and Auditor General requires an address by both Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The removal address must be passed by a special majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Proved misbehaviour or incapacity is required for removal of the Comptroller and Auditor General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
The CAG is removed like a **Supreme Court Judge** — by an **address by both Houses** with a **special majority** on **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**.
xa: Basis: **Article 148(1)** read with **Article 124(4)**.
**Article 148(4):** **complete bar** on further office under GoI or any State after retirement.
Tenure: **six years** or **65 years**, whichever is earlier.

71.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Article)
a. Article 148
b. Article 149
c. Article 150
d. Article 151

List-II (Subject)
i. Form of Accounts of the Union and States
ii. Duties and Powers of the CAG
iii. Comptroller and Auditor General of India
iv. Audit Reports of the Union and States
71.x: Article 148 – the CAG; 149 – duties and powers; 150 – form of accounts; 151 – audit reports.
71.tq: Recall Articles 148–151 in order.
n: Article 148 deals with the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Article 149 deals with the duties and powers of the Comptroller and Auditor General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Article 150 deals with the form of accounts of the Union and the States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Article 151(1) deals with the audit reports of the Union. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Article 151(2) deals with the audit reports of the States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: The correct code is **a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv** — option **(1)**.
**148** = **CAG of India**; **149** = **duties and powers**.
**150** = **form of accounts** of Union and States; **151** = **audit reports**.
xa: **Article 150:** form prescribed by the **President** on the CAG's **advice**.
**151(1):** Union reports → **President**; **151(2):** State reports → **Governor**.
Ultimate action rests with **Parliament** / **State Legislature**.

71.s:
Assertion (A): The CAG’s audit report on Union accounts is submitted to the President.
Reason (R): The President causes the report to be laid before both Houses of Parliament.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
71.x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the President laying the report before Parliament is a later step; it does not explain why the report goes to the President first.
71.tq: A next step does not explain the first step.
n: Article 151(1) deals with the audit reports of the Union. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Union audit reports are submitted to the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The President causes Union audit reports to be laid before both Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — option **(2)**.
A: Union audit reports go to the **President** (**Article 151(1)**).
R: the President lays them before **both Houses of Parliament** — a later step that does not explain A.
xa: State reports → **Governor** → **State Legislature** (**Article 151(2)**).
Union reports are examined by the **Public Accounts Committee**.
⚠ False claim: "CAG submits reports **directly** to the PAC".

71.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The CAG audits expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India.
II. The CAG audits transactions relating to Contingency Funds and Public Accounts.
III. The CAG audits stores, stocks and government companies.
IV. The CAG exercises day-to-day control over the issue of money from the treasury.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
71.x: I, II and III are correct: the CAG audits Consolidated Fund spending, Contingency Funds and Public Accounts, and stores, stocks and government companies. IV is wrong: he does not control treasury issues day to day.
71.tq: The Indian CAG audits; he does not control withdrawals.
n: The Comptroller and Auditor General audits all expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General audits all transactions relating to the Contingency Funds of the Union and the States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General audits all transactions relating to the Public Accounts of the Union and the States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General audits government stores and stocks. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General audits public sector undertakings. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General does not exercise day-to-day control over the exchequer. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General does not control the issue or drawal of money from the treasury. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: Statements **I, II and III only** are correct — option **(2)**.
I and II: the CAG audits expenditure from the **Consolidated Fund**, and **Contingency Funds** and **Public Accounts**.
III: it audits **stores and stocks** and **public sector undertakings** / government companies.
IV is wrong: the CAG has **no day-to-day control** over issue of money from the treasury.
xa: Audit is **post-expenditure** (ex-post facto).
The CAG **cannot audit secret service expenditure**.
Bodies **substantially financed** by government are also audited.

71.s:
How many of the following are functions of the CAG?
1. Auditing government companies
2. Conducting performance audits
3. Initiating criminal prosecutions
4. Controlling the issue of money from the treasury
71.x: Two: auditing government companies and performance audits are CAG functions. He cannot prosecute or control treasury withdrawals.
71.tq: Separate audit functions from executive powers.
n: The Comptroller and Auditor General audits public sector undertakings. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General conducts performance audits. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General does not control the issue or drawal of money from the treasury. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General has no power to initiate criminal prosecutions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: **Only two** are CAG functions — option **(2)**: auditing **government companies** and **performance audits**.
The CAG **cannot initiate criminal prosecutions**.
The CAG does **not control the issue of money** from the treasury — unlike the **British** CAG.
xa: No power to **disallow expenditure** or **enforce recovery**.
He is **only an Auditor-General, not a Comptroller**.
⚠ "CAG controls the entire financial system" is the **wrong** statement (APPSC-G2 2017).

71.s: The CAG’s performance audit evaluates which three dimensions of government schemes and outlays?
71.x: A performance audit checks the 3 Es: economy, efficiency and effectiveness of schemes and spending.
71.tq: Recall the 3 Es.
n: Performance audits by the Comptroller and Auditor General evaluate economy, efficiency and effectiveness. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: Performance audit tests **Economy, Efficiency and Effectiveness** — option **(3)**.
It is a **discretionary** audit of schemes and outlays.
xa: **Propriety** audit is also discretionary — wisdom, faithfulness, economy.
**Obligatory** audits: **legal and regulatory** and **financial attest**.
CAG audits **101 cities** for ease of living.

71.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The CAG has no power to disallow expenditure.
II. The CAG cannot enforce recovery.
III. The CAG cannot initiate criminal prosecutions.
IV. The CAG can itself impose punishment for irregular expenditure.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
71.x: I, II and III are correct: the CAG cannot disallow expenditure, enforce recovery or prosecute. IV is wrong: he has no power to punish; he only reports to the legislature.
71.tq: The CAG reports; he does not punish.
n: The Comptroller and Auditor General has no power to disallow expenditure. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General has no power to enforce recovery. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General has no power to initiate criminal prosecutions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: Statements **I, II and III only** are correct — option **(1)**.
The CAG has **no power** to **disallow expenditure**, **enforce recovery** or **initiate criminal prosecutions**.
IV is wrong: the CAG cannot itself punish; reports go to the legislature for action.
xa: **Ultimate responsibility** for action lies with **Parliament** / **State Legislature**.
**PAC** recommendations are **not binding**; final action rests with the **executive** through Action Taken Notes.
The CAG does **not** control issue of money — unlike the **British** CAG.

71.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
a. Audit report of the Union
b. Audit report of a State
c. Assistance to the Public Accounts Committee
d. Ultimate action on CAG findings

List-II
i. Governor
ii. Parliament or State Legislature
iii. Friend, Philosopher and Guide
iv. President
71.x: Union report – President; State report – Governor; for the PAC – 'friend, philosopher and guide'; final action – Parliament or State Legislature.
71.tq: Match each step of audit follow-up.
n: Union audit reports are submitted to the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
State audit reports are submitted to the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General acts as the Friend, Philosopher and Guide of the Public Accounts Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The ultimate constitutional responsibility for taking action on the findings in Union audit reports rests with Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The ultimate constitutional responsibility for taking action on the findings in State audit reports rests with the State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: The correct code is **a-iv, b-i, c-iii, d-ii** — option **(4)**.
**Union** report → **President**; **State** report → **Governor**.
To the **PAC** the CAG is "**friend, philosopher and guide**"; ultimate action → **Parliament or State Legislature**.
xa: **PAC (2026-27):** **22 members** (**15 LS + 7 RS**); chair from the **Opposition since 1967**.
PAC was set up in **1921**.
AP reports go to the **Governor of AP** (**Art. 151(2)**).

71.s: In relation to the Public Accounts Committee, the CAG functions as its:
71.x: The CAG is the 'friend, philosopher and guide' of the Public Accounts Committee, helping it examine audit reports line by line. He is not its chairman.
71.tq: Recall the PAC description.
n: The Comptroller and Auditor General acts as the Friend, Philosopher and Guide of the Public Accounts Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General attends Public Accounts Committee meetings. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General assists the Public Accounts Committee in the line-by-line examination of audit reports. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: The CAG is the PAC's **Friend, Philosopher and Guide** — option **(4)**.
He attends its meetings and assists its **line-by-line examination** of audit reports.
xa: PAC chairperson is appointed by the **Speaker**; currently **K.C. Venugopal**.
PAC members are elected annually by **STV**; **no minister**.
PSU reports go to the **Committee on Public Undertakings**.

71.s:
Assertion (A): The form of accounts of the Union and the States is prescribed by the President.
Reason (R): The President prescribes the form of accounts on the advice of the CAG.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
71.x: Both are true and R explains A: under Article 150 the President prescribes the form of Union and State accounts, on the CAG's advice.
71.tq: Check whether R states how A is done.
n: The President prescribes the form of Union and State accounts on the advice of the Comptroller and Auditor General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General advises on the form of accounts but does not prescribe it unilaterally. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Union and State accounts are kept in the form prescribed by the President upon the advice of the Comptroller and Auditor General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
Under **Article 150**, the **President** prescribes the **form of accounts** of Union and States on the **advice** of the CAG.
xa: The CAG does **not** prescribe it unilaterally.
**Article 149** = duties and powers; **Article 151** = audit reports.
The **1976** reform separated accounting from auditing.

71.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
 a. Audit report on Union accounts
 b. Audit report on State accounts
 c. Form of accounts of the Union and States
 d. Appointment of the CAG

List-II
 i. Submitted to the President
 ii. Submitted to the Governor
 iii. Prescribed by the President on the CAG's advice
 iv. By warrant under the President's hand and seal
71.x: Union audit reports go to the President and State reports to the Governor (Article 151), the form of accounts is prescribed by the President on the CAG's advice (Article 150), and the CAG is appointed by warrant under the President's hand and seal (Article 148), giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
71.tq: Link each step to the authority named in Articles 148 to 151.
n: Under Article 149, the Comptroller and Auditor General audits the receipts, expenditures, stores and accounts of the Union and the States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: The correct code is **a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv** — option **(2)**.
**Union** report → **President**; **State** report → **Governor** (**Article 151**).
**Form of accounts** → **President** on the CAG's advice (**Article 150**); **appointment** → **warrant under the President's hand and seal** (**Article 148(1)**).
xa: Oath before the President, form in the **Third Schedule**.
Salary equals an **SC judge**; fixed by **Parliament** (**Second Schedule**).
**Leave** is granted by the **President**.

71.s:
Assertion (A): In India, the CAG does not control the issue or drawal of money from the treasury.
Reason (R): The CAG functions as an Auditor General and exercises audit after expenditure rather than prior exchequer control.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
71.x: Both are true and R explains A: the Indian CAG is only an Auditor General whose audit is after spending, so he does not control the issue of money from the treasury.
71.tq: Ask whether post-audit explains no prior control.
n: The Comptroller and Auditor General does not exercise day-to-day control over the exchequer. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General does not control the issue or drawal of money from the treasury. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General is an Auditor General and not a Comptroller in the Indian system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The audit conducted by the Comptroller and Auditor General is post-expenditure or ex-post facto. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
The Indian CAG is **only an Auditor-General, not a Comptroller**; audit is **post-expenditure**, so he has **no control** over issue or drawal of money.
xa: In **Britain** the C&AG does control issue.
No power to **disallow expenditure** or **enforce recovery**.
⚠ False claim: "CAG ensures no money is drawn from the CFI without **prior sanction**".

71.s:
How many of the following statements are correct?
1. The CAG was relieved of preparing Union accounts from 1 March 1976.
2. The CAG continues to compile and maintain accounts of most States.
3. Union account compilation is handled by the CGA under the Ministry of Finance.
4. The 1976 reform merged accounting and auditing functions.
71.x: Three are correct: the CAG stopped compiling Union accounts from 1 March 1976, still keeps most States' accounts, and the CGA compiles Union accounts. Statement 4 is wrong: the reform separated, not merged, the two functions.
71.tq: Check the direction of the 1976 reform.
n: The 1976 departmentalization reform separated accounting from auditing. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General was relieved of the responsibility of preparing Union accounts from 1 March 1976. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General continues to compile and maintain the accounts of most States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Central Government Accounts authority handles Union account compilation under the Ministry of Finance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: **Only three** statements are correct — option **(3)**.

1, 2, 3: the CAG was relieved of **Union accounts** from **1 March 1976**, still keeps **most State** accounts, and Union accounts are compiled by the **Central Government Accounts** authority under the **Ministry of Finance**.
4 is wrong: the **1976** reform **separated** accounting from auditing.
xa: The governing Act: **CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971**.
CAG heads the **Indian Audit and Accounts Department**.
Current CAG: **K. Sanjay Murthy**.

71.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The administrative expenses of the CAG are non-votable.
Statement B: The salaries, allowances and pensions of the CAG and staff are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
71.x: Both are true: the CAG's administrative expenses, including salaries, allowances and pensions of him and his staff, are charged on the Consolidated Fund and so are not voted.
71.tq: Charged expenditure is non-votable.
n: The administrative expenses of the Comptroller and Auditor General are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The charged administrative expenses are governed by Article 148(6). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The salaries of the Comptroller and Auditor General and staff are charged expenses. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The allowances of the Comptroller and Auditor General and staff are charged expenses. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The pensions of the Comptroller and Auditor General and staff are charged expenses. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Charged expenses are non-votable. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)** is correct.
Under **Article 148(6)**, **salaries, allowances and pensions** of the CAG and staff (and office expenses) are **charged** on the **Consolidated Fund of India** — **non-votable**.
xa: Salary and conditions are fixed by **Parliament** (**Article 148(3)**, **Second Schedule**).
They cannot be varied to his **disadvantage** after appointment.
**No minister** represents the CAG in Parliament.

71.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The CAG submits audit reports directly to the Public Accounts Committee.
Statement B: The CAG assists the Public Accounts Committee after the reports reach the Committee for examination.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
71.x: A is false: audit reports go first to the President or Governor, who lay them before the legislature. B is true: the CAG then helps the PAC examine them.
71.tq: Trace the report's path before it reaches the PAC.
n: The Comptroller and Auditor General assists the Public Accounts Committee in the line-by-line examination of audit reports. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General does not submit audit reports directly to the Public Accounts Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General submits reports first to the President or Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The claim that the Comptroller and Auditor General submits audit reports directly to the Public Accounts Committee is false. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General does not submit audit reports directly to Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: **Statement A is false, Statement B is true** — option **(4)** is correct.
A is wrong: reports go first to the **President or Governor**, not directly to the PAC.
B: the CAG assists the **PAC** in its **line-by-line examination** as its "**friend, philosopher and guide**".
xa: Union reports are laid before **both Houses**, then examined by the **PAC**.
Three Union reports: **appropriation accounts**, **finance accounts**, **public undertakings**.
PAC recommendations are **not binding**.

71.s:
Assertion (A): The President of India removes the Comptroller and Auditor General through the parliamentary removal process.
Reason (R): The removal mechanism of the Comptroller and Auditor General is governed by Article 148(1) read with Article 124(4).
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
71.x: Both are true and R explains A: Article 148(1) read with Article 124(4) applies the Supreme Court judge's removal process, which ends with the President's order after Parliament's address.
71.tq: Check whether R gives the legal basis of A.
n: The President of India removes the Comptroller and Auditor General through the parliamentary removal process. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The removal mechanism of the Comptroller and Auditor General is governed by Article 148(1) read with Article 124(4). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
**Article 148(1)** read with **Article 124(4)** applies the **Supreme Court judge** removal process: the **President** removes on an **address by both Houses**.
xa: Address must pass by **special majority** on **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**.
The CAG does **not** hold office at the President's pleasure.
**Article 148(4):** no further office after retirement.

71.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The British Comptroller and Auditor General controls the issue or drawal of money from the treasury.
Statement B: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India does not control the issue or drawal of money from the treasury.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
71.x: Both are true: the British CAG controls the issue of money from the treasury, whereas India's CAG is only an Auditor General without that control.
71.tq: Contrast the British and Indian CAG.
n: The British Comptroller and Auditor General controls the issue or drawal of money from the treasury. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)** is correct.
A: the **British** C&AG controls the issue of money.
B: the **Indian** CAG is **only an Auditor-General** — **no control** over issue or drawal of money from the treasury.
xa: Indian audit is **post-expenditure**.
No power to **disallow expenditure**, **enforce recovery** or **prosecute**.
⚠ "CAG controls the entire financial system" — **wrong** (APPSC-G2 2017).

71.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
 a. Chairman of the Union Public Service Commission
 b. Judges

List-II
 i. Can head commissions after retirement
 ii. Cannot take another job after retirement

Choose the correct code:
71.x: The UPSC Chairman cannot take any further government job after retirement, whereas retired judges often head commissions and tribunals.
71.tq: Compare post-retirement rules of the two offices.
n: The Chairman of the Union Public Service Commission cannot take another job after retirement. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Judges can head commissions after retirement. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: The correct code is **a-ii, b-i** — option **(2)**.
The **UPSC Chairman** cannot take another job after retirement; **judges can** head commissions.
xa: The CAG too faces a **complete bar** under **Article 148(4)**.
CAG tenure: **6 years or 65**; UPSC: **6 years or 65**.
SPSC: **6 years or 62**.

71.s:
Assertion (A): The retirement age of a High Court Judge is 62 years.
Reason (R): The 15th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963, raised the retirement age of High Court Judges from 60 to 62 years.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
71.x: Both are true: High Court judges retire at 62 because the 15th Amendment (1963) raised the age from 60. R explains A.
71.tq: Recall the 15th Amendment's change.
n: A High Court Judge retires at 62 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The retirement age of High Court Judges was raised from 60 to 62 years by the 15th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
xs: **Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A** — option **(1)**.
HC judges retire at **62** because the **15th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963** raised it from **60 to 62**.
xa: Basis: **Article 217(1)**; also applies to **Additional and Acting** judges (**224(3)**).
**Supreme Court judge:** retires at **65**, **no fixed tenure** (**124(2)**).
**SPSC** members: **6 years or 62**.

71.s:
Assertion (A): A Supreme Court Judge has a fixed tenure of six years.
Reason (R): A Supreme Court Judge retires strictly on attaining 65 years of age under Article 124(2).
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
71.x: A is false: a Supreme Court judge has no fixed term in years. R is true: they retire at 65 under Article 124(2).
71.tq: Discriminate a retirement age from a fixed term.
n: A Supreme Court Judge retires at 65 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
Article 124(2) governs the retirement age of a Supreme Court Judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
A Supreme Court Judge has no fixed tenure in years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
A Supreme Court Judge retires upon turning 65 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
xs: **A is false, but R is true** — option **(4)**.
A is wrong: a **Supreme Court Judge** has **no fixed tenure** in years.
R: SC judges retire on turning **65** (**Article 124(2)**).
xa: **CAG** and **UPSC**: **6 years or 65**, whichever earlier.
**CEC/ECs**: **6 years or 65** under the **Election Commission Act, 1991/2023**.
President / Vice-President: **5 years**.

71.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) High Court Judge
(b) Supreme Court Judge
(c) UPSC Chairman and Members
(d) SPSC Chairman and Members

List-II
(i) 65 years; no fixed tenure in years
(ii) 62 years or six years, whichever is earlier
(iii) 62 years
(iv) 65 years or six years, whichever is earlier
71.x: High Court judges retire at 62, Supreme Court judges at 65 with no fixed term, UPSC members at 65 or after six years, and State PSC members at 62 or after six years. The answer is a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
71.tq: Discriminate the 62-year group from the 65-year group.
n: A High Court Judge retires at 62 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
A Supreme Court Judge retires at 65 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
A Supreme Court Judge has no fixed tenure in years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
A Supreme Court Judge retires upon turning 65 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The Chairman and Members of the UPSC have a tenure of 6 years or until 65 years of age, whichever is earlier. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The UPSC Chairman and Members retire at 65 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The Chairman and Members of an SPSC have a tenure of 6 years or until 62 years of age, whichever is earlier. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The SPSC Chairman and Members retire at 62 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
xs: The correct code is **a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii** — option **(4)**.
**HC Judge** = **62**; **SC Judge** = **65**, no fixed tenure.
**UPSC** = **65 or six years**; **SPSC** = **62 or six years**, whichever is earlier.
xa: UPSC and SPSC both under **316(2)**.
HC age raised from **60 to 62** by the **15th Amendment, 1963**.
The **CAG** also has **6 years or 65**.

71.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. High Court Judges and SPSC Chairmen or Members fall under the 62-year retirement category.
II. Supreme Court Judges and UPSC Chairmen or Members fall under the 65-year retirement category.
III. The CAG and CEC/ECs fall under the 62-year retirement category.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
71.x: I and II are correct: High Court judges and State PSC members retire at 62, and Supreme Court judges and UPSC members at 65. III is false because the CAG and Election Commissioners are in the 65 group.
71.tq: Discriminate the 62-year group from the 65-year group.
n: A High Court Judge retires at 62 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
A Supreme Court Judge retires at 65 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners have a tenure of 6 years or until 65 years of age, whichever is earlier. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The UPSC Chairman and Members retire at 65 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The SPSC Chairman and Members retire at 62 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The Comptroller and Auditor General retires at 65 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
xs: Statements **I and II only** are correct — option **(3)**.
I: **HC judges** and **SPSC** members retire at **62**; II: **SC judges** and **UPSC** members at **65**.
III is wrong: the **CAG** and **CEC/ECs** are in the **65** group (**6 years or 65**).
xa: CAG basis: **148(3)** and the **CAG Act, 1971**.
CEC/ECs: **Election Commission Act, 1991/2023**.
The CAG has the longest fixed term among President, VP and MP (APPSC-G2 2017).

71.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The retirement provisions of the Comptroller and Auditor General are governed by Article 148(3) and the CAG Act, 1971.
Statement B: The tenure and retirement conditions of the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners are statutory and are linked to the Election Commission Act, 1991/2023.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
71.x: Both are true: the CAG's tenure comes from Article 148(3) and the CAG Act, 1971, and the Election Commissioners' from the Election Commission Act (1991, now 2023).
71.tq: Recall the source of each tenure rule.
n: The Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners have a tenure of 6 years or until 65 years of age, whichever is earlier. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The tenure and retirement condition of the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners is statutory. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The Election Commission condition is governed by the Election Commission Act, 1991/2023. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The Comptroller and Auditor General has a tenure of 6 years or until 65 years of age, whichever is earlier. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
Article 148(3) and the CAG Act, 1971 govern the tenure and retirement condition of the Comptroller and Auditor General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
xs: **Both Statement A and Statement B are true** — option **(1)** is correct.
A: CAG tenure comes from **Article 148(3)** and the **CAG Act, 1971**.
B: CEC/ECs tenure is **statutory** — **Election Commission Act, 1991/2023**.
xa: Both: **6 years** or **65**, whichever is **earlier**.
**UPSC** retirement is under **316(2)**.
**SC judge** retirement is under **124(2)**.

72.s: Which of the following statements regarding the removal of the Attorney General for India is correct?
o: Removal can be ordered only by the Supreme Court
Removal requires impeachment by both Houses of Parliament
The Constitution specifies detailed grounds and a special removal procedure
The Constitution does not specify grounds or a separate removal procedure; the office is held during the President's pleasure
72.x: The Constitution does not prescribe specific grounds or a special procedure for removal of the Attorney General. The office is held during the pleasure of the President.
72.tq: Distinguish an office held during pleasure from constitutional offices having a prescribed removal procedure.
xs: The Constitution specifies **no grounds or removal procedure**; the AG holds office **during the pleasure of the President** — so option **(4)** is correct.
There is no impeachment and no Supreme Court role in removal.
xa: **Term not fixed** by the Constitution.
The AG resigns to the **President**; by convention, also when the **Council of Ministers** goes.
⚠ The **Advocate General** likewise holds office during the **Governor's pleasure**.

72.s: The Attorney General is consulted through the Ministry of Law primarily on:
o: All administrative matters of the Union Government
72.x: References to the Attorney General are made through the Ministry of Law, and consultation is confined to legal matters of real importance.
72.tq: Watch for the overbroad word 'all' and identify the carefully limited scope of consultation.
xs: The AG is consulted through the **Ministry of Law** only on **legal matters of real importance** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The AG does not handle all administrative matters; the **Law Minister** handles legal matters at government level.
xa: Duties: advise GoI on legal matters referred by the **President**; appear for GoI in all **Supreme Court** cases.
The AG represents GoI in **Art. 143** references and may appear in any **High Court**.
The AG is the **chief legal adviser** to GoI.

72.s: Which one of the following is NOT a duty of the Attorney General of India?
o: Advising the Government of India on legal matters
Appearing for the Government of India in the Supreme Court
Appearing in references made under Article 143
Presiding over joint sittings of Parliament
72.x: The Attorney General advises the Government of India, appears for it in the Supreme Court, and appears in Article 143 references. The Attorney General does not preside over joint sittings of Parliament.
72.tq: Reject the option assigning a parliamentary presiding function to the chief law officer.
xs: **Presiding over joint sittings of Parliament** is not the AG's duty — so option **(4)** is the answer.
The AG **advises GoI**, appears for GoI in the **Supreme Court**, and represents it in **Art. 143** references.
xa: The AG may also appear in any **High Court** when required.
Under **Art. 88** the AG can speak in Parliament; privileges under **Art. 105(4)**.
Exam angle: the **highest law officer** is the AG — not the **CJI** or the **Law Minister**.

72.s:
Consider the following statements about the Attorney General for India:
1. He is the highest law officer of the country.
2. He is a member of the Union Cabinet.
3. The Constitution gives him a fixed term of five years.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
