IV is wrong: for the **armed forces** it may only **seek a report from the Central Government**.
xa: **Time bar**: no inquiry **after one year** from the alleged act.
⚠ Action taken: **one month** (general) vs **three months** (armed forces).
Since **2006**, NHRC may visit jails **even without intimating the State Govt**.

126.s: Which of the following statements regarding the NHRC's High-Level Selection Committee is incorrect?
o: The committee consists of six members, including the Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Prime Minister is the Chairperson of the Selection Committee
The President of India appoints the NHRC based on the committee's recommendations
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is a member of the Selection Committee
126.x: Option D is incorrect: the Rajya Sabha's Deputy Chairman, not its Chairman, sits on the NHRC selection committee. The Prime Minister chairs the six-member committee, and the President appoints on its advice.
126.tq: Recall the NHRC selection committee's members.
n: The President of India appoints the NHRC Chairperson and members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The President of India makes appointments to the NHRC based on the recommendations of a six-member High-Level Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The Prime Minister is the Chairperson of the High-Level Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha is a member of the High-Level Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is not a member of the High-Level Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The Deputy Chairman represents the Rajya Sabha on the High-Level Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is a member of the High-Level Selection Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 68-70]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** is a committee member — option **(4)**.
The **Deputy Chairman** of the Rajya Sabha represents the House on the **six-member** committee.
The **Prime Minister** chairs it, the **Speaker** of the Lok Sabha sits on it, and the **President** appoints on its recommendation.
xa: Other members: **Union Home Minister**, **Leaders of the Opposition** in both Houses.
A **vacancy** in the committee does not invalidate its decisions.
SHRC committee is headed by the **Chief Minister**; SHRC members are **removable only by the President**.
First NHRC Chairperson: **Justice Ranganath Misra**.

127.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Case)
a. Nilabati Behera v State of Orissa
b. Joginder Kumar v State of Uttar Pradesh
c. D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal
d. Arnesh Kumar v State of Bihar

List-II (Principle)
i. No automatic arrest for offences punishable up to seven years
 ii. Compensation for custodial death; sovereign immunity is no defence
 iii. Arrest must be justified and a friend or relative may be informed
 iv. Mandatory arrest safeguards including arrest memo and medical examination

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
127.x: Nilabati Behera concerns compensation, Joginder Kumar concerns justified arrest and informing relatives, D.K. Basu concerns arrest safeguards, and Arnesh Kumar restricts automatic arrest for offences up to seven years.
127.tq: Start from the sure case-principle pair and eliminate codes with swapped custodial safeguards.
xs: The match is **a–ii, b–iii, c–iv, d–i** — option **(1)**.
**Nilabati Behera (1993)** — **compensation** for custodial death; **sovereign immunity no defence**.
**Joginder Kumar (1994)** — arrest must be **justified**; a **friend/relative** may be informed.
**D.K. Basu (1997)** — **arrest memo**, officer ID, informing kin, **medical check**; **Arnesh Kumar (2014)** — no automatic arrest up to **7 years**.
xa: ⚠ **1993 – 1994 – 1997 – 2014** = **Nilabati – Joginder – D.K. Basu – Arnesh**.
Arnesh Kumar's checklist: **CrPC s.41**, now **BNSS s.35**.
Nilabati compensation is under **Arts 32/226**.

127.s: Which of the following is NOT a mandatory safeguard associated with D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal?
o: Automatic arrest in every offence punishable up to seven years
127.x: D.K. Basu required safeguards such as an arrest memo, identification of officers, informing kin and medical examination. Automatic arrest for offences up to seven years is contrary to the safeguard approach associated with Arnesh Kumar.
127.tq: Find the one proposition that reverses the arrest-safeguard principle.
xs: **Automatic arrest in every offence up to seven years** is not a D.K. Basu safeguard — option **(3)**.
**D.K. Basu (1997)** mandated an **arrest memo**, **ID of officers**, **informing kin** and a **medical check**.
In fact **Arnesh Kumar (2014)** barred **automatic arrest** for offences up to **7 years**.
xa: **Joginder Kumar (1994)**: arrest must be justified, not routine.
**Nilabati Behera (1993)**: compensation for custodial death.
**PUCL v Maharashtra (2014)**: **16-point** encounter guidelines.

127.s: Which provision makes a judicial inquiry mandatory in custodial deaths, with the corresponding current BNSS provision being Section 196?
127.x: CrPC Section 176(1A) made judicial inquiry mandatory in custodial deaths; the corresponding BNSS provision is Section 196.
127.tq: Match the old and new procedural section numbers without confusing arrest and sanction provisions.
xs: **CrPC s.176(1A)** made a **judicial inquiry mandatory in custodial deaths**; it is now **BNSS s.196** — option **(1)**.
**BNSS s.218** is government sanction for prosecuting public servants; **CrPC s.41** became **BNSS s.35** (arrest checklist); **BNSS s.479** is undertrial relief.
xa: Only **3 convictions** for **2,253** police-custody deaths (**1999-2023**).
NHRC norms: custodial/encounter deaths need **mandatory reporting** and **post-mortem videography**.
**Bihar** records the most police-custody deaths.

127.s: What was the reported relationship between police-custody deaths and convictions during 1999–2023?
127.x: The reported data recorded 2,253 police-custody deaths and only three convictions during 1999–2023.
127.tq: Pair the large denominator with the exceptionally small number of convictions.
xs: There were **2,253** police-custody deaths and only **3 convictions** (**1999-2023**) — option **(1)**.
**122** is the number of prison **suicides** in NCRB **2024** data, not convictions.
xa: **Bihar** records the most custody deaths, then **Rajasthan** and **UP**.
Debate: the custodial-death **conviction rate near zero**.
**CrPC s.176(1A)** / **BNSS s.196**: mandatory judicial inquiry.

127.s: Which State records the highest number of deaths in police custody, followed by Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh?
127.x: Bihar records the most police-custody deaths, followed by Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh. Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan come after Bihar, and Maharashtra is not named among the leading States.
127.tq: Custody deaths: Bihar first, then Rajasthan and UP.
xs: **Bihar** records the most **police-custody deaths**, followed by **Rajasthan** and **UP** — option **(2)**.
UP and Rajasthan come after Bihar; Maharashtra is not named.
xa: Only **3 convictions** for **2,253** custody deaths (**1999-2023**).
**Delhi** has the highest prison occupancy (**194.6%**).
AP case: **Gade Sai Krishna** (**Krishnalanka** police, **Vijayawada**).

127.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the directives in Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006):
1. A State Security Commission was envisaged.
2. The DGP was to be selected from a UPSC panel and given a two-year tenure.
3. Field officers were to receive a two-year tenure.
4. Police Establishment Boards were recommended.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
127.x: All four are among the police-reform measures associated with Prakash Singh (2006): the State Security Commission, UPSC-panel selection of the DGP with a two-year tenure, two-year tenure for field officers and Police Establishment Boards.
127.tq: Verify each institutional reform separately before choosing the comprehensive combination.
xs: All four are correct — option **(4)**.
**Prakash Singh (2006)** envisaged a **State Security Commission** and a **DGP from a UPSC panel** with a **2-year** tenure.
It gave **field officers** a **2-year** tenure and created **Police Establishment Boards**.
xa: Also: **separate investigation from law and order**, **National Security Commission**, **PCAs**.
Total: **7 directives**.
The colonial **Police Act 1861** still remains in force.

127.s:
Consider the following statements about Police Complaints Authorities (PCAs) under the Prakash Singh framework:
1. The State PCA is headed by a retired judge.
2. The State PCA handles serious misconduct including custodial death, rape and grievous hurt.
3. PCAs are envisaged only at the State level, not at the district level.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
127.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the State PCA, headed by a retired judge, handles serious misconduct such as custodial death, rape and grievous hurt. Statement 3 is wrong: Prakash Singh (2006) envisaged PCAs at both State and district levels. So '1 and 2 only' is right; the other options include statement 3.
127.tq: PCAs at State + district; State PCA = retired judge.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **State PCA** is headed by a **retired judge**.
Statement 2 correct: it handles **serious misconduct** — **custodial death, rape, grievous hurt**.
Statement 3 wrong: PCAs are at **State and district levels**.
xa: There is a call for **PCAs with statutory backing**.
Prakash Singh (**2006**) issued **7 directives**.
⚠ PCAs are a Prakash Singh directive, not a creation of the **Police Act 1861**.

127.s: How many directives on police reform did the Supreme Court issue in Prakash Singh v Union of India (2006)?
127.x: Prakash Singh (2006) issued seven directives: State Security Commission, DGP from a UPSC panel with a 2-year tenure, 2-year tenure for field officers, separation of investigation from law and order, Police Establishment Board, National Security Commission and Police Complaints Authorities. Five, six and ten are wrong counts.
127.tq: Prakash Singh 2006 = 7 directives.
xs: **Prakash Singh v UOI (2006)** issued **seven** directives — option **(3)**.

They are: **State Security Commission**; **DGP from UPSC panel** (**2-year** tenure); **2-year** tenure for field officers; separate investigation; **Police Establishment Board**; **National Security Commission**; **PCAs**.
xa: ⚠ **PUCL (2014)** has **16** points; Prakash Singh has **7** directives.
**Arnesh Kumar (2014)**: no automatic arrest up to **7 years**.
PCAs exist at **State and district levels**.

127.s: The guidelines in PUCL v State of Maharashtra (2014) concerning encounter deaths consisted of how many points?
127.x: PUCL v State of Maharashtra (2014) laid down 16-point guidelines for encounter deaths.
127.tq: Recall the exact count attached to the leading encounter-death guidelines case.
xs: **PUCL v Maharashtra (2014)** laid down guidelines of **16 points** on **encounter deaths** — option **(2)**.
⚠ Do not confuse with the **7 directives** of **Prakash Singh (2006)** on police reform.
xa: Key points: record the **tip-off**, register an **FIR**, independent probe by **CID or another police station**, **magisterial inquiry**.
Also: inform **NHRC/SHRC**, medical aid, inform kin, **forensic check of weapons**.
**No out-of-turn promotion or gallantry award** until cleared.

127.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the PUCL guidelines on encounter deaths:
1. The tip-off should be recorded.
2. An FIR should be registered.
3. An independent investigation should be conducted by the CID or another police station.
4. An out-of-turn promotion should be granted immediately to the officers involved.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
127.x: The guidelines require recording the tip-off, registering an FIR and an independent investigation by the CID or another police station. They prohibit out-of-turn promotion or a gallantry award until the officers are cleared.
127.tq: Spot the statement that reverses the rule on rewards before clearance.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
The **PUCL** guidelines require recording the **tip-off**, registering an **FIR** and an independent probe by the **CID or another police station**.
Statement 4 wrong: **no out-of-turn promotion or gallantry award** until the officers are **cleared**.
xa: A **magisterial inquiry** is also required.
Inform **NHRC/SHRC**; **forensic check** of weapons.
PUCL (**2014**) has **16** points.

127.s: Which of the following correctly states the position of the NHRC regarding encounter deaths?
o: They are treated as serious violations requiring mandatory reporting, post-mortem videography and independent investigation.
They can be investigated only by the armed forces.
They require only an internal police report and no post-mortem.
They are treated as routine police actions requiring no special reporting.
127.x: The NHRC treats encounter deaths as serious violations and requires mandatory reporting, post-mortem videography and independent investigation.
127.tq: Match the rights-protection body with its prescribed procedural safeguards.
xs: The **NHRC** treats encounter deaths as **serious violations** needing **mandatory reporting, post-mortem videography and independent investigation** — option **(1)**.
They are not routine police actions and are not left to internal reports or the armed forces.
xa: **PUCL (2014)**: **16-point** guidelines, including a **magisterial inquiry**.
Way forward: **body-worn cameras** (Delhi Police) and better **forensic capacity**.
Only **3 convictions** for **2,253** custody deaths.

127.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. India signed the UN Convention against Torture (UNCAT) in 1997 but has not ratified it.
2. The Prevention of Torture Bill, 2010 became India's standalone anti-torture law after the Lok Sabha passed it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
127.x: Statement 1 is correct: India signed UNCAT in 1997 but has not ratified it. Statement 2 is wrong: the 2010 Bill was passed by the Lok Sabha but lapsed, and India still has no standalone anti-torture law. So '1 only' is right; the other options accept the false statement or reject the true one.
127.tq: UNCAT: signed 1997, not ratified; 2010 Bill lapsed.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: India **signed UNCAT in 1997** but has **not ratified** it.
Statement 2 wrong: the **Prevention of Torture Bill, 2010** passed the **Lok Sabha** but then **lapsed**; India has **no standalone anti-torture law**.
xa: **Law Commission 273rd Report (2017)** recommended **UNCAT ratification** and a draft Bill.
Way forward: **standalone law** + **PEACE model** of interviewing.
⚠ **262nd** = death penalty; **273rd** = torture.

127.s: The 273rd Law Commission Report recommended which of the following?
o: Replacement of the Seventh Schedule by a new prison list
Ratification of UNCAT and a draft Prevention of Torture Bill, 2017
Confirmation of all death sentences by the Supreme Court
127.x: The 273rd Law Commission Report (2017) recommended ratification of UNCAT and proposed a draft Prevention of Torture Bill, 2017.
127.tq: Match the Law Commission report number with its specific subject and recommendation.
xs: The **273rd Report (2017)** recommended **UNCAT ratification** and a draft **Prevention of Torture Bill, 2017** — option **(3)**.
Prison manuals, the Seventh Schedule and death-sentence confirmation were not its subject.
xa: ⚠ **262nd (2015)** = death penalty; **273rd** = torture.
India **signed UNCAT in 1997**, not ratified.
The **2010** torture Bill **lapsed** after passing the Lok Sabha.

127.s: Under the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India, prisons are included in which of the following?
127.x: Prisons are a State subject under Entry 4 of the State List in the Seventh Schedule.
127.tq: Test the exact List and Entry instead of relying on the general subject classification.
xs: **Prisons** are in the **State List, Entry 4** of the Seventh Schedule — option **(4)**.
They are not a Union or Concurrent subject.
xa: Prisons are governed by the **Prisons Act 1894** and **State jail manuals**.
**BPR&D** issues **advisory** guidelines.
**Model Prisons Act 2023** — prepared by **MHA** as a guide for States.

127.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the administration of prisons is correct?
o: Prisons are governed exclusively by the Union Government under the Prisons Act, 1894.
The Supreme Court directly administers all prisons through BPR&D.
Prisons are governed by the Prisons Act, 1894 and State jail manuals, while BPR&D issues advisory guidelines.
State jail manuals have no role after the enactment of the Model Prisons Act, 2023.
127.x: Prisons continue to be governed by the Prisons Act, 1894 and State jail manuals; BPR&D issues advisory guidelines.
127.tq: Identify the correct combination of governing law, State rules and advisory authority.
xs: Prisons are governed by the **Prisons Act 1894** and **State jail manuals**, while **BPR&D** issues **advisory guidelines** — option **(3)**.
Prisons are a **State List (Entry 4)** subject — not run by the Union or the Supreme Court.
The **Model Prisons Act 2023** is only a **guide** for States, so jail manuals still apply.
xa: The **Mulla Committee** (**1980-83**) sought a **national prison policy**.
NCRB **2024**: occupancy **112.7%**; undertrials **~73%**.
**SC (Aug 2025)**: immediate release of prisoners held beyond sentence.

127.s:
Consider the following statements about the Model Prisons Act, 2023:
1. It was prepared by the Ministry of Home Affairs.
2. It is intended to guide States in replacing the colonial Prisons Act, 1894.
3. It automatically operates as a binding Central law in every State.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
127.x: The Model Prisons Act, 2023 was prepared by the Ministry of Home Affairs as a guide for States to replace the colonial 1894 Act. It is not automatically a binding Central law in every State.
127.tq: Separate a model guide for States from an automatically binding Central enactment.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1 correct: the **Model Prisons Act 2023** was prepared by the **MHA**.
Statement 2 correct: it is a **guide for States** to replace the colonial **1894** Act.
Statement 3 wrong: prisons are a **State List** subject, so it is not automatically binding.
xa: Prisons = **State List, Entry 4**.
**BPR&D** issues advisory guidelines.
Justice **Amitava Roy Committee** (**2018**): overcrowding, undertrials, legal aid, speedy trial.

127.s: With reference to parole and furlough, which one of the following is correct?
o: They are available only to undertrial prisoners.
They are governed by identical Central rules applicable to every State.
They are not absolute rights, and each State has its own prisoner-release rules.
They constitute an absolute constitutional right available uniformly throughout India.
127.x: Parole and furlough are not absolute rights. Each State frames its own prisoner-release or parole rules.
127.tq: Distinguish a non-absolute release facility from a uniform constitutional entitlement.
xs: Parole and furlough are **not absolute rights**, and **each State has its own prisoner-release rules** — option **(3)** (UPSC **2021**: the only correct statement).
They are not uniform Central rules, not limited to undertrials and not constitutional rights.
xa: Prisons are a **State List (Entry 4)** subject.
**BNSS s.479**: undertrial release after **half** the maximum term (**one-third** for first-time offenders).
SC (**Aug 2025**): immediate release of prisoners held beyond sentence completion.

127.s: Under Section 479 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, an undertrial prisoner is generally eligible for release after undergoing which period of the maximum imprisonment prescribed, subject to the statutory conditions?
127.x: BNSS Section 479 provides release after one-half of the maximum term, reduced to one-third for first-time offenders, subject to the statutory conditions.
127.tq: Recall the paired fractions and avoid reversing the general and first-offender thresholds.
xs: **BNSS s.479**: release after **one-half** of the maximum term; **one-third** for **first-time offenders** — option **(2)**.
It is an **undertrial relief** provision, subject to the statutory conditions.
xa: Undertrials are **~73%** of inmates; **9,028** held over **5 years** (NCRB **2024**).
The **Justice Amitava Roy Committee** (**2018**) addressed undertrials and speedy trial.
The **Mulla Committee** wanted **separate undertrials**.

127.s:
Consider the following statements regarding prisoners according to NCRB Prison Statistics 2024:
1. Undertrials constituted approximately 73% of inmates.
2. About 9,028 prisoners had been held for more than five years.
3. Women constituted 14.3% of inmates.
4. There were only 34 women’s prisons.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
127.x: Undertrials constituted approximately 73%, 9,028 had been held over five years and there were 34 women’s prisons. Women constituted 4.14%, not 14.3%.
127.tq: Check each numerical statement independently, especially the altered percentage trap.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Undertrials ~73%**; **9,028** held over **5 years**; only **34** women's prisons.
Statement 3 wrong: women are **4.14%** of inmates, not 14.3%.
xa: **21** States/UTs lack a women's prison.
Prisons **1,333**; inmates **5.11 lakh** against ~**4.53 lakh** capacity.
About **37%** of staff posts vacant; **122 suicides**.

127.s:
Match the following committees with their principal focus:

List-I (Committee)
a. Mulla Committee
b. Krishna Iyer Committee
c. Justice Amitava Roy Committee

List-II (Focus)
i. Women prisoners and greater representation of women in police
 ii. Overcrowding, undertrials, legal aid and speedy trial
 iii. National prison policy, All India Prison Service and separate undertrials

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
127.x: The Mulla Committee focused on comprehensive jail reforms, the Krishna Iyer Committee on women prisoners and women in police, and the Justice Amitava Roy Committee on overcrowding, undertrials, legal aid and speedy trial.
127.tq: Start with the distinctive women-prisoners focus and then eliminate the remaining mismatches.
xs: The match is **a–iii, b–i, c–ii** — option **(1)**.
**Mulla (1980-83)** — **national prison policy, All India Prison Service, separate undertrials**.
**Krishna Iyer (1987)** — **women prisoners**, more women in police; **Amitava Roy (2018)** — **overcrowding, undertrials, legal aid, speedy trial**.
xa: The Amitava Roy Committee was **SC-appointed**.
**Law Commission 262nd (2015)**: death penalty; **273rd (2017)**: torture.
Women are **4.14%** of inmates; only **34** women's prisons.

127.s:
Match List-I (Case) with List-II (Holding):
a. Jagmohan Singh v State of UP (1973)
b. Bachan Singh v State of Punjab (1980)
c. Machhi Singh v State of Punjab (1983)

i. Categories of rarest cases; balancing aggravating and mitigating factors
ii. Death penalty held constitutional
iii. 'Rarest of rare' doctrine: life is the rule, death the exception

Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
127.x: Jagmohan Singh (1973) upheld the death penalty (a–ii); Bachan Singh (1980) laid down 'rarest of rare', life the rule and death the exception (b–iii); Machhi Singh (1983) set categories of rarest cases and the aggravating-mitigating balance (c–i). Option B swaps Jagmohan and Bachan; option C swaps Bachan and Machhi; option D swaps Jagmohan and Machhi.
127.tq: Chronology helps: 1973 upheld, 1980 doctrine, 1983 categories.
xs: The match is **a–ii, b–iii, c–i** — option **(1)**.
**Jagmohan Singh (1973)** — **death penalty constitutional**.
**Bachan Singh (1980)** — **"rarest of rare"**; **life the rule, death the exception**.
**Machhi Singh (1983)** — **categories of rarest cases**; balance **aggravating vs mitigating** factors.
xa: **Epuru Sudhakar (2006)**: pardon/remission open to limited **judicial review**.
**Shatrughan Chauhan (2014)**: inordinate delay → **commute to life**.
**Law Commission 262nd (2015)**: abolish except **terrorism and waging war**.

127.s: A death sentence imposed by a Sessions Court becomes executable only after confirmation by which court?
127.x: A death sentence passed by a Sessions Court requires confirmation by the High Court.
127.tq: Identify the higher authority whose confirmation is mandatory before execution.
xs: A Sessions Court death sentence needs **High Court confirmation** — option **(3)**.
The NHRC, District Court and Cabinet play no confirmation role.
xa: Appeal to SC under **Arts 132, 134, 136**.
**Art. 72**: the **President** can pardon a death sentence.
**Art. 161**: the **Governor** cannot pardon a death sentence but can commute/remit/suspend.

127.s: An appeal against a death sentence may reach the Supreme Court under which combination of constitutional provisions?
127.x: Appeals in such matters may lie to the Supreme Court under Articles 132, 134 and 136.
127.tq: Recall the exact constitutional Article cluster instead of nearby judicial provisions.
xs: Appeals reach the Supreme Court under **Articles 132, 134 and 136** — option **(1)**.
First the Sessions Court sentence needs **High Court confirmation**.
xa: **Nilabati Behera** compensation is under **Arts 32/226** — writ jurisdiction, not appeals.
**Art. 72** (President) can pardon death sentences and **court-martial** cases.
Capital offences now in the **BNS** (murder **s.103**).

127.s: According to Amnesty International’s execution ranking referred to here, which country was identified as the world’s biggest state executioner?
127.x: China was identified as the world’s biggest state executioner.
127.tq: Test the named country directly without importing unrelated current ranking figures.
xs: **China** was named the **world's biggest state executioner** by **Amnesty International** — option **(1)** (UPPSC **2014**).
India, Iran and the USA are not named as the biggest executioner in the notes.
xa: India: **Bachan Singh (1980)** "**rarest of rare**" doctrine.
**Law Commission 262nd (2015)**: abolish death penalty except for **terrorism and waging war**.
Debate: **retributive** vs **reformative** justice.

127.s: Which one of the following correctly matches the Law Commission report with its subject?
o: 262nd Report (2015) — abolition of the death penalty for all crimes except terrorism and waging war
273rd Report (2017) — classification of rarest-of-rare cases under Machhi Singh
262nd Report (2015) — ratification of UNCAT and draft Prevention of Torture Bill, 2017
273rd Report (2017) — creation of the All India Prison Service
127.x: The 262nd Report (2015) recommended abolishing the death penalty for all crimes except terrorism and waging war. The 273rd Report concerned UNCAT ratification and a draft anti-torture Bill.
127.tq: Discriminate between the two Law Commission reports by subject and year.
xs: **262nd Report (2015)** — abolish the death penalty for all crimes **except terrorism and waging war** — option **(1)**.
The **273rd (2017)** dealt with **UNCAT ratification** and a draft torture Bill; rarest-of-rare categories come from **Machhi Singh**; the All India Prison Service from the **Mulla Committee**.
xa: ⚠ **262nd** = death penalty; **273rd** = torture.
**Jagmohan Singh (1973)** held the death penalty constitutional.
**Shatrughan Chauhan (2014)**: **14 days** between mercy rejection and execution.

127.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Articles 72 and 161:
1. The President’s power under Article 72 extends to death sentences.
2. The Governor’s power under Article 161 includes an unrestricted power to pardon a death sentence.
3. The President’s power under Article 72 extends to court-martial cases.
4. The Governor may commute, remit or suspend a death sentence.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
127.x: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct. Statement 2 is false because the Governor cannot pardon a death sentence, though the Governor may commute, remit or suspend it.
127.tq: Use the President–Governor power distinction to identify the reversed constitutional authority.
xs: Statements **1, 3 and 4** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Art. 72**: the **President** can pardon, including **death sentences** and **court-martial** cases.
Statement 2 wrong: under **Art. 161** the **Governor cannot pardon a death sentence**.
Statement 4 correct: the Governor can **commute, remit or suspend** it.
xa: ⚠ **Art 72** = President can pardon death; **Art 161** = Governor cannot.
**Epuru Sudhakar (2006)**: pardon/remission open to limited **judicial review**.
**Shatrughan Chauhan (2014)**: delay in mercy → commutation.

127.s:
Consider the following statements in the context of Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India (2014):
1. Inordinate and unexplained delay in deciding a mercy petition may justify commuting death to life imprisonment.
2. Solitary confinement before rejection of a mercy petition is illegal.
3. A minimum period of 14 days should ordinarily be available between rejection of mercy and execution.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
127.x: All three statements reflect the safeguards recognised in Shatrughan Chauhan (2014): unexplained delay may support commutation, pre-rejection solitary confinement is illegal, and 14 days should separate rejection from execution.
127.tq: Treat each safeguard as an independent proposition and select the combination containing all the established protections.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(1)**.
**Shatrughan Chauhan (2014)**: **inordinate, unexplained delay** in mercy petitions justifies **commuting death to life**.
**Solitary confinement** before rejection is **illegal**; **14 days** must separate rejection and execution.
xa: **Art. 72** (President) and **Art. 161** (Governor) are the mercy powers.
**Epuru Sudhakar (2006)**: limited **judicial review** of pardon.
**Bachan Singh (1980)**: **life is the rule**, death the exception.

127.s: The decision in Epuru Sudhakar v. Government of Andhra Pradesh (2006) is associated with which proposition?
o: Mercy powers are completely immune from judicial scrutiny.
Pardon and remission are open to limited judicial review.
Only the Supreme Court may decide mercy petitions.
A Governor may pardon every death sentence.
127.x: Epuru Sudhakar (2006) established that the exercise of pardon or remission powers is subject to limited judicial review.
127.tq: Identify the precise extent of judicial review without confusing limited review with complete judicial control.
xs: **Epuru Sudhakar v Govt of AP (2006)**: **pardon and remission** are open to **limited judicial review** — option **(2)**.
So mercy powers are not immune; the **Governor** still cannot pardon a death sentence (**Art. 161**).
xa: **Art. 72**: the **President** can pardon a death sentence.
**Shatrughan Chauhan (2014)**: unexplained delay → **commute to life**.
**Machhi Singh (1983)**: categories of rarest cases.

127.s: According to NCRB Prison Statistics 2024, the prison occupancy rate and the proportion of undertrials were respectively:
127.x: NCRB Prison Statistics 2024 reported prison occupancy at 112.7%, with undertrials constituting 73% of the prison population.
127.tq: Keep the percentage pair together and reject options that alter one figure while retaining the other.
xs: NCRB **2024**: occupancy **112.7%** and undertrials **73%** — option **(4)**.
**112.7%** is a **decade-low**; the other percentages are not in the data.
xa: **Delhi** highest occupancy **194.6%**, **Meghalaya** **163.5%**.
**9,028** undertrials held over **5 years**.
Released on **3 Jun 2026**.

127.s: Gade Sai Krishna’s custodial-death case in Andhra Pradesh was associated with which police station and city?
127.x: The case concerned the Krishnalanka police station in Vijayawada.
127.tq: Match the incident with its precise local jurisdiction instead of the wider State alone.
xs: The **Gade Sai Krishna** custodial death involved the **Krishnalanka police station, Vijayawada** — option **(1)**.
It is the **AP angle** of custodial violence; Tirupati figures only because the **Tirupati MP** was later summoned.
xa: NHRC sought reports (**Jun 2026**).
SC gave the SIT (IGP **M. Ravi Prakash**) **7-day** custody of suspended CI **Nagaraju** (**31 Jul 2026**).
A Vijayawada court summoned the **Tirupati MP** to record his statement (**11 Aug 2026**).

128.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Patriarchy is a system in which men hold primary power and status in family and society.
2. Matrilineal tribes are an exception to the general pattern of patriarchy.
3. Patriarchy means the unequal treatment by society of men and women.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
128.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: 'unequal treatment by society of men and women' is the definition of gender discrimination (APPSC 2024), not patriarchy. Hence A (1 and 2 only); B, C and D include the wrong statement 3.
128.tq: Patriarchy = male dominance; gender discrimination = unequal treatment.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **Patriarchy** = male dominance, men holding **primary power and status** in family and society — correct.
Statement 2: **Matrilineal tribes** are the exception — correct.
Statement 3: "unequal treatment by society of men and women" defines **gender discrimination** (APPSC **2024**), not patriarchy — wrong.
xa: Patriarchy has been critiqued by **Nivedita Menon**, author of **Seeing Like a Feminist**.
**Uma Chakravarti** wrote on **Brahmanical patriarchy** vs Dalit patriarchy.
**Gail Omvedt**: Dalit/Bahujan feminism.

128.s: The term ‘Missing women’ was coined by
128.x: Amartya Sen coined the term ‘missing women’ to refer to the consequences of discrimination against women, including intra-household discrimination.
128.tq: Use the person–concept association without confusing it with other gender scholars.
xs: **Amartya Sen** coined **'Missing women'** for intra-household discrimination — option **(2)** (APPSC **2019**).
**Uma Chakravarti**: **Brahmanical patriarchy**; **Bina Agarwal**: **A Field of One's Own**; **Gail Omvedt**: Dalit/Bahujan feminism.
xa: Sen also gave the **capability approach** and **cooperative conflict**.
Causes of a low sex ratio: **son preference**, female foeticide/infanticide, dowry, neglect of girls.
Sex ratio at birth rose from **904 (2017-19)** to **917 (2021-23)** (MoSPI, Women and Men in India **2025**).

128.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Uma Chakravarti — A Field of One’s Own
Gail Omvedt — Seeing Like a Feminist
Bina Agarwal — Land rights and A Field of One’s Own
128.x: Bina Agarwal is associated with land rights and authored A Field of One’s Own. Seeing Like a Feminist is associated with Nivedita Menon, while ‘missing women’ was coined by Amartya Sen.
128.tq: Start from the sure author–work pair and eliminate swapped scholars.
xs: **Bina Agarwal** — **land rights** and **A Field of One's Own** — option **(3)** is correctly matched.
**A Field of One's Own** is not Uma Chakravarti's; she wrote on **Brahmanical patriarchy**.
**Seeing Like a Feminist** is by **Nivedita Menon**, not Gail Omvedt; **'Missing women'** is **Amartya Sen's** term.
xa: **Gail Omvedt**: Dalit/Bahujan feminism.
**The High-Caste Hindu Woman**: **Pandita Ramabai**; **Stri Purush Tulana**: **Tarabai Shinde**.
**Manushi** was founded by **Madhu Kishwar**.

128.s: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes gender mainstreaming from a gender audit?
o: Mainstreaming concerns only biological differences, whereas auditing concerns only employment.
Mainstreaming is limited to personal law, whereas auditing is limited to criminal law.
There is no conceptual distinction between the two.
Mainstreaming is a Beijing strategy, whereas a gender audit checks whether policies and budgets affect women and men equally.
128.x: Gender mainstreaming involves building a gender lens into every policy and was adopted as a Beijing strategy. A gender audit examines whether policies and budgets affect women and men equally.
128.tq: Compare two closely related concepts by their function and scope.
xs: **Gender mainstreaming** is a **Beijing (1995)** strategy; a **gender audit** checks whether policies and budgets affect women and men equally — option **(4)**.
Mainstreaming puts a **gender lens in every policy**, assessing each policy's impact on women and men — not biology or personal law.
The two are distinct: one builds gender into policy, the other **audits** its effects.
xa: The Beijing **Fourth World Conference on Women (1995)** adopted the **Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action**.
The Platform has **12 critical areas**, including the **girl child**.
**NPEW 2001** goals include **gender mainstreaming** and ending discrimination and violence.

128.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the status of women in different periods:
1. Women enjoyed an honourable position during the Vedic period.
2. Women were referred to as Ardhangini or the better half.
3. Gargi and Maitreyi were women scholars.
4. Purdah became a prominent feature of the early Vedic period.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
128.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the status of women declined in the later Vedic and medieval periods, when practices such as purdah became prominent.
128.tq: Find the period-based false statement by checking the time attached to a custom.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1–2: in the **Vedic/ancient** period women had an **honourable place**, called **'Ardhangini'** (better half) — correct.
Statement 3: **Gargi** and **Maitreyi** were women scholars — correct.
Statement 4: **purdah** belongs to the **later Vedic and medieval** decline, not the early Vedic period — wrong.
xa: Vedic women had **equal standing** and a role in **sacred rites**.
In the later period women were **confined to the home** and social evils rose.
Customs: **Niyoga**, **Sati** (widow immolation), **Devadasi** (girls dedicated to temples).

128.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Child marriage — Marriage below the legally prescribed age
Devadasi — Dedication of girls to temples
128.x: Niyoga did not mean prohibition of widow remarriage; it involved a childless widow or wife bearing a son by the husband’s brother or kinsman.
128.tq: Find the wrong definition among closely related social customs.
xs: **Niyoga — Prohibition of widow remarriage** is wrongly matched — option **(2)**.
**Niyoga** = a **childless widow/wife bearing a son** by the husband's **brother or kinsman**.
**Devadasi** = girls dedicated to temples; **Sati** = widow immolation — both correctly matched.
xa: Devadasi was banned by the **Madras Act 1947** and the **AP Devadasis (Prohibition of Dedication) Act 1988**.
**Sati** was abolished in **1829** (Raja Rammohan Roy); the **Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act** is of **1987**.
**Vidyasagar**: **Widow Remarriage Act 1856**.

128.s: The Devadasi system was prohibited in Andhra Pradesh by the
o: AP Devadasis (Prohibition of Dedication) Act, 1988 only
both the Madras Act, 1947 and the AP Devadasis (Prohibition of Dedication) Act, 1988
128.x: The practice was banned by the Madras Act of 1947 and, in Andhra Pradesh, by the AP Devadasis (Prohibition of Dedication) Act, 1988.
128.tq: Combine a general regional law with the specific Andhra Pradesh enactment.
xs: Devadasi dedication was banned by **both** the **Madras Act 1947** and the **AP Devadasis (Prohibition of Dedication) Act 1988** — option **(3)**.
Picking only one of the two Acts is incomplete; the **Child Marriage Restraint Act (1929)** deals with minimum marriage age, not Devadasis.
xa: **Devadasi** = girls dedicated to temples.
Other customs: **Niyoga** (son by husband's kinsman) and **Sati** (widow immolation).
**Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act 1987** bans Sati and its **glorification**.

128.s: The Child Marriage Restraint Act, commonly known as the Sarda Act, was enacted in
128.x: The Child Marriage Restraint or Sarda Act was enacted in 1929 and dealt with the minimum marriage age.
128.tq: Separate the Sarda Act’s year from the nearby years of women’s organisations.
xs: The **Child Marriage Restraint (Sarda) Act** was enacted in **1929** — option **(4)**; it fixed a **minimum marriage age**.
**1917** = **WIA**; **1925** = **NCWI**; **1927** = **AIWC** — organisations, not this Act.
xa: **Female Infanticide Prevention Act**: **1870** (APPSC **2018**).
**Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act**: **1956**; **Dowry Prohibition Act**: **1961**.
**Vidyasagar** opposed **child marriage** and polygamy.

128.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Reformer)
 a. Raja Rammohan Roy
 b. Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar
 c. Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule
 d. Pandita Ramabai

List-II (Contribution)
 i. Arya Mahila Samaj
 ii. Brahmo Samaj
 iii. Widow Remarriage Act
 iv. Satyashodhak Samaj

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
128.x: Raja Rammohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj; Vidyasagar was associated with the Widow Remarriage Act; the Phules founded the Satyashodhak Samaj; and Pandita Ramabai founded the Arya Mahila Samaj.
128.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes with a swapped reformer and reform.
xs: **a–ii, b–iii, c–iv, d–i** — option **(1)**.
**Raja Rammohan Roy** – **Brahmo Samaj**; **Vidyasagar** – **Widow Remarriage Act 1856**.
**Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule** – **Satyashodhak Samaj (1873)**; **Pandita Ramabai** – **Arya Mahila Samaj (1881)**.
xa: Rammohan Roy: abolition of **Sati (1829)**.
Vidyasagar: **Bethune School (1849)**; against child marriage and polygamy.
Phules: **first girls' school, Pune 1848**; Savitribai the **first woman teacher**.
⚠ **1881** = Ramabai's Arya Mahila Samaj and **Veeresalingam's** first Telugu widow remarriage.

128.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Kandukuri Veeresalingam — Women's personal and sexual freedom through the novel Stree
Raja Rammohan Roy — Abolition of Sati
Pandita Ramabai — The High-Caste Hindu Woman
128.x: The statement is not correctly matched. Stree was written by Chalam, while Kandukuri Veeresalingam promoted widow remarriage and women's education in Telugu society.
128.tq: Find the wrong author–work association rather than relying on the broad reform theme.
xs: **Kandukuri Veeresalingam — Stree** is wrongly matched — option **(2)**: **Stree** is by **Chalam (Gudipati Venkata Chalam)**.
Veeresalingam brought **widow remarriage** and **women's education** to Telugu society.
The rest are correct: **Tarabai Shinde** – Stri Purush Tulana; **Rammohan Roy** – Sati abolition; **Pandita Ramabai** – The High-Caste Hindu Woman.
xa: Chalam wrote for women's **personal and sexual freedom**.
Veeresalingam's first Telugu widow remarriage: **1881, Rajahmundry**.
**Durgabai Deshmukh** founded the **Andhra Mahila Sabha (1937)**.

128.s: Kandukuri Veeresalingam performed the first widow remarriage in Telugu society at:
128.x: Kandukuri Veeresalingam performed the first widow remarriage in Telugu society at Rajahmundry in 1881.
128.tq: Use the place–year pair to distinguish this event from Veeresalingam's broader reform activities.
xs: Veeresalingam performed the first Telugu widow remarriage at **Rajahmundry in 1881** — option **(1)**.
He brought **widow remarriage** and **women's education** to Telugu society.
xa: ⚠ **1881** is also the year of **Pandita Ramabai's Arya Mahila Samaj**.
**Durgabai Deshmukh**: **Andhra Mahila Sabha (1937)**; first chair, **Central Social Welfare Board (1953)**.
**Chalam** wrote **Stree** on women's personal and sexual freedom.

128.s: The Female Infanticide Prevention Act was enacted during British rule in the year:
128.x: The Female Infanticide Prevention Act was passed in 1870 (APPSC 2018). 1829 is the abolition of Sati, 1856 the Widow Remarriage Act and 1929 the Sarda (Child Marriage Restraint) Act.
128.tq: Infanticide 1870; Sati 1829; Widow Remarriage 1856; Sarda 1929.
xs: The **Female Infanticide Prevention Act** dates from **1870** — option **(3)** (APPSC **2018**).
**1829** = abolition of **Sati**; **1856** = **Widow Remarriage Act**; **1929** = **Sarda Act**.
xa: The Phules ran a **Home for Prevention of Infanticide** (**1863**).
**PCPNDT Act 1994** bans sex selection and pre-natal sex determination.
Low sex ratio causes: **son preference**, female foeticide/infanticide, dowry.

128.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the women's movement in India:
1. Its 19th-century phase focused on reform issues such as sati, widow remarriage and education.
2. By the early 20th century its focus had shifted to economic liberalisation and industrial employment.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
128.x: Statement 1 is correct: the first phase took up sati, widow remarriage and education. Statement 2 is wrong: in the early 20th century the focus shifted to political rights. Hence 1 only (A); B, C and D are wrong.
128.tq: Phase 1 = social reform; early 20th c. = political rights.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: the **19th-century** phase focused on **sati, widow remarriage, education** — correct.
Statement 2: in the early 20th century the focus shifted to **political rights**, not economic liberalisation — wrong.
xa: **WIA (1917)**: **Annie Besant, Margaret Cousins** — votes for women and the right to sit in councils.
**NCWI (1925)** and **AIWC (1927)** followed.
**Towards Equality (1974)** sparked the **modern women's movement**.

128.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Women's Indian Association (1917) was founded by Annie Besant and Margaret Cousins.
2. The WIA worked for votes for women and the right to sit in councils.
3. The National Council of Women in India (1925) was linked to the International Labour Organization.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
128.x: Statements 1 and 2 on the WIA are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: the NCWI (1925) was linked to the International Council of Women, not the ILO. Hence A; B, C and D include statement 3.
128.tq: WIA 1917 = Besant + Cousins, votes; NCWI 1925 = International Council of Women.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statements 1–2: **WIA (1917)** was founded by **Annie Besant and Margaret Cousins** for **votes for women** and seats in councils — correct.
Statement 3: the **NCWI (1925)** was linked to the **International Council of Women**, not the ILO — wrong.
xa: **AIWC (1927)**: **Margaret Cousins** — education, social upliftment, legal rights.
⚠ Margaret Cousins appears in **both WIA and AIWC**.
Early 20th c.: the movement's focus shifted to **political rights**.

128.s: Which of the following was a principal area of work of the All India Women’s Conference?
o: Education, social upliftment and legal rights
Only the abolition of international borders
128.x: The AIWC focused on education, social upliftment and legal rights.
128.tq: Select the option that combines the organisation’s three stated areas of work.
xs: The **AIWC** worked on **education, social upliftment and legal rights** — option **(2)**.
Banking, defence or borders were never its concerns.
xa: AIWC was founded in **1927**, linked with **Margaret Cousins**.
**WIA (1917)**: votes for women; **NCWI (1925)**: linked to the International Council of Women.
**Andhra Mahila Sabha (1937)**: **Durgabai Deshmukh**.

128.s:
Consider the following statements regarding ‘Towards Equality’:
1. It was a report of the Committee on the Status of Women in India.
2. Vina Mazumdar was its Member-Secretary.
3. It exposed the declining status of women.
4. It had no influence on the modern women’s movement.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
128.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 4 is false because the report helped spark the modern women’s movement.
128.tq: Reject the absolute negative statement that reverses the report’s impact.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(2)**.
**Towards Equality** was the report of the **Committee on the Status of Women in India**, with **Vina Mazumdar** as Member-Secretary — correct.
It **exposed women's declining status** — correct.
Statement 4 is wrong: it **sparked the modern women's movement**.
xa: The report dates from **1974**.
Vina Mazumdar later founded **CWDS**; **Neera Desai** founded the first Women's Studies Centre (**SNDT**).
**Madhu Kishwar** founded **Manushi**.

128.s: Who founded the first Women’s Studies Centre at SNDT?
128.x: Neera Desai founded the first Women’s Studies Centre at SNDT.
128.tq: Discriminate among women’s movement leaders by their specific institutional contribution.
xs: **Neera Desai** founded the first **Women's Studies Centre** at **SNDT** — option **(4)**.
**Vina Mazumdar** founded **CWDS**; **Madhu Kishwar** founded **Manushi**; **Margaret Cousins** was in **WIA** and **AIWC**.
xa: These belong to the **post-1970s autonomous movement**, after **Towards Equality (1974)**.
**Chipko (1973)**: women of **Chamoli** hugged trees.
**Anti-Arrack Movement** began **1992** at **Dubagunta (Nellore)**.

128.s:
Arrange the following developments associated with the Anti-Arrack Movement in chronological order:

A. Prohibition of arrack
B. Beginning of the movement at Dubagunta
C. Ban on arrack

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
128.x: The movement began at Dubagunta in 1992, led to the arrack ban in 1993, and was followed by prohibition in 1995.
128.tq: Anchor the sequence to the dated starting event and then place the two policy outcomes.
xs: Order **B, C, A** — option **(1)**.
**Dubagunta** beginning (**1992**) → **arrack ban** (**1993**) → **prohibition** (**1995**).
xa: The movement began among **literacy-campaign women** in **Nellore**.
**Chipko (1973)**: women of **Chamoli** hugged trees.
**Towards Equality (1974)** sparked the modern women's movement.

128.s: Durgabai Deshmukh, founder of the Andhra Mahila Sabha, was also the first chairperson of the:
o: Committee on the Status of Women in India (1974)
128.x: Durgabai Deshmukh founded the Andhra Mahila Sabha in 1937 and was the first chair of the Central Social Welfare Board, set up in 1953. The NCW came in 1992, the Committee on the Status of Women produced Towards Equality in 1974 (Vina Mazumdar as Member-Secretary), and the AIWC is linked with Margaret Cousins.
128.tq: Durgabai: Andhra Mahila Sabha 1937, CSWB chair 1953.
xs: Durgabai Deshmukh was the first chair of the **Central Social Welfare Board (1953)** — option **(2)**.
The **NCW** was set up in **Jan 1992**; the **Committee on the Status of Women** (Towards Equality, **1974**) had **Vina Mazumdar** as Member-Secretary.
The **AIWC (1927)** is linked with **Margaret Cousins**.
xa: Durgabai founded the **Andhra Mahila Sabha** in **1937**.
NCW: **Act 1990**; Chairperson + **5 members** + Member-Secretary.
⚠ NCW **Act 1990** but **set up Jan 1992**.

128.s: Which Article of the Constitution provides for special provisions for women and children?
128.x: Article 15(3) enables the State to make special provisions for women and children.
128.tq: Identify the specific sub-clause rather than the broader equality provision.
xs: **Article 15(3)** permits **special provisions for women and children** — option **(3)**.
**Art. 14**: equality; **Art. 15(1)**: no discrimination on ground of **sex**; **Art. 16(2)**: no sex discrimination in **public employment**.
xa: **Art. 42**: just and humane work conditions, **maternity relief**.
**Art. 44**: **Uniform Civil Code**.
**Arts. 243D / 243T**: at least **one-third** seats for women in Panchayats / Municipalities.

128.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 243D — reservation of seats and chairperson offices in Panchayats
Article 42 — reservation of seats in State Assemblies
128.x: Article 243D provides for at least one-third reservation of seats and chairperson offices in Panchayats. Article 243T relates to Municipalities.
128.tq: Use the local-body distinction between Panchayats and Municipalities.
xs: **Art. 243D** reserves at least **one-third** seats and **chairpersons' offices** in **Panchayats** — option **(3)**.
**Art. 243T** is for **Municipalities**, not Panchayats; Art. 243D is not about Municipalities.
**Art. 42** is about **maternity relief**; Assembly seats are under **Art. 332A**.
xa: **AP** gives **50%** to women in panchayats and municipalities — above the **1/3** floor.
About **46%** of PRI representatives are women (**26 Jan 2026**).
**Sashakt Panchayat Netri Abhiyan** trains women elected representatives.

128.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Article 42 provides for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief.
2. Articles 330A and 332A, inserted by the 106th Amendment, reserve one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies.
3. Article 243T provides for reservation of seats for women in Panchayats.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
128.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong: Article 243T covers Municipalities; Panchayat reservation is under Article 243D. So '1 and 2 only' is right, and every other option includes statement 3 or leaves out a correct statement.
128.tq: 42 = maternity relief; 330A/332A = LS/Assembly quota; 243D Panchayats, 243T Municipalities.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **Art. 42** — just and humane work conditions and **maternity relief** — correct.
Statement 2: **Arts. 330A / 332A** (**106th Amendment**) — **1/3** seats in Lok Sabha / State Assemblies — correct.
Statement 3: **Art. 243T** covers **Municipalities**; Panchayats are under **Art. 243D** — wrong.
xa: The **33%** quota came into effect in the **J&K and Puducherry** Assemblies on **17 Apr 2026**.
The **131st Amendment Bill, 2026** (to speed up the quota) was defeated on **17 Apr 2026**.
**Art. 44**: Uniform Civil Code.

128.s: Which of the following correctly describes women's reservation in Andhra Pradesh local bodies?
o: 50% only in municipalities and 33⅓% in panchayats
50% in panchayats and municipalities, above the one-third floor
33⅓% in panchayats and municipalities, equal to the constitutional floor
One-third in panchayats and 50% only in nominated posts
128.x: Andhra Pradesh provides 50% reservation for women in panchayats and municipalities, which is above the one-third floor.
128.tq: Compare the State share with the constitutional minimum instead of confusing the two percentages.
xs: AP gives **50%** to women in **panchayats and municipalities**, above the **1/3** floor — option **(2)**.
The Constitution's **Arts. 243D / 243T** require only **at least one-third**.
xa: AP also gives **50% of nominated posts and work contracts** to women (**14 Apr 2026**).
AP direct recruitment: **33 1/3% horizontal** reservation for women.
About **46%** of PRI representatives nationally are women.

128.s:
Consider the following statements regarding reservation for women in Andhra Pradesh:
1. Women get 50% of nominated posts and work contracts.
2. Women get 50% horizontal reservation in direct recruitment.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
128.x: Statement 1 is correct: AP reserves 50% of nominated posts and work contracts for women. Statement 2 is wrong: the horizontal reservation in direct recruitment is 33 1/3%, not 50%. Hence 1 only (A); B, C and D are wrong.
128.tq: AP: 50% local bodies and nominated posts; 33 1/3% in jobs.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: AP gives women **50% of nominated posts and work contracts** — correct.
Statement 2: direct recruitment has **33 1/3% horizontal** reservation, not 50% — wrong.
xa: AP local bodies: **50%** for women in panchayats and municipalities.
AP daughters' property law dates from **1985** (passed under **NTR**).
**APSES 2024-25 (SDG 5)** gaps: women in the labour force, institution building, crime against women.

128.s: The 33% women's quota under the 106th Constitutional Amendment (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) came into effect on 17 April 2026 in the Legislative Assemblies of:
128.x: The 33% quota came into effect in the Jammu and Kashmir and Puducherry Assemblies on 17 April 2026. Ladakh has no legislature, and neither Delhi nor the States named are the ones where it took effect on that date.
128.tq: 106th CAA quota: first in J&K + Puducherry Assemblies (17 Apr 2026).
xs: The **33%** quota took effect in the **J&K and Puducherry** Assemblies on **17 Apr 2026** — option **(3)**.
It comes from the **106th CAA (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam)**, which inserted **Arts. 330A / 332A**.
xa: The **Constitution (131st) Amendment Bill, 2026**, to speed up the quota by redistributing Lok Sabha seats, was defeated on **17 Apr 2026**.
Elsewhere the quota (**2023** Act) still waits for **Census and delimitation**.
**Arts. 243D / 243T**: **1/3** in Panchayats / Municipalities.

128.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India and CEDAW:
1. India signed CEDAW in 1980.
2. India ratified CEDAW in 1993.
3. India adopted CEDAW only after the Beijing Conference of 1995.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
128.x: India signed CEDAW in 1980 and ratified it in 1993. Statement 3 is false because both events preceded the Beijing Conference of 1995.
128.tq: Use the chronological relationship among signature, ratification and conference dates.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
India **signed** CEDAW in **1980** and **ratified** it in **1993** — both correct.
Statement 3 is wrong: both came **before Beijing (1995)**.
xa: CEDAW was adopted by the UNGA in **1979**.
India's **reservation** is on **Art. 29(1)** (arbitration/ICJ).
Declaration on **16(2)** concerns **marriage registration**.

128.s:
Consider the following statements regarding India and CEDAW:
1. India made declarations on Articles 5(a), 16(1) and 16(2) of CEDAW.
2. India's reservation under CEDAW relates to Article 16(2) on marriage registration.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
128.x: Statement 1 is correct: India's declarations cover Arts 5(a), 16(1) and 16(2). Statement 2 is wrong: Art. 16(2) is a declaration; India's reservation is on Art. 29(1) (arbitration/ICJ). Hence 1 only (A); B, C and D are wrong.
128.tq: Declarations = 5(a), 16(1), 16(2); reservation = 29(1).
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: India made **declarations** on Arts **5(a), 16(1)** and **16(2)** — correct.
Statement 2: **16(2)** (marriage registration) is a declaration; India's **reservation** is on **Art. 29(1)** (arbitration/ICJ) — wrong.
xa: The 5(a)/16(1) declarations mean **no interference in personal affairs without community consent**.
India signed in **1980**, ratified in **1993**.
CEDAW: UNGA, **1979**.

128.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action:
1. It was adopted at the Fourth World Conference on Women in 1995.
2. It identifies 10 critical areas of concern, including the girl child.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
128.x: Statement 1 is correct: Beijing was the Fourth World Conference on Women, 1995. Statement 2 is wrong: the Platform identifies 12 critical areas (the girl child is one of them), not 10. Hence 1 only (A); B, C and D are wrong.
128.tq: Beijing = 4th conference, 1995, 12 critical areas.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: the **Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action** came from the **Fourth World Conference on Women, 1995** — correct.
Statement 2: it lists **12 critical areas**, not 10 (the **girl child** is one) — wrong.
xa: Areas include poverty, education, health, violence, armed conflict, economy, decision-making, media, environment.
**Gender mainstreaming** is a Beijing strategy.
Earlier conferences: Mexico City **1975**, Copenhagen **1980**, Nairobi **1985**.

128.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Commission on the Status of Women:
1. It was set up in 1946.
2. It functions under the UN General Assembly.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
128.x: Statement 1 is correct: the CSW dates from 1946. Statement 2 is wrong: it functions under ECOSOC, not the General Assembly. Hence 1 only (A); B, C and D are wrong.
128.tq: CSW = 1946, under ECOSOC.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: the **Commission on the Status of Women** was set up in **1946** — correct.
Statement 2: it works under **ECOSOC**, not the General Assembly — wrong.
xa: **CSW-70 (2026)** adopted non-binding **Agreed Conclusions** on women's **access to justice**.
**CEDAW** was adopted by the **UNGA** in **1979**.
**International Women's Year**: **1975**.

128.s: The International Women’s Year and the First World Conference on Women were associated with
128.x: The International Women’s Year and the First World Conference on Women were held in Mexico City in 1975.
128.tq: Match the conference milestone with its city and year.
xs: **International Women's Year** and the **1st World Conference** were in **Mexico City, 1975** — option **(4)**.
**Copenhagen 1980** was the 2nd, **Nairobi 1985** the 3rd, **Beijing 1995** the 4th.
xa: The **UN Decade for Women** ran **1976-85**.
Beijing produced the **Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action**.

128.s: The UN Decade for Women covered the period
128.x: The UN Decade for Women extended from 1976 to 1985.
128.tq: Recall the exact decade following the 1975 Mexico City conference.
xs: The **UN Decade for Women** ran **1976-85** — option **(4)**.
It followed **International Women's Year (1975)** and the Mexico City conference.
xa: Within the Decade: **CEDAW (1979)**, **Copenhagen (1980)**, **Nairobi (1985)**.
**Beijing (1995)** was the 4th World Conference.
Commission on the Status of Women: **1946**.

128.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
128.x: The Beijing Conference was held in 1995, not 1980. Copenhagen was the second World Conference in 1980, and Nairobi was the third in 1985.
128.tq: Find the shifted year in a sequence of closely spaced international milestones.
xs: **Beijing Conference — 1980** is wrong — option **(4)**: Beijing was in **1995**.
**Nairobi — 1985**, **CEDAW — 1979** and **Copenhagen — 1980** are correct.
xa: ⚠ Mexico City **1975** (1st) – Copenhagen **1980** (2nd) – Nairobi **1985** (3rd) – Beijing **1995** (4th).
India signed CEDAW in **1980**, ratified **1993**.
Beijing identified **12 critical areas**.

128.s: The National Policy for Empowerment of Women, 2001 was associated with which of the following developments?
o: The shift in the Eighth Plan from development to empowerment
The replacement of empowerment by welfare
128.x: The Eighth Plan marked a shift in policy emphasis from development of women to empowerment of women. The year 2001 was also observed as the Year of Women’s Empowerment.
128.tq: Identify the policy milestone by its distinctive planning-period shift.
xs: The **8th Five Year Plan** marked the **shift from 'development' to 'empowerment'** of women, the line that the **NPEW 2001** carried forward — option **(2)**.
Commercial surrogacy is **banned** (Surrogacy Act **2021**), and Family Courts come from the **Family Courts Act 1984** — neither belongs to NPEW.
Welfare did not replace empowerment; the move was **towards** empowerment.
xa: **2001** was the **Year of Women's Empowerment** (APPSC **2019**).
NPEW goals: advancement and empowerment; equal access to health, education, employment; ending discrimination and violence; **gender mainstreaming**.
**Draft National Policy for Women 2016 (MWCD)** later added environment and climate change.

128.s: Which of the following is NOT an objective of the National Policy for Empowerment of Women, 2001?
o: Promoting commercial surrogacy as an employment opportunity
Ending discrimination and violence against women
Ensuring equal access to health, education and employment
128.x: The policy objectives included advancement and empowerment, equal access to health, education and employment, ending discrimination and violence, and gender mainstreaming. Commercial surrogacy is not a policy objective listed here.
128.tq: Find the unrelated legal concept inserted among genuine policy objectives.
xs: **Promoting commercial surrogacy** is not an NPEW goal — option **(1)**; the **Surrogacy (Regulation) Act 2021** bans commercial surrogacy.
NPEW goals: **ending discrimination and violence**, **equal access to health, education, employment**, and **gender mainstreaming**.
xa: NPEW **2001**; **2001** was the **Year of Women's Empowerment**.
The **8th Plan** shifted from 'development' to **'empowerment'**.
Only **altruistic** surrogacy is allowed (medical costs, insurance).

128.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Draft National Policy for Women, 2016 included food security and nutrition under health.
2. It included governance and decision-making as a priority area.
3. It excluded environmental and climate-change concerns.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
128.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because environment and climate change were expressly included as priority areas.
128.tq: Detect the negative reversal of a listed policy priority.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: **Health incl. food security and nutrition** is a priority area of the **Draft National Policy for Women 2016** — correct.
Statement 2: **Governance and decision-making** is a priority area — correct.
Statement 3: **environment and climate change** is included — wrong.
xa: Other areas: **education**, **economy**, **violence against women**, **enabling environment**.
The Draft Policy came from the **MWCD**.
Earlier: **NPEW 2001** (APPSC **2019**).

128.s:
Consider the following statements:

1. The Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act was enacted in 1987.
2. The Act bans Sati and its glorification.
3. The National Policy for Empowerment of Women was adopted in 2001.
4. The year 2001 was also observed as the Year of Empowerment of Women.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
128.x: All four statements are correct. The 1987 Act addressed Sati and its glorification, while 2001 marked both the National Policy and the Year of Empowerment of Women.
128.tq: Check whether the year and the substantive provision are both present before choosing the code.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4)**.
**Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act** (**1987**) bans **Sati and its glorification**.
**NPEW** was adopted in **2001**, also the **Year of Empowerment of Women**.
xa: ⚠ **1986** = **Indecent Representation Act**; **1987** = **Sati Act**.
**Raja Rammohan Roy**: abolition of Sati (**1829**).
The **8th Plan** shifted from development to **empowerment** of women.

128.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 — Decision within 60 days
Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013 — Internal Complaints Committee at the workplace
Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013 — Right to Residence under Section 17
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 — Right to Residence under Section 17
128.x: Right to Residence under Section 17 belongs to the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005. The 2013 workplace law provides for an Internal Complaints Committee and a Local Complaints Committee in the district.
128.tq: Distinguish provisions of two neighbouring women-protection laws rather than matching only their subject.
xs: **Workplace Act 2013 — Right to Residence (Sec. 17)** is wrongly matched — option **(3)**.
**Right to Residence (Sec. 17)** and decision within **60 days** belong to the **Domestic Violence Act 2005**.
The **2013 Act** provides an **Internal Complaints Committee** at the workplace.
xa: The 2013 Act also has a **Local Complaints Committee** in the district.
The **DV Act 2005** is a **civil law**.
Crimes against women: **4,41,534** in **2024**; **32%** spousal violence (NFHS-5).

128.s:
Which of the following chronological orders of enactment is correct?
A. Dowry Prohibition Act
B. Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act
C. Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act
D. Prohibition of Child Marriage Act
128.x: The years are 1961 for the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1986 for the Indecent Representation of Women Act, 1987 for the Commission of Sati Act and 2006 for the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act.
128.tq: Arrange the enactments by their years, checking the close 1986–1987 sequence.
xs: Order **A, B, C, D** — option **(1)**.
**Dowry Prohibition Act** (**1961**) → **Indecent Representation Act** (**1986**) → **Commission of Sati Act** (**1987**) → **Prohibition of Child Marriage Act**, the last.
xa: ⚠ **1986** = Indecent Representation; **1987** = Sati — a common swap.
The earlier **Child Marriage Restraint (Sarda) Act** was of **1929**.
**Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act**: **1956**.

128.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.

List-I (Law)
a. Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act
b. Dowry Prohibition Act
c. PCPNDT Act
 d. Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act

List-II (Year)
i. 1994
ii. 1956
iii. 2019
iv. 1961
128.x: The Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act dates to 1956, the Dowry Prohibition Act to 1961, the PCPNDT Act to 1994 and the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act to 2019.
128.tq: Start with the sure year-law pairs and eliminate codes that disturb them.
xs: **a–ii, b–iv, c–i, d–iii** — option **(1)**.
**Immoral Traffic Act** – **1956**; **Dowry Prohibition Act** – **1961**.
**PCPNDT Act** – **1994**; **Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act** – **2019**.
xa: The **2019** Act was Parliament's response to **Shayara Bano**, passed **30 July 2019**.
**PCPNDT** bans sex selection and pre-natal sex determination.
Dowry: minimum **5 years** + fine of at least **Rs 15,000**.

128.s: Which one of the following is correct about the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956?
o: It criminalises prostitution itself in all forms.
It penalises brothel-keeping, soliciting and living on the earnings of prostitution, but not prostitution itself.
It was enacted in 1986 to replace the Indian Penal Code provisions on trafficking.
It deals only with child marriage.
128.x: The ITPA, 1956 penalises brothel-keeping, soliciting and living on the earnings of prostitution, but does not make prostitution itself an offence. It is a 1956 law (1986 is only its amendment year) and has nothing to do with child marriage.
128.tq: ITPA 1956: punishes the trade around prostitution, not prostitution itself.
xs: The **ITPA 1956** penalises **brothel keeping, soliciting, living on earnings** — **not prostitution itself** — option **(2)**.
It dates from **1956**, not 1986, and has nothing to do with child marriage.
xa: Child marriage: **Sarda Act (1929)** fixed the minimum marriage age.
**1986** = **Indecent Representation of Women Act**.
**Dowry Prohibition Act**: **1961**.

128.s: In which case was the right of a daughter to be a coparcener by birth recognised, irrespective of whether the father was alive on 9 September 2005?
128.x: Vineeta Sharma (2020) recognised that a daughter is a coparcener by birth, whether or not the father was alive on 9 September 2005.
128.tq: Use the precise legal consequence to distinguish similar women’s-rights judgments.
xs: **Vineeta Sharma (2020)** held a daughter a **coparcener by birth**, whether or not the father was alive on **9 Sept 2005** — option **(3)**.
**Shayara Bano**: triple talaq; **Sarla Mudgal**: conversion to remarry; **Shah Bano**: maintenance under **s.125 CrPC**.
xa: The **2005 amendment** to the HSA made daughters **equal coparceners**.
**AP** had made unmarried daughters coparceners earlier (**1986** amendment; Assembly passed it **24 Sept 1985** under **NTR**).
HSA does **not apply to notified STs** (**s.2(2)**).

128.s: The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 is associated with which of the following reforms?
o: Abolition of the female heir’s limited estate and equal inheritance for women
Mandatory registration of every inter-faith marriage under one uniform law
128.x: The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 gave women equal inheritance and abolished the female heir’s limited estate. Civil marriage irrespective of religion is associated with the Special Marriage Act.
128.tq: Distinguish personal-law reform from marriage and labour legislation.
xs: The **HSA 1956** gave **equal inheritance** to women and **abolished the female heir's limited estate** — option **(1)**.
**Civil marriage irrespective of religion** = **Special Marriage Act 1954**; **equal pay** = **Equal Remuneration Act 1976**.
xa: **2005 amendment**: daughters = **equal coparceners**.
**AP amendment (1986)** made unmarried daughters coparceners well before 2005.
STs are excluded under **s.2(2)**.

128.s: The Hindu Succession Act does not apply to
o: all persons belonging to Scheduled Castes
all women belonging to Scheduled Tribes notified under the Act’s exclusion
128.x: Under Section 2(2) the Hindu Succession Act does not apply to notified Scheduled Tribes. The Supreme Court (8 Oct 2025) upheld this exclusion, so the Act cannot be extended to tribals whatever their religion; it does apply to Scheduled Castes and to residents of Andhra Pradesh generally.
128.tq: Test the statutory exception and avoid replacing Scheduled Tribes with Scheduled Castes.
xs: The HSA does **not apply to notified STs** under **s.2(2)** — option **(3)**.
It applies to **Scheduled Castes** and to AP residents generally; inter-faith marriages are not its exclusion.
The **SC (8 Oct 2025)** upheld the **exclusion of STs** — the Act cannot be extended to tribals whatever their religion.
xa: HSA **1956**: equal inheritance; limited estate abolished.
**2005 amendment**: daughters equal coparceners.
**Vineeta Sharma (2020)**: daughter a **coparcener by birth**.

128.s: The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 is primarily associated with
128.x: The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 provides for monogamy and specifies grounds of divorce under Hindu personal law.
128.tq: Identify the subject matter of the personal law statute without confusing it with succession law.
xs: The **Hindu Marriage Act 1955** provides for **monogamy and divorce grounds** — option **(1)**.
Local-body reservation is under **Arts. 243D/243T**; statutory **floor wage** is in the **Code on Wages, 2019**.
xa: **Special Marriage Act 1954**: civil marriage irrespective of religion.
**Sarla Mudgal (1995)**: a Hindu man's **conversion** cannot validate his second marriage.
**HSA 1956**: equal inheritance for women.

128.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Hindu Succession Act enacted
B. Andhra Pradesh Assembly passed the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act under NTR
C. Central amendment making daughters coparceners by birth
D. *Vineeta Sharma* judgment
128.x: The correct sequence is 1956, 1985, 2005 and 2020. Andhra Pradesh passed its amendment on 24 September 1985 under N.T. Rama Rao.
128.tq: Anchor the sequence to the four supplied years and check the middle events.
xs: Order **A, B, C, D** — option **(1)**.
**HSA** (**1956**) → AP Assembly's amendment under **NTR** (**24 Sept 1985**) → central **2005 amendment** → **Vineeta Sharma** (**2020**).
xa: The AP amendment is dated **1986** — unmarried daughters made coparceners well before 2005.
Vineeta Sharma: the right holds **whether or not the father was alive** on **9 Sept 2005**.
AP angle: daughters' property law (**1985**) + **50%** quotas.

128.s: Which State had already made unmarried daughters coparceners through its amendment before the national Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005?
128.x: Andhra Pradesh made unmarried daughters coparceners through an earlier amendment. The Andhra Pradesh Assembly passed the relevant Act on 24 September 1985 under NTR.
128.tq: Identify the State-level precursor to the later central reform.
xs: **Andhra Pradesh** made **unmarried daughters coparceners** well before **2005** — option **(1)**.
The AP Assembly passed its Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act on **24 Sept 1985** under **NTR**.
xa: The AP amendment is dated **1986**.
Central **2005 amendment**: daughters = **equal coparceners**.
**Vineeta Sharma (2020)**: daughter a **coparcener by birth**.

128.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 was passed after the Shah Bano judgment.
2. The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 was Parliament's response to the Shamim Ara judgment.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
128.x: Statement 1 is correct: the 1986 Act followed Shah Bano (1985). Statement 2 is wrong: the 2019 Act was Parliament's response to Shayara Bano (2017); Shamim Ara (2002) was an earlier SC ruling on triple talaq. Hence 1 only (A); B, C and D are wrong.
128.tq: Pair each Act with its case: 1986 - Shah Bano; 2019 - Shayara Bano.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1)**.
Statement 1: the **1986** Act was passed after **Shah Bano** — correct.
Statement 2: the **2019** Act answered **Shayara Bano**, not **Shamim Ara (2002)** — wrong.
xa: ⚠ Case → law: **Shah Bano** → **1986** Act; **Shayara Bano** → **2019** Act.
**Allahabad High Court** had held triple talaq illegal (PYQ BPSC **1994**).
The **2019** Act: **cognisable, non-bailable**, up to **3 years** jail.

128.s: The judgment in Shah Bano (1985) is associated with which of the following issues?
o: Entry of women aged 10–50 into the Sabarimala temple
Permanent commission for women Army officers
Maintenance of a divorced Muslim woman under Section 125 of the CrPC
128.x: The Shah Bano judgment recognised the entitlement of a divorced Muslim woman to maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC and also urged the adoption of a Uniform Civil Code.
128.tq: Match the landmark case with its distinctive legal issue.
xs: **Shah Bano (1985)**: a divorced Muslim wife is entitled to **maintenance under s.125 CrPC** — option **(4)**.
**Sabarimala** dealt with women aged **10-50**; **Babita Puniya** with **permanent commission** for women Army officers.
xa: The Court also **urged a UCC**.
The **Muslim Women (Divorce) Act, 1986** followed.
Today's secular route: **Sec. 144 BNSS**, replacing **Sec. 125 CrPC**.

128.s: Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) primarily dealt with which of the following?
o: Conversion to Islam to contract a second Hindu marriage
Adultery under Section 497 of the IPC
128.x: Sarla Mudgal held that conversion to Islam cannot be used to validate a second marriage by a Hindu man and stressed the need for a Uniform Civil Code.
128.tq: Use the wrong-person or wrong-issue trap in landmark-judgment questions.
xs: **Sarla Mudgal (1995)**: a Hindu man **converting to Islam to remarry** — option **(2)**.
**Conversion cannot validate his second marriage**; the Court stressed the **UCC**.
Workplace harassment is the **2013 Act**; adultery (**s.497 IPC**) was **Joseph Shine (2018)**.
xa: **Hindu Marriage Act 1955**: **monogamy**.
**Shah Bano (1985)** also urged a UCC.
UCC vs **Art. 25/29** remains a debate.

128.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Sabarimala judgment?
o: The entry restriction was upheld unanimously.
