The Protection of Human Rights Act established the National Human Rights Commission. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 39-42]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii** — option **(4)**.
**Protection of Civil Rights Act** **punishes the practice of untouchability**; **PoA Act 1989** prevents atrocities against **SCs/STs**.
The **Manual Scavengers Act 2013** **eliminates manual scavenging**; the **Protection of Human Rights Act** establishes the **NHRC**.
xa: PCR was **renamed** in **1976** from the **Untouchability (Offences) Act**.
The Manual Scavengers Act came into force on **December 6, 2013**.
**PoA Rules 1995**: special courts and **60-day** limit for investigation.

133.s: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 primarily prescribes penalties for which of the following?
o: Denying forest rights to traditional forest dwellers
Enforcing religious and social disabilities arising from untouchability
133.x: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955, punishes enforcing religious and social disabilities that come from untouchability. Child labour and sex determination fall under other Acts.
133.tq: Match each Act to the wrong it punishes.
n: The Protection of Civil Rights Act was passed in 1955. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 87-89]
The Protection of Civil Rights Act prescribes penalties for enforcing religious and social disabilities arising from untouchability. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 87-89]
The Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act completely bans employing children below 14 in all occupations. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 87-89]
The PCPNDT Act strictly prohibits sex determination. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 87-89]
xs: The **PCR Act, 1955** prescribes penalties for **enforcing religious and social disabilities arising from untouchability** — option **(2)**.
It **enforces Article 17** and **punishes the practice of untouchability**.
xa: It came into force on **June 1, 1955**.
Offences include barring entry to **public worship** and **justifying untouchability**.
A conviction **disqualifies** from elections under **Sec. 8, RP Act 1951**.

133.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The 2013 Act prohibits hazardous manual cleaning of sewer and septic tanks.
The Act permits hazardous manual cleaning when carried out by private contractors.
The Act concerns the prohibition of employment as manual scavengers and their rehabilitation.
The Act mandates mechanization and alternative livelihood rehabilitation.
133.x: Option B is incorrect: the 2013 manual scavengers Act fully bans hazardous manual cleaning of sewers and septic tanks, by anyone. It requires mechanisation and rehabilitation with other livelihoods.
133.tq: Watch for a made-up exception.
n: The Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act was passed in 2013. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 87-89]
The Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act completely prohibits hazardous manual cleaning of sewer tanks. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 87-89]
The Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act completely prohibits hazardous manual cleaning of septic tanks. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 87-89]
The Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act mandates mechanization. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 87-89]
The Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act mandates alternative livelihood rehabilitation. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 87-89]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the Act **permits hazardous manual cleaning** by **private contractors** — option **(2)**.
The **2013** Act **completely prohibits** hazardous manual cleaning of **sewer and septic tanks**.
It **mandates mechanization** and **alternative livelihood rehabilitation**.
xa: It also **totally bans** manual cleaning of **unsanitary latrines** and **open drains** without protective gear.
An earlier **1993** Act prohibited manual scavengers and dry latrines.
**SRMS** (**2007**) was subsumed in **NAMASTE**, goal **zero sanitation deaths**.

133.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Protection of Civil Rights Act commenced on June 1, 1955.
The Act prescribes penalties for practising untouchability.
The Act was renamed in 1976 from the Untouchability Offences Act.
133.x: Option B is incorrect: the Civil Rights Act came into force on 1 June 1955. 30 January 1990 is the start date of the SC/ST Atrocities Act.
133.tq: Match each Act to its start date.
n: The Protection of Civil Rights Act came into force on June 1, 1955. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 102-103]
The Protection of Civil Rights Act was renamed in 1976 from the Untouchability Offences Act. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 102-103]
The Protection of Civil Rights Act prescribes penalties for practicing untouchability. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 102-103]
The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act came into force on January 30, 1990. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 102-103]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the PCR Act **commenced on January 30, 1990** — option **(2)**; it came into force on **June 1, 1955**.
The Act **prescribes penalties** for **practicing untouchability** and was **renamed** in **1976** from the **Untouchability Offences Act**.
xa: **January 30, 1990** is when the **SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act** came into force.
The PCR Act enforces **Article 17**.
Only **24 cases** were registered nationwide under the PCR Act in **2023**.

133.s: The Bhikhu Ramji Idate Commission led directly to the formulation of which scheme?
133.x: The Idate Commission surveyed denotified, nomadic and semi-nomadic tribes, and led to the SEED scheme for their economic empowerment.
133.tq: Recall the Idate Commission's outcome.
n: The Bhikhu Ramji Idate Commission led directly to the formulation of the SEED Scheme. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
The Bhikhu Ramji Idate Commission concerned Scheduled Castes and De-Notified Tribes (DNTs). [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
xs: The **Bhikhu Ramji Idate Commission** **led directly** to the **SEED Scheme** — option **(4)**.
It was constituted in **2017** by the **Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment**.
It **surveyed** **De-Notified**, **Nomadic** and **Semi-Nomadic Tribes**.
xa: **Justice K.G. Balakrishnan Commission** (**2022**): SC status for Dalit converts to **Christianity and Islam**.
**Rajiv Gauba Committee** (**2024**): the **most backward SC sub-castes** (e.g. **Madigas**).

133.s: Which of the following statements about the Rajiv Gauba Committee is incorrect?
o: It was formed to explore equitable administrative mechanisms for the most backward SC sub-castes.
It was a Cabinet Secretary panel constituted in 2024.
It was associated with alternative interventions for groups such as Madigas.
It was set up by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs to examine ST status for the Madigas.
133.x: Option D is incorrect: the Rajiv Gauba panel dealt with Scheduled Caste sub-castes such as the Madigas, not ST status, and was not a Tribal Affairs body. It was a 2024 Cabinet Secretary panel on the most backward SC sub-castes.
133.tq: Check which category, SC or ST, the Madigas belong to.
n: The Rajiv Gauba Committee explored equitable administrative mechanisms for the most backward sub-castes among Scheduled Castes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
The Rajiv Gauba Committee was a Cabinet Secretary panel formed in 2024. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
The Rajiv Gauba Committee explored alternative interventions for the most backward sub-castes among Scheduled Castes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
Madigas were cited as an example of the most backward Scheduled Caste sub-castes considered by the Rajiv Gauba Committee. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
The Rajiv Gauba Committee was formed by the Central Government through the Department of Personnel and Training. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
The Rajiv Gauba Committee concerned Scheduled Castes (SCs). [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the **Rajiv Gauba Committee** was set up by **Tribal Affairs** to examine **ST status** — option **(4)**.
It was a **Cabinet Secretary panel** formed in **2024** through the **Department of Personnel and Training**.
It explored **equitable administrative mechanisms** and **alternative interventions** for the **most backward SC sub-castes**, citing **Madigas**.
xa: **Idate Commission** (**2017**) → **SEED Scheme**.
**K.G. Balakrishnan Commission** extended till **10 June 2026**.
**Davinder Singh** (**2024**) allowed sub-classification within SCs.

133.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(a) Bhikhu Ramji Idate Commission
(b) Justice K.G. Balakrishnan Commission
(c) Rajiv Gauba Committee
(d) Justice Rajindar Sachar Committee

List-II
(i) Legal feasibility of SC status for certain converted Dalits
(ii) Socio-economic status of the Muslim community
(iii) Survey of DNTs, NTs and SNTs
(iv) Equitable mechanisms for the most backward SC sub-castes
133.x: Idate surveyed DNTs, NTs and SNTs, Balakrishnan examined SC status for Dalits who converted, Gauba the most backward SC sub-castes, and Sachar the status of Muslims. The answer is a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
133.tq: Match each body to its subject.
n: The Bhikhu Ramji Idate Commission surveyed De-Notified Tribes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
The Bhikhu Ramji Idate Commission surveyed Nomadic Tribes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
The Bhikhu Ramji Idate Commission surveyed Semi-Nomadic Tribes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]

The Justice K.G. Balakrishnan Commission examined the legal feasibility of according Scheduled Caste status to Dalits who converted to religions other than Hinduism, Sikhism, and Buddhism. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
The Rajiv Gauba Committee explored equitable administrative mechanisms for the most backward sub-castes among Scheduled Castes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
The Justice Rajindar Sachar Committee assessed the socio-economic status of the Muslim community in India. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
The Bhikhu Ramji Idate Commission concerned Scheduled Castes and De-Notified Tribes (DNTs). [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
The Justice K.G. Balakrishnan Commission concerned Scheduled Castes (SCs). [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
The Rajiv Gauba Committee concerned Scheduled Castes (SCs). [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
The Justice Rajindar Sachar Committee concerned minorities. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 90-92]
xs: The correct match is **a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii** — option **(3)**.
**Idate Commission**: survey of **DNTs, NTs and SNTs**; **K.G. Balakrishnan Commission**: **legal feasibility** of **SC status** for converted Dalits.
**Rajiv Gauba Committee**: equitable mechanisms for the **most backward SC sub-castes**; the remaining pair is **Sachar** with the Muslim community.
xa: Balakrishnan examined converts to religions other than **Hinduism**, **Sikhism** and **Buddhism**.
Idate (**2017**) and Balakrishnan (**2022**) were both set up by the **Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment**.

134.s: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 derives its constitutional basis primarily from:
134.x: The Act was enacted to give effect to Article 17 of the Constitution, which abolishes untouchability.
134.tq: Match the legislation with its specific constitutional provision.
xs: The **PCR Act** was enacted under **Article 17**, which abolishes untouchability — option **(4)** is correct.
It began as the **Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955** and was **renamed in 1976**.
xa: It extends to the **whole of India** (APPSC **2019** key).
**PCR Rules** were notified in **1977**.
⚠ **PCR 1955** vs **PoA 1989** (in force **30 January 1990**, Rules **1995**).

134.s: Which of the following is correctly matched under the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955?
o: Section 3 — Religious disabilities relating to entry into public places of worship
Section 6 — Collective fine on inhabitants of an area
Section 15A — Refusal to sell goods or render services
134.x: Section 3 deals with religious disabilities, including barring entry to or worship in public places of worship. Section 6 concerns refusal to sell goods or render services, Section 10A concerns collective fines and Section 15A concerns State duties.
134.tq: Start with the sure section–subject pair and eliminate the shifted provisions.
xs: **Section 3 — religious disabilities** (entry to or worship in public places of worship) is correct — option **(1)**.
**Sec. 4** = social disabilities; **Sec. 14** = offences by companies.
**Sec. 10A** = collective fine; **Sec. 6** = refusing to sell goods or render services; **15A** = State duties.
xa: **Sec. 5** = refusing admission to **hospitals, dispensaries, educational institutions, hostels**.
**Sec. 12** = court **presumes** the untouchability ground when the victim is an SC member.
**Sec. 7(1)(d)** = insulting an SC member on this ground.

134.s: The first-offence punishment under the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 is generally stated as:
o: Imprisonment from one to six months and fine from ₹100 to ₹500
Imprisonment up to three years without fine
Imprisonment from six months to one year and fine from ₹500 to ₹1,000
134.x: For a first offence, the stated punishment is imprisonment of one to six months and a fine of ₹100 to ₹500. The older wording is also expressed as imprisonment up to six months or fine up to ₹500 or both.
134.tq: Read the range carefully and avoid replacing a statutory range with a single figure.
xs: First offence: **imprisonment 1-6 months** and **fine ₹100-500** — option **(1)** is correct.
Older wording: "up to **6 months** or fine up to **₹500** or both".
xa: Offences are **cognizable**, triable **summarily** and **non-compoundable** (**Sec. 15**).
A convict is **disqualified** from contesting Parliament/State legislature.
**Sec. 10A** allows a **collective fine** on an area's inhabitants.

134.s: A person convicted under the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 is also subject to which electoral consequence mentioned in the law?
o: Permanent disqualification from voting in all elections
Disqualification from holding any private office
Disqualification from contesting elections to Parliament and State Legislatures
134.x: A person convicted under the Act is disqualified from contesting elections to Parliament or a State Legislature.
134.tq: Distinguish the specified electoral consequence from broader penalties not attached to the provision.
xs: A PCR convict is **disqualified from contesting** elections to **Parliament and State Legislatures** — option **(4)** is correct.
The law does not bar voting or remove a person from employment.
xa: ⚠ PCR offences also cover **justifying untouchability** and insulting SC persons.
First-offence punishment: **1-6 months** and **₹100-500** fine.
Offences are **cognizable**.

134.s:
Which of the following statements regarding the expression 'untouchability' is correct?
1. It is expressly defined in the Constitution.
2. It is expressly defined in the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955.
3. The Mysore High Court interpreted it as a historically developed caste practice.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
134.x: The expression is not defined in either the Constitution or the Act. The Mysore High Court interpreted it as the historically developed caste practice.
134.tq: Watch for the common trap that an important constitutional expression must have a statutory definition.
xs: Only statement 3 is correct — option **(3) 3 only**.
Statements 1 and 2 are wrong: "untouchability" is **not defined** in the **Constitution** or the **Act**.
Statement 3: the **Mysore HC** read it as the **historically developed caste practice**.
xa: The Act is based on **Art. 17**.
**Sukanya Shantha (2024)** held Art. 17 bars **caste-based purity stigma**.

134.s: At the Union level, which Ministry is the nodal ministry for implementation of the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955, with the Ministry of Home Affairs also associated with implementation?
o: Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment
134.x: The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is the nodal ministry, with the Ministry of Home Affairs also associated with implementation.
134.tq: Use the nodal-ministry distinction to avoid selecting a neighbouring social-sector ministry.
xs: The nodal ministry is **Social Justice and Empowerment** (with **Home Affairs**) — option **(1)** is correct (UKPSC **2025** key).
⚠ **Minority Affairs** is a trap — it is **not** involved.
xa: On the ground, the Act is implemented by **State Govts/UT administrations**.
MoSJE also administers the **2013 manual scavenging Act**.

134.s:
With reference to the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955, consider the following statements:
1. It was originally enacted as the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955.
2. It was renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act in 1976.
3. It extends to the whole of India except Jammu and Kashmir and the north-eastern States.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
134.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: the Act was enacted under Article 17 as the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955 and renamed in 1976. Statement 3 is wrong: the Act extends to the whole of India (APPSC 2019 and GS 2019 keys). Hence A; B, C and D wrongly include statement 3.
134.tq: PCR: 1955 Act, renamed 1976, extends to the whole of India.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: originally the **Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955**, under **Art. 17**.
Statement 2: **renamed in 1976** as the **PCR Act**.
Statement 3 is wrong: it extends to the **whole of India** (APPSC **2019**, GS **2019** keys).
xa: ⚠ The old UPSC note that the **PoA Act** excludes **J&K** is outdated — it applies there since **2019**.
PCR Rules: **1977**.

134.s:
Consider the following pairs relating to the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955:
1. Section 5 - Refusing admission to hospitals, dispensaries or educational institutions on the ground of untouchability
2. Section 12 - Court presumes the offence was committed on the ground of untouchability when committed against a member of a Scheduled Caste
3. Section 10A - Offences by companies
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
134.x: Pairs 1 and 2 are correct (both MPPSC 2019 key facts): Section 5 covers refusal of admission to hospitals, dispensaries and educational institutions, and Section 12 raises a presumption when the victim is an SC member. Pair 3 is wrong: Section 10A provides for a collective fine; offences by companies fall under Section 14. Hence A.
134.tq: Sec 5 hospitals/schools; Sec 10A collective fine; Sec 12 presumption; Sec 14 companies.
xs: Pairs 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only** (MPPSC **2019** key facts).
**Sec. 5**: refusing admission to **hospitals, dispensaries, educational institutions**.
**Sec. 12**: court **presumes** the untouchability ground when the victim is an **SC member**.
Pair 3 is wrong: **Sec. 10A** = **collective fine**; offences by companies = **Sec. 14**.
xa: ⚠ **PCR Sec. 14** = companies; **PoA Sec. 14** = Special Courts.
**Sec. 6** = refusing to sell goods or render services.

134.s: Offences under the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 are:
o: Non-cognizable and triable only by a Sessions Court
Cognizable only with prior sanction of the State Government
134.x: Under Section 15, offences under the PCR Act are cognizable and may be tried summarily; they are also non-compoundable (MPPSC 2019 accepted both descriptions). They are not non-cognizable or compoundable, are not reserved for Sessions Courts, and need no prior sanction.
134.tq: PCR offences: cognizable, summary trial, non-compoundable.
xs: PCR offences are **cognizable and triable summarily** — option **(2)** is correct (**Sec. 15**).
They are also **non-compoundable**; MPPSC **2019** accepted both descriptions.
They are not non-cognizable, not Sessions-only, and need no prior sanction.
xa: First offence: **1-6 months** and **₹100-500** fine.
**PoA** offences are also **cognizable** — arrest without warrant.

134.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989:
1. Section 3 deals with atrocities committed by persons who are not members of a Scheduled Caste or a Scheduled Tribe.
2. The Act creates certain offences which are not covered by the Protection of Civil Rights Act or the Indian Penal Code.
3. The Act applies only when the accused and the victim belong to the same Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
134.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the Act principally covers offences by non-SC/ST persons against SC/ST persons.
134.tq: Split the options by checking the scope of the accused and victim rather than accepting a broad statement about applicability.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **Sec. 3** atrocities are by **non-SC/ST** offenders.
Statement 2: atrocities are offences **not in the PCRA/IPC** (now BNS).
Statement 3 is wrong: the Act applies only to offences by **non-SC/ST persons** against SCs/STs.
xa: PoA Act: passed **1989**, in force **30 January 1990**, **23 sections**.
**Sec. 4** punishes **wilful neglect of duty** by public servants.

134.s:
Consider the following pairs relating to the SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989:
1. Section 4 - Punishment for wilful neglect of duty by public servants
2. Section 19 - Appeal to the High Court within 90 days
3. Section 23 - Rule-making power of the Central Government
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
134.x: Pair 1 is correct: Section 4 punishes wilful neglect of duty by public servants. Pair 2 is wrong: Section 19 bars probation for convicts; the 90-day appeal to the High Court is Section 14A. Pair 3 is correct: Section 23 gives the Central Government rule-making power. Hence B; A, C and D wrongly include pair 2.
134.tq: Sec 4 neglect, 14A appeal (90 days), 18 no anticipatory bail, 19 no probation, 23 rules.
xs: Pairs 1 and 3 are correct — option **(2) 1 and 3 only**.
**Sec. 4** = **wilful neglect of duty** by public servants; **Sec. 23** = Centre's **rule-making power** (Rules **1995**).
Pair 2 is wrong: **Sec. 19** = **no probation**; the **90-day** appeal is **Sec. 14A**.
xa: **Sec. 18** bars **anticipatory bail**; **18A** (**2018**) = no preliminary enquiry.
**Sec. 14** = **Special Courts**; Exclusive Special Courts from **2015**.

134.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the special judicial structure under the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989?
o: Special Courts are established only by the Supreme Court without consultation with the State judiciary.
Special Courts are established in every district with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of the High Court.
Exclusive Special Courts existed in the original 1989 Act and were not affected by later amendments.
Trials under the Act can be conducted only by ordinary Magistrates.
134.x: Special Courts are set up in each district with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court. Exclusive Special Courts were added by the 2015 amendment.
134.tq: Use the ‘who establishes or concurs’ method to avoid confusing the State Government, High Court and Supreme Court.
xs: **Special Courts** are set up in each district **with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of the High Court** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Exclusive Special Courts** were **added in 2015**, not part of the original Act.
Trials are not left to ordinary Magistrates; **Special Public Prosecutors** are appointed.
xa: **Sec. 14** = Special Courts; **14A** = appeal to the HC within **90 days**.
AP: **14 Special Sessions Courts + 1 Exclusive Court** (**Laxmipet, Srikakulam**).

134.s: Which of the following is NOT a provision associated with the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989?
o: Grant of arms licences to members of SCs and STs
Enhanced punishment for public servants in specified circumstances
Cancellation of arms licences in atrocity-prone areas
Automatic dissolution of every local authority located in an atrocity-prone area
134.x: The Act provides for cancellation of arms licences of potential offenders in atrocity-prone areas, licences for SC/ST persons and enhanced punishment for public servants. It does not provide for automatic dissolution of local authorities.
134.tq: Find the option that introduces an institutional consequence not connected with the Act’s stated safeguards.
xs: **Automatic dissolution of local authorities** is not a PoA provision — option **(4)** is the answer.
The Act **cancels arms licences** of potential offenders in **atrocity-prone areas** and gives **licences to SC/ST persons**.
It gives **enhanced minimum punishment** for public servants.
xa: States identify **atrocity-prone areas**.
**Sec. 4** punishes **wilful neglect of duty**.

134.s: An appeal from an order of a Special Court under the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, including an order relating to bail, lies to the High Court within:
134.x: An appeal, including an appeal against a bail order, lies to the High Court within 90 days.
134.tq: Test the appellate time limit separately from the investigation and trial timelines.
xs: Appeal from a Special Court order (incl. bail) lies to the **High Court within 90 days** — option **(3)** is correct.
This is **Sec. 14A**, added in **2015**.
**60 days** is the charge-sheet limit under the **Rules, 1995**.
xa: **Sec. 19** = no probation for convicts.
**Sec. 18** = anticipatory bail barred.

134.s:
With reference to the SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, consider the following statements:
1. Section 18 bars anticipatory bail for persons accused of offences under the Act.
2. Section 19 bars the benefit of probation for persons convicted under the Act.
3. The Act came into force on 30 January 1991.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
134.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Section 18 bars anticipatory bail (CrPC Sec. 438, now Sec. 482 BNSS) and Section 19 denies probation to convicts. Statement 3 is wrong: the Act, passed in 1989, came into force on 30 January 1990. Hence A; B, C and D include the wrong date.
134.tq: Sec 18 no anticipatory bail; Sec 19 no probation; in force 30 Jan 1990.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **Sec. 18** bars **anticipatory bail** (CrPC **438**, now **Sec. 482 BNSS**).
Statement 2: **Sec. 19** bars **probation** for convicts.
Statement 3 is wrong: the Act came into force on **30 January 1990**.
xa: **18A** (**2018**): no preliminary enquiry or approval before arrest.
**Kiran v Rajkumar Jivaraj Jain (2025)**: Sec. 18 bar applies where a **prima facie case** exists.

134.s: Which one of the following is the correct combination regarding investigation under the SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Rules, 1995?
o: Investigation by an officer not below DSP rank; charge-sheet within 60 days
Investigation by an officer not below Inspector rank; charge-sheet within 30 days
Investigation by an officer not below Superintendent of Police rank; charge-sheet within 90 days
Investigation by an Executive Magistrate; charge-sheet within 60 days
134.x: Investigation is to be conducted by a police officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police, and the investigation and filing of the charge-sheet are to be completed within 60 days.
134.tq: Start from the sure pair of investigating rank and then verify the prescribed time limit.
xs: Investigation by an officer **not below DSP**; charge-sheet within **60 days** — option **(1)** is correct.
These are the **PoA Rules, 1995**.
xa: A High Court questioned a probe that changed hands **six** times, **26 months** past the **60-day** limit.
**97%** pendency rate.
Annual report goes to **Parliament**.

134.s:
Consider the following statements regarding institutional machinery for prevention of atrocities:
1. The State Vigilance and Monitoring Committee is chaired by the Chief Minister.
2. The District Vigilance and Monitoring Committee is chaired by the Collector.
3. A nodal officer is designated at the Secretary level in each State.
4. SC/ST Protection Cells function under an Inspector General or Additional Director General of Police.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
134.x: All four statements correctly describe the institutional machinery: State-level chairmanship by the Chief Minister, district-level chairmanship by the Collector, a Secretary-level nodal officer, and Protection Cells under an IG or ADGP.
134.tq: Verify the level, chairperson and police rank in each institutional arrangement.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
State **Vigilance and Monitoring Committee** = **Chief Minister**; district committee = **Collector**.
**Nodal officer** at **Secretary level**; **SC/ST Protection Cells** under an **IG/ADGP**.
xa: AP drew up an **SOP** with Police, Revenue, Judiciary and Welfare.
AP's Director of Prosecutions held a review in **Vijayawada** (**19 Jul 2026**) on **digital evidence**.

134.s:
Consider the following statements regarding offences added or rephrased by the 2015 amendment:
1. Denying access to irrigation facilities may constitute an atrocity.
2. Forcing a person to perform manual scavenging may constitute an atrocity.
3. Preventing SC/ST candidates from contesting an election may constitute an atrocity.
4. Calling a woman a witch is included among the specified atrocities.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
134.x: All four statements describe acts included among the new or rephrased atrocities under the 2015 amendment.
134.tq: Use complete-list recognition: verify each concrete act before selecting the coded combination.
xs: All four statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2, 3 and 4**.
**Denying irrigation access** and forcing **manual scavenging** are atrocities.
**Preventing SC/ST candidates from contesting** and calling a woman a **witch** are atrocities.
xa: Also: **obstructing voting**; digging graves; **social or economic boycott**.
The amendment came **in force from 2016**.

134.s: Under the 2015 amendment, the trial in an Exclusive Special Court is intended to be completed within:
o: 60 days of filing of the charge-sheet
90 days of arrest of the accused
30 days of registration of the FIR
134.x: The amendment envisages completion of trial within two months, that is, 60 days, from the filing of the charge-sheet.
134.tq: Convert the stated period of two months into the precise numerical option and note the starting point.
xs: Trial is to finish, as far as possible, **within two months** (**60 days**) of the **charge sheet** — option **(2)** is correct.
This came with the **2015** amendment's **Exclusive Special Courts**.
xa: Special Courts can take **direct cognizance**.
Charge-sheet itself is due within **60 days** (Rules, 1995).

134.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the 2015 amendment to the SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act:
1. It provided for Exclusive Special Courts and Exclusive Special Public Prosecutors.
2. Special Courts may take cognizance of offences only after prior approval of the Central Government.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
134.x: Statement 1 is correct: the 2015 amendment added Exclusive Special Courts and Exclusive Special PPs. Statement 2 is wrong: the amendment empowered Special Courts to take direct cognizance, with no prior approval needed. Hence A; B and C wrongly accept statement 2, and D wrongly rejects statement 1.
134.tq: 2015: Exclusive Special Courts + PPs, direct cognizance, trial in two months.
xs: Only statement 1 is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
Statement 1: **2015** added **Exclusive Special Courts** and **Exclusive Special PPs**.
Statement 2 is wrong: Special Courts can take **direct cognizance**.
xa: Trial within **two months** of the charge sheet.
New chapter on **rights of victims and witnesses**.

134.s: The 2015 amendment introduced a new chapter dealing with:
134.x: A new chapter on the rights of victims and witnesses was introduced by the 2015 amendment.
134.tq: Match the amendment with its distinctive new chapter rather than with unrelated social legislation.
xs: The **2015** amendment added a chapter on **rights of victims and witnesses** — option **(4)** is correct.
It came **in force from 2016**, with many new offences.
xa: It also added **Exclusive Special Courts** and direct cognizance.
PoA Rules give **travel/maintenance** for victims and witnesses.
Centre's task force (**2026**) suggested **counselling** and **State relief cells**.

134.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched under the 2015 amendment to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act?
o: Economic boycott and social boycott — defined and made atrocities
Economic boycott and social boycott — removed from the Act
Economic boycott — removed; social boycott — made a civil wrong only
Social boycott — defined only under the Protection of Civil Rights Act
134.x: The 2015 amendment defined economic boycott and social boycott and made them offences amounting to atrocities under the Act.
134.tq: Distinguish the two paired expressions and remember that both were added as atrocities by the amendment.
xs: The 2015 amendment **defined economic boycott and social boycott** and **made them atrocities** — option **(1)** is correct.
"**Economic boycott**" is defined in **Sec. 2(1)(bea)**.
xa: ⚠ They were added, not removed, and are in the **PoA Act**, not just the PCR Act.
PCR **Sec. 10A** = collective fine; atrocity-prone areas allow cancelling arms licences.

134.s: Which of the following cases is associated with the Supreme Court directions that were perceived as diluting the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989?
o: Prithvi Raj Chauhan v. Union of India
Subhash Kashinath Mahajan v. State of Maharashtra
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
134.x: In Subhash Kashinath Mahajan v. State of Maharashtra, decided on 20 March 2018, the Supreme Court issued directions concerning preliminary enquiry, anticipatory bail and prior approval for arrest.
134.tq: Use the case-name and outcome association to distinguish closely related judgments.
xs: **Subhash Kashinath Mahajan v State of Maharashtra** (**20 March 2018**) was seen as **diluting** the Act — option **(2)** is correct (APPSC G2 **2024** key).
**Prithvi Raj Chauhan** (**2020**) **upheld** the 2018 restoring amendment; **Kiran (2025)** cancelled an anticipatory bail.
**Indra Sawhney** is a reservation case.
xa: Mahajan: **preliminary enquiry** before FIR, **anticipatory bail**, **prior approval** before arrest.
The **2018** Amendment inserted **Sec. 18A** to undo it.

134.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the directions issued in Subhash Kashinath Mahajan v. State of Maharashtra:
1. A preliminary enquiry was contemplated before registration of an FIR.
2. Anticipatory bail could be granted where no prima facie case existed.
3. Prior approval of the appointing authority was required before arresting a public servant.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
134.x: All three statements correctly describe the directions issued in the Mahajan case, which were viewed as curbing possible misuse of the Atrocities Act.
134.tq: Verify each procedural safeguard separately before selecting the coded combination.
xs: All three statements are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
**Preliminary inquiry by DSP** before FIR.
**Anticipatory bail** where **no prima facie case**; arrest of public servants needs the **appointing authority's approval**.
xa: The directions were **recalled** on review (Oct **2019**).
⚠ **2018** sequence: Mahajan → **18A** → review → **Chauhan** (Feb **2020**).

134.s:
With reference to Prithvi Raj Chauhan v. Union of India, consider the following statements:
1. The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the 2018 amendment.
2. Courts may grant anticipatory bail where no prima facie case exists.
3. Courts may quash proceedings where a prima facie case exists, without examining the allegations further.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
134.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The power to grant relief or quash proceedings is available where no prima facie case exists; statement 3 reverses this condition.
134.tq: Find the reversed condition in a legally qualified statement.
xs: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: **Prithvi Raj Chauhan** (Feb **2020**) **upheld** the 2018 amendment.
Statement 2: courts may grant anticipatory bail where **no prima facie case** exists.
Statement 3 is wrong: quashing is allowed only where **no prima facie case** exists.
xa: **Kiran (2025)**: no "**mini-trial**" at the bail stage.
Debate: **misuse** claims vs **low convictions**.

134.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Decision in Prithvi Raj Chauhan v. Union of India
B. Judgment in Subhash Kashinath Mahajan v. State of Maharashtra
C. Recall of the Mahajan directions on review
D. Decision in Kiran v. Rajkumar Jivaraj Jain
134.x: The correct sequence is Mahajan judgment in March 2018, recall in October 2019, Prithvi Raj Chauhan in February 2020 and Kiran in 2025.
134.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the two intervening developments.
xs: Correct order is **B, C, A, D** — option **(1)**.
**Mahajan** (Mar **2018**) → **recall on review** (Oct **2019**).
**Prithvi Raj Chauhan** (Feb **2020**) → **Kiran** (**2025**).
xa: **Sec. 18A** came by the **2018** Amendment Act.
Model answer angle: the **2018** episode (**Mahajan → 18A**).

134.s: In Kiran v. Rajkumar Jivaraj Jain (2025), the Supreme Court:
o: Declared Section 18 of the Atrocities Act unconstitutional.
Directed that a preliminary enquiry must precede every arrest.
Cancelled an anticipatory bail granted by a High Court and held that no mini-trial should be conducted at the bail stage.
Upheld anticipatory bail despite the existence of a prima facie case.
134.x: The Supreme Court cancelled the High Court's anticipatory bail, held that Section 18 applies where a prima facie case exists and stated that a mini-trial is impermissible at the bail stage.
134.tq: Match the latest case with its precise procedural holding, not with the earlier Mahajan directions.
xs: **Kiran v Rajkumar Jivaraj Jain (2025)** **cancelled an HC anticipatory bail** and barred a **mini-trial** at the bail stage — option **(3)** is correct.
It held the **Sec. 18** bar applies where a **prima facie case** exists — so Sec. 18 was not struck down.
xa: **Madras HC**: **no preliminary inquiry** before an FIR.
**Chauhan (2020)** allowed bail only where **no prima facie case** exists.

134.s: Which legislation prohibited the employment of manual scavengers and the construction of dry latrines?
o: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955
The Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993
The Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013
134.x: The 1993 Act prohibited employing manual scavengers and constructing dry latrines. The 2013 Act subsequently widened the prohibition and rehabilitation framework.
134.tq: Discriminate between the similarly named 1993 and 2013 enactments by their distinct scope.
xs: The **1993 Act** banned employing **manual scavengers** and **construction of dry latrines** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **2013 Act** later added the sewer/septic-tank ban and rehabilitation.
xa: **Safai Karamchari Andolan v UoI (2014)**: **₹10 lakh** per sewer death since **1993**.
Raised to **₹30 lakh** in **2023** (**Balram Singh**).

134.s: The National Safai Karamcharis Finance and Development Corporation was established in which year and serves as the nodal agency for which scheme?
o: 1997 — Self-Employment Scheme for Rehabilitation of Manual Scavengers
134.x: NSKFDC was established in 1997 and is the nodal agency for the Self-Employment Scheme for Rehabilitation of Manual Scavengers.
134.tq: Combine the founding year with the exact scheme name to avoid confusing it with later programmes.
xs: **NSKFDC** was set up in **1997** and is the nodal agency for the **Self-Employment Scheme for Rehabilitation of Manual Scavengers** — option **(2)** is correct.
**1993** is the dry latrines Act; **2013** the Manual Scavengers Act; **2014** the SC compensation order.
xa: **NAMASTE (2023)** subsumed SRMS.
**Swachhata Udyami Yojana (2026)**: capital subsidy **₹5 lakh → ₹7.5 lakh**.

134.s: Which body monitors the implementation of measures relating to manual scavenging and rehabilitation?
134.x: The National Commission for Safai Karamcharis monitors implementation in this field.
134.tq: Match the specialised statutory subject with the institution specifically associated with it.
xs: The **National Commission for Safai Karamcharis (NCSK)** monitors — option **(1)** is correct.
**Vigilance Committees** also oversee the **2013 Act**.
xa: The Act is administered by **Social Justice & Empowerment**.
⚠ Sewer-death compensation: **₹10 lakh** (**2014**) → **₹30 lakh** (**2023**).

134.s: Which of the following correctly reflects the compensation developments relating to sewer deaths?
o: ₹10 lakh was ordered in 2014 and raised to ₹30 lakh in 2023
₹30 lakh was ordered in 2014 and reduced to ₹10 lakh in 2023
₹10 lakh was ordered in 1993 and raised to ₹50 lakh in 2014
₹5 lakh was ordered in 2014 and raised to ₹10 lakh in 2023
134.x: Safai Karamchari Andolan v. Union of India involved ₹10 lakh compensation, which was raised to ₹30 lakh in 2023 in Balram Singh.
134.tq: Track the sequence of the original ruling and the later enhancement rather than reversing the amounts.
xs: Sewer-death compensation: **₹10 lakh** was ordered in **2014** and **raised to ₹30 lakh in 2023** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Safai Karamchari Andolan v Union of India (2014)**: the SC ordered **₹10 lakh** for each sewer death since **1993**.
The **₹30 lakh** figure came in **2023** in the **Balram Singh** case — compensation was raised, never reduced, so option (2) reverses the order.
xa: The **Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013** bans hazardous cleaning of **sewers and septic tanks** without protective gear.
Under the 2013 Act, hazardous sewer cleaning is punishable with up to **2 years / ₹2 lakh**.
The earlier **Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993** banned employing manual scavengers and building dry latrines.
**NAMASTE (2023)** aims at **zero sanitation fatalities**.

134.s: NAMASTE, launched in 2023, is associated with which of the following objectives?
o: Replacing all State Vigilance and Monitoring Committees
Formalising sewer and septic-tank workers and achieving zero sanitation fatalities
Constructing only dry latrines in rural areas
Providing compensation exclusively for denial of public-space access
134.x: NAMASTE formalises sewer and septic-tank workers, subsumed the Self-Employment Scheme for Rehabilitation of Manual Scavengers, and aims at zero sanitation fatalities.
134.tq: Identify the programme through its worker-formalisation and safety objective, not through a general sanitation function.
xs: **NAMASTE (2023)** aims at **formalising sewer and septic-tank workers** and achieving **zero sanitation fatalities** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It **subsumed SRMS** — the **Self-Employment Scheme for Rehabilitation of Manual Scavengers**.
**Vigilance and Monitoring Committees** are bodies under the **PoA Rules 1995**, not replaced by NAMASTE; the **2013 Act** in fact requires building **sanitary latrines**, not dry latrines.
xa: **NSKFDC (1997)** was the nodal agency for the Self-Employment Scheme for Rehabilitation of Manual Scavengers.
**Swachhata Udyami Yojana (2026)**: individual capital subsidy raised from **₹5 lakh → ₹7.5 lakh** (Aug 2026).
The **2013 Act** makes local authorities **survey** manual scavengers and build sanitary latrines within **3 years**; the **NCSK** monitors it.
⚠ Sewer-death compensation: **₹10 lakh** (2014, Safai Karamchari Andolan) → **₹30 lakh** (2023, Balram Singh).

134.s: Offences under the Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013 are:
o: Civil wrongs punishable only with fine
Compoundable and triable only by the NCSK
134.x: Offences under the 2013 Act are cognizable and non-bailable; a first contravention attracts up to 1 year or Rs 50,000, and hazardous sewer cleaning up to 2 years or Rs 2 lakh. They are not non-cognizable or bailable, not mere civil wrongs, and the NCSK monitors the Act; it does not try offences.
134.tq: MS Act 2013 offences: cognizable + non-bailable.
xs: Offences under the **2013 Manual Scavengers Act** are **cognizable and non-bailable** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Punishment: first contravention up to **1 year / ₹50,000**; hazardous sewer cleaning up to **2 years / ₹2 lakh** — so they are crimes, not mere civil wrongs.
The **NCSK** only **monitors** the Act; it does not try offences.
xa: Oversight under the Act is through **Vigilance Committees**; it is administered by the **Dept of Social Justice & Empowerment**.
Local authorities must **survey** manual scavengers and build **sanitary latrines** within **3 years**.
The Act also bans hazardous cleaning of **sewers and septic tanks** without protective gear.
⚠ Compare: **PCR Act** offences are **cognizable** and **non-compoundable** / triable **summarily**.

134.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the NCRB data for 2024:
1. Crimes against Scheduled Tribes declined by 23.1%.
2. Crimes against Scheduled Castes declined by 3.6%.
3. Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Bihar were among the States reporting the highest number of crimes against Scheduled Castes.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
134.x: All three statements are correct. Crimes against Scheduled Tribes declined by 23.1%, crimes against Scheduled Castes by 3.6%, and Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Bihar were the leading States mentioned for crimes against Scheduled Castes.
134.tq: Check each percentage and the State grouping independently before selecting the combined code.
xs: All three statements are correct — so option **(4) 1, 2 and 3** is correct.
Statement 1 is correct: crimes against **STs** fell **23.1%** in **Crime in India 2024**.
Statement 2 is correct: crimes against **SCs** were **55,698**, **down 3.6%** from **57,789** in **2023**.
Statement 3 is correct: most cases were in **UP, MP and Bihar**.
xa: The **NCRB** released Crime in India 2024 in **May 2026**.
In **2023**, crimes against SCs had risen **+0.4%** and against STs **+28.8%**.
Denial of access to public spaces (PoA): **180** cases in **2023**, **173 in UP**; **305** in **2022** (**300** in UP).
**AP**: crime rate **27.4 per lakh SC population** (**SDG India Index 2023-24**).

134.s: Which of the following correctly describes the institutional arrangement in Andhra Pradesh?
o: Fourteen Special Sessions Courts and one Exclusive Court at Amaravati, supported by Police and Judiciary alone
Fourteen Exclusive Courts and one Special Sessions Court at Vijayawada, supported only by the Police Department
One Special Sessions Court and fourteen Exclusive Courts at Laxmipet, Srikakulam, supported by the Revenue Department alone
Fourteen Special Sessions Courts and one Exclusive Court at Laxmipet, Srikakulam, supported by an SOP involving Police, Revenue, Judiciary and Welfare departments
134.x: Andhra Pradesh has 14 Special Sessions Courts and one Exclusive Court at Laxmipet in Srikakulam. The SOP involves the Police, Revenue, Judiciary and Welfare departments.
134.tq: Check the court count, location and participating departments as one integrated factual unit.
xs: AP has **14 Special Sessions Courts + 1 Exclusive Court at Laxmipet, Srikakulam**, backed by an **SOP** with **Police, Revenue, Judiciary and Welfare** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The Exclusive Court is at **Laxmipet (Srikakulam)**, not Amaravati or Vijayawada; the numbers are not reversed.
The SOP is multi-departmental, not Police or Revenue alone.
xa: Crimes against SCs/STs in AP **fell 24.32% in 2025** (Home Minister, 1 Jan 2026); the DGP reported a **30%** fall.
The Director of Prosecutions held a State-level review in **Vijayawada** (19 Jul 2026) → guidelines on **digital evidence** and timely charge-sheets.
AP crime rate: **27.4 per lakh SC population** (**SDG India Index 2023-24**).
Relief is paid under a **centrally sponsored scheme**, **50:50** Centre-State.

134.s: The Madras High Court has held, in the context of offences under the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, that:
o: A preliminary inquiry is mandatory before registration of every FIR.
An FIR may be registered only after approval by the State relief cell.
No preliminary inquiry is required before registration of an FIR.
A preliminary inquiry is required only where a counter-FIR is filed.
134.x: The Madras High Court held that a preliminary inquiry is not required before registration of an FIR in such cases.
134.tq: Test the judicial position by distinguishing a mandatory preliminary inquiry from direct FIR registration.
xs: The **Madras HC** held that **no preliminary inquiry** is required before registering an FIR — option **(3)**.
This follows **Sec. 18A** (2018 Amendment): **no preliminary enquiry**, **no approval** before arrest, FIR registered **immediately**.
A mandatory preliminary inquiry was the **Mahajan (2018)** direction that the 2018 Act overturned.
xa: **Mahajan (20 March 2018)** had directed a **preliminary inquiry by DSP** before FIR and approval before arresting public servants.
The SC **recalled** the Mahajan directions on review in **Oct 2019**.
**Prithvi Raj Chauhan (Feb 2020)** upheld the 2018 amendment; anticipatory bail or quashing only where **no prima facie case** exists.
⚠ **APPCA** calls the provision "**Section 4A**"; the correct number is **18A**.

134.s: The Andhra Pradesh Devadasis (Prohibition of Dedication) Act, 1989 is primarily associated with prohibition of which practice?
134.x: The Andhra Pradesh Devadasis (Prohibition of Dedication) Act, 1989 was enacted against the Jogini system.
134.tq: Identify the legislation through its specific social practice rather than through a general rights category.
xs: The **A.P. Devadasis (Prohibition of Dedication) Act, 1989** targets the **Jogini system** — option **(4)**.
It also provides for **rehabilitation of Jogini women**.
Manual scavenging is covered by separate laws (**1993** and **2013** Acts), not this Act.
xa: The **2015 PoA Amendment** made dedicating an SC/ST woman as a **devadasi** an atrocity.
Other 2015 atrocities: **tonsuring**, garlanding with footwear, **witchcraft** atrocities, **abusing by caste name**.
The PoA Act itself was also passed in **1989** (in force **30 January 1990**).

134.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the significance of the Supreme Court's decision in Sukanya Shantha (2024)?
o: Article 17 applies only to physical exclusion from public wells and temples.
Article 17 permits purity-based distinctions when followed by customary communities.
Article 17 concerns only untouchability imposed by private employers.
134.x: The Sukanya Shantha decision held that Article 17 bars caste-based purity stigma, expanding the understanding of untouchability beyond narrow physical exclusion.
134.tq: Apply the constitutional provision to the precise form of discrimination identified by the judgment.
xs: **Sukanya Shantha (2024)** held that **Article 17 bars caste-based purity stigma** — option **(2)**.
The case came up again when a post-rally "**Shuddhikaran**" ritual revived the **untouchability** debate (2 Sep 2026).
So Art. 17 is not limited to physical exclusion and does not permit purity-based distinctions.
xa: "Untouchability" is **not defined** in the Constitution or the Act; the **Mysore HC** read it as the historically developed caste practice.
The **PCR Act** was enacted under **Art. 17** as the **Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955**, renamed in **1976**.
**PCR Sec. 7** punishes **preaching or justifying untouchability** and insulting an SC member on this ground.

134.s: The National Toll-Free Helpline associated with casteism and atrocities is numbered:
134.x: 14566 is the national helpline against caste atrocities. 1098 is Childline, 181 the women's helpline, and 1930 the cyber-crime helpline.
134.tq: Match each helpline number to its purpose.
n: The National Toll-Free Helpline number for casteism and atrocities is 14566. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 79-81]
xs: The **National Toll-Free Helpline** for casteism and atrocities is **14566** — option **(4)**.
It is the **NGRS** under the **Department of Social Justice and Empowerment**, operating **24/7**.
xa: It gives **immediate grievance escalation** under the **POA Act** and the **PCR Act**.
Mechanism: **automatic FIR registration** without a **preliminary inquiry**.
PoA relief: **₹85,000 to ₹8.25 lakh** (fixed in **2016**).

134.s: The Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Amendment Act was enacted in which year?
134.x: The SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Amendment Act was passed in 2018, restoring safeguards after a Supreme Court ruling. The Protection of Civil Rights Act dates from 1955.
134.tq: Discriminate the 1955 Act from the 2018 amendment.
n: The SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Amendment Act was enacted in 2018. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 79-81]
xs: The **SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Amendment Act** was enacted in **2018** — option **(3)**.
**1955** is the year of the **Protection of Civil Rights Act**.
xa: The 2018 Act inserted **Sec. 18A**: no **preliminary enquiry** and no **approval** before arrest.
It answered **Subhash Kashinath Mahajan** (**20 March 2018**).
**Prithvi Raj Chauhan** (Feb **2020**) upheld the 2018 amendment.

134.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the mechanism for casteism and atrocities:

I. It includes central assistance for atrocity victim relief.
II. It includes incentives for inter-caste marriage.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
134.x: Both are correct: the response to caste atrocities includes central help for victims and incentives for inter-caste marriage.
134.tq: Recall the caste-atrocity measures.
n: The mechanism for addressing casteism and atrocities includes central assistance for atrocity victim relief. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 79-81]
The mechanism for addressing casteism and atrocities includes incentives for inter-caste marriage. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 79-81]
xs: Both statements are correct — option **(3)**.
I: the mechanism includes **central assistance for atrocity victim relief** — correct.
II: it includes **incentives for inter-caste marriage** — correct.
xa: It also provides **automatic FIR registration** without a **preliminary inquiry**.
Helpline: **14566**.
Relief is paid under a **centrally sponsored scheme**, **50:50** Centre-State.

134.s:
Assertion (A): The SC & ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 prevents atrocities.
Reason (R): Section 18A of the Act bars anticipatory bail and removes the requirement of a preliminary inquiry before arrest.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
134.x: Both are true: the Atrocities Act prevents atrocities, and Section 18A bars anticipatory bail and the need for a preliminary inquiry before arrest. Section 18A is a procedure, not the reason the Act exists, so R does not explain A.
134.tq: Ask whether a procedure explains the purpose.
n: The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act prevents atrocities. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 102-103]
Section 18A of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act bars anticipatory bail. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 102-103]

Section 18A of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act removes the requirement of a preliminary inquiry before arrest. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 102-103]
xs: Both A and R are true, but **R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — option **(2)**.
The **PoA Act, 1989** **prevents atrocities** against SCs and STs — true.
**Section 18A** **bars anticipatory bail** and removes the **preliminary inquiry** before arrest — true, but it is a procedure, not the Act's purpose.
xa: ⚠ Sources differ: other notes put the anticipatory bail bar in **Sec. 18**, with 18A adding "notwithstanding any court order".
⚠ APPCA calls it "**Section 4A**" — the correct number is **18A**.
**Sec. 19**: **no probation** for convicts.

134.s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the SC & ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.

List-I
(a) Year of enactment
(b) Date of commencement
(c) Date of amendment
(d) Relevant provision

List-II
(i) August 20, 2018
(ii) Section 18A
(iii) January 30, 1990
(iv) 1989
134.x: The Atrocities Act was passed in 1989 and came into force on 30 January 1990. It was amended on 20 August 2018, adding Section 18A. The answer is a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii.
134.tq: Match each date to its event.
n: The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act was enacted in 1989. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 102-103]
The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act came into force on January 30, 1990. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 102-103]
The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act was amended on August 20, 2018. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 102-103]
Section 18A of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act bars anticipatory bail. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 102-103]
xs: The correct match is **a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii** — option **(4)**.
The PoA Act was **enacted** in **1989** and **came into force** on **January 30, 1990**.
It was **amended** on **August 20, 2018**, which added **Section 18A**.
xa: The Act has **23 sections**.
The Act applies in **Jammu & Kashmir** since **2019**.

135.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Constitution expressly defines the term 'backward classes'.
2. Article 340 enables the President to appoint a commission to investigate the conditions of SEBCs.
3. The Mandal Commission was appointed under Article 340.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. The Constitution does not define the expression 'backward classes'; Article 340 provides for a commission to investigate their conditions and recommend remedies.
135.tq: Use the negative constitutional fact to eliminate the statement that sounds formally plausible but is incorrect.
xs: Statements **2 and 3** are correct — option **(3) 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1 is wrong: "**Backward Classes**" is **not defined** in the Constitution (APPSC G2 **2017** key).
Statement 2 is correct: under **Art. 340** the **President** appoints a commission to investigate conditions of **SEBCs** and recommend remedies.
Statement 3 is correct: both **Kalelkar** and **Mandal** commissions were appointed under **Art. 340**.
xa: **Kaka Kalelkar** (**1953**) was the first Backward Classes Commission; **B.P. Mandal** (**1979**) the second.
Correct term = **Socially and Educationally** Backward Classes — ⚠ IYB's "Socially and Economically" is wrong.
**Art. 366(26C)** defines SEBCs by reference to **Art. 342A** (102nd).
**First AP BC Commission**: **Anantharaman Commission**, report **1970**.

135.s: Before the 102nd Constitutional Amendment, Article 338(10) provided that references to Scheduled Castes would include such backward classes as were specified by the
135.x: Before the 102nd Amendment, Article 338(10) treated references to Scheduled Castes as including such backward classes as the President specified. Consequently, complaints relating to backward classes could go to the SC Commission.
135.tq: Identify the constitutional authority named in the transitional provision.
xs: Before **2018**, **Art. 338(10)** treated references to SCs as including backward classes specified by the **President** — option **(4)**.
Hence **BC complaints** went to the **SC commission** until the **102nd Amendment**.
The **NCBC** got constitutional status only through the **102nd (2018)** under **Art. 338B**, so it could not be the specifying authority earlier.
xa: **102nd (2018)** also inserted **Art. 342A** (SEBC lists) and **Art. 366(26C)**.
The statutory **NCBC Act 1993** was **repealed** in 2018; the present (**8th**) NCBC is constitutional.
102nd = **123rd Bill**; 105th = **127th Bill**; 103rd = **124th Bill**.
**Niranjan Jyoti** was appointed **NCBC Chairperson** (2026).

135.s: Which of the following statements about the expression “Backward Classes” in the Constitution is correct?
o: It is exhaustively defined in Article 15.
It is defined in Article 340 itself.
It is defined only in the Fifth Schedule.
It is not defined in the Constitution.
135.x: The Constitution does not define the expression “Backward Classes”; constitutional provisions instead provide mechanisms concerning their identification and welfare.
135.tq: Test the exact constitutional status of a frequently misattributed definition.
xs: "**Backward Classes**" is **not defined in the Constitution** — option **(4)**.
APPSC G2 **2017** key: the statement saying it is "defined" was the wrong one.
**Art. 340** only lets the **President** appoint a commission to investigate their conditions — it does not define the term.
xa: Under **Indra Sawhney**, **Art. 16(4)** backward classes are identified mainly by **caste/social backwardness**.
Correct term = **Socially and Educationally** Backward Classes (SEBCs).
For the **CEI Act**, OBCs are classes "so determined by the **Central Government**".
**Art. 366(26C)** defines SEBCs by reference to **Art. 342A**.

135.s: According to the Indra Sawhney judgment, the backward classes referred to in Article 16(4) are to be identified mainly on the basis of:
135.x: Indra Sawhney held that backward classes under Article 16(4) are identified mainly by caste and social backwardness, not by economic criteria alone.
135.tq: Indra Sawhney: caste can be the starting point for backwardness under 16(4).
xs: **Indra Sawhney**: **Art. 16(4)** backward classes are identified mainly by **caste and social backwardness** — option **(1)**.
It held **caste can be the main criterion** of backwardness, overruling **Balaji** on this.
Income alone is not the test; it is used to exclude the **creamy layer**, which Indra Sawhney introduced.
xa: Indra Sawhney fixed the **50%** ceiling except in extraordinary cases, applied year by year.
It confined reservation to **initial appointment**, not promotion → answered by the **77th** (**Art. 16(4A)**).
It directed a **permanent statutory body** for OBC lists → the **NCBC**.

135.s:
With reference to the two National Backward Classes Commissions, consider the following statements:
1. The First Backward Class Commission was chaired by Kaka Kalelkar.
2. The Second Backward Class Commission was chaired by B.P. Mandal.
3. The First Commission was set up in 1979.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: Kaka Kalelkar chaired the First Commission and B.P. Mandal chaired the Second. The First Commission was set up in 1953, whereas the Second was set up in 1979.
135.tq: Separate the correct chairmen from the deliberately shifted year.
xs: Statements **1 and 2** are correct — option **(1) 1 and 2 only**.
Statement 1: the First Commission was chaired by **Kaka Kalelkar**.
Statement 2: the Second was chaired by **B.P. Mandal**.
Statement 3 is wrong: the First Commission was set up in **1953**; **1979** is the **Mandal** year.
xa: Kalelkar reported in **1955**; Mandal in **1980**, estimating OBCs at **52%** of population.
Mandal used **11 indicators** — social, educational, economic.
Mandal recommended **27%** for OBCs; implemented by **V.P. Singh** in **1990**.

135.s: The First Backward Classes Commission was appointed in which year, and its report was submitted in which year?
135.x: The First Backward Classes Commission was appointed in 1953 and submitted its report in 1955. It was headed by Kaka Kalelkar.
135.tq: Separate the appointment year from the report year instead of treating them as the same date.
xs: The First Backward Classes Commission was appointed in **1953** and reported in **1955** — option **(1)**.
It was headed by **Kaka Kalelkar**, set up under **Art. 340** by the **Nehru** Government.
**1979 and 1980** are the **Mandal** Commission's set-up and report years; **1990 and 1993** are Mandal's implementation years.
xa: Kalelkar listed about **2,399** castes; its report was **not implemented**.
Its criteria: low caste status, lack of education, poor representation in govt service, trade and industry.
First **AP** BC Commission: **Anantharaman**, report **1970**.

135.s: The Second Backward Classes Commission, popularly known as the Mandal Commission, was set up in 1979 by the
135.x: The B.P. Mandal Commission was established in 1979 by the Janata Government headed by Morarji Desai.
135.tq: Avoid the common trap of confusing the government that appointed a commission with the government that implemented its recommendations.
xs: The Mandal Commission was set up in **1979** by the **Janata Government** of **Morarji Desai** — option **(1)**.
The **Nehru** Government set up the first commission (**Kalelkar**, **1953**).
The **V.P. Singh** Government **implemented** Mandal in **1990** — it did not set it up.
xa: Mandal reported in **1980**; OBCs = **52%** of population.
It used **11 indicators** and recommended **27%** for OBCs.
**27%** of central civil posts were reserved in **1993** (UPSC, IYB).

135.s: Which of the following correctly describes the implementation of the Mandal Commission recommendations?
o: They were implemented by the V.P. Singh Government in 1990, and 27 per cent of Central civil posts were reserved in 1993.
They were implemented by the V.P. Singh Government in 1993, and posts were reserved in 1995.
They were implemented by the Morarji Desai Government in 1979, and posts were reserved in 1980.
They were implemented by the Nehru Government in 1955, and posts were reserved in 1990.
135.x: The V.P. Singh Government implemented the Mandal recommendations in 1990, and 27 per cent of Central civil posts were reserved for OBCs in 1993.
135.tq: Track the sequence of appointment, report, political implementation and operational reservation.
xs: Mandal was implemented by the **V.P. Singh Government in 1990**, and **27%** of central civil posts reserved in **1993** — option **(1)**.
**Morarji Desai** (**1979**) only set the commission up; it reported in **1980**.
**1955** is the **Kalelkar** report year under the Nehru era — not Mandal.
xa: Creamy layer criteria: **DoPT Office Memorandum of Sept 1993**, based on **Justice R.N. Prasad** committee.
Creamy-layer income limit: **₹1 lakh (1993)** → **₹8 lakh (2017)**.
Mandal Commission = reservation in **government employment** (APPSC **2019** key).

135.s: Which commission is associated with recommending reservation for backward classes in government employment, leading to the 27 per cent OBC quota?
135.x: The B.P. Mandal Commission (1979) is the commission on reservation in government employment (APPSC 2019, GS 2019); it recommended 27 per cent for OBCs. Kalelkar's report (1955) was not implemented; Rohini deals with OBC sub-categorisation; R.N. Prasad framed creamy-layer criteria.
135.tq: Govt employment reservation commission = Mandal.
xs: The **B.P. Mandal Commission** recommended reservation in **government employment**, leading to the **27%** OBC quota — option **(2)**.
**Kalelkar** (report **1955**) was **not implemented**.
**Rohini** deals with OBC **sub-categorisation**; **R.N. Prasad** framed **creamy-layer** criteria.
xa: GS **2019** / APPSC **2019** key: "commission on reservation in government employment" = **Mandal**.
Implemented by **V.P. Singh** in **1990**; central posts reserved in **1993**.
**Oversight Committee (M. Veerappa Moily, 2006)** raised total seats so general-category seats did not shrink.

135.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Indra Sawhney judgment:
1. Caste may be the main criterion for determining backwardness.
2. Total reservation should ordinarily not exceed 50 per cent.
3. The creamy layer among OBCs should be excluded.
4. Reservation for OBCs was extended to promotions as a general rule.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: Indra Sawhney accepted caste as a possible main criterion, prescribed the general 50 per cent ceiling and excluded the creamy layer. It confined reservation to initial appointments and did not extend it to promotions as a general rule.
135.tq: Locate the single reversal in the statement dealing with promotion.
xs: Statements **1, 2 and 3** are correct — option **(1) 1, 2 and 3 only**.
Statement 1: **caste can be the main criterion** of backwardness (overruled **Balaji**).
Statement 2: total reservation **not above 50%** except in extraordinary cases. Statement 3: the **creamy layer** is excluded from OBCs.
Statement 4 is wrong: reservation was confined to **initial appointment**, not promotion.
xa: The **77th (1995)** answered it with **Art. 16(4A)** — promotion reservation for SCs/STs.
Indra Sawhney directed a **permanent statutory body** → the **NCBC**.
**Carry-forward** allowed within the **50%** ceiling, applied year by year.

135.s: Which one of the following statements correctly reflects the ruling in Indra Sawhney regarding carry-forward vacancies?
o: Carry-forward is allowed, but it must operate within the 50 per cent ceiling on a year-by-year basis.
Carry-forward is prohibited in every situation.
Carry-forward applies only to EWS vacancies.
Carry-forward is unlimited and is calculated only once in a decade.
135.x: Indra Sawhney permitted carry-forward of vacancies, subject to the 50 per cent ceiling being applied year by year.
135.tq: Combine the carry-forward rule with the year-by-year ceiling rather than treating either as absolute.
xs: **Carry-forward** is allowed but must stay **within the 50% ceiling**, applied **year by year** — option **(1)**.
Indra Sawhney fixed total reservation **not above 50%** except in extraordinary cases.
It is not limited to EWS; EWS (**103rd**) came much later.
xa: The **81st (2000)** made unfilled **backlog vacancies** a separate class, outside the **50%** ceiling (**Art. 16(4B)**).
**Janhit Abhiyan**: the **50% cap** applies to backward-class quotas.
The **76th (1994)** put Tamil Nadu's **69%** law in the **Ninth Schedule**.

135.s: The permanent statutory body for backward-class lists directed by the Supreme Court in Indra Sawhney subsequently became the:
135.x: The permanent statutory body directed for backward-class lists subsequently became the National Commission for Backward Classes.
135.tq: Match the judicially directed institutional role with the body that performs it.
xs: The permanent statutory body directed in **Indra Sawhney** became the **National Commission for Backward Classes** — option **(4)**.
The statutory **NCBC Act 1993** was **repealed** in **2018**; the NCBC is now constitutional under **Art. 338B** (**102nd**).
xa: **NCBC role**: examines **inclusion/exclusion** requests for OBC lists.
Present NCBC is the **8th**; **Niranjan Jyoti** appointed Chairperson (2026).
Before 2018, **Art. 338(10)** sent BC complaints to the **SC commission**.

135.s: Which amendment-clause pair is correctly matched?
135.x: The First Amendment, 1951 inserted Article 15(4). Article 16(4A) was inserted by the 77th Amendment, Article 16(4B) by the 81st, Article 15(5) by the 93rd and Article 16(6) by the 103rd Amendment.
135.tq: Start with the sure amendment-clause pair and eliminate the swapped clauses.
xs: **First Amendment — Article 15(4)** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**Art. 15(4)** was added to overcome **Champakam Dorairajan**.
xa: **81st (2000)** = **Art. 16(4B)** backlog vacancies.
**85th (2001)** = **consequential seniority**, nullifying the "catch-up" rule.

135.s:
With reference to the 93rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2005, consider the following statements:
1. It inserted Article 15(5).
2. It enabled reservation in educational institutions, including private unaided institutions.
3. Minority educational institutions were excluded from its scope.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
135.x: The 93rd Amendment inserted Article 15(5) and enabled reservation in educational institutions, including private unaided institutions, while excluding minority institutions.
135.tq: Test the main provision together with its important constitutional exception.
xs: All three are correct — option **(4) 1, 2 and 3**.
Statement 1: the **93rd (2005)** inserted **Art. 15(5)**.
Statement 2: reservation in educational institutions incl. **private aided or unaided**.
Statement 3: **minority institutions excluded**.
xa: It overcame **P.A. Inamdar (2005)**.
It is the base for the **CEI Act, 2006** — **27% OBC** seats, in force **Jan 2007**.
GS **2007** key: the CEI Act rests on the **93rd Amendment**.

135.s: Which one of the following statements is NOT correct?
o: The 82nd Amendment concerns relaxation of qualifying standards in promotion for SCs and STs.
The 81st Amendment deals with unfilled backlog vacancies.
The 89th Amendment introduced the relaxation of qualifying marks under Article 335.
The 77th Amendment deals with reservation in promotion for SCs and STs.
135.x: The 89th Amendment did not introduce the relaxation of qualifying marks; that change was made by the 82nd Amendment Act, 2000. The 89th Amendment is associated with the bifurcation of the SC/ST Commission.
135.tq: Find the wrong amendment-provision association among closely related reservation amendments.
xs: The NOT-correct statement is that the **89th Amendment introduced relaxation of qualifying marks** — option **(3)**.
Relaxation (proviso to **Art. 335**) came by the **82nd (2000)**; the **89th** split the **SC/ST Commission**.
Other statements are correct: **81st** = backlog vacancies; **77th** = promotion reservation for SCs/STs.
xa: ⚠ APPSC G2 **2024** keyed relaxation to the "**89th**" — WRONG.
**85th (2001)**: consequential seniority.
**76th (1994)**: TN **69%** law in the **Ninth Schedule**.

135.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below.
List-I (Constitutional Amendment)
 a. 77th Amendment
 b. 81st Amendment
 c. 82nd Amendment
 d. 85th Amendment
List-II (Provision)
 i. Consequential seniority in promotion
 ii. Backlog vacancies as a separate class
 iii. Reservation in promotion under Article 16(4A)
 iv. Relaxation in qualifying marks for promotion
135.x: The 77th Amendment inserted Article 16(4A), the 81st dealt with backlog vacancies, the 82nd inserted the proviso to Article 335, and the 85th provided consequential seniority.
135.tq: Start from the sure amendment-purpose pair and eliminate codes with a misplaced provision.
xs: Correct code: **a–iii, b–ii, c–iv, d–i** — option **(1)**.
**77th** → **Art. 16(4A)** promotion; **81st** → **backlog vacancies** as a separate class.
**82nd** → **relaxation in qualifying marks** (**Art. 335**); **85th** → **consequential seniority**.
xa: The **85th (2001)** nullified the "**catch-up**" rule.
**77th (1995)** answered **Indra Sawhney**.
**81st**: backlog vacancies sit outside the **50%** ceiling.

135.s: The 76th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1994 is associated with which one of the following?
o: Inserting Article 16(4A) for reservation in promotion
Placing Tamil Nadu's 69 per cent reservation law in the Ninth Schedule
Giving constitutional status to the NCBC
135.x: The 76th Amendment (1994) placed Tamil Nadu's 69 per cent reservation law in the Ninth Schedule. Article 16(4A) came through the 77th (1995), consequential seniority through the 85th (2001), and constitutional status of the NCBC through the 102nd (2018).
135.tq: 76th = TN 69% in Ninth Schedule; 77th = 16(4A).
xs: The **76th (1994)** put **Tamil Nadu's 69%** reservation law in the **Ninth Schedule** — option **(2)**.
**Art. 16(4A)** = **77th (1995)**; consequential seniority = **85th (2001)**; NCBC status = **102nd (2018)**.
xa: Indra Sawhney: total reservation **not above 50%** except in extraordinary cases.
SC reserved verdict on TN's BC (Muslim) quota for converts (8 Aug 2026).
**103rd (2019)**: **10% EWS** — over and above existing reservation.

135.s: Which clause was added to the Constitution to overcome the judgment in State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan?
135.x: Article 15(4) was inserted by the First Amendment, 1951 to overcome Champakam Dorairajan. Article 16(4) was in the original Constitution; Article 15(5) came by the 93rd Amendment (2005) and Article 16(4B) by the 81st (2000).
135.tq: Champakam Dorairajan -> 1st Amendment -> 15(4).
xs: **Article 15(4)** was added to overcome **Champakam Dorairajan** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 15(5)** = **93rd** (to overcome **P.A. Inamdar**); **Art. 16(4B)** = **81st** (backlog).
xa: Exam angle: "which article was added to overcome Champakam Dorairajan" → **15(4)**.
**Art. 16(4A)**: promotion reservation (**77th**).

135.s: The Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006, providing 27 per cent OBC reservation, came into force in:
135.x: Although enacted in 2006, the Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act came into force in 2007.
135.tq: Separate the enactment year from the commencement year.
xs: The **CEI (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006** came into force in **Jan 2007** — option **(3)**.
It gives **27% OBC** seats in central institutions; based on **Art. 15(5)** (**93rd, 2005**).
**2006** is the enactment year, **2005** the 93rd Amendment year — not the commencement.
xa: GS **2007** key: **93rd Amendment** underlies the CEI Act.
**Oversight Committee (M. Veerappa Moily, 2006)** expanded seats (about **54%**, phased).

135.s: Which one of the following was the principal objective of the Oversight Committee headed by M. Veerappa Moily in 2006?
o: To prepare the Central List of Scheduled Tribes
To implement OBC reservation by expanding seats so that general-category seats did not shrink
To identify the creamy layer among SCs and STs
To abolish reservation in Central educational institutions
135.x: The Oversight Committee headed by M. Veerappa Moily planned implementation through expansion of seats, thereby protecting the existing number of general-category seats.
135.tq: Use the committee’s stated implementation purpose rather than its year alone.
xs: The **Moily Oversight Committee (2006)** aimed to implement OBC reservation by **expanding seats** so **general-category seats did not shrink** — option **(2)**.
It proposed raising total seats by about **54%**, **phased**.
